target_language_example: Le ciliegie sono dolci quando sono mature.
native_language_example: Cherries are sweet when they are ripe.

meaning: 'at the top of' or 'on top of' (followed by a masculine singular noun introduced by 'il' contracted to 'al').
additional_notes: Used to indicate the highest point or upper surface of something. 'Cima' means 'summit/top'; when followed by 'il' the contraction 'al' is used (cima al = cima + al). You can also see 'in cima a' before feminine or without article (in cima del/la/dei/degli depending on gender/number). Common in literal (mountain, object) and figurative (feeling on top of the world) uses.
target_language_example: Siamo in cima al colle e vediamo tutto il paese.
native_language_example: We are at the top of the hill and can see the whole village.

meaning: the top/summit of (feminine noun) — 'the top of the…'
additional_notes: Used before a feminine singular noun (la collina, la montagna). 'Cima' means summit/top; 'della' is the contraction of di + la ('of the'). Use 'cima del' for masculine nouns (e.g. 'cima del monte'). Common in geographic/descriptive contexts.
target_language_example: Siamo saliti fino alla cima della collina.
native_language_example: We climbed up to the top of the hill.

meaning: 'cheers' (a toast when drinking)
additional_notes: Used when clinking glasses to offer a toast. Informal and common in spoken Italian; pronounced like 'chin chin'. Often said alone or before taking a sip. Not related to the English 'chin'.
target_language_example: Cin cin! Alla nostra salute.
native_language_example: Cheers! To our health.

meaning: lit. 'cinema with' — used to describe a film that includes something (e.g., 'cinema with subtitles', 'cinema with commentary'); a short form often followed by a noun or phrase.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom on its own; it's the noun 'cinema' followed by the preposition 'con' ('with'). You will usually see it as part of a longer phrase: e.g. 'cinema con sottotitoli' (film with subtitles) or 'cinema con audio descrizione' (film with audio description). Word order is the same as in English: 'cinema con' + [feature].
target_language_example: Abbiamo scelto un cinema con sottotitoli in inglese.
native_language_example: We chose a film with English subtitles.

meaning: at the cinema yesterday / went to the movies yesterday
additional_notes: Combines 'cinema' (movie theater) and 'ieri' (yesterday). Used to say someone went to or was at the movies the previous day. Word order can vary: 'al cinema ieri', 'ieri al cinema', or simply 'cinema ieri' in short notes or headlines. Often appears with time words like 'ieri sera' (yesterday evening/last night). Remember verbs and past participles follow Italian agreement rules when using auxiliary 'essere' (e.g. 'sono andata' vs 'sono andato').
target_language_example: Sono andata al cinema ieri.
native_language_example: I went to the cinema yesterday.

meaning: 'five and' — used as part of a time or range expression (e.g. "cinque e mezzo" = 5:30) or in numeric ranges with 'e' connecting parts of a compound time/number phrase.
additional_notes: In Italian, 'e' means 'and'. 'Cinque e' appears when saying times like 'cinque e mezzo' (five thirty) or in constructions giving an approximate range with 'fra/tra ... e ...' (between five and six). Alone 'cinque e' is incomplete; you need the following word or number. In the example sentences, 'fra/tra le cinque e le sei' = 'between five and six' (times or counts).
target_language_example: Torniamo a casa verso le cinque e mezzo.
native_language_example: We'll return home around five thirty.

meaning: 'five mistakes' or 'five errors'.
additional_notes: Literal, basic count phrase: number + noun. Used to state that someone made five mistakes/errors (in a test, text, lines, etc.). Can appear with past tenses (fece, ha fatto) and with location phrases like 'in altrettante righe/linee' (in as many lines). No special idiomatic meaning.
target_language_example: Ha fatto cinque errori nell'esercizio di grammatica.
native_language_example: He/She made five mistakes in the grammar exercise.

cinque fette di pizza al mese

target_language_multi_word_term: cinque fette di pizza al mese
meaning: five slices of pizza per month
additional_notes: A simple quantity/time phrase: 'cinque fette' = five slices, 'di pizza' specifies what, 'al mese' = per month. Commonly used to talk about how often or how much someone eats something. You can replace the number, food, or time period (e.g., 'tre fette di torta a settimana').
target_language_example: Di solito mangi cinque fette di pizza al mese?
native_language_example: Do you usually eat five slices of pizza per month?

meaning: five minutes (a short time period of five minutes)
additional_notes: Used to refer to a duration of five minutes or to say 'in five minutes' (future) or 'five minutes ago' depending on context. Common in time expressions: 'Ho cinque minuti?' = Do you have five minutes?; 'Torno fra cinque minuti' = I'll be back in five minutes. Can describe how long something takes (Sono cinque minuti a piedi = it's a five-minute walk) or indicate a specific portion of time (negli ultimi cinque minuti = in the last five minutes).
target_language_example: Posso parlare con te cinque minuti?
native_language_example: Can I talk to you for five minutes?

meaning: 'five times' or 'five per' (depends on context); can mean the multiplication phrase "five times" or indicate an amount 'five for (something)'.
additional_notes: Used in two main ways: 1) as part of arithmetic/multiplication (cinque per tre = five times three). 2) colloquially to indicate giving/setting aside five units for something (cinque per la benzina = five [euros/dollars] for gas). Context tells whether it's mathematical or 'per/for' meaning. In spoken Italian the currency or unit is often omitted when understood from context.
target_language_example: Dammi cinque per il taxi, per favore.
native_language_example: Give me five for the taxi, please.

meaning: seat belt; safety belt.
additional_notes: Used to refer to the strap in vehicles or other situations that secures a person for safety. Commonly used in instructions and safety rules (e.g., "Allacciare la cintura di sicurezza" = "Fasten your seat belt"). "Cintura" = belt; "di sicurezza" = of safety.
target_language_example: Per favore allaccia la cintura di sicurezza prima di partire.
native_language_example: Please fasten your seat belt before we leave.

meaning: hot chocolate (hot cocoa).
additional_notes: A common drink made from melted chocolate or cocoa powder with milk or water, served hot. Used as a noun phrase; can be countable (una cioccolata calda = a cup of hot chocolate) or uncountable (della cioccolata calda = some hot chocolate).
target_language_example: Stasera prendo una cioccolata calda invece del caffè.
native_language_example: Tonight I'll have a hot chocolate instead of coffee.

meaning: about / approximately (followed by a feminine noun or expression).
additional_notes: Used to give an approximate measurement, age, size, etc. 'Circa' means 'about/around' and often appears before the article + noun (here 'la') when referring to a feminine noun or expression (e.g., la stessa altezza, la mia età). For masculine nouns you'd hear 'circa il' or just 'circa'. Can be used with numbers (circa 10) or with nouns (circa la stessa età).
target_language_example: Quella valigia è circa la stessa grandezza della mia.
native_language_example: That suitcase is about the same size as mine.

meaning: 'vicious circle' — a self-reinforcing negative cycle that is hard to break.
additional_notes: Used to describe situations where one problem causes another, which in turn worsens the first, creating a loop. Common in social, economic, personal contexts. English equivalent: 'vicious circle' or 'vicious cycle'.
target_language_example: Dobbiamo intervenire prima che si formi un circolo vizioso.
native_language_example: We need to intervene before a vicious circle forms.

meaning: big city; a large town.
additional_notes: Used to describe a city of considerable size or population. Word order is flexible in Italian (more common: "grande città"), but both forms are understood. "Città" is feminine, so adjectives agree: una città grande or una grande città. Context usually implies an urban area with many people, services, or buildings.
target_language_example: Mary vive da sola in una città grande.
native_language_example: Mary lives alone in a big city.

meaning: 'old town' or 'old part of a city' (historic district)
additional_notes: Refers to the historic, older quarter of a city or town — often with narrow streets, old buildings and tourist attractions. In many Italian cities it is called 'la città vecchia' or 'il centro storico' (both used). Use città vecchia when pointing out the old quarter; note that città is feminine, so you may see "la città vecchia."
target_language_example: Facciamo una passeggiata nella città vecchia.
native_language_example: Let's take a walk in the old town.

meaning: the city is in / the city is under (a state or condition).
additional_notes: Used to describe the current state, condition, location, or situation of a city. Followed by a noun phrase indicating condition (quarantena, rovina, difficoltà) or place (riva al mare, Francia). In natural speech you might also hear 'la città è' + adjective (es. 'la città è bella') or 'questa città è in...' for 'this city is in...'.
target_language_example: La città è in festa per il torneo.
native_language_example: The city is celebrating because of the tournament.

meaning: 'what they have' / 'what they (have) did' — i.e., 'what they did' or 'what they have done'.
additional_notes: Combines 'ciò che' (that which / what) + 'hanno' (they have). In most contexts it refers to actions: 'what they did' or 'what they have done'. Use with past context (often followed by a past participle: ciò che hanno fatto). Can introduce a noun clause and appear as subject or object in a sentence.
target_language_example: Non capisco perché dobbiamo pagare per ciò che hanno fatto.
native_language_example: I don't understand why we have to pay for what they did.

meaning: '(the) class is' or part of comparative/negative sentences about the class/group.'
additional_notes: This is the verb 'è' (is) used with 'classe' (class). Often appears in sentences comparing or stating something about everyone in a class/group (e.g. no one in the class is X, or the class is X). Watch subject-verb agreement: 'la classe è' (singular) vs. 'i ragazzi della classe sono' (plural). In negative comparative constructions Italian often uses 'nessun/nessuno' + singular verb (e.g. 'Nessun ragazzo della classe è alto come Bill' = 'No boy in the class is as tall as Bill').
target_language_example: La classe è molto rumorosa oggi.
native_language_example: The class is very noisy today.

meaning: No way; absolutely not (strong, vulgar refusal or disbelief).
additional_notes: Very vulgar slang used to express strong rejection, refusal, or disbelief—like 'no way' or 'as if'. Often followed by a clause contradicting or rejecting something. Do not use in formal contexts or around people you should respect. Rough English equivalents: 'No freakin' way', 'Hell no'.
target_language_example: Col cazzo che accetto di lavorare gratis per loro.
native_language_example: No way I'm agreeing to work for them for free.

meaning: over time; with time; as time passes
additional_notes: Used to indicate that something happens gradually or eventually as time goes by. It's a contraction of "con il tempo" and commonly appears at the start or middle of a sentence. Can introduce a change, improvement, habit, or gradual development.
target_language_example: Col tempo imparerai a gestire lo stress.
native_language_example: Over time you'll learn to manage stress.

meaning: have breakfast at (someone's place) or by oneself; 'colazione' = breakfast, 'da' indicates location or company (at someone's place / alone).
additional_notes: Used with a person pronoun or noun after 'da' to say you have breakfast at that person's place (e.g., "colazione da noi" = breakfast at our place). With pronouns like 'solo/a' or reflexive forms it can mean 'have breakfast alone' ("colazione da sola"). Common construction: "fare colazione da + (noi/lei/loro)" or simply "a colazione da + ...".
target_language_example: Domani faccio colazione da Marco.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I'll have breakfast at Marco's.

meaning: on/around the neck of (someone or something)
additional_notes: Literal phrase made of 'collo' (neck) + preposition 'di' indicating possession/position. Used to say that something is located on, attached to, or belongs to someone's neck (e.g., a necklace, weapon, mark). Context determines whether it's physical placement ('on the neck of') or possession ('the neck of').
target_language_example: Aveva una catena d'oro al collo di sua madre.
native_language_example: He had a gold chain on his mother's neck.

meaning: 'interview for' (followed by the type of interview, e.g. lavoro = job interview).
additional_notes: Used to indicate the type of interview: colloquio di lavoro (job interview), colloquio di ammissione (admissions interview), etc. Usually followed by a noun that specifies the interview type. In everyday speech Italians often say simply "un colloquio" to mean a job interview when context is clear.
target_language_example: Ho un colloquio di lavoro domani mattina.
native_language_example: I have a job interview tomorrow morning.

meaning: the color of (the)
additional_notes: A common phrase used to say what color something has. 'Colore' = color; 'del' = contraction of 'di' + 'il' meaning 'of the'. Followed by a noun (colore del + noun). Change 'del' if noun requires different article (della, dei, degli, delle) or if speaking generally use 'di'.
target_language_example: Mi piace il colore del vestito.
native_language_example: I like the color of the dress.

meaning: 'what color is' (used to ask about the color of something) / 'the color is' (to state a color)
additional_notes: Commonly appears in the question formula 'Di che colore è...?' meaning 'What color is...?' Use 'Di che colore sono...?' for plural nouns. To state the color, use 'Il/Il suo colore è ...' or simply 'È ...' + color (e.g. 'È rosso').
target_language_example: Di che colore è la tua macchina?
native_language_example: What color is your car?

meaning: 'the fault/blame is' (used to assign responsibility)
additional_notes: Used to state who or what is responsible for something. Commonly followed by a person (tua, mia, sua), an entity (del diavolo), or a cause. Often appears in the fixed phrase "la colpa è...". Tone can be neutral, accusatory, or self-blaming depending on context.
target_language_example: La colpa è sua, non nostra.
native_language_example: The fault is his, not ours.

meaning: hit/struck by; affected by (passive: someone/something is struck or impacted by something).
additional_notes: A passive construction: past participle 'colpito' + preposition 'da' indicates the agent or cause (e.g. struck by a ball, hit by a car, struck by lightning, or emotionally affected by someone). Can describe physical impact or being emotionally impressed/affected. Agreement in gender/number when used with essere (colpita, colpiti, colpite).
target_language_example: Sono rimasto colpito da quel film.
native_language_example: I was impressed/affected by that movie.

meaning: hit/struck the (masculine singular object).
additional_notes: Past participle 'colpito' (from colpire) means 'hit', 'struck', or 'affected' depending on context. When followed by a definite article like 'il' it introduces the masculine singular direct object (e.g., 'colpito il muro' = 'hit the wall'). Can describe deliberate hitting or accidental contact (e.g., a head hitting an edge). Word form must agree with gender/number of the object when using compound tenses with essere (e.g., 'è stato colpito' for 'he was hit').
target_language_example: Ho colpito il tavolo per sbaglio.
native_language_example: I hit the table by mistake.

meaning: a lucky stroke; a piece of good luck
additional_notes: Used to describe an unexpected fortunate event or chance that leads to a positive outcome. Can refer to meeting someone by chance, getting a job unexpectedly, or winning because of luck. Common in exclamations (Che colpo di fortuna!).
target_language_example: Ho trovato l'ultimo biglietto per il concerto per un vero colpo di fortuna.
native_language_example: I found the last ticket for the concert by a real stroke of luck.

meaning: coup d'état; an illegal, sudden seizure of government power (a coup).
additional_notes: Used to describe an abrupt overthrow of a government by a small group (military, politicians, etc.). Formal term; literal translation is 'blow/strike of state.' Often shortened in conversation to 'colpo' in context.
target_language_example: Il generale ha tentato un colpo di stato la scorsa notte.
native_language_example: The general attempted a coup last night.

target_language_multi_word_term: fare colpo su (qualcuno) / far colpo su (qualcuno)
meaning: to impress someone, to make an impression on someone (often to attract or win their admiration)
additional_notes: Commonly used with the preposition su and a person (su di me, su di lei, etc.). Often implies trying to attract someone's attention or admiration (romantically or socially). Conjugation: fare colpo (infinitive), fa/faceva/ha fatto colpo, far colpo (elided form before a vowel: far colpo). Informal everyday expression.
target_language_example: Sta cercando di fare colpo su di me con la sua macchina nuova.
native_language_example: He's trying to impress me with his new car.

meaning: kitchen knife; a knife used for food preparation.
additional_notes: Commonly refers to larger knives used for chopping, slicing, and general cooking tasks (chef's knife, utility knife). Used in everyday speech when asking for or referring to a knife in the kitchen. 'Da cucina' specifies purpose (for the kitchen).
target_language_example: Mi passi il coltello da cucina, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you pass me the kitchen knife, please?

meaning: 'the knife is' (simple sentence starter describing a knife)
additional_notes: This is the verb 'essere' (è = is) used with 'coltello' (knife). Use to state a property or ownership of a knife: e.g. condition (affilato = sharp, arrugginito = rusty) or possession (mio = mine). 'Coltello' is masculine singular, so it takes 'il' (il coltello) and 'la lama del coltello' for the blade. You normally say just 'il coltello è...' rather than the two-word chunk as a fixed phrase.
target_language_example: Il coltello è arrugginito.
native_language_example: The knife is rusty.

meaning: like two / as two (used to compare someone/something to a pair or to describe how two people acted together)
additional_notes: A common colloquial simile meaning 'like two' or 'as if they were two'. Often completes a phrase comparing someone's condition, behavior, or manner to a pair of things or to acting together. Context determines exact nuance (e.g., insult, vivid image, or describing paired action). Not a fixed idiom with one single translation; translate depending on the noun that follows. Frequently used in spoken Italian.
target_language_example: Se se ne vanno così, sembrano come due ladri.
native_language_example: If they leave like that, they look like two thieves.

meaning: as ours / like ours
additional_notes: Phrase combining 'come' (like/as) + possessive adjective 'nostro' (our/ours). Grammatically, 'nostro' normally agrees in gender and number with the noun it modifies (nostra, nostri, nostre), so the sequence 'come nostro' appears when the article or context supplies agreement or when referring to a masculine singular noun omitted after the phrase (elliptical usage). More commonly Italians say 'come il nostro' or 'come la nostra' to be explicit. Use 'come nostro' in contexts where the noun is understood or in fixed expressions.
target_language_example: Il loro è più grande, ma il tuo è come nostro.
native_language_example: Theirs is bigger, but yours is like ours.

meaning: as our representative
additional_notes: Used to say someone acts on behalf of a group or organization (e.g., company, team). Common in formal contexts such as meetings, conferences, or official events. Structure: 'come' (as) + 'nostro' (our) + 'rappresentante' (representative). Adjust possessive gender/number if needed (nostra/nostri/nostre).
target_language_example: È venuto alla fiera come nostro rappresentante.
native_language_example: He came to the fair as our representative.

meaning: like his/her (someone); in the same way as his/her (someone).
additional_notes: Used to compare a person to another family member (or person) introduced by a possessive (sua = his/her/its). word order: 'come' + possessive + noun (e.g. come sua madre = like his/her mother). Context determines whether 'sua' means his, her, or its; Italian often repeats the subject elsewhere to clarify. Can be followed by a name when saying someone was named like a relative (e.g. È stata chiamata Alice come sua zia = She was named Alice like her aunt).
target_language_example: Luca è timido, proprio come sua sorella.
native_language_example: Luca is shy, just like his sister.

meaning: like a
additional_notes: Used to make a comparison with a feminine singular noun: come una ragazza = like a girl. In some contexts, una can also mean 'one' and refer back to a feminine noun already understood.
target_language_example: Parla come una vera esperta.
native_language_example: She talks like a real expert.

meaning: 'how should I' or 'how must I' (asks for the correct way to do/say something).
additional_notes: Used to ask for guidance about the correct action, wording, or behavior. Followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., chiamarla, parlare, rispondere). Tone is neutral; can be polite or practical depending on context. Equivalent to 'how do I (ought to)...' in English.
target_language_example: Come devo comportarmi in ufficio?
native_language_example: How should I behave in the office?

meaning: how to do
additional_notes: Used to ask or state knowledge about the method or ability to do/make something. Followed by an infinitive or a noun phrase (often with an implied infinitive). In questions it means "do you know how to..." or "does he/she know how to..."
target_language_example: Sai come fare una torta al cioccolato?
native_language_example: Do you know how to make a chocolate cake?

meaning: how did they
additional_notes: "Come" means "how" and "hanno" means "they have." In questions, it is often followed by a past participle to ask about what a group of people did in the past: for example, "Come hanno fatto?" = "How did they do it?" In English, this is often translated with the simple past ("did they") rather than "have they."
target_language_example: Come hanno trovato la soluzione così in fretta?
native_language_example: How did they find the solution so quickly?

meaning: Why? / How come?
additional_notes: Used to ask for an explanation or reason in conversational Italian. Slightly more curious or surprised than a neutral 'perché'. Can be used with present/past contexts (e.g., 'Come mai sei qui?' / 'Come mai è tornata?').
target_language_example: Come mai non sei venuto alla festa?
native_language_example: How come you didn't come to the party?

meaning: 'of course' / 'sure' (used to agree, sometimes sarcastic)
additional_notes: Informal conversational phrase used to agree emphatically. Tone depends on context and intonation: can be sincere ('sure, of course') or ironic/sarcastic ('yeah, right'). Often stands alone or precedes a name/pronoun.
target_language_example: — Puoi venire domani? — Come no, ci sarò.
native_language_example: — Can you come tomorrow? — Of course, I'll be there.

meaning: more than ever; like never before.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something is happening to a greater degree than at any previous time. Common in written and spoken Italian; often follows a verb or adjective (e.g., 'sono felice come non mai', 'lavora come non mai').
target_language_example: Oggi sono concentrato come non mai.
native_language_example: Today I'm more focused than ever.

meaning: 'how dare you' (expresses shock/anger at someone's action or words).
additional_notes: Used to challenge or scold someone — strong, confrontational phrase. Often followed by an infinitive (e.g., dirmelo) or a clause describing the offending action. Can be rude or offensive depending on tone and context; avoid with strangers or in polite situations.
target_language_example: Come osi parlare così davanti a tutti?
native_language_example: How dare you speak like that in front of everyone?

meaning: 'as before' / 'like before' (returning to a previous state or situation)
additional_notes: Used to say that things will go back to how they were earlier. Common in everyday speech to talk about returning to normal or to a prior arrangement. Often follows verbs like tornare, essere, or phrases meaning 'go back' or 'resume'.
target_language_example: Spero che tutto torni come prima entro l'estate.
native_language_example: I hope everything goes back to how it was before by summer.

meaning: how (it/they/he/she) looks or seems
additional_notes: Used to ask about appearance or impression. Can refer to visual appearance (e.g., clothes, photos) or general impression/feeling (e.g., how something appears to be going). Context and intonation determine whether it asks about looks (appearance) or perceived state. Often followed by a subject or demonstrative (questa, questo, mio marito) or by a subordinate clause with che + verb.
target_language_example: Come sembra questo vestito?
native_language_example: How does this dress look?

meaning: 'what is (his/her/its/your) name?' or 'what is it called?'.
additional_notes: Used to ask the name of a person, animal, object, or place. Literally 'how is it called' (come = how, si chiama = is called). Can be used politely for people (formal: 'Come si chiama?' when speaking to ask someone else's name) and casually for pets/objects/places. For asking someone's own name directly you can also say 'Come ti chiami?'.
target_language_example: Come si chiama questo fiore?
native_language_example: What is this flower called?

meaning: properly; correctly; as one should; in the right / proper way.
additional_notes: Used to say that something is done in the correct, appropriate, or respectable manner. Can imply thoroughness or doing something with proper attention or respect (e.g., a proper farewell, to thank properly). Often appears after a verb or phrase (fare qualcosa come si deve, ringraziare come si deve).
target_language_example: Vorrei festeggiare come si deve per il suo compleanno.
native_language_example: I want to celebrate properly for his birthday.

meaning: how are you
additional_notes: Polite/formal way to ask about someone's well-being or condition. Use 'come stai' for informal singular (tu). Context and intonation determine whether it's addressing 'you' (formal lei) or asking about a third person ('how is she/he/it'). Often used when speaking to someone respectfully (e.g., a doctor, elder, or stranger).
target_language_example: Dottor Rossi, come sta oggi?
native_language_example: Doctor Rossi, how are you today?

meaning: How are you? (informal singular)
additional_notes: Used to ask about someone's well-being in informal contexts or with people you know (friends, family, peers). For formal situations or when addressing one person respectfully, use "come sta". Can be followed by additions like "oggi" (today) or "tutto a posto?" (is everything okay?).
target_language_example: Come stai oggi? Ti senti bene?
native_language_example: How are you today? Do you feel well?

meaning: like you
additional_notes: Two common uses: 1) literal/comparative — 'like you' or 'as you do' (e.g. comparing feelings or abilities). 2) in colloquial questions and expressions with pronominal verbs (come te la cavi?, come te la prendi?, come te la spiego?) the phrase combines come + te + a verb + clitic object (la) — meaning 'how do you manage/cope?', 'how dare you/take it?', 'how do I explain it to you?'. Context determines translation. Informal and used in spoken Italian.
target_language_example: Come te non conoscevo nessuno che parlasse così.
native_language_example: I didn't know anyone like you who spoke like that.

meaning: 'What's your name?' (informal)
additional_notes: Used to ask someone's name in informal situations or with people of similar age. Literally: 'how do you call yourself'. With strangers you can use the more polite 'come si chiama?'. Can be said with first-name expectation; 'ti' indicates familiar 'you'.
target_language_example: Ciao! Come ti chiami?
native_language_example: Hi! What's your name?

meaning: 'as you like' / 'however you prefer' (telling someone they can decide or do things their way)
additional_notes: Informal way to give someone freedom or show indifference about how they do something. Often used in conversation to mean 'do it the way you think best' or 'suit yourself'. Tone can be neutral, permissive, or slightly dismissive depending on context and intonation.
target_language_example: Se vuoi mettere le sedie così, fallo come ti pare.
native_language_example: If you want to put the chairs like that, do it however you like.

meaning: how's it going
additional_notes: Common informal greeting meaning 'how are you' when used alone (e.g. "Come va?"). Can also be used with a noun to ask about the condition of something or someone (e.g. "Come va la gamba?" = "How's the leg doing?"). Use in casual contexts; for more formal situations use "come sta?".
target_language_example: Ciao Maria, come va il lavoro?
native_language_example: Hi Maria, how's work going?

meaning: 'how to get' or 'how to arrive' (used to ask for directions)
additional_notes: Used to ask or report how to reach a place. Often followed by a preposition + place (a, al, alla, in, etc.). Common in questions: "Mi può dire come arrivare a..." or "Ditemi come arrivare a..." Can also be used in reported speech (Tom mi disse come arrivare a casa sua).
target_language_example: Mi puoi dire come arrivare alla stazione?
native_language_example: Can you tell me how to get to the station?

meaning: 'how to get to (the)'.
additional_notes: Used to ask for directions to a feminine singular place (la + noun). Swap 'alla' for other articles as needed (al, allo, ai, alle) depending on the destination's article and number. Commonly appears in polite questions: Mi può dire come arrivare alla stazione? / Ditemi come arrivare alla banca.
target_language_example: Mi può spiegare come arrivare alla biblioteca?
native_language_example: Can you tell me how to get to the library?

meaning: 'how one feels' or 'what it's like' (used to ask or state how someone experiences something).
additional_notes: Often appears as 'come ci si sente' (literally 'how one feels there'), used to describe or ask about a general/impersonal experience (equivalent to 'how it feels' or 'what it's like'). The 'si' makes it impersonal/one-people construction; sometimes examples drop 'si' in casual speech but 'come ci si sente' is the common full form. Use when talking about feelings or experiences in general or when asking someone to imagine being in a situation.
target_language_example: Prova a chiudere gli occhi e immagina: come ci si sente a perdere tutte le certezze?
native_language_example: Try closing your eyes and imagine: what is it like to lose all certainty?

meaning: how to delete my account
additional_notes: A phrase used to ask for instructions on deleting (closing) an online account. 'Come' = how; 'eliminare' = to delete/remove; 'il mio account' = my account. Polite variations in examples show different verb forms (dimmi, ditemi, mi dica) for informal/formal and singular/plural requests. Common in customer support or tutorials.
target_language_example: Puoi spiegarmi come eliminare il mio account di posta elettronica?
native_language_example: Can you explain how to delete my email account?

meaning: how this works / how this functions
additional_notes: Used to ask for an explanation of how a specific thing (machine, device, system, or situation) operates. Word order can change: 'come funziona questa macchina?' or 'questa macchina, come funziona?'. Formality: neutral — appropriate in both polite and casual contexts. You can replace 'questa' with 'questa macchina', 'questa cosa', or a different demonstrative (questa/questa cosa/quella) to point to the item.
target_language_example: Puoi mostrarmi e spiegare come funziona questa stampante?
native_language_example: Can you show me and explain how this printer works?

meaning: how (the) ... work / how things work (in a place or system).
additional_notes: Used to ask or explain the way things operate in a specific context. Often followed by a noun (e.g., cose, regole, macchine). In the example sentences it's used with 'cose' (things) to mean 'how things work here' or in general. Literal components: 'come' = how, 'funzionano' = they work, 'le' = the (plural feminine).
target_language_example: Devo imparare come funzionano le regole dell'ufficio.
native_language_example: I need to learn how the office rules work.

meaning: 'how to solve the' (used before a masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: This phrase combines 'come' (how), the verb 'risolvere' (to solve), and the definite article 'il' (the, masculine singular). It's used when explaining or saying you know the method to solve a specific masculine problem or issue (e.g., 'il problema'). In spoken/written Italian you'll often see the noun following immediately: 'come risolvere il problema'.
target_language_example: Non so ancora come risolvere il problema tecnico.
native_language_example: I still don't know how to solve the technical problem.

meaning: as if
additional_notes: Used to introduce a hypothetical or imagined situation that contrasts with reality. It is followed by a verb in the subjunctive in Italian when expressing something contrary to fact or unlikely (e.g., "come se fosse"), but in casual speech indicative can also appear. Common in comparisons and to describe people's behavior or appearances.
target_language_example: Parla con me come se mi conoscesse.
native_language_example: He speaks to me as if he knew me.

meaning: 'how do you use this' or 'how is this used' (asking how to operate or use an object).
additional_notes: Common phrase to ask for instructions or a demonstration. Verb form can change (Sai/Sa/Sapete) depending on the pronoun/formality: 'Sai come si usa questa?' (informal you), 'Sa come si usa questa?' (formal you), 'Sapete come si usa questa?' (plural you). 'Questa' refers to a nearby feminine noun (e.g., macchina fotografica). For a masculine object, use 'questo' instead.
target_language_example: Scusi, sa come si usa questa fotocamera?
native_language_example: Excuse me, do you know how to use this camera?

meaning: 'how to use' or 'how to operate'.
additional_notes: Used to introduce instructions or knowledge about operating something (a tool, device, system, etc.). Commonly followed by a noun (come usare il computer, come usare il dizionario) or an infinitive/object. Neutral, suitable for formal and informal contexts.
target_language_example: Mi puoi spiegare come usare questa macchina?
native_language_example: Can you explain to me how to use this machine?

meaning: how (something) turns out / how (it) ends.
additional_notes: Used with verbs like finire (to end) to ask or state how a situation/story will turn out. Often appears as 'come va a finire' meaning 'how it will end' or 'how it turns out'. Informal to neutral spoken usage; common in conversation when anticipating an outcome.
target_language_example: Non spoilerare: voglio vedere come va a finire da sola.
native_language_example: Don't spoil it: I want to see how it ends on its own.

meaning: ‘the ... begins’ or ‘the ... starts’ (3rd-person singular + definite article).
additional_notes: Comincia is the 3rd-person singular present of cominciare (to begin/start). Paired with the masculine singular definite article il, it introduces a specific event or thing (e.g., il concerto, il test). Common in questions about time (A che ora comincia il concerto?). Word order can vary: the article + noun can follow (Comincia il test) or precede in questions.
target_language_example: Comincia il film alle otto.
native_language_example: The film starts at eight.

meaning: started to read / began reading
additional_notes: Past participle form (cominciato) + preposition a + infinitive leggere. Used to say someone began the action of reading. Can be paired with different subjects and objects; tense here is passato prossimo (e.g., 'Ho cominciato a leggere' = I started to read). Equivalent: 'ha iniziato a leggere'.
target_language_example: Ho cominciato a leggere un romanzo ieri.
native_language_example: I started to read a novel yesterday.

meaning: 'committed some' (past participle + partitive) — used with errors/acts: 'have committed some' or 'made some (mistakes)'
additional_notes: Combines the past participle commesso (from commettere — to commit/make) with the partitive degli (some/of the) before a plural noun (e.g., errori). Commonly used to say someone has made or committed some mistakes or wrongdoings. In spoken/written Italian you can also say abbiamo commesso errori (without degli) or abbiamo fatto degli errori (we made some mistakes). Agreement: commesso doesn't change for gender when used with avere; the plural noun after degli must match (e.g., degli errori, degli sbagli).
target_language_example: Ho commesso degli errori, ma imparerò da essi.
native_language_example: I committed some mistakes, but I will learn from them.

meaning: literally 'committed the' — part of a phrase used when talking about committing (an act, crime, error) followed by a masculine singular noun.
additional_notes: This is not a standalone fixed phrase but the verb participle 'commesso' (committed) plus the definite article 'il' (the). You'll typically see it in contexts like 'commesso il reato' (committed the crime) or 'commesso l'errore' (committed the mistake — note l' instead of il before a vowel). Use it when describing that someone has carried out an action; adjust the article/gender/number to match the noun (commessa la, commessi i, commesse le).
target_language_example: È stato commesso il furto nella notte.
native_language_example: The theft was committed during the night.

meaning: committed the crime.
additional_notes: Used to say someone carried out a criminal act. Often appears with verbs like 'ammettere' or 'confessare' (to admit/confess) followed by 'di aver' + past participle (di aver commesso). Literal: 'committed the crime.' Suitable in both formal and neutral contexts.
target_language_example: Ha ammesso di aver commesso il crimine la scorsa notte.
native_language_example: He admitted he committed the crime last night.

meaning: roommate; person you share a room or apartment with.
additional_notes: Used to refer to someone you live with who shares your room or living space. Common in casual and formal contexts. If you want to specify gender-neutral, 'coinquilino' (flatmate) or 'compagno/compagna di stanza' can be used.
target_language_example: Il mio compagno di stanza è molto ordinato.
native_language_example: My roommate is very tidy.

meaning: 'homework now' or 'do homework now' (indicates doing homework at this moment)
additional_notes: Compiti = homework; adesso = now. Together they emphasize that the homework is being done or should be done right now. Common in imperative or descriptive sentences (e.g., saying someone is doing their homework now, or telling someone they should do it now). Word order can vary (e.g., 'fare i compiti adesso', 'sta facendo i compiti adesso').
target_language_example: Dovresti iniziare i compiti adesso.
native_language_example: You should start the homework now.

meaning: tasks/homework to (do) — indicates tasks that need to be done or an action to be completed.
additional_notes: Commonly used with verbs or infinitives after 'da' to show purpose or necessity (e.g., 'compiti da finire' = tasks to finish, 'compiti da correggere' = tasks to correct). 'Compiti' usually means school homework, but can also mean general tasks. Word order: 'compiti da' + infinitive or past participle.
target_language_example: Ho dei compiti da studiare stasera.
native_language_example: I have homework to study tonight.

meaning: French homework (assignments for French class).
additional_notes: Used to refer to exercises, homework or assignments in the French language subject. 'Compiti' is the plural of 'compito' (task/homework). You can change the language: 'compiti di matematica', 'compiti di storia', etc. To specify possessive: 'i miei compiti di francese' = 'my French homework'.
target_language_example: Devo finire i compiti di francese prima di cena.
native_language_example: I have to finish my French homework before dinner.

meaning: homework now / do your homework now.
additional_notes: Used to tell someone to do (their) homework immediately. 'Compiti' = homework (plural). 'Ora' = now. In full sentences you'll usually see a verb (fare, fare i compiti) plus this phrase as object/time: e.g. 'Fai i compiti ora.' Imperative or modal verbs (dovresti/dovreste) are common: 'Dovresti fare i compiti ora' = 'You should do your homework now.'
target_language_example: Devi fare i compiti ora, poi puoi giocare.
native_language_example: You must do your homework now, then you can play.

meaning: someone's birthday (female family member): 'the birthday of my...'.
additional_notes: Used to say 'the birthday of my [female relative]'. 'Mia' is the possessive 'my' for feminine singular nouns (mia madre, mia figlia, mia sorella). In Italian word order the noun (compleanno) comes before the possession introduced by 'di' + pronoun. You can replace 'mia' with other possessives (mio, tuo, suo) and the following noun determines gender: use 'mio' with masculine nouns (compleanno di mio padre) and 'mia' with feminine nouns.
target_language_example: Vado a Firenze per il compleanno di mia sorella.
native_language_example: I'm going to Florence for my sister's birthday.

meaning: 'completely convinced' or 'fully convinced'.
additional_notes: Used to state strong certainty or belief about something or someone (often followed by 'di' + noun/pronoun or a clause). Can be used with different subjects and pronouns (la tua innocenza, della sua innocenza, che... ). Formality: neutral — suitable in both spoken and written contexts.
target_language_example: Sono completamente convinto che abbia detto la verità.
native_language_example: I am completely convinced that he/she told the truth.

meaning: acts/behaves as if (something were true).
additional_notes: Used to say someone behaves in a way that suggests a hypothetical or imagined situation. Often followed by a subjunctive clause (e.g. 'comporta come se nulla fosse' or 'comporta come se niente fosse'). Common in spoken and written Italian to describe manner or attitude.
target_language_example: Si comporta come se non lo conoscesse.
native_language_example: He behaves as if he didn't know him.

meaning: literally 'behavior me' — used with verbs to say someone's behavior affects me (e.g. 'his/her behavior annoys/upsets me').
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase on its own; it's the noun comportamento ('behavior') followed by an indirect object pronoun mi ('to me' / 'me'). In Italian you commonly say 'Il suo comportamento mi fa arrabbiare', 'mi dà sui nervi', 'mi rende malato/a', or 'mi confonde' — the verb after mi expresses how the behavior affects you. Agreement of adjectives (malato/malata) matches the speaker's gender.
target_language_example: Il suo comportamento mi dà sui nervi.
native_language_example: His behavior gets on my nerves.

meaning: 'behaved like a' or 'acted like a'.
additional_notes: Used to describe how someone behaved, followed by a noun (often a person type or quality): e.g. 'si comportò come un santo' = 'he/she behaved like a saint.' Commonly seen in past tense (comportò) or with reflexive pronoun (si comportò). You can replace the noun with character traits (gentiluomo, santo, espertо, bambino, etc.).
target_language_example: Lei si comportò come un'amica quando ne avevo bisogno.
native_language_example: She behaved like a friend when I needed her.

meaning: 'buys the' (he/she/it buys the) or an informal imperative 'buy the' (tu) depending on context.
additional_notes: Comprare = to buy. 'Compra il' can be the 3rd-person singular present (lui/lei compra il = he/she buys the) or the informal imperative (tu compra il = buy the) though the imperative more commonly appears without pronoun. Followed by a masculine singular noun introduced by the definite article 'il' (e.g., il libro, il pane). In questions use subject inversion or context to indicate who is buying (e.g., 'Dove compra il pane?' = 'Where does he/she buy the bread?').
target_language_example: Marco compra il giornale ogni mattina.
native_language_example: Marco buys the newspaper every morning.

meaning: I bought a pair (of ...).
additional_notes: Used to say you bought two matching items (a pair) such as shoes, gloves, glasses, scissors. 'Comprai' is the passato remoto (past simple) first-person singular of 'comprare' — commonly used in written or formal past narration in Italian; in spoken language many Italians use 'ho comprato'. The phrase is followed by 'di' + item (e.g., 'un paio di scarpe').
target_language_example: Comprai un paio di stivali la settimana scorsa.
native_language_example: I bought a pair of boots last week.

meaning: to buy the
additional_notes: A common verb + article sequence used before a masculine singular noun (il + noun). In English it corresponds to "to buy the..." or simply "to buy" when followed by a specific masculine item (e.g. il biglietto, il televisore, il pane). Remember that in Italian the article agrees with the noun (e.g. comprare la + feminine; comprare i/le for plural). Often appears with infinitive structures after verbs like dovere, ricordarsi, dimenticare, omettere (e.g. devo comprare il...).
target_language_example: Devo comprare il pane prima di uscire.
native_language_example: I have to buy the bread before going out.

meaning: to buy this (feminine singular item).
additional_notes: Combines the verb comprare (to buy) with the demonstrative adjective questa (this, feminine singular). Use when pointing to or referring to a specific feminine noun: questa casa, questa giacca, questa scarpa, etc. For masculine nouns use "comprare questo" (e.g., comprare questo libro). In questions and statements the verb is conjugated as needed (e.g., "Voglio comprare questa...", "Hai deciso di comprare questa...").
target_language_example: Voglio comprare questa giacca per l'inverno.
native_language_example: I want to buy this jacket for the winter.

meaning: buy this
additional_notes: Literal phrase meaning 'to buy this' (direct object 'questo' = 'this' — must agree in gender with the noun it refers to in full form: questo (m.)/questa (f.)/questi/queste). Commonly used when pointing to or referring to a specific item you intend to purchase. In natural speech you often include the noun (comprare questo libro/questo vestito) or use a pronoun/gesture.
target_language_example: Devo ricordarmi di comprare questo libro domani.
native_language_example: I must remember to buy this book tomorrow.

meaning: bought the (masculine plural) — literal past participle + definite article used before a plural masculine noun
additional_notes: Combines the past participle 'comprato' (bought) with the definite article 'i' (the, masculine plural). In sentences it precedes a masculine plural noun (e.g., i biglietti, i fiori, i regali). Common in passato prossimo constructions with avere: 'abbiamo comprato i biglietti' = 'we bought the tickets'. Word order: 'comprato i' is followed by the noun. If the noun is feminine plural, the article would be 'le' (e.g., 'comprato le scarpe').
target_language_example: Ho comprato i libri per il corso.
native_language_example: I bought the books for the course.

meaning: 'bought that' (past participle + demonstrative: 'bought that/that ...')
additional_notes: Comprato is the past participle of comprare (to buy). Quel is a demonstrative adjective meaning 'that' (masculine singular, used before a noun: quel libro, quel cavallo, quel maglione). Together they appear when talking about having bought a specific item in the past. Word order in Italian places the past participle (comprato) with any object pronoun/auxiliary as needed; in questions the auxiliary (hai/ha/hanno) appears before comprato: "Quando hai comprato quel maglione?"
target_language_example: Ho comprato quel libro ieri.
native_language_example: I bought that book yesterday.

meaning: 'bought those' (literally: 'bought those') — used to ask or say where/when someone bought certain items.
additional_notes: Comprato = past participle of comprare (to buy). Quelle = feminine plural demonstrative meaning 'those' (for feminine plural nouns like 'mutande', 'mutandine', 'scarpe'). Common in questions: Dove ha comprato quelle...? (Where did he/she buy those...?) or Quando hai comprato quelle...? (When did you buy those...?). If referring to masculine plural items, use 'quei/quegli' instead. Word order: 'comprato' often appears with a form of avere (ha, hai, abbiamo) when forming the passato prossimo: 'ha comprato'.
target_language_example: Dove hai comprato quelle scarpe?
native_language_example: Where did you buy those shoes?

meaning: bought this kind/type (of ...)
additional_notes: Used to ask or refer to why someone bought a particular kind or model of something. Often appears as 'comprato questo tipo di [oggetto]' (e.g. macchina, auto, telefono). The structure: 'comprato' (past participle of comprare) + 'questo tipo (di...)' meaning 'this kind/type of...'. Common in questions: 'Perché hai comprato questo tipo di macchina?'
target_language_example: Perché hai comprato questo tipo di telefono?
native_language_example: Why did you buy this kind of phone?

meaning: 'bought this' (past participle + demonstrative; 'have/has/have you bought this?')
additional_notes: Combines the past participle comprato (from comprare) with the demonstrative questo (‘this’). Used in perfect constructions with a form of avere (e.g., ho comprato questo = I bought this / I have bought this) or in questions (Avete comprato questo? = Did you buy this?). Word order can also be questo comprato in spoken language, but the common neutral order is ho comprato questo. Use appropriate subject/auxiliary for person and number: hai comprato, ha comprato, abbiamo comprato, hanno comprato.
target_language_example: L'ho comprato questo per il compleanno.
native_language_example: I bought this for his birthday.

meaning: bought a pair (of ...)
additional_notes: Used with 'di' + noun to say you bought two of something that forms a pair (e.g. shoes, gloves, chairs). Common in past tense: 'ho comprato un paio di...' or 'abbiamo comprato un paio di...'. Can also imply 'a couple of' in some contexts, but usually means a pair (two items meant to be used together).
target_language_example: Ho comprato un paio di scarpe nuove.
native_language_example: I bought a pair of new shoes.

meaning: bought a gift for (a specific occasion)
additional_notes: Used to say someone bought a present for a particular occasion (di + occasion: di compleanno, di Natale, etc.). Often appears with an indirect object indicating the recipient (gli, le, ti, vi). Literally: 'bought a gift of [occasion]'.
target_language_example: Le ho comprato un regalo di compleanno.
native_language_example: I bought her a birthday present.

meaning: bought a gift for
additional_notes: Used to say someone purchased a present intended for someone else. Comprato is the past participle of comprare (to buy); un regalo = a gift; per introduces the recipient or purpose (for). Commonly followed by a person (e.g., per mio padre) or an occasion (e.g., per il compleanno di...). Word order: Ho comprato un regalo per + recipient.
target_language_example: Ho comprato un regalo per il mio migliore amico.
native_language_example: I bought a gift for my best friend.

meaning: bought a bottle
additional_notes: Past participle phrase using 'comprare' (to buy). 'Comprato' is the past participle and here implies 'ho comprato' (I bought) or another subject (e.g. 'ha comprato', 'abbiamo comprato'). 'Una bottiglia' = a bottle (of water, wine, etc.). In speech the auxiliary (essere/avere) is usually included: 'Ho comprato una bottiglia.'
target_language_example: Ieri ho comprato una bottiglia d'acqua al supermercato.
native_language_example: Yesterday I bought a bottle of water at the supermarket.

meaning: a buyer for (something); 'compratore' = buyer, 'per' = for
additional_notes: Used to say there is (or to find) a buyer for a specific item or property. Common in contexts like real estate or selling goods. You can replace the noun after 'per' (e.g., 'un compratore per la casa', 'un compratore per queste' (these items)). Verb phrases often used: 'avere un compratore per...' (to have a buyer for...), 'trovare un compratore per...' (to find a buyer for...).
target_language_example: Spero di trovare un compratore per la mia macchina.
native_language_example: I hope to find a buyer for my car.

meaning: bought a pair (of ...).
additional_notes: Past simple (passato remoto) or literary past of comprare + 'un paio di' meaning 'a pair of'. Commonly used when referring to items sold in pairs (shoes, socks, gloves, etc.). In everyday spoken Italian speakers often use the passato prossimo ('ha comprato un paio di...') instead of 'comprò un paio di...'.
target_language_example: Lei comprò un paio di guanti nuovi per l'inverno.
native_language_example: She bought a pair of new gloves for the winter.

meaning: 'in common with' / 'shared with'.
additional_notes: Used to say that people or things share characteristics, interests, or belongings. Often appears in the fixed expression "avere (molto/niente) in comune (con)" — e.g. "abbiamo molto in comune con loro" (we have a lot in common with them). Can also mean 'shared' when describing shared spaces or ceremonies (e.g. "camera in comune" = shared room; "sposato in comune" = married in a civil/communal ceremony).
target_language_example: Abbiamo molti amici in comune con Marco.
native_language_example: We have many mutual friends with Marco.

con burro di arachidi e gelatina

target_language_multi_word_term: con burro di arachidi e gelatina
meaning: with peanut butter and jelly (as a sandwich filling).
additional_notes: Common phrase describing the classic sandwich combination (peanut butter and fruit jelly/jam). In Italian 'gelatina' can mean jelly or gelatine; in this culinary context it refers to fruit jelly or jam. Used to describe what a sandwich is made with: e.g., 'un panino con burro di arachidi e gelatina.'
target_language_example: Vorrei un panino con burro di arachidi e gelatina, per favore.
native_language_example: I'd like a peanut butter and jelly sandwich, please.

meaning: with whom is/has (someone) — asks who accompanied a person
additional_notes: Used to ask about the companion of a third person. 'È' is the third-person singular of 'essere' and can be part of the passato prossimo (e.g. 'è andato' = 'has gone') or present ('è' = 'is') depending on context and following verb. Common structure: 'Con chi è + past participle?' (Who did they go with?) or 'Con chi è + adjective/noun?' in some contexts.
target_language_example: Con chi è partita Laura per Milano?
native_language_example: Who did Laura leave with for Milan?

meaning: take your time; don't rush; make yourself comfortable
additional_notes: A polite expression telling someone to act without hurry or to be relaxed. Commonly used when inviting someone to proceed at their own pace (e.g., eat, sit, do something) or to reassure them. Variants: 'fai con comodo', 'fate con comodo', 'faccia con comodo' (informal/formal and singular/plural forms).
target_language_example: Prego, faccia con comodo.
native_language_example: Please, take your time.

meaning: with both (the) — used before a feminine plural or singular noun introduced by the definite article 'le' (often for body parts or objects).
additional_notes: Common in instructions to tell someone to hold or use something with both hands/fingers/etc. 'Entambe' agrees with feminine; for masculine you'd say 'con entrambi i' or 'con entrambe le' before feminine nouns. Often followed by a body part (le mani) or a feminine noun. Formal and neutral register.
target_language_example: Tieni il pacco con entrambe le mani quando scendi dalla macchina.
native_language_example: Hold the package with both hands when you get out of the car.

meaning: as (the) ... passed / as ... went by (e.g. with the passing of time).
additional_notes: Used to introduce something that changed gradually as time or another period progressed. Usually followed by a noun of time: 'con il passare del tempo' = 'as time went by'. Can be used with past tenses (passato prossimo or passato remoto) to describe a change that occurred over time.
target_language_example: Con il passare del tempo ho capito che avevo ragione.
native_language_example: As time went by I realized I was right.

meaning: with her to / with her at (used before a verb or place to show going with a female person).
additional_notes: This sequence appears when describing accompanying a woman (lei) to do something or to go somewhere. Often followed by an infinitive verb (con lei a vedere = with her to see/watch) or a place (con lei a Boston = with her in Boston). In spoken Italian the 'a' may link to the verb of motion or the place; word order can vary (e.g., 'va spesso con lei a vedere film' or 'va spesso con lei a guardare film'). 'Con lei' = 'with her'; 'a' here functions like 'to' or 'in' depending on the context.
target_language_example: Vado spesso con lei a fare una passeggiata.
native_language_example: I often go with her to take a walk.

meaning: with her for / with her alone (depends on context).
additional_notes:
This string appears in two different patterns in the example sentences:
- con lei da sola = "with her alone" / "alone with her" (used when asking to speak privately to a woman). Here da sola modifies lei (feminine) and means alone/privately.
- sta con lei da + time = "(he/they) have been with her for + duration" (da introduces a duration). In this pattern con lei means "with her" and da indicates how long.
Be careful: do not separate 'da sola' from 'lei' when you mean 'alone with her'.
target_language_example: Vorrei restare con lei da sola per parlare.
native_language_example: I'd like to stay alone with her to talk.

meaning: with her (and)... — 'con lei' = 'with her'; 'e' can add 'and' or be part of a following phrase
additional_notes: This sequence appears when 'con lei' (with her) is followed by another element introduced by 'e' (and) or when 'e' is part of a larger expression like 'e basta' (and that's it). Common uses: 'con lei e basta' (just with her), 'con lei e i suoi amici' (with her and her friends), 'con lei e il suo bambino' (with her and her baby). Pronunciation and meaning are literal; context determines whether 'e' links another noun or completes a phrase.
target_language_example: Sono partito con lei e il suo cane.
native_language_example: I left with her and her dog.

meaning: with the scandal / connected to the scandal (usually in negative sentences: 'to have something to do with the scandal')
additional_notes: Often appears in the fixed expression avere (nulla/niente) a che fare con lo scandalo = 'to have nothing to do with the scandal'. Used to deny involvement or connection. In positive contexts you could say avere a che fare con lo scandalo = 'to be involved with the scandal'.
target_language_example: Non voglio essere coinvolto: non ho niente a che fare con lo scandalo.
native_language_example: I don't want to be involved: I have nothing to do with the scandal.

meaning: 'with the aim' or 'with the purpose'.
additional_notes: Used to introduce the intention or goal behind an action. Often followed by di + infinitive (con lo scopo di migliorare) or a noun phrase. Formal-neutral register, common in written and spoken Italian.
target_language_example: Ha studiato tutta la notte con lo scopo di superare l'esame.
native_language_example: He studied all night with the aim of passing the exam.

meaning: with me, just in case / in case anything happens
additional_notes: Used to ask someone to stay in contact or be with you as a precaution. 'Per ogni evenienza' means 'for any eventuality' or 'just in case'. Common in spoken and written Italian when giving safety instructions or contingency plans. The phrase often follows a verb like restare/stare (to stay) or contattare (to contact).
target_language_example: Resta con me, per ogni evenienza.
native_language_example: Stay with me, just in case.

meaning: with my
additional_notes: A simple preposition + possessive combination meaning 'with my' (masculine singular). Used before a masculine singular noun (e.g. mio figlio, mio padre, mio fratello, mio zio). In speech you may also hear the full phrase with the article (con il mio, con lo mio — though con lo mio is uncommon); when referring to people Italians often omit the article: con mio padre, not *con il mio padre. For feminine nouns use con mia (e.g. con mia madre).
target_language_example: Esco con mio amico stasera.
native_language_example: I'm going out with my friend tonight.

meaning: with my uncle last (as in 'last week').
additional_notes: This is a fragment you see in sentences like 'Io sono stato/a con mio zio la scorsa settimana.' It combines: 'con mio zio' (with my uncle) and 'la scorsa' as a truncated form of 'la scorsa settimana' (last week). Remember to add the noun 'settimana' (week) or another time word after 'la scorsa' (e.g. 'la scorsa estate' = last summer). Verb agreement: past participle and auxiliary must match the speaker's gender and number (sono stato / stata / stati / state).
target_language_example: Io sono stata con mio zio la scorsa settimana.
native_language_example: I was with my uncle last week.

meaning: with my uncle last week (fragment used to say you stayed or were with your uncle the previous week).
additional_notes: This is a fragment; complete sentence usually adds a past-tense verb (e.g. sono stato/a, sono rimasto/a). Gender of the speaker affects the past participle: 'sono stato' (male speaker), 'sono stata' (female speaker). 'La settimana scorsa' = 'last week'. Use 'con mio zio la settimana scorsa' for a full time expression.
target_language_example: Sono rimasta con mio zio la settimana scorsa.
native_language_example: I stayed with my uncle last week.

meaning: with us in (followed by a place or language).
additional_notes: Used to indicate being together with 'us' inside a location or using a language. Commonly appears before a noun or phrase: e.g. 'con noi in questa stanza' (with us in this room) or 'con noi in francese' (with us in French). Verb forms in examples show different moods/persons (ha provato a parlare — tried to speak; resta/restate/stai/stia — imperative or indicative forms).
target_language_example: Vieni con noi in cucina.
native_language_example: Come with us into the kitchen.

meaning: with all my heart; very sincerely or deeply (used for emotions or thanks).
additional_notes: Common idiom to emphasize strong feelings (love, hate, gratitude, missing someone). Can be used literally (deep emotional feeling) or figuratively to show sincerity. Often appears after verbs like amare, mancare, detestare, ringraziare. Tone can be affectionate or intense depending on context.
target_language_example: Ti ringrazio con tutto il cuore per il tuo aiuto.
native_language_example: I thank you with all my heart for your help.

meaning: with all my (used to express full intensity, usually followed by a noun like 'cuore' or 'amore').
additional_notes: A common romantic or emphatic phrase meaning 'with all my...' — most often completed as 'con tutto il mio cuore' (with all my heart) or 'con tutto il mio amore' (with all my love). Used to stress total commitment or feeling. Usually followed by a singular masculine noun (mio + noun). For different persons or genders you would change the possessive (e.g. 'con tutto il tuo cuore', 'con tutta la mia anima').
target_language_example: Ti sosterrò con tutto il mio cuore.
native_language_example: I will support you with all my heart.

meaning: with a pair of / with a couple of (depending on context).
additional_notes: Literal meaning: 'with a pair' (used with plural nouns like 'occhiali', 'forbici'). Can also be used more loosely to mean 'with a couple of' (a small number of) when followed by countable items or actions (e.g., 'con un paio di spari' = 'with a couple of shots'). Common in everyday speech. Choose meaning from context: physical pair (tools, clothing) vs. informal 'a couple of'.
target_language_example: Ho risolto il problema con un paio di telefonate.
native_language_example: I solved the problem with a couple of phone calls.

meaning: with a (baseball) bat; used to say someone hit or attacked using a bat
additional_notes: Followed by the sport/type of bat (e.g. mazza da baseball). Common in contexts describing hitting or attacking. Word order: 'colpire/attaccare qualcuno con una mazza da baseball.' 'Mazza' = bat; 'da' links purpose/type (mazza da baseball = baseball bat).
target_language_example: Lo hanno colpito con una mazza da baseball.
native_language_example: They hit him with a baseball bat.

meaning: with one
additional_notes: Literally means "with one." In phrases like "con uno dei/delle...", it means "with one of ...". When "uno" stands alone, it can refer to a male person ("a guy/man") from context; after verbs like "stare" or "uscire," it often suggests being with or dating a guy. Use "una" for a female person.
target_language_example: Non voglio uscire con uno che non conosco.
native_language_example: I don't want to go out with a guy I don't know.

meaning: 'the concert is' or 'the concert has' (depending on context).
additional_notes: A phrase combining 'concerto' (concert) with the verb 'essere' (to be). Use 'Il concerto è ...' to state when a concert takes place (e.g. domenica prossima), to say its state (e.g. finito), or with past forms (è stato) to say the concert 'was' or 'has been' something. Word order is subject + verb in Italian: 'Il concerto è...'.
target_language_example: Il concerto è stasera alle otto.
native_language_example: The concert is tonight at eight.

meaning: shared his/her/its (something).
additional_notes: Literal phrase: 'condiviso' is the past participle of 'condividere' (to share). 'Il suo' means 'his/her/its/your (formal)/their' depending on context — Italian uses the same possessive for different genders and persons; gender/number of the noun that follows must agree (e.g., 'il suo dessert', 'la sua mela', 'i suoi panini'). Commonly used to say someone shared a specific item with someone else.
target_language_example: Luca ha condiviso il suo panino con me.
native_language_example: Luca shared his sandwich with me.

meaning: shared his/her lunch with (someone).
additional_notes: Past participle phrase (condiviso = shared). Use with a subject: e.g., 'Ha condiviso il suo pranzo con me' = 'He/She shared his/her lunch with me.' Replace 'suo' with 'mio/tuo/nostro' for different owners. Common structure: [Subject] ha condiviso il suo pranzo con [object].
target_language_example: Maria ha condiviso il suo pranzo con un collega.
native_language_example: Maria shared her lunch with a colleague.

meaning: 'conditions of' or 'state/terms of'.
additional_notes: Used to describe the state, circumstances, or terms relating to something or someone. Can refer to living conditions (condizioni di vita), ability/fitness (nelle condizioni di), working terms (condizioni di lavoro), or the state in which something is returned (nelle stesse condizioni di). Commonly followed by a noun or a clause.
target_language_example: Le condizioni di viaggio non erano buone.
native_language_example: The travel conditions were not good.

meaning: compared to; in comparison with
additional_notes: Used to compare two people, places, times, or things. Often appears as the fixed phrase "in confronto a/di" + noun or pronoun. Can introduce a direct comparison (e.g., "In confronto a Tokyo, Londra è piccola") or emphasize contrast ("Tom non era niente in confronto a lei"). Tone is neutral and common in both spoken and written Italian. "In confronto a" and "in confronto con" are both used; choose either based on preference.
target_language_example: In confronto a ieri, oggi siamo molto più rilassati.
native_language_example: Compared to yesterday, today we are much more relaxed.

meaning: he/she/it knows the (plural feminine) / you (formal) know the (plural feminine).
additional_notes: From the verb conoscere (to know, to be acquainted with). Conosce is the third-person singular or formal second-person singular (Lei) present tense. 'Le' is the direct object pronoun or the article for feminine plural nouns. Most often 'conosce le' appears before a feminine plural noun (e.g., 'conosce le regole' — 'he/she knows the rules') or with 'le' as a pronoun (less common: 'Conosce le?' — 'Do you (formal) know them?'). For informal 'you' use 'conosci le'.
target_language_example: Lei conosce le regole della casa.
native_language_example: She/You (formal) knows the house rules.

meaning: to know the
additional_notes: Compositional phrase: conoscere means "to know" or "to be familiar with," and la is the feminine singular definite article ("the"). The article changes depending on the noun: for example conoscere il, conoscere i, conoscere le. In many contexts, Italian also contrasts conoscere with sapere: conoscere is often used with nouns, people, or things one is familiar with.
target_language_example: È importante conoscere la differenza.
native_language_example: It's important to know the difference.

meaning: to know (someone/something) fairly/quite/rather well; 'piuttosto' modifies 'conoscere' to indicate a moderate-to-high degree of familiarity
additional_notes: 'Piuttosto' here functions as an adverb modifying conoscere, often appearing with other adverbs like 'bene' (conoscere piuttosto bene). Commonly used with direct objects or pronouns (la, le, li, lui, il posto, ecc.). Word order can vary: conoscere piuttosto [bene] or [pronoun] conoscere piuttosto. Tone is neutral; fits both formal and informal contexts depending on surrounding language.
target_language_example: La devi conoscere piuttosto bene.
native_language_example: You must know her fairly well.

meaning: that he/she/it knew everything (imperfect subjunctive + object)
additional_notes: Literally 'knew everything.' 'Conoscesse' is the third-person singular imperfect subjunctive of conoscere. This form appears in subordinate clauses after verbs or expressions that require the subjunctive (e.g., doubt, desire, emotion, hypothetical or non-real situations). Context determines tense/meaning: often used for hypothetical past situations (e.g., 'If he had known everything...') or in reported/indirect speech. For English, translate depending on context as 'knew everything,' 'were to know everything,' or 'had known everything.'
target_language_example: Se lui conoscesse tutto, potrebbe aiutare più facilmente.
native_language_example: If he knew everything, he could help more easily.

meaning: 'do you (plural) know who...'? (asking whether you all know who did something)
additional_notes: Conoscete is the second-person plural present of conoscere (voi). Use 'conoscete chi...' to ask a group if they know the identity of a person or people who performed an action. In spoken Italian, voi is often omitted because 'conoscete' already indicates 'you (plural)'. Followed by a clause with a verb (e.g., 'ha rotto', 'li ha uccisi'). Pronouns (li, le) refer to masculine/feminine plural direct objects in the subordinate clause.
target_language_example: Conoscete chi ha chiamato ieri sera?
native_language_example: Do you (all) know who called last night?

meaning: 'do you (plural) know a...?' — asking if the listeners know someone or something (one, unspecified).
additional_notes: Conoscete is the second-person plural (voi) form of conoscere (to know). Use 'conoscete un/una' to ask a group if they know a person, place, or professional (e.g., 'Conoscete un buon ristorante?'). For singular informal 'you' (tu) use 'conosci un'. Often followed by a noun or clause identifying the person/thing (e.g., 'conoscete un uomo che si chiama...').
target_language_example: Conoscete un buon avvocato in città?
native_language_example: Do you (all) know a good lawyer in town?

meaning: 'knew the' (imperfect past tense of conoscere + definite article).
additional_notes: Conosceva is the third-person singular imperfect of conoscere (to know, be familiar with). Use this for ongoing/past habitual knowledge or background information. It is followed by a noun with the definite article (il). Can refer to knowing people, places, facts, systems, etc. English often translates it as "knew the" or "was familiar with the".
target_language_example: Lei conosceva il ragazzo del quartiere.
native_language_example: She knew the boy from the neighborhood.

meaning: I knew (them/him) for/since (a period of time).
additional_notes: Conoscevo is the imperfect of conoscere (to know someone/be acquainted with). 'Da' introduces the duration or starting point (e.g., 'da molto tempo' = for a long time; 'da quando...' = since when...). Commonly used to describe ongoing or repeated past acquaintance. Replace 'conoscevo' with other persons (conoscevo, conoscevi, conoscevamo...) to match subject.
target_language_example: Li conoscevo da quando erano piccoli.
native_language_example: I had known them since they were little.

meaning: 'do you know the boy' / 'do you know the guy'.
additional_notes: A common spoken question asking whether someone is acquainted with or recognizes a male person (ragazzo). Often used with an object pronoun lo: "Lo conosci il ragazzo?" or more naturally "Conosci il ragazzo?" or "Lo conosci?" Word order can vary in casual speech. Use 'conoscere' for knowing people or places (to be familiar with).
target_language_example: Conosci il ragazzo che lavora qui?
native_language_example: Do you know the boy who works here?

meaning: 'do you know my...?' (familiar form: conoscere + possessive)
additional_notes: Used to ask if someone knows a person you are related to or connected with. 'Conosci' is the tu (informal singular) form of conoscere (to know). Follow with the family noun: marito (husband), padre (father), figlio (son), fratello (brother). In Italian possessive adjectives usually take the definite article (il mio padre), but in casual speech, especially in questions starting with 'Conosci...', the article is often dropped (Conosci mio padre?). Use 'Conosce' for formal/third-person (Conosce mio padre?) and 'conoscete' for plural 'you'.
target_language_example: Conosci mio cugino?
native_language_example: Do you know my cousin?

meaning: met/have met some (people).
additional_notes: A combination of the past participle/conjugated form of conoscere (conosciuto or ha conosciuto/hai conosciuto) plus the partitive article 'dei' meaning 'some' before a plural noun (e.g. 'dei canadesi' = 'some Canadians'). Used to ask or say whether someone has met some members of a group. In sentences the verb will change with person and tense (Hai conosciuto dei..., Ha conosciuto dei..., Avete conosciuto dei...).
target_language_example: Hai conosciuto dei nuovi colleghi in ufficio?
native_language_example: Have you met some new colleagues at the office?

meaning: ‘met/learned (about) my…’ — used when saying you met or came to know someone or something belonging to you (my name, my boyfriend, my teacher).
additional_notes: This phrase is the past participle conosciuto (met / got to know) followed by a possessive (il mio = my + masculine noun). In natural Italian you often include the noun after il mio (e.g., il mio fidanzato, il mio nome). For people, common verbs are conoscere (to meet/get to know) vs. incontrare (to meet). Conosciuto il mio can mean 'met my…' or 'learned my…' depending on context (e.g., Come ha conosciuto il mio nome? = How did he learn my name?).
target_language_example: Ieri ho conosciuto il mio nuovo vicino.
native_language_example: Yesterday I met my new neighbor.

meaning: 'I have known (someone) for...'.
additional_notes: Used with a person pronoun or name plus a time expression to say how long you've known them. Conjugate 'conoscere' to match the subject (e.g., 'conosco', 'conosci', 'conosce', 'conosciamo', 'conoscete', 'conoscono') and follow with 'da' + time period (da due anni) or 'da quando' + clause (da quando è nata).
target_language_example: La conosco da tre anni.
native_language_example: I've known her for three years.

meaning: I know the (feminine plural) / I am familiar with them.
additional_notes: Conosco is the first-person singular present of conoscere (to know, be familiar with). When followed by le, it refers to feminine plural nouns (e.g., le regole, le storie) or to a previously mentioned group of feminine things/people. For masculine plural use 'li' (conosco i / li) and for singular feminine use 'la' (conosco la). In sentences like 'Mi scusi, non conosco le leggi.' the negative uses non before the verb: 'non conosco le...'.
target_language_example: Conosco le tradizioni del mio paese.
native_language_example: I know the traditions of my country.

meaning: I don't know anyone / I know nobody.
additional_notes: Common negative construction with the verb conoscere (to know people). In Italian the negation usually uses non before the verb (Non conosco nessuno). 'Conosco nessuno' without 'non' is ungrammatical in neutral Italian; examples show different contexts (places, names, groups). Use when you want to say you do not know any person in a group or place.
target_language_example: Non conosco nessuno a scuola.
native_language_example: I don't know anyone at school.

meaning: they know the (masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: Conoscono is the third-person plural present of conoscere (to know, be familiar with). Followed by the definite article il when the noun is masculine singular (il mare, il fatto, il signor...). Use conosco (I), conosci (you sing.), conosce (he/she), conosciamo (we), conoscete (you pl.) accordingly. If the noun is feminine singular use la (e.g., conoscono la città).
target_language_example: Loro conoscono il mio amico Gianni.
native_language_example: They know my friend Gianni.

meaning: delivered / handed in (followed by a masculine singular noun - 'the')
additional_notes: Past participle 'consegnato' (from consegnare) + definite article 'il' appears before a masculine singular noun (e.g., il compito, il messaggio, il rapporto). Used to say someone handed in, delivered, or gave something. Can be part of compound past (e.g., 'Ho consegnato il rapporto') or in questions ('Hai consegnato il messaggio?').
target_language_example: Ho consegnato il pacco al corriere ieri.
native_language_example: I delivered the package to the courier yesterday.
