additional_notes: Used to indicate that an action or state began in the past and has continued up to now. Common with verbs of knowing, being ill, sending, not doing something, etc. Can be replaced by "da molto tempo" for emphasis.
target_language_example: Studio italiano da tempo.
native_language_example: I've been studying Italian for a long time.

meaning: hard to find / difficult to find (literally: 'to find' with a phrase indicating difficulty or necessity).
additional_notes: Used after an adjective (difficile) or a comment to indicate that something will be difficult or rare to locate. Often follows the word it modifies: 'difficile da trovare' = 'difficult to find.' Can also be used alone as a short comment: 'Difficile da trovare!' or just 'Da trovare!' in context meaning 'worth looking for' or 'to be found'.
target_language_example: Questa varietà è davvero difficile da trovare qui.
native_language_example: This variety is really difficult to find here.

meaning: by/from everyone; compared to everyone else (depending on context).
additional_notes: Literally 'from everyone' or 'by everyone'. Common uses: 1) in comparisons or distinctions: '... diverso da tutti gli altri' = 'different from everyone else' (here da tutti can be part of 'da tutti gli altri'); 2) to indicate agency/passive agent: 'accettata da tutti i membri' = 'accepted by all the members' (here 'da tutti' = 'by all'); 3) to indicate being surrounded: 'circondato da tutti i suoi amici' = 'surrounded by all his/her friends'. The exact meaning depends on the surrounding words. Often appears as part of longer phrases like 'da tutti gli altri' (from/than everyone else) or 'da tutti i membri' (by all members).
target_language_example: Era felice di essere diverso da tutti gli altri.
native_language_example: He was happy to be different from everyone else.

meaning: for a long time / since many (used with time expressions)
additional_notes: Informal expression meaning 'for a long time' or 'a lot of' when referring to time or quantity. Commonly used with time nouns (tempo, anni, giorni) or verbs to indicate duration (e.g., 'da un sacco di tempo' = 'for ages'). Can be used in present tense to say something has been true for a long period (with 'da' + duration).
target_language_example: Non lo vedo da un sacco di tempo.
native_language_example: I haven't seen him in ages.

meaning: 'for ages' / 'for a very long time' (informal)
additional_notes: Used to say someone has known/been doing something for a very long time. Common in spoken Italian; often interchangeable with 'da molto tempo' or 'da tanto tempo'. Can refer to knowing a person, living somewhere, or experiencing something. Tone is informal/casual.
target_language_example: Ti conosco da una vita, dobbiamo prendere un caffè insieme.
native_language_example: I've known you for ages, we should grab a coffee together.

meaning: from one
additional_notes: Used with numbers to indicate the starting point of a range, especially in expressions like "da uno a dieci" = "from one to ten." In these examples, it is part of counting or number sequences.
target_language_example: I bambini imparano a contare da uno a venti.
native_language_example: The children learn to count from one to twenty.

meaning: 'to sell' or 'for selling' (indicates that something is available to be sold or has a certain quality in abundance).
additional_notes: Literally 'to sell'. Used after a noun to say the item is available/has to be sold (e.g., 'biglietti da vendere' = tickets to sell). Also used idiomatically with abstract nouns to indicate abundance of a trait (e.g., 'coraggio da vendere' = courage to spare / plenty of courage). Often follows verbs like 'avere', 'restare', or 'rimanere' (e.g., 'non resta niente da vendere' = there's nothing left to sell).
target_language_example: Ho tre biciclette da vendere.
native_language_example: I have three bicycles to sell.

meaning: up close; closely (physically or in observation).
additional_notes: Used to say looking or observing something closely or from a short distance. Can refer to physically seeing someone/something up close (Da vicino sembra diverso) or to monitoring/observing carefully (osservare da vicino). Often appears with verbs like vedere, guardare, osservare, or in passive constructions.
target_language_example: Vorrei vedere il dipinto da vicino.
native_language_example: I would like to see the painting up close.

meaning: from scratch; starting again from the beginning.
additional_notes: Used to say you start something anew with no prior progress or using basic/raw ingredients. Common with verbs like ricominciare (to start again) or fare (to make) — e.g., ricominciare da zero = start over; fare qualcosa da zero = make something from scratch.
target_language_example: Ho cucinato la salsa da zero, senza usare conserve.
native_language_example: I made the sauce from scratch, without using canned products.

meaning: 'Go for it!' / 'Give it your all!' (encouragement to try hard or hurry up).
additional_notes: Informal imperative phrase used to urge someone to start enthusiastically, work hard, hurry up, or put a lot of energy into something. Can be said to one person or a group. Tone can be encouraging or pushy depending on context (e.g., 'Zitta e dacci dentro!' = 'Shut up and go for it!'). Literal components: dacci = 'give us' (da' + ci), dentro = 'inside', but meaning is idiomatic here.
target_language_example: Dacci dentro con quel progetto, possiamo finirlo entro la settimana.
native_language_example: Go for it with that project; we can finish it by the week.

meaning: give (something) to; feed (someone/animal).
additional_notes: Common imperative/second-person singular or present-tense form of 'dare' + partitive or direct object phrase 'da mangiare' meaning 'to give (food)'. In the examples 'dai da mangiare' = 'you give/are giving food' or as a request 'please give (food)'. Often followed by a prepositional phrase indicating the recipient (al cane, ai pesci, alle galline). Use 'dai' for tu (you), 'dà' (with accent) is third person/Lei in some dialects but standard third person is 'dà'.
target_language_example: Dai da bere al gatto quando torni a casa.
native_language_example: Give the cat something to drink when you come home.

meaning: from the king / by the king (literally 'from the King')
additional_notes: A short phrase made of preposition + article + noun: da + il = dal, Re = King. Used literally to indicate origin, gift, order, or authority coming from a king (or as a historical/formal expression). Can also appear in names/titles (e.g., 'decreto dal Re' = 'decree from the King'). Context determines whether it means 'from' (origin) or 'by' (agent).
target_language_example: Il documento è stato firmato dal Re.
native_language_example: The document was signed by the King.

meaning: because; since; given that.
additional_notes: Used to introduce a reason or cause. Equivalent to 'since' or 'because' in English and often appears at the start of a sentence or clause. Neutral register (suitable for formal and informal contexts). Can be followed by indicative verbs.
target_language_example: Dal momento che piove, restiamo a casa.
native_language_example: Since it's raining, we'll stay home.

meaning: 'out of nowhere' or 'from nowhere'.
additional_notes: Used to describe something or someone appearing suddenly and unexpectedly. Equivalent to English 'out of nowhere'. Common in spoken and written Italian.
target_language_example: Il gatto è spuntato dal nulla nel corridoio.
native_language_example: The cat appeared out of nowhere in the hallway.

meaning: by/with the noise of the cars; because of the car noise.
additional_notes: This phrase is used to indicate the cause or source of annoyance or disturbance. 'Dal' = 'da' + 'il' (from/by the). 'Rumore delle automobili' = 'noise of the cars' (often shortened in speech to 'rumore delle auto'). Common in sentences expressing being bothered: 'siamo infastiditi dal rumore delle automobili' = 'we are annoyed by the car noise.'
target_language_example: La notte non dormo dal rumore delle automobili.
native_language_example: I can't sleep at night because of the car noise.

meaning: by/with the noise of the cars; from the sound of the cars (i.e., bothered by car noise).
additional_notes: Literal prepositional phrase: 'dal' = 'da + il' (from/by the), 'rumore' = noise/sound, 'delle macchine' = of the cars. Commonly used after verbs like 'essere infastidito/a' (to be annoyed/bothered) or 'disturbato/a' to say you're bothered by traffic or car noise. Gender/number of adjectives/participles must agree with the speaker (in the examples, 'infastidita' = female singular, 'infastiditi' = male plural).
target_language_example: La finestra è aperta e non dormo dal rumore delle macchine.
native_language_example: The window is open and I can't sleep because of the noise of the cars.

meaning: from the (hand)bag / out of the bag.
additional_notes: A combination of dalla (di + la) meaning 'from the' and borsa meaning 'bag' or 'handbag'. Used to say someone took or pulled something out of their bag. Common in everyday speech; context determines if 'bag', 'purse', or 'handbag' is best in English.
target_language_example: Ha tirato fuori il portafoglio dalla borsa.
native_language_example: She pulled the wallet out of her bag.

meaning: literally 'from the balls'; vulgar slang meaning 'annoying' or 'a pain (in the butt)'.
additional_notes: Very informal and vulgar. Used to describe people or things that are irritating, annoying, or troublesome. Often appears as 'che ti/mi/ci/lo/le/… fa/sono dalle palle' or in expressions like 'sei dalle palle' (you're a pain). Avoid in formal contexts or with strangers; use milder alternatives like 'fastidioso' or 'scocciante'.
target_language_example: Quel vicino è proprio dalle palle.
native_language_example: That neighbor is really annoying / a real pain.

meaning: the damage was already done / it was too late to fix it
additional_notes: Used to say that harm or negative consequences have already occurred and cannot easily be reversed. Often appears as 'il danno era ormai fatto' or shortened to 'il danno era fatto'. Can refer to physical damage, mistakes, or irreversible consequences.
target_language_example: Quando abbiamo chiuso la porta, il danno era fatto e non si poteva più recuperare.
native_language_example: When we closed the door, the damage was done and couldn't be undone.

meaning: to give birth; to deliver (a baby); also used figuratively to mean 'to bring into the world' (e.g., an idea, a work).
additional_notes: Common idiom for childbirth. Used both literally (a woman giving birth) and figuratively (publishing or creating something). Conjugates like other verbs: e.g., "dà alla luce" (she gives birth), "ha dato alla luce" (she gave birth). Often followed by the newborn or the thing brought forth: "ha dato alla luce un figlio" or "ha dato alla luce un romanzo".
target_language_example: Maria ha deciso di dare alla luce il suo bambino in ospedale.
native_language_example: Maria decided to give birth to her baby in the hospital.

meaning: to make someone feel dizzy, arrogant, or overwhelmed (lit. 'to give to the head') — often used for alcohol, success, or strong feelings that 'go to one's head'.
additional_notes: Idiom used when something (e.g., alcohol, praise, success, strong emotions) affects someone's judgment or makes them feel lightheaded or conceited. Context determines whether physical dizziness or figurative arrogance is meant. Typical constructions: 'Mi dà alla testa' (It makes me dizzy/goes to my head) or 'Gli è salita alla testa'/'Gli ha dato alla testa' (It has gone to his head / it's made him arrogant).
target_language_example: Quella birra mi dà alla testa e mi sento strano.
native_language_example: That beer is going to my head and I feel strange.

meaning: to listen to, to heed, to pay attention to (someone or something).
additional_notes: Used when someone pays attention to advice, warnings, or requests. Often followed by a person or thing introduced with a preposition (e.g., 'a' or directly the pronoun). Similar to 'ascoltare' but emphasizes heeding or taking someone's words seriously.
target_language_example: Dovresti dare ascolto a quello che ti dicono i medici.
native_language_example: You should listen to what the doctors tell you.

meaning: to give a high five (to slap hands in celebration or greeting).
additional_notes: Informal expression used when two people slap their open palms together as a friendly gesture of celebration, agreement, or encouragement. Conjugated like the verb 'dare' (e.g., 'gli ho dato cinque' = 'I gave him a high five'). Common in casual contexts among friends, teammates, or to congratulate someone.
target_language_example: Vuoi dare cinque dopo la partita?
native_language_example: Do you want to give a high five after the game?

meaning: to give to (for someone to do something)
additional_notes: Literal components mean “to give” + preposition “to/for.” Often used before an infinitive or a noun to indicate giving something to someone (e.g., give food to an animal) or in a causative/colloquial construction meaning “have/get someone to give/do something” (e.g., "fartelo dare da [name]" = get [name] to give it to you/do it). Context determines whether it's simple give or a causative sense. Common with verbs like "mangiare" (to feed) or with pronouns and names.
target_language_example: Devo dare da mangiare al cane.
native_language_example: I have to give the dog something to eat / I have to feed the dog.

meaning: to go crazy / to lose one's mind (behave irrationally, become very angry or panic).
additional_notes: Informal idiomatic expression. Often used to describe a sudden, temporary loss of self-control—extreme anger, panic, or irrational behavior—not a clinical diagnosis. Common in spoken Italian and colloquial writing.
target_language_example: Ha cominciato a dare di matto quando ha visto il conto.
native_language_example: He started to go crazy when he saw the bill.

meaning: to set fire to; to burn (something) intentionally.
additional_notes: A common phrase for deliberately starting a fire to an object or place (often used with a direct object: dare fuoco a + qualcosa). Usually used in contexts of arson, threats, or violent actions. Can be followed by 'a' + noun (dare fuoco a casa/auto/foresta) or by a clause (minacciare di dare fuoco a...).
target_language_example: Hanno minacciato di dare fuoco alla macchina.
native_language_example: They threatened to set the car on fire.

meaning: to act crazy, to talk nonsense, to be confused or incoherent
additional_notes: Informal idiom used to describe someone who is behaving irrationally, saying nonsense, or losing their sense (could be temporary confusion, jokingly or critically). Often used in present tense: 'sta dando i numeri' (he/she is acting crazy). Not literal — 'numeri' (numbers) doesn't refer to actual numbers here.
target_language_example: Non fare lo stronzo e smettila di dare i numeri.
native_language_example: Don't be an idiot and stop talking nonsense.

meaning: to hunt or chase (after someone or something); to pursue.
additional_notes: Commonly used for literal hunting (animals) and figurative chasing (pursuing a person, idea, or opportunity). Often followed by a noun or a prepositional phrase: dare la caccia a qualcosa/qualcuno. More formal alternatives: cacciare, inseguire. Can imply persistent pursuit.
target_language_example: La polizia ha dato la caccia al fuggitivo per tre giorni; hanno continuato a dare la caccia fino a catturarlo.
native_language_example: The police chased the fugitive for three days; they kept hunting him until they caught him.

meaning: to give one's hand; to help someone (offer physical help) or, in some contexts, to shake hands; figuratively 'to assist' or 'lend a hand'.
additional_notes: Used with an indirect object: dare la mano a qualcuno. Context determines literal (physical help or handshake) vs. figurative meaning (help/assistance). Not a false cognate; literal translation is meaningful. Common in both formal and informal speech.
target_language_example: Mi ha detto «Vieni, ti do la mano» quando sono scivolato.
native_language_example: He said 'Come on, I'll give you my hand' when I slipped.

meaning: to consider/regard (someone/something) as; to assume or take for (something).
additional_notes: Used with a noun, adjective, or past participle to express that someone/something is regarded in a certain way. Common in expressions like 'dare per morto' (to consider someone dead) and 'dare per scontato' (to take for granted). Can be used in active constructions (dare per + complemento) and impersonal/plural forms (Lo danno per ...). Formality: neutral.
target_language_example: Lo danno per disperso dopo la tempesta; molti lo danno per morto.
native_language_example: They consider him missing after the storm; many take him for dead.

meaning: to take (something/someone) for granted; to assume without questioning
additional_notes: Used when someone assumes a fact, help, feeling, or presence will always be there without appreciating it or checking. Often followed by a direct object (e.g., 'dare per scontato qualcosa/qualcuno') or by a clause introduced with 'che'. Can be used in negative to warn against assumptions: 'Non dare per scontato...'.
target_language_example: Non dare per scontato il supporto dei tuoi amici.
native_language_example: Don't take your friends' support for granted.

meaning: 'give more' or 'give more (time/space/etc.)' — used to say someone should allow or provide additional amount of something (often time).
additional_notes: Commonly used with an object and often with 'tempo' (time): 'dare più tempo' = 'give more time / allow more time'. Conjugate 'dare' for the subject (devo/puoi/ci devono ...) and place indirect object pronouns before the verb (mi, gli, le). In English you might say 'give him more time' or 'you should give her more time.'
target_language_example: Gli devi dare più tempo per finire il lavoro.
native_language_example: You must give him more time to finish the work.

meaning: to listen to someone / to pay attention to someone's advice or warnings
additional_notes: Used when following (or not following) someone's advice or paying attention to what they say. Often appears in negative form (non gli do retta) meaning 'I don't heed him.' Informal, conversational. Commonly used with indirect object pronouns: dare retta a qualcuno = to listen to someone.
target_language_example: Non gli do retta quando parla di affari.
native_language_example: I don't listen to him when he talks about business.

meaning: to get on someone's nerves; to annoy or irritate someone
additional_notes: Idiomatic expression used when a person, sound, behavior, or situation is irritating. Commonly used in the form "mi dà sui nervi" (it annoys me) or "mi danno sui nervi" (they annoy me). Conjugate verb dare as needed and keep the prepositional phrase "sui nervi". Often used in informal spoken Italian.
target_language_example: Quel vicino con la musica alta sa solo dare sui nervi a tutti.
native_language_example: That neighbor with the loud music only knows how to get on everyone's nerves.

meaning: to give respite; to relent or stop (for a while)
additional_notes: Used when something (often pain, bad weather, a problem, or a person) "gives a break" or eases up. Commonly appears in negative contexts: "non dà tregua" = it doesn't stop/let up. Tregua literally means "truce" or "ceasefire".
target_language_example: La pioggia non sembra voler dare tregua oggi.
native_language_example: The rain doesn't seem willing to let up today.

meaning: to give a (single) blow/hit; to strike once. Can also be used figuratively for attempting something quickly or making a quick attempt (colloquial).
additional_notes: Literal meaning: 'to give a blow'. Common with physical objects or people (dare un colpo a qualcuno/qualcosa). Figuratively: e.g., dare un colpo di telefono (to give someone a call) or dare un colpo di prova (to try briefly). Context and object determine whether the use is physical or idiomatic. Often followed by a direct object or prepositional phrase (a qualcuno, a qualcosa, di prova).
target_language_example: Gli ha detto di dare un colpo alla porta prima di entrare: "Non dimenticare di dare un colpo, così sapranno che sei lì."
native_language_example: He told him to give a knock on the door before entering: "Don't forget to give a knock so they'll know you're there."

meaning: to give someone a ride (in a vehicle).
additional_notes: Common Italian phrase used when offering or saying you gave someone a lift/ride. Often followed by a person (mi, lui, a Marco). Can be used in past (gli ho dato un passaggio) or future (ti do un passaggio). Informal to neutral register; widely used in spoken Italian.
target_language_example: Posso dare un passaggio a Marco fino alla stazione.
native_language_example: Can I give Marco a ride to the station?

meaning: to take a quick look; to glance or have a quick look at something.
additional_notes: Common everyday phrase used when you want someone to quickly check or look at something. Often used with indirect object or preposition: dare un'occhiata a qualcosa / dare un'occhiata a qualcuno (to take a look at something/someone). Can be used politely: "Posso dare un'occhiata?" (Can I take a look?).
target_language_example: Dammi un secondo, voglio dare un'occhiata al calendario.
native_language_example: Give me a second, I want to take a quick look at the calendar.

meaning: to give someone a lesson; literal: to teach or instruct someone; figurative: to reprimand, put someone in their place, or teach them a harsh lesson.
additional_notes: Can be used literally (teaching a class or explaining something) or figuratively (punishing or humiliating someone to correct their behavior). Tone and context determine whether it's neutral or negative. Often used with indirect object pronouns (ti, gli, le) or a person: dare una lezione a qualcuno.
target_language_example: Se continui a comportarti così, ti darò una lezione e vedrai di non rifarlo più.
native_language_example: If you keep behaving like that, I will give you a lesson and you'll see not to do it again (i.e. I'll reprimand you).

meaning: to give someone a hand; to help (someone).
additional_notes: A common idiom meaning to help or assist. Used in everyday speech for both casual and slightly more formal situations. Can be followed by a person (dare una mano a qualcuno) or by a task (dare una mano con qualcosa).
target_language_example: Dopo mi dovrai dare una mano.
native_language_example: Afterwards you'll have to give me a hand.

meaning: to give away (something), to give for free or dispose of; sometimes to sell cheaply
additional_notes: Commonly used when you give something you no longer want to someone else (give away) or when an item is being let go cheaply (e.g., "l'ho dato via" = I gave it away). Often followed by the item and, if relevant, the recipient (a qualcuno) or a preposition (a qualcuno / per pochi soldi). Not to be confused with "dare via" meaning to start sending something — that usage is rare.
target_language_example: Ho deciso di dare via i vecchi vestiti a un'associazione.
native_language_example: I decided to give away my old clothes to a charity.

meaning: to give life to; to create or bring something into existence
additional_notes: Commonly used both literally (to give life/birth) and figuratively (to create, start, or animate an idea, project, story, character). Often appears with nouns like 'un'idea', 'un progetto', 'una storia' or 'vita' in contexts about creation. Verb 'dare' + noun; context determines literal vs. figurative meaning.
target_language_example: Gli autori hanno deciso di dare vita a un nuovo personaggio nel prossimo capitolo.
native_language_example: The authors decided to give life to a new character in the next chapter.

meaning: to give me the (…)
additional_notes: Combines the verb dare (to give) + indirect object pronoun mi (to me) + the definite article il. Used when asking someone to hand or give something to the speaker (e.g., darmi il telefono = give me the phone). In sentences the object follows il (the noun): darmi il libro, darmi il permesso. Can be used both as a request and to describe someone giving something.
target_language_example: Puoi darmi il libro, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you give me the book, please?

meaning: to make an effort; to busy oneself; to work hard to get something done.
additional_notes: Common reflexive expression used to indicate someone is putting in effort, being active, or taking initiative. Often followed by an infinitive (darsi da fare per trovare un lavoro) or used in past forms (Mi sono dato da fare). Suitable for everyday conversation and neutral/formal contexts depending on tone.
target_language_example: Devi darti da fare se vuoi finire il progetto in tempo.
native_language_example: You need to make an effort if you want to finish the project on time.

meaning: to be bothered/annoyed (by someone or something); to annoy one another
additional_notes: Used reflexively to indicate that something or someone causes annoyance to someone (e.g., "Mi dà fastidio...") or that people irritate each other (e.g., "Ci diamo fastidio"). Common constructions: "darsi fastidio di + infinitive" (rare), "Mi dà fastidio + [noun/che clause]", and reciprocal uses: "Ci diamo fastidio". Register: neutral/informal depending on context.
target_language_example: Ci diamo fastidio quando discutiamo a voce alta.
native_language_example: We annoy each other when we argue loudly.

meaning: to calm down; to take it easy (used to tell someone to relax or quiet down).
additional_notes: Informal reflexive phrase commonly used in spoken Italian to tell someone (or oneself) to relax, stop being upset/angry, or behave more calmly. Often used in the imperative (e.g., "Datti una calmata", "Datevi una calmata") or in infinitive/reflexive form. Can be followed by a brief reason or stand alone.
target_language_example: Darsi una calmata prima di prendere decisioni importanti è sempre una buona idea.
native_language_example: Calming down before making important decisions is always a good idea.

meaning: to hurry up; to get a move on.
additional_notes: Informal idiom used to tell someone (or yourself) to be quicker or to start doing something. Often used in the imperative: «Datti una mossa!» or reflexively: «Devo darmi una mossa.» Tone can be encouraging or slightly impatient.
target_language_example: Devo darmi una mossa se voglio arrivare in tempo.
native_language_example: I have to hurry up if I want to arrive on time.

meaning: 'to get oneself under control' / 'to calm down' / 'to behave' (tells someone to settle down or moderate their behavior)
additional_notes: Informal expression used to tell someone (or oneself) to control emotions, tone, or actions — e.g. stop exaggerating, calm down, be more sensible. Often used in imperative: "datti una regolata" (to one person) or "datevi una regolata" (to a group). Not literal; 'regolata' here means 'adjustment' but the phrase means self-control or moderation.
target_language_example: Se non ti dai una regolata, finirai per rovinare tutto.
native_language_example: If you don't get yourself under control, you'll end up ruining everything.

meaning: 'I will give a (masculine singular) ...' or part of 'I will give you a ...' expressed in future tense.
additional_notes: Darò is the first-person singular future of dare (to give). 'Un' is the indefinite article for masculine singular nouns. Together they begin a statement meaning 'I will give a ...'. In conversational contexts it can also be used idiomatically in threats or promises (e.g., 'ti darò un bel calcio' — 'I'll give you a good kick'). Remember to add an object after 'un' (e.g., 'darò un regalo', 'darò un lavoro'). When addressing someone directly, the indirect object pronoun (ti, gli, le, ci, etc.) often appears before the verb: 'ti darò un libro' = 'I'll give you a book.'
target_language_example: Ti darò un libro domani.
native_language_example: I'll give you a book tomorrow.

meaning: 'I will give a' (feminine singular direct object) — future tense first person singular of dare + indefinite article una.
additional_notes: Used to promise or offer to give something (a feminine noun) in the future. 'Darò' = I will give. 'Una' agrees with a feminine singular noun (una lezione, una bicicletta, una pista, una copia). Can introduce both literal gifts and figurative things (a hint, a lesson). Often followed by the noun being given; the noun may be omitted when context makes it clear.
target_language_example: Domani darò una sorpresa a Maria.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I will give Maria a surprise.

meaning: date of birth
additional_notes: Used to ask or give someone's birth date (day/month/year). Common on forms and ID documents. Formal/neutral phrase.
target_language_example: Per favore, scriva la sua data di nascita sul modulo.
native_language_example: Please write your date of birth on the form.

meaning: 'give (plural imperative) the' — the imperative form of dare (to give) for voi + feminine singular direct object/article 'la'.
additional_notes: Used when speaking to a group (voi) telling them to give something. 'Date' is the imperative (or present indicative) for voi, but in commands it means 'give'. 'La' is the feminine singular direct object article or pronoun (the/it/her). Context determines whether 'la' is an article before a noun (date la chiave = give the key) or a pronoun replacing a feminine noun (ci siamo date la mano = we gave each other the hand — here 'date' is past participle feminine plural, not imperative; note: watch forms: 'ci siamo date la mano' uses 'date' as feminine plural past participle of dare). In imperative examples (commands) use 'Date la ... a [someone]' = Give the ... to [someone].
target_language_example: Date la torta a Maria, per favore.
native_language_example: Give the cake to Maria, please.

meaning: Give me the (plural or specific) ... (imperative, polite/neutral plural form).
additional_notes: Datemi is the imperative form of dare (to give) for voi (you plural) directed to one or more people: 'give me'. Followed by i plus a plural noun or a specific masculine plural noun phrase (i miei occhiali, i punti, i telefoni, i vostri soldi). Use 'datemi' when asking multiple people to hand something over; for one person use 'dammi'. Can be strong or urgent depending on tone.
target_language_example: Datemi i documenti, per favore.
native_language_example: Give me the documents, please.

meaning: 'given to' or part of idiomatic phrases like 'ha dato alla luce' (gave birth to) or 'ha dato alla testa' (went to one's head).
additional_notes: Dato is the past participle of dare (to give). 'Dato alla' often appears as part of fixed expressions: - 'ha dato alla luce' = 'gave birth to' (literally 'gave to the light') - 'ha dato alla testa' = 'went to her head' / 'got to her head' (popularity/success). Context determines meaning; you usually need the following noun (e.g. 'una figlia', 'la testa').
target_language_example: Ieri ha dato alla luce un bambino.
native_language_example: Yesterday she gave birth to a baby.

meaning: 'given the' or 'gave the' (past participle + definite article 'i') — part of a verb phrase meaning 'gave the' or 'have given the'.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom but the combination of the past participle 'dato' (given/gave) with the plural masculine definite article 'i' (the). It appears in sentences like 'Mi hanno dato i loro indirizzi' (They gave me their addresses) or 'Vi ho già dato i documenti' (I have already given you the documents). Context (subject and tense) determines whether 'dato' is simple past/preterite meaning 'gave' (e.g. 'Gli ho dato i soldi' = 'I gave him the money' using passato prossimo) or functions as 'given' in other constructions.
target_language_example: Le ho dato i biglietti per il concerto.
native_language_example: I gave her the tickets for the concert.

meaning: gave the
additional_notes: Not a fixed expression: this is dato, the past participle of dare ('to give'), followed by il ('the'). In context it often means 'gave the' or forms part of a passive such as 'was given the'. With some nouns, dare is translated less literally, for example dare il buongiorno = 'say good morning'.
target_language_example: Il professore ci ha dato il compito ieri.
native_language_example: The teacher gave us the homework yesterday.

meaning: given my / gave my (thing); used when referring to something belonging to the speaker that was given
additional_notes: A short sequence combining the past participle 'dato' (given) with a possessive 'il mio' (my + masculine noun implied). The exact English translation depends on the noun implied (indirizzo, nome, messaggio, paese, etc.). In questions with indirect object pronouns (gli, le, ti, vi) the structure asks who was given the speaker's X: e.g. 'Perché gli avete dato il mio indirizzo?' = 'Why did you give him my address?'. Word order and verb forms change with tense/person (hai dato, ha dato, avete dato).
target_language_example: Perché gli hai dato il mio numero di telefono?
native_language_example: Why did you give him my phone number?

meaning: literally 'given his/her/its' or 'given the ... of his/her/its'; part of a phrase meaning 'gave (something) belonging to him/her/it'.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom but a sequence: 'dato' is the past participle of 'dare' (to give) used with an auxiliary (ha dato = he/she gave). 'la sua' is a feminine singular possessive ('his/her/its/their' depending on context) agreeing with a feminine noun that follows or is understood. In many examples the noun is explicit (la sua vita = his/her life, la sua chiave = his/her key). In sentence fragments like 'Ha dato la sua.' the object may be clear from context. Word order and gender must agree (e.g. 'dato il suo' for masculine).
target_language_example: Ha dato la sua testimonianza al giudice.
native_language_example: He/She gave his/her testimony to the judge.

meaning: the phrase 'dato le' is part of the compound verb 'dare le dimissioni' meaning 'to resign' (literally 'to give the resignations').
additional_notes: You won't use 'dato le' alone. It's the past participle 'dato' (given) plus the definite article 'le' introducing a feminine plural noun, most commonly 'dimissioni' (resignation). Common full expression: 'ha dato le dimissioni' = 'he/she resigned'. Use appropriate past tense and agreement: e.g. 'ha dato le dimissioni', 'hanno dato le dimissioni'.
target_language_example: Maria ha dato le dimissioni dopo la riunione.
native_language_example: Maria resigned after the meeting.

meaning: given something; (someone) gave (someone) something.
additional_notes: Literal past participle 'dato' (given) + 'qualcosa' (something). Common in passive or active constructions: 'mi ha dato qualcosa' = 'he/she gave me something'; 'gli fu dato qualcosa' = 'something was given to him' (formal/older style). Use with indirect objects to show who received it (mi, gli, le).
target_language_example: Mi ha dato qualcosa da leggere.
native_language_example: He/she gave me something to read.

meaning: given that; literally 'given that/that ...' or 'having given that/that ...' depending on context.
additional_notes: This phrase combines the past participle 'dato' (given, or gave when used as part of a compound) with the demonstrative 'quel' (that). It can appear in two common uses: 1) as part of a passive/active construction meaning 'gave that (thing)': e.g. 'Gli ha dato quel libro?' = 'Did he/she give him that book?'; here 'dato' is the past participle of 'dare' used in a compound tense. 2) as a short clause meaning 'given that' (dando per scontato), but this meaning usually appears as 'dato che' rather than 'dato quel'. For beginners, focus on recognizing 'dato' as 'given/gave' and 'quel' as 'that' and that together they often occur when saying someone 'gave that (object)'.
target_language_example: Mi ha dato quel regalo ieri.
native_language_example: He/She gave me that gift yesterday.

meaning: 'given all the' or 'having given all the' (past participle + 'all the')
additional_notes: This phrase combines the past participle 'dato' (given) with 'tutti i' (all the). It's used when saying someone gave all of something (e.g., all the money, all the CDs). The noun that follows 'tutti i' must be plural and masculine (e.g., soldi, dischi). Word order: 'dare' in past (ha/ho dato) + 'tutti i' + plural noun. Examples in the input use indirect objects (gli, mi) or direct objects depending on context.
target_language_example: Mi ha dato tutti i suoi libri.
native_language_example: He/She gave me all his/her books.

meaning: having given all the (something) / gave all the (something)
additional_notes: This phrase is a combination of the past participle 'dato' (given) + 'tutto il' (all the). It appears in sentences where someone has given all of a specific masculine singular noun (e.g., 'tutto il suo denaro' = all his money). Word order and agreement: 'tutto il' is used before a masculine singular noun; for feminine nouns use 'tutta la' (tutta la sua roba). The pronouns (gli, le, lui, lei) indicate the indirect or direct object depending on context.
target_language_example: Gli ho dato tutto il mio tempo.
native_language_example: I gave him all my time.

meaning: given a
additional_notes: Combination of the past participle 'dato' (given/gave) + the indefinite article 'un' (a). Used in past contexts to say someone gave or provided something: 'gave a...' or 'given a...'. Translate as 'gave a' when describing a past action (e.g. 'they gave a gift'), or 'given a' when used adjectivally. Remember agreement and tense come from the verb (e.g. 'ho dato', 'hai dato', 'hanno dato').
target_language_example: Gli ho dato un consiglio.
native_language_example: I gave him a piece of advice.

meaning: given a gift / gave a gift
additional_notes: Past participle construction using dare (to give). 'Dato un regalo' often appears in sentences like 'ha dato un regalo' (he/she gave a gift) or 'mi ha dato un regalo' (he/she gave me a gift). Use with appropriate subject and auxiliary verb (avere) for passato prossimo: [subject] ha/hanno/davamo + dato un regalo. Can include indirect object (a lui, mi, ti) to show who received the gift.
target_language_example: Le ho dato un regalo per il suo compleanno.
native_language_example: I gave her a gift for her birthday.

meaning: given a lot (of) / gave a lot (of)
additional_notes: Informal expression used with 'dare' to mean giving or receiving a large quantity of something (money, food, blows, etc.). Usually followed by 'di' + noun (e.g., 'dato un sacco di soldi'). Can also appear in past forms (ha dato un sacco). Equivalent to English 'gave a lot' or 'gave loads'.
target_language_example: Gli ho dato un sacco di vestiti che non uso più.
native_language_example: I gave him a lot of clothes I no longer use.

meaning: given one / gave one (feminine singular object)
additional_notes: Literal combination of the past participle 'dato' (given) and the feminine indefinite article 'una'. Used when referring to giving someone a feminine singular thing (una camera, una di queste). Often part of a larger clause (mi ha dato una, ci hanno dato una). Word order and auxiliary depend on tense/person: e.g. 'mi ha dato una' = 'he/she gave me one'.
target_language_example: Mi ha dato una camera senza balcone.
native_language_example: He/She gave me a room without a balcony.

meaning: given one of (something) / considering one of (something)
additional_notes: This phrase appears to be a clipped or colloquial combination of 'dato' (given) + 'una di' (one of). In Italian standard usage you would more often see 'dato che' (given that), 'dato uno di...' or 'dato una di quelle...' depending on context. 'Dato una di' could introduce a condition or point referring to a single item or example among many: 'given one of (these)...'. It is not a fixed set phrase in standard Italian and likely context-specific; you may need to adjust word order or add nouns (e.g. 'data una di queste situazioni' or 'dato uno di loro').
target_language_example: Dato una di queste opzioni, sceglierei la più semplice.
native_language_example: Given one of these options, I would choose the simplest.

meaning: given a
additional_notes: Usually used in formal or explanatory language to introduce something assumed or taken as the starting point. Here uno is normally the indefinite article "a/an" before certain masculine nouns (for example, uno studente, uno spazio), not the number "one".
target_language_example: Dato uno spazio limitato, abbiamo invitato poche persone.
native_language_example: Given a limited space, we invited only a few people.

meaning: 'in front of' or 'before' (spatially or figuratively).
additional_notes: Used to indicate physical location in front of something (davanti alla casa) or figurative situations like being before/face-to-face with something (davanti a un giudice = facing a judge). Followed by a noun with the appropriate preposition contraction (davanti al, davanti allo, davanti alla, davanti ai, ecc.).
target_language_example: Siamo rimasti a parlare davanti a un bar.
native_language_example: We stayed talking in front of a café.

meaning: to really/be truly (do something); 'davvero' = really, 'essere' = to be — used to emphasize the verb that follows.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom but the adverb 'davvero' placed before a verb (here 'essere') to add emphasis. In examples it stresses sincerity or degree (e.g., 'really be dangerous' or 'really want to be'). Word order can vary: 'essere davvero' is also possible depending on nuance. Use 'davvero' before adjectives, verbs, or entire clauses to mean 'really' or 'truly'.
target_language_example: Vuoi davvero essere parte del progetto?
native_language_example: Do you really want to be part of the project?

meaning: really happy to / really glad to
additional_notes: Used to emphasize being happy about something (meeting someone, seeing someone, being in a situation). 'Davvero' strengthens 'felice'; followed by 'di' + infinitive or 'di' + a verb phrase (e.g., 'di conoscerti', 'di vederti', 'di essere qui'). Equivalent to 'very' or 'truly' in English emphasis.
target_language_example: Sono davvero felice di conoscere la tua famiglia.
native_language_example: I'm really happy to meet your family.

meaning: "my" with emphasis (really my / truly my).
additional_notes: Davvero means "really/truly" and is used to emphasize the possession expressed by "il mio" (my + masculine singular noun implied). In natural speech you might hear "davvero il mio" before or after the noun it refers to (e.g., "davvero il mio lavoro" or "il mio lavoro davvero"). Use the appropriate possessive form (la mia, i miei, le mie) to match the noun's gender and number.
target_language_example: Mi manca davvero il mio cane.
native_language_example: I really miss my dog.

meaning: really your / I really (like/appreciate) your ...
additional_notes: Used to emphasize sincere appreciation for something that belongs to or is produced by the listener (companionship, music, help, visit, personality, etc.). Typically appears in phrases like "Mi piace davvero la tua ..." or "Apprezzo davvero la tua ...". Word order: adverb "davvero" (really) comes before the possessive phrase "la tua" (your + feminine noun).
target_language_example: Mi piace davvero la tua risata.
native_language_example: I really like your laugh.

meaning: really a / truly a (used to emphasize a noun phrase).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize or express surprise about someone's role, quality or possession. 'Davvero' adds intensity ('really'/'truly'); 'un' begins the following noun phrase. Can be used with professions, characteristics, or possessions (e.g. 'davvero un bravo studente', 'davvero un bel sorriso'). In questions it conveys surprise or doubt ('Lei è davvero un giornalista?').
target_language_example: È davvero un amico leale.
native_language_example: He is really a loyal friend.

meaning: to really live / to truly live — used to ask or emphasize whether someone genuinely wants to live (in a place, in a certain way, or forever).
additional_notes: Combines 'davvero' (really/truly) + the infinitive 'vivere' (to live). Often appears in questions or emphatic statements: word order can be 'Davvero vuoi vivere...?' or 'Vuoi davvero vivere...?'. Common complements: locations (e.g., 'a Boston') or durations/conditions (e.g., 'per sempre'). Tone can be neutral or incredulous depending on context.
target_language_example: Volete davvero vivere per sempre?
native_language_example: Do you really want to live forever?

meaning: to have a soft spot for; to be fond of someone/something.
additional_notes: Used after 'avere' (e.g., 'ha un debole per...') to say you really like or are easily charmed by someone or something. Can refer to people, foods, activities, etc. Tone is informal to neutral and expresses affection or a weakness/tendency rather than strong love.
target_language_example: Ho un debole per il caffè del mattino.
native_language_example: I have a soft spot for morning coffee.

meaning: to decide to study (something).
additional_notes: Commonly used to talk about choosing to study a subject, language, or topic. Followed by a noun (with or without definite article: studiare francese / studiare il francese). 'Decidere' is conjugated according to the subject (decido, decidi, decide, decidiamo, decidete, decidono). Often appears in questions about motivation (e.g., Che cosa vi ha fatto decidere di studiare?).
target_language_example: Che cosa vi ha fatto decidere di studiare francese?
native_language_example: What made you decide to study French?

meaning: a decision like that / such a decision (usually emphasizing degree: important, sudden, etc.)
additional_notes: Used to comment on the quality or intensity of a decision already described (e.g. important, sudden, risky). Often follows an adjective (decisione così importante, così improvvisa). Can appear after verbs like prendere (to make/take) or esserci (to be) and is used to stress caution or surprise.
target_language_example: Non prendere una decisione così senza parlarne prima.
native_language_example: Don't make a decision like that without talking about it first.

meaning: a decision to (do something) / someone's decision
additional_notes: Used to express that a choice was made. Often followed by an infinitive verb (decisione di + verb) to mean 'a decision to [do something]'. Can also be used with a noun or possessive to indicate whose decision it was (una decisione di tua madre = a decision of your mother). Common in both formal and everyday contexts.
target_language_example: Ho preso la decisione di trasferirmi all'estero.
native_language_example: I made the decision to move abroad.

meaning: decided to become (someone/a profession).
additional_notes: Used to say someone made a decision to take on a role, job, or identity (often followed by a noun for a profession or role). Form: past participle 'deciso' + preposition 'di' + infinitive 'diventare'. Common in spoken and written Italian to describe a choice about the future.
target_language_example: Ho deciso di diventare un insegnante.
native_language_example: I decided to become a teacher.

meaning: dedicated to her/it (feminine singular).
additional_notes: Formed from the past participle 'dedicato' (dedicated) plus the feminine singular direct object pronoun/article 'la'. In Italian this sequence can appear when saying something is dedicated to a feminine noun (e.g., 'dedicato la canzone') or less commonly when 'la' is a clitic referring to 'her'/'it'. More natural phrasing usually places the article or pronoun differently (e.g., 'dedicato a lei' or 'dedicata a lei' depending on gender/agreement). Watch agreement: when the subject or the thing dedicated is feminine, use 'dedicata'.
target_language_example: Ho dedicato la canzone a mia sorella.
native_language_example: I dedicated the song to my sister.

meaning: I dedicate this (often followed by what is being dedicated).
additional_notes: Commonly used when dedicating a song, speech, message, or item to a person or group. 'Dedico' is the first-person singular present of 'dedicare' (to dedicate). The word order can vary: you can also say 'questa canzone la dedico a...' or omit 'questa' if context makes the object clear. Formal and neutral; suitable in speeches, dedications, or casual statements.
target_language_example: Dedico questa canzone a mia madre.
native_language_example: I dedicate this song to my mother.

meaning: of the Men / of Men (the people).
additional_notes: A possessive/genitive phrase: 'degli' = 'di' + 'gli' (of the). 'Uomini' is the plural of 'uomo' (man). Used to indicate something belonging to or related to men/people. In some contexts (literary/fantasy) 'Uomini' with capital U can mean humankind or a specific group (e.g. 'the Men'). English translation depends on context: 'of the men', 'of men', or 'of humankind'.
target_language_example: La voce degli Uomini rimbalzò nella valle.
native_language_example: The voice of the Men echoed in the valley.

meaning: one of the most / one of the [adjective]+est (used to form superlative groups)
additional_notes: Used after "uno/una" (uno dei più, una delle più) to say something is among the most of a group (e.g. one of the oldest, one of the biggest). It combines with an adjective (vecchi, grandi, profondi, alti) and often appears as "uno dei più + adjective". Literal components: "dei" = of the, "più" = more/most.
target_language_example: È uno dei più interessanti libri che abbia letto.
native_language_example: It's one of the most interesting books I've read.

meaning: of his/her/their restaurants; some of his/her/their restaurants
additional_notes: A possessive phrase: 'dei' is the plural partitive/article (di + i) and here can mean 'of the' or 'some'. 'Suo/suoi' agrees with the noun in number/gender and can mean his, her, its, or their depending on context. Use 'dei suoi ristoranti' to refer to restaurants that belong to or are run by someone (plural: restaurants).
target_language_example: Ho provato dei suoi ristoranti e mi sono piaciuti molto.
native_language_example: I tried some of his/her restaurants and I liked them a lot.

meaning: some advice to / give (someone) some advice
additional_notes: Dei consigli is the plural partitive 'some advice' (consiglio = advice/suggestion). When followed by a person use 'a' or the contracted 'al' (a + il) before a masculine singular noun: 'dei consigli a Marco' or 'dei consigli al mio collega'. More commonly you will see the verb form 'dare dei consigli a/ al' (to give someone some advice).
target_language_example: Vorrei dare dei consigli al nuovo studente.
native_language_example: I would like to give some advice to the new student.

meaning: some pancakes for (e.g. a meal or person).
additional_notes: Dei = plural indefinite article ('some') used with plural nouns. 'Pancake' is an English loanword commonly used in Italian (plural often stays 'pancake' or 'pancakes'); context determines whether speaker treats it as invariable. 'Per' means 'for' and introduces purpose, meal, or recipient (e.g. 'per colazione' = 'for breakfast'). Together 'dei pancake per colazione' = 'some pancakes for breakfast.'
target_language_example: Ho fatto dei pancake per la colazione di domani.
native_language_example: I made some pancakes for tomorrow's breakfast.

meaning: of the Quran / of the Koran (possessive phrase referring to the Islamic holy book)
additional_notes: Del is the contraction of di + il and means "of the". Used to show possession or that something is a copy, a part, or related to the Quran (il Corano). Common in phrases like "una copia del Corano" (a copy of the Quran).
target_language_example: Ho letto alcuni passaggi del Corano.
native_language_example: I read some passages of the Quran.

meaning: of the world; worldly; relating to the world (often used in superlatives or names).
additional_notes: Literal combination of preposition + noun: 'del' = 'di' + 'il' (of the) and 'Mondo' = 'world'. Commonly appears in phrases like 'il migliore del mondo' (the best in the world), 'cup del mondo' contexts (though English loan 'mondiale' is used too), or names/titles (e.g., 'Gioco del Mondo'). Capitalization: 'mondo' is usually lowercase except in titles where 'Mondo' may be capitalized.
target_language_example: È considerato il migliore del mondo nel suo sport.
native_language_example: He is considered the best in the world in his sport.

meaning: of the Lord / belonging to the Lord (religious or formal reference)
additional_notes: A contraction of di + il Signore. Common in religious contexts (e.g., references to God or Jesus) or in formal phrases like 'la volontà del Signore' (the will of the Lord). Capitalized 'Signore' usually refers to God; lowercase 'signore' would mean 'the gentleman' or 'Mr.'.
target_language_example: La misericordia del Signore dura per sempre.
native_language_example: The mercy of the Lord endures forever.

meaning: 'of the Sun' or 'of/from the Sun'; can be part of names/titles (e.g. newspaper, place) or literal 'belonging to the sun'.
additional_notes: Del is the contraction of di + il (of the). Sole means 'sun'. Together 'del Sole' appears in proper names (Il Sole 24 Ore — an Italian newspaper), place names, poetic expressions, or literal phrases like 'la luce del sole' (sunlight). Use according to context: sometimes part of a title and not translated. Pronunciation: /del ˈso.le/.
target_language_example: La luce del sole entra dalla finestra.
native_language_example: Sunlight comes in through the window.

meaning: of/from Vecchio (a surname or place name); 'del' = 'di' + 'il' (of the).
additional_notes: Used as a part of names or phrases to indicate belonging or origin. Commonly appears in family names (e.g., Mario del Vecchio) or to mean 'of the old man' if used descriptively—Vecchio can be a surname or an adjective meaning 'old'. 'Del' is the contraction of 'di' + 'il'. Capitalization: when part of a surname it is often written 'del Vecchio' (lowercase d) or 'Del Vecchio' depending on convention.
target_language_example: Il signor Del Vecchio è il nuovo professore.
native_language_example: Mr. Del Vecchio is the new teacher.

meaning: of the wind / from the wind (literally)
additional_notes: Del Vento is the contraction of 'di' + 'il Vento' and literally means 'of the wind' or 'from the wind'. You will see it in names, titles, place names, or poetic expressions (e.g., 'la luce del vento', 'la casa del Vento'). Capitalization: 'Vento' is normally lowercase ('del vento') unless part of a proper name or title. Use when showing possession or origin related to 'vento' (wind).
target_language_example: La canzone del vento è molto bella.
native_language_example: The song of the wind is very beautiful.

meaning: partitive + 'coffee' used in choices: 'some coffee or some...'; often appears in the pattern 'del X o del Y' meaning 'coffee or tea' (would you like coffee or tea?).
additional_notes: This chunk is part of the expression 'del X o del Y' where 'del' is the contraction of 'di + il' used as a partitive article meaning 'some' (or to offer/ask about a drink). In questions or offers (Volete del caffè o del tè?) it functions like English 'Would you like some coffee or some tea?' Often only one 'del' is used in casual speech (Volete del caffè o tè?), but repeating 'del' is common and sounds natural.
target_language_example: Vuoi del caffè o del tè?
native_language_example: Do you want some coffee or some tea?

meaning: 'of (the) football' / 'of soccer' (used to indicate relation to the sport football/soccer)
additional_notes: Del is the contraction of di + il (of the). 'Calcio' in Italian normally means the sport known as football (soccer in American English). 'Del calcio' appears in phrases like 'regole del calcio' (rules of football) or 'fan del calcio' (football fan). Use 'del' before masculine singular nouns when expressing possession, origin, type, or relation.
target_language_example: Sono un tifoso del calcio italiano.
native_language_example: I am a fan of Italian football.

meaning: 'of the case' / 'about the case' (refers to a specific legal or described case)
additional_notes: Commonly used to refer to a particular case (legal, investigative, or a described situation) previously mentioned or understood from context. Often appears after a noun (e.g., 'il caso') as 'del caso' to mean 'of the case' or 'regarding the case'.
target_language_example: Ho letto tutti i documenti del caso.
native_language_example: I read all the documents of/about the case.

meaning: 'of the horse' or part of a fixed phrase meaning 'the (move/scene) of the horse' depending on context.
additional_notes: Literally 'of the horse' (di + il = del). Used literally to indicate possession or relation (e.g., something belonging to or about a horse). In your examples it's used idiomatically: 'scena del cavallo' = 'the horse scene' (e.g. a scene involving a horse, here 'the scene of the dead horse'), and 'mossa del cavallo' = 'the knight's move' / 'horse move' in chess (the piece called 'cavallo' in some informal speech). Keep in mind context decides the exact translation; translate whole phrase, not word-by-word.
target_language_example: Abbiamo girato la scena del cavallo ieri.
native_language_example: We filmed the horse scene yesterday.

meaning: a vulgar intensifier meaning 'f---ing' or 'damn' used to express annoyance, contempt, or emphasis
additional_notes: Very informal and vulgar. Often attached to nouns or exclamations to insult, belittle, or add strong emphasis (e.g., 'traffico del cazzo' = 'f---ing traffic'). Tone is rude; avoid in polite/company or formal situations. Can be used alone as an expletive ('Cazzo!') or combined with other words ('quel tipo del cazzo').
target_language_example: Quella macchina del cazzo non parte mai.
native_language_example: That f---ing car never starts.

meaning: a phrase meaning 'some chili with some' (used to talk about mixing a bit of chili with something else); literally 'some chilli with some'.
additional_notes: This is a colloquial, partly redundant construction combining partitive articles (del...della) with nouns. It appears in questions about mixing 'chilli' with another ingredient (here, 'senape' = mustard). In normal speech you could also say 'del chilli e della senape' (chili and mustard) or use partitives separately: 'un po' di chilli e un po' di senape'. 'Chilli' is a loanword; pronunciation like English 'chili'.
target_language_example: Hai mai mescolato del chilli con della marmellata?
native_language_example: Have you ever mixed some chili with some jam?

meaning: of the heart; heartfelt / relating to the heart (literal or figurative).
additional_notes: Can be literal (anatomical: 'of the heart', e.g. 'chirurgo del cuore') or figurative (emotional: 'heartfelt' or 'close', e.g. 'amici del cuore' = very close friends; 'dal profondo del cuore' = from the bottom of one's heart). Context determines which meaning applies. Commonly appears in expressions like 'amico del cuore' (close friend) or 'dal più profondo del cuore' (from the deepest part of the heart).
target_language_example: Siamo amici del cuore.
native_language_example: We are close friends (literally: friends of the heart).

meaning: of/from French; about the French language
additional_notes: A contraction of di + il + francese. Commonly used to indicate possession, knowledge, topic or origin related to the French language (e.g. knowledge of French, a book about French). Context determines exact English translation: 'of French', 'about French', or 'from French'.
target_language_example: Ha una buona conoscenza del francese.
native_language_example: He has a good knowledge of French.

meaning: like that
additional_notes: Used to refer to something of a certain type or manner mentioned or implied. Common in expressions like "una cosa del genere" (something like that) or "cose del genere" (things like that). Can be used to show surprise, disapproval, or to generalize.
target_language_example: Non mi aspettavo una reazione del genere.
native_language_example: I didn't expect a reaction like that.

meaning: 'of the big' or 'of the great' (combination of preposition + adjective in Italian).
additional_notes: Del is the contraction of di + il ('of the'). Grande can mean 'big/large' or 'great' (famous/important) depending on context. Together 'del grande' appears before a noun to indicate possession or relation ('of the big...') or to describe someone notable ('of the great...'). Make sure gender/number and article match the noun (del = di + il, singular masculine). For feminine or plural nouns you'd use 'della', 'dei', 'delle', 'degli' as appropriate.
target_language_example: La stanza del grande castello era fredda.
native_language_example: The room of the big/large castle was cold.

meaning: some milk in his/her/one's (own) — used to say someone put milk into their coffee (or another drink).
additional_notes: Del = partitive 'some' (di + il). 'Nel' = in + the. 'Suo' agrees with the possessor (his/her/one's) and refers back to the subject; context determines gender of possessor in English (his/her/one's). Common in sentences like 'Ha messo del latte nel suo caffè' = 'He/She put some milk in his/her coffee.'
target_language_example: Luca ha versato del latte nel suo tè.
native_language_example: Luca poured some milk into his tea.

meaning: some work to (do) / work that needs to be done
additional_notes: Used to say there is work that needs completing. Followed by an infinitive (da + verb) or an implied verb like fare/sbrigare. Common in spoken and written Italian. 'Del lavoro' = 'some work' and 'da' introduces the action required.
target_language_example: Ho del lavoro da finire prima di uscire.
native_language_example: I have some work to finish before going out.

meaning: some honey in his/her/its (e.g., his/her) — used to indicate adding honey into someone's (or something's) drink or food.
additional_notes: Del miele = 'some honey' (partitive). Nel = in + the (in the). Suo agrees with possessor (his/her/its); gender/number of the following noun determines the article after 'nel' (here 'tè' is masculine so 'nel suo tè'). Common in sentences about putting something into someone's drink or food: 'mettere del miele nel suo tè' = 'to put some honey in his/her tea.'
target_language_example: Lei mette sempre del miele nel suo tè al mattino.
native_language_example: She always puts some honey in her tea in the morning.

meaning: before I arrived / before my arrival.
additional_notes: Literal phrase composed of 'di + il' (del) + 'mio' (my) + 'arrivo' (arrival). Used to place an action or event in time relative to the speaker's arrival. Common in past-tense statements. Can be replaced with 'prima che arrivassi/arrivassi io' in some contexts (subjunctive required when followed by a clause).
target_language_example: Tutto era già finito del mio arrivo.
native_language_example: Everything was already finished before I arrived.

meaning: anyway / besides / after all / moreover (depends on context)
additional_notes: A versatile connector used to add supporting information, introduce a contrasting/confirming remark, or refer to 'the rest' (remaining things). In many contexts it means 'besides' or 'after all' (e.g. Del resto, era allegro = After all, he was cheerful). It can also mean 'as for the rest' or 'the rest' when referring to remaining items (Hai del resto? = Do you have anything else?/Do you have the rest?). Placement varies: often at the start of a sentence (Del resto, ...) or after a noun/phrase.
target_language_example: Non mi dispiace, del resto l'ho già visto.
native_language_example: I don't mind, besides I've already seen it.

meaning: some curry rice yesterday (lit. 'of/ some rice with curry yesterday').
additional_notes: This phrase combines: 'del' (partitive = 'some' or 'of the'), 'riso al curry' (rice with curry), and 'ieri' (yesterday). It's not a fixed idiom — it's simply a short sentence fragment meaning you ate or had some curry-flavored rice yesterday. To make a full sentence, add a verb: e.g. 'Ho mangiato del riso al curry ieri' = 'I ate some curry rice yesterday.' 'Ieri notte' = last night; 'ieri sera' = last evening/last night (evening).
target_language_example: Ho mangiato del riso al curry ieri sera.
native_language_example: I ate some curry rice last night.

meaning: has (some) talent; shows talent for ...
additional_notes: Used after a person (often with 'ha') to say they possess talent or ability in a certain area. Literal structure: 'ha del talento per [X]' or 'ha del talento [adjective/noun]'. The phrase 'del' here implies 'some' or 'a certain amount of' talent. Can be used neutrally or colloquially; final example shows a rude/contextual comment — be careful with tone and register.
target_language_example: Marco ha del talento per il disegno.
native_language_example: Marco has talent for drawing.

meaning: some time with her / time spent with her.
additional_notes: Used after verbs like passare (to spend) or voler (to want) to indicate spending time with a female person (lei = her). 'Del tempo' literally means 'some time' or 'time' — common phrasing: 'passare del tempo con...' For speaking about 'him' use 'con lui'; for 'with you' (formal/informal) use 'con lei/te' depending on context.
target_language_example: Vorrei passare del tempo con lei questo weekend.
native_language_example: I'd like to spend some time with her this weekend.

meaning: of the treasure / treasure's (of the treasure)
additional_notes: A prepositional phrase: 'del' = 'di' + 'il' (of the). Used to show possession or relation to a treasure (e.g. mappa del tesoro = treasure map; parte del tesoro = part of the treasure). Can appear in idiomatic contexts referring to a treasure or figurative 'treasure'.
target_language_example: Ha trovato la mappa del tesoro nella soffitta.
native_language_example: He found the treasure's map in the attic.

meaning: completely; entirely; wholly
additional_notes: Used to emphasize totality or completeness. Commonly appears in negative contexts with 'non del tutto' meaning 'not completely' or 'not entirely'. Can modify verbs, adjectives, or clauses. Formal and neutral register.
target_language_example: Non sono del tutto sicuro della risposta.
native_language_example: I'm not completely sure of the answer.

meaning: of the Snow (a surname or poetic name); literally 'of the Snow'
additional_notes: Della Neve is most likely a proper name or part of a surname (capitalized Neve). It literally combines the partitive/genitive article 'della' (di + la = 'of the'/'from the') with 'Neve' (Snow). You may see it in names (e.g., family names, historical references) or in poetic/place names. It is not a common everyday phrase and is used like any other surname or proper noun.
target_language_example: La famiglia Della Neve vive in questa villa.
native_language_example: The Della Neve family lives in this villa.

meaning: 'of the great' or 'of the big/important (feminine noun)'.
additional_notes: Della = di + la (of the). Grande means 'big', 'great', or 'important'. Together they modify a following feminine singular noun (e.g., 'della grande presentazione' = 'of the big/important presentation'). Context determines whether 'grande' is literal size or figurative (important, major). Can appear in idiomatic phrases ('la grande svolta' = 'the big turning point').
target_language_example: Aveva paura della grande decisione.
native_language_example: She was afraid of the big/important decision.

meaning: because of the illness / due to illness
additional_notes: A common phrase used to explain a reason tied to sickness. 'Della' is the contraction of 'di' + 'la' (of the). Often appears in contexts like 'per via della malattia' or 'a causa della malattia' to mean 'because of the illness'. Can refer to someone's own illness or someone else's (the illness in question).
target_language_example: Sono rimasto a casa per via della malattia.
native_language_example: I stayed home because of the illness.

meaning: of his/her life in (used to say how long someone spent living or being somewhere)
additional_notes: This phrase is a combination: "della sua vita" = "of his/her life" and the preposition "in" introduces the place or situation (e.g., in carcere, in galera, in prigione). Commonly used to say someone spent a large portion of their life in a particular place or condition. Adjust "sua" to context (mio/tuo/nostra, etc.).
target_language_example: Ha passato metà della sua vita in città.
native_language_example: He/She spent half of his/her life in the city.

meaning: of the women / some women (depending on context)
additional_notes: This is the feminine plural partitive/genitive form: 'di' + 'le' → 'delle'. It can mean 'of the women' (possession or relation) or 'some women' when used partively (e.g., 'delle donne hanno detto...' = 'some women said...'). Capitalization matters: 'delle Donne' with a capital D looks like a proper name (e.g., the title of an organization or publication); normally you would see 'delle donne'.
target_language_example: Ho parlato delle donne del quartiere.
native_language_example: I spoke with the women from the neighborhood.

meaning: some Canadian women / some Canadians (female).
additional_notes: Plural partitive + adjective + noun. "delle" is the plural partitive/article (some) used before feminine plural nouns. "canadesi" is the plural of "canadese" and here refers to female people because of context; Italian often doesn't distinguish gender in the adjective form "canadese" in plural, but agreement can be shown by article/other words. Used to ask whether someone met some (unspecified) Canadian women.
target_language_example: Hai conosciuto delle canadesi al bar ieri?
native_language_example: Did you meet some Canadian women at the bar yesterday?

meaning: some decisions / (making) decisions (indefinite plural).
additional_notes: Delle is the plural indefinite article (di + le) used before feminine plural nouns; here it makes 'decisioni' indefinite: 'some decisions' or simply 'decisions' in English. Common in phrases about being able to make decisions (prendere decisioni). You will often see it with verbs like prendere (to make/take), avere difficoltà a prendere, riuscire a prendere. Can be omitted in English or translated as 'decisions' depending on context.
target_language_example: Riesco a prendere delle decisioni da sola.
native_language_example: I can make decisions by myself.

meaning: 'some apples at/to the' (part of a phrase: 'some apples at the [market/place]').
additional_notes: This string combines: 'delle' (indefinite plural article = 'some'), 'mele' (apples), and 'al' (preposition 'a' + definite article 'il' = 'to the' or 'at the'). It is not a fixed phrase by itself but a common chunk in sentences like 'hai venduto delle mele al mercato' = 'you sold some apples at the market.' Remember: 'delle' agrees with plural feminine nouns (mele), and 'al' contracts 'a + il' used before masculine singular nouns (al mercato).
target_language_example: Ho comprato delle mele al negozio.
native_language_example: I bought some apples at the shop.

meaning: some threats of / threats of (plural)
additional_notes: Used before a type of threat (e.g. 'delle minacce di morte' = 'threats of death'). 'Delle' is the plural partitive/indefinite article meaning 'some' or simply marking plural unspecified quantity. Common in questions and statements about receiving or making threats. Word order: 'delle minacce di + [noun]' or 'delle minacce di + [verb/noun phrase]'.
target_language_example: Hai ricevuto delle minacce di morte?
native_language_example: Have you received threats of death?

meaning: some vegetables at (the)... (a partial phrase: 'delle verdure' = 'some vegetables'; 'al' = 'at the' or 'to the')
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom but a sequence of common pieces: "delle verdure" is the partitive plural meaning "some vegetables"; "al" is the contraction of "a + il" meaning "at the" or "to the". In full sentences you will usually see it followed by a place (e.g. "al mercato" = "at the market") or an article+noun. Word order: verb + (delle verdure) + (al + place).
target_language_example: Ho comprato delle verdure al mercato.
native_language_example: I bought some vegetables at the market.

meaning: 'money that' or 'the money (which/that)'.
additional_notes: Used to introduce a relative clause describing money someone has or carries. Often appears as part of phrases like "tutto il denaro che..." (all the money that...) or "il poco denaro che..." (the little money that...). Equivalent to English 'the money that' or 'money which'.
target_language_example: Mi ha dato il poco denaro che aveva.
native_language_example: He gave me the little money that he had.

meaning: baby tooth; milk tooth
additional_notes: Refers to the first set of teeth that children have before they are replaced by permanent teeth. Used in everyday speech and in medical/dental contexts. Plural: denti da latte. Can be used literally or figuratively (e.g., to describe something small or early).
target_language_example: Il bimbo ha perso il suo primo dente da latte ieri.
native_language_example: The child lost his first baby tooth yesterday.

meaning: 'teeth of a certain type/for a certain animal or stage' — used to describe a kind or origin of teeth (e.g. baby teeth, horse teeth).
additional_notes: Commonly appears in expressions like "denti da latte" (baby/deciduous teeth) or "denti da cavallo" (horse teeth). The structure is compositional: "denti" = teeth, "da" introduces the type/source. Use it to label teeth by species or developmental stage. In some contexts (e.g. museums, collections) it can refer to actual teeth kept as objects.
target_language_example: I bambini perdono i denti da latte intorno ai sei anni.
native_language_example: Children lose their baby teeth around age six.

meaning: 'dentist' with the preposition 'in' used before a time expression like 'in futuro' (e.g. 'a dentist in the future').
additional_notes: The core phrase is 'dentista' (dentist). Here 'in' is the Italian preposition meaning 'in' used to form time expressions (e.g. 'in futuro' = 'in the future'). For beginners: say 'diventare dentista' or 'diventare una dentista' (to become a dentist). Common collocations: 'andare dal dentista' (go to the dentist) — note the different preposition 'dal'.
target_language_example: Spero di diventare una dentista in futuro.
native_language_example: I hope to become a dentist in the future.

meaning: 'inside' or 'in (somewhere)' used with a following action; literally 'inside and' — often part of a clause meaning 'go/come/be inside and (do something)'.
additional_notes: This sequence combines 'dentro' (inside) with a conjunction 'e' that links to a verb or result. It's commonly used in spoken Italian to say enter/stay/be inside and then do or experience something. Depending on context, 'dentro' can describe physical location (1–2) or an internal/psychological feeling (3). The literal words translate directly into English, but the 'e' simply connects to what happens next ('and' = then/and so').
target_language_example: Vado dentro e chiudo la porta a chiave.
native_language_example: I go inside and lock the door.

meaning: 'desire is' — literal combination of the noun desiderio (desire/wish) and the verb è (is).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom by itself; it's simply the noun 'desiderio' followed by the verb 'è' (third-person singular of essere). You'll see this structure when someone defines or describes a desire: e.g. 'Il mio desiderio è...'. In most contexts you will use 'il desiderio è' or possessive forms ('il mio desiderio è') rather than 'desiderio è' alone. Remember to include the article or possessive for grammatically complete sentences.
target_language_example: Il mio desiderio è viaggiare per il mondo.
native_language_example: My desire is to travel the world.

meaning: 'said to me' or 'told me' (passive/participial phrase referring to something someone told the speaker)
additional_notes: Literally the past participle 'detto' (said) + prepositional phrase 'a me' (to me). Used to refer to words or information that another person addressed to the speaker. Common in reported-speech contexts: asking whether someone told the speaker something or instructing someone to repeat what they told the speaker. Can appear in different grammatical forms (e.g., with pronouns: 'detto a me' → 'mi ha detto').
target_language_example: Puoi ripetere quello che hai detto a me?
native_language_example: Can you repeat what you said to me?

meaning: said to everyone that he/she was ... (used to report what someone told many people about their state or situation).
additional_notes: This is a past participle construction (detto) + indirect object (a tutti) + reported clause (che era ...). Use to report that someone told many people about something concerning themselves (e.g., feelings, status, background). The verb and subject can change: e.g., "Ha detto a tutti che ero...", "Hanno detto a tutti che sarebbero...". Common in spoken and written Italian. Literal translation: "said to everyone that was" (follow with an adjective or noun phrase).
target_language_example: Luisa ha detto a tutti che era stanca dopo il viaggio.
native_language_example: Luisa told everyone that she was tired after the trip.

meaning: told everyone that they were (…)
additional_notes: A past-passive/perfect construction: 'hanno detto a tutti che erano...' means 'they told everyone that they were...' followed by an adjective or state (e.g., in pensione, interessati, nervosi). Used to report what someone told a group. In English the clause after 'that' completes the meaning. Pronoun subject (they) is often explicit in the surrounding sentence (hanno).
target_language_example: Hanno detto a tutti che erano felici.
native_language_example: They told everyone that they were happy.

meaning: said that she likes (something).
additional_notes: This phrase is a combination: detto che = 'said that' (reported speech), a lei piace = 'she/it pleases her' but here used to mean 'she likes' (indirect object pronoun + piacere construction). Common in reported speech: 'X ha detto che a lei piace ...' = 'X said that she likes ...'. English uses a subject-verb structure ('she likes'), while Italian uses piacere with an indirect object (a lei).
target_language_example: Marco ha detto che a lei piace andare in barca.
native_language_example: Marco said that she likes going boating.

meaning: said that she liked (something).
additional_notes: A reported-speech phrase: 'detto che' = 'said that'; 'a lei piaceva' = 'she liked' (imperfect tense, often used to describe general likes or past habitual preferences). Common in sentences where someone reports what a third person (female) liked. If the person is named (e.g., Mary), you can omit 'a lei' and say 'Mary ha detto che le piaceva...' or use 'le' instead of 'a lei'.
target_language_example: Luca mi ha detto che a lei piaceva il gelato.
native_language_example: Luca told me that she liked ice cream.

detto che a loro piaceva la

target_language_multi_word_term: detto che a loro piaceva la
meaning: they said that they (liked) the ...
