additional_notes: This phrase is part of reported speech. "Hanno detto che" or "Mi hanno detto che" = "They said that" / "They told me that". "a loro piaceva la..." means "they liked the..." (imperfect tense, indicating a past or habitual liking). For English, combine as "They said (to me) that they liked the [noun]." Replace the final "la" with the correct article for the noun (la for feminine singular nouns like "neve", la pizza).
target_language_example: Mi hanno detto che a loro piaceva la musica italiana.
native_language_example: They told me that they liked Italian music.

meaning: literally 'said that to him' or 'having told him that' (used to report something said to a male person).
additional_notes: This is a short sequence combining passato participle 'detto' (said) + conjunction 'che' (that/to) + indirect object 'a lui' (to him). It appears in reported-speech or explanatory contexts: e.g. 'Gli ho detto che a lui...' — 'I told him that to him...' Often in natural Italian you'd find a slightly different word order ('gli ho detto che...') or omit 'a lui' if context is clear. Use 'a lui' for emphasis or contrast (to him, not to someone else).
target_language_example: Gli ho detto che a lui non interessava, ma ha insistito.
native_language_example: I told him that he wasn't interested, but he insisted.

meaning: said that (he/she) needed
additional_notes: A reported-speech phrase: detto (said) + che (that) + aveva bisogno (he/she needed). Used to report what someone said they needed. Subject can change (mi ha detto = he/she told me). For English, 'aveva' is imperfect past (was needing / needed) but usually translated simply as 'needed'. Followed by di/di + noun or di + verb (di + infinitive).
target_language_example: Luca mi ha detto che aveva bisogno di tempo.
native_language_example: Luca told me that he needed time.

meaning: '(he/she) said (that) (he/she) had something' — introduces that someone reported having something to give or say.
additional_notes: Common structure: [Name/Subject] + ha detto che + aveva qualcosa (+ per voi / da dirti/dirle/dirvi). Used to report what someone said in the past (reported speech). 'Aveva' is imperfect tense indicating a past state; context clarifies whether 'something' is an object, information, or a message. To specify the recipient add phrases like 'per voi' (for you all) or 'da dirti' (to tell you).
target_language_example: Luca ha detto che aveva qualcosa da dirti.
native_language_example: Luca said he had something to tell you.

meaning: 'said that (he/she) had a…' — reports what someone said they possessed or experienced
additional_notes: Common spoken/written sequence used to report indirect speech. 'Detto' is the past participle of 'dire' (to say) and with a person omitted it often implies 'he/she/they said'. 'Aveva' is the imperfect of 'avere' (to have) and usually describes possession, states, conditions, or background information. The noun that completes the phrase follows (un alibi, un problema, un piano, etc.). Use it to relay what someone told you in the past.
target_language_example: Lui ha detto che aveva un problema con la macchina.
native_language_example: He said that he had a problem with the car.

meaning: 'said that (he/she/they) must' or 'said (someone) has to'
additional_notes: Combines passato prossimo of 'dire' (detto = 'said') + subordinate clause with 'che' + present of 'dovere' (deve = 'must/has to'). Used to report what someone said is necessary or required. Subject of 'deve' can be the same person who spoke or a different person mentioned in context. English translations often use 'said (that) he/she has to' or 'said (that) they must.'
target_language_example: Luca ha detto che deve partire domani.
native_language_example: Luca said that he has to leave tomorrow.

meaning: said (that) he/she had to go / said (that) they had to go
additional_notes: Common reported-speech phrase: 'ha detto che doveva andare' = '(he/she) said that (he/she/they) had to go.' Subject of 'detto' (the speaker) can be explicit (es. Mary) or implied. 'Doveva' is imperfect of 'dovere' expressing obligation in the past or a past intention. Use with indirect object pronouns: 'mi ha detto che doveva andare' = 'he/she told me that he/she had to go.'
target_language_example: Lui mi ha detto che doveva andare prima di cena.
native_language_example: He told me that he had to go before dinner.

meaning: 'said that he/it was the' or 'said that it was the' (intro to reported information about a masculine noun)
additional_notes: A fragment used in reported speech. 'Detto' is the past participle of 'dire' (to say). 'Che era il' introduces what was said about a masculine singular noun (e.g., 'il padre', 'il lavoro', 'il vostro impiego'). Often appears inside questions: e.g., 'Ma non ha detto che era il padre?' = 'Didn't he/she say he was the father?'. You can replace 'il' with other articles/pronouns as needed (la, i, le, un, etc.).
target_language_example: Hai detto che era il responsabile?
native_language_example: Did you say he was the person in charge?

meaning: said (that) she was in love with
additional_notes: This is a reported-speech phrase: detto (past participle of dire) + che (that) + era (imperfect of essere) + innamorata di (in love with). It reports what a female speaker or subject said about her feelings. Replace pronouns/names after di for the person: di me/te/lei/lui/voi/nomi. For a male speaker use innamorato instead of innamorata.
target_language_example: Anna ha detto che era innamorata di Marco.
native_language_example: Anna said that she was in love with Marco.

meaning: they/people said that they were really (…),
additional_notes: A phrase combining 'detto' (said), 'che' (that), 'erano' (they were) and 'davvero' (really). Used to report what others said about a group's state or quality. Agreeing adjectives that follow must match gender/number (arrabbate/arrabbati/riche/ricchi/etc.). Common in reported speech: Hanno detto che erano davvero + adjective.
target_language_example: Hanno detto che erano davvero felici.
native_language_example: They said that they were really happy.

meaning: said they were very
additional_notes: A reporting phrase used to introduce what someone else felt or was like. Usually follows verbs like 'hanno detto' or 'mi hanno detto'. The adjective that completes the phrase (e.g., 'tristi', 'stanchi', 'affamate') matches the subject in gender and number. You can drop 'molto' to soften the intensity ('detto che erano' = 'said they were').
target_language_example: Mi hanno detto che erano molto stanchi dopo il viaggio.
native_language_example: They told me they were very tired after the trip.

meaning: said that they were too (adjective) — introduces a reported statement about being 'too' something to do something.
additional_notes: Common structure for reported speech: 'Hanno detto che erano troppo + adjective + per + infinitive' (They said they were too [adjective] to [verb]). 'Erano' is the imperfect of 'essere' used for reported/descriptive past. Agreement of adjective (stanco/stanca/stanchi/stanche) matches the subject (gender/number).
target_language_example: Hanno detto che erano troppo impegnati per venire.
native_language_example: They said they were too busy to come.

meaning: they said that they were really / they said (that) they were very
additional_notes: A fixed combination made from the verb 'dire' in passato prossimo ('hanno detto') followed by a subordinate clause introduced by 'che' and 'erano veramente' + adjective. Use to report what others said about a group's state or feelings. 'Veramente' strengthens the adjective (really, very). Subject agreement (gelose/gelosi, stanche/spaventati) matches the people described.
target_language_example: Hanno detto che erano veramente contenti.
native_language_example: They said that they were really happy.

meaning: said that he/she has
additional_notes: Not a fixed expression, but a common fragment in reported speech. It often appears in sentences like ha detto che ha..., where the first ha is part of ha detto ('said'), and the second ha is usually the auxiliary for another past action: ha trovato, ha sentito, ha aiutato, etc. In natural English, this whole pattern is often translated with a simple past: 'said that he/she found/heard/helped...'
target_language_example: Luca ha detto che ha perso le chiavi.
native_language_example: Luca said that he lost the keys.

meaning: '(they) said that they have' or 'said that they' (perfect of dire + subordinate clause with avere/auxiliary).
additional_notes: This is a combination of detto (past participle of dire: 'said') usually in a passive or reporting structure, followed by che hanno introducing a subordinate clause with hanno (they have / auxiliary 'they' for compound tenses). In English it's often translated as 'they said that they...' or 'have said that they...'. Use it when reporting what people said. Word order: subject (optional) + detto che + hanno + past participle or verb (e.g. hanno chiamato = 'they called').
target_language_example: Maria ha detto che hanno finito il lavoro.
native_language_example: Maria said that they finished the work.

meaning: ‘(I) said that I have/ I …’ — part of a sentence reporting what someone told someone else about themselves (past: told + present perfect clause).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom but a combination: passato prossimo of dire (ho detto/ti ho detto) plus a subordinate clause introduced by che + ho (present perfect of another verb). It appears when reporting that you told someone something about yourself (e.g., 'I told him that I have/that I did...'). Word order and subject/object clitics matter: 'Gli/le/ti/vi ho detto che ho...'. Use depending on the indirect object (gli = to him, le = to her, ti = to you, vi = to you(pl)).
target_language_example: Le ho detto che ho visto quel film.
native_language_example: I told her that I have seen that film.

meaning: literally 'said that the' — used to introduce a reported clause about a plural noun (i + plural noun).
additional_notes: Combines the past participle detto (said) with the conjunction che (that) and the plural definite article i. Common in reported speech: 'Ha detto che i...' = 'He/She said that the...'. The definite article i marks a plural noun (e.g., i genitori = the parents). You can replace detto with other forms (dice, ha detto, mi hanno detto) depending on the subject and tense.
target_language_example: Mi hanno detto che i negozi chiudono alle otto.
native_language_example: They told me that the shops close at eight.

meaning: literally 'said that his/their' — a clipped phrase used in speech when referring back to something someone said about someone's (m) possession or situation
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom but a fragment: detto (said) + che (that) + il suo (his/its/their, masculine). You will most often see it inside a larger sentence (e.g., «Detto che il suo amico…» = 'He said that his friend…'). The gender/number of 'suo' must agree with the thing possessed (il suo, la sua, i suoi, le sue). In spoken Italian fragments like this can appear when reporting speech or summarizing what someone said.
target_language_example: Ho sentito Marco, ha detto che il suo cane è malato.
native_language_example: I heard Marco, he said that his dog is sick.

meaning: literally "said that the..." — a piece of reported speech introducing what someone said about a feminine noun or phrase starting with 'la'.
additional_notes: Composed of "detto" (past participle of dire, 'said'), the conjunction "che" ('that'), and the feminine definite article "la". Used to introduce reported speech when the thing reported refers to a feminine noun or a clause beginning with 'la' (e.g., la terra, la tua vita, la festa). In many contexts you will also see variations without the article ("ha detto che...") or with other articles/pronouns ("detto che il", "detto che lo", "detto che l'", "detto che le").
target_language_example: Mi ha detto che la festa è stata annullata.
native_language_example: He/she told me that the party was canceled.

meaning: '(someone) said that she liked the ...' (introduces reported speech about a woman's likes)
additional_notes: This phrase combines past participle 'detto' (said) with a subordinate clause 'che le piaceva la ...' meaning 'that she liked the ...'. 'Le' is the indirect object pronoun for 'to her' (or 'her'), and 'piaceva' is the imperfect of 'piacere' used for past habitual or descriptive statements. The noun that follows 'la' fills what she liked (e.g. 'neve', 'pioggia'). In English you usually say 'she said she liked the snow'. Word order in Italian can omit the subject because 'le' clarifies who liked it.
target_language_example: Marco mi ha detto che le piaceva la musica classica.
native_language_example: Marco told me that she liked classical music.

meaning: "(someone) said that she..." — reports what someone said about a female or 'she'.
additional_notes: Combines passato participle 'detto' (said) + conjunction 'che' (that) + pronoun 'lei' (she). Used to report speech: "[Someone] mi ha detto che lei..." = "[Someone] told/me that she..." The subject who said it can be explicit (e.g. "Tom mi ha detto che lei...") or implied. Pay attention to tense agreement after 'che'.
target_language_example: Marco mi ha detto che lei arriverà domani.
native_language_example: Marco told me that she will arrive tomorrow.

meaning: literally 'having said that it doesn't have' — used to report that someone said something does not exist or is not available
additional_notes: This phrase is a clipped sequence often found inside reported speech or recounting: e.g. «Ha detto che non ha...», meaning 'He/She said that he/she doesn't have...'. Alone, 'detto che non ha' is incomplete and normally followed by an object (tempo, soldi, informazioni, ecc.). Use when reporting what someone said about lacking or not possessing something.
target_language_example: Mi ha detto che non ha soldi per il biglietto.
native_language_example: He told me that he doesn't have money for the ticket.

meaning: '(I/he/she) said that I (do not)...' — part of a clause reporting what someone said about the speaker (followed by a verb or complement).
additional_notes: This is the fixed sequence 'detto che' (said that) plus the clitic 'mi' (to/for me or reflexive/part of a verb phrase) used before a past participle, verb, or adjective. In English it usually becomes 'said that I ...' or 'said that he/she ... me ...' depending on the subject. The exact translation depends on the verb or phrase that follows (e.g. 'mi ricordo' = 'I remember', 'mi sento' = 'I feel', 'mi ha visto' = 'has seen me'). Word order: subject + 'ha detto che non mi ...' or 'ho detto che non mi ...'.
target_language_example: Lei ha detto che non mi sento a mio agio.
native_language_example: She said that I don't feel comfortable.

meaning: said that (he/she) thought that… — introduces reported speech with a past-tense opinion or belief.
additional_notes: Used to report what someone said they believed or thought in the past. Often followed by a subordinate clause with the imperfect (pensava) plus a subjunctive or indicative in the subordinate clause depending on truth/stance (e.g., fossi, sembrassi, avesse). Common in indirect speech: 'Ha detto che pensava che + [clause]'.
target_language_example: Lui ha detto che pensava che non fosse colpa mia.
native_language_example: He said that he thought it wasn't my fault.

meaning: said that (he/she/it) could/might
additional_notes: Combines 'detto' (said/told) + clause introduced by 'che' + 'potrebbe' (conditional of potere). Used to report what someone said about a possible action. English equivalents: 'told me that he/she might' or 'said that it could'. Verb agreement depends on subject in reported clause (e.g., 'potrebbe farlo' = 'he/she/it might do it'). Often appears in indirect speech.
target_language_example: Mi ha detto che potrebbe venire domani.
native_language_example: He told me that he might come tomorrow.

meaning: a phrase introducing a reported conditional: 'I/they said that if...'.
additional_notes: Combines detto (said) + che (that) + se (if). Used to report what someone said about a hypothetical or conditional situation. Common in sentences like 'Ho detto che se...,' 'Mi ha detto che se...,' or 'Ti aveva detto che se...' Word order can vary (e.g. 'Le ho detto che se le potevo essere utile...'). Often followed by a verb in a conditional or subjunctive, depending on tense and speaker's perspective.
target_language_example: Mi ha detto che se avessi tempo, verrebbe con noi.
native_language_example: He told me that if he had time, he would come with us.

meaning: said (that) he/she/they feel(s) — introduces reported speech about someone's physical or emotional state.
additional_notes: A fixed sequence combining 'detto' (said) + 'che' (that) + the reflexive verb 'si sente' (he/she/they feel). Used to report what someone said about how they feel (e.g., sick, tired, well). The subject of 'detto' (who said it) appears before 'ha detto' (has said/said). The reflexive 'si' agrees with the reported person (third person). Tense and agreement can change (e.g., 'ha detto che mi sento' = 'he/she said that I feel...').
target_language_example: Maria ha detto che si sente stanca oggi.
native_language_example: Maria said that she feels tired today.

meaning: said that (he/she) felt
additional_notes: Used to report what someone said about their feelings or physical state. "Detto" is the past participle of "dire" (to say) used here with an implied subject (e.g., "ha detto" = "(he/she) said"). "Si sentiva" is the imperfect of "sentirsi" (to feel) and describes a continuing or repeated feeling/state in the past ("felt", "was feeling"). In English reporting, you can translate as "said that (he/she) felt" or simply "said (they) felt."
target_language_example: Luca ha detto che si sentiva stanco dopo il lavoro.
native_language_example: Luca said that he felt tired after work.

meaning: said that (he/she) felt very…
additional_notes: Used to report what someone said about their feelings or condition. "Detto" is the past participle of "dire" (to say); the structure "ha detto che si sentiva..." = "(he/she) said that (he/she) felt..." The reflexive verb "sentirsi" means "to feel" (emotionally or physically). The subject gender/number is shown in adjectives (nervoso/nervosa, sola/solo/stanca).
target_language_example: Marco ha detto che si sentiva molto felice.
native_language_example: Marco said that he felt very happy.

meaning: literally 'said that they have' — introduces reported speech with a reflexive/plural past action (they ... themselves + past participle).
additional_notes: Used to report what people said about actions they did (plural 'they') expressed with a reflexive or pronominal verb in the passato prossimo (si sono + past participle). Common in sentences like 'Hanno detto che si sono accorti...' or 'hanno detto che si sono divertiti...'. The subject of 'hanno detto' (they said) and the subject of 'si sono' is the same group (they). In English it's usually translated as 'they said that they ...' or 'they said they had ...'.
target_language_example: Gli studenti hanno detto che si sono preparati per l'esame.
native_language_example: The students said that they had prepared for the exam.

meaning: 'said that (someone) wanted to' — reports that a person wanted or intended to do something
additional_notes: A reported-speech construction. 'Detto' is the past participle of 'dire' (to say). 'Si voleva' uses the impersonal/passive 'si' with the imperfect of 'volere' (to want) and refers back to the person mentioned (e.g., 'ha detto che si voleva...' = 'he/she said that he/she wanted...'). It often appears after a clause like '[Nome] ha detto che si voleva...' In English you normally add the subject ('he wanted', 'she wanted').
target_language_example: Marco ha detto che si voleva trasferire all'estero.
native_language_example: Marco said that he wanted to move abroad.

meaning: said that (he/she/it) was
additional_notes: Combination of 'detto' (said/told) + 'che' (that) + imperfect of 'stare' used with a gerund or adjective to report what someone was doing or how they were (e.g. 'stava scherzando' = 'was joking', 'stava mentendo' = 'was lying', 'stava arrivando'/'venendo' = 'was arriving/coming'). Common in reported speech. The subject of 'stava' is usually he/she/it (lui/lei) or an impersonal subject understood from context.
target_language_example: Gli ho detto che stava esagerando.
native_language_example: I told him that he was exaggerating.

meaning: said that (he/she/they) was about to / was going to
additional_notes: Used to report what someone said about an action that was imminent in the past. "Stava per + infinitive" expresses that something was on the point of happening (past continuous + 'about to'). The subject of "stava" is the person referred to in the reported speech. Common in reported/indirect speech: "Ha detto che stava per + verb_inf".
target_language_example: Luca mi ha detto che stava per partire.
native_language_example: Luca told me he was about to leave.

meaning: literally 'said that you' — used to report what someone said about the person 'you'.
additional_notes: This is the combination of the past participle 'detto' (said) + the conjunction 'che' (that) + the subject 'tu' (you). It appears when reporting speech about 'you' (direct or indirect reported speech). Word order and tense in the reporting clause follow normal Italian: e.g., "Ha detto che tu eri..." (He said that you were...). In casual speech speakers may drop 'tu' if context is clear.
target_language_example: Marco ha detto che tu sei molto bravo.
native_language_example: Marco said that you are very good.

meaning: 'said that (he/she) wanted a…' — part of a reported speech phrase introducing what someone wanted
additional_notes: This is a fragment used in indirect/reported speech. 'Detto' (past participle of 'dire') + 'che' introduces the content: 'he/she said that…' followed by 'voleva' (imperfect of 'volere', 'wanted') and an indefinite article + noun. You will typically see a noun after 'un' (masculine singular) — e.g. 'detto che voleva un caffè' = 'said that he/she wanted a coffee'. The subject of 'voleva' is usually implied from context (lui/lei/egli/ella).
target_language_example: Ha detto che voleva un panino per pranzo.
native_language_example: He/she said that (he/she) wanted a sandwich for lunch.

meaning: said that he/she wants to
additional_notes: Usually part of a longer phrase such as ha detto che vuole... or mi ha detto che vuole.... Italian often omits the subject pronoun, so vuole can mean "he wants" or "she wants" depending on context.
target_language_example: Mi ha detto che vuole imparare l'italiano.
native_language_example: He/She told me that he/she wants to learn Italian.

meaning: said that he/she is
additional_notes: Used in reported speech, usually as part of ha detto che... or mi ha detto che... ('said that...' / 'told me that...'). Italian often omits the subject pronoun after che, so English usually needs 'he' or 'she'. Here è can mean 'is' or be an auxiliary before a past participle, as in è andato = 'he went / has gone'.
target_language_example: Luca mi ha detto che è arrivato presto.
native_language_example: Luca told me that he arrived early.

meaning: said that she/it went (or has gone).
additional_notes: A reported-speech phrase: 'detto' is the past participle of dire (to say) used with a subject (e.g., 'gli/le/mi/ha detto') + 'che' (that) + 'è andata' (she/it has gone or went). 'È andata' is passato prossimo of andare for feminine subject (or feminine noun). Use with masculine subjects you'd hear 'è andato'. Context indicates someone reported that a (female) person or feminine thing went/has gone somewhere.
target_language_example: Ti ho detto che è andata al lavoro stamattina.
native_language_example: I told you that she went to work this morning.

meaning: having said that; that said; that being said (used to introduce a comment after stating something).
additional_notes: Often used as a discourse marker to add a remark, qualification, or contrast after giving information. Can also appear in sentences like "ti ho detto ciò che..." where "ciò" = "that/what" and the phrase means "I told you that/what..." Context determines whether it's a connector ('that said') or part of a clause ('told you what'). Formal to neutral register.
target_language_example: Detto ciò, possiamo procedere con il piano.
native_language_example: That said, we can proceed with the plan.

meaning: told (someone) not to tell (it) to (someone else); a reported-speech construction meaning 'I/He/She told [someone] not to tell [others]'.
additional_notes: This is part of a larger structure: past participle "detto" (said/told) + "di non dirlo a" (to not tell it to). Change the pronouns for who was told (mi, ti, gli, le, vi) and for whom not to tell (a lui/lei/loro/niente = nobody). "Dirlo" = 'to say/tell it' (dir + lo). Common in warning someone to keep a secret: "Ti ho detto di non dirlo a nessuno."
target_language_example: Le ho detto di non dirlo a nessuno.
native_language_example: I told her not to tell anyone.

meaning: told (someone) to stop (doing something).
additional_notes: Literally 'told to stop of' — used after verbs like dire (to tell) to report that someone instructed or asked another person to stop a specific action. Followed by an infinitive verb: 'smettere di' + infinitive (e.g., smettere di fumare). Common in past (ho detto, ha detto, ti ho detto).
target_language_example: Mi hanno detto di smettere di bere caffè dopo cena.
native_language_example: They told me to stop drinking coffee after dinner.

meaning: 'told (me/you) where' — indicates that someone has said the location or place (where to go/live/work/etc.).
additional_notes: Combines the past participle detto (from dire — 'to tell/say') with the interrogative dove ('where'). Used to report or ask about information on a place or destination. In examples, auxiliary verbs and pronouns change (e.g., 'mi ha detto dove...' = 'he/she told me where...'; 'ti ha detto dove?' = 'did he/she tell you where?'). Common in both statements and questions. Word order may vary: 'mi ha detto dove andare' (infinitive) vs 'mi ha detto dove vivi' (finite clause).
target_language_example: Mi ha detto dove posso trovare la farmacia.
native_language_example: He told me where I can find the pharmacy.

meaning: said the same (thing).
additional_notes: Used to say someone said the same thing as someone else. Often part of phrases like "ho detto la stessa cosa" or "mi ha detto la stessa cosa". The word "cosa" (thing) is frequently implied or included. Verb form (detto) is the past participle of "dire" (to say). Word order may vary: "ho detto la stessa cosa", "mi ha detto la stessa cosa", or "hai detto la stessa cosa".
target_language_example: Gli ho detto la stessa cosa ieri.
native_language_example: I told him the same thing yesterday.

meaning: told them not to (do something).
additional_notes: Combination of passato prossimo of 'dire' (detto) + indirect object 'loro' (to them) + the infinitive negated by 'di non' before a verb. Use to report that you instructed or warned a group not to perform an action. Common in spoken and written Italian. Followed by an infinitive verb: e.g. 'venire', 'guidare', 'usare'.
target_language_example: Ho detto loro di non parlare durante la riunione.
native_language_example: I told them not to speak during the meeting.

meaning: 'said anything to' (used in negative sentences: 'didn't tell anyone' / 'didn't say anything to')
additional_notes: Commonly appears in negative constructions with non, mai, or nessuno (e.g. 'non ho detto niente a nessuno' = 'I didn't tell anyone'). 'Niente' means 'nothing'/'anything' here; 'a' introduces the person or topic (a riguardo = about it; a [name] = to [name]). Word order: 'non' + passato prossimo/imperfetto + 'detto niente a ...' or 'non hanno detto niente a riguardo'.
target_language_example: Non ho detto niente a Marco della festa.
native_language_example: I didn't tell Marco anything about the party.

meaning: "told (me) why" or "said why" (past participle + conjunction introducing a reason).
additional_notes: Combines detto (past participle of dire = 'to tell/say') with perché ('why' / 'because'). Used when reporting that someone explained the reason for something. In English it corresponds to 'told (me) why' or 'said why'. The subject and indirect object may be stated elsewhere (e.g., 'mi hai detto perché' = 'you told me why').
target_language_example: Mi hanno detto perché il volo è in ritardo.
native_language_example: They told me why the flight is delayed.

meaning: 'told (me) why (she/he/it) was...'.
additional_notes: This is a clipped sequence showing reported speech: detto (past participle of dire) + perché (why) + era (imperfect of essere: 'was'). It appears when someone reports that another person told them the reason for a past state or action. Subject and adjective/agreement change depending on the person (era qua/qui, era arrabbiata/arrabbiato, era in ritardo). Often used with an indirect object (mi/ti/ci) or named subject (Tom mi ha detto perché era...).
target_language_example: Marco mi ha detto perché era stanco.
native_language_example: Marco told me why he was tired.

meaning: 'said about' or 'told about' (referring to something said regarding someone or something).
additional_notes: Used to refer to information or comments spoken concerning a person or topic. Often appears in questions (Cosa gli hai detto su di me? = What did you tell him about me?) or statements (Quello che ho detto su di lui = What I said about him). In everyday speech, Italians may also say 'detto di' or simply 'su' (e.g., 'Cosa gli hai detto di me?/Cosa gli hai detto su di me?').
target_language_example: Non mi piace quello che hai detto su di lei.
native_language_example: I don't like what you said about her.

meaning: must get up / has to get up.
additional_notes: Formed from the modal verb dovere (deve = he/she/you formal must) + alzare (to get up). Often used with a reflexive pronoun si (si deve alzare = he/she must get up). Can refer to needing to wake up or to rise/stand up. In sentences with imperative or indirect speech, pronouns change (Dille che si deve alzare = Tell her she must get up).
target_language_example: Devi dirle che si deve alzare domani presto.
native_language_example: You must tell her that she has to get up early tomorrow.

meaning: This sequence is not a correct or natural Italian phrase; it appears to combine 'deve fare' (must do) and 'è' (is) from different clauses. As written, it is ungrammatical and should be rephrased depending on intent.
additional_notes:
'Deve fare' = 'he/she/it/you(formal) must do' (use 'deve' + infinitive for obligation). 'È' = 'is' (third-person singular of 'essere'). They are not normally adjacent as 'deve fare è'. Possible corrections:
- Obligation + action: 'Deve fare [qualcosa].' (Deve fare i compiti.)
- Deduction about a state: 'Deve essere [aggettivo/partecipio].' (Deve essere stanco.)
- If trying to link clauses, use appropriate connectors: e.g. 'Deve fare, e è...' with a comma and 'e' (and) as separate words: 'Deve fare il lavoro, e è pronto a finirlo.' Note that 'deve fare è' without punctuation is incorrect.
target_language_example: *Incorrect/ungrammatical in Italian, shown with context:* "Quando parla veloce, sembra che deve fare è confuso."
native_language_example: *Incorrect/ungrammatical English translation:* "When he speaks fast, it seems that must do is confused."

meaning: must take in / has to take in (someone or something)
additional_notes: This is part of a verb phrase using 'prendere in' (often followed by 'considerazione', 'conto', 'cura', 'affitto', etc.). Alone it feels incomplete — you usually need an object or complement (e.g., 'prendere in considerazione' = 'take into consideration'; 'prendere in affitto' = 'rent; take on lease'; 'prendere in cura' = 'take into care'). 'Deve' indicates obligation ('must' / 'has to').
target_language_example: Deve prendere in considerazione tutte le opinioni.
native_language_example: He/She must take all opinions into consideration.

meaning: 'he/she/it/you (formal) must study the' or 'has to study the'.
additional_notes: This is a short sequence combining the modal verb 'dovere' in the third person singular ('deve' = must/has to), the infinitive 'studiare' (to study), and the definite article 'il' (the). It begins a phrase that needs a noun after 'il' (e.g., 'deve studiare il libro' = 'he must study the book'). Subject is implied by the verb form. For 'you must' (informal) use 'devi'; for plural 'you' use 'dovete'; for 'I must' use 'devo'.
target_language_example: Luca deve studiare il libro per l'esame.
native_language_example: Luca must study the book for the exam.

meaning: 'you owe (me/someone) a ...' or 'you owe someone something (often used to say someone deserves/should give something)'.
additional_notes: Formed with the verb dovere (devi = you must/you owe) + an indefinite object (un/una + noun). Commonly used to say someone owes someone a favor, a meal, a kiss, etc. Can be literal (debt) or colloquial (you should give me/you owe me). In examples with strong language (un cazzo, un accidente) it expresses that someone doesn't owe anything — rude/informal. Word order: subject + mi/ti/le + devi + un + noun (Tu mi devi un favore / Mi devi un pranzo).
target_language_example: Mi devi un favore per quello che hai fatto.
native_language_example: You owe me a favor for what you did.

meaning: I have to do many (something).
additional_notes: Phrase combines the verb dovere (devo = I must/have to) + fare (to do) + molte (many, feminine plural). It's incomplete on its own—usually followed by a feminine plural noun (e.g., 'devo fare molte commissioni', 'devo fare molte cose'). Use 'molti' before masculine plural nouns. Conveys obligation to perform many tasks or items.
target_language_example: Devo fare molte cose oggi.
native_language_example: I have to do many things today.

meaning: I must apologize / I have to apologize
additional_notes: Devo scusare is the first-person singular of dovere + the verb scusare (to apologize). More commonly Italians say "devo scusarmi" (reflexive) or "devo scusare qualcuno" when apologizing on someone's behalf. With a person: "Mi devo scusare con lei/lui" = I must apologize to her/him. With a reason: use "per" + clause (e.g. "per non aver scritto..."). Can be used in questions: "Quante volte mi devo scusare?".
target_language_example: Mi devo scusare con te per ieri sera.
native_language_example: I must apologize to you for last night.

meaning: I owe (some) — used to say you owe someone money or something.
additional_notes: Combines the verb dovere (devo = I must / I owe) + partitive 'dei' to indicate an unspecified amount ('some'). Commonly followed by 'soldi' (money) or another object. Word order can vary: direct or indirect object pronouns (mi/ti/lo/le/gli/vi) can come before the verb (Gli devo dei soldi) or after in spoken questions with emphasis (Io vi devo dei soldi?). 'Devo dei' is not used to state a specific amount; use 'devo €10' or 'devo dieci euro' for exact sums.
target_language_example: Ti devo dei soldi per il biglietto.
native_language_example: I owe you some money for the ticket.

meaning: I owe my (something) to... / I owe (my) [success/etc.] to...
additional_notes: Used to say you attribute something (often success, gratitude, thanks) to someone or something. Structure: (Io) devo il mio + [noun] + a/ai/al/alla + [person or thing]. More natural Italian often omits 'il mio' if context is clear (e.g. 'Gli devo il successo' or 'Gli devo tutto'). Verb 'devo' is from 'dovere' meaning 'to owe' or 'must' — here 'to owe'.
target_language_example: Devo il mio lavoro alla sua raccomandazione.
native_language_example: I owe my job to his recommendation.

meaning: of Cocco / by Cocco (indicating origin, authorship, or family name)
additional_notes: Likely a surname phrase: 'di' + family name Cocco. Used to show possession, origin, authorship, or noble/family affiliation (e.g., la casa di Cocco = Cocco's house; un dipinto di Cocco = a painting by Cocco). Capitalize 'Cocco' as a proper name. Not a standalone fixed expression.
target_language_example: Questa ricetta è di Cocco.
native_language_example: This recipe is by Cocco.

meaning: of Donna / belonging to Donna (possessive); can also be part of a name or phrase meaning 'woman's' or 'female' when Donna is a noun.
additional_notes: di means 'of' or 'from' in Italian. When followed by a proper name like Donna, di Donna usually indicates possession or origin (e.g., il libro di Donna = Donna's book). Note: Donna is also an Italian word meaning 'woman' (la donna), but capitalized Donna is a personal name in English/Italian. Context tells you whether it's a name (possessive) or part of a phrase meaning 'of the woman'. If you mean 'of the woman' in Italian, you'd normally say 'della donna' (di + la = della).
target_language_example: Il cappello è di Donna.
native_language_example: The hat is Donna's.

meaning: of Halloween; relating to Halloween (used to describe events, costumes, decorations, etc.).
additional_notes: A simple prepositional phrase: 'di' + 'Halloween'. Commonly used to indicate that something belongs to or is for Halloween (festa di Halloween, costume di Halloween, decorazioni di Halloween). Used with singular nouns; English often uses 'Halloween' as an adjective (Halloween party).
target_language_example: Siamo andati a una festa di Halloween ieri sera.
native_language_example: We went to a Halloween party last night.

meaning: a surname or family name (literally 'of May'); used as part of a person's full name
additional_notes: Appears after a given name to form a full name (e.g., Nihad di Maggio). 'Di' + capitalized month or name often indicates a surname or a locative/familial particle in Italian names. Not a prepositional phrase meaning 'in May' in this context — when referring to the month, 'di maggio' is usually lowercase and not attached to a personal name.
target_language_example: Conosci il signor Marco di Maggio?
native_language_example: Do you know Mr. Marco di Maggio?

meaning: of the sea / from the sea; relating to the sea (used with nouns, often in culinary or descriptive contexts)
additional_notes: A prepositional phrase: 'di' (of/from) + 'mare' (sea). Commonly used in compound expressions like 'frutti di mare' (seafood) or to indicate origin/relationship to the sea (e.g., 'profumo di mare'). Use after a noun it modifies: 'pesce di mare' = fish from the sea. Literal translation is possible.
target_language_example: Abbiamo mangiato un piatto di frutti di mare.
native_language_example: We ate a seafood dish.

meaning: of Christmas
additional_notes: Used to indicate something related to Christmas (e.g., Christmas gifts, Christmas cake, Christmas holidays). Commonly follows the noun it modifies in Italian (torta di Natale = Christmas cake). Can also appear in time expressions meaning 'around Christmas' (prima di Natale = just before Christmas).
target_language_example: La mia famiglia mangia il panettone di Natale ogni anno.
native_language_example: My family eats the Christmas panettone every year.

meaning: to (someone) to lower; 'to lower' after a verb like chiedere/dirre (infinitive marker + 'to lower').
additional_notes: This is the infinitive form of abbassare preceded by the particle di, used after verbs that require 'di' before another verb (e.g., chiedere di, pregare di, consigliare di). In the examples it appears in requests: 'asked (someone) to lower' (voice, music, etc.). Use di + infinitive when the main verb governs an infinitive in Italian. The subject receiving the request can be expressed with a + person (chiedere a Maria di...).
target_language_example: Ti chiedo di abbassare la radio, per favore.
native_language_example: I'm asking you to turn down the radio, please.

meaning: of friendship / friend (as in 'friend request')
additional_notes: 'Di amicizia' is used to form phrases related to friendship, most commonly in 'richiesta di amicizia' (friend request) on social networks. Literally 'of friendship' — it links a noun (richiesta, gesto, rapporto) to the idea of friendship.
target_language_example: Ho ricevuto una richiesta di amicizia ieri.
native_language_example: I received a friend request yesterday.

meaning: of/ to kill; used after verbs or expressions to indicate killing (literal or figurative).
additional_notes: The phrase di ammazzare appears when a verb or phrase requires a following infinitive (ammazzare = to kill). It can be literal (to kill a person or animal) or figurative (e.g., 'ammazzare il tempo' = 'to kill time' = to pass time). Pay attention to context and tone—literal use is serious; figurative use is common in everyday speech. Grammar: di introduces the infinitive after certain verbs (cercare di, dire di, finire di, etc.).
target_language_example: Sto cercando di ammazzare la noia leggendo un libro.
native_language_example: I'm trying to kill boredom by reading a book.

meaning: one-way (as in a ticket) / outward (journey)
additional_notes: Often used with biglietto or viaggio: "biglietto di andata" = one-way ticket. Opposite is "di ritorno" (return). Can describe the outward leg of a journey (andata) or a single-direction ticket. Common in travel contexts (trains, buses, flights).
target_language_example: Vorrei un biglietto di andata per Napoli.
native_language_example: I would like a one-way ticket to Naples.

meaning: 'of animals' / 'about animals' (used to indicate relation to animals)
additional_notes: This phrase combines the preposition di ('of', 'about') with animali (animals). It appears in questions (Che tipo di animali? = What kind of animals?) and in descriptions of interests (appassionato/a di animali = passionate about animals). Depending on context, di animali can describe type, content, or a person's interest. Remember agreement: appassionato (m.sg.), appassionata (f.sg.), appassionati (m.pl.), appassionate (f.pl.).
target_language_example: Mio fratello studia libri di animali.
native_language_example: My brother studies books about animals.

meaning: to tell someone to wait (in a specific place).
additional_notes: This construction combines the infinitive aspettare ('to wait') with di after a verb of telling (dire, chiedere, etc.) to introduce a command or request: [dire] + di + aspettare + in + [place]. Commonly used with 'in macchina' (in the car), 'in cucina', etc. Word order: subject + dire + di + aspettare + in + luogo. The preposition 'in' is followed by the place (e.g. macchina).
target_language_example: Mi ha detto di aspettare in giardino.
native_language_example: He/She told me to wait in the garden.

meaning: of having said / that (someone) said (used after verbs or expressions to report speech or a belief)
additional_notes: This is a compound of the preposition 'di' + the perfect infinitive 'aver detto' (to have said). Common after verbs or nouns that introduce reported speech, opinions, or claims: e.g. 'pensare di aver detto' or 'il fatto di aver detto'. Often appears in subordinate constructions: 'Mi dispiace di aver detto quelle cose.'
target_language_example: Mi scuso di aver detto qualcosa di offensivo.
native_language_example: I apologize for having said something offensive.

meaning: of having received the (feminine) — used to refer to an action that was completed before another (perfect infinitive).
additional_notes: This is the perfect infinitive construction (di + avere + past participle) used after verbs or expressions that link events in time. 'La' is the feminine singular direct article (e.g. la lettera). In the examples it means 'before having received the letter.' In spoken Italian, simpler forms like "prima di ricevere la" are more common; both are correct, but "di avere ricevuto" emphasizes the completion of the action.
target_language_example: Era già partito di avere ricevuto la lettera.
native_language_example: He had already left before having received the letter.

meaning: to need (something); 'to have need of'.
additional_notes: Used after verbs like dire, pensare, sapere to report that someone needs something. Literally 'of having need' — common in constructions like 'dice di avere bisogno di...' followed by the thing needed or an infinitive. For simpler use, you can say 'ho bisogno di...' (I need...).
target_language_example: Marco dice di avere bisogno di riposare.
native_language_example: Marco says he needs to rest.

meaning: to have many (of something); used after verbs like dire/dire che to report someone saying they have many X.
additional_notes: This phrase combines the preposition/connector di (used after verbs like dire, credere, pensare when introducing reported content) + avere molti (to have many). Use it to report what someone says they possess or have to do. Followed by a noun (amici, soldi, compiti). Word order: [person] + dice/dicono + di avere molti + [noun].
target_language_example: Luca dice di avere molti libri da leggere.
native_language_example: Luca says he has many books to read.

meaning: of adventure / adventure (as a genre).
additional_notes: Used after nouns (e.g., libri di avventura) to indicate the genre or type: 'adventure books'. Di + noun often marks 'of' or 'made of' relationships; here it marks genre. Common with books, films, storie, film, romanzi.
target_language_example: Ho comprato un film di avventura per i bambini.
native_language_example: I bought an adventure movie for the children.

meaning: basically; fundamental; at a basic level
additional_notes: Used to indicate the basic, core, or fundamental aspect of something (e.g., idea, problem). Can also mean 'basically' as an adverb to summarize or simplify a point. Context determines whether it's describing a foundational element ("la teoria di base") or giving a general summary/opinion ("sono di base sulla costa occidentale" — here meaning 'basically, I'm on the west coast' or 'I’m based on the west coast').
target_language_example: Il problema di base è la mancanza di fondi.
native_language_example: The basic problem is the lack of funding.

meaning: 'to beat' or 'to strike' (infinitive form used after verbs that require 'di' + infinitive).
additional_notes: This is the preposition 'di' + the infinitive 'battere'. In Italian certain verbs, adjectives, or expressions are followed by 'di' + infinitive (e.g., 'ho paura di battere' — although that exact collocation is rare). More commonly you will see 'di battere' after verbs expressing possibility, obligation, desire, or after nouns/expressions that link to another action (e.g., 'la possibilità di battere' = 'the possibility of beating/defeating'). 'Battere' can mean to beat (someone), hit/strike, defeat (in a game), or to beat (as in a heart). Use depends on context.
target_language_example: La squadra ha la possibilità di battere gli avversari domani.
native_language_example: The team has the possibility of beating the opponents tomorrow.

meaning: to type (on a typewriter or keyboard) — used with 'battere a macchina' = to type
additional_notes: This construction appears as 'battere a macchina' meaning 'to type' (literally 'to strike at the machine'). The particle 'di' appears when the verb is used after certain adjectives (e.g., 'capace di', 'stanco di') or other verbs requiring 'di' before an infinitive. Use the full phrase 'battere a macchina' for 'to type'. In modern Italian you may also hear 'digitare' or 'scrivere al computer'.
target_language_example: Sono stanco di battere a macchina tutto il giorno.
native_language_example: I'm tired of typing all day.

meaning: 'something nice/interesting' or 'what nice/interesting things' (depends on context)
additional_notes: Used after words like 'cosa', 'niente', 'qualcosa' or verbs to describe something pleasant, attractive, or noteworthy. In questions 'Cosa fai di bello?' it asks 'What are you up to?' or 'What nice/interesting thing are you doing?'. With 'niente' it means 'nothing special/interesting'. In descriptive sentences it means 'something nice' (e.g. 'qualcosa di bello' = 'something beautiful/nice'). Tone is neutral; common in spoken Italian.
target_language_example: Hai fatto qualcosa di bello oggi?
native_language_example: Did you do anything nice today?

meaning: 'very' or 'really' (intensifier); also 'badly' when describing something negative.
additional_notes: Used colloquially to intensify an adjective, verb or situation. Often emphasizes severity (very bad/serious) or degree (really). Can be informal and strong — sometimes coarse in tone depending on context. When paired with negative nouns/verbs it can mean 'badly' or 'seriously'; with adjectives it works like 'very' or 'extremely'.
target_language_example: Ha pianto di brutto dopo il film.
native_language_example: He cried really hard after the movie.

meaning: relating to hunting; 'hunting' (used to describe things for or about hunting)
additional_notes: Used after a noun to indicate purpose, type, or relation to hunting (e.g. licenza di caccia = hunting license; baracca di caccia = hunting shack; incidente di caccia = hunting accident). Common in compound phrases. Not slang.
target_language_example: Ha trovato una giacca di caccia nel negozio.
native_language_example: He found a hunting jacket in the shop.

meaning: of socks / (used after a quantity) socks
additional_notes: Commonly appears after a number or quantity word to indicate how many pairs of socks (paio/paia di calze). Italian uses 'paio' (singular) and 'paia' (plural) with 'di calze' to say 'a pair of socks' or 'pairs of socks'. You can also see 'un paio di calze' = 'a pair of socks' and 'tre paia di calze' = 'three pairs of socks'.
target_language_example: Ho comprato un paio di calze nere.
native_language_example: I bought a pair of black socks.

meaning: of changing the / to change the (literal phrase used after verbs like cercare, decidere, pensare).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom but the combination of the preposition 'di' + infinitive 'cambiare' + definite article 'il'. You'll see it after verbs that require 'di' before another verb (e.g., cercare di, decidere di, pensare di). The article 'il' agrees with a masculine singular noun that follows (il mondo, il comportamento, il nome). For feminine nouns use 'la' (di cambiare la) and for plural use 'i/ le' (di cambiare i / di cambiare le).
target_language_example: Sto pensando di cambiare il mio lavoro.
native_language_example: I'm thinking of changing my job.

meaning: 'in a bad (mood)' or 'bad' (used in phrases like "di cattivo umore" or to describe something unpleasant).
additional_notes: Often appears in the fixed phrase "di cattivo umore" meaning "in a bad mood." Alone, "cattivo" means bad/evil/spoiled; "di" marks the state (literally "of bad"). Use "di cattivo umore" for people. For things or actions, "di cattivo" can imply something unpleasant or of poor quality, but this use is less common without a noun.
target_language_example: Dopo la notizia, è rimasto di cattivo umore tutto il giorno.
native_language_example: After the news, he stayed in a bad mood all day.

meaning: 'of/like an asshole' or 'fucking' (very vulgar insult; denotes contempt or worthlessness).
additional_notes: Highly offensive slang used to insult people or things. Often attached to nouns (e.g., pezzo di cazzo, testa di cazzo) to call someone a jerk/asshole or to express that something is worthless. Do not use in polite contexts. Tone is aggressive; may provoke strong reactions.
target_language_example: Non essere quel pezzo di cazzo, chiedi scusa.
native_language_example: Don't be that asshole, apologize.

meaning: certainly; for sure; definitely (used to affirm or emphasize).
additional_notes: Used to confirm or emphasize certainty about a fact or opinion. Can appear at the start of a sentence (Di certo..., 'Certainly...') or alone as a short affirmation (Di certo.). When negated (Non di certo! / No di certo!) it expresses strong disagreement or 'certainly not'. Tone can be formal or informal depending on context.
target_language_example: Di certo verrò alla festa domani.
native_language_example: I will certainly come to the party tomorrow.

meaning: of/from champagne; (used after a measure word) '...of champagne' or 'champagne' as the substance.
additional_notes: Used after words indicating quantity (un bicchiere di, una bottiglia di) to say what the container holds. 'Di' here means 'of' or 'made from' and connects the measure noun to the beverage. Common in spoken and written Italian when naming drinks.
target_language_example: Vorrei un bicchiere di champagne, per favore.
native_language_example: I'd like a glass of champagne, please.

meaning: to call the (used before a feminine noun like 'polizia' or 'sicurezza').
additional_notes: This is part of an infinitive phrase: 'di chiamare' = 'to call' and 'la' is the feminine definite article 'the' (e.g., la polizia, la sicurezza). You'll see it in constructions after verbs or expressions that require 'di' plus an infinitive (e.g., 'ha minacciato di chiamare la...'; 'ti raccomando di chiamare la...'). Use 'il' for masculine nouns (es. 'di chiamare il 118' for emergency number).
target_language_example: Ti consiglio di chiamare la polizia immediatamente.
native_language_example: I advise you to call the police immediately.

meaning: of/to close the (feminine singular noun follows).
additional_notes: This is part of an infinitive construction using the verb 'dimenticare', 'chiedere', 'scordare', etc. 'Di' introduces the infinitive 'chiudere' (to close). 'La' is the definite article for a feminine singular noun (la porta, la finestra). You'll usually see it in phrases like 'dimenticare di chiudere la porta' (to forget to close the door).
target_language_example: Devi ricordarti di chiudere la finestra prima di uscire.
native_language_example: You must remember to close the window before leaving.

meaning: of Chinese / (related) to Chinese (language).
additional_notes: Used to indicate possession/relationship with the Chinese language (e.g., teacher, lesson, book) or describe someone as an expert in Chinese. Commonly follows nouns: 'insegnante di cinese' = Chinese teacher. 'Cinese' here refers to the language; context may also mean 'Chinese' (nationality/ethnicity) but with 'di' it typically links items to the language.
target_language_example: Ho comprato un dizionario di cinese.
native_language_example: I bought a Chinese dictionary.

meaning: 'of color' / 'colored' (relating to color or, in some contexts, referring to a person as non-white)
additional_notes: Primary literal meaning: 'of color' — used to describe the color of objects (e.g., 'scarpe di colore rosso' = 'shoes of red color'). In social contexts, especially when referring to people, 'di colore' can mean 'a person of color' or 'non-white'. Be careful: when used about people it can sound dated or potentially insensitive depending on context and region; more neutral alternatives are 'persona di colore', 'persona non bianca', or specifying nationality/ethnicity if appropriate. Word order: often appears after a noun (ragazzo di colore, scarpe di colore rosso).
target_language_example: Ha una giacca di colore blu scuro.
native_language_example: He has a dark blue jacket.

meaning: 'suddenly' or 'all of a sudden'.
additional_notes: Used to describe something that happens quickly and unexpectedly. Usually placed before or after the verb or phrase it modifies (e.g., 'Di colpo è successo...' or 'È successo di colpo'). Informal-neutral register; common in spoken and written Italian.
target_language_example: Di colpo ha cominciato a piovere.
native_language_example: Suddenly it started to rain.

meaning: a phrase used to say 'to buy some' (used before an uncountable noun or partitive quantity).
additional_notes: This is the verb 'ricordarsi/ricordare' or similar + 'di' + the infinitive 'comprare' + the partitive 'del' (de + il) meaning 'some' or 'some of the'. Used when asking/reminding someone to buy a non-count item or a portion of something (e.g., del latte, del pane). The structure is: [verb] di comprare del + noun. 'Del' contracts with masculine singular definite article; for feminine use 'della' (della frutta), for plural 'dei/degli'.
target_language_example: Mi ricordi di comprare del formaggio?
native_language_example: Can you remind me to buy some cheese?

meaning: of/to buy a (masculine/some) — part of infinitive phrase meaning 'to buy a...'
additional_notes: This is not a standalone phrase but a common combination: the preposition/particle di (often after verbs like 'decidere', 'dimenticare', 'avere bisogno', 'dire' + indirect object) + the infinitive comprare + the indefinite article un. It introduces the action 'to buy a...' (usually followed by a masculine noun). English equivalents: 'to buy a', 'of buying a' depending on context. The noun that follows must agree in gender/number (un → uno before certain consonant clusters; una for feminine nouns).
target_language_example: Ho deciso di comprare un nuovo computer.
native_language_example: I decided to buy a new computer.

meaning: of/to buy a (feminine singular noun) — indicates the action of buying something specific.
additional_notes: This sequence combines the infinitive verb comprare (to buy) with the preposition di, which often follows verbs or expressions that introduce another verb (e.g., essere in grado di, decidere di). Una is the indefinite article for feminine singular nouns (a/an). Use di comprare un/uno/una depending on the gender and form of the noun that follows (un/uno for masculine, una for feminine).
target_language_example: Ho deciso di comprare una bicicletta nuova.
native_language_example: I decided to buy a new bicycle.

meaning: of rabbit / rabbit (meat).
additional_notes: Used to indicate something made from or relating to rabbit, most commonly rabbit meat (carne di coniglio). In Italian the preposition 'di' + animal name often means 'made from' or 'meat of'. Can appear after nouns (carne di coniglio) or in recipes (ravioli di coniglio).
target_language_example: Preferisco il ragù di coniglio alla pasta al sugo.
native_language_example: I prefer rabbit ragù to tomato sauce pasta.

meaning: 'as a result' / 'consequently'.
additional_notes: Used to link an action or situation to its result or consequence. Can appear at the start, middle, or end of a sentence and is fairly neutral/formal. Synonyms: 'quindi', 'pertanto'.
target_language_example: Ha perso il treno e, di conseguenza, è arrivato tardi al lavoro.
native_language_example: He missed the train and, as a result, arrived late to work.

meaning: 'in cash' or 'of cash' (refers to money in physical bills/coins)
additional_notes: Used to talk about physical money (bills/coins) as opposed to cards, transfers, or checks. Often appears after verbs like avere bisogno (ho bisogno di contanti) or to describe an amount (un mucchio di contanti). In English you usually say "in cash" or simply "cash."
target_language_example: Ho pagato il regalo di contanti.
native_language_example: I paid for the gift in cash.

meaning: to continue (to) — introduces an action that will keep happening
additional_notes: Used after verbs or expressions of intention/decision (e.g., 'hai intenzione di', 'ho deciso di') to mean 'to keep doing' something. Followed by an infinitive verb: 'continuare a + infinitive' (e.g., continuare a studiare). In some varieties, 'continuare + a' can also be replaced by 'continuare + infinitive' without 'a' (less common).
target_language_example: Ho deciso di continuare a imparare l'italiano.
native_language_example: I decided to continue learning Italian.

meaning: continuously; all the time; repeatedly without long breaks
additional_notes: Used adverbially to describe actions that happen repeatedly or without interruption. Common in everyday speech to emphasize frequency (e.g., crying, eating, listening, receiving messages). Can be placed after the verb or verb phrase.
target_language_example: Mi chiama di continuo anche quando sono al lavoro.
native_language_example: He calls me all the time, even when I'm at work.

meaning: of/ to check/control the (feminine singular noun that follows).
additional_notes: This is a fragment that combines the preposition/infinitive marker 'di' + verb 'controllare' + definite article 'la'. It usually appears before a feminine singular noun (e.g., la rabbia, la posta) and indicates attempting or needing to check, control, or examine that thing. Context determines whether 'controllare' means 'to control' (e.g., emotions) or 'to check/review' (e.g., mail/documents). The subject and tense are shown elsewhere in the sentence (e.g., 'Cercarono di controllare la...'; 'Ho bisogno di controllare la...').
target_language_example: Devo cercare di controllare la mia rabbia.
native_language_example: I must try to control my anger.

meaning: to control his/her/its (something) — used after verbs like 'cercare' (to try) or modal constructions.
additional_notes: This phrase combines the preposition 'di' + verb infinitive 'controllare' + possessive 'la sua' (feminine singular). 'La sua' agrees with the noun it refers to (e.g., paura, rabbia). In English you'd usually say 'to control his/her/its [fear/anger]'. The subject (he/she/it) is indicated by context; Italian uses 'sua' for 'his' or 'her'. If the noun is masculine, use 'il suo' instead (e.g., 'di controllare il suo nervosismo'). Common with verbs like 'cercare di' (try to), 'essere in grado di' (to be able to), and progressive forms.
target_language_example: Cercò di controllare la sua paura.
native_language_example: He tried to control his fear.

meaning: to (try) to control the… (feminine plural noun follows)
additional_notes: This is part of the infinitive construction 'cercare di controllare le...' meaning 'to try to control the…'. 'Le' is the feminine plural direct article, so it will be followed by a feminine plural noun (e.g., emozioni). The phrase itself is not standalone — you need a subject and the noun after 'le' to complete the idea.
target_language_example: Lui ha cercato di controllare le emozioni davanti a tutti.
native_language_example: He tried to control his emotions in front of everyone.

meaning: of/from courage; expressing possession or quality related to courage (e.g. 'a show of courage', 'full of courage').
additional_notes: Used after nouns to indicate that something is made of, characterized by, or shows courage: 'un esempio di coraggio' = 'an example of courage'. In exclamations, 'un po' di coraggio!' = 'a bit of courage!' or 'come on, have some courage!'. Can appear in negative constructions: 'manca di coraggio' = 'lacks courage'.
target_language_example: Ha affrontato la prova con molto di coraggio.
native_language_example: He faced the test with a lot of courage.

meaning: used in expressions (e.g., 'voce di corridoio') meaning 'rumor' or 'hearsay' (literally 'of the corridor').
additional_notes: Commonly appears in the phrase 'voce di corridoio' or 'una voce di corridoio' to refer to an unofficial rumor, gossip, or unconfirmed report. It implies information passed informally (like whispered in hallways). Not formal evidence. Use when talking about things you heard but don't know are true.
target_language_example: Ho sentito una voce di corridoio che cambieranno i dirigenti.
native_language_example: I heard a rumor that they will change the managers.

meaning: quickly; in a hurry; at speed.
additional_notes: Common adverbial phrase meaning to do something hurriedly or quickly. Can describe running physically (coming 'running') or acting in a rush (doing things 'in a hurry'). Often used after a verb: 'venire di corsa' = 'to come running'. Neutral register; very common in spoken and written Italian.
target_language_example: Sono arrivato di corsa perché ero in ritardo.
native_language_example: I arrived in a hurry because I was late.

meaning: 'about what' or 'what ... about' (used before a verb to ask or refer to the topic someone is speaking/acting about).
additional_notes: Commonly appears in questions and statements with verbs like parlare (to speak) or sapere (to know). Word-by-word: di (of/about) + cosa (what) + sta (he/she/it is / you formal are). Often continued by a gerund or present participle (e.g., 'di cosa sta parlando' = 'what he/she is talking about'). Used to ask for or refer to the subject/topic of someone's speech or thought.
target_language_example: Di cosa sta parlando il professore?
native_language_example: What is the professor talking about?

meaning: things
additional_notes: Used after a quantity or expression (e.g., un paio di, molte di) or alone to refer vaguely to items, matters, or things. Common in phrases like "un paio di cose" (a couple of things) or "ho delle cose da dire" (I have things to say). Not a standalone phrase meaning anything without context; it attaches to a preceding noun or number.
target_language_example: Ho un paio di cose da insegnarti.
native_language_example: I have a couple of things to teach you.

meaning: of which/whom he/she/it had (used to introduce a relative clause referring to something previously mentioned, with past-tense auxiliary 'aveva').
additional_notes: A combination of the relative pronoun 'di cui' (meaning 'of which' or 'of whom') and the imperfect of 'avere' ('aveva' = 'he/she/it had' or 'you formal had'). 'Di cui' links back to a noun already mentioned; 'aveva' gives past or ongoing context. Typical in sentences like: 'Il libro di cui aveva parlato' = 'the book he had talked about'.
target_language_example: Il film di cui aveva parlato era interessante.
native_language_example: The film he had talked about was interesting.

meaning: from the heart; sincerely / heartily (depending on context).
additional_notes: Used in two main senses: 1) idiomatic: 'di cuore' after thanks or wishes means 'sincerely' or 'heartfelt' (e.g., Grazie di cuore = Thank you very much / Thank you from the bottom of my heart). 2) describing emotion or action: 'ridere di cuore' = laugh heartily/with genuine feeling. Note: do not confuse with 'attacco di cuore' which literally means 'heart attack' — there 'di cuore' is part of the noun phrase referring to the organ, not the idiom meaning 'sincerely'.
target_language_example: Ti auguro buona fortuna di cuore.
native_language_example: I wish you good luck from the bottom of my heart.

meaning: to feed (someone or an animal) / to give food to
additional_notes: This is the infinitive phrase used after verbs like dimenticare/scordare (to forget) or modal verbs: e.g. 'Ho dimenticato di dare da mangiare...' = 'I forgot to feed...'. Literally 'to give to eat'. Commonly used for pets, children, or plants (colloquially).
target_language_example: Ho dimenticato di dare da mangiare al gatto stamattina.
native_language_example: I forgot to feed the cat this morning.

meaning: 'of debts' / 'in debt' (used to say someone has debts)
additional_notes: Often appears after quantity words (e.g., un sacco di, una montagna di, un paio di) to indicate an amount of debt. In English you would usually say 'in debt' or 'has a lot of debts' rather than literally 'of debts.' The phrase di + noun is a common way to link quantities to what is being counted.
target_language_example: Ha un sacco di debiti da pagare.
native_language_example: He has a lot of debts to pay.

meaning: 'of resignation' or 'resignation (letter)'.
additional_notes: Used after words like 'lettera' to indicate something related to resigning from a job or position. Common collocation: 'lettera di dimissioni' = 'resignation letter'. 'Dimissioni' is plural in Italian but refers to the act of resigning. You usually see it in formal contexts (work, politics).
target_language_example: Ho preparato la mia lettera di dimissioni e la consegnerò domani.
native_language_example: I prepared my resignation letter and I will hand it in tomorrow.

meaning: of something fun / something fun (descriptive phrase)
additional_notes: Used after words like 'qualcosa', 'niente', or 'nulla' to describe that the thing is 'fun' or 'entertaining'. 'Di' here links the noun/pronoun to an adjective. Common in questions and statements: 'qualcosa di divertente' = 'something fun'. Word order: noun (qualcosa) + di + adjective.
target_language_example: Cerchiamo qualcosa di divertente da fare stasera.
native_language_example: We're looking for something fun to do tonight.

meaning: of example; example (used to label or describe something as an example).
additional_notes: Commonly used after a noun to indicate that the item is an example or sample. Often appears in phrases like "frase di esempio" (example sentence) or "campione di esempio" (sample). It is literal and compositional: di = of, esempio = example. Use to mark illustrative or non-final content.
target_language_example: Questa è una frase di esempio per l'esercizio.
native_language_example: This is an example sentence for the exercise.

meaning: of experience; relating to experience (often used to describe amount or type of experience).
additional_notes: Commonly follows nouns to indicate possession or quality related to experience (e.g., 'mancanza di esperienza' = lack of experience, 'livello di esperienza' = level of experience). Used in contexts like jobs, skills, or personal encounters. Not idiomatic — literal composition of 'of' + 'experience'.
target_language_example: Ha bisogno di più anni di esperienza per quel ruolo.
native_language_example: He needs more years of experience for that role.

meaning: 'to be washed' (passive infinitive: expresses that something, feminine singular, needs or should be washed).
additional_notes: Passive infinitive construction: di + essere + past participle (lavata = washed, feminine singular). Commonly follows verbs/phrases expressing necessity or obligation (e.g., ha bisogno di, deve, bisogna). The past participle agrees in gender and number with the noun it refers to (lavato/lavata/lavati/lavate). You can replace lavare with other verbs to form similar passive phrases (es. di essere riparata = to be repaired).
target_language_example: Ha bisogno di essere lavata.
native_language_example: It needs to be washed.

meaning: to be proven wrong / to be contradicted (female plural).
additional_notes: Passive infinitive phrase: 'di' + infinitive 'essere' + past participle 'smentite' (feminine plural). Used when speakers (female or a mixed group referred to as feminine) expect or hope that their statements will be contradicted or shown to be false. Commonly appears after verbs like aspettare/attendere (to wait) or sperare (to hope). Change gender/number of 'smentite' as needed: smentito (m. sing.), smentita (f. sing.), smentiti (m. pl.).
target_language_example: Aspettiamo di essere smentite da nuovi dati.
native_language_example: We are waiting to be proven wrong by new data.

meaning: 'to be proven wrong' or 'to be contradicted' (literally 'to be denied/refuted').
additional_notes: This phrase uses the infinitive passive construction (essere + past participle) after 'di' and often follows verbs of waiting, expecting or fearing (es. aspettare, attendere, temere). It expresses the idea of anticipating that someone or something will show that your statement, prediction, or belief is incorrect. 'Smentiti' is plural masculine (can be used generically or with plural subjects).
target_language_example: Aspettiamo con trepidazione di essere smentiti.
native_language_example: We wait with trepidation to be proven wrong.

meaning: to be home by (a certain time); used to tell someone to return home before a deadline.
additional_notes: This phrase is the verb phrase used after verbs like dire (to tell) to give an instruction about being at home by a specific time. 'Entro' means 'by' or 'no later than'. The full construction often appears as 'dire di essere a casa entro [ora]'. Time expression follows 'entro' (e.g., entro mezzanotte = by midnight).
target_language_example: Ti dico di essere a casa entro le dieci stasera.
native_language_example: I'm telling you to be home by ten tonight.

meaning: 'to be already' (used in reported speech: 'that [someone] is already...').
additional_notes: Commonly appears after verbs of saying (dire, raccontare) to report what someone told you. 'Di' introduces an infinitive clause with 'essere' (to be); 'già' means 'already' and goes before the adjective or past participle (e.g. sposato/a). Agreement (sposato vs sposata) matches the subject being described. Used for reported speech: English often uses 'that' or 'to be' (e.g. 'told me (that) she was already...').
target_language_example: Mi ha detto di essere già pronto.
native_language_example: He/She told me that he/she was already ready.

meaning: a phrase used to report someone's state or quality: 'to be very...' (used after verbs like pensare/dire).
additional_notes: This sequence appears when reporting what someone thinks or says about themselves. It combines the preposition 'di' (introducing a subordinate clause), the infinitive 'essere' (to be), and 'molto' (very). Common verbs before it: pensare di, dire di, credere di. You will usually see it followed by an adjective (stanco, felice, fortunato, occupato).
target_language_example: Credo di essere molto stanco oggi.
native_language_example: I believe I am very tired today.

meaning: 'to be (allowed/entitled/qualified) to' in expressions like 'Who do you think you are to...?'
additional_notes: Used in questions that challenge someone's right, authority, or entitlement to do or say something. Common structure: Chi (credi/pensi) di essere per + infinitive or per + verb phrase. Often expresses indignation or disbelief. Equivalent English: "Who do you think you are to..."
target_language_example: Chi credi di essere per dirmi come vivere la mia vita?
native_language_example: Who do you think you are to tell me how to live my life?

meaning: to be here / of being here (used after verbs like 'permesso' or expressions of thanks).
additional_notes: Commonly appears after verbs or nouns that require 'di' + infinitive (e.g., 'permesso di essere qua' = permission to be here) or after 'grazie' to thank someone for being present ('grazie di essere qua'). 'Qua' is informal for 'here' (vs. 'qui').
target_language_example: Sono felice di essere qua oggi.
native_language_example: I'm happy to be here today.

meaning: to be his/her (someone's) — used after verbs like chiedere/cercare to indicate 'to be his/her [role]'.
additional_notes: This is a fragment combining the infinitive 'essere' (to be) with the possessive adjective 'sua' (his/her/its, feminine) and the preposition 'di' used after verbs that take an infinitive (e.g., chiedere di, cercare di). In the examples the full idea is 'to be his/her mother/friend'. 'Sua' agrees with the noun that follows (suo/sua/suoi/sue depending on gender and number of the thing possessed). In English you'd translate the whole phrase with the verb + 'to be' + possessive (e.g., 'asked me to be her friend').
target_language_example: Mi ha chiesto di essere sua insegnante.
native_language_example: She asked me to be her teacher.

meaning: 'in danger of extinction' / 'endangered (becoming extinct)'.
additional_notes: Used after nouns (often with 'in via') to say a species or thing is facing extinction. Common collocation: 'in via di estinzione' = 'endangered'. Can be used with animals, plants, or species. Typical structure: 'una specie in via di estinzione' or 'è in via di estinzione.'
target_language_example: Quella rana è in via di estinzione nel nostro paese.
native_language_example: That frog is endangered in our country.

meaning: a short sequence used to introduce an infinitive action (to do/make) followed by a feminine plural direct object (the ...); literally 'to do the...'.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom but the combination of the preposition 'di' + infinitive 'fare' + feminine plural article 'le'. It appears when a verb or expression requires 'di' before an infinitive (e.g., 'suggerire di fare') and the action takes a feminine plural object (le valigie, le stesse cose, le riprese). The exact translation depends on the noun that follows: 'di fare le valigie' = 'to pack the suitcases' (or 'to pack up'), 'di fare le stesse cose' = 'to do the same things', 'di fare le riprese' = 'to make/do the recordings/shots'.
target_language_example: Mi ha detto di fare le pulizie prima di uscire.
native_language_example: He told me to do the cleaning before going out.

meaning: 'to do that' or 'to do what/that (something)' (used after verbs or expressions to introduce the action someone does or is able/unable to do).
additional_notes: This is a combination: 'di' (part of an infinitive construction), 'fare' (to do/make) and 'quello' (that/what). It commonly appears after verbs like credere, essere capace/essere in grado, finire, impedire, dire, etc., and refers back to a previously mentioned action or to a generic action ('that thing'). In English it often corresponds to 'to do that', 'to do what...', or 'to do what we asked (them) to do.' The phrase is compositional and literal—translate the parts directly when possible.
target_language_example: Non so se sono capace di fare quello che chiede il capo.
native_language_example: I don't know if I'm able to do what the boss asks.

meaning: to do it (by oneself) / to do it alone
additional_notes: This phrase combines 'di fare' (to do) in the infinitive with 'lo' (it) and 'da' + 'solo/a' implied after it: in the examples the full idea is 'di farlo da solo/da sola' = 'to do it by himself/herself'. Use 'da solo' for a male subject and 'da sola' for a female subject. Common after verbs like 'dire', 'essere in grado', 'avere bisogno', 'avere intenzione' to express doing something alone or without help.
target_language_example: Non voglio aiuto: posso di farlo da solo.
native_language_example: I don't want help: I can do it by myself.

meaning: in fact / actually / as a matter of fact
additional_notes: Used to state a fact that may contrast with expectations, clarify reality, or confirm something. Common at start of a sentence or clause and can be followed by a comma. Similar to 'in realtà' or 'effettivamente'.
target_language_example: Di fatto, non avevo più tempo per finire il progetto.
native_language_example: In fact, I didn't have time to finish the project.

meaning: made of iron; (figuratively) very strong, tough, or unflinching.
additional_notes: Literally means 'of iron' and is used both literally (an object made of iron) and figuratively (a person with great strength, courage, or emotional toughness — e.g., 'cuore di ferro' = 'heart of iron'). Context shows literal use for a piece of iron and idiomatic use about a person. Placement: usually follows the noun (pezzo di ferro, cuore di ferro).
target_language_example: Ha le gambe di ferro dopo anni di lavoro duro.
native_language_example: He has legs of iron after years of hard work.

meaning: beside; next to; alongside.
additional_notes: Used to indicate physical position next to someone or something. Often appears as 'di fianco a' + noun (e.g. 'di fianco a lui' = 'next to him'). Can be used alone in short phrases (e.g. 'Proprio di fianco' = 'Right next to it/him/her').
target_language_example: Mi sono seduto di fianco a Maria.
native_language_example: I sat down next to Maria.

meaning: 'trusted' / 'of trust' — indicates someone or something reliable or related to trust.
