additional_notes: Used to describe a person, object, or relationship that is trustworthy or relied upon. Can appear after nouns (e.g., 'uomo di fiducia' = 'trusted man/agent') or in phrases about trust (e.g., 'problemi di fiducia' = 'trust issues'). Not to be confused with 'fiducia' on its own meaning 'confidence' or 'trust' in abstract contexts.
target_language_example: Ho bisogno di una persona di fiducia per custodire le chiavi.
native_language_example: I need a trusted person to hold the keys.

meaning: of signing the (masculine singular noun) — part of an infinitive phrase indicating the action 'to sign the ...'.
additional_notes: This is not a standalone phrase but a sequence inside a sentence: 'di' can introduce an infinitive after certain verbs or expressions (e.g., 'ha deciso di firmare il contratto' = 'he decided to sign the contract'). 'Firmare' is the infinitive 'to sign'. 'Il' is the masculine singular definite article ('the') and will agree with the noun that follows (il contratto, il documento). You will see similar forms with other articles (di firmare la, di firmare l', di firmare i, di firmare gli).
target_language_example: Ha deciso di firmare il contratto domani.
native_language_example: He decided to sign the contract tomorrow.

meaning: to sign his/her (name) / to sign one's (name).
additional_notes: This is part of the infinitive construction 'dimenticare/ricordare/scordare/rifiutarsi di firmare il suo nome' — literally 'to forget/refuse to sign his/her name'. In Italian the possessive + noun (il suo nome) agrees normally with the noun, not the owner; for a person you might also hear 'firmare il proprio nome' (sign one's own name). Use 'di firmare' after verbs that require 'di' before another infinitive (e.g., dimenticare di, ricordare di, rifiutarsi di).
target_language_example: Ho dimenticato di firmare il suo nome sul modulo.
native_language_example: I forgot to sign his/her name on the form.

meaning: fundamental / underlying; (also) background (noise, context).
additional_notes: Used to indicate something deep-rooted or underlying (problema di fondo = underlying problem). Can also mean 'background' when referring to noise, context, or setting (rumore di fondo = background noise). Context determines translation.
target_language_example: Il vero problema di fondo è la mancanza di comunicazione.
native_language_example: The real underlying problem is the lack of communication.

meaning: temporary, makeshift, or improvised (lit. 'of luck' but used for something put together quickly or as a stopgap).
additional_notes: Often used after a noun to describe something done or made roughly, cheaply, or temporarily — e.g. una soluzione di fortuna (a makeshift solution), una sistemazione di fortuna (a temporary arrangement). It suggests it's not ideal but works for the moment.
target_language_example: Abbiamo trovato una sedia di fortuna per tutti gli ospiti.
native_language_example: We found a makeshift chair for all the guests.

meaning: of strength; indicating force, power, or intensity
additional_notes: Used in different contexts: describing physical strength or talents (punti di forza = strengths/strong points), the intensity of wind or force (vento di forza moderata = wind of moderate strength), demonstrations or acts of force (dimostrazione di forza), or power relations (rapporti di forza = power relations). Often part of fixed phrases (punti di forza, dimostrazione di forza, rapporti di forza).
target_language_example: Ha mostrato i suoi punti di forza durante il colloquio.
native_language_example: He showed his strengths during the interview.

meaning: in front (of); facing; opposite
additional_notes: Used to indicate physical position (in front of, opposite) or figurative confrontation (facing someone/something). Commonly followed by 'a' or 'al/la/alla' when specifying the object: 'di fronte a qualcuno/qualcosa' or 'di fronte al negozio'. Can also be used alone as 'sono di fronte' (I'm in front).
target_language_example: Il bar è di fronte alla stazione.
native_language_example: The café is in front of the station.

meaning: of smoking two years ago / about having smoked two years ago
additional_notes: This phrase is not a fixed expression but a short fragment that would appear in sentences referring to someone having smoked (or started/stopped smoking) two years ago. 'Di' often links to a verb or noun (e.g., 'ho il ricordo di fumare due anni fa' — I have the memory of smoking two years ago) or after verbs that govern an infinitive ('ho smesso di fumare due anni fa' — I stopped smoking two years ago). The key parts: 'fumare' = to smoke; 'due anni fa' = two years ago.
target_language_example: Ho smesso di fumare due anni fa.
native_language_example: I quit smoking two years ago.

meaning: for theft / of theft (used to indicate the crime of theft)
additional_notes: Used after verbs like essere (to be) or accusare (to accuse) to state the crime someone committed or is accused of. Equivalent to English 'for theft' or 'of theft'. Common in legal or formal contexts. The noun 'furto' means 'theft' (petty stealing); for 'robbery' you'd use 'rapina'.
target_language_example: La polizia lo ha arrestato di furto.
native_language_example: The police arrested him for theft.

meaning: about playing mahjong / to play mahjong (with 'di' introducing a verb or phrase: 'about' or part of an infinitive structure).
additional_notes: This phrase includes the preposition 'di' + the verb 'giocare' (to play) + the game name 'mahjong'. 'Giocare a mahjong' means 'to play mahjong'. When you see 'di giocare a mahjong' it often appears after verbs or expressions that require 'di' before an infinitive or noun clause (e.g., 'parlare di giocare a mahjong' = 'to talk about playing mahjong', or 'ho deciso di giocare a mahjong' = 'I decided to play mahjong').
target_language_example: Abbiamo parlato di giocare a mahjong questo fine settimana.
native_language_example: We talked about playing mahjong this weekend.

meaning: of game / related to play (used to describe type or relation to a game)
additional_notes: Commonly used after a noun like tipo, razza, compagno to indicate 'of the game' or 'related to the game' (e.g., tipo di gioco = type of game; compagno di gioco = playing partner). 'Di' is the preposition 'of' and combines with 'gioco' (game/play).
target_language_example: Quale tipo di gioco preferisci?
native_language_example: Which type of game do you prefer?

meaning: of days / (part of time expressions) 'days' used in phrases like 'a couple of days', 'in a few days'.
additional_notes: Commonly appears in time expressions with quantities or phrases: 'un paio di giorni' (a couple of days), 'fra/tra ... giorni' (in ... days), 'un paio di giorni fa' (a couple of days ago). 'Di' links the quantity to 'giorni'. Use 'giorno' (singular) after 'un giorno' or numbers ending with 1 (except 11); otherwise use 'giorni'.
target_language_example: Resto qui per un paio di giorni.
native_language_example: I'll stay here for a couple of days.

meaning: already (used to express surprise that something has happened sooner than expected).
additional_notes: Common adverbial phrase. Often used alone or in short questions to show surprise or disbelief (e.g., 'Di già?' = 'Already?'). Placed after a verb or at the end of a question. Tone can be neutral or slightly surprised/annoyed depending on context.
target_language_example: Te ne vai di già?
native_language_example: Are you leaving already?

meaning: by far; far and away (used to emphasize a large difference)
additional_notes: An adverbial phrase used before comparatives or superlatives to stress that something is much more (better, worse, bigger, etc.). Common in both spoken and written Italian. Equivalent to 'far and away' or 'by far' in English.
target_language_example: È di gran lunga il miglior studente della classe.
native_language_example: He is by far the best student in the class.

meaning: 'of mercy' / 'mercy' (used in legal/administrative contexts: requests for clemency); also an idiom meaning 'please' or used to express surprise/politeness.
additional_notes: In the provided examples, 'istanze di grazia' means 'requests for clemency' or 'petitions for mercy' (legal/official). Alone, 'di grazia' can appear in polite phrases ('mi dai, di grazia...') or in surprised/exasperated questions ('Di grazia, cosa intendi?') — context determines meaning. For beginners: when you see 'istanze di grazia' treat it as a fixed legal phrase = 'clemency petitions'.
target_language_example: Ci sono tre istanze di grazia da valutare oggi.
native_language_example: There are three clemency petitions to review today.

meaning: big; important; major (used after qualcosa/qualcuno to mean 'something/someone big or significant').
additional_notes: Commonly appears after words like qualcosa/qualcuno (e.g., qualcosa di grosso) to indicate something large in size, importance, impact, or seriousness. Tone depends on context: can be neutral (large size) or imply a major event/problem/opportunity. Not used alone—it's a modifier following a noun or pronoun.
target_language_example: Sento che sta arrivando qualcosa di grosso.
native_language_example: I feel like something big is coming.

meaning: of/ to drive; marks the infinitive 'guidare' after verbs or expressions (e.g., 'permittere di guidare' = 'to allow someone to drive').
additional_notes: This is the preposition 'di' + the infinitive 'guidare' (to drive). In Italian, certain verbs, adjectives, and expressions are followed by 'di' + infinitive to link actions (e.g., 'permettere di', 'capace di', 'dire di'). The construction does not translate word-for-word in every case; often it becomes 'to do something' or 'to be able to do something' in English. Use 'di' before the verb when the governing word requires it.
target_language_example: Mi ha permesso di guidare la sua macchina.
native_language_example: He/she allowed me to drive his/her car.

meaning: of identity; relating to identity (used in phrases like 'documento di identità' or 'furto di identità').
additional_notes: Commonly appears after a noun to indicate the type or relation to identity. Examples: 'documento di identità' = identity document/ID; 'furto di identità' = identity theft; 'verifica di identità' = identity verification. Not used alone; usually part of a compound noun or phrase.
target_language_example: Puoi mostrare il tuo documento di identità per la verifica di identità?
native_language_example: Can you show your identity document for identity verification?

meaning: 'of idiots' — used after a noun to insult a group (a bunch/pack of idiots).
additional_notes: A derogatory phrase used to call a group foolish or stupid. Often follows words like 'banda', 'mucchio', 'branco', or 'razza' to form insults (e.g. 'banda di idioti' = 'a bunch of idiots'). Strong informal and rude language; avoid in polite situations.
target_language_example: Un gruppo di idioti ha lasciato la porta aperta.
native_language_example: A group of idiots left the door open.

meaning: to mail/drop this (letter/package).
additional_notes: Used after verbs like ricordarsi/ricordare (to remember/to remind) to ask someone to put a letter or parcel in the mailbox or post it. Imbucare = put into the mailbox/send by post. 'Questa' agrees with a feminine noun understood from context (usually 'lettera').
target_language_example: Per favore, ricordati di imbucare questa lettera domani mattina.
native_language_example: Please remember to mail this letter tomorrow morning.

meaning: to wear a (piece of clothing) — used after verbs like dire (to tell) or avere bisogno (to need) to indicate wearing one item.
additional_notes: This is a verb phrase: 'di' introduces the infinitive 'indossare' (to wear) and 'una' is the indefinite article 'a' agreeing in gender with a feminine noun (e.g. una cravatta = a tie). You'll often see it after verbs that require an infinitive: 'dire di indossare una...' (to tell someone to wear a...), 'avere bisogno di indossare una...' (to need to wear a...). Change the article to 'un' for masculine nouns (di indossare un), or change the noun gender/number as needed (di indossare il/la/lo/le/i).
target_language_example: Le ho detto di indossare una giacca.
native_language_example: I told her to wear a jacket.

meaning: to tell (someone) to let (the) ... in (literal components: 'to let enter the')
additional_notes: This phrase is part of an indirect command: 'Dille/ditele/ditegli/Le dica...' = 'Tell her/them/him/you (formal) to...'. 'di lasciare entrare il' introduces what should be allowed inside (e.g. 'il cane' = the dog). Replace 'il' with the appropriate article (la, i, gli, etc.) to match the noun. Common in spoken and written instructions.
target_language_example: Dille di lasciare entrare il gatto.
native_language_example: Tell her to let the cat in.

meaning: to leave him/it (alone); to let him/it be.
additional_notes: Di lasciarlo is the infinitive construction with the verb lasciare + direct object pronoun lo (him/it) preceded by the subordinating preposition di. It often follows verbs of saying, asking, promising, or commanding (e.g., dire, chiedere, promettere) and means 'to leave him/it' or 'to let him/it do something' depending on context. 'Lasciarlo in pace' = leave him alone/in peace; 'lasciarlo andare' = let him go. The pronoun lo can refer to a person (masculine) or a masculine/neutral thing.
target_language_example: Ti consiglio di lasciarlo perdere.
native_language_example: I advise you to leave him/it alone.

meaning: tell/ask someone to leave me (alone); 'di' introduces a command/request, 'lasciarmi da' appears in set phrase meaning 'leave me' + adjective (solo/sola).
additional_notes: This sequence appears in sentences where someone tells or asks another person to 'leave me alone.' Grammatically: verb of saying/requesting (dire, chiedere) + di + lasciarmi + da + adjective (solo/sola). In modern usage you can often omit 'da' and say 'lasciarmi solo/sola' — both are understood. Gender of the speaker affects the adjective (solo = male speaker, sola = female).
target_language_example: Gli ho detto di lasciarmi da sola.
native_language_example: I told him to leave me alone.

meaning: of washing the (plural masculine noun).
additional_notes: This is a fragment that combines the preposition 'di' (of), the infinitive verb 'lavare' (to wash), and the plural masculine definite article 'i' (the). It commonly appears inside larger sentences to indicate purpose, instruction, or possession related to washing multiple items (e.g., 'la macchina di lavare i piatti' is incorrect — correct would be 'la macchina per lavare i piatti' — but you might see 'di lavare i vestiti' after verbs or nouns that require 'di' + infinitive). Pay attention to article agreement: 'i' is used before masculine plural nouns (i piatti, i vestiti).
target_language_example: Ho bisogno di lavare i piatti dopo cena.
native_language_example: I need to wash the dishes after dinner.

meaning: of/for reading the book that... (part of a clause meaning 'to finish reading the book that...')
additional_notes: This phrase appears in constructions like "finire di leggere il libro che..." meaning someone finished reading a specific book identified by a relative clause ("che..." = "that.../which..."). "Che" introduces the relative clause giving more information about the book (who gave it, when, etc.). The phrase itself isn't used alone — it's a segment inside larger verbs/phrases (e.g., "ha finito di leggere il libro che le ho prestato").
target_language_example: Hai finito di leggere il libro che ti ho prestato?
native_language_example: Did you finish reading the book that I lent you?

meaning: "of them is" / "one of them is" — used to indicate that one (or none) among a group has a characteristic or performs an action. Often appears after a quantifier or negative (e.g. nessuno, nessuna, uno).
additional_notes: Commonly used with expressions like 'uno/una', 'nessuno/nessuna', 'alcuni/alcune' or numerals: the quantifier usually precedes 'di loro' (e.g. 'Uno di loro è...','Nessuna di loro è...'). The verb agrees in number and gender with the noun following the phrase (singular with 'uno/nessuno', plural with numerals/alcuni). 'Di loro è' can often be translated literally as 'of them is' or more naturally as 'one of them is' / 'none of them is'.
target_language_example: Nessuno di loro è presente.
native_language_example: None of them is present.

meaning: a sequence of words meaning 'to eat the' (di + mangiare + il) — appears in contexts like 'the need/desire to eat the ...' or after verbs/nouns that require 'di' before an infinitive.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but a common combination: 'di' can introduce an infinitive (e.g., dopo 'volevo di mangiare' is nonstandard; correct is 'di mangiare' after certain nouns/expressions like 'ho voglia di mangiare' — 'voglia di mangiare il pane' = 'a desire to eat the bread'). The proper structure depends on the preceding word: many verbs use 'di' + infinitive (e.g., 'ho bisogno di mangiare il pranzo'), while others use the infinitive without 'di'. Be careful: Italian normally says 'ho voglia di mangiare il gelato' (I want to eat the ice cream).
target_language_example: Ho voglia di mangiare il gelato.
native_language_example: I feel like eating the ice cream.

meaning: 'of the sea' / 'sea- (related to seafood, sea creatures, sea-themed)'.
additional_notes: Commonly used to describe things that come from or relate to the sea. In food contexts, 'di mare' often means 'seafood' (e.g., 'frutti di mare' = 'seafood/seafood platter'). It can modify nouns (conchiglie di mare = seashells) and is widely used in everyday speech. Gender and number agreement depends on the noun it describes (di mare does not change form).
target_language_example: Preferisco la pasta di mare al pesce alla griglia.
native_language_example: I prefer seafood pasta to grilled fish.

meaning: 'of medicine' / 'medical' (used to show relation to medicine, e.g. schools, books, studies)
additional_notes: A prepositional phrase combining di (of) + medicina (medicine). Commonly used to indicate that something belongs to, is about, or is related to the field of medicine: scuola di medicina (medical school), libri di medicina (medical books), studentessa di medicina (medical student). Word order: di medicina follows the noun it modifies. No article is required if the noun already appears (e.g. scuole di medicina).
target_language_example: Lavora in un ospedale di medicina generale.
native_language_example: She works in a general medicine hospital.

meaning: of apple / apple (as a type of) — used to indicate something made from or related to apple (e.g., apple juice, apple seed).
additional_notes: A partitive or descriptive phrase: 'di' + noun shows the material, flavor, origin, or type. Common with food/drink (succo di mela = apple juice). Usage depends on context and article: 'del succo di mela' (some apple juice), 'il succo di mela' (the apple juice), 'un bicchiere di succo di mela' (a glass of apple juice). Not idiomatic—literal meaning.
target_language_example: Vorrei una torta di mela, per favore.
native_language_example: I would like an apple pie, please.

meaning: shitty
additional_notes: A coarse, insulting modifier attached to nouns to express strong contempt or low quality. Equivalent to adding "shitty" after a noun in English (e.g., "shitty job", "shitty tape"). Often used in informal, angry or vulgar speech. Avoid in polite contexts. Can be combined with people (insult), objects, situations, or abstract nouns.
target_language_example: Questo lavoro di merda non finisce mai.
native_language_example: This shitty job never ends.

meaning: 'of messages' (used after quantities or expressions to indicate what is being counted/left)
additional_notes: Commonly appears after words like 'un paio', 'molti', 'alcuni' to specify the item counted (e.g., 'un paio di messaggi' = 'a couple of messages'). Often used in contexts of leaving or receiving messages (telefonate/voicemail). The preposition 'di' links the quantity to the noun; word order is quantity + di + noun.
target_language_example: Ho lasciato un paio di messaggi sul suo telefono.
native_language_example: I left a couple of messages on his phone.

meaning: a fragment meaning 'to put the' or 'of putting the' (part of a verb phrase with direct object)
additional_notes: This is not a standalone phrase but a common sequence: di (of/to) + mettere (to put) + il (the, masc. singular). It appears inside larger constructions like "parlare di mettere il..." (to talk about putting the...) or "l'idea di mettere il tavolo in salotto" (the idea of putting the table in the living room). Pay attention to agreement: il changes to la/lo/i/gli when the noun differs (e.g. di mettere la, di mettere lo, di mettere i).
target_language_example: L'idea di mettere il libro sullo scaffale sembra buona.
native_language_example: The idea of putting the book on the shelf seems good.

meaning: to put the laundry in (e.g. the basket).
additional_notes: This is a verb phrase used after verbs like chiedere (to ask) or dire (to tell). 'Il bucato' means 'the laundry' (clothes to be washed or already washed). The phrase is usually completed by a location (e.g., 'nella cesta' = in the basket). Common in commands or reminders: 'Quante volte devo chiederti di mettere il bucato nella cesta?' = 'How many times do I have to ask you to put the laundry in the basket?'.
target_language_example: Per favore, ricordati di mettere il bucato nella cesta prima di uscire.
native_language_example: Please remember to put the laundry in the basket before you leave.

di mettersi della crema solare ad alta

target_language_multi_word_term: di mettersi della crema solare ad alta
meaning: to put on high (SPF) sunscreen / to apply high-protection sunscreen
additional_notes: This phrase appears in commands or reported speech telling someone to apply sunscreen with high protection (ad alta protezione). 'Mettersi' means 'to put on' (reflexive: to put on oneself). In natural sentences you'd usually include 'protezione' after 'alta' (ad alta protezione) or state the SPF (es. SPF 50). Pronouns and subjects change the verb forms: 'di mettersi' follows verbs like 'dire' in reported commands (Ho detto loro di mettersi...). For direct commands use the imperative: 'Mettiti la crema solare ad alta protezione.'
target_language_example: Ho detto a Marco di mettersi della crema solare ad alta protezione prima di uscire.
native_language_example: I told Marco to put on high-protection sunscreen before going out.

meaning: 'of middle' used in the expression 'di mezza età' meaning 'middle-aged' or in time expressions like 'mezza estate' (mid-.../half...).
additional_notes: Usually appears as part of fixed expressions. Most common: 'di mezza età' = 'middle-aged' (for people). 'Di mezza estate' or 'di mezza notte' can mean 'mid-summer' or 'midnight/around midnight' depending on context. In practice, learners will most often see 'di mezza età' to describe someone's age. Word order: 'una donna di mezza età' = 'a middle-aged woman.'
target_language_example: È la storia di una coppia di mezza età che va in vacanza.
native_language_example: It's the story of a middle-aged couple who go on holiday.

meaning: 'involved', 'in the middle', or 'between/among' (depending on context).
additional_notes: Common multiword expression with a few uses: 1) To say someone/something is 'involved' or 'implicated' (e.g., 'c'è di mezzo un ragazzo' = 'is a boy involved?'). 2) In commands like 'levatevi di mezzo' or 'togliti di mezzo' it means 'get out of the way' or 'remove yourself (from the situation)'. Tone can be neutral when describing involvement and rude/forceful in imperatives. Context determines whether it means 'in the middle/between,' 'involved,' or 'out of the way.'
target_language_example: Non voglio problemi: togli quelle persone di mezzo.
native_language_example: I don't want trouble: get those people out of the way.

meaning: 'fashionable' or 'in fashion'.
additional_notes: Used to describe something that is currently stylish or trendy (clothing, styles, people, etc.). Often follows the noun (e.g., "una gonna di moda") or appears in phrases like "tornare di moda" (to come back into fashion). Can also appear in occupational phrases like "stilista di moda" (fashion designer).
target_language_example: Quella giacca è di moda quest'anno.
native_language_example: That jacket is fashionable this year.

meaning: 'to move' (infinitive with particle; used after verbs/adjectives to indicate ability, obligation, or action).
additional_notes: Literally 'to move oneself'. Appears after verbs or expressions (e.g., poter, essere in grado, smettere, avere bisogno) to form infinitive clauses: 'smettere di muoversi' = 'stop moving', 'essere in grado di muoversi' = 'be able to move'. Used for people or animals moving their body or changing position.
target_language_example: Non riesce più di muoversi dopo l'incidente.
native_language_example: He can no longer move after the accident.

meaning: secretly; stealthily; without being seen or noticed.
additional_notes: Used to describe actions done in secret or stealthily to avoid detection. Common with verbs of movement (entrare, tornare) or verbs like mostrare, prendere. Suitable in both formal and informal contexts. Literal components: 'di' (of) + 'nascosto' (hidden), so compositional in form but functions as an adverbial phrase.
target_language_example: Lui è uscito di nascosto dal lavoro per fare una sorpresa.
native_language_example: He left work secretly to make a surprise.

meaning: one of us should speak (to someone).
additional_notes: Used to suggest that a single person from a group should talk to someone (e.g., Tom, her, them). In Italian the phrase commonly appears as 'una di noi dovrebbe parlare' (for a female group member) or 'uno di noi dovrebbe parlare' (for a male/mixed group). The preposition 'con' + object indicates who they should speak to. It expresses obligation or recommendation (should).
target_language_example: Una di noi dovrebbe parlare con il professore.
native_language_example: One of us should speak with the professor.

meaning: 'of us' + direct object pronoun 'it' (literally: 'of us it').
additional_notes: This sequence appears when talking about people in the group (di noi = 'of us' / 'among us') followed by the clitic direct object pronoun lo ('it' / 'him'). In natural English you would translate the whole phrase as 'most of us will do it', 'many of us do it', 'none of us wanted it', etc. Word order in Italian places the pronoun after the noun phrase (di noi lo). The pronoun agrees in gender/number with the object, not with 'noi'.
target_language_example: Quasi tutti di noi lo capiscono.
native_language_example: Almost all of us understand it.

meaning: 'is one of us' / part of constructions meaning 'one/none of us is...'
additional_notes: Appears in expressions with quantifiers like uno/nessuno/nessuna/alcuni + di noi + è + adjective/noun/phrase. Translation depends on the quantifier: "uno di noi è..." = "one of us is...", "nessuno/nessuna di noi è..." = "none of us is...". Agreement (nessuno/nessuna, bravo/brava) follows gender and number of the omitted noun referring to people. Often used to identify membership or state among a group.
target_language_example: Uno di noi è stanco, ma nessuno di noi è debole.
native_language_example: One of us is tired, but none of us is weak.

meaning: called / with the name; 'by name' or 'named'.
additional_notes: Used to say someone's name or that you know someone only by their name. Often follows a noun (e.g., 'tre ragazzi di nome Tom' = 'three boys named Tom') or a verb of knowing ('conosco... di nome' = 'I only know them by name').
target_language_example: Conosco solo di nome la nuova vicina.
native_language_example: I only know the new neighbor by name.

meaning: to (tell someone) not to say; to instruct someone not to say something.
additional_notes: This is the infinitive construction with a verb of telling/asking (e.g., dire, chiedere, promettere) + 'di' + the negative infinitive 'non dire'. It expresses an instruction, promise, or request that someone refrain from saying something. Common in reported speech: "mi ha detto di non dire..." = "he told me not to say..."
target_language_example: Mi ha consigliato di non dire tutto subito.
native_language_example: He advised me not to say everything right away.

meaning: 'to pretend not to hear' (used after verbs like 'fare finta' = to pretend)
additional_notes: This phrase usually follows verbs such as fare finta (di) or sembrare, and expresses intentionally ignoring someone or something by acting as if you didn't hear. The literal parts are compositional, but the whole is typically used in the fixed expression fare finta di non sentire.
target_language_example: Ha fatto finta di non sentire quando gli ho chiesto aiuto.
native_language_example: He pretended not to hear when I asked him for help.

meaning: 'at night' (during the nighttime)
additional_notes: Used to indicate that something happens during the night hours. Can describe habitual actions (Fa i turni di notte = She works night shifts) or specific times (arrivare di notte = arrive at night). Common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Preferisco studiare di notte quando è silenzioso.
native_language_example: I prefer to study at night when it's quiet.

meaning: 'you're welcome' or 'it's nothing' (used to respond to thanks); can also mean 'about nothing' or 'of nothing' in literal/other uses.
additional_notes: Most commonly used as a short, polite response to grazie (like 'you're welcome' or 'no problem'). Alone it's often said simply as "Di nulla." In other contexts, part of phrases like "lamentarsi di nulla" (to complain about nothing) or "discutere di nulla" (to discuss nothing). Tone and context determine whether it's a fixed polite reply or a literal prepositional phrase.
target_language_example:
—Grazie per il tuo aiuto.
—Di nulla, figurati!
native_language_example:
—Thanks for your help.
—It's nothing, don't mention it!

meaning: again
additional_notes: Means that something happens one more time or returns to a previous state. Very common with verbs: parlare di nuovo = talk again, provare di nuovo = try again. In expressions like di nuovo in piedi, it can mean back on one's feet / standing again.
target_language_example: Proviamo di nuovo più tardi.
native_language_example: Let's try again later.

meaning: 'of every other' / 'than anything else' (used to mean 'more than anything else' or 'before anything else').
additional_notes: Often appears in expressions like "prima di ogni altra cosa" (before anything else) or "più importante di ogni altra cosa" (more important than anything else). It emphasizes priority or superiority over all other things. Common in both formal and everyday speech.
target_language_example: La famiglia viene prima di ogni altra cosa.
native_language_example: Family comes before anything else.

meaning: of something horrible / terrible
additional_notes: Used after verbs or nouns to describe an unspecified terrible event or action. Literally 'of horrible' — the adjective orribile is describing an implied noun (qualcosa di orribile = something horrible). Commonly appears with verbs like succedere, fare, accadere, capitare and with expressions like 'qualcosa di...'.
target_language_example: Sembra che sia successo qualcosa di orribile.
native_language_example: It seems that something horrible happened.

meaning: ‘to park’ (infinitive with the preposition 'di' used after verbs/expressions)
additional_notes: This is the infinitive verb parcheggiare ('to park') preceded by 'di', which appears after certain verbs or expressions (e.g., avere il permesso di, dire di) to introduce the action. Literally 'of to park' but functions like English 'to park' after verbs: Avete avuto il permesso di parcheggiare = You had permission to park. Not a fixed phrase—it's a combination of the preposition + infinitive.
target_language_example: Mi ha chiesto di parcheggiare davanti al negozio.
native_language_example: He asked me to park in front of the shop.

meaning: part of a verb phrase meaning 'to speak (the)' as in 'to speak the French language'.
additional_notes: This combination appears when a verb construction uses the infinitive 'parlare' with the preposition 'di' (e.g. 'dire di', 'pensare di', 'voler essere in grado di') followed by a definite article + language (il francese). In natural Italian you can also say 'parlare francese' (without article). Using 'parlare il/lo/la + language' is common with some speakers and contexts, but omitting the article is more neutral.
target_language_example: Penso di parlare il tedesco abbastanza bene.
native_language_example: I think I speak German quite well.

meaning: on (someone's) side; biased in favor of someone or something.
additional_notes: Used to describe partiality or favoritism. Often appears after verbs or nouns: essere di parte (to be biased), prendere posizione di parte (to take a partisan stance). Can refer to personal bias or political/party allegiance.
target_language_example: Il giudice non dovrebbe essere di parte durante il processo.
native_language_example: The judge should not be biased during the trial.

meaning: 'particularly' / 'of particular ...' — used to single out something specific
additional_notes: Often appears before a noun or adjective to highlight something specific or noteworthy (e.g., di particolare importanza = of particular importance). Can also be used adverbially to mean 'particularly' or 'especially'. Common in formal and neutral registers.
target_language_example: Questa caratteristica è di particolare importanza.
native_language_example: This feature is of particular importance.

meaning: nothing special/to say; nothing in particular to (do/say).
additional_notes: Used after words like 'niente' or 'nulla' to mean 'nothing in particular' about an action (often followed by an infinitive: 'da dire', 'da fare', 'da trascrivere'). Common in replies to questions like 'Hai qualcosa da dire?' or 'C'è qualcosa da segnalare?'. Word order: 'niente/nulla di particolare da + infinitive'.
target_language_example: Non ho niente di particolare da aggiungere.
native_language_example: I don't have anything in particular to add.

meaning: passing through, brief/temporary visit or stop; not staying long.
additional_notes: Used to describe someone or something that is just passing by or stopping briefly. Can refer to people (Sono di passaggio in città — I'm just passing through the city), visits (una visita di passaggio), or things that are temporary. Often interchangeable with 'di passaggio per' + place. Tone: neutral, common in spoken and written Italian.
target_language_example: Sono solo di passaggio, torno domani.
native_language_example: I'm just passing through; I'll be back tomorrow.

meaning: 'pen pal' (used after amico/amica: amico di penna = pen pal).
additional_notes: Literally 'of pen' — used with amico/amica to mean someone you correspond with by letter or email. Common phrases: amico di penna (male pen pal), amica di penna (female pen pal). It's a compositional expression (pen + of) but the full meaning is idiomatic when combined with amico/amica.
target_language_example: Vorrei essere la tua amica di penna.
native_language_example: I would like to be your pen pal.

meaning: by itself; in itself; inherently (without other factors).
additional_notes: Used to say that something considered alone has a certain quality (often neutral), but that other factors may change the overall judgment. Common in formal and everyday speech. Usually follows the noun or adjective it qualifies: 'X non è ... di per sé.'
target_language_example: Questa decisione non è sbagliata di per sé, ma le conseguenze possono esserlo.
native_language_example: This decision isn't wrong in itself, but the consequences may be.

meaning: in person
additional_notes: Used to ask or say whether someone met or saw a person face-to-face, or did something personally rather than via phone/online/secondhand. Can translate as "in person" (physical presence) or "personally" (done by oneself). Often follows the person: e.g. "Hai visto Marco di persona?"
target_language_example: Hai parlato con lei di persona o solo al telefono?
native_language_example: Did you speak with her in person or only on the phone?

meaning: 'a burden' / 'of weight' (depends on context).
additional_notes: Two main uses: 1) Idiomatic: 'essere di peso a qualcuno' = to be a burden/annoyance to someone. 2) Literal/neutral: used with aumentare/problema to talk about body weight or weight-related issues (increase in weight / weight problem). Context tells which meaning is intended.
target_language_example: Non voglio essere di peso alla tua famiglia.
native_language_example: I don't want to be a burden to your family.

meaning: 'to be liked by' or 'to please' (used with a person as the indirect object: piacere a qualcuno).
additional_notes: In Italian the verb piacere works differently than English. Instead of saying 'I like someone', you say 'to be pleasing to someone' (piacere a qualcuno). Phrases like 'pensare di piacere a Tom' mean 'to think that Tom likes me'. The structure is: [subject that is liked] + piacere + a + [person who likes]. When used after verbs of interest (interessarsi di) it appears as 'interessarsi di piacere (a qualcuno)' — 'to care about pleasing someone'.
target_language_example: Spero di piacere ai miei nuovi colleghi.
native_language_example: I hope to be liked by my new colleagues.

meaning: of/from a pistol; (used to describe) pistol-related (e.g., a gunshot, wound).
additional_notes: Commonly appears after words like colpo (colpo di pistola = gunshot) or ferita (ferita da colpo di pistola = gunshot wound). Literally 'of pistol' or 'from a pistol'. Used to indicate the source or type (that something was caused by a pistol).
target_language_example: Ha trovato una ferita di pistola sul campo.
native_language_example: He found a pistol-related wound on the field.

meaning: '(I/you/he/etc.) like ... more' — used to compare preferences (literally 'more the ...').
additional_notes: This phrase appears in comparative sentences where you say you prefer one thing over another. Word order: 'Mi/piacciono di più le X (delle Y)' or 'A me piacciono di più le X.' Often followed by 'di' or 'delle' to introduce what it's preferred to (e.g. 'di/le mele' or 'delle mele'). The verb agrees with the noun (piace/piacciono). 'Di più' alone means 'more' or 'anymore', and here it modifies preference.
target_language_example: Mi piacciono di più le pasta senza carne.
native_language_example: I like pasta without meat more.

meaning: more
additional_notes: Usually means 'more' or 'to a greater extent'. After verbs it often stands alone: leggere di più = 'read more'. In sentences like avere bisogno di più tempo, the di is required by the earlier expression, and più gives the idea of 'more' before the noun.
target_language_example: Voglio studiare di più quest'anno.
native_language_example: I want to study more this year.

meaning: of plagiarism / for plagiarism (accused of plagiarism)
additional_notes: Used after verbs like 'accusare' (to accuse) or 'essere accusato/a' to indicate the charge of plagiarism. 'Plagio' is a masculine noun meaning 'plagiarism'. Common in academic or legal contexts. In English you'd usually say 'accused of plagiarism' or 'charged with plagiarism.'
target_language_example: L'università mi ha sospeso per essere stato accusato di plagio.
native_language_example: The university suspended me for being accused of plagiarism.

meaning: of little / not much; slightly (used to downplay amount, value, quality, or degree)
additional_notes: Commonly used to soften or minimize something. Can modify nouns (un vestito di poco valore — a dress of little value), adjectives or adverbs (una cosa di poco conto — a trivial thing), or to mean 'a little' in expressions (sono arrivato di poco — I arrived a little late/just recently). Often placed after the noun or expression it qualifies. Tone can be neutral or dismissive depending on context.
target_language_example: È un regalo di poco valore, ma fatto con il cuore.
native_language_example: It's a gift of little value, but made with heart.

meaning: to take out (something, e.g. the trash).
additional_notes: Used after verbs like dimenticare/scordare (to forget) or modal verbs: 'si è dimenticato di portare fuori...' = 'he forgot to take out...'. 'Portare fuori' is a separable-like verb phrase meaning to carry something outside (trash, dog, etc.). Commonly used for 'pattume' or 'spazzatura' (garbage/trash).
target_language_example: Si è dimenticata di portare fuori la spazzatura questa mattina.
native_language_example: She forgot to take out the trash this morning.

meaning: to bring the (feminine singular) — used after verbs that introduce a request or command (e.g., 'ask someone to bring the...').
additional_notes: This phrase combines the infinitive 'portare' (to bring) with the preposition 'di' used after verbs like 'chiedere' (to ask) or 'dire' (to tell) to introduce an action someone should do. 'La' is the feminine singular definite article (the) and agrees with a feminine noun (e.g., 'la chitarra', 'la tua faccia'). Change the article for masculine nouns ('il'/'lo') or use possessives as in the examples ('sua', 'tua'). Word order: [verb] + a + [person] + di portare la + [noun].
target_language_example: Chiedi a Marco di portare la torta alla festa.
native_language_example: Ask Marco to bring the cake to the party.

meaning: 'to bring/take it' (used after verbs that require 'di' + infinitive: 'to bring/take it')
additional_notes: Combines the preposition 'di' (used after certain verbs like 'decidere', 'chiedere', 'dire' + infinitive) + 'portare' (to bring/take) + object pronoun 'lo' (it/he). Use when referring to bringing or taking something/someone previously mentioned. Word order: the pronoun attaches to the infinitive (portare → portarlo). In spoken/written Italian you will often see it after verbs like 'decidere di...', 'chiedere di...', 'dire di...'.
target_language_example: Mi hanno chiesto di portarlo alla festa.
native_language_example: They asked me to bring it to the party.

meaning: of places / (number) of seats or spots
additional_notes: Composed of the preposition di (of, some) + posti (places, seats). Often links a noun of quantity or possession to 'posti' (e.g., 'un sacco di posti' = 'lots of places'). Can also appear in fixed expressions about capacity ('numero di posti' = 'number of seats'). Meaning depends on context and surrounding words.
target_language_example: Qual è il numero di posti su questo aereo?
native_language_example: What is the number of seats on this plane?

meaning: of/to take the (used when an infinitive verb + definite article follow a preceding verb or expression)
additional_notes: This sequence appears when a verb or expression requires an infinitive (prendere = to take/get) followed by a masculine singular noun with the definite article il (the). In English it often translates as "to take the" or "to catch the" depending on context (e.g., prendere il treno = to catch/take the train). The preceding words (like essere in grado di = to be able to) determine the full meaning: "essere in grado di prendere il treno" = "to be able to take the train."
target_language_example: Sarà in grado di prendere il treno domani?
native_language_example: Will he be able to take the train tomorrow?

meaning: 'to take his/her/its' (part of a verb phrase meaning to stop or start taking someone's medicine or something belonging to someone)
additional_notes: This phrase is the infinitive verb 'prendere' (to take) with a possessive object 'la sua' (his/her/its — feminine noun). It often appears after verbs like 'smettere/cessare' (to stop) or 'cominciare' (to begin): e.g. 'ha smesso di prendere la sua medicina' = 'he/she stopped taking his/her medicine.' The gender of the possessive agrees with the noun it replaces (here 'medicina' is feminine, so 'la sua').
target_language_example: Ha iniziato di prendere la sua medicina ogni mattina.
native_language_example: She started to take her medicine every morning.

di prendere una tazza di tè

target_language_multi_word_term: di prendere una tazza di tè
meaning: to take/get a cup of tea (for someone).
additional_notes: This phrase is used when asking or telling someone to bring or get a cup of tea for someone else. It often appears after verbs like chiedere (Potrei chiederti di prendere...) or chiedere a qualcuno di... The structure 'di + verb' introduces the action requested. Note: 'una tazza di tè' = a cup of tea; agreement errors in the examples ('la nostro' should be 'il nostro' or 'per il nostro ospite') are unrelated to the phrase itself.
target_language_example: Potrei chiederti di prendere una tazza di tè per l'ospite?
native_language_example: Could I ask you to get a cup of tea for the guest?

meaning: to take/get some of it/them; to buy one of them (depending on context).
additional_notes: 'Prenderne' = 'prendere' (to take/get/buy) + clitic pronoun 'ne' (of it/of them/from it/from them). Used when referring back to something already mentioned (e.g. some cookies, one of those). 'Di' often begins a clause after verbs like 'dire' (che ne dici di prenderne...) or follows verbs expressing intention/need (Ho bisogno di prenderne...). English translations depend on context: 'to get some', 'to take one', 'to buy one of them'.
target_language_example: Ho intenzione di prenderne una domani.
native_language_example: I intend to get/buy one of them tomorrow.

meaning: to take care (of someone or oneself); to look after
additional_notes: Common reflexive expression using prendersi cura (di + person/thing). Often used with an infinitive marker (di) after verbs like dire, chiedere, promettere: e.g. 'dire di prendersi cura del cane' = 'tell (someone) to take care of the dog'. For oneself use 'prendersi cura di sé' or 'prendersi cura di me/te'.
target_language_example: Dì a Marco di prendersi cura di nonna quando sei via.
native_language_example: Tell Marco to take care of Grandma while you're away.

meaning: to worry (about); used after verbs to introduce the reflexive infinitive 'preoccuparsi' (lit. 'to worry oneself')
additional_notes: This is the reflexive infinitive form of preoccuparsi. It commonly appears after verbs that require 'di' before an infinitive (e.g. dire, chiedere, smettere, fingere). Examples: 'Dite loro di smettere di preoccuparsi' (Tell them to stop worrying). Use prepositions like 'per' or 'di' after preoccuparsi when specifying the object (e.g. 'di preoccuparsi per il ritardo' or 'di preoccuparsi di ciò che non può controllare').
target_language_example: Dite loro di smettere di preoccuparsi.
native_language_example: Tell them to stop worrying.

meaning: earlier; just before (earlier today or previously mentioned time)
additional_notes: Commonly used to refer back to something that happened a short time ago or earlier in the day or conversation. Often appears in phrases like "di prima/l'altro giorno/di prima mattina" or after verbs: "te l'ho detto di prima" (I told you earlier). Context determines how recent the event is.
target_language_example: Ho visto Marco di prima, gli ho chiesto come stava.
native_language_example: I saw Marco earlier; I asked him how he was.

meaning: on purpose; intentionally.
additional_notes: Used to say that an action was done deliberately (or to deny that it was deliberate). Common in spoken and written Italian. Synonym: 'volontariamente'. Often follows the verb or object (e.g., 'l'ha fatto di proposito' or 'non l'ho fatto di proposito').
target_language_example: Non l'ho fatto di proposito; è stato un incidente.
native_language_example: I didn't do it on purpose; it was an accident.

meaning: for protection / of protection (indicating purpose or type related to protection).
additional_notes: Used after a noun to indicate purpose (e.g., "strumento di protezione" = protective tool) or after verbs expressing need ("ho bisogno di protezione" = I need protection). Common in both literal (physical safety) and figurative contexts (legal, diplomatic). 'Di' links the noun to 'protezione' and is not a reflexive or conjugated form.
target_language_example: Cerco un casco di protezione per la bici.
native_language_example: I'm looking for a protective helmet for my bike.

meaning: "to clean the" (part of an infinitive phrase)
additional_notes: This is not a standalone phrase but a fragment: di + infinitive (pulire) + direct article (la). In Italian, di can introduce an infinitive after certain verbs or expressions (e.g., avere bisogno di pulire la casa = to need to clean the house). The article la agrees with a feminine singular noun that follows (la casa, la cucina, la macchina [fem.]). Watch word order: the full phrase will include the noun (e.g., di pulire la casa) or be rephrased with a pronoun (di pulirla = of/to clean it).
target_language_example: Ho bisogno di pulire la cucina prima di uscire.
native_language_example: I need to clean the kitchen before going out.

meaning: to clean his/her/its/their (something) — part of an infinitive construction ('to clean' + 'his/her').
additional_notes: This string combines the preposition 'di' used after verbs like 'chiedere', 'dire', 'continuare' + the infinitive 'pulire' (to clean) and the possessive phrase 'la sua' (his/her/its/their, feminine singular). It's not a fixed phrase by itself but appears in sentences like "chiedere/dire a qualcuno di pulire la sua stanza" = 'ask/tell someone to clean their room.' The gender and number of the noun after the possessive must match (e.g., 'la sua camera' or 'il suo garage'). In English, the infinitive 'to clean' follows verbs like 'ask' or 'tell'.
target_language_example: Ho detto a Lucia di pulire la sua cucina.
native_language_example: I told Lucia to clean her kitchen.

meaning: on this side of / over here from (used to indicate location relative to the speaker or a point)
additional_notes: Used to point out something that is on this side or nearby relative to the speaker or a reference point. Often appears in spoken Italian and in expressions like 'di qua' (over here) plus 'da' when specifying direction or relation (e.g., 'di qua da noi' = 'here with us / on our side'). Can be followed by a person, place, or time.
target_language_example: Vieni di qua da me, così parliamo tranquilli.
native_language_example: Come over here to my place so we can talk calmly.

meaning: literally 'of something of' — used to mean 'something' plus a qualifier (e.g. 'something more', 'something different', 'something real', 'something bigger'). It links 'qualcosa' with a following adjective or phrase introduced by 'di'.
additional_notes: Structure: 'di' + 'qualcosa' + 'di' + [qualifier]. Common in spoken and written Italian to express 'something' qualified by an adjective/phrase (più, diverso, reale, più grande, etc.). Not idiomatic as a standalone unit without the following qualifier. Translate contextually (e.g. 'something more', 'something different', 'something real').
target_language_example: A me piace perché mi fanno sentire parte di qualcosa di più grande.
native_language_example: I like it because they make me feel part of something bigger.

meaning: of/about what you have (done/said/heard).
additional_notes: This phrase combines 'di' (of/about) + 'quello che' (what/that which) + a second-person present perfect 'hai' (you have). In context it refers to something the listener has done, said, or heard. Common in questions and statements: e.g. asking for explanation ('Hai idea di quello che hai fatto?') or expressing pride/responsibility ('Sono fiera di quello che hai fatto.'). The exact English phrasing depends on the verb implied (done, said, heard).
target_language_example: Sono orgoglioso di quello che hai fatto.
native_language_example: I'm proud of what you did.

meaning: of these before; (used to ask or say if someone has seen/been given one of these previously).
additional_notes: Commonly appears in questions or statements like "Hai mai visto una di queste prima?" meaning "Have you ever seen one of these before?" 'di queste' = 'of these' (feminine plural); 'prima' = 'before/previously'. Word order can vary: "una di queste" (one of these) + 'prima'. Used in everyday speech. Make sure gender/number matches the noun (e.g., 'uno di questi' for masculine).
target_language_example: Hai mai provato una di queste prima?
native_language_example: Have you ever tried one of these before?

meaning: these days; nowadays
additional_notes: Used to talk about the current period or recent times, often with a slightly negative or generalizing tone (e.g., problems or conditions these days). Can appear at the beginning or end of a sentence.
target_language_example: Di questi tempi è difficile trovare lavoro stabile.
native_language_example: These days it's hard to find steady work.

meaning: 'one of these before' — used with 'hai/avete mai visto' or 'mi hai dato' to mean 'have you ever seen one of these before' / 'you gave me one of these before'.
additional_notes: Commonly appears after words like 'uno' (uno di questi prima) or with verbs like 'vedere' (Hai mai visto uno di questi prima?) and 'dare' (Mi hai dato uno di questi prima). Literally: 'of these before'. In questions with 'mai' it asks if someone has ever seen one of these before; in statements it says someone gave one of these to someone earlier. Word order can vary (e.g., 'uno di questi prima' is the full phrase).
target_language_example: Hai già ricevuto uno di questi prima?
native_language_example: Have you received one of these before?

meaning: recently; lately.
additional_notes: Used to ask or say that something happened in the near past. Can appear at the end of a sentence (most common) or before the verb in some constructions (e.g., "ha cambiato di recente"). Equivalent to "recentemente" but slightly more conversational.
target_language_example: Hai letto qualcosa di recente?
native_language_example: Have you read anything recently?

meaning: 'to recite' or 'to perform (as an actor)'.
additional_notes: Form is the preposition di + infinitive recitare, commonly used after verbs that require 'to' (e.g., essere in grado di recitare, decidere di recitare, smettere di recitare). Recitare can mean to recite aloud (poem, prayer, Quran) or to act/perform in theatre/film. Context determines whether it means recite (spoken) or act (perform).
target_language_example: Ha deciso di recitare in una commedia al teatro locale.
native_language_example: He decided to act in a comedy at the local theatre.

meaning: 'of responsibility' / 'related to responsibility' (used to describe a role, duty, or quality connected to responsibility).
additional_notes: Often appears after nouns to specify that something is a responsibility or a role involving responsibility (e.g., ruolo di responsabilità = a position of responsibility). Also used in phrases describing someone's sense or feeling of responsibility (senso di responsabilità). Common in formal and everyday speech.
target_language_example: Ha ottenuto un ruolo di responsabilità nell'azienda.
native_language_example: He got a position of responsibility in the company.

meaning: 'to stay (somewhere)'; used with a verb meaning 'to stay' plus a place introduced by a (e.g., stay at home, stay in Boston).
additional_notes: Formed from the infinitive 'restare' preceded by 'di' when linked to another verb (e.g., decidere di, chiedere a qualcuno di). Followed by a place introduced by 'a' (a casa, a Boston). Use without 'di' after some verbs? Many verbs require 'di' before an infinitive (decidere di, chiedere di, avere bisogno di, non avere intenzione di).
target_language_example: Ho chiesto a Marco di restare a scuola oggi.
native_language_example: I asked Marco to stay at school today.

meaning: 'to recognize' (infinitive form used after certain verbs or expressions)
additional_notes: This is the preposition 'di' + the infinitive 'riconoscere' (to recognize). In Italian, many verbs, adjectives, or nouns are followed by 'di' + infinitive (e.g., 'ho bisogno di riconoscere', 'è difficile di riconoscere' — note: some combinations use 'che' or no preposition instead). 'Riconoscere' can mean to identify someone/something, to acknowledge (a fact), or to admit. The literal translation is possible. Watch word order: after verbs like 'decidere di', 'cercare di', 'smettere di', you put the infinitive with 'di'.
target_language_example: Ho deciso di riconoscere il problema e di parlare con il team.
native_language_example: I decided to acknowledge the problem and talk with the team.

meaning: 'to laugh' (used after verbs like smettere, smettersi — e.g., 'to stop laughing').
additional_notes: Literally 'of/to laugh'. Commonly appears after verbs that require 'di' before an infinitive (e.g., smettere di ridere = to stop laughing; pregare di ridere = to ask to laugh). In everyday commands you'll often see the reflexive or imperative forms: 'Smettila di ridere' or 'Smettete di ridere' (Stop laughing). Use 'di' when the preceding verb governs an infinitive.
target_language_example: Per favore, smettila di ridere e ascolta.
native_language_example: Please stop laughing and listen.

meaning: to stay for a long time / to remain for a long time
additional_notes: A verbal phrase used after expressions like "avere intenzione" (to intend) or other verbs to express the idea of staying somewhere for an extended period. "Rimanere" = to stay; "a lungo" = for a long time. Can be shortened to "rimanere" or paired with different time expressions (es. "per molto tempo").
target_language_example: Ho intenzione di rimanere a lungo a Roma quest'estate.
native_language_example: I intend to stay in Rome for a long time this summer.

meaning: 'to repair' (infinitive with the preposition 'di' used after verbs that require it, e.g. 'cercare di', 'chiedere di').
additional_notes: This is the infinitive verb 'riparare' (to repair) preceded by 'di'. Many Italian verbs (like cercare, provare, chiedere, promettere) are followed by 'di' + infinitive to express trying, asking, or intending to do something. The literal translation is 'of/to repair', but in English you usually just say 'to repair' (e.g. 'try to repair', 'ask to repair').
target_language_example: Ha deciso di riparare la bicicletta domani.
native_language_example: He decided to repair the bike tomorrow.

meaning: spare, reserve, backup; kept in case it's needed
additional_notes: Used to describe something or someone kept as a substitute or backup (e.g., a spare question, reserve player, backup supply). Can also mean 'reservation' in the sense of doubts or objections when used in plural or with 'avere riserve' ('to have reservations'). Context determines whether it means a physical reserve/backup or personal reservations.
target_language_example: Ho preparato una risposta di riserva nel caso cambiassero le domande.
native_language_example: I prepared a spare answer in case they change the questions.

meaning: of/ to solve the (used with a specific problem or issue).
additional_notes: This is a fragment showing the infinitive verb risolvere ('to solve') with the preposition di linking a verb of attempt (cercare di, tentare di) and the definite article il before a masculine singular noun (e.g., problema). Common full pattern: [cercare/tentare] di risolvere il + noun. Use when saying someone tries/attempts to solve a specific problem. Word order: verb of trying + di + risolvere + il + noun.
target_language_example: Sto cercando di risolvere il problema del computer.
native_language_example: I'm trying to solve the computer problem.

meaning: of/to return; used after verbs to indicate the action of returning.
additional_notes: This is the infinitive verb 'ritornare' (to return) preceded by the preposition 'di', which appears after certain verbs or expressions (e.g., sperare di, avere intenzione di) to link them to another action. In English it corresponds to 'to return' or 'of returning' depending on the verb. Use 'a' + place (ritornare a Roma) to say 'return to [city]'.
target_language_example: Spero di ritornare in Italia il prossimo anno.
native_language_example: I hope to return to Italy next year.

meaning: back; returned; on the way back
additional_notes: Used to say someone has returned or is coming back/returning. Often follows a verb (essere, tornare) or appears after a name: 'essere di ritorno' = 'to be back/returning'. Can refer to imminent return ('di ritorno presto') or already returned ('È già di ritorno?').
target_language_example: Domani sarò di ritorno nel pomeriggio.
native_language_example: I'll be back tomorrow afternoon.

meaning: of stuff / of things (informal way to talk about unspecified items or kinds)
additional_notes: Used informally to refer to unspecified objects, things, or kinds of activity. Common in questions (Che tipo di roba? = What kind of stuff?) and in phrases like un sacco di roba (a lot of stuff). Tone is casual; avoid in very formal contexts.
target_language_example: Che tipo di roba vuoi portare alla festa?
native_language_example: What kind of stuff do you want to bring to the party?

meaning: of shoes / (used after 'paio') indicating 'pair of shoes'.
additional_notes: Commonly appears after words like 'paio' (un paio di scarpe = a pair of shoes). 'Di' is the preposition 'of' or partitive here linking quantity to the noun. Used for talking about buying, owning, or describing shoes. Not idiomatic—literal meaning.
target_language_example: Ho comprato un paio di scarpe nuove per la festa.
native_language_example: I bought a new pair of shoes for the party.

meaning: 'to choose' (infinitive with the preposition 'di') — used after verbs or expressions that require 'di' before an infinitive.
additional_notes: This is the infinitive verb scegliere (to choose) preceded by the preposition di. In Italian many verbs, nouns, or expressions require 'di' before another verb (e.g., diritto di scegliere, trattarsi di scegliere, prima di scegliere). Not a fixed idiom — it's a common grammatical pattern. Use it when you want to say 'to choose' as a complement (e.g., 'the right to choose' = il diritto di scegliere).
target_language_example: Hanno il diritto di scegliere il proprio medico.
native_language_example: They have the right to choose their own doctor.

meaning: 'of the scene' / 'for show' — used to indicate something theatrical, dramatic, or meant to impress; also appears in the fixed expression "colpo di scena" (plot twist).
additional_notes: Depending on context, "di scena" can describe something theatrical or staged (e.g., "roba di scena" = for show, ostentatious) or appear in phrases like "colpo di scena" meaning a sudden dramatic turn (plot twist). In questions like "Chi è di scena?" it means "who's on stage/who's performing?". Tone can be neutral or slightly colloquial.
target_language_example: Non fare tanto lo spettacolo: non è roba di scena.
native_language_example: Don't put on such a show: it's not for show.

meaning: 'to apologize' (infinitive phrase using the preposition di + reflexive verb scusarsi).
additional_notes: Used when the verb scusarsi (to apologize) appears after another verb, adjective, or expression that requires the preposition di (e.g., avere paura di scusarsi, cercare di scusarsi). The reflexive pronoun (mi/ti/si/ci/vi/si) is used according to the subject: chiedere a qualcuno di scusarsi (to ask someone to apologize).
target_language_example: Gli ho consigliato di scusarsi prima che la situazione peggiori.
native_language_example: I advised him to apologize before the situation gets worse.

meaning: 'second-hand' or 'from a secondary/indirect source'.
additional_notes: Commonly used both for physical goods (used/preowned) and for information (not firsthand — received via someone else). Context tells which meaning applies: with objects it means used/previously owned; with news or reports it means indirect/rumored information.
target_language_example: Ho comprato una giacca di seconda mano in centro.
native_language_example: I bought a second-hand jacket downtown.

meaning: ever; of all time (used to emphasize superlatives) or 'always'/'the same as always' in some contexts.
additional_notes: Commonly attached to superlatives to mean 'of all time' (e.g., la migliore di sempre = the best ever). Can also appear after adjectives referring to a person's usual state: 'lo stesso di sempre' = 'the same as always'. Tone is neutral; often used in enthusiastic or emphatic statements.
target_language_example: Questo è il miglior gelato di sempre!
native_language_example: This is the best ice cream ever!

meaning: literally 'to hear the' — used when saying someone hears or refuses to hear (something).
additional_notes: This phrase combines the preposition 'di' + the verb 'sentire' (to hear) + the definite article 'le' (the, feminine plural). It appears before a feminine plural noun like 'notizie' (news) or 'scuse' (apologies). Often used in constructions like 'essere sorpresi/essere felice di sentire le...' (to be surprised/happy to hear the...) or 'mi rifiuto di sentire le...' (I refuse to hear the...). The full clause usually follows with the noun (e.g. 'di sentire le notizie' or 'di sentire le tue scuse').
target_language_example: Non voglio di sentire le tue scuse adesso.
native_language_example: I don't want to hear your excuses right now.

meaning: in the evening; during the evening hours.
additional_notes: Used to indicate something habitually or generally happening in the evening (opposite of 'di giorno' = by day). Can describe routines, preferences, times (e.g. 'alle otto di sera' = at eight in the evening) or ask whether something can occur in the evening.
target_language_example: Di sera guardiamo la TV insieme.
native_language_example: In the evening we watch TV together.

meaning: of/related to snake; used in compounds like 'snake bite' or descriptive phrases (literally 'of snake').
additional_notes: Di + noun indicates possession, material, origin, or relation. With 'serpente' it's often used in set phrases: 'morso di serpente' (snake bite), 'lingua di serpente' (snake's tongue or a spiteful comment), or to describe something made of/like snake (e.g., 'pelle di serpente' = snake skin). Word order is noun + di + serpente when indicating 'of the snake' or 'snake's ...'.
target_language_example: Ha una ferita da morso di serpente.
native_language_example: He has a snake-bite wound.

meaning: 'of duty' / 'service' — used to describe something related to work, duty, or a service role (e.g. service staff, service entrance, military service, on duty).
additional_notes: Used after a noun to indicate that the noun is connected to service/work or a duty. Context determines exact translation: e.g. 'donna di servizio' = cleaning woman/housekeeper; 'agenti di servizio' = officers on duty; 'accesso di servizio' = service/access entrance; 'servizio militare' = military service; 'giorno di servizio' = day on duty. Common in formal and neutral registers.
target_language_example: Oggi sono di servizio al ricevimento.
native_language_example: Today I'm on duty at the reception.

meaning: 'of weeks' or used in time expressions meaning 'weeks (apart/long)' — often appears in phrases like 'a distanza di settimane' or 'un paio di settimane' meaning 'weeks' or 'a couple of weeks'.
additional_notes: Commonly used in time expressions. Often appears after a quantity (un paio di settimane = a couple of weeks) or in phrases indicating separation in time (a distanza di settimane = weeks apart). Use 'settimana' (singular) for one week and 'settimane' (plural) for more than one. Prepositions like 'in', 'fra', 'tra', 'a' combine with time expressions: 'fra un paio di settimane' = 'in a couple of weeks'.
target_language_example: Ci vediamo fra un paio di settimane.
native_language_example: We'll see each other in a couple of weeks.

meaning: certainly / for sure / definitely
additional_notes: Used to express certainty or strong probability. Can appear before or after the verb/object: 'Di sicuro non...' (definitely not) or 'mangeranno di sicuro' (they will definitely eat). It's neutral register and common in spoken and written Italian.
target_language_example: Di sicuro arriverà in tempo.
native_language_example: He/She will definitely arrive on time.

meaning: of meaning; meaningful / meaningfulness (depends on context).
additional_notes: Used to describe whether something has meaning or significance. Often appears in negative phrases with 'privo/priva di significato' = 'devoid of meaning' or in positive contexts like 'pieno di significato' = 'full of meaning / meaningful'. English translation depends on construction: sometimes translated as 'meaningful', 'meaningless' (with 'privo di'), or literally 'of meaning'.
target_language_example: Questo regalo è pieno di significato per me.
native_language_example: This gift is full of meaning for me.

meaning: 'money for' or 'of money for' — indicates an amount of money related to a purpose or recipient.
additional_notes: Commonly appears in phrases like 'un sacco di soldi per...' (a lot of money for...) or 'ho bisogno di soldi per...' (I need money to...). Use to express purpose (to buy, to pay) or to describe how much money is involved for someone/something. Literally composed from 'di' (of), 'soldi' (money) and 'per' (for).
target_language_example: Ho bisogno di soldi per pagare l'affitto.
native_language_example: I need money to pay the rent.

meaning: usually
additional_notes: Adverbial phrase used to describe habitual or typical actions. Commonly placed before the verb (especially compound verbs) or after the subject. Equivalent to 'generally' or 'as a rule' in many contexts.
target_language_example: Di solito prendo il treno per andare al lavoro.
native_language_example: I usually take the train to go to work.

meaning: upstairs
additional_notes: Commonly means 'upstairs' (in a house/building) or more generally 'above' (a higher location). Used with people/objects and with verbs of motion (andare di sopra, portare di sopra) or to indicate location (sono di sopra). Context determines whether physical upstairs (inside a building) or simply 'above' is meant.
target_language_example: Sono di sopra, sali tu?
native_language_example: I'm upstairs, will you come up?

meaning: by surprise; unexpectedly.
additional_notes: Used after verbs like 'colgere' (colto di sorpresa) or 'prendere' (prendere di sorpresa) to indicate being surprised or caught unprepared. Can be used impersonally (È stato colto di sorpresa) or with people (Mi ha colto di sorpresa). Common in past/perfect contexts.
target_language_example: Mi ha preso di sorpresa con la torta.
native_language_example: He took me by surprise with the cake.

meaning: below average; under the average level
additional_notes: Used to describe something (a score, performance, quality, etc.) that is lower than the average. More common phrasing is 'sotto la media' or 'al di sotto della media'. 'Di sotto della media' is understandable but slightly less idiomatic than the alternatives.
target_language_example: Il suo punteggio è di sotto della media per la classe.
native_language_example: His score is below the class average.

meaning: 'downstairs' or 'below'.
additional_notes: Used to indicate a lower location or movement to a lower level. Common in everyday speech when giving directions (Vai di sotto = Go downstairs) or describing where someone/something is (Venne di sotto = He/She came up from downstairs / came from below). Can pair with verbs of motion (andare, venire) or with state verbs (stare, essere).
target_language_example: Sali di sopra e poi torna giù; io vado di sotto a controllare.
native_language_example: Go upstairs and then come back down; I'll go downstairs to check.

meaning: for (someone) that is special; something special for (someone).
additional_notes: Used to say you want to do or get something special intended for someone. Often appears after words like 'qualcosa' (something) or 'qualcuno' and followed by the person (per te, per lei, per voi). Tone is neutral; common in everyday and formal speech.
target_language_example: Ho preparato qualcosa di speciale per te.
native_language_example: I prepared something special for you.

meaning: of/ (a) bunch of jerks; used to describe a group as rude, mean, or despicable people.
additional_notes: Informal and vulgar. 'Stronzi' is plural of 'stronzo' (insult = jerk/asshole). 'Di' + plural noun here marks a group (una banda di, una compagnia di). Common in colloquial speech to complain about a group: 'che banda/che compagnia/che famiglia di stronzi' = 'what a bunch of jerks'. Avoid in polite contexts.
target_language_example: Che banda di stronzi: hanno rovinato la festa.
native_language_example: What a bunch of jerks: they ruined the party.

meaning: 'of students' or 'students' (used to show possession/association or to indicate a group composed of students).
additional_notes: Formed by the preposition di + studenti (plural of studente). Used to link a noun to a group of students (e.g., il numero di studenti = the number of students) or to describe something made up of or involving students (e.g., un gruppo di studenti). Common in everyday speech and neutral register.
target_language_example: C'è una classe di studenti in biblioteca.
native_language_example: There is a class of students in the library.

meaning: to study more / to study longer or harder (used as part of a larger clause where 'di' links to a preceding verb or expression)
additional_notes: This sequence combines the preposition 'di' (often required after certain verbs or expressions) + the infinitive 'studiare' + 'più' meaning 'more'. 'Studiare di più' is the more natural order when the phrase stands alone; 'di studiare più' occurs when 'di' belongs to an earlier verb or expression (e.g., 'ho paura di studiare più del necessario'). On its own it is not a complete sentence and word order may vary depending on the surrounding clause.
target_language_example: Ho deciso di studiare più per superare l'esame.
native_language_example: I decided to study more to pass the exam.

meaning: successful; having achieved success.
additional_notes: Used after a noun or adjective to describe someone or something that has achieved success (e.g., una pièce di successo, un avvocato di successo). Can modify people (Tom è di successo) or things/projects. Equivalent to English 'successful' or 'a successful (X)'.
target_language_example: Ha pubblicato un libro di successo l'anno scorso.
native_language_example: He published a successful book last year.

meaning: of juice / (a container) of juice
additional_notes: Used to indicate quantity or content (a bottle/box/glass of juice). Commonly follows a container noun (bottiglia, bicchiere, scatola) or is used in constructions like 'succo di mela' (apple juice) where 'di' links the type/flavor. In English you'd say 'a bottle of juice' or 'apple juice'.
target_language_example: Vorrei una bottiglia di succo d'arancia, per favore.
native_language_example: I'd like a bottle of orange juice, please.

meaning: occasionally; from time to time
additional_notes: Used to say something happens now and then, not often. Interchangeable with occasional adverbs like "ogni tanto" or "di tanto in poi" (less common). Placed before or after the verb: "Di tanto in tanto vado al cinema" or "Vado al cinema di tanto in tanto."
target_language_example: Di tanto in tanto vado a trovare i miei genitori.
native_language_example: I visit my parents from time to time.

meaning: 'to return to (someone) / to get back together with (someone)' — used after verbs expressing decision, intention, or time.
additional_notes: Commonly appears after verbs like decidere (to decide) or pensare (to think) and refers to going back or resuming a relationship or companionship with a person. The preposition con means "with"; context determines whether it's physical return or reuniting romantically. You will often see it preceded by an infinitive (tornare) and introduced by di when linked to another verb (e.g., decidere di tornare con...).
target_language_example: Quando hai deciso di tornare con Maria?
native_language_example: When did you decide to get back together with Maria?

meaning: away; out of the way; (to get) rid of someone/something nearby
additional_notes: Used in expressions like "levare/togliere (qcn./qc.) di torno" or "stare di torno" to mean removing someone/something from one's vicinity or telling someone to go away. Can be literal or colloquial; often follows verbs like levare, togliere, togliersi. In the proverb example ("leva il medico di torno") it means 'keeps the doctor away' (i.e., prevents the need for the doctor).
target_language_example: Togliti di torno: devo studiare in pace.
native_language_example: Get out of the way; I need to study in peace.

meaning: of all
additional_notes: Used to indicate possession, inclusion or relation with a whole group. Often appears before a noun (di tutte le spese, di tutte queste bugie) or as part of comparative/superlative expressions (più bella di tutte). Can be followed by singular/plural nouns and determiners (tutte le, tutte queste, tutte quelle). Literal translation is usually possible as "of all" or "of all the."
target_language_example: Sono stanca di tutte queste scuse.
native_language_example: I'm tired of all these excuses.

meaning: everyday; ordinary; of daily life.
additional_notes: Used to describe things that are common, routine, or part of daily life. Can modify nouns (la vita di tutti i giorni = everyday life) or be used adjectivally (le cose di tutti i giorni = everyday things). Neutral register; often conveys boredom or mundanity in context.
target_language_example: Cerco qualcosa di speciale, non la solita cosa di tutti i giorni.
native_language_example: I'm looking for something special, not the usual everyday thing.

meaning: of all time; ever (the best/worst/etc. in history).
additional_notes: Used after a noun or phrase to say someone or something is the best, worst, greatest, etc., across all history or in all periods. Common in superlative expressions (il più ___ di tutti i tempi, il migliore di tutti i tempi, la peggior ___ di tutti i tempi).
target_language_example: Maria è la miglior insegnante di tutti i tempi.
native_language_example: Maria is the best teacher of all time.

meaning: of/for a hug; (need/want) a hug
additional_notes: Commonly appears after verbs or expressions of need, desire, or suggestion (e.g., 'ho bisogno di un abbraccio' = 'I need a hug'; 'che ne dici di un abbraccio?' = 'how about a hug?'). 'Abbraccio' is masculine singular; the phrase is literal and used in both emotional and casual contexts.
target_language_example: Stasera dopo la brutta giornata ho bisogno di un abbraccio.
native_language_example: Tonight after the bad day I need a hug.

meaning: of a bath / of a bathroom; here used in the phrase 'ha/avete bisogno di un bagno' meaning 'needs a bath' or 'needs a bathroom'.
additional_notes: Directly, 'di un bagno' means 'of a bath' or 'of a bathroom'. In the example sentences it appears in the fixed expression 'avere bisogno di un bagno' (to need a bath / to need a bathroom). Context decides whether it means someone needs to take a bath (cleaning) or needs to use/find a bathroom (toilet). For people/pets, 'ha bisogno di un bagno' often means 'needs a bath' (to be washed).
