additional_notes: Used to say you provide emotional or practical support to someone. Often followed by a person or occasionally an infinitive. Common in spoken and written Italian: essere lì per te / essere lì per aiutare. Neutral tone; implies availability and solidarity.
target_language_example: Ti prometto che sarò lì per te quando ne avrai bisogno.
native_language_example: I promise I'll be there for you when you need it.

meaning: 'to be very proud of' (said to/of a group of females or addressing women)
additional_notes: Literal components: essere = to be; molto = very; fiere = proud (feminine plural); di = of/about. Because fiere is feminine plural, this phrase is used when the subject (those who are proud) is a group of women or when addressing women using voi. To use for mixed-gender or masculine subjects, change fiere → fieri. For singular: fiera (feminine) / fiero (masculine).
target_language_example: Dovete essere molto fiere di quello che ha fatto vostra figlia.
native_language_example: You should be very proud of what your daughter did.

meaning: 'to be in' (followed by a noun indicating location, situation or state)
additional_notes: Literally 'to be in the ...'. Used to indicate physical location (e.g. nei sotterranei = in the basements) or figurative situations/states (e.g. nei guai = in trouble; nei tuoi panni = in your shoes/in your situation). The preposition changes with the article (nei = in + i).
target_language_example: Non vorrei essere nei suoi panni.
native_language_example: I wouldn't want to be in his shoes.

meaning: to be crazy
additional_notes: Used literally (mentally unwell) and figuratively (crazy, foolish, or extreme). Often appears with verbs like essere, sembrare, fingere di (to pretend to be). Can express surprise or strong opinion (e.g., "Devi essere pazzo" = "You must be crazy"). Not formal medical language when used figuratively.
target_language_example: Devi essere pazzo se lo fai di nuovo.
native_language_example: You must be crazy if you do it again.

meaning: to be exactly
additional_notes: Depends on context. "Proprio" can add emphasis meaning "exactly/precisely" (Dovrebbe essere proprio qui = It should be right here) or add subjective emphasis meaning "really/truly/indeed" (Devo essere proprio noiosa = I must really be boring). In comparisons it can mean "just/just like" (essere proprio come = to be just like). It often appears before or after the adjective or noun it emphasizes.
target_language_example: Deve essere proprio qui, non altrove.
native_language_example: It must be right here, not elsewhere.

target_language_multi_word_term: essere se (short for essere se stessi)
meaning: 'to be oneself' (to behave or feel naturally, true to one's own identity)
additional_notes: Usually appears as essere se stessi (reflexive form) or with a reflexive pronoun (essere sé stesso/a, essere se stessi). Used to talk about authenticity, personal identity, and staying true to oneself. Commonly appears with verbs like poter (to be able to), sentire (to feel), or constructions about society, style, dreams, etc. Accent on 'sé' is optional in informal writing but recommended in formal texts to avoid ambiguity.
target_language_example: È importante cercare di essere se stessi, anche quando è difficile.
native_language_example: It's important to try to be yourself, even when it's difficult.

meaning: to be an alien (i.e., an extraterrestrial) or figuratively 'to be strange/very different'.
additional_notes: Usually literal: someone is an extraterrestrial. Can be used jokingly or figuratively to say someone seems very odd or unlike others. Common in questions or speculation (e.g., 'Pensi che Tom potrebbe essere un alieno?'). Verb agrees with subject (essere).
target_language_example: Pensi che Marco potrebbe essere un alieno?
native_language_example: Do you think Marco might be an alien?

meaning: 'ago' used with 'we have' (noi abbiamo) to mean 'we ... ago' or 'ago we have ...' — actually the correct sequence is 'fa' + time expression + 'abbiamo' to say something happened a while ago involving 'we'.
additional_notes: In Italian time expressions use 'fa' after the time period to mean 'ago'. When describing past actions with 'we', you often see '... fa abbiamo + past participle' only in narration; more commonly the structure is 'qualche settimana fa abbiamo festeggiato' = 'a few weeks ago we celebrated.' 'Fa' is invariable and follows the time phrase (e.g. 'anni fa', 'poco fa', 'molto tempo fa').
target_language_example: Due anni fa abbiamo visitato Roma.
native_language_example: Two years ago we visited Rome.

meaning: makes (someone/something) seem so (easy/etc.).
additional_notes: Used with direct object pronouns or nouns: fa (pronoun/noun) sembrare così + adjective/infinitive. Literally 'makes ... appear so.' Common to describe that someone causes a task or person to look very easy or a certain way. Word order: subject + fa + (lo/la/li/le/noun) + sembrare + così + adjective/infinitive.
target_language_example: Lei lo fa sembrare così semplice.
native_language_example: She makes it seem so simple.

meaning: 'manage to' / 'be able to (do something)' in constructions like 'ce la fa a...' or in questions 'come fa a...?' ; also appears in colloquial phrases 'fa a botte' (fights) and in weather question 'che tempo fa a...?' meaning 'what's the weather like in...?'
additional_notes: This is not a fixed two-word verb by itself; 'fa' is third-person singular of 'fare' and combines with particles/pronouns or with 'a' + infinitive to form expressions. Common patterns: 'ce la fa a + infinitive' = 'manage to (do)'; 'come fa a + infinitive' = 'how can/does (someone) ...?'; 'fa a botte (con)' = 'fights with'; 'che fa a [place]?' = 'what's the weather like in [place]?'. Use depends on context. Formal equivalent for ability/possibility is often 'riesce a' (e.g. 'riesce a finire?').
target_language_example: Come fa a sapere se è commestibile?
native_language_example: How can he/she know if it's edible?

meaning: 'equals two' or 'makes two' (used with numbers or to say 'he/she does two' in contexts with verbs like fare).
additional_notes: Commonly appears in math questions: Quanto fa due per due? = How much is two times two? Here 'fa' = 'is'/'equals' in calculations. In other contexts, 'fa due' can occur when 'fa' (he/she/it does/makes) is followed by the number two: e.g. 'Tom fa due lavori' = 'Tom does two jobs' (there 'fa due' means 'does two [of something]'). Pay attention to context: in math sentences 'fa' is a neutral verb meaning 'equals', while with people it means 'does/has'.
target_language_example: Questa somma fa due.
native_language_example: This sum equals two.

meaning: It's the same / it doesn't matter / that's fine (no problem).
additional_notes: Used to say that something makes no difference or that you're okay with a situation. Can be neutral or casual depending on tone. Common responses: 'Fa lo stesso.' (It doesn't matter.) and 'Fa lo stesso!' (No problem!/Never mind!).
target_language_example: Se non puoi venire, fa lo stesso, ci vediamo un'altra volta.
native_language_example: If you can't come, it's fine, we'll see each other another time.

meaning: is doing here
additional_notes: Used to ask or state what someone/something is doing or doing in a particular place. Often appears with 'ci' or 'che' (e.g. 'che ci fa qui?') to form questions meaning 'what is (he/it) doing here?' or 'what is (it) doing here?'. Can be used in statements to indicate someone is present and doing something in that location (e.g. 'So cosa fa qui Tom.' = 'I know what Tom is doing here.').
target_language_example: Che ci fa qui Marco?
native_language_example: What is Marco doing here?

meaning: face to face; in person; directly (confrontation or meeting).
additional_notes: Used to describe a direct, personal meeting or confrontation between people (literal or figurative). Often implies speaking directly rather than by phone/email or confronting someone. Can be used for neutral meetings or tense encounters.
target_language_example: Dobbiamo parlare faccia a faccia domani.
native_language_example: We need to talk face to face tomorrow.

meaning: 'shamelessness' or 'nerve' (used to call someone brazen or bold in a rude way).
additional_notes: Informal idiom used to describe someone who behaves boldly without shame or embarrassment. Often used with avere (avere la faccia tosta) or as an exclamation (Che faccia tosta!). Can be translated as 'what nerve!' or 'the nerve!' depending on context.
target_language_example: Hai una faccia tosta a non scusarti dopo quello che hai fatto.
native_language_example: You have the nerve not to apologize after what you did.

meaning: 'do your best' (polite/formal imperative)
additional_notes: Formal or polite imperative using the verb fare in the formal usted/Lei form: faccia (Lei) + del suo meglio = 'please do your best' or 'do your best.' Common in formal requests or advice (to one person). You can drop 'suo' in less formal contexts: 'faccia del meglio' is uncommon; more natural informal forms are 'fa' il tuo meglio' or 'fai del tuo meglio.'
target_language_example: Stia calma e faccia del suo meglio.
native_language_example: Stay calm and do your best.

meaning: 'show me how' (formal/polite request)
additional_notes: A polite/formal way to ask someone to demonstrate how to do something. 'Mi faccia vedere come...' literally means 'Make me see how...' but functions as 'show me how to...'. Used with third-person polite form (Lei) or formal address; in informal situations you would say 'fammi vedere come' or 'mostrami come'. Followed by an infinitive describing the action (es. farla, farlo).
target_language_example: Mi faccia vedere come usarlo, per favore.
native_language_example: Please show me how to use it.

meaning: how do we (do) ...? / how can we ...?
additional_notes: Used in questions to ask how something can be done or how to accomplish/know something. Literally from 'facciamo' (we do/make) + 'a' but functions as part of the fixed question 'come facciamo a + infinitive'. Common in spoken and written Italian.
target_language_example: Come facciamo a risolvere questo problema?
native_language_example: How can we solve this problem?

meaning: 'how do I know that...' or 'how can I tell that...'
additional_notes: Used to ask for proof, evidence or a way to be sure about something. Commonly appears as the question 'Come faccio a sapere che...?' followed by the statement you doubt. 'Faccio' comes from 'fare' (to do/make); this is an idiomatic construction meaning 'how can I (do) to know...'.
target_language_example: Come faccio a sapere che mi hai detto la verità?
native_language_example: How do I know that you told me the truth?

target_language_multi_word_term: faccio ad / ce la faccio ad
meaning: 'faccio ad' (in questions) = 'how do I...?' ; 'ce la faccio ad' = 'I can / I manage to...'; 'non ce la faccio ad' = 'I can't / I can't manage to...'
additional_notes: Uses the verb fare + preposition a before an infinitive. In questions 'Come faccio ad...?' asks how to do something. 'Ce la faccio (a)...' is an idiomatic expression meaning to succeed or manage; add 'non' to negate. In spoken Italian 'ad' is used instead of 'a' before a vowel (e.g. 'ad andare').
target_language_example: Non ce la faccio ad alzarmi così presto domani.
native_language_example: I can't manage to get up so early tomorrow.

meaning: 'I do that' or 'I do what...'.
additional_notes: Often appears as part of the phrase 'faccio ciò che...' meaning 'I do what...'. 'Ciò' is a formal/demonstrative pronoun meaning 'that' or 'what' and is commonly followed by 'che' to introduce a clause. In casual speech Italians more often say 'faccio quello che' or simply 'faccio quello che...' rather than 'faccio ciò che...'. Can be used to state compliance ('I do what is asked') or asserting one's will ('I do what I want').
target_language_example: Faccio ciò che mi serve per finire il lavoro.
native_language_example: I do what I need to finish the job.

meaning: I do/make the (masculine plural noun that follows).
additional_notes: This is the first-person singular of fare (faccio) followed by the masculine plural definite article i and a plural noun (e.g., i compiti, i migliori auguri). It can mean 'I do the...' (actions: faccio i compiti = I do the homework) or 'I give/make the...' (expressions: faccio i miei auguri = I give my best wishes). Word order may vary for emphasis (Le faccio i miei migliori auguri = I give her my best wishes).
target_language_example: Stasera faccio i compiti prima di cena.
native_language_example: Tonight I do the homework before dinner.

meaning: 'I do that' or used as part of 'faccio quello che...' = 'I do what.../I do what I want.'
additional_notes: Commonly appears in the structure 'faccio quello che...' followed by a clause (e.g. 'faccio quello che voglio' = 'I do what I want'). Used to state what someone does or to insist on personal choice or action. Can be neutral (describing actions) or emphatic/defensive depending on tone. The bare phrase 'faccio quello' without a following clause is less common and may sound incomplete; learners will usually use the full pattern 'faccio quello che...'.
target_language_example: Faccio quello che devo per aiutare la mia famiglia.
native_language_example: I do what I must to help my family.

meaning: present progressive + plural direct object or noun phrase: 'doing the...' or 'doing (plural noun)'.
additional_notes: Facendo is the gerund of fare (to do/make). When followed by the definite article i it introduces plural nouns (e.g., i compiti = the (school) exercises/homework). In context this structure appears in the present continuous (stare + gerund): stanno facendo i compiti = they are doing the homework. The exact English translation depends on the noun after i (often omitted in examples: 'facendo i compiti' = doing the homework).
target_language_example: Stiamo facendo i preparativi per la festa.
native_language_example: We are doing the preparations for the party.

meaning: making a
additional_notes: Gerund of fare ('to do/make') plus una ('a/an' for a feminine singular noun). It is used before a feminine noun: facendo una torta = 'making a cake', facendo una copia = 'making a copy', facendo una lista = 'making a list'. In some expressions, English uses a different verb, such as farsi una doccia = 'take/have a shower'.
target_language_example: Sto facendo una lista per il viaggio.
native_language_example: I'm making a list for the trip.

meaning: manage to
additional_notes: Usually appears in the pattern come fai a + infinitive, meaning “how do/can you ...?” when asking how someone is able to do something. fai is the tu form of fare, so this is specifically for speaking to one person informally.
target_language_example: Come fai a svegliarti così presto ogni giorno?
native_language_example: How do you manage to wake up so early every day?

meaning: 'do with' / 'are you doing with' (part of questions like 'what are you doing with...') or in fixed phrases 'fai con calma' = 'take it easy / do it calmly'.
additional_notes: In questions like 'Che ci fai con...?' or 'Cosa fai con...?' it asks what someone is doing/what they intend to do with an object (English: 'What are you doing with this...? / What do you want with...?'). The pronoun 'ci' is optional and often used for emphasis or colloquial rhythm. 'Fai con calma' is a separate use: an imperative/advice meaning 'do it calmly' or 'take your time'. Context decides meaning; not a single fixed idiom. Verbal form corresponds to 'tu' (you).
target_language_example: Che ci fai con quel vecchio libro?
native_language_example: What are you doing with that old book?

meaning: 'do/are ... anymore' or 'do/are ... no longer' (second-person singular informal)
additional_notes: Combines the verb fai (you do/you are doing) with più (no more/anymore). Used to say someone no longer does something, is no longer part of something, or to ask what someone will do later (with 'più tardi' = later). Context determines meaning: with time expressions like 'più tardi' it means 'later'; alone before an adjective or noun it often means 'no longer' (e.g. 'non fai più parte' = 'you are no longer part'). It's informal (tu form).
target_language_example: Non fai più gli esercizi con noi?
native_language_example: You don't do the exercises with us anymore?

meaning: Go ahead / feel free (do it); an informal encouragement to proceed.
additional_notes: Used to give permission or encourage someone to do something. Tone ranges from polite permission to casual encouragement depending on context and intonation. Often followed by an infinitive or another clause (e.g., 'fai pure e...'). It is informal/conversational.
target_language_example: Fai pure, prendi un pezzo di torta.
native_language_example: Go ahead, take a piece of cake.

meaning: do that / do it (imperative: you do that)
additional_notes: Informal imperative form using 'fare' (to do) for 'tu' (fai) + 'quello' (that/what I/you/others indicated). Often followed by 'che' + clause (fai quello che devi fare = do what you have to do) or used to point to an action someone should copy (fai quello che fa lui = do what he does). Tone is direct; common in spoken Italian.
target_language_example: Fai quello che ti ho detto, per favore.
native_language_example: Do what I told you, please.

meaning: do only (you do only) / just do (imperative or statement addressing 'tu')
additional_notes: Used with the informal tu form (fai) plus solo meaning 'only' or 'just'. Can be an instruction (imperative tone) or a description of what someone does. Context determines whether it's a command ('Just do ...') or an observation ('You only ...'). Often followed by a verb or clause (es. 'fai solo quello che ti dico' = 'just do what I tell you'). Tone can be blunt or scolding.
target_language_example: Fai solo quello che ti dico, per favore.
native_language_example: Just do what I tell you, please.

meaning: 'failure is' — the phrase 'fallimento è' begins a statement defining or describing failure.
additional_notes: Used to introduce a characterization, cause, or definition of 'fallimento' (failure). Common in proverbs or explanatory sentences (e.g., "Il fallimento è la madre del successo"). When specifying cause, it often appears in a structure like "Questo fallimento è dovuto a..." (This failure is due to...).
target_language_example: Il fallimento è spesso un'opportunità per migliorare.
native_language_example: Failure is often an opportunity to improve.

meaning: 'family and' — the noun famiglia followed by the conjunction e (and).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase: it's simply the word famiglia (family) used together with the conjunction e (and) to link 'family' with another noun or phrase. You'll see it in lists or paired ideas (e.g. 'famiglia e il paese' = 'family and the hometown'). Word order and agreement remain regular: famiglia is singular feminine; any adjectives or articles for the second element follow normal rules.
target_language_example: Penso sempre alla mia famiglia e ai miei amici.
native_language_example: I always think about my family and my friends.

meaning: 'the family is' (used to say how a family is doing/feeling)
additional_notes: This is the noun 'famiglia' (family) followed by the verb 'stare' in the 3rd person singular (sta). Use to describe the state or wellbeing of a family: 'La famiglia sta bene' = 'The family is well/doing fine.' Can be used with possessives (la sua, la vostra, tutta la) and adverbs (molto). For questions, invert intonation or add question marks: 'La vostra famiglia sta bene?'
target_language_example: La mia famiglia sta bene dopo il trasloco.
native_language_example: My family is doing well after the move.

meaning: 'famous in' — used to say someone or something is well-known within a particular place, field or group.
additional_notes: Combine famoso (famous) with the preposition in + place/field to indicate where someone/something is famous: famoso in Italia, famoso in città, famoso in rete, famoso in ambito musicale. Can be used for people, works, brands, events. For feminine/plural nouns use famosa/famosi/famose as needed (famosa in, famosi in).
target_language_example: È famoso in tutta la regione per i suoi formaggi.
native_language_example: He/It is famous throughout the region for its cheeses.

meaning: famous everywhere / famous throughout (a place or among people).
additional_notes: Used to say someone or something is well-known everywhere or throughout a certain area or group. Often followed by a place or phrase indicating scope (e.g., famoso in tutto il mondo = famous all over the world). Can be shortened to 'famoso' with context, or expanded (famoso in tutto il paese, famoso in tutto il quartiere, ecc.).
target_language_example: Quel ristorante è famoso in tutto per la qualità del suo servizio.
native_language_example: That restaurant is famous everywhere for the quality of its service.

meaning: 'they do/they make a' (used before a noun or activity).
additional_notes: Plural third-person present of fare + indefinite article una. Used to say that 'they' perform, organize or create something (an event, activity, thing). Can describe habitual actions (fanno una partita = they have/play a match), appearances (fanno una bella coppia = they make a nice couple), or preparations (fanno una cioccolata = they make a hot chocolate). The exact translation into English depends on the noun that follows: 'they have/hold/put on/make/do a…'.
target_language_example: Ogni venerdì fanno una cena tra amici.
native_language_example: Every Friday they have a dinner with friends.

meaning: to do anything else / to do nothing but (depending on context).
additional_notes: Often appears in fixed expressions: "non può far altro che + infinitive" means "can only/there's nothing to do but..." (i.e. nothing else is possible). With "non far altro che + infinitive" it means "to do nothing but/only" (repetitive or limiting action). Alone it can mean "to do something else" when used literally.
target_language_example: Non può far altro che aspettare notizie.
native_language_example: He can only wait for news.

meaning: to be extremely annoying, awful, or to disgust (colloquial, vulgar)
additional_notes: Informal and vulgar expression. Used to say that something or someone is really bad, boring, annoying, or makes you angry/disgusted. Commonly appears in conjugated forms like 'fa cagare' (it sucks) or 'mi fa cagare' (it disgusts/angers me). Avoid in formal or polite contexts.
target_language_example: Mi fa cagare quando la gente parla al cinema; fa cagare davvero.
native_language_example: It disgusts me when people talk in the cinema; it really sucks.

meaning: 'to make (someone) understand' or 'to cause (someone) to understand'
additional_notes: A causative construction: far (infinitive) = to have/make someone do or experience something. Far capire is used to indicate causing understanding or explaining so that someone understands. Can appear in various forms (ti faccio capire, mi vuoi far capire, farsi capire). Used in neutral and informal registers depending on context.
target_language_example: La capisci questa parola, o te la devo far capire io?
native_language_example: Do you understand this word, or do I have to make you understand it?

meaning: to make (someone or something) known; to introduce or publicize
additional_notes: Usually used with a direct object (a person, idea, product, etc.) or with a reflexive/indirect object to mean 'introduce someone to others' or 'help something become known/publicized'. Commonly appears as far conoscere + a/a qualcuno or far conoscere + qualcosa. Verb form: far is the shortened form of fare (far conoscere = fare conoscere).
target_language_example: Voglio far conoscere il mio progetto alla comunità.
native_language_example: I want to make my project known to the community.

meaning: to be part of; to belong to; to join (a group, family, team, etc.).
additional_notes: Commonly used with di/da (far parte di + noun) or with verbs like entrare (entrare a far parte = to join). Often expresses membership or inclusion. Infinitive form is far parte; conjugate using fare + parte (e.g., faccio parte, fa parte, fanno parte).
target_language_example: Mi piacerebbe far parte del team.
native_language_example: I would like to be part of the team.

meaning: to start (something), to set (something) off or in motion; to make something begin
additional_notes: A causative construction using the infinitive partire with far (a contracted form of fare + infinitive). Commonly used to say you make a machine, event, vehicle, program, process, or action start. Far is often contracted to 'far' instead of 'fare' in combination with another verb (e.g., far partire). Can be followed by a thing or person: far partire la macchina, far partire un progetto, far partire i corridoi.
target_language_example: Ho bisogno di far partire il generatore prima del temporale.
native_language_example: I need to start the generator before the storm.

meaning: to make (someone) think; to cause someone to consider or reflect; to suggest or imply.
additional_notes: Often used with an indirect object (e.g., 'far pensare a qualcuno') or with a clause ('far pensare che...'). Common in both literal and figurative senses. Typically appears conjugated as fare + infinitive (e.g., 'fa pensare', 'faceva pensare', 'farà pensare'), but the base infinitive 'far pensare' is used in dictionaries and instructional examples.
target_language_example: Quella frase può far pensare che qualcosa non vada.
native_language_example: That sentence can make one think that something is wrong.

meaning: 'to blow up' or 'to make explode; to cause something to jump/collapse'.
additional_notes: A transitive phrase meaning to cause something to explode, collapse, or be destroyed (literal: 'make jump'). Used with objects like 'il palazzo', 'la torre', or figuratively (e.g., 'far saltare la copertura' = to compromise/expose one's cover). Often followed by 'in aria' when emphasizing an explosion. Context determines whether literal (bombs, demolition) or figurative (ruin plans, reveal).
target_language_example: Non possiamo far saltare l'edificio: ci sono persone dentro.
native_language_example: We can't blow up the building; there are people inside.

meaning: 'to let (someone) know' or 'to inform'.
additional_notes: Commonly used in the expression far sapere a qualcuno (to let someone know). Often appears in future, imperative, or infinitive contexts: Fammi sapere (let me know) is a frequent colloquial shortening of 'fammi far sapere' historically; more precisely 'fammi sapere' uses sapere as causative in spoken use. 'Far sapere' can be used for giving information, asking for a reply, or promising to inform someone. It is regular and neutral in register but can appear in both formal and informal contexts depending on phrasing.
target_language_example: Voglio far sapere a tutti la decisione prima di domani.
native_language_example: I want to let everyone know the decision before tomorrow.

meaning: 'to make sure that' / 'to ensure that' / 'to cause (something) to happen'.
additional_notes: Used with a subordinate clause (usually followed by a verb in the subjunctive or indicative depending on context). Commonly means causing or ensuring that something happens or someone does something (e.g. far sì che accada = make sure it happens). Formality: neutral; often used in both spoken and written Italian.
target_language_example: Farò di tutto per far sì che tu sia al sicuro.
native_language_example: I'll do everything to make sure that you are safe.

meaning: to show
additional_notes: Common compound of the verb fare + vedere used to mean 'to show (something) to someone' or 'allow someone to see.' Can be followed by a direct object (far vedere qualcosa) or an indirect object with a/ a+person (far vedere qualcosa a qualcuno). In some contexts (colloquial) it can mean 'to make an appearance' or 'to let oneself be seen' (non volersi far vedere = not want to be seen).
target_language_example: Posso far vedere il mio disegno a Marco?
native_language_example: Can I show my drawing to Marco?

meaning: you will (do) the ... (used with nouns/expressions to indicate becoming/acting in a certain way).
additional_notes: Farai is the future tense of fare (tu farai = you will do/make). When followed by la + noun/adjective phrase, it often means 'you will be/act like a (specified thing)' or 'you will have (a certain end)'. Common in expressions: 'farai la brava' = 'you'll behave (well)', 'farai la fine di ...' = 'you'll end up like ...'. Context decides whether 'la' is part of a fixed phrase (la brava, la fine) or a colloquial object pronoun construction.
target_language_example: Farai la brava e poi usciremo insieme.
native_language_example: You'll behave (be good) and then we'll go out together.

meaning: you will (do) a / will you (do) a — future tense 'you' + indefinite article
additional_notes: Farai is the second-person singular future of fare (to do/make). Combined with an indefinite noun (un/una/un') it forms 'you will do/make a ...' or a question 'will you ... a ...?'. Context and noun determine exact translation: e.g. 'Farai un viaggio?' = 'Will you take a trip?' In exclamations it can express a warning or surprise: 'Farai un buco nel pavimento!' = 'You'll make a hole in the floor!' Pronunciation: farai = fa-RAI.
target_language_example: Farai un favore a Marco?
native_language_example: Will you do Marco a favor?

meaning: 'do without' / 'manage without' (to be able or unable to live/operate without someone or something).
additional_notes: Used with a pronoun like 'ne' when referring to something already mentioned (ne fare a meno = do without it/them). Often appears in negative or ability contexts: 'non può fare a meno' = 'cannot do without' (i.e. needs it). 'Potere fare a meno di + noun/pronoun' = 'to be able to do without'.
target_language_example: Posso fare a meno del computer per un giorno.
native_language_example: I can do without the computer for one day.

meaning: to do business; to do deals; to trade (with someone).
additional_notes: Used to talk about engaging in business, trading, or making commercial deals. Can be general (doing business) or refer to a specific deal/partnership (doing business with someone). Common in both formal and informal contexts.
target_language_example: Vuoi fare affari con me?
native_language_example: Do you want to do business with me?

meaning: to make friends; to become friends with someone
additional_notes: Commonly used to talk about forming friendships or getting to know people. Often followed by con + person (e.g., fare amicizia con qualcuno). Neutral register; suitable for everyday use.
target_language_example: È facile fare amicizia quando si partecipa a corsi o attività.
native_language_example: It's easy to make friends when you join classes or activities.

meaning: be careful; pay attention
additional_notes: Common impersonal or exhortative phrase used to warn or advise someone to be cautious or to pay attention to something. Often followed by a preposition (a, di, con) plus an action or noun: fare attenzione a + [verb/thing] (e.g. fare attenzione a nuotare / fare attenzione al traffico). Can be used in various persons: bisogna fare attenzione (one must be careful), dovete fare attenzione (you all should be careful).
target_language_example: Bisogna fare attenzione quando si va in bicicletta dopo averla presa.
native_language_example: You need to be careful when you ride a bicycle after taking it.

meaning: to do well; to be good/beneficial (for someone)
additional_notes: Two common uses: 1) perform well or succeed (fare bene in un esame = do well in an exam); 2) to be beneficial or good for health/well‑being (questo ti farà bene = this will do you good). Often used with an indirect object introduced by 'a' (fare bene a qualcuno) or followed by an infinitive. Context determines precise translation.
target_language_example: Fare bene a qualcuno non significa sempre rendere felice quella persona.
native_language_example: Doing good for someone does not always mean making that person happy.

meaning: to build a career / to get ahead professionally
additional_notes: Used to talk about advancing in one's job or social standing through work, connections, or opportunistic behavior. Can be neutral (to have a career ambition) or negative if implying using people or tactics to climb the ladder. Commonly followed by context (in un'azienda, nella politica, ecc.).
target_language_example: Vuole fare carriera in azienda entro cinque anni.
native_language_example: He wants to build a career in the company within five years.

meaning: 'to make a mess' / 'to make a lot of noise' / 'to cause a commotion' (colloquial)
additional_notes: Informal phrase used to describe loud, chaotic, or disorderly behaviour — can mean making a physical mess, causing trouble, or being noisy. Common in spoken Italian; context decides whether it refers to noise, disorder, or creating problems. Often used with avere/essere in compound tenses (e.g., hanno fatto casino).
target_language_example: I bambini hanno fatto casino in salotto tutto il pomeriggio.
native_language_example: The children made a mess/noise in the living room all afternoon.

meaning: to pay attention; to notice (often used in negative: 'non fare caso' = to not pay attention/notice).
additional_notes: Commonly used with non/nessuno to mean 'don't pay attention' or 'don't mind'. Can be followed by a direct object (fare caso a qualcosa/qualcuno = to notice someone/something or to pay attention to them). Often appears in expressions like "non farci caso" (don't pay attention to it).
target_language_example: Non fare caso al rumore: è solo il vento.
native_language_example: Don't pay attention to the noise: it's just the wind.

meaning: 'to sue' or 'to take legal action (against someone or something)'.
additional_notes: Used when someone brings a lawsuit against a person, organization, or the state. Common construction: fare causa a + [persona/ente]. In English the verb is 'to sue (someone)'. Can also appear with 'fare causa contro'.
target_language_example: Dobbiamo consultare un avvocato prima di fare causa al datore di lavoro.
native_language_example: We need to consult a lawyer before suing the employer.

meaning: 'to do stupid/messy things' or 'to do nonsense/idiotic stuff'.
additional_notes: Informal and vulgar. Used to warn someone not to act recklessly, make foolish mistakes, or cause trouble. Tone ranges from friendly (Don't do anything dumb) to stern (Don't screw things up). Avoid in formal situations.
target_language_example: Non fare cazzate con quella macchina.
native_language_example: Don't do anything stupid with that car.

meaning: to impress someone; to make an impression (often to attract someone's attention or admiration).
additional_notes: Commonly used with su + person (fare colpo su di qualcuno). Often implies trying to impress romantically or socially. Can be used in past, present, or infinitive forms (ha fatto colpo, sta cercando di fare colpo). Neutral register.
target_language_example: Sta cercando di fare colpo su di me con quella macchina nuova.
native_language_example: He's trying to impress me with that new car.

meaning: to be convenient; to suit someone (to fit someone's needs, schedule, or preferences).
additional_notes: Often used impersonally with an indirect object: e.g. 'Mi fa comodo' / 'Ti fa comodo' meaning 'It's convenient for me/you.' Can refer to time, arrangements, or situations that make something easier. Not typically used for physical comfort—use 'essere comodo' for that. Common in both formal and informal contexts.
target_language_example: Mi fa comodo se possiamo fare comodo spostando l'appuntamento alle cinque?
native_language_example: Is it convenient for me if we can make it convenient by moving the appointment to five?

meaning: to keep someone company; to stay with someone so they are not alone.
additional_notes: Common, everyday expression used when you spend time with someone to provide companionship or comfort. Often used with indirect objects: fare compagnia a qualcuno (e.g. fare compagnia a mia nonna). Can be used for short visits or longer stays. Neutral register (not formal or slang).
target_language_example: Vengo a fare compagnia a tua madre questo pomeriggio.
native_language_example: I'll come keep your mother company this afternoon.

meaning: do with
additional_notes: Used to ask or say what someone should/ wants/ did (or could) do involving something. Often appears in questions: "Cosa/ Che vuoi fare con... ?" — equivalent to English "What do you want to do with...?/ What should we do with...?" Can also express hypothetical use (e.g. "what we could have done with those money"). The literal components (fare = to do/make, con = with) match the English translation.
target_language_example: Cosa dovremmo fare con quel vecchio computer?
native_language_example: What should we do with that old computer?

meaning: to make conversation; to chat (engage in polite or casual talk)
additional_notes: Used for engaging in polite or casual talk with someone — often small talk rather than deep discussion. Common in social settings (parties, waiting areas, visits). Constructed with fare (to do/make) + conversazione (conversation).
target_language_example: Abbiamo deciso di fare conversazione per passare il tempo.
native_language_example: We decided to make conversation to pass the time.

meaning: do our best / do what we can
additional_notes: Usually appears in the fixed phrase 'fare del nostro meglio' meaning 'to do our best.' It implies making a sincere effort or doing as much as possible in a situation. Commonly used with modal verbs (dobbiamo, dovremmo, cerchiamo di) and followed by an infinitive or context describing what one is trying to achieve.
target_language_example: Dobbiamo fare del nostro meglio per aiutare.
native_language_example: We must do our best to help.

meaning: to go for walks (alone); literally 'to make some walks by/from' — often used with 'solo/sola' to mean walking alone.
additional_notes: This phrase is used to say someone enjoys taking walks. In the examples it appears with 'da solo/da sola' (alone). The core verb phrase is 'fare delle passeggiate' (to take/go for walks); adding 'da' before 'solo/sola' is a common Italian way to say 'alone' (da solo = by oneself). You can also use it without 'da' and simply say 'fare delle passeggiate da solo' or 'fare delle passeggiate' alone/with others depending on context.
target_language_example: Mi piace fare delle passeggiate da sola nel parco.
native_language_example: I like to go for walks alone in the park.

meaning: to do anything; to do everything possible (often 'do whatever it takes')
additional_notes: Used to say someone can do many different things or will do everything to achieve something. Context determines if it's literal (able to do any task) or idiomatic (make any effort, do whatever it takes). Common in positive and cautionary contexts.
target_language_example: Devi parlare con lui e fare di tutto per risolvere il problema.
native_language_example: You must talk to him and do everything you can to solve the problem.

meaning: to have an effect; to impress or make an impact (on someone or something).
additional_notes: Used to indicate that something produces an emotional reaction, visual impact, or influence. Often constructed with impersonal forms or with indirect objects/pronouns (e.g., "fa effetto a me" / "mi fa effetto"). Can be literal (e.g., a medicine "fa effetto") or figurative (e.g., a film, outfit, or gesture "fa effetto"). Frequently modified by adverbs like "davvero" or "molto" ("fa molto effetto").
target_language_example: Questo vestito sa come fare effetto.
native_language_example: This dress knows how to make an impact.

meaning: to celebrate / to party
additional_notes: Used to say someone is partying or celebrating (having fun, often with music, food, drinks). Can be used intransitively (fare festa) or with a direct object or preposition (fare festa per/di). Common in spoken Italian for informal celebrations.
target_language_example: Stasera vogliamo fare festa per il compleanno di Anna.
native_language_example: Tonight we want to party to celebrate Anna's birthday.

meaning: to pretend; to make believe or act as if something is true when it is not.
additional_notes: Commonly followed by di + infinitive (fare finta di non vedere = pretend not to see) or by che + subjunctive/indicative (fare finta che abbia capito / fare finta che è tutto a posto). Used for pretending, faking emotions or actions, or play-acting (children often 'fare finta' while playing). Informal and widely used in spoken Italian.
target_language_example: Ha deciso di fare finta di niente quando gli ho chiesto del progetto.
native_language_example: He decided to pretend nothing had happened when I asked him about the project.

meaning: 'to kill' (colloquial); also 'to get rid of' or 'to finish off' (things or people).
additional_notes: Colloquial and somewhat strong/violent. Commonly used in spoken Italian to mean murdering someone (slang), but can also be used figuratively: e.g., to finish a task or to eliminate an obstacle/object. Context determines whether it's literal (kill) or figurative (get rid of/finish). Avoid in formal situations.
target_language_example: Hanno deciso di fare fuori il testimone.
native_language_example: They decided to get rid of/kill the witness.

meaning: to reckon/compute; to deal with the consequences; to face reality (depending on context).
additional_notes: Literally 'to do the counts'. Common uses: fare i conti con (to come to terms with / deal with someone/something), fare i conti sui numeri (to calculate/figure out numbers or costs). Often implies calculating results, consequences, or budgeting. Verb phrase; conjugate 'fare' as needed.
target_language_example: Dobbiamo fare i conti con le spese del mese.
native_language_example: We need to deal with the month's expenses.

meaning: to harshly scold, punish, or defeat someone; to give someone a very hard time (can be physical or figurative)
additional_notes: Very informal and vulgar. Literally 'to do the ass' — used for strong reproach, threatening to beat someone, or saying you'll make someone suffer (physically or in terms of criticism). Avoid in polite contexts. Often used with a direct object (fare il culo a qualcuno). Tone ranges from joking among close friends to aggressive; context and intonation determine severity.
target_language_example: Se continui a mentire, ti farò fare il culo!
native_language_example: If you keep lying, I'll beat the hell out of you!

meaning: to fill up (a vehicle with fuel); to refuel
additional_notes: Commonly used when talking about cars, motorbikes, or any vehicle: fare il pieno alla macchina / alla moto. Can also be used figuratively to mean 'to replenish' or 'to top up' (less common). Typical phrase at gas stations: "Devo fare il pieno."
target_language_example: Prima del viaggio devo fare il pieno.
native_language_example: Before the trip I need to fill up (the tank).

meaning: to make sure / to arrange (that something happens); to ensure
additional_notes: Used to indicate someone takes action or makes arrangements so that a particular result occurs. Often followed by a subordinating clause introduced by 'che' (e.g. fare in modo che + subj./indic.). Can be translated as 'ensure that', 'make sure (that)', or 'arrange for'.
target_language_example: Farò in modo che tu riceva le informazioni in tempo.
native_language_example: I'll make sure that you receive the information on time.

meaning: to break in / to burst in (forcefully enter a place)
additional_notes: Commonly used for entering a building or room suddenly and often forcefully (by police, burglars, or people surprising others). Can be literal (physically entering) or figurative (interrupting a meeting). Often used with prepositions: fare irruzione in (fare irruzione in casa) or fare irruzione dentro. Typically conjugated as fare irruzione + preposition or with auxiliary avere in compound tenses (ha fatto irruzione).
target_language_example: La polizia ha deciso di fare irruzione nell'appartamento questa mattina.
native_language_example: The police decided to burst into the apartment this morning.

meaning: to poop; to have a bowel movement (childish/informal).
additional_notes: Common, informal and somewhat childish way to say 'to defecate'. Used with children or in casual speech. More polite or neutral alternatives: 'fare i bisogni', 'defecare' (medical/formal), or 'andare di corpo'.
target_language_example: Il bambino deve fare la cacca.
native_language_example: The child needs to poop.

meaning: to make a difference; to matter or have a significant impact.
additional_notes: Used when something or someone changes an outcome or has notable influence. Can refer to small or large effects (e.g., a gesture, a decision, a person). Common in both spoken and written Italian. Conjugate 'fare' as needed: 'fa la differenza', 'ha fatto la differenza', etc.
target_language_example: Un piccolo gesto può fare la differenza.
native_language_example: A small gesture can make a difference.

meaning: to teach a class / to give a lesson
additional_notes: Used when a teacher or instructor leads a class or gives a lesson. Can refer to a single lesson (fare la lezione) or regular teaching (fare lezione di storia). Commonly used with a subject: fare lezione di matematica. Also used impersonally about classes taking place: Oggi non si fa lezione (more natural: oggi non c'è lezione).
target_language_example: Oggi il professore deve fare lezione di storia alle nove.
native_language_example: Today the professor has to teach a history class at nine.

meaning: to shed light on; to explain or clarify (also: to illuminate physically)
additional_notes: Used both figuratively (to clarify a fact, make something clear) and literally (to provide light). Common in contexts like investigations, explanations, or describing light sources. Typical constructions: fare luce su + topic (to clarify/bring to light something) or fare luce in/nel + place (to light up a place).
target_language_example: Dobbiamo fare luce su quello che è successo ieri sera.
native_language_example: We need to shed light on what happened last night.

meaning: to make peace; to reconcile (with someone).
additional_notes: Used when two people or groups resolve a dispute and restore friendly relations. Commonly used with the preposition 'con' to specify with whom: 'fare pace con qualcuno'. Can appear in various tenses (e.g., 'fanno pace', 'hanno fatto pace') and occasionally in reflexive colloquial form 'farsi pace' (less formal).
target_language_example: Dopo anni di litigi hanno deciso di fare pace.
native_language_example: After years of arguing, they decided to make peace.

meaning: 'do for you' — used to ask or offer what action/service you can do for someone.
additional_notes: Common in offers of help or service. Often appears in questions: "Cosa posso fare per te?" (How can I help you?/What can I do for you?). Can be formal or informal depending on context and pronoun (per Lei = formal). The verb fare is general — could mean help, fix, get, or perform a task depending on context.
target_language_example: Dimmi cosa devo fare per te e lo farò.
native_language_example: Tell me what I should do for you and I'll do it.

meaning: to be pleasing; to make someone happy; to please (someone).
additional_notes: Usually used impersonally with an indirect object pronoun to indicate who is pleased: mi fa piacere (it pleases me / I'm glad), ti farà piacere (you will be pleased). Common in polite reactions: "Mi fa piacere conoscerti" = "I'm pleased to meet you." Often followed by an infinitive, a noun phrase, or a clause. Tense and agreement follow fare: Mi fa piacere (singular), Ci fanno piacere (plural objects).
target_language_example: Mi fa piacere che tu sia venuto; fare piacere a qualcuno è importante.
native_language_example: I'm glad you came; making someone happy is important.

meaning: to make room / to make space (for someone or something).
additional_notes: Commonly used when asking someone to move so there is space (e.g., on a bench, in a seat, in a car) or when arranging things to free up space. Often found in imperative or infinitive forms: 'Mi puoi fare posto?' or 'Puoi fare posto?' Can be used literally (physical space) or more loosely (creating opportunity).
target_language_example: Mi puoi fare posto sul divano?
native_language_example: Can you make room for me on the sofa?

meaning: to put pressure on; to pressure (someone) — to try to influence or persuade forcefully
additional_notes: Commonly used when someone exerts influence, pressure, or coercion on a person, group, or institution (e.g., fare pressione su qualcuno, fare pressione per ottenere qualcosa). Can be physical but is more often social/political/negotiation pressure. Conjugate 'fare' as needed and follow with 'su' + object when specifying who/what is pressured.
target_language_example: I sindacati stanno a fare pressione sull'azienda per migliori condizioni di lavoro.
native_language_example: The unions are putting pressure on the company for better working conditions.

meaning: to do (something) before (doing something else) — indicates one action must be completed prior to another
additional_notes: Usually followed by an infinitive (e.g., 'fare qualcosa prima di + infinitive'). Can appear with verbs like 'dovere' or expressions such as 'avere da fare'. 'Prima di poter' is the modern preferred form; 'prima di potere' is older/less common. The phrase can express tasks to complete before an event (e.g., 'fare le commissioni prima di partire').
target_language_example: Ho ancora molto da fare prima di poter andare a casa.
native_language_example: I still have a lot to do before I can go home.

meaning: to make something one's own; to embrace or adopt something fully; colloquially, to really like or take to something or to appropriate/claim something.
additional_notes: Meaning depends on context: 1) take ownership/adopt (a habit, an object) — often with reflexive/object pronouns; 2) express strong liking/enjoyment (similar to 'mi piace molto' in some constructions); 3) appropriate or claim something. Common in colloquial speech; register is informal. Word-for-word literal translation is possible ('to do own'), but idiomatic senses vary with pronouns and tense (e.g., 'me lo sono fatto proprio', 'gliel'ho fatto proprio').
target_language_example: Ho deciso di fare proprio quel metodo per studiare e ora funziona.
native_language_example: I decided to make that study method my own and now it works.

meaning: to do anything; to do whatever (often with a negative or careless sense: do anything, even something inappropriate).
additional_notes: Literally 'to do whatever'. Used to express willingness to do anything or to criticize someone who acts without care or standards (e.g., 'fa qualunque' = 'he/she does anything' meaning 'does anything, even wrong things'). Can appear with infinitive or clauses (fare qualunque cosa, fare qualsiasi cosa). More common variants: 'fare qualsiasi cosa' or 'fare qualunque cosa'.
target_language_example: Non fare qualunque: pensaci prima di agire.
native_language_example: Don't do just anything: think before you act.

meaning: to report (to a superior); to give a report or account
additional_notes: Used when someone must inform a person in authority about events, progress, or a situation. Common in military, workplace, or official contexts. Can be followed by a person (fare rapporto a/ al + person) or used without specifying the recipient when context is clear.
target_language_example: Devo fare rapporto al comandante prima di uscire.
native_language_example: I have to report to the commander before leaving.

meaning: to refer to; to make reference to (something or someone).
additional_notes: Commonly used in formal and everyday contexts to indicate pointing to information, a source, a document, or a person. Often followed by a preposition (a, su, or con) or a direct object: fare riferimento a qualcosa / a qualcuno, fare riferimento a quanto detto, fare riferimento al documento. Can also mean 'consult' in contexts like 'fare riferimento al manuale'.
target_language_example: Per maggiori dettagli, puoi fare riferimento al sito ufficiale.
native_language_example: For more details, you can refer to the official website.

meaning: to be disgusting / to be awful; to disgust someone (colloquial)
additional_notes: Common informal expression. Can be used impersonally (qualcosa fa schifo — something is disgusting/terrible) or with a person as object (mi fa schifo — it disgusts me; also mi fa schifo can mean 'I feel disgusted'). Often used to express strong dislike or poor quality. Tone is colloquial and can be rude in polite contexts.
target_language_example: Questa pizza fa schifo, non la mangio.
native_language_example: This pizza is awful/This pizza is disgusting, I won't eat it.

meaning: to be quiet; to be silent; to quiet down.
additional_notes: Common imperative/requests to ask someone or a group to stop making noise. Can be polite or firm depending on tone and context. Often used with verbs like 'devi' (you must), 'chiediamo' (we ask), or in reported commands. Usable with singular or plural subjects and in both formal and informal contexts depending on accompanying pronouns or tone.
target_language_example: Devi fare silenzio!
native_language_example: You must be quiet!

meaning: to make progress / to advance (literally 'to make/do road'); to go far in life or in a career.
additional_notes: Used both literally (to travel or cover distance) and figuratively (to progress, become successful, or 'get far' in something). Commonly appears in phrases like 'fare molta strada' (to go a long way / make a lot of progress). Can be used with personal subjects or impersonal constructions.
target_language_example: Se continua così, potrà fare strada nella sua carriera.
native_language_example: If he keeps going like this, he will be able to go far in his career.

meaning: 'all you have to do is follow his/her/its' (used to say the only required action).
additional_notes: This pattern appears in sentences like "Tutto ciò che (devi/dovete/deve) fare è seguire il suo consiglio." The core structure is "Tutto ciò che + [subject] + dovere + fare è + [action]" meaning "All you (he/you(pl)) have to do is [action]." "Il suo" must be completed by a noun (e.g., "il suo consiglio" = "his/her advice"). Verb agreement: fare is infinitive; auxiliary (devi/dovete/deve) changes with subject. Can be used with any object after "il suo" (il suo piano, il suo esempio, ecc.).
target_language_example: Tutto ciò che devi fare è seguire il suo piano.
native_language_example: All you have to do is follow his plan.

meaning: 'would (do) the' — part of a conditional construction using the verb fare (to do/make) plus the definite article; often translates as "would [do] the..." or appears in idiomatic questions like "What would the world do without..."
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself but a combination: farebbe (conditional of fare = would do/make) + the definite article il. You will see it in conditional sentences (often questions) where the verb is followed by a noun introduced by il. Translate according to context (e.g. "Che farebbe il mondo senza il tè?" = "What would the world do without tea?"). Word order can vary: subject may follow the verb (especially in questions).
target_language_example: Che farebbe il paese senza i suoi insegnanti?
native_language_example: What would the country do without its teachers?

meaning: 'would ... if' — conditional + 'if' used to ask about hypothetical situations
additional_notes: Used to form polite or speculative questions about what someone would do in an imagined situation. 'Farebbe' is the third-person singular conditional of 'fare' (would do). Often followed by a clause in the imperfect subjunctive (e.g. 'fosse', 'sapesse', 'incontrasse') to express hypothetical conditions.
target_language_example: Cosa farebbe se vincesse la lotteria?
native_language_example: What would you do if you won the lottery?

meaning: 'would (do) a' — conditional form used to say someone 'would do' something (followed by a noun or phrase).
additional_notes: Combines the conditional of fare (farebbe = he/she/you formal would do) with the indefinite article una. Common in questions or exclamations to ask who would do such a thing (Chi farebbe una cosa del genere?). Often followed by nouns like cosa, cosa del genere, cosa simile, or by clauses: farebbe una cosa così. Context expresses hypothetical or rhetorical disbelief.
target_language_example: Chi farebbe una cosa simile?
native_language_example: Who would do a thing like that?

meaning: 'I would never (do) ... harm to' (part of the phrase "non farei mai del male a ..." meaning "I would never hurt ...").
additional_notes: This sequence appears in negative conditional sentences: non farei mai del male a + person (or non le/le farei mai del male). In natural Italian you usually say "non farei mai del male a [qualcuno]" or simply "non farei mai del male". The verb tense is conditional present (farei = I would do), mai = never, del male = harm/evil; the indirect object pronoun (le, gli, ti) can appear before the verb.
target_language_example: Non farei mai del male a un animale.
native_language_example: I would never hurt an animal.

meaning: 'we will do everything' (usually followed by 'possibile' → 'we will do everything possible')
additional_notes: This is the future tense of 'fare' (faremo = we will do) plus 'tutto il' meaning 'all the' and is typically completed by 'possibile' (possible). Used to reassure someone — 'we'll do everything (we can)'. Can be followed by other nouns too (e.g., 'faremo tutto il necessario' = 'we will do everything necessary').
target_language_example: Faremo tutto il possibile per risolvere il problema.
native_language_example: We will do everything possible to fix the problem.

meaning: you would do well (to) / it would be wise for you (to)
additional_notes: Polite suggestion or advice directed at 'tu' (second person singular). Often followed by 'a' + infinitive (e.g. faresti bene a dire) and implies that doing the action is advisable. Can be softened by adding 'penso che' or used directly for stronger warning. Used in everyday and formal contexts.
target_language_example: Faresti bene a riposare prima dell'esame.
native_language_example: You would do well to rest before the exam.

meaning: to make a long story short; to be brief
additional_notes: Used to summarize or skip details before giving the main point or conclusion. Commonly appears in the phrase 'Per farla breve' = 'To make a long story short'. Informal but widely used in spoken and written Italian.
target_language_example: Per farla breve, ho detto di no e se ne è andato.
native_language_example: To make a long story short, I said no and he left.

meaning: to do it (with)... — used to say how something should be done (with care, attention, etc.).
additional_notes: Farla con combines the verb fare (to do/make) in the pronoun form 'farla' (do it) with 'con' (with). It appears before a noun or phrase that describes the manner or attitude (con attenzione, con cura, con gli occhi bendati). Common in instructions or statements about how to perform an action. Use appropriate pronoun/verb form depending on subject (e.g., farlo con, farla con, farle con).
target_language_example: Devi farla con calma, non correre.
native_language_example: You must do it calmly, don't rush.

meaning: to stop (doing something); to put an end to it; to quit.
additional_notes: Informal expression used to tell someone to stop a behaviour or to end a situation. Often appears as an imperative (Falla finita! / Basta, falla finita!) or in constructions like 'farla finita con...' (to put an end to something). Equivalent to English 'cut it out', 'stop it', or 'put an end to it'.
target_language_example: Per favore, falla finita con quelle battute, non è divertente.
native_language_example: Please, stop it with those jokes, it's not funny.

meaning: do it too / do it as well
additional_notes: A combination of the verb phrase 'farlo' (to do it) plus 'anche' (also/too). Used to invite or warn someone to do (or not do) the same action as someone else. Tone depends on context and may be affirmative, encouragement, or prohibition when negated ('non farlo anche...'). Commonly followed by a pronoun or noun indicating who is addressed (tu, voi, tuo figlio, etc.).
target_language_example: Se hai finito i compiti, puoi farlo anche tu.
native_language_example: If you finished your homework, you can do it too.

meaning: never do it again; to not let something be done again
additional_notes: A forceful phrase used to tell someone to stop an action permanently or to ensure something will not happen again. Often appears after a command or threat: 'Non farlo mai più' = 'Don't ever do it again.' 'Farlo mai più' by itself is the infinitive construction with 'mai più' (never again). Tone can be strong depending on context.
target_language_example: Non farlo mai più, o ti mando via.
native_language_example: Don't ever do it again, or I'll send you away.

meaning: to get scared; to chicken out (become afraid or lose courage)
additional_notes: Informal/slang expression. Literally 'to do it under oneself' but idiomatic: used when someone becomes frightened or decides not to go through with something because of fear. Commonly appears as 'farsela sotto' (infinitive) or conjugated with reflexive pronoun and auxiliary: e.g. 'me la sono fatta sotto' = 'I got scared'. Primarily used in spoken Italian.
target_language_example: All'inizio voleva saltare dal ponte, ma poi ha deciso di farsela sotto.
native_language_example: At first he wanted to jump off the bridge, but then he decided to chicken out.

meaning: to make someone wait (for you); to keep someone waiting
additional_notes: Reflexive construction: the subject is the person who causes the waiting. Used when apologizing or explaining that you were late or kept someone waiting. Conjugates like farsi + past participle (mi sono fatto aspettare) or in infinitive (farsi aspettare). Often appears with time expressions (farti aspettare un'ora) or with da/per. Can be used in various tenses and persons.
target_language_example: Mi dispiace di averti fatto farti aspettare, non era mia intenzione.
native_language_example: I'm sorry to have made you wait, it wasn't my intention.

meaning: to step forward; to come forward (volunteer, speak up, or approach)
additional_notes: Used both literal (physically step forward) and figurative (volunteer, admit something, speak up). Often reflexive with person who should 'farsi avanti' — e.g. to volunteer for a task, to present oneself, or to speak up about knowledge. Can be followed by 'con' or an infinitive (e.g. 'farsi avanti e salutare').
target_language_example: Se qualcuno sa la verità, è ora di farsi avanti.
native_language_example: If anyone knows the truth, it's time to come forward.

meaning: to step aside; to move out of the way (literally and figuratively).
additional_notes: Used both physically (move out of someone's path) and figuratively (make room, withdraw from a role or let someone else take over). Common reflexive construction: farsi + da parte. Can be used in imperative (Fatti da parte!) or intransitively (Si è fatto da parte).
target_language_example: Per favore, puoi farti da parte? Devo passare con la valigia.
native_language_example: Please, can you step aside? I need to pass with the suitcase.

meaning: to play (a game) or to act in a way that benefits someone else; commonly used in the expression 'farsi il gioco di qualcuno' meaning 'to play into someone's hands' (to be outwitted or to unintentionally help someone).
additional_notes: Formed from the reflexive 'farsi' + 'gioco' (game). Standalone 'farsi gioco' is uncommon; it's usually used in fuller expressions like 'farsi il gioco di qualcuno'. Can be literal (to play a game oneself) but more often idiomatic (to unwittingly help someone).
target_language_example: Non devi farti farsi gioco di lui — non lasciare che ti usi.
native_language_example: You mustn't let him play you — don't let him use you.

meaning: 'to shave (one's face)' — to shave oneself
additional_notes: Reflexive construction: farsi + article + noun (la barba). Used when the subject shaves their own beard or face. Common present-tense forms: mi faccio la barba (I shave), ti fai la barba (you shave), si fa la barba (he/she shaves). Can also be used with past or future tenses (mi sono fatto la barba, mi farò la barba).
target_language_example: Ogni mattina devo farsi la barba prima di uscire.
native_language_example: Every morning I have to shave before going out.

meaning: to hurt oneself
additional_notes: Reflexive construction meaning someone causes injury to themselves. Used with modal verbs (potere, dovere) and in past forms (potuto, avrebbe potuto). Can imply physical harm; context may allow minor injuries. Common patterns: (non) dovere + farsi male, potere + farsi male, poter(si) + essere/avere + potuto farsi male (past).
target_language_example: Nessuno deve farsi male.
native_language_example: No one must hurt themselves.

meaning: to make oneself noticed; to attract attention to oneself
additional_notes: Reflexive verb phrase: 'farsi' + past participle 'notare'. Used when someone actively seeks or succeeds in getting others' attention (visually, verbally, or by actions). Can be neutral (simply being noticed) or imply trying to stand out. Commonly followed by da/da parte di + people or just used intransitively (Mi sono fatto notare = I made myself noticed).
target_language_example: Ha cercato di farsi notare con un vestito colorato.
native_language_example: He tried to make himself noticed with a colorful outfit.

meaning: to make oneself heard; to get in touch / let someone know you're there
additional_notes: Literally 'to make oneself heard.' Used for speaking up so others hear your opinion or for contacting someone (letting them hear from you). Often appears with reflexive 'farsi' + past participle 'sentire'; context decides whether it means asserting oneself vocally or simply getting in touch (phone, message, email).
target_language_example: È importante farsi sentire quando non sei d'accordo.
native_language_example: It's important to make yourself heard when you disagree.

meaning: to accept something; to come to terms with (often unpleasant) reality.
additional_notes: Used when someone needs to stop resisting or hoping and accept a situation. Often used reflexively (farsi) and followed by 'di' + verb or nothing: e.g. 'Devi farti una ragione' (You must accept it). Can be used for both minor disappointments and serious matters. Tone is neutral to slightly blunt.
target_language_example: Devi farti una ragione di quello che è successo; non puoi cambiare il passato.
native_language_example: You must come to terms with what happened; you can't change the past.

meaning: 'to be seen' / 'to show oneself' (often 'to let oneself be seen' or 'to go to see someone' depending on context).
additional_notes: Common pronominal verb. Can mean: 1) to make oneself visible or appear in public (letting others see you), 2) to go and see someone (e.g. a doctor) when used reflexively with context like 'dovrebbe farsi vedere' = 'he/she should get checked/see someone'). Often used with negative/privative forms (non farsi vedere = to avoid being seen). Context determines whether it's about visibility or visiting/checking up.
target_language_example: Dovrebbe farsi vedere da un medico prima che peggiori.
native_language_example: He should go see a doctor before it gets worse.

meaning: to get in touch (with someone); to make oneself heard/seen — i.e., to contact someone or respond after a period of silence.
additional_notes: Commonly used when asking someone to contact you or to respond after a period of silence. Often used reflexively with a pronoun: 'fatti vivo' (informal singular imperative: 'get in touch'), 'fatevi vivi' (plural). Can refer to calling, texting, emailing, or showing up in person. Tone can be casual or slightly urging.
target_language_example: Dovresti farti vivo quando arrivi in città; così ci organizziamo.
native_language_example: You should get in touch when you arrive in town; that way we can make plans.

meaning: will cause (someone) harm / will do (something) of (a quality) — depends on context
additional_notes: This phrase combines the future of fare (farà = he/she/it will do/make) with del (partitive 'of the' or 'some'). In contexts with 'male' (farà del male) it means 'will hurt/harm (someone)'. With expressions like 'farà del suo meglio' it means 'will do his best' (literally 'will do of his best'). The object (who is harmed or who does the best) is shown by an indirect or direct pronoun or name. Common structure: [subject] farà del + [noun].
target_language_example: Non ti farà del male, stai tranquillo.
native_language_example: He won't hurt you, don't worry.

meaning: 'I will do (some) / I will do my' — part of phrases like "farò del mio meglio" (I'll do my best) or "farò del male" (I will harm).
additional_notes: Farò = future of fare (to do/make). Del is the contraction of di + il and combines with a following noun (del mio = of my). Alone, "farò del" is incomplete and needs a noun or expression after it. Common fixed phrase: "farò del mio meglio" = I'll do my best. Context determines literal vs. idiomatic meaning (e.g. "farò del male" = I'll harm).
target_language_example: Farò del mio meglio per aiutarti domani.
native_language_example: I'll do my best to help you tomorrow.

meaning: 'I will (do) a' — the future first-person singular of fare + the indefinite article una, used to say you will do or give something (an action, a thing, a question, a favor, etc.).
additional_notes: Farò = 'I will do/make'. When followed by una + noun, it indicates you'll perform or give one of that noun (e.g., una sorpresa, una domanda, una doccia). Can also appear in idiomatic expressions (e.g., non te ne farò una colpa = I won't blame you for it). Use for planned future actions. Replace una with other articles/genders as needed (farò un, farò delle).
target_language_example: Domani farò una telefonata al dottore.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I'll make a phone call to the doctor.

meaning: 'do that' or 'do what (someone/something does or says)'.
additional_notes: Imperative form (voi) of fare + quello. Used to tell a group (you all) to do a specific thing or to follow instructions/behaviour already mentioned. Often appears in patterns like 'Fate quello che...' = 'Do what...'. 'Quello' can refer to an action, instruction, or example just mentioned. For singular you would say 'Fai quello' (informal) or 'Faccia quello' (formal).
target_language_example: Fate quello che vi ho spiegato.
native_language_example: Do what I explained to you.

meaning: 'made/treated myself a' or 'I did myself a' (reflexive past: I had/did for myself)
additional_notes: Combination of the reflexive past participle fatta (feminine of fatto) plus the indefinite article un. Used with verbs where the subject does something for themselves: mi sono fatta un + noun/verb (e.g. mi sono fatta un bagno = I took a bath). Gender and agreement matter: a woman speaker uses fatta; a man would say fatto. Context shows completed action (past).
target_language_example: Ieri mi sono fatta un caffè prima di uscire.
native_language_example: Yesterday I made myself a coffee before going out.

meaning: A short structure using the feminine past participle 'fatta' + the indefinite article 'una' to indicate having done or experienced something (e.g., had a laugh, taken a shower, made a promise, built a new life). The form reflects a feminine subject; masculine would be 'fatto una'.
additional_notes: Not a fixed idiom but a common, compositional structure: 'fatta' (feminine past participle of 'fare') + a noun. Used with appropriate auxiliary or context (e.g., 'mi sono fatta', 'ti sei fatta', 'è stata fatta una...'). Subject gender matters: a woman or feminine noun uses 'fatta', a man uses 'fatto'. Can translate literally as 'made a/ had a' depending on context.
target_language_example: La storia era così divertente che mi sono fatta una risata.
native_language_example: The story was so funny that I had a laugh.

meaning: An insulting command meaning 'go f*** yourself' or 'screw you'.
additional_notes: Very rude and vulgar. Literally 'get yourself fucked' (reflexive imperative). Used to tell someone off or express strong anger/hostility. Do not use in polite conversation; common in heated arguments or coarse slang. Tone and context make it offensive.
target_language_example: Se non vuoi aiutarmi, fatti fottere.
native_language_example: If you don't want to help me, go f*** yourself.

meaning: 'mind your own business' (imperative, telling someone to stay out of others' matters).
additional_notes: Shortened form of 'fatti gli affari tuoi'. Common, direct, sometimes rude. Used as an imperative to tell someone to stop interfering or asking questions. Can be softened with tone or added words; usually addressed informally (tu).
target_language_example: Fatti gli affari tuoi e non immischiarti in questa discussione.
native_language_example: Mind your own business and don't get involved in this discussion.

meaning: homemade; made at home (not store-bought).
additional_notes: Used to describe food, goods, or products prepared or made at home rather than bought ready-made. Often implies freshness, tradition, or family recipe. Can modify nouns (e.g., 'pasta fatta in casa', 'dolce fatto in casa').
target_language_example: Questa marmellata è fatta in casa.
native_language_example: This jam is homemade.

meaning: done that / done it / done what (was needed or said).
additional_notes: Used to refer back to an action just mentioned or implied: 'fatto ciò che...' = 'done what...'. Common in past contexts. Often appears with verbs like 'fare' in passato (ho fatto) and relative clauses (che era necessario, che mi è stato chiesto). Can translate as 'done that' or 'done what was required.'
target_language_example: Ho fatto ciò che mi hai chiesto, quindi ora possiamo partire.
native_language_example: I did what you asked me, so we can leave now.

meaning: have/made some (used with plural nouns): 'have made some' or 'made some'.
additional_notes: Combination of the past participle fatto (from fare, 'to do/make') with the partitive article degli (plural 'some' before consonant clusters). Used in passato prossimo: [avere] + fatto + degli + [plural noun]. Common in sentences like "Ho fatto degli errori" = "I made some mistakes."
target_language_example: Abbiamo fatto degli esercizi ieri.
native_language_example: We did/made some exercises yesterday.

meaning: caused some
additional_notes: This phrase is a combination of the verb 'fare' (to do/make) in a past participle form ('fatto') followed by 'del' (de + il) and is used before nouns to mean 'caused some [harm/chaos/effort/etc.]' or 'did some [of something]'. Common uses in the examples: 'fatto del male' = 'caused some harm', 'fatto del casino' = 'made a mess/caused trouble', 'fatto del tuo meglio' (with possessive) = 'did your best' (note word order: fatto del mio/tuo/nostro meglio). Context and the noun after 'del' determine the exact translation. 'Del' may also contract with other articles (della, dei, delle) depending on gender/number.
target_language_example: Hai fatto del bene quando hai aiutato i vicini.
native_language_example: You did some good when you helped the neighbors.

meaning: done his/her part; did what they could (often followed by 'meglio' = 'their best')
additional_notes: Literally 'made of his/hers'. Commonly appears in the phrase 'ha fatto del suo meglio' meaning 'he/she did his/her best' or more literally 'he/she did what they could best'. Used to state someone tried or contributed as much as they could. Often used in past tense (ha fatto).
target_language_example: Ha fatto del suo meglio per aiutare, ma non è bastato.
native_language_example: He did his best to help, but it wasn't enough.

meaning: made (someone) do; caused (someone) to do.
additional_notes: Compound of passato participle 'fatto' + infinitive 'fare' used in causative constructions (far + infinitive) in the past: 'ha fatto fare' = 'he/she/it had (someone) do' or 'made (someone) do'. Often appears with a pronoun to show who was caused to act (e.g., 'ti ha fatto fare' = 'he made you do'). Can express both direct causation (someone made someone do something) and indirect (had something done by someone). Context determines whether it's literal coercion or more neutral causation. Common in conversational Italian.
target_language_example: Mi hanno fatto fare un lavoro che non sapevo fare.
native_language_example: They made me do a job I didn't know how to do.

meaning: 'pretended' or 'made as if' (to have done something that wasn't real).
additional_notes: Common structure: 'fare finta di + infinitive' (to pretend to do something). In past tense use 'ha fatto finta', 'ho fatto finta', etc. Often followed by 'di' + verb (e.g. 'di non sentire', 'di essere'). Used to describe deliberate pretense or acting like something is true when it isn't.
target_language_example: Lei ha fatto finta di non vedermi per tutta la serata.
native_language_example: She pretended not to see me the whole evening.

meaning: done the
additional_notes: past participle of fare + the masculine singular article il. This is not a fixed expression: it is followed by a masculine singular noun, and in full sentences often appears as ho/hai/ha/hanno fatto il ... . In English it may be 'did the', 'made the', or something more idiomatic depending on the noun: fare il bagno = have/take a bath, fare il giro = go around/take a tour, fare il dottorato = do a PhD.
target_language_example: Stamattina ho fatto il letto prima di uscire.
native_language_example: This morning I made the bed before leaving.

meaning: lit. 'made/done the' — used as part of past‑tense phrases meaning 'did/made the (something)'.
additional_notes: This phrase is not idiomatic on its own; it's the past participle 'fatto' (done/made) followed by the feminine singular definite article 'la' and a noun (e.g. la chiamata, la spesa, la cosa). Use with auxiliary 'avere' (ho/ha/abbiamo/avete) to form the passato prossimo: (avere) + fatto + la + [noun]. Agreement: 'fatto' does not change for feminine singular when used with avere. Context tells the full meaning (e.g. 'ha fatto la chiamata' = 'he/she made the call').
target_language_example: Ho fatto la cena prima che arrivassero gli ospiti.
native_language_example: I made dinner before the guests arrived.

meaning: made the (right) choice / chose (something).
additional_notes: Literal components: fatto (made/done) + la scelta (the choice). Commonly appears as 'fare la scelta giusta' (to make the right choice). In sentences it indicates someone has decided or chosen; context determines whether 'right' (giusta) is implied. Verb forms often include avere (ha/hanno fatto).
target_language_example: Hai fatto la scelta giusta a venire con noi.
native_language_example: You made the right choice by coming with us.
