meaning: would have done better / should have (done) — used to say someone would have been better off doing something different.
additional_notes: Often appears in conditional constructions with a past infinitive introduced by 'a' (e.g., 'avrebbe fatto meglio a...'). Used to express regret, advice, or criticism about what someone ought to have done. Can be followed by an infinitive verb. In questions ('Avresti fatto meglio?') it asks whether someone would have been better off doing so.
target_language_example: Avresti fatto meglio a chiamare prima.
native_language_example: You would have done better to call earlier.

meaning: made a lot
additional_notes: Literal components: fatto = done/made; molto = much/a lot/very. Meaning depends on context: 'ha fatto molto denaro' → 'made a lot of money'; 'ha fatto molto lavoro' → 'has done a lot (of work)'; in temporal phrases 'fatto molto tempo fa' the adverb molto modifies 'tempo' meaning 'a long time' (this is slightly different structure: 'fatto molto tempo fa' = 'done a long time ago'). Verb tense/person is given by the surrounding verb (e.g. 'ha fatto' = he/she/it has made/done; 'ho fatto' = I have made/done).
target_language_example: Ho fatto molto lavoro quest'anno.
native_language_example: I have done a lot of work this year.

meaning: did nothing (of) / made nothing (of) — part of a structure meaning 'didn't do anything (to/for)'
additional_notes: This phrase is a colloquial combination: fatto (past participle of fare) + niente (nothing) + di (of/to). It typically appears inside larger sentences like «Non ho fatto niente di speciale» (I didn't do anything special) or «Non ha fatto niente di male» (He/She didn't do anything wrong). Alone as given it is incomplete; expect a negative subject or auxiliary before 'fatto' (e.g., non ho fatto niente di ...).
target_language_example: Non ho fatto niente di interessante ieri.
native_language_example: I didn't do anything interesting yesterday.

meaning: 'done nothing (wrong) / haven't done anything (wrong)'.
additional_notes: Used in negative sentences with verbs like 'dire' or 'avere' to say someone did nothing (often nothing wrong). The full negative phrase is usually 'non ... ha/hanno/ho fatto niente/nonnulla di [agg./sbagliato/ male]'. 'Nulla' and 'niente' are interchangeable (both mean 'nothing'). Word order: 'non ho fatto nulla di sbagliato' = 'I haven't done anything wrong.'
target_language_example: Non ho fatto nulla di male, ve lo giuro.
native_language_example: I haven't done anything wrong, I swear.

meaning: "done today" or "did today" (past action that happened today)
additional_notes: Used after verbs (e.g., 'hai fatto oggi?') to ask or state what someone did during the current day. Can appear in questions ('Che cosa hai fatto oggi?') or in statements describing something completed today. In sentence 1 the structure is different: 'sei la ragazza più bella che mi sono fatto oggi' uses 'fatto' as past participle of 'fare' in a colloquial reflexive expression meaning 'I've had (sex with)' or 'I've been with' today—this is informal and can be vulgar.
target_language_example: Che cosa hai fatto oggi dopo la scuola?
native_language_example: What did you do today after school?

meaning: 'done earlier' / 'done before' or (in some contexts) 'did it earlier' / 'did it before'.
additional_notes: Commonly appears after a verb in passive forms (È stato fatto prima = it was done earlier) or after a subject in perfect constructions (ho fatto prima = I did it earlier/ as soon as possible depending on context). With 'mai' it can mean 'ever before' (non l'abbiamo mai fatto prima = we've never done it before). Context and auxiliary verbs determine tense and voice. Literal translation to English usually works.
target_language_example: Non l'avevo mai fatto prima.
native_language_example: I had never done it before.

meaning: literally 'done that' or 'made that' — combination of past participle fatto + demonstrative quel ('that'), used to refer to something done/made on a specific day or that specific thing/person.
additional_notes: Not a fixed idiom on its own; it's just the past participle fatto followed by the demonstrative adjectivequel. Meaning depends on context: can describe an action (what was done that day), a thing made (that dress I made), or be part of expressions about someone causing something (What did that ... do to you?). Word order, gender and number may change (fatto quel vestito / fatta quella cosa / fatti quei giorni). Pay attention to auxiliaries (avere/essere) and agreement when necessary.
target_language_example: Che ha fatto quel ragazzo quel giorno?
native_language_example: What did that boy do that day?

meaning: done that
additional_notes: Literally 'done that' or 'done what'. Often used to refer back to an action previously mentioned or implied (e.g. 'what needed to be done' or 'what you asked me to do'). Context determines whether it means a specific task ('done that') or a completed obligation ('done what had to be done').
target_language_example: Ho fatto quello che mi hai detto di fare.
native_language_example: I did what you told me to do.

meaning: has done what (he/she) has (promised/asked) — used to say someone did what they said or were asked to do.
additional_notes: This fragment appears in sentences like 'Ha fatto quello che ha promesso di fare' or 'Ho fatto quello che ha chiesto.' It often follows a subject (Ha, Mary, Tom, Ho) and is completed by an infinitive or a clause (di fare, chiesto). In English it corresponds to 'did what (someone) said/asked/promised.' The tense and subject depend on the verb before the phrase (e.g. 'Ha' = he/she has/did, 'Ho' = I have/did).
target_language_example: Luca ha fatto quello che ha promesso di fare per la squadra.
native_language_example: Luca did what he promised to do for the team.

meaning: 'referred to my...' (used before a family member or person)
additional_notes: This phrase is the perfect participle construction of 'fare riferimento a' (to refer to). 'Fatto riferimento a mio' is followed by a noun like 'padre', 'fratello', etc. In correct Italian you usually include the definite article with family members: 'fatto riferimento a mio padre' is common in spoken Italian, though more formally you might say 'fatto riferimento a mio padre' or 'ha fatto riferimento a mio padre' (both acceptable). Verb forms change with subject: 'ho fatto', 'hai fatto', 'ha fatto', 'abbiamo fatto', 'avete fatto', 'hanno fatto'.
target_language_example: Hai fatto riferimento a mio fratello durante la riunione.
native_language_example: You referred to my brother during the meeting.

meaning: had (something) repaired; caused/arranged for someone to repair something.
additional_notes: Common construction using fare + past participle (fatto + riparare) to indicate that you arranged for someone else to repair an item. Focus is on having the action done by another person or a service (not repairing it yourself). Can be followed by the person or place who did the repair (e.g., da mio fratello, in quel negozio).
target_language_example: Ho fatto riparare il telefono in un negozio vicino.
native_language_example: I had the phone repaired in a nearby shop.

meaning: made (someone) feel ...; caused (someone) to feel ...
additional_notes: Commonly used with a subject + "ha/mi/ti... fatto sentire" to describe how an action made someone feel (emotion, state, or identity). Often followed by adjectives, nouns, or clauses introduced by "come se" or "di/da". Literal components: "fatto" (made) + "sentire" (to feel/hear), but here it means 'caused to feel.'
target_language_example: Le sue parole mi hanno fatto sentire importante.
native_language_example: His words made me feel important.

meaning: alone; done/managed by oneself (literally: 'made/done alone').
additional_notes: Can describe a person being alone (e.g., Sono fatto solo is uncommon — prefer Sono da solo / Sono solo) or more naturally describe an action done by one person: l'ho fatto solo = I did it alone / by myself. Word order and auxiliary matter: when used with past participle, più common is 'l'ho fatto da solo' or 'l'ho fatto da me'. 'Fatto solo' without context may sound incomplete; add pronouns or subject for natural sentences.
target_language_example: L'ho fatto solo, non avevo aiuto.
native_language_example: I did it by myself, I had no help.

meaning: had (someone) cut the (hair). Indicates having something done by someone else (passive/causative).
additional_notes: This is the past participle construction of 'farsi + fare' used to express a causative action: someone caused/arranged for their hair to be cut (usually by a barber/hairdresser). It typically appears with a reflexive pronoun (mi/si/ci/vi) + essere (sono/è/si è) + fatto/fatta/i/e + tagliare + definite article + body part (i capelli). Use agreement (fatto/fatta/fatti) with the subject when required. Common in spoken Italian to say you 'got your hair cut.'
target_language_example: Mi sono fatto tagliare i capelli ieri dal parrucchiere.
native_language_example: I had my hair cut yesterday by the hairdresser.

meaning: literally 'done three' — indicates that someone did something three times or completed three of something.
additional_notes: Used after verbs (with avere/essere + past participle) or with 'ho fatto' to state quantity: e.g. 'l'ho fatto tre volte' (I did it three times) or 'ho fatto tre domande' (I asked three questions). Common in spoken and written Italian. Word order: 'fatto' (past participle) + number; you can also say 'tre volte' after the verb ('l'ho fatto tre volte').
target_language_example: L'ho fatto tre volte prima di capire.
native_language_example: I did it three times before I understood.

meaning: done everything (that)...
additional_notes: Used to say someone completed all actions or did everything possible, often followed by a clause introduced by che (e.g., fatto tutto quello che...). Can be shortened informally (fatto tutto quello) to mean 'did everything' without specifying what. Common in past or perfect constructions (ha fatto...).
target_language_example: Ha fatto tutto quello che gli ho chiesto.
native_language_example: He did everything I asked him to.

meaning: made a good (e.g., decision, impression, choice) — 'fatto' = made/done; 'un buon' = a good
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself but a common sequence: 'fatto un buon' is followed by a noun (e.g., 'fatto un buon lavoro', 'fatto un buon affare', 'fatto un buon primo impatto'). Use when saying someone did or made something good. 'Fatto' is the past participle of 'fare' and often used in passato prossimo: 'ho fatto un buon…' or 'hai fatto un buon…'.
target_language_example: Ho fatto un buon affare comprando quel computer.
native_language_example: I made a good deal buying that computer.

meaning: '(he/she) did his/her homework'.
additional_notes: Literal past tense phrase: 'fatto' = done (past participle of fare), 'i suoi compiti' = his/her homework or assignments. Used to say someone completed their homework; subject determines gender/number of 'suo/suoi'. In spoken Italian you might also hear 'ha fatto i compiti' (without 'suoi').
target_language_example: Anna ha fatto i suoi compiti prima di uscire.
native_language_example: Anna did her homework before going out.

meaning: made/done many (used before a feminine plural noun).
additional_notes: ‘Fatto’ is the past participle of fare (to do/make) and agrees with the auxiliary in passato prossimo (ha fatto = he/she has done/made). 'Molte' is the feminine plural of 'molto' meaning 'many' or 'a lot of' and must match the gender/number of the noun that follows (molte foto, molte cose, molte domande). English often omits a separate auxiliary adjective, so translate as 'has/had done/made many ...'.
target_language_example: Lei ha fatto molte domande durante la lezione.
native_language_example: She asked many questions during the lesson.

meaning: made/did some (a small number of) — used before a singular noun to indicate a few or some instances
additional_notes: Combines the past participle 'fatto' (made/done) with 'qualche' (literally 'some/each'), which is followed by a singular noun (qualche commento, qualche errore). 'Qualche' implies a small, indefinite number and always takes a singular noun in Italian. Use 'fatto qualche + [singular noun]' to say someone made/did some of that thing. For general plural ideas, Italian uses 'alcuni/qualche' differences: 'alcuni' takes a plural noun (alcuni commenti).
target_language_example: Ha fatto qualche domanda durante la lezione.
native_language_example: He asked some questions during the lesson.

meaning: done everything that / did all that
additional_notes: Used to say someone has completed all possible actions described by a following clause. Often followed by a verb phrase introduced by 'poteva', 'può', 'riesce', etc., to indicate ability or effort (past or present). Common in sentences like 'Ha fatto tutto quello che poteva' = 'He/She did everything he/she could.'
target_language_example: Ho fatto tutto quello che potevo per aiutarti.
native_language_example: I did everything I could to help you.

meaning: 'the fact is' or 'the truth is'.
additional_notes: Used to introduce or emphasize a fact, explanation, or reality—often followed by 'che' + clause (Il fatto è che...). Common in spoken and written Italian to present the main point or a reason.
target_language_example: Il fatto è che non ho abbastanza tempo per venire.
native_language_example: The fact is that I don't have enough time to come.

meaning: 'please, call me' or 'please call (me)'.
additional_notes: A polite request using 'per favore' (please) followed by the imperative 'chiamami' (call me). 'Chiamami' is the informal singular imperative of 'chiamare' + object pronoun 'mi' (me). Use to ask someone to call you (by phone) or to call you by a name (less common: 'chiamami Taro' = 'call me Taro'). For formal situations, use 'mi chiami' or 'mi chiami per favore' (subjunctive/conditional polite form) or 'mi chiami, per favore' with lei: 'Per favore, mi chiami.'
target_language_example: Per favore, chiamami quando arrivi a casa.
native_language_example: Please call me when you arrive home.

meaning: 'please, call me' (polite request asking someone to call you)
additional_notes: This combines 'per favore' (please) and the imperative/formal request 'chiamatemi' (call me). 'Chiamatemi' is the polite or plural imperative form (voi or Lei with full form); in casual speech you might hear 'chiamami' (call me — singular/informal). Placement: 'Per favore' usually comes at the start of the sentence. Time words (domani, stanotte, stasera) are added after to specify when.
target_language_example: Per favore, chiamatemi domani mattina.
native_language_example: Please, call me tomorrow morning.

meaning: Please, bring me... (polite request asking someone to bring something or take you to someone).
additional_notes: Combines 'per favore' (please) and the imperative form 'portatemi' (bring me — second person plural imperative, polite or addressing multiple people). Use 'portami' for informal singular 'you'. Can request objects (una bistecca, una sedia) or movement to a person/place (da lui, da loro).
target_language_example: Per favore, portatemi il conto.
native_language_example: Please, bring me the bill.

meaning: in favor of; supporting (something).
additional_notes: Used to express support for a proposal, idea or person. Often appears as 'a favore di' or 'a favore della' (with article) depending on the noun that follows. Common in voting or giving opinions: 'essere a favore' (to be in favor), 'votare a favore' (to vote in favor).
target_language_example: Sono a favore della nuova regola.
native_language_example: I am in favor of the new rule.

meaning: 'in favor of or against (the)'.
additional_notes: Used to ask whether someone supports or opposes a specific thing (project, plan, proposal). Gender agreement: 'favorevole' is neutral (same for both genders), while 'contrario/contraria' changes with the person's gender — use 'contrario' for a male speaker, 'contraria' for a female speaker. You can replace 'al' with other prepositions (e.g., 'alla', 'allo', 'ai') to match the noun that follows.
target_language_example: Sei favorevole o contraria al nuovo regolamento?
native_language_example: Are you in favor of or against the new regulation?

meaning: did some / made some (used to say someone did an action or made an effort); often appears in the phrase "fece del suo meglio" = "she/he did her/his best".
additional_notes: Fece is the past (passato remoto) of fare (to do/make). Del is the contraction of di + il and here often means 'some' or links to a noun (fece del pane = made some bread). In the fixed expression "fece del suo meglio" it means 'did their best' (made an effort). Context decides whether it's literal (made some of something) or idiomatic (made an effort).
target_language_example: Fece del suo meglio per finire il lavoro in tempo.
native_language_example: She did her best to finish the job on time.

meaning: he/she pretended (to).
additional_notes: Past simple (passato remoto or passato prossimo sense depending on region) of 'fare finta (di)' meaning 'to pretend (to)'. Used with an infinitive or 'di' + verb/noun: e.g. "fece finta di non sentire" = 'he/she pretended not to hear.' Common in storytelling; for spoken past you may also hear 'ha fatto finta' (passato prossimo).
target_language_example: Fece finta di non vedere il messaggio.
native_language_example: He/she pretended not to see the message.

meaning: 'he/she/it made/did the' or 'he/she/it did (something)'.
additional_notes: Fece is the passato remoto (simple past) of fare (to do/make). Followed by il + noun it often means 'made the [noun]' (e.g. fece il the = made the tea) or with some nouns it means 'did the [noun/action]' (fece il contrario = did the opposite; fece il lavoro = did the work). In spoken modern Italian the passato prossimo (ha fatto) is more common for past events except in some regions, formal writing, or storytelling.
target_language_example: Ieri fece il caffè per tutti.
native_language_example: Yesterday he made the coffee for everyone.

meaning: did nothing / did not do anything.
additional_notes: Past simple (passato remoto) or literary/ formal past of fare (fece) + nulla = 'did nothing'. Commonly used to deny action: 'he/she did nothing' or 'didn't do anything.' In everyday spoken Italian, passato prossimo (non ha fatto niente) or non fece niente (formal) are more common depending on region and register. Can be followed by purpose phrases (per aiutare) or by 'di + adjective' to mean 'did nothing wrong/illegal.'
target_language_example: Non fece nulla per risolvere il problema.
native_language_example: He did nothing to solve the problem.

meaning: did that / did what (was said or needed)
additional_notes: Past tense (passato remoto or passato prossimo contextually) of fare + quello. Commonly used to say someone 'did that' or 'did what was said/expected.' Often appears in structures like 'fece quello che...' = 'he/she did what...'. Can be used with a direct object omitted (e.g. 'Fece quello.') to mean 'He/She did it/that.'
target_language_example: Lei fece quello che le avevano chiesto.
native_language_example: She did what they had asked her.

meaning: wedding ring; marriage ring.
additional_notes: Refers to the ring exchanged at a wedding to show marriage. Commonly used in everyday speech when talking about wearing, losing, or removing the ring. 'Fede' alone can mean 'faith' in other contexts, but 'fede nuziale' specifically means wedding ring.
target_language_example: Ho perso la mia fede nuziale ieri sera.
native_language_example: I lost my wedding ring last night.

meaning: happy that you (have/are...); expresses happiness about something the listener did or is doing
additional_notes: Used with the subjunctive verb form (e.g., sia, abbia) after 'tu'. Common in spoken and written Italian to say you're glad about the listener's presence, feelings, or actions. Translate as 'I'm happy that you...' or 'glad you...'. Tone is neutral and polite; often followed by a clause describing what the person did or their state.
target_language_example: Sono felice che tu sia venuto oggi.
native_language_example: I'm happy that you came today.

meaning: happy for me (i.e., pleased on my behalf)
additional_notes: Used when asking or saying that someone should feel happiness or be pleased about something that happened to the speaker. Often appears with modal verbs (dovrebbe, dovresti, può) to express expectation, request, or mild reproach. 'Per' here means 'for' in the sense of 'on behalf of'.
target_language_example: Dovresti essere felice per me, ho finalmente il lavoro!
native_language_example: You should be happy for me, I finally got the job!

meaning: happy if; would be happy if (conditional).
additional_notes: Used to express happiness or willingness under a condition. Often appears with the conditional tense (sarei, sarebbe) or present tense depending on context. Can indicate a wish, polite request, or a factual statement about when someone is happy. Combine with clauses introduced by 'se' (if).
target_language_example: Sarei felice se potessi venire alla festa.
native_language_example: I would be happy if you could come to the party.

meaning: happy for (someone); glad about someone else's good situation
additional_notes: Used with people or pronouns (per loro, per te, per voi) to express that you feel happiness on someone else's behalf. 'Felici' is the plural of 'felice' (happy); agree with the subject (sono felice, siamo felici, sii felice). Common in contexts of congratulations or empathy.
target_language_example: Siamo felici per te e per il tuo nuovo lavoro.
native_language_example: We are happy for you and for your new job.

meaning: 'happiness is' — used to define or describe what happiness consists of.
additional_notes: Commonly appears at the start of sentences that give a definition, opinion, or description of happiness. 'Felicità' is a feminine noun; 'è' is the third-person singular of 'essere' (to be). Useful for making simple statements like 'Happiness is...'.
target_language_example: La felicità è apprezzare le piccole cose ogni giorno.
native_language_example: Happiness is appreciating the small things every day.

meaning: wounded in / injured in (used with a body part or location)
additional_notes: Combines the past participle ferito (wounded/injured) with the preposition in to indicate where someone is injured (e.g., ferito in testa, ferito in modo lieve). Often used in news reports or medical contexts. Requires a following noun or phrase specifying the place or manner. Can appear with auxiliary essere (È stato ferito in scontro) or as an adjective (Un ragazzo ferito in più punti).
target_language_example: È stato ferito in testa durante l'incidente.
native_language_example: He was injured in the head during the accident.

meaning: injured in an accident
additional_notes: Used to describe a person who has been hurt as a result of an accident (car crash, fall, workplace incident, etc.). 'Ferito' is the past participle of 'ferire' (to wound/hurt) and agrees in gender/number (ferita, feriti, ferite). Commonly used in news reports and everyday reports about injuries.
target_language_example: Sono stato ferito in un incidente d'auto la settimana scorsa.
native_language_example: I was injured in a car accident last week.

meaning: wounded in/at (a body part).
additional_notes: Used to say someone was injured in a specific body part. 'Ferito' is the past participle of 'ferire' (to wound); it agrees in number and sometimes gender when used with essere (e.g., 'fu ferito', 'fu ferita', 'furono feriti'). 'Alla' = a + la, used before feminine singular body parts (alla spalla, alla gamba). Use 'al' (a + il) for masculine parts (es. 'ferito al braccio').
target_language_example: È stato ferito alla mano durante l'incidente.
native_language_example: He was wounded in the hand during the accident.

meaning: 'wounded in a' (used to specify the body part or area where someone was injured)
additional_notes: This phrase combines the past participle ferito (wounded) with the preposition in and an article (un) to introduce the injured area: e.g. 'ferito in un braccio' = 'wounded in an arm'. Often used in news reports or medical contexts. You will more commonly see 'ferito a' (ferito a un braccio) in everyday Italian; 'in' can emphasize being inside or within an area (e.g. 'ferito in un ospedale' would mean 'wounded in a hospital' but that meaning is less common).
target_language_example: È stato ferito in un braccio durante l'incidente.
native_language_example: He was wounded in an arm during the accident.

meaning: birthday party.
additional_notes: Common phrase used to invite or talk about a celebration for someone's birthday. 'Festa' = party, 'compleanno' = birthday; word order is the same as in English. Can be used with verbs like 'fare/avere' (to have a party) or 'venire'/'andare' (to come/go to a party).
target_language_example: Hai organizzato la festa di compleanno per Marco?
native_language_example: Did you organize Marco's birthday party?

meaning: 'the party was' (simple past description)
additional_notes: Combines the noun festa (party) with the imperfect/preterite form era (3rd person singular of essere: 'was'). Used to describe the party in the past (its state, atmosphere, who organized it, etc.). In spoken/written Italian you'd more often see 'la festa era...' or just 'era...' depending on context. Verb tense: era is the imperfect (used for descriptions/background) but can describe a completed past state in narrative.
target_language_example: La festa era divertente e tutti ballavano.
native_language_example: The party was fun and everyone was dancing.

meaning: literally 'party the week' — not a standard fixed phrase in Italian; likely a mistaken or non-idiomatic string. Depending on intent it could be interpreted as 'a party this week' or 'a party during the week' but the phrasing is ungrammatical or uncommon.
additional_notes:
This exact sequence 'festa la settimana' is not a common or standard Italian expression. More natural alternatives:
- 'una festa questa settimana' — 'a party this week'
- 'festa in settimana' — 'a party on a weekday / during the week'
- 'festa della settimana' — uncommon, 'the week's party'
- 'festeggiare la settimana' — 'to celebrate the week' (verb form)
Use 'una festa questa settimana' to say 'a party this week' or 'festa in settimana' to contrast with weekend parties. If you see 'festa la settimana' in written text, it is likely a typo or non-native phrasing.
target_language_example: Ho visto scritto 'festa la settimana' sul volantino, ma credo sia un errore.
native_language_example: I saw 'festa la settimana' written on the flyer, but I think it's a mistake.

meaning: beside me / next to me.
additional_notes: Used to say someone or something is positioned at your side (physically next to you). Common with verbs like abitare (live), sedere/sedersi (sit). More natural variants: "di fianco a me" or simply "accanto a me"; both mean the same. Informal everyday usage.
target_language_example: Si è seduto di fianco a me al cinema.
native_language_example: He sat down next to me at the cinema.

meaning: next to a library / alongside a library
additional_notes: A spatial phrase indicating position beside a library. 'Fianco' (flank/side) emphasizes being alongside the side of the building; usage often includes the preposition variant 'di fianco a' or the contracted 'fianco a' with 'ad' before a vowel ('una' here colloquially uses 'ad una'). 'Accanto a una biblioteca' and 'vicino a una biblioteca' are more common in everyday speech. Use 'una' or 'la' depending on indefiniteness/definiteness.
target_language_example: Il negozio è al fianco ad una biblioteca.
native_language_example: The shop is next to a library.

meaning: a girlfriend 'for' (used to indicate purpose, duration, or reason).
additional_notes: fidanzata = 'girlfriend' (female partner). When followed by 'per' + noun or time expression, it expresses receiving a girlfriend for a specific occasion or period (e.g., 'per Natale' = for Christmas; 'per la settimana' = for the week). 'Per' can also mark a reason/duration: in sentence 5 ('tradì la sua fidanzata per mesi') it means 'for months' (duration). Note word order: 'fidanzata per [X]' is natural when specifying purpose/occasion/duration. If you mean 'to have a girlfriend by/for (a date)', Italians might also say 'una fidanzata per Natale' or 'una fidanzata entro Natale'.
target_language_example: Vorrei una fidanzata per l'estate.
native_language_example: I'd like a girlfriend for the summer.

meaning: my girlfriend is / the girlfriend is (used to describe someone).
additional_notes: Combines fidanzata (girlfriend, feminine) with the verb essere (to be). Used to state facts or descriptions about a girlfriend (nationality, profession, qualities). In English you would usually say 'my girlfriend is...' — in Italian include a possessive (la mia) when specifying whose girlfriend. Word order: La mia fidanzata è + noun/adjective. If talking about a boyfriend, use fidanzato.
target_language_example: La mia fidanzata è italiana e lavora in una scuola.
native_language_example: My girlfriend is Italian and works in a school.

meaning: ‘my/your/his/her boyfriend is…’ — the verb phrase used to describe a boyfriend.
additional_notes: Fidanzato means 'boyfriend' (male partner); followed by è (3rd-person singular of essere = 'is') to state a quality, opinion or fact about him. Example sentences show adjectives (possessive, stupid), nouns used as insults (un idiota), or traits (ateo = atheist). Change the possessive before fidanzato (mio, tuo, suo) to match the speaker and use è to link to the description. For a female partner use fidanzata. Tone can be informal or rude depending on the adjective/noun used.
target_language_example: Il mio fidanzato è gentile e premuroso.
native_language_example: My boyfriend is kind and considerate.

meaning: 'to trust (someone)'.
additional_notes: Used with the reflexive verb fidarsi (voi form: vi fidate di ...) followed by a person or pronoun introduced by di. Commonly appears as a question: Vi fidate di me? = Do you trust me? The subject is voi (you plural) or implied in conversational Vi. Use di before names/pronouns: di Tom, di lei, di qualcuno.
target_language_example: Vi fidate di Marco per questa decisione?
native_language_example: Do you trust Marco with this decision?

meaning: I trusted (someone).
additional_notes: First-person singular imperfect of 'fidarsi di' (to trust). Used to describe past, ongoing, or habitual trust (e.g., 'I used to trust him', 'I trusted him [at that time]'). It requires 'di' before the person or thing trusted: 'fidavo di lui/lei/te'. Common in spoken and written Italian.
target_language_example: Mi fidavo di lei, ma ora ho dei dubbi.
native_language_example: I trusted her, but now I have doubts.

meaning: will trust
additional_notes: Usually seen as si fiderà di, from the reflexive verb fidarsi di, meaning 'to trust someone' or 'to trust in something'. It is future tense: 'will trust'. After di, you normally name the person or thing trusted: di te, di voi, di lei, etc.
target_language_example: Un giorno si fiderà di me.
native_language_example: One day she will trust me.

meaning: children who / sons (or children) that
additional_notes: Combination of figli (children/sons) + relative pronoun che (who/that). Used to introduce a clause describing what the children did or became. 'Figli' is plural; verb agreement follows (e.g., sono diventati / diventarono). Can refer to sons or children of any gender in general contexts.
target_language_example: Ha tre figli che lavorano in città.
native_language_example: He has three children who work in the city.

meaning: 'children to' or 'children to be/for' used with verbs that require an object or purpose (e.g. da soli = alone; da mantenere = to support).
additional_notes: Not a fixed phrase by itself; 'figli' (children) combines with 'da' plus another word (an adjective, past participle, or infinitive) to express relationships like 'children alone' (figli da soli), 'children to support/maintain' (figli da mantenere), or 'children to prepare/dress' (figli da preparare). Word order: 'figli da' is followed by the descriptor (adjective or infinitive). Common in spoken and written Italian.
target_language_example: Ho tre figli da mantenere e lavoro tutto il giorno.
native_language_example: I have three children to support and I work all day.

meaning: 'a daughter who/that' — used to introduce a relative clause giving information about a daughter.
additional_notes: Combines figlia (daughter) with the relative pronoun che (who/that). Used to describe or identify a specific daughter (e.g. name, characteristics, age). In Italian che is the common, neutral relative pronoun for people and things. In the sentence È di mia figlia che si sta parlando!, che introduces a cleft construction ('it is my daughter who is being talked about').
target_language_example: Ho una figlia che vive a Roma.
native_language_example: I have a daughter who lives in Rome.

meaning: insult: 'son/daughter of a bitch' — very strong insult meaning 'bitch' or 'jerk'.
additional_notes: Very vulgar and offensive. Literally 'daughter of a whore' (similar to English 'son/daughter of a bitch'). Used to insult or express anger at someone. Can be directed at a person (outrage, anger) or used to describe someone who behaved very badly. Avoid in polite company; only used in informal, heated, or coarse contexts.
target_language_example: Non parlare così a tuo fratello, non chiamarlo 'figlia di puttana'.
native_language_example: Don't speak to your brother like that; don't call him a 'daughter of a bitch'.

meaning: ‘(my/your/her) daughter is in…’ — used to say where a daughter is (location or state).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase; it's a simple combination: noun (figlia) + verb (è) + preposition (in) followed by a place or condition (e.g., in ospedale, in casa, in coma, in un canale). Change the possessive (mia, tua, sua, nostra) and the place to fit context. Common in everyday speech for reporting someone's location or situation.
target_language_example: La mia figlia è in ospedale da ieri.
native_language_example: My daughter has been in the hospital since yesterday.

meaning: son of a bitch
additional_notes: A strong insult in Italian used to angrily attack someone's character or actions. Very vulgar — use only in informal, heated contexts or when translating/emphasizing anger. Can be directed at a person (you are a 'figlio di puttana') or shouted about someone (e.g. to express outrage after an action).
target_language_example: A terra, figlio di puttana!
native_language_example: Get down, you son of a bitch!

meaning: his/ her son was a ... (past description)
additional_notes: A short sequence showing possession (suo), subject (figlio) and a past-state description using the imperfect tense (era) plus an indefinite article (un). Used to describe what someone's son was like in the past: 'suo figlio era un [noun/adjective]'. The gender/number of the noun/adjective that follows should agree with 'figlio' (masculine singular). 'Suo' can mean his, her, or your (formal) depending on context.
target_language_example: Ha detto che suo figlio era un bravo dottore.
native_language_example: He said that his son was a good doctor.

meaning: a son involved in an accident
additional_notes: Literal phrase: figlio = son, in un incidente = in an accident. Used to state that someone's son was or is involved in an accident; may imply injury depending on context. Not idiomatic; a straightforward descriptive phrase. For more natural sentences, speakers usually add verbs or possessives (e.g., "mio figlio in un incidente" appears inside a larger clause: "Ho saputo del mio figlio in un incidente").
target_language_example: Ho ricevuto la telefonata: mio figlio in un incidente, è urgente.
native_language_example: I received the call: my son in an accident, it's urgent.

meaning: only child (male) — a child with no siblings.
additional_notes: Literal: 'figlio' = son/child, 'unico' = only. Used to say someone has no brothers or sisters. For a female speaker, use 'figlia unica'. Can describe past or present (ero figlio unico / sono figlio unico).
target_language_example: Sono figlio unico, quindi conosco solo i miei genitori.
native_language_example: I'm an only child, so I only know my parents.

meaning: lines up for / queues for (someone/something); stands in line to get or do something.
additional_notes: Literal components: fila (line/row) + per (for). Commonly used with a person or activity following 'per' (e.g., fila per i biglietti — lines up for tickets). In speech you may also hear stare in fila (to be standing in line) or fare la fila. Use with appropriate verb if needed: 'fa la fila per...' or 'fila per...' as a shortened description.
target_language_example: Fila per i biglietti al cinema.
native_language_example: He/She lines up for the movie tickets.

meaning: in line/queue for (something); next in line for (something).
additional_notes: Used to say someone is in a queue or is next to receive something (e.g., a promotion, a turn, a photo). Often appears as part of phrases like "in fila per la foto" or "il prossimo in fila per la promozione." The noun after "la" specifies what they're waiting for. If gender/number requires, the article can change (e.g., "in fila per il", "per l'", "per le").
target_language_example: Siamo in fila per la biglietteria da mezz'ora.
native_language_example: We've been in line for the ticket office for half an hour.

meaning: 'the film was' or 'what film was' depending on context (past tense of 'essere' with 'film').
additional_notes: Used to talk about a film in the past. As a phrase, 'film era' can appear inside questions (Che film era... = Which film was/what film was) or statements (Quel film era... / Il film era... = That film was... / The film was...). 'Era' is the imperfect past of essere (to be) and describes past states or repeated/habitual actions or background information.
target_language_example: Quel film era interessante, ma la trama era confusa.
native_language_example: That film was interesting, but the plot was confusing.

meaning: 'the film is' — subject (il film) + verb essere (è) used to describe the film's state or a passive construction with 'è' + past participle or 'è' + adjective.
additional_notes: Commonly appears as 'Il film è ...' to say the film is in a certain state (already started, changed, directed by...) or as part of a passive/perfect structure (often with passato prossimo: 'è stato' + past participle). The phrase itself is just the noun + present of 'essere' (to be). Watch for verb combinations: 'è già cominciato/è già iniziato' (it has already begun), 'è stato girato' (it was filmed/has been filmed).
target_language_example: Il film è stato presentato al festival la scorsa settimana.
native_language_example: The film was shown at the festival last week.

meaning: 'from the very' or 'since the very' (short for fin dall'inizio = from the very beginning).
additional_notes: Contraction of fin da + l' (used before words starting with a vowel). Commonly followed by nouns like inizio, principio, or a time expression. Emphasizes that something was true from the very start. Formality: neutral, used in both spoken and written Italian.
target_language_example: Lo sapevo fin dall'inizio.
native_language_example: I knew it from the very beginning.

meaning: 'you finally have' or 'you finally did' (informal, when speaking to one person - tu).
additional_notes: Combines 'finalmente' (finally) + 'hai' (second-person singular of avere or auxiliary for passato prossimo). Used with a noun: 'Finalmente hai un lavoro' = 'You finally have a job.' Used with past participle to mean 'you finally did' (with passato prossimo): 'Finalmente hai finito' = 'You finally finished.' Spoken to one person (tu).
target_language_example: Finalmente hai trovato le chiavi!
native_language_example: You finally found the keys!

meaning: 'finally' + impersonal/reflective 'si' used with verbs to mean 'finally [someone] ...' or 'finally it is possible to ...'.
additional_notes: Finalmente = 'finally'. The 'si' here is the impersonal/reflective pronoun used with verbs (si comincia, si sono incontrati, si sposerà) to indicate actions happening to people in general or reflexive/reciprocal actions (they met, they got married, she fell asleep). In many examples 'si' combines with auxiliary verbs (è/sono) to form reflexive/reciprocal past tenses. Use 'Finalmente si + verb' to express relief or long-awaited completion.
target_language_example: Finalmente si sono laureati ieri.
native_language_example: They finally graduated yesterday.

meaning: weekend
additional_notes: Used to refer to the weekend (Saturday and Sunday). Can appear with articles (il fine settimana, quel fine settimana) or without (nei fine settimana) and combined with prepositions: 'nel fine settimana', 'per il fine settimana', 'ogni fine settimana'. Common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Andiamo al mare questo fine settimana.
native_language_example: We're going to the beach this weekend.

meaning: ‘the weekend with’ — used to say you spent or will spend the weekend with someone.
additional_notes: Commonly appears after verbs like passare, trascorrere, invitare. Use with a person or pronoun (e.g., con lei, con loro, con le mie amiche). Gender/number can affect agreement of past participles when clitics are used (e.g., ci hanno invitate vs. ci hanno invitati) but does not affect simple prepositional phrases like “fine settimana con + [noun/pronoun]”.
target_language_example: Ho passato il fine settimana con lei.
native_language_example: I spent the weekend with her.

meaning: literally 'window for' — used to indicate a window (opening) or a time/opportunity for something; meaning depends on context.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom: 'finestra' can mean a physical window or a figurative time/opportunity ('finestra temporale'). When followed by 'per' + verb/noun, it shows purpose or reason (e.g. 'finestra per le zanzare' = closing because of mosquitoes) or a time-slot/opportunity (e.g. 'ultima finestra per i pit stop' = last opportunity for pit stops). Translate according to context.
target_language_example: C'è una finestra per le domande alla fine della presentazione.
native_language_example: There is a window for questions at the end of the presentation.

meaning: to finish my (something); often refers to homework or personal tasks
additional_notes: This phrase is incomplete on its own and normally needs a noun after 'miei' (e.g., compiti = homework). In examples it refers to 'finire i miei compiti' (to finish my homework). 'Finire' is a regular verb meaning 'to finish' or 'to end'. Use with the appropriate past/infinitive/compound forms (devo ancora finire i miei = I still have to finish mine).
target_language_example: Devo finire i miei compiti prima di uscire.
native_language_example: I have to finish my homework before going out.

meaning: to finish this (thing/something currently mentioned).
additional_notes: Used to refer to completing a specific task, object, or piece of work that is known from context. Common with verbs like 'devo', 'voglio', 'lasciami' (let me) and time expressions (entro..., prima di...). 'Finire' is a regular -ire verb meaning 'to finish' or 'to end'; 'questo' means 'this'. Word order can change (e.g. 'finire questo progetto' or 'questo progetto finire').
target_language_example: Devo finire questo compito stasera.
native_language_example: I have to finish this assignment tonight.

meaning: 'finisce il' = 'the ... ends' or 'does the ... end' (third-person singular of finire + definite article)
additional_notes: Combination of the verb finire (to finish/end) in third person singular (finisce) followed by the masculine singular definite article il. Used to ask or state when/if something (a masculine-noun event: corso, film, gioco) ends. Word order may vary in questions (e.g., A che ora finisce il corso? / Quando finisce il gioco?). Replace il with la/lo/i/le to match the noun's gender and number (e.g., finisce la partita, finiscono i corsi).
target_language_example: Finisce il film alle dieci?
native_language_example: Does the movie end at ten?

meaning: 'ever finishes' or 'finishes (something) ever' — used in negative or rhetorical contexts to say someone/something never finishes.
additional_notes: Commonly appears with non/nessuno/niente/mai to express that something never ends or someone never completes tasks. In positive questions it can mean 'does ... ever finish?' In everyday speech Italians often say "non finisce mai" (it never ends) or "non finisce mai niente" / "non finisce mai nulla" (he/she never finishes anything).
target_language_example: Non finisce mai i suoi compiti.
native_language_example: He never finishes his homework.

meaning: 'end up like this' / 'finish like this' — used to express that something has (or will) end in a particular (often predictable or unfortunate) way.
additional_notes: Usually appears in the fixed phrase "(sarebbe) finita così" meaning "(would) end up like this". Common in sentences expressing resignation, prediction, or that the outcome was expected. Often follows verbs like sapere, credere, dire (e.g., "sapevo che sarebbe finita così"). Tense of the auxiliary (sarebbe, è, è finita) changes the nuance (conditional for expected/predicted outcome, past or present for actual end).
target_language_example: Sapevo che sarebbe finita così, ma non potevo fare niente.
native_language_example: I knew it would end up like this, but I couldn't do anything.

meaning: finished washing (something); have/has finished washing
additional_notes: Form of 'finire di' + verb in infinitive; used to say someone completed an action (here: 'lavare i piatti' = to wash the dishes). Can be used in different persons/tenses (Ho finito, Hai finito, Ha finito, Abbiamo finito, etc.). 'Appena' before the verb means 'just' (Ho appena finito = I have just finished).
target_language_example: Abbiamo finito di lavare le stoviglie.
native_language_example: We have finished washing the dishes.

meaning: 'finished the' (masculine plural direct object) — past participle used with avere to say someone has finished something (masculine plural).
additional_notes: Finito is the past participle of finire (to finish). With the auxiliary avere it forms the passato prossimo (e.g., ho finito). The following article/possessive (i, i miei, i tuoi, i preparativi, i compiti, i proiettili) marks a masculine plural object. In English you usually translate the whole phrase as 'finished the/your/my ...' or 'finished (my/your) ...'. Word order: Hai finito i compiti? = Have you finished the homework?
target_language_example: Ha finito i documenti prima della riunione.
native_language_example: He finished the documents before the meeting.

meaning: finished the
additional_notes: "finito" is the past participle of "finire" and "il" means "the" for a masculine singular noun. It is usually followed by a noun, as in "finito il caffè" or "finito il lavoro." After forms of "avere" ("ho/ha/hanno finito..."), it means someone finished something. In expressions like "È finito il tempo," it means something is over or has ended.
target_language_example: Ho finito il libro ieri sera.
native_language_example: I finished the book yesterday evening.

meaning: have finished their (something).
additional_notes: Finito is the past participle of finire (to finish). 'Hanno finito il loro...' is used with avere (hanno) to say someone has finished something they own or were using. 'Loro' (their) agrees in meaning but not in gender/number with the noun; it stays 'loro' before the noun. You may also see 'il loro' abbreviated to just the noun if context makes the possession clear (e.g. 'Hanno finito.' = They've finished). For feminine plurals referring to people who finished, auxiliary and past participle agreement uses essere (e.g. 'sono andate' after finishing work and going home).
target_language_example: Hanno finito il loro pranzo e sono usciti.
native_language_example: They have finished their lunch and went out.

meaning: I've finished my / my ... is finished (literally: 'finished my')
additional_notes: Used with a masculine singular noun (mio + noun) to say you have finished something that belongs to you. Often appears as part of 'Ho finito il mio [oggetto/compito]' (I finished my [thing/assignment]). Note the verb 'finire' requires the auxiliary 'avere' in passato prossimo: 'Ho finito'. In sentence 5 the structure changes: 'finito' is used with 'dove sia finito il mio...' meaning 'where my ... has ended up/gone' (passive/result).
target_language_example: Ho finito il mio libro ieri sera.
native_language_example: I finished my book last night.

meaning: 'to end up in' (somewhere or in some situation)
additional_notes: Used to say someone or something ended up in a place or situation, often unexpectedly or negatively (e.g., prison, a bad place, a diary). Common in spoken Italian. Followed by a noun or location introduced directly (finire in prigione, finire in galera) or by a noun phrase (finire in quel diario).
target_language_example: Dopo la perdita del lavoro, sono finito in difficoltà.
native_language_example: After losing my job, I ended up in trouble.

meaning: until
additional_notes: Marks an endpoint or limit in time, place, quantity, or degree: fino a domani = until tomorrow, fino a qui = up to/as far as here, contare fino a dieci = count up to ten. It can also be used before an infinitive to mean 'to the point of': fino a puzzare = until/to the point of stinking.
target_language_example: Resto qui fino a domani.
native_language_example: I'm staying here until tomorrow.

meaning: up to a certain (point/limit); to some extent
additional_notes: Used to indicate a limit or degree that is not exact or is somewhat vague. Often followed by a noun (e.g., punto, livello) or used before clauses to mean 'to a certain extent'. Can be shortened in speech to 'fino a un certo punto' for 'up to a certain point'.
target_language_example: Posso aiutarti fino a un certo punto.
native_language_example: I can help you up to a certain point.

meaning: up to one's neck; deeply (involved, overwhelmed, or in trouble).
additional_notes: Used figuratively to say someone is deeply involved in a situation (often negative): debt, trouble, problems, or responsibilities. Can be used alone for emphasis. Common in informal speech; can be combined with contexts like 'nei debiti fino al collo' (deeply in debt) or 'dentro fino al collo' (deeply involved).
target_language_example: Sono nei debiti fino al collo.
native_language_example: I'm up to my neck in debt.

meaning: until the end; all the way to the end.
additional_notes: Used to indicate continuing something up to its conclusion (time, place, action, or text). Can be literal (to the physical end) or figurative (to completion, persevering). Often followed by a noun with 'di' for time periods (e.g. 'fino alla fine del mese').
target_language_example: Ho letto il libro fino alla fine senza fermarmi.
native_language_example: I read the book until the end without stopping.

meaning: since / from (a specific time or point in the past)
additional_notes: Used to indicate that something has been true starting at a particular time or point (often with a date, age, or event). It is commonly followed by a noun, a date, an age, or a phrase indicating a moment: e.g. fino da bambino (since childhood), fino da marzo (since March), fino da quando ero giovane (since I was young). Can be interchangeable with 'da' in many contexts, but 'fino da' emphasizes the starting point.
target_language_example: Frequento il coro fino da bambino.
native_language_example: I have been in the choir since I was a child.

meaning: completely; all the way; to the very end
additional_notes: Used to say that something is done thoroughly, fully, or carried through to its conclusion. Can be literal (to the bottom/end) or figurative (to finish a task, follow through with an action). Often used with verbs like andare (go), essere (be) or in imperative/advice contexts.
target_language_example: Devi impegnarti e portare il progetto fino in fondo.
native_language_example: You must commit yourself and carry the project through to the end.

meaning: snowflake
additional_notes: A compound noun meaning a single crystal or flake of snow. Can be used literally (a physical snowflake) or figuratively (e.g., describing something delicate or unique). Articles (un/il) change whether you mean 'a snowflake' or 'the snowflake'.
target_language_example: Un fiocco di neve si posò sul suo naso.
native_language_example: A snowflake landed on his nose.

meaning: a flower (given) to — indicates giving a flower to someone.
additional_notes: Built from 'fiore' (flower) + preposition 'a' (to). Common in sentences with verbs like 'dare' (to give) or 'offrire' (to offer): 'dare un fiore a qualcuno' = to give someone a flower. The recipient follows 'a'. Use definite/indefinite articles as needed (un fiore a mio padre / il fiore a Marco).
target_language_example: Ho comprato un fiore a mia madre per il suo compleanno.
native_language_example: I bought a flower for my mother for her birthday.

meaning: literally 'flowers have'; likely part of a sentence meaning 'the flowers have...' (e.g. the flowers have bloomed, the flowers have been watered).
additional_notes: This is not a standalone phrase; it's the verb phrase 'hanno' (they have) following the noun 'fiori' (flowers). In Italian, subject can follow verb or be repeated for emphasis, so you'll often see 'i fiori hanno' or 'fiori hanno' inside a larger sentence. To express completed actions with 'have', Italian often uses avere + past participle: 'i fiori hanno fiorito' (the flowers have bloomed) or more naturally 'i fiori sono sbocciati' (the flowers have bloomed — using 'essere').
target_language_example: I fiori hanno bisogno d'acqua ogni giorno.
native_language_example: The flowers need water every day.

meaning: flowers in the / flowers in the (inside of) — literal phrase used to say flowers are located in a place (nel = in + il).
additional_notes: This is a combination of 'fiori' (flowers) and the contraction 'nel' (in + il = in the). It is used before a masculine singular noun (e.g., 'nel giardino', 'nel vaso'). The phrase is literal and compositional; you will commonly see it in descriptions of where flowers are planted or placed.
target_language_example: Ci sono fiori nel vaso sul tavolo.
native_language_example: There are flowers in the vase on the table.

meaning: flowers for (someone).
additional_notes: A simple phrase used to say you buy or have flowers intended for a person. 'Per' means 'for' and is followed by the recipient (name or pronoun). Can be used with verbs like comprare (to buy), avere (to have), portare (to bring). Word order: 'dei fiori per [nome/te]'.
target_language_example: Ho portato dei fiori per te.
native_language_example: I brought flowers for you.

meaning: to sign (the) — used with a plural or specific noun (e.g., 'i documenti', 'i loro nomi').
additional_notes: Literally 'to sign the'. In Italian, verbs combine with the definite article when referring to specific plural items: 'firmare i documenti' = 'to sign the documents'. Often appears with pronouns (i loro = their). Use appropriate article/gender/number for the noun: e.g., 'firmare il contratto' (singular), 'firmare le carte' (feminine plural).
target_language_example: Devo firmare i contratti domani.
native_language_example: I have to sign the contracts tomorrow.

meaning: This looks like 'fiume' (river) followed by the preposition 'per' (for/to). By itself it isn't an established fixed phrase; it appears in sentences where 'fiume' is the noun and 'per' begins a purpose, reason, or object phrase (e.g. 'per salvare...' = 'to save...'; 'per costruire...' = 'to build...'; 'per tutto il suo mais' = 'for all his corn').
additional_notes: Treat 'fiume' (river) and 'per' (for/to) as separate words. Common uses: 'tuffarsi nel fiume per...' (to jump into the river to...), 'bisogno di un fiume per...' (need a river for...), or 'controllare il fiume per...' (check/control the river in order to...). The meaning depends on the clause following 'per' (purpose, intended use, or beneficiary). Not an idiom—just noun + preposition.
target_language_example: Si tuffò nel fiume per salvare il cane.
native_language_example: He jumped into the river to save the dog.

meaning: “a sheet of” or “a piece of” (used before a material or noun, e.g. foglio di carta = a sheet of paper).
additional_notes: Common short phrase used to indicate a single thin flat piece of something (paper, metal, etc.). Usually followed by the material or type (carta, alluminio, calcolo, etc.). In requests or commands with polite forms, it appears in simple phrases: "Dammi un foglio di carta" = "Give me a sheet of paper." Not idiomatic on its own—you need the noun after di.
target_language_example: Mi serve un foglio di carta per prendere appunti.
native_language_example: I need a sheet of paper to take notes.

meaning: the bottom of (the)... — used to refer to the lowest part of something (well, river, sea, container).
additional_notes: ‘Fondo’ means 'bottom' or 'depth'. When followed by a definite article + noun (here 'del' = 'di' + 'il'), it specifies the bottom of a particular place or object: 'fondo del pozzo' (bottom of the well), 'fondo del mare' (sea floor). Commonly used with verbs like vedere (see), trovare (find), scendere (go down), venire trovato (be found).
target_language_example: Ho trovato una bottiglia sul fondo del lago.
native_language_example: I found a bottle at the bottom of the lake.

meaning: used to describe a type of oven or what the oven uses (e.g., forno a gas = gas oven, forno a legna = wood-fired oven).
additional_notes: Forno means 'oven'. When followed by a preposition a and a noun, it specifies the oven's fuel, style, or function. Common examples: 'forno a gas' (gas oven), 'forno a legna' (wood-fired oven), 'forno a microonde' is NOT correct — say 'forno a microonde' is used colloquially but standard is 'forno a microonde' or simply 'microonde'. You will often see labels like 'pizza al forno a legna' meaning pizza cooked in a wood-fired oven.
target_language_example: Abbiamo comprato un forno a gas per la cucina nuova.
native_language_example: We bought a gas oven for the new kitchen.

meaning: microwave oven; microwave
additional_notes: Common household appliance used to heat or defrost food quickly using microwaves. In casual speech Italians may also say semplicemente 'microonde' (il microonde) to mean the microwave oven. Used with verbs like usare, mettere (nel), scaldare, riscaldare, scongelare.
target_language_example: Ho riscaldato la zuppa nel forno a microonde.
native_language_example: I warmed the soup in the microwave oven.

meaning: 'maybe (to) her/them' or 'maybe you (will) find them/her'
additional_notes: Forse = maybe. Le is a clitic pronoun that can mean 'to her', 'to them' (feminine), or 'them' (feminine direct object) depending on context. Word order in Italian often places the clitic before the verb (le dovrei aiutare = I should help her/them). In conversational speech you may also hear 'forse le trovi' (maybe you'll find them/her). Pay attention to whether le refers to a feminine singular indirect object (to her), feminine plural direct object (them, feminine), or feminine plural indirect object, based on the sentence.
target_language_example: Forse le parlerò domani.
native_language_example: Maybe I'll talk to her/them tomorrow.

meaning: maybe we / perhaps we
additional_notes: Combines 'forse' (maybe/perhaps) with the subject pronoun 'noi' (we). Used to suggest a possibility or tentative action involving 'we'. In spoken Italian the pronoun 'noi' is often optional (Forse dovremmo...), but including it adds emphasis or clarity (especially when contrasting with others).
target_language_example: Forse noi dovremmo chiedere aiuto prima di continuare.
native_language_example: Maybe we should ask for help before continuing.

meaning: maybe I can / perhaps I can
additional_notes: Used to express uncertainty about one's ability to do something. 'Forse' = maybe/perhaps; 'posso' = I can (from potere). Common in tentative offers or guesses. Can be followed by an infinitive (e.g., 'forse posso aiutare') or a clause introduced by a verb.
target_language_example: Forse posso aiutarti domani.
native_language_example: Maybe I can help you tomorrow.

meaning: 'perhaps this' or 'maybe this'.
additional_notes: Used to introduce a tentative idea or suggestion about 'this' (something just mentioned or shown). 'Forse' = maybe/perhaps; 'questo' = this. Common in spoken and written Italian to express uncertainty about a specific thing or situation.
target_language_example: Forse questo è quello che ci serve.
native_language_example: Maybe this is what we need.

meaning: perhaps you are / maybe you are
additional_notes: Forse = 'perhaps/maybe'. Sei = second-person singular of essere ('you are'). Used to suggest something about the listener with some uncertainty. Can start a sentence or clause. Tone depends on context: neutral, speculative, flattering, accusatory, etc. Common in spoken and written Italian.
target_language_example: Forse sei stanco; riposati un po'.
native_language_example: Maybe you are tired; rest a little.

meaning: maybe you / perhaps you ( + verb).
additional_notes: Forse = 'maybe/perhaps'. Ti is the familiar indirect/direct object pronoun 'you' (singular, informal). Together they commonly start sentences where the speaker suggests, guesses, or offers something about the listener (e.g., advice, possibility, opinion, or question). After 'forse ti' follow a verb conjugated for the subject (often impersonal or the speaker), e.g. 'dovresti' (you should), 'sbagli' (you are wrong), 'serve' (do you need). Tone can be tentative/polite. Use 'le'/'gli' for formal or plural forms instead of 'ti' when needed.
target_language_example: Forse ti conviene portare un ombrello.
native_language_example: Maybe you should bring an umbrella.

meaning: 'strong' (used before a clause or relative phrase) — describes someone/something strong or powerful; here 'che' introduces the clause that follows.
additional_notes: Not a fixed idiom: 'forte' is the adjective 'strong/forceful/powerful' and 'che' is the conjunction/relative pronoun 'that/who/which'. Together they appear when 'forte' is followed by a clause (e.g., 'forte che si nota', 'forte che ha superato...') or when specifying the strongest item ('più forte che ha' — colloquial; more standard: 'il più forte che ha' or 'il più forte che abbiamo'). In some examples, word order or articles may be slightly informal or elliptical. 'Forte' meanings include physically strong, emotionally/mentally strong, intense (e.g., strong flavor), or powerful/robust (e.g., equipment).
target_language_example: È un ragazzo forte che non si lascia intimidire.
native_language_example: He is a strong boy who doesn't let himself be intimidated.

meaning: 'loud and clear' — heard or understood very well
additional_notes: Used when confirming you heard or understood a message (often in radio/phone contexts) or to say someone's voice/statement is strong and unmistakable. Equivalent to English 'loud and clear.' Can be used alone as a short reply.
target_language_example: Ti sento forte e chiaro.
native_language_example: I hear you loud and clear.

meaning: 'fortune' or 'luck' with the preposition 'to' or 'for'; used either to wish luck to someone (augurare fortuna a) or to indicate leaving a fortune to someone (lasciare una fortuna a).
additional_notes: This phrase combines fortuna (fortune, luck, or a large sum of money) with the preposition a. Context decides meaning: "auguro fortuna a [nome]" = I wish [name] luck; "lasciare/lasciò una grande fortuna a [nome]" = to leave a large inheritance to someone. Also appears in idiomatic uses where "fortuna" means chance or fate. Use the indirect object after 'a'.
target_language_example: Le auguro buona fortuna a te per l'esame.
native_language_example: I wish you good luck for the exam.

meaning: 'luck with' or 'good/bad luck regarding (someone or something)'
additional_notes: Used to talk about having good or bad luck relating to a person, thing or situation. Typically appears as part of phrases like 'avere fortuna con' (to be lucky with) or 'non avere fortuna con' (to be unlucky with). Followed by a noun or pronoun (e.g., 'fortuna con gli esami', 'fortuna con le persone').
target_language_example: Non ho molta fortuna con gli aerei.
native_language_example: I don't have much luck with airplanes.

meaning: to be fortunate to (have/do something); 'the luck of' when talking about someone's fortunes
additional_notes: Used to say someone is lucky to have or experience something: 'ho la fortuna di...' = 'I'm fortunate to...'. Can also refer to a person's wealth or fortunes (la fortuna di [name]) meaning someone's assets or fate, depending on context. Common structure: 'la fortuna di + infinitive' or 'la fortuna di + noun'.
target_language_example: Ho la fortuna di avere amici così gentili.
native_language_example: I'm fortunate to have such kind friends.

meaning: “luck and” — the conjunction 'and' following the noun 'fortuna' (luck/fortune).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom by itself; it's simply the noun fortuna (luck, fortune) followed by the coordinating conjunction e (and). You'll see it in lists or comparisons (e.g., 'fortuna e duro lavoro' = 'luck and hard work'). Fortuna can mean luck, good fortune, or (financial) wealth depending on context. Pronounce e like English 'eh' or the vowel in 'bed' (but shorter).
target_language_example: Fortuna e preparazione vanno spesso insieme.
native_language_example: Luck and preparation often go together.

meaning: luck (has) [me] — used to talk about luck affecting the speaker (e.g., 'luck has abandoned me').
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom by itself but a common word order in Italian where 'fortuna' (luck) is the subject and 'mi' (to me) is the indirect object. Often appears with verbs like 'abbandonare', 'voltar(e) le spalle', 'odiare' to say that luck is behaving badly toward the speaker. Translate according to context: 'luck has left me', 'luck has turned its back on me', or 'why does luck hate me?'.
target_language_example: La fortuna mi ha voltato le spalle proprio oggi.
native_language_example: Luck has turned its back on me today.

meaning: lucky to find the (…).
additional_notes: A phrase used after a subject to say they were lucky to find something. The adjective 'fortunati' agrees in gender/number with the subject (fortunato/fortunata/fortunati/fortunate). 'Trovare le' is followed by a feminine plural noun (e.g., 'chiavi' = keys). For other nouns adjust the article (il/lo/la/i/gli) and agreement as needed: e.g., 'fortunato a trovare il portafoglio'.
target_language_example: Siamo stati fortunati a trovare le chiavi nel parco.
native_language_example: We were lucky to find the keys in the park.

meaning: ‘it/he/she were’ or ‘that it/he/she was’ in subjunctive; often used to suggest or speculate that someone is the cause or the person involved.
additional_notes: Fosse is the imperfect subjunctive (congiuntivo imperfetto) of essere. 'Fosse lei' appears in indirect/subjunctive clauses after verbs like pensare, chiedere, or in hypothetical questions (E se il problema fosse lei?). Can mean 'that it/she/he was' or 'were she' in a tentative/speculative sense. In spoken Italian, the subjunctive is often used with or without che (Pensavo (che) fosse lei).
target_language_example: Se fosse lei, dovremmo parlarle subito.
native_language_example: If it were her, we should talk to her right away.

meaning: 'it/he were him' — used to talk about someone being the person responsible or the one involved (subjunctive)
additional_notes: Fosse is the imperfect subjunctive form of essere (to be). 'Fosse lui' is used in hypothetical, doubtful, or reported contexts: questions (E se fosse lui? — What if it were him?), conjecture (Penso che fosse lui — I think it was him), or contrary-to-fact/possibility (Anche se fosse lui — Even if it were him). In English you can often translate it as 'were it him,' 'if it were him,' 'that it was him,' or simply 'it was him' depending on context.
target_language_example: Non importa se fosse lui, dobbiamo risolvere il problema comunque.
native_language_example: It doesn't matter if it were him, we must solve the problem anyway.

meaning: was/were in (subjunctive + feminine/neutral 'in the') — used in subordinate clauses requiring the imperfect subjunctive (congiuntivo imperfetto) + preposition 'in' + feminine/neutral definite noun or possessive.
additional_notes: This phrase combines the imperfect subjunctive of 'essere' (fosse) with 'nella' (in + la). It appears in reported thoughts, doubts, wishes, or with verbs that trigger the subjunctive (pensare, chiedersi, pensava che, etc.). Change 'nella' to 'nel' for masculine nouns (es. fosse nel giardino), or to 'nello', 'negli', 'nelle' depending on the following noun. The English equivalent is often '…was in…' or '…might have been in…' depending on context.
target_language_example: Pensavo che Maria fosse nella cucina quando sono arrivato.
native_language_example: I thought Maria was in the kitchen when I arrived.

meaning: 'were a' / 'was a' in subordinate (past) clauses — subjunctive form used after verbs expressing thought, opinion, desire, etc.
additional_notes: Fosse is the imperfect subjunctive of essere (to be). 'Fosse una' appears in dependent clauses introduced by verbs like pensare, volere, desiderare, and in reported speech or hypothetical/wish contexts. It can translate as 'that she/he/it was a' or 'that it were a' depending on register. Subject is often omitted and understood from context. Common in sentences like 'Pensavo fosse una donna' (I thought she was a woman) or 'Volevo che fosse una sorpresa' (I wanted it to be a surprise).
target_language_example: Credevo fosse una buona idea.
native_language_example: I thought it was a good idea.

meaning: literally 'photographic is' — not a standalone phrase; likely part of a sentence (e.g., 'l'impressione fotografica è...').
additional_notes: This combination is not an independent expression in Italian. 'Fotografica' is the feminine singular adjective meaning 'photographic' (from 'fotografico/a'). 'È' is the third-person singular of 'essere' ('is'). You will commonly see 'fotografica è' when the adjective directly precedes the verb in a clause (often due to inversion or emphasis) or when part of a larger phrase like 'l'immagine fotografica è...' (the photographic image is...). For beginners: learn 'fotografico/fotografica' (adjective) and 'è' (is) separately and use them together only within a full sentence.
target_language_example: L'immagine fotografica è molto nitida.
native_language_example: The photographic image is very sharp.

meaning: between me and (someone); among me and (others).
additional_notes: Used to indicate something involving 'me' and one or more other people — often followed by a pronoun (e.g., lui, lei, loro). 'Fra' (or 'tra') means 'between' or 'among'. In spoken Italian 'fra' and 'tra' are interchangeable. Common in phrases like 'fra me e te' (between you and me).
target_language_example: Questo segreto rimane fra me e te.
native_language_example: This secret stays between you and me.

meaning: 'between us' or 'among us' (used to indicate something shared privately or within a group).
additional_notes: Commonly used to mark confidentiality or to refer to relationships/feelings within a small group (e.g., between two people or among colleagues). Can mean both literal physical/relational 'between us' and idiomatic 'let's keep this secret.' Interchangeable with 'tra noi' (same meaning).
target_language_example: Questo rimane fra noi, non dirlo a nessuno.
native_language_example: This stays between us, don't tell anyone.

meaning: in a little while; soon; shortly.
additional_notes: Used to indicate that something will happen soon or after a short amount of time. Common in everyday speech. Can be used alone (A fra poco = See you soon) or before a verb (Fra poco arriva = It will arrive soon). Interchangeable with 'tra poco' — both are correct.
target_language_example: Fra poco vado al negozio.
native_language_example: I'll go to the store in a little while.

meaning: in (a) + time period; indicates an event will happen after the stated amount of time (e.g. in a minute, in a year).
additional_notes: Used before a time expression to say something will occur after that interval. 'Fra' and 'tra' are interchangeable (fra un / tra un). Common with expressions like 'fra un minuto', 'fra un anno', 'fra un paio di settimane', 'fra un quarto d'ora'. Can be used with singular or quantifier phrases (un, un paio di).
target_language_example: Ci vediamo fra un'ora.
native_language_example: See you in an hour.

meaning: 'in French at' or 'French at' — indicates the language (French) used in a specific place or context.
additional_notes: This phrase combines the noun for the language (francese) with the preposition a to show where or in what setting the language is spoken or learned. In English you'd usually say 'French at home' or 'French at school' (often reordering to 'we speak French at home' / 'Tom learned French at school'). The article il is often used with imparare (imparò il francese) but can be omitted in casual speech.
target_language_example: Parliamo francese a scuola durante le lezioni.
native_language_example: We speak French at school during lessons.

meaning: French like him / as well as he does (i.e., the same level of French as he has).
additional_notes: Used after verbs of ability (parlare, riuscire, sapere) to ask whether someone can speak French to the same standard as another person ('lui' = he). Word order: language + come + pronoun. Can be adapted: 'francese come te' (like you), 'inglese come lei' (English like her).
target_language_example: Puoi parlare in francese come lui?
native_language_example: Can you speak French like him?

meaning: in/into French with her (or with you formal) — i.e., speak in French when talking to her.
additional_notes: Used after verbs of speaking (parlare) to indicate the language used with a particular person. 'Lei' can mean 'her' (third person) or the formal 'you' (polite form). Word order is flexible: 'parlare in francese con lei' or 'in francese con lei parlare' (less common). You can replace 'francese' with other languages (es. 'in inglese con lui').
target_language_example: Domani parlerò in francese con lei durante la riunione.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I'll speak in French with her during the meeting.

meaning: French yesterday (i.e. 'French' as in the subject/language + 'yesterday' — used to ask whether someone studied French yesterday).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase; it's simply the word francese (French) followed by ieri (yesterday). In questions like the examples, Italian often omits the definite article before languages (e.g. Hai studiato francese?) but can include it (Hai studiato il francese?) — both are possible with little change in meaning. Word order: subject + avere + past participle + object/time expression (Hai studiato francese ieri?).
target_language_example: Hai parlato francese ieri?
native_language_example: Did you speak French yesterday?

meaning: 'the sentence/phrase is' (used to state something about a sentence or phrase).
additional_notes: This is simply the noun frase ('sentence' or 'phrase') followed by the verb è (3rd-person singular of essere = 'is'). It's used to describe the state or action related to a sentence/phrase (e.g., 'is deleted', 'is commonly used', 'is approved'). In Italian the past passive uses è stata + past participle for feminine nouns (la frase è stata cancellata = the sentence was deleted).
target_language_example: Questa frase è nuova e può essere modificata.
native_language_example: This sentence is new and can be edited.

meaning: ‘sentences are’ — combination of the noun frasi (sentences) and the verb sono (they are).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but a simple subject–verb sequence: frasi (plural of frase) + sono (3rd person plural of essere). Use it to describe properties of sentences (e.g., difficulty, length). You can replace frasi with another plural noun and sono with other adjectives or complements. Word order: subject + sono + adjective/complement (Le frasi sono lunghe).
target_language_example: Le frasi sono chiare e facili da capire.
native_language_example: The sentences are clear and easy to understand.

meaning: '(my/your/his/her) brother is more/—er' (used to compare a brother to someone or describe a quality as greater).
additional_notes: This phrase combines 'fratello' (brother) + the verb 'essere' (è = is) + 'più' (more/er). Use 'più' with an adjective to make comparisons (più forte = stronger, più vecchio = older, più paziente = more patient). You can add 'di' + person/object to say 'than' (e.g. più alto di me = taller than me). 'Suo'/'mio'/'tuo' etc. change the possessor (his/her/my/your brother).
target_language_example: Il mio fratello è più alto di me.
native_language_example: My brother is taller than me.

meaning: in a hurry to (do something); eager/pressured to
additional_notes: Used with a verb (infinitive) or noun phrase to indicate urgency, haste, or desire to act. Common construction: avere fretta di + [infinitive] = to be in a hurry to do something. Negated (non avere fretta di) means not in a hurry. Can describe positive eagerness or impatience; context determines level of urgency.
target_language_example: Ho fretta di prendere il treno.
native_language_example: I'm in a hurry to catch the train.

meaning: in front of me; facing me; opposite me.
additional_notes: Used to indicate something or someone positioned directly in front of the speaker or facing the speaker. Often appears as "di fronte a me" (more common), but "fronte a me" is understood in similar contexts. Can refer to physical placement (an object or person) or to arranging people (e.g., lining up facing the speaker).
target_language_example: Si mise di fronte a me e cominciò a parlare.
native_language_example: He stood in front of me and started to speak.

meaning: seafood (literally: 'fruit of the sea') — often used for shellfish and other seafood items
additional_notes: Used in singular or plural (frutto di mare / frutti di mare). Commonly appears on menus (e.g., spaghetti ai frutti di mare). Can refer to a single type of seafood or a mixed seafood dish. Formal/neutral register.
target_language_example: Il piatto contiene un frutto di mare in evidenza.
native_language_example: The dish contains a standout seafood item.

meaning: 'it was then' / 'that was when' (introduces the moment when something happened)
additional_notes: Used to narrate past events; often appears at the start of a clause to highlight the exact time something occurred. 'Fu' is the passato remoto (literary/simple past) of 'essere' and gives a formal or narrative tone. In spoken Italian, speakers might use 'fu allora che' less often and prefer 'è stato allora che' or 'è allora che' (present perfect / present) depending on region and style.
