For masculine nouns use 'del' (di + il) or 'dello' before s+consonant/z, and 'dei/degli' for plurals. Common in spoken Italian to say someone is in the process of eating.
target_language_example: Marco sta mangiando della pasta adesso.
native_language_example: Marco is eating some pasta right now.

meaning: to feed the dogs (give food to the dogs).
additional_notes: Literal phrase made of 'dare da mangiare' (to give something to eat) + 'ai cani' (to the dogs). Used when someone gives food to dogs or takes care of feeding them. Common simple past or present forms: 'ho dato da mangiare ai cani' (I fed the dogs), 'devo dare da mangiare ai cani' (I must feed the dogs).
target_language_example: Ogni mattina devo dare da mangiare ai cani prima di uscire.
native_language_example: Every morning I have to feed the dogs before leaving.

meaning: to feed the fish / to give food to the fish
additional_notes: A common, literal expression used when asking or stating how often someone feeds fish (e.g., pet fish or fish at a pond). The verb phrase is 'dare da mangiare' (to give something to eat) followed by the indirect object 'ai pesci' (to the fish). You can replace 'ai pesci' with other animals (e.g., 'al cane', 'agli uccelli'). Tense and person change the verb (dai, date, dà, etc.).
target_language_example: Ogni mattina do da mangiare ai pesci nell'acquario.
native_language_example: Every morning I feed the fish in the aquarium.

meaning: to feed my dog (literally: 'to give something to eat to my dog')
additional_notes: In Italian the construction 'dare da mangiare a + [animal/person]' means 'to feed (someone/something)'. You often see it with verbs like 'dare' or in past forms ('diedi/ho dato/dimenticai di dar da mangiare'). Here 'mangiare al mio cane' is the complement phrase meaning 'to my dog' and is normally used with 'dare' (dar da mangiare). Use 'non do mai da mangiare al mio cane' to say 'I never feed my dog...' or 'dimenticai di dar da mangiare al mio cane' for 'I forgot to feed my dog.'
target_language_example: Devo ricordarmi di dare da mangiare al mio cane stasera.
native_language_example: I must remember to feed my dog tonight.

meaning: to feed (someone/something); literally 'to give to eat to'.
additional_notes: This appears as part of the verb phrase dare da mangiare a + [animal/person]. In your examples the full idea is 'dare da mangiare alle ...' where 'alle' = a + le (to the, plural feminine). Use dare (conjugated) + da mangiare + a/allo/alla/alle to say 'feed (the) ...'. If the direct object is singular/plural or masculine/feminine, the preposition changes (al, allo, alla, ai, agli, alle).
target_language_example: Ho dato da mangiare alle galline stamattina.
native_language_example: I fed the chickens this morning.

meaning: to eat (somewhere) / to eat (at a place); also used in constructions like "nothing to eat"
additional_notes: Used with a place or occasion: "mangiare da [qualcuno/qualcosa]" = to eat at someone's house or at a specific place. In questions about meals (e.g. "mangiare da cena") it means "to eat for dinner" or "to eat at dinner time." Can also appear in negative constructions with "nulla/ nient'altro da mangiare" meaning "nothing to eat." Context determines whether "da" indicates location (at) or purpose/time (for).
target_language_example: Preferisci mangiare da me stasera?
native_language_example: Do you prefer to eat at my place tonight?

meaning: to eat more / to eat more (something) or to eat more + adverb (e.g., more slowly).
additional_notes: Used with a noun to mean 'eat more [of something]' (e.g., mangiare più verdure = eat more vegetables) or with an adverb to form comparative expressions (e.g., mangiare più lentamente = eat more slowly). Context and sentence structure determine whether it modifies the verb (more) or the object (more of). Common with verbs of consumption and advice from doctors or guides.
target_language_example: Dovresti mangiare più frutta ogni giorno.
native_language_example: You should eat more fruit every day.

meaning: to eat here / eat in this place.
additional_notes: Common phrase used to say you want to eat at the current location or ask/suggest eating here. Can be used in statements, questions, or invitations. 'Mangiare' = to eat; 'qui' = here. Word order is flexible in spoken Italian (e.g., 'voglio mangiare qui' or 'mangiare qui voglio' is possible but less common).
target_language_example: Preferisco mangiare qui stasera.
native_language_example: I prefer to eat here tonight.

meaning: you eat the
additional_notes: Compositional phrase from mangiate + il. Mangiate can mean either "you all eat / are eating" (with voi) or a command to more than one person: "eat!". Il means "the" before many masculine singular nouns, so the full phrase changes depending on the noun that follows.
target_language_example: Mangiate il pesce stasera?
native_language_example: Are you eating the fish tonight?

meaning: ate meat (past participle + noun) — used to say someone has eaten meat or a specific kind of meat.
additional_notes: This is the past participle mangiato (from mangiare) plus the noun carne. It often appears with a specific type of meat after carne (e.g., carne di maiale = pork). In Italian you'd more naturally say "ho mangiato carne" (I ate meat) or include the subject and auxiliary verb (e.g., "hai mangiato carne?"). The phrase itself is not idiomatic or fixed — it's just a literal description of having eaten meat. Can appear with qualifiers like "solo/soltanto/ma solo/ma soltanto/ però solo" to limit frequency.
target_language_example: Ieri ho mangiato carne di manzo alla griglia.
native_language_example: Yesterday I ate grilled beef.

meaning: ate (some) bread / has eaten bread.
additional_notes: Literal past participle construction: mangiato (eaten) + del pane (some bread). Used to say someone ate bread (unspecified amount). In Italian, 'del' is partitive meaning 'some' — common for food. Can be adapted for different subjects (Ho mangiato del pane = I ate some bread).
target_language_example: Lei ha mangiato del pane con l'olio.
native_language_example: She ate some bread with oil.

meaning: eaten rice (followed by a specification, e.g. a place or style).
additional_notes: This is not a complete fixed phrase by itself — it's a fragment meaning 'ate some rice' and normally continues with a preposition or adjective (for example 'mangiato del riso al sugo' = 'ate rice with sauce', or 'mangiato del riso al ristorante' = 'ate rice at the restaurant'). Use it as part of a full sentence: subject + 'ha/ho/mangiato del riso...' The part 'del riso' means 'some rice' and 'al' is the start of a following phrase (a contraction of 'a' + 'il' or part of 'al + [flavor/condiment/place]').
target_language_example: Ieri ho mangiato del riso al sugo per cena.
native_language_example: Yesterday I ate rice with sauce for dinner.

meaning: 'eaten my' (past participle + possessive) — indicates someone/something ate something that belongs to the speaker.
additional_notes: Mangiato is the past participle of mangiare (to eat). 'Il mio' means 'my' (masculine singular). Together they appear in sentences like 'Chi ha mangiato il mio dessert?' or 'Hai mangiato il mio sandwich?' — English word order is usually 'eaten my X' but in Italian you include the thing after (mangiato il mio sandwich). Change 'il mio' to agree with the gender/number of the noun (la mia, i miei, le mie). Use appropriate auxiliary (avere) and subject pronouns as needed.
target_language_example: Marco ha mangiato il mio panino senza chiedere.
native_language_example: Marco ate my sandwich without asking.

meaning: eaten in this (context/place/time) — literal phrase, often incomplete; needs more words to be a full sentence.
additional_notes: This is a sequence of words: mangiato (past participle of mangiare = 'eaten') + in questo ('in this'). Alone it is not a complete, natural sentence in Italian. You will typically see it as part of longer phrases, for example: "È mangiato in questo ristorante" (it is eaten in this restaurant) or "L'ho mangiato in questo momento" (I ate it at this moment) — note that the latter would normally use a different structure ("l'ho mangiato ora"). Be careful: word order and auxiliary verbs are important for past actions (e.g. "l'ho mangiato in questo bar").
target_language_example: L'ho mangiato in questo ristorante.
native_language_example: I ate it in this restaurant.

meaning: 'eaten his/her/its' (past participle + possessive)
additional_notes: Combines the past participle mangiato (eaten) with the possessive la sua (her/his/its — feminine singular object). Use la sua when the thing eaten is a feminine noun (la cena, la farina, la colazione, la insalata). Gender of the possessor (his/her) is not shown by la sua; context or a name clarifies who it belongs to. For a masculine singular object use il suo (e.g. ha mangiato il suo panino).
target_language_example: Marco ha già mangiato la sua cena.
native_language_example: Marco has already eaten his dinner.

meaning: ate a lot / have eaten a lot
additional_notes: A past participle phrase using 'mangiare' (to eat) + 'molto' (a lot). Can be used in passato prossimo: (io) ho mangiato molto = I ate a lot / I have eaten a lot. Also appears in questions (Hai mangiato molto?) and comparisons (ha mangiato molto più di...). 'Molto' modifies quantity (how much).
target_language_example: Abbiamo mangiato molto alla festa ieri.
native_language_example: We ate a lot at the party yesterday.

meaning: ate only / have only eaten (something).
additional_notes: Used to say you ate only a specific food or only a small amount. 'Mangiato' is the past participle of 'mangiare' (to eat); 'solo' means 'only' or 'just'. Word order can vary: you can also say 'ho mangiato solo...' or emphasize quantity with 'solo un/una' (only one). Common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Ho mangiato solo un panino, non ho preso altro.
native_language_example: I only ate a sandwich; I didn't take anything else.

meaning: literally 'eaten all (feminine)', used to say someone/thing ate everything or finished all of something (feminine agreement).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase on its own but a combination of the past participle mangiato (eaten) and tutta (all, feminine). Agreement in Italian: tutta matches a feminine singular noun (e.g., 'la torta') — 'ho mangiato tutta la torta' = 'I ate the whole cake.' For masculine nouns you'd say 'mangiato tutto'. Pronoun subjects and auxiliary verbs (avere/essere) may appear: 'Ho mangiato tutta' is colloquial/elliptical and usually needs the noun or context ('l'ho mangiato tutto' or 'l'ho mangiata tutta').
target_language_example: Ho mangiato tutta la pizza.
native_language_example: I ate the whole pizza.

meaning: ate all (of it/them).
additional_notes: Compound of the past participle mangiato (eaten) + tutti (all). Used to say someone consumed all of something (e.g., all the cookies). Word order can vary: 'ha mangiato tutti i biscotti' or subject after. If the noun is feminine plural use 'tutte' (e.g., 'ha mangiato tutte le fragole').
target_language_example: Ha mangiato tutti i panini prima della festa.
native_language_example: He ate all the sandwiches before the party.

meaning: ate everything / finished all of it
additional_notes: Past participle phrase meaning someone has eaten all of the food (or everything available). Commonly used after an auxiliary (e.g., 'ho mangiato tutto') or as a short question/report ('Hai mangiato tutto?'). Can refer to a specific dish, plate, or all food in a place (fridge, table).
target_language_example: Ho mangiato tutto quello che c'era nel piatto.
native_language_example: I ate everything that was on the plate.

meaning: ate a cake
additional_notes: Simple past (passato prossimo) phrase: mangiato is the past participle of mangiare. Usually used with an auxiliary verb (ho mangiato una torta = I ate a cake). Alone it may appear in answers or clipped sentences where the auxiliary is understood from context.
target_language_example: Ieri ho mangiato una torta al cioccolato.
native_language_example: Yesterday I ate a chocolate cake.

meaning: ate all of (something) — indicates a completed action in the past where the subject consumed the entire item.
additional_notes: Compound of the past tense verb 'mangiò' (he/she/it ate — passato remoto or passato prossimo depending on context) and 'tutta' (whole/entire, agrees in gender with feminine singular noun). Use 'tutto' for masculine singular nouns (e.g. 'mangiò tutto il panino') and plural forms 'tutti/tutte' for plural nouns. Common in stories and narratives to say someone finished all of a food item.
target_language_example: Luca mangiò tutta la ciambella in pochi minuti.
native_language_example: Luca ate the whole donut in a few minutes.

meaning: 'hands on (someone)' — to touch someone, usually in a forceful, inappropriate, or non-consensual way (often implying assault).
additional_notes: Used to describe someone putting their hands on another person. Often negative: can mean unwanted touching, assault, or physical aggression. Common in exclamations and accusations. Literal words are 'hands' (mani) + 'on'/'onto' (addosso).
target_language_example: Non ti permettere di mettermi le mani addosso!
native_language_example: Don't you dare put your hands on me!

meaning: Hands behind the... (an instruction to put hands behind a specified body part).
additional_notes: Common short command used by police, security, or authority figures. The phrase is typically completed by a noun (e.g. schiena = back, testa = head) — here examples show 'mani dietro la schiena' (hands behind your back) and 'mani dietro la testa' (hands behind your head). It's an imperative/formal or neutral command; context is usually urgent or authoritative.
target_language_example: Mani dietro la schiena, per favore.
native_language_example: Hands behind your back, please.

meaning: "hands and" (the word 'e' means 'and')
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself — it's simply the plural noun mani (hands) followed by the conjunction e (and). It appears in examples when listing body parts (mani e piedi = hands and feet) or in constructions like alza le mani e girati (raise your hands and turn around). Use le mani for "the hands" (feminine plural).
target_language_example: Si è lavato le mani e i piedi prima di uscire.
native_language_example: He washed his hands and feet before going out.

meaning: 'hands up' (raise your hands; often an order)
additional_notes: Used as an imperative command telling someone to raise their hands. Common in contexts of authority or danger (e.g., police, robberies) and also used figuratively or playfully. Pronounced with stress on 'alto'. Can be plural exclamation: 'Mani in alto!'.
target_language_example: Mani in alto, per favore!
native_language_example: Hands up, please!

meaning: hands before eating (used in instructions/phrases about washing hands before a meal).
additional_notes: This phrase appears as part of commands, questions, or statements about washing hands before eating. In Italian you normally say lavarsi le mani prima di mangiare (to wash one's hands before eating). The examples show variations: imperative (Lavati le mani...), questions (Ti lavi le mani...?), and reflexive infinitive constructions (lavarmi/le mani). Useful when talking about hygiene or asking where to wash hands.
target_language_example: Per favore, lavati le mani prima di mangiare.
native_language_example: Please wash your hands before eating.

meaning: "in such a way" or "so (adjective)" — used to describe the manner or way something is done (often followed by an adjective).
additional_notes: Commonly appears as "in maniera così + adjective" or "in modo così + adjective" to emphasize how (often unexpectedly) someone behaves or speaks. It is neutral; tone depends on adjective (e.g., "stupida" is insulting, "divertente" is positive). You may also hear shortened forms like "così" alone (e.g., "Perché fai così?").
target_language_example: Perché parli in maniera così veloce?
native_language_example: Why are you speaking so fast?

meaning: literally 'hand that'; used to introduce a clause describing a hand or metaphorical 'hand' (action, situation) — often part of phrases like 'la mano che...' or 'una mano che...'.
additional_notes: This is not an idiom by itself but a common construction: mano (hand) + che (that). It can be literal (the physical hand that...) or figurative (a hand as an action, fate, or situation). The following clause describes or qualifies the hand. Translation depends on context: sometimes 'the hand that...', 'a hand that...', or 'which...'.
target_language_example: La mano che tieni stretta era fredda.
native_language_example: The hand that you hold was cold.

meaning: help me with this / give me a hand with this (literally: 'a hand with this')
additional_notes: Used after verbs like 'dare' (dammi/mi dia) or modal verbs to ask someone to help lift, carry, or deal with something nearby. Common polite forms: 'Dammi una mano con questa...' (informal), 'Mi dia una mano con questa...' (formal). Replace 'questa' with 'questo' for masculine nouns (e.g. 'con questo pacco').
target_language_example: Dammi una mano con questa valigia, per favore.
native_language_example: Give me a hand with this suitcase, please.

meaning: 'hand in hand' — holding hands; also used figuratively to mean 'together' or 'closely connected'.
additional_notes: Literally describes people holding hands (romantic or friendly). Commonly used figuratively to describe groups or ideas working closely together or being allied (sometimes with negative connotations, e.g. 'the police and the Klan go hand in hand'). Word order is fixed; you can also say 'a mano' in other contexts but not as a substitute here.
target_language_example: Camminavano mano nella mano lungo il fiume.
native_language_example: They walked hand in hand along the river.

meaning: 'the beef is' (manzo = beef/cattle; è = is).
additional_notes: This is simply the noun manzo (beef) followed by the verb è (is). Use to state facts or opinions about beef (price, quality, taste). Manzo can also mean 'steer' or 'ox' in other contexts, but in food contexts it means 'beef'. Word order is subject + verb as in English. Replace è with other verbs or adjectives as needed (e.g., 'Il manzo è buono' = 'The beef is good').
target_language_example: Il manzo è tenero e saporito.
native_language_example: The beef is tender and tasty.

meaning: Used with 'che' to comment on or question 'husband' — often to emphasize, express surprise, disbelief, or to introduce a remark about the husband.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom; it shows how 'che' can be used after or before a noun to add emphasis, surprise, irony, or to introduce a follow-up comment. Examples: 'Che buon marito che hai!' = 'What a good husband you have!' ('che' before adjective + repetition with 'che' + subject). 'E il marito che fa?' = 'And what about the husband?' or 'And the husband, what does he do?' 'Mio marito, che!' is an exclamation (often trailing off) expressing strong feeling about 'my husband' (pride, annoyance, disbelief) depending on tone and context. Note: word order and intonation matter in spoken Italian.
target_language_example: Che marito che hai — sempre disponibile!
native_language_example: What a husband you have — always helpful!

meaning: my/your/his/her husband is in (somewhere/state).
additional_notes: This is the phrase 'marito è in' (husband is in) used with a following noun or place: e.g. 'in prigione', 'in carcere', 'in pericolo', 'in vacanza'. Replace the possessive (mio/suo/tuo) as needed: 'Mio marito è in...' = 'My husband is in...'. Commonly followed by locations or conditions.
target_language_example: Il mio marito è in vacanza questa settimana.
native_language_example: My husband is on vacation this week.

meaning: my/your/his/her husband is a... (used to state someone's husband's profession or role).
additional_notes: This phrase combines marito (husband) + the verb è (is) + the indefinite article un (a). Change the subject pronoun (mio, suo, etc.) before marito to show whose husband it is: mio marito (my husband), suo marito (his/her/your formal husband). The article un agrees with masculine singular nouns (un dottore, un insegnante). For feminine or plural nouns you'd use different forms (e.g., mia moglie è una...).
target_language_example: Tuo marito è un musicista molto talentuoso.
native_language_example: Your husband is a very talented musician.

meaning: cardiac massage; chest compressions (CPR) — manual pressing on the chest to help the heart pump.
additional_notes: Used in medical/first-aid contexts. Refers to external chest compressions performed during cardiopulmonary resuscitation (RCP/CPR). Can appear in questions asking if someone knows how to perform it (Conosci il massaggio cardiaco?) or statements saying someone received it (Gli hanno fatto un massaggio cardiaco).
target_language_example: Se perdi conoscenza, qualcuno deve fare il massaggio cardiaco.
native_language_example: If you lose consciousness, someone needs to perform cardiac massage (chest compressions).

meaning: favorite school subject
additional_notes: Used to say which subject (in school or study) someone likes best. 'Materia' = subject; 'preferita' = preferred/favorite. Commonly preceded by a definite article (la mia materia preferita) or the subject name (La matematica è la mia materia preferita).
target_language_example: La storia è la mia materia preferita.
native_language_example: History is my favorite subject.

meaning: to give/loan a pencil to (someone).
additional_notes: This phrase combines the noun matita (pencil) with the preposition a (to) and is used when indicating the recipient of an action involving a pencil (lend, give, pass, lose at a place). Common verbs with this structure: prestare la matita a (lend the pencil to), passare la matita a (pass the pencil to), perdere la matita a (lose the pencil at [a place]) — note perdere la matita a scuola means 'lose one's pencil at school'. The word order is typically verb + la/mi/tu + matita + a + recipient.
target_language_example: Ho dato la mia matita a Luca.
native_language_example: I gave my pencil to Luca.

meaning: "pencil and" — the noun matita (pencil) followed by the conjunction e (and).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase; it's simply the word matita (a pencil) used with the conjunction e (and) to join items or actions. In sentences it can appear in subject or object position (e.g., 'Ha preso la matita e ha cominciato a scrivere' = 'He/She took the pencil and started to write'). The noun agrees only in number (matita → matite for plural).
target_language_example: Ho una matita e un quaderno nella borsa.
native_language_example: I have a pencil and a notebook in my bag.

meaning: Likely a mistaken or incomplete phrase; appears to combine 'matrimonio' (marriage/wedding) with the article 'la' ('the'), yielding an unfinished fragment rather than a standard expression.
additional_notes: 'Matrimonio e la' is not a standard fixed phrase in Italian. Possible correct forms: 'il matrimonio' (the marriage/wedding) or a full coordinated phrase like 'il matrimonio e la famiglia' (marriage and family). As written, it's probably a typo or a fragment that needs another word after 'la'.
target_language_example: Il matrimonio e la festa sono stati splendidi, ma la frase 'matrimonio e la' così com'è è incompleta.
native_language_example: The wedding and the party were wonderful, but the phrase 'matrimonio e la' by itself is incomplete.

meaning: a formula used to introduce a comment/opinion about marriage (literally: 'marriage is a...').
additional_notes: This phrase is not a fixed idiom but the structure 'Il matrimonio è una + [noun/phrase]' is commonly used to state beliefs, judgments, or metaphors about marriage (e.g. 'una cosa seria', 'una lotteria'). Change the article (Il/Il) or gender/number as needed: 'Il matrimonio è importante', 'Il matrimonio sono...'(rare). Keep 'Il matrimonio' for 'marriage' in general.
target_language_example: Il matrimonio è una scelta importante nella vita.
native_language_example: Marriage is an important choice in life.

meaning: 'from morning to evening' (all day; continuously throughout the day).
additional_notes: Used to say something happens or is true for the whole day, often emphasizing continuity or repetition. Can be literal (working all day) or idiomatic (doing nothing all day, or always). Common in both neutral and informal contexts; tone depends on surrounding words.
target_language_example: Lavora dalla mattina alla sera senza pausa.
native_language_example: He works from morning to evening without a break.

meaning: 'me' (object pronoun) + 'now' — meaning 'me now' or 'to/for me now' depending on context.
additional_notes: Me is the unstressed first-person object pronoun (me). Adesso means 'now'. Together they usually appear in sentences like 'per me adesso' (for me now), 'con me adesso' (with me now), or simply as 'me adesso' where adesso modifies the time related to the speaker (e.g. 'what do you think of me now?'). Word order is flexible in Italian; 'me adesso' is colloquial/neutral and common in spoken and written language.
target_language_example: Cosa pensi di me adesso?
native_language_example: What do you think of me now?

meaning: 'me and' (used before naming another person or people)
additional_notes: Informal spoken construction used to mean 'me and ...' as the subject or object (e.g. 'me e Tom' = 'me and Tom'). Standard written Italian prefers 'io e...' as subject (though 'io e...' is awkward — better to use 'Tom ed io' or 'io e Tom') or 'me e...' as object after prepositions (colloquial). In many dialects and casual speech 'me e' is common. Watch word order and politeness: placing oneself after others (e.g. 'Tom ed io') is more formal/polite.
target_language_example: Me e Luca andremo al cinema domani.
native_language_example: Me and Luca will go to the cinema tomorrow.

meaning: I miss (someone/something) / I lack (something) — expresses that someone or something is missing to me (literally 'to me is missing').
additional_notes: Standard construction uses an indirect object pronoun (mi manca / mi mancano); 'me manca' is a stressed form (A me manca...) used for emphasis or contrast. Use singular (manca) for one item/person and plural (mancano) for multiple. Can also mean 'I lack' or 'I don't have enough' in contexts like 'Me manca il tempo' (I lack time). 'Me manca' without an explicit object can be used elliptically to mean 'I miss (them/it)' or 'I feel something is missing.' Informal register is common in spoken Italian.
target_language_example: A me manca Parigi.
native_language_example: I miss Paris.

meaning: 'I miss (them)' — used to say you miss multiple people or things (plural).
additional_notes: "Me mancano" is a colloquial short form of "a me mancano" and uses the verb mancare with an indirect object pronoun (me). In Italian mancare works like 'to be lacking to someone': the thing(s) missing is/are the grammatical subject and the person who misses is the indirect object. The more standard clitic form is "mi mancano"; "me mancano" is often used for emphasis or in spoken, regional, or informal registers, sometimes after "a" as in "A me mancano...". For a singular missing item use "mi manca" / "me manca."
target_language_example: A me mancano davvero molto i miei genitori.
native_language_example: I really miss my parents.

meaning: I don't care at all / I couldn't care less.
additional_notes: Colloquial and somewhat blunt; expresses strong indifference. Often used with 'non' (non me ne frega niente) or emphatically (a me non me ne frega niente). Can sound rude in formal contexts. 'Fregare' here means 'to matter' in this expression, not its literal sense 'to steal/cheat'.
target_language_example: Davvero pensi che cambi qualcosa? Non me ne frega niente.
native_language_example: Do you really think it will change anything? I couldn't care less.

me ne frega un cazzo di

target_language_multi_word_term: me ne frega un cazzo di
meaning: I don't give a damn about / I couldn't care less about (vulgar).
additional_notes: Very strong, vulgar expression used to say you don't care at all about someone or something. Use with caution: inappropriate in formal settings or with people you don't know. Structure: 'Non me ne frega un cazzo di ...' + noun, clause, or verb (often introduced by 'cosa', 'che', or a relative clause). Informal/explicit; there are milder alternatives like 'non me ne importa niente' or 'non mi interessa'.
target_language_example: Non me ne frega un cazzo di quello che dicono su di me.
native_language_example: I don't give a damn about what they say about me.

meaning: I don't like (them/people/things).
additional_notes: This is a colloquial word order used for emphasis: 'A me non piacciono ...' stresses 'me' (as for me). Literally 'to me they are not pleasing.' Use with plural subjects (piacciono). For singular use 'A me non piace ...'. You can drop 'A' in casual speech ('Me non...' is possible but less common than 'A me non...').
target_language_example: A me non piacciono i film d'orrore.
native_language_example: I don't like horror movies.

meaning: to me it doesn't seem / it doesn't seem to me
additional_notes: Used to give a personal opinion or impression that something is not the case. Often appears with 'a me' at the start (A me non sembra) to emphasize 'to me.' Can comment on facts (e.g., not dry, not correct, not a helmet) or on feelings/perceptions. Common in spoken Italian. Word order can vary: 'A me non sembra' or simply 'Non mi sembra' (both mean the same; 'non mi sembra' is more common).
target_language_example: A me non sembra una buona idea.
native_language_example: It doesn't seem like a good idea to me.

meaning: to me, (it) has never (been/liked/etc.).
additional_notes: This phrase combines 'a me' (to me) with the negative perfect 'non è mai' (has never). It's used to say you have never experienced or liked something. In spoken Italian 'a me' often appears before the verb (A me non è mai piaciuto...), and agreement of past participle depends on the object when using 'piacere' (piaciuto/piaciuta).
target_language_example: A me non è mai piaciuto il calcio.
native_language_example: I've never liked soccer.

meaning: 'for me ... is not' / 'to me ... is not' (used to express a personal opinion or state that something is not the case for the speaker)
additional_notes: This sequence appears in phrases like 'a me non è...' or 'per me non è...' and is followed by an adjective, noun phrase, or verb phrase introduced by 'un/una/di...'. It emphasizes the speaker's personal perspective (contrast: 'a me'/'per me' = 'for me'/'to me'). Word order can vary: 'Per me non è un problema' or 'A me non è mai importato'. The standalone fragment 'me non è' without 'a'/'per' before it is uncommon; learners should use 'a me non è' or 'per me non è'.
target_language_example: Per me non è un problema andare domani.
native_language_example: For me, it's not a problem to go tomorrow.

meaning: I like (plural things).
additional_notes: Used to say that you like multiple items or activities. 'Piacciono' is the third-person plural form of 'piacere' and requires a plural subject (the things you like). 'A me' is optional and adds emphasis ('as for me' / 'I'). In Italian the grammar is different: you literally say 'to me (are pleasing) X'. For singular things use 'mi piace' (e.g. 'mi piace la musica').
target_language_example: A me piacciono i film d'avventura.
native_language_example: I like adventure movies.

meaning: I really like (them).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that the speaker likes something. 'Me' is the tonic/emphatic form of 'mi' (to me); 'piacciono' is plural form of 'piacere' (to be pleasing). Use 'mi piace veramente' for singular nouns. Common in spoken and written Italian to stress genuine liking.
target_language_example: A me piacciono veramente i film italiani.
native_language_example: I really like Italian films.

meaning: I like
additional_notes: Usually the standard Italian form is mi piace. In sentences like a me piace, a me adds emphasis: “I like” / “as for me, I like”. The form me piace by itself is colloquial or nonstandard in many contexts; beginners should normally learn mi piace.
target_language_example: A me piace cucinare la sera.
native_language_example: I like cooking in the evening.

meaning: I like to be / I enjoy being (emphatic).
additional_notes: Used to express a personal preference about being in a certain state or role. 'A me' adds emphasis or contrast (e.g., 'as for me'); it can be omitted in neutral statements ('Mi piace essere...'). Followed by an adjective, noun, or clause: 'essere spontanea' (to be spontaneous), 'essere un insegnante' (to be a teacher). Verb agrees with the speaker's gender/number if an adjective is used.
target_language_example: A me piace essere onesta.
native_language_example: I like to be honest.

meaning: I like to talk / I enjoy speaking.
additional_notes: This phrase emphasizes the speaker's personal liking (the 'A me' is a stressed form of 'mi'). It's followed by an infinitive or by 'con'/'a' + person/thing or a language (e.g., 'parlare con lei', 'parlare in francese'). More neutral/common: 'Mi piace parlare'. Use 'A me' for contrast or emphasis (e.g., 'A me piace parlare, a te no').
target_language_example: A me piace parlare con gli amici la sera.
native_language_example: I like to talk with friends in the evening.

meaning: 'I would like' (expresses a desire or wish).
additional_notes: Usually appears as 'mi piacerebbe' in standard Italian; 'a me piacerebbe' adds emphasis ('as for me, I would like'). Follows the conditional form 'piacerebbe' + infinitive or noun. Use to politely state wishes or preferences.
target_language_example: A me piacerebbe visitare Roma la prossima estate.
native_language_example: I would like to visit Rome next summer.

meaning: 'I liked' (past, imperfect) or 'it used to please me'.
additional_notes: Used to express a past or habitual liking. The full phrase is normally 'a me piaceva' for emphasis on 'me' (contrast with others) — you can also say simply 'mi piaceva'. 'Piaceva' is the imperfect of 'piacere', so it describes ongoing or repeated liking in the past (e.g., 'I used to like' or 'I liked' with no single completed moment). The thing that was liked follows the verb (e.g., 'A me piaceva il vino').
target_language_example: A me piaceva quel ristorante quando vivevo in città.
native_language_example: I used to like that restaurant when I lived in the city.

meaning: 'I liked' (something plural) — emphatic/colloquial form.
additional_notes: This is the imperfect tense of piacere used for plural things (piacevano). With 'a me' or simply 'me' it adds emphasis or clarifies the person: 'A me piacevano...' = 'I (personally) liked...'. Note Italian uses an indirect-object structure: literal order is '[to me] they were pleasing.' Common in spoken and informal contexts; in more neutral style you might say 'Mi piacevano...'.
target_language_example: A me piacevano i film d'avventura quando ero giovane.
native_language_example: I liked adventure movies when I was young.

meaning: 'I need' (used to indicate that something is needed by the speaker; informal/colloquial variant emphasising 'to me')
additional_notes: 'Me serve' is a colloquial, regional, or emphatic variant of the standard 'mi serve' or 'a me serve'. Often used in spoken Italian to stress that the need belongs to the speaker. Can be followed by a noun, partitive, infinitive, or clause: e.g. 'me serve del caffè', 'me serve sapere...'. More formal/standard: 'mi serve' or 'a me serve' (the latter adds emphasis).
target_language_example: A me serve del caffè.
native_language_example: I need some coffee.

meaning: (To) me they are needed — I need (plural items). Used to express that plural things are needed by the speaker. The verb 'servire' is impersonal/experiential and agrees with the thing(s) needed.
additional_notes: This form is typically spoken as 'a me servono' for emphasis (literally 'to me are needed'). In everyday Italian the unstressed indirect object pronoun 'mi' is more common (e.g. 'Mi servono...'), but 'a me servono' or shortened 'me servono' adds emphasis or contrast ('I need... (as for me)'). Use 'me serve' or 'mi serve' when the item is singular. The verb agrees with the thing(s) needed (servono for plural, serve for singular).
target_language_example: A me servono delle forbici.
native_language_example: I need a pair of scissors.

meaning: myself (reflexive, feminine singular).
additional_notes: Used as the feminine singular reflexive pronoun after verbs or prepositions to refer back to the female speaker. For a male speaker use "me stesso". Can appear with emphasis (e.g., "solo me stessa") and in negative or emotional statements ("odio me stessa"). Often follows the verb or preposition: "credere in me stessa", "dare la colpa a me stessa".
target_language_example: Devo imparare a fidarmi di me stessa.
native_language_example: I need to learn to trust myself.

meaning: myself (emphatic reflexive pronoun).
additional_notes: Used for emphasis or reflexive actions referring to the speaker. 'Me stesso' agrees with the speaker (first person). In spoken Italian you may also hear 'me' alone in informal contexts (e.g. 'posso essere me'). Use 'me stessa' if the speaker identifies as female.
target_language_example: A volte devo difendermi e pensare prima a me stesso.
native_language_example: Sometimes I have to defend myself and think of myself first.

meaning: I liked (it) — feminine singular object; emphasis with 'a me'.
additional_notes: This is a focused/emphatic way to say 'I liked it' in Italian. 'A me' adds emphasis or contrast (e.g., 'as for me'). 'Piaciuta' agrees in gender and number with the thing liked (here feminine singular). For a masculine singular use 'mi è piaciuto', for plural 'mi sono piaciuti/e'. In everyday speech 'a me' can be omitted: 'Mi è piaciuta la festa.'
target_language_example: A me è piaciuta la canzone che hai scelto.
native_language_example: I liked the song you chose.

meaning: for me, (he/she/it) is like… / to me, it’s like…
additional_notes: Usually appears after 'per' as 'per me è come' meaning 'in my opinion/for me, (someone or something) is like...'. Used to compare a person or thing to something familiar (a brother, a king, a drug, etc.). Common in spoken Italian. Structure: Per me è come + noun.
target_language_example: Per me è come una famiglia.
native_language_example: To me, he/she is like family.

meaning: bronze medal (third-place prize)
additional_notes: Used to say someone finished third in a competition or event. Common in sports/awards contexts. 'Medaglia d'oro' = gold (first), 'medaglia d'argento' = silver (second). Verbs: vincere (to win) una medaglia di bronzo.
target_language_example: Ha vinto una medaglia di bronzo alle gare.
native_language_example: He/she won a bronze medal at the competition.

meaning: ‘this average’ — refers to the average for the current period (e.g., this semester/trimester).
additional_notes: Literal order 'media questo' is colloquial and less formal; standard Italian more commonly uses 'la media di questo [periodo]' or 'la media di questo semestre/trimestre'. However, in spoken or informal written contexts you may hear or see 'la media questo semestre/trimestre' (omitting 'di'). 'Media' is feminine singular (la media). Context determines whether the noun phrase is acceptable without 'di'.
target_language_example: I suoi voti sono stati ben al di sotto della media questo semestre.
native_language_example: His grades were well below the average this semester.

meaning: medicine/medication for (someone or something).
additional_notes: Used to say that a medicine is intended for a person or to treat a condition. 'Per' can be followed by a person (e.g., 'per mio padre' = for my father) or a condition/ailment (e.g., 'per la febbre' = for fever). Common in everyday speech when giving, buying, or describing purpose of medicine.
target_language_example: Ho comprato una medicina per la tosse.
native_language_example: I bought a medicine for the cough.

meaning: 'medicine is' — the verb è (is) following medicina (medicine).
additional_notes: This phrase is simply the noun medicina followed by the verb è (third-person singular of essere). It appears in sentences that describe or ask about medicine (e.g., what kind of medicine it is, its taste, effectiveness, or readiness). Useful for basic statements or questions: Che medicina è? / La medicina è pronta. Note word order: in Italian the verb often follows the subject or comes after it in simple statements.
target_language_example: La medicina è fredda; scaldala prima di prenderla.
native_language_example: The medicine is cold; warm it up before taking it.

meaning: had better / would be better to (do something).
additional_notes: Used with a conditional or modal verb form (faremmo/faresti/etc.) + 'a' + infinitive to give advice or say one action is preferable. In sentence 6 ('gioca meglio a tennis') 'meglio' + 'a' is part of a different structure meaning 'better at' (skill with a sport or activity). Context tells which meaning is intended.
target_language_example: Faresti meglio a studiare prima dell'esame.
native_language_example: You'd better study before the exam.

meaning: 'would be better not to' (used to give advice or say someone should avoid doing something)
additional_notes: Usually appears in conditional constructions with verbs like "avresti/avreste/faresti/farebbe/fareste" + "fatto meglio a non" or the simpler "farebbe/faresti meglio a non". It's a formula for polite or strong advice/warning. After "meglio a non" the verb is in the infinitive (e.g., "fumare", "aprire"). In English you can translate it as "you would be better off not..." or "it would be better not to..."
target_language_example: Faresti meglio a non dire nulla.
native_language_example: You would be better off not saying anything.

meaning: would be better to / would have been better to (suggesting a preferred action).
additional_notes: Used with a conditional verb (often the conditional of fare: farebbe/farei/avrebbe fatto meglio) + 'ad' + an infinitive verb. Expresses advice or a counterfactual suggestion (what someone should do or should have done). In everyday English: 'you'd better' / 'it would be better to' / 'would have been better to.'
target_language_example: Faresti meglio ad accettare l'offerta.
native_language_example: You'd be better off accepting the offer.

meaning: It's better this way / that's better.
additional_notes: Used to say that the current situation or outcome is preferable to an alternative (often implied). Can be said neutrally, approvingly, or resignedly. Common in spoken Italian as a short comment; context determines if it's emphatic (È meglio così!) or questioning (Meglio così?).
target_language_example: Hai cambiato piano? Meglio così, sarà più semplice.
native_language_example: You changed the plan? That's better this way, it'll be simpler.

meaning: better for (someone/something); in someone's/something's best interest
additional_notes: Used to compare what is preferable for a person, group, or thing. Often appears in phrases like "è meglio per..." (it's better for...) or with verbs: "sarebbe stato meglio per..." (it would have been better for...). Can be followed by a noun, pronoun, or clause. Not idiomatic slang.
target_language_example: È meglio per noi aspettare un giorno in più.
native_language_example: It's better for us to wait one more day.

meaning: 'better for' (used to talk about what is best or preferable for someone/something)
additional_notes: Often appears in phrases like 'il meglio per [qualcuno]' (the best for someone) or 'del nostro meglio per [fare qualcosa]' (our best to do something). Can indicate a preference, wish, or suitability. 'Del nostro meglio per' means 'our best to' (make an effort); 'il meglio per loro' means 'what is best for them'.
target_language_example: Faremo il meglio per la tua famiglia.
native_language_example: We will do what's best for your family.

meaning: '(to do) one's best to help' or 'better to help' depending on context; here it appears as part of the phrase fare del (mio/suo/nostro) meglio per aiutare — to do one's best to help.
additional_notes: In the examples the full idiom is "fare del (mio/suo/nostro) meglio per aiutare [qualcuno]" meaning to try as hard as possible to help someone. "Meglio per aiutare" by itself is not a standalone fixed phrase; it usually appears after "fare del mio/suo/nostro meglio" or in comparative senses ("è meglio per aiutare..." = "it's better to help..."). Use the structure: fare del + possessive + meglio + per + aiutare + [persona].
target_language_example: Farò del mio meglio per aiutare i miei colleghi domani.
native_language_example: I will do my best to help my colleagues tomorrow.

meaning: literally 'apple was' — the past-tense phrase 'the apple was' used to describe an apple in the past.
additional_notes: This is simply the noun 'mela' (apple) followed by the past-tense form of 'essere' (era = he/she/it was). You will see it in sentences describing the state or quality of an apple in the past (e.g., delicious, ripe). Replace 'mela' with other nouns and 'era' with different tenses/persons as needed (e.g., 'la mela è' = 'the apple is').
target_language_example: Quella mela era molto matura.
native_language_example: That apple was very ripe.

meaning: literally 'apple for' — used to indicate an apple intended for or prepared for someone.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom; it's simply the noun mela (apple) followed by the preposition per (for). Commonly appears in sentences where someone peels or prepares an apple for another person (e.g. 'una mela per lui' = 'an apple for him'). Use per to show purpose, recipient, or intended beneficiary.
target_language_example: Ho comprato una mela per te.
native_language_example: I bought an apple for you.

meaning: This looks like the noun 'mele' (apples) followed by the conjunction 'e' (and). Alone it has no special meaning beyond 'apples and...'.
additional_notes: Not a fixed multiword expression. In the example sentences the intended phrase is likely just 'sacchetto di mele' and the 'e' would start a continuation; however the provided examples actually use 'e ne' ('and of them' with the clitic 'ne') to say 'and ate a third of them'. For beginners: 'mele' = plural of 'mela' (apple). 'e' = 'and'. 'ne' is a clitic pronoun meaning 'of them' or 'from it' used to replace a quantity (e.g. 'ne ha mangiate un terzo' = 'he ate one third of them').
target_language_example: Ho comprato delle mele e ne darò alcune ai miei amici.
native_language_example: I bought some apples and I'll give some of them to my friends.

meaning: unless (you) ...
additional_notes: Used in subordinate clauses to introduce an exception or condition: 'a meno che tu non...' = 'unless you...'. Often followed by a verb in the subjunctive (e.g., chieda, possa, voglia, abbia). The word 'non' is commonly included in Italian after 'a meno che' even though the clause already expresses a negative/exception; in English translate simply as 'unless'.
target_language_example: Non vieni, a meno che tu non cambi idea.
native_language_example: You won't come, unless you change your mind.

meaning: thankfully; luckily; it's a good thing
additional_notes: Used as an interjection to express relief that something turned out well or that a bad outcome was avoided. Often stands alone ("Meno male!") or followed by a clause introduced by "che" ("Meno male che..."). Tone can be casual to neutral and is common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Meno male che siamo arrivati in tempo!
native_language_example: Thankfully we arrived on time!

meaning: 'as little as possible' or 'the least possible'.
additional_notes: Used to say to minimize an action, amount, or involvement. Often follows verbs (pensarci il meno possibile = think about it as little as possible). Can stand alone as a short phrase (Il meno possibile = as little as possible).
target_language_example: Prova a parlare il meno possibile durante la lezione.
native_language_example: Try to speak as little as possible during the lesson.

mentire alla sua famiglia riguardo al suo

target_language_multi_word_term: mentire alla sua famiglia riguardo al suo
meaning: to lie to her/their family about her/their (something — typically a romantic partner).
additional_notes: This phrase is followed by a noun (e.g., fidanzato, moroso, ragazzo) that specifies what the person is lying about. 'Mentire a qualcuno' = to lie to someone. 'Riguardo a' = about/regarding. The possessive 'sua' agrees with the subject (his/her/their in context); in these examples it refers to the woman's partner. Common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Deve mentire alla sua famiglia riguardo al suo lavoro.
native_language_example: She has to lie to her family about her job.

meaning: lied to (someone).
additional_notes: Past participle form of mentire (to lie) used with a plural indirect object introduced by the preposition a + plural article (ai = a + i). 'Mentito ai' is followed by the people who were lied to: e.g. 'Ho mentito ai miei genitori' = 'I lied to my parents.' The subject can be io/lei/lui/etc.; the auxiliary used is avere (ho/ha).
target_language_example: Abbiamo mentito ai nostri amici per proteggerli.
native_language_example: We lied to our friends to protect them.

meaning: lied to (someone) about / lied for (a reason)
additional_notes: Built from the past participle mentito (lied) plus the preposition per. Often used with an indirect object or reason: e.g. "Mi ha mentito per paura" (He/she lied to me out of fear) or "Ha mentito per coprirlo" (He/she lied to cover for him). The exact nuance depends on the rest of the sentence: 'mentito a' is more common when specifying the person who was lied to (mentire a qualcuno), while 'per' typically introduces the motive or purpose.
target_language_example: Mi ha mentito per proteggermi.
native_language_example: He lied to me to protect me.

meaning: 'market of' or 'the ... market' (used to refer to a specific market or market sector).
additional_notes: A common phrase used before a noun to indicate a particular market or sector (e.g. mercato del lavoro = labor/job market; mercato del pesce = fish market). Often followed by the thing being traded or the sector. In everyday speech it can mean a physical marketplace or an economic market depending on context. The article 'del' is the contraction of 'di' + 'il'.
target_language_example: Il mercato del lavoro è cambiato molto negli ultimi anni.
native_language_example: The job market has changed a lot in recent years.

meaning: 'the market yesterday' (used to refer to the market on the previous day).
additional_notes: This phrase combines mercato (market) and ieri (yesterday). It commonly appears in questions or statements about whether someone went to the market the day before. Word order in Italian is flexible; more natural alternatives include 'ieri al mercato' or 'al mercato ieri'. When used with verbs of motion like 'andare', the past tense uses the auxiliary 'essere' and the past participle agrees in gender and number (e.g., sono andato/andata, siete andati/siete andate).
target_language_example: Non sono andato al mercato ieri.
native_language_example: I didn't go to the market yesterday.

meaning: 'damn' / 'shitty' (insulting intensifier used before a noun)
additional_notes: Vulgar and offensive. 'Merda di' is used as an intensifier to insult or degrade the noun that follows (e.g., 'merda di camion' = 'damn truck' or 'shitty truck'). Tone is aggressive; avoid in polite conversation. Can appear in many contexts to express anger, disgust, or contempt. Literal meaning is 'shit of', but it functions idiomatically as an expletive phrase.
target_language_example: Non toccare quella merda di macchina!
native_language_example: Don't touch that damn/shitty car!

meaning: ‘months in’ — used to indicate how many months someone spent in a place or situation.
additional_notes: Combine a number of months (e.g., tre mesi, sei mesi) with in + location or situation to say where/time was spent. Often appears with verbs like trascorrere, passare, trascorrere/ passare (passato) or studiare. Word order: [number] mesi in [luogo/situazione].
target_language_example: Ho passato sei mesi in Spagna.
native_language_example: I spent six months in Spain.

meaning: 'months later' or 'more months' (used to indicate a time a certain number of months after)
additional_notes: Used after a number or time expression to say how many months later something happened. Often appears as 'tre mesi più tardi' (three months later). Can also appear in comparative phrases about months (e.g. 'nei mesi più freddi' = 'in the coldest months') — context determines whether it means 'later' or 'more/most'.
target_language_example: Tre mesi più tardi, la situazione era molto diversa.
native_language_example: Three months later, the situation was very different.

meaning: a message to (someone) — used to say you give/send/pass on a message to a person.
additional_notes: Often appears with verbs like dare, mandare, trasmettere, or poter/dovrei to ask or say someone will send a message to a named person. Use 'un messaggio a [nome]' to mean 'a message for/to [name]'. In polite requests use 'per favore' or conditional forms (Daresti/ Potresti...).
target_language_example: Posso dare un messaggio a Maria?
native_language_example: Can I give/send a message to Maria?

meaning: “message to” (a message sent/directed to someone or something).
additional_notes: Used to indicate the recipient of a message or communication. 'Al' is the contraction of 'a' + 'il' (to the) and changes depending on the article: e.g., 'messaggio alla' (to the, feminine), 'messaggio ai' (to the, plural). Often appears with people (fidanzato, ragazzo) or institutions (Presidente, mondo).
target_language_example: Ho inviato un messaggio al professore dopo la lezione.
native_language_example: I sent a message to the professor after class.

meaning: a message for (someone); 'per' indicates the recipient
additional_notes: Used to say that a message is intended for a specific person or group. 'Messaggio' = message; 'per' = for. Commonly followed by a name or pronoun (es. per te, per voi, per Marco). Can be used for spoken or written messages.
target_language_example: Ho lasciato un messaggio per Maria.
native_language_example: I left a message for Maria.

meaning: a message for her / a message for you (formal).
additional_notes: Used to say someone left or has a message intended for a female person or when addressing someone formally (lei = formal 'you' or 'she' depending on context). In spoken Italian, context tells whether lei means 'her' (third person) or the formal 'you' (second person). You can replace 'lei' with 'te' (informal you) or a name/pronoun as needed.
target_language_example: Ho lasciato un messaggio per lei dall'ufficio.
native_language_example: I left a message for her/for you (formal) from the office.

meaning: 'the message is' — a way to describe or identify a message.
additional_notes: Used to state or ask about the characteristics, clarity, or intended recipient of a message. Commonly followed by adjectives (chiaro, semplice, molto chiaro) or prepositional phrases (per lui/te/loro/voi). Word order in Italian places the noun before the verb: 'Il messaggio è...'.
target_language_example: Il messaggio è per te.
native_language_example: The message is for you.

meaning: began to
additional_notes: Often appears as part of the reflexive verb mettersi a + infinitive (mi sono messo a guidare = I began to drive). Use 'messo a' to indicate the start of an action. In other contexts 'mettere a' can combine with nouns (mettere a disagio = to embarrass/make uncomfortable). When asking about duration, 'ci hai messo a ...?' means 'how long did it take you to ...?'.
target_language_example: Mi sono messo a studiare italiano ieri sera.
native_language_example: I started studying Italian last night.

meaning: put/placed to (used before a masculine singular noun or verb phrase: 'messo al' = 'put to' / 'placed at/on' / 'assigned to')
additional_notes: Compound of 'messo' (past participle of mettere = 'put') + preposition 'al' (a + il). Usually appears in passive or perfect constructions: e.g., 'È stato messo al sicuro' (He/It was put to safety), or in expressions like 'messo al lavoro' (put to work/assigned to work). The exact translation depends on context and the following noun/verb. Agreement: 'messo' can change to 'messa', 'messi', 'messe' to match gender/number.
target_language_example: Il nuovo stagista è stato messo al lavoro subito.
native_language_example: The new intern was put to work immediately.

meaning: put down (feminine object) / hung up (the phone) (feminine object).
additional_notes: Literal past participle of mettere (messo) + giù (down) + feminine direct article la. Used when the thing put down or the phone hung up is feminine: e.g. 'ho messo giù la borsa' (I put the bag down) or 'ha messo giù la chiamata' (she hung up the call). In speech you may also hear 'ha messo giù' without the article when context is clear. Verb tense and subject will change (ho messo giù, ha messo giù, abbiamo messo giù).
target_language_example: Ho messo giù la borsa prima di entrare in casa.
native_language_example: I put the bag down before going into the house.

meaning: put down her/his (something).
additional_notes: Literal phrase meaning someone placed an object on a surface. 'Messo giù' = 'put down' (past participle of mettere + giù). 'La sua' means 'his/her' (feminine singular object). Use gender/number agreement: la sua (fem. sing.), il suo (masc. sing.), le sue (fem. pl.), i suoi (masc. pl.). Common in simple past (passato prossimo) with avere: [Name] ha messo giù la sua [cosa].
target_language_example: Anna ha messo giù la sua borsa sul tavolo.
native_language_example: Anna put down her bag on the table.

meaning: put the
additional_notes: "messo" is the past participle of mettere, so this usually appears with forms of avere: ho messo, hai messo, ha messo, etc. It is used for putting or placing something somewhere: "Dove hai messo il libro?" It can also appear in expressions like "metterci il cuore" = "to put your heart into it."
target_language_example: Hai messo il latte in frigo?
native_language_example: Did you put the milk in the fridge?

meaning: placed/put (my) — used in questions like 'Where did you put my...?'
additional_notes: Messo is the past participle of mettere (to put). 'Messo il mio' appears in questions about where someone put the speaker's possession. You will usually see it with an object (cappello, portatile, ombrello, quaderno). In spoken Italian the subject and auxiliary vary (hai/ha/avete) depending on who did the action. For a female possession you may hear 'messa la mia' if the noun is feminine and you make agreement (rare with avere), but standard is to keep 'messo' and agree the article and noun: e.g. 'il mio quaderno', 'la mia borsa'.
target_language_example: Dove hai messo il mio telefono?
native_language_example: Where did you put my phone?

meaning: past participle of mettere (messo) + feminine definite article 'la' — 'placed/put the (feminine noun)'.
additional_notes: Used when describing that someone put or placed a specific feminine noun (la + noun). In Italian the past participle 'messo' combines with the auxiliary (avere/essere) to form past tenses; examples above show omission of the following noun (spoken/informal) or slight mistakes. Make sure the noun after 'la' is present (e.g., 'la macchina', 'la guida') or understood from context. Watch agreement: with direct object pronouns the participle doesn't change for gender when using 'avere' unless the pronoun precedes the verb.
target_language_example: Ho messo la giacca sull'attaccapanni.
native_language_example: I put the jacket on the coat rack.

meaning: placed/put (something of mine).
additional_notes: This is the past participle phrase using mettere (messo) + definite article + mia (my, feminine). It appears when talking about where you put a feminine noun you own (la guida, la borsa, la valigia). In spoken Italian word order often drops the subject pronoun (io/tu). For masculine nouns you'd say 'messo il mio' or for plural 'messi i miei / messe le mie'.
target_language_example: Ho messo la mia borsa sotto il tavolo.
native_language_example: I put my bag under the table.

meaning: put/placed a (masculine or general) — past participle construction: 'put a/one ...'
additional_notes: Combines the past participle 'messo' (from mettere = to put) with the indefinite article 'un'. Used in the passato prossimo or other compound tenses to say someone 'put/placed a ...' or more generally 'took (time) to ...' when used with 'ci ho messo' (I took...). Context determines the noun that follows. Note: agreement of 'messo' doesn't change for the object; it can be followed by masculine nouns (un libro, un francobollo) or used in idiomatic expressions (ci ho messo un anno = it took me a year).
target_language_example: Ho messo un cappotto prima di uscire.
native_language_example: I put on a coat before going out.

meaning: 'puts/starts (to)'.
additional_notes: Commonly appears as part of verbs with 'a' + infinitive to mean 'begins to (do something)' (si mette a + infinitive = 'he/she/it starts to...'). It can also mean 'puts (someone) into a state' when followed by a noun (mettere a disagio = 'to make [someone] uncomfortable', mettere a tacere = 'to silence [someone]'). Subject and reflexive pronouns change the meaning: 'mi mette a disagio' = 'it makes me uncomfortable'; 'si mette a lavorare' = 'he/she starts to work'.
target_language_example: Si mette a leggere non appena arriva a casa.
native_language_example: He/she starts to read as soon as he/she gets home.

meaning: to do one's best; to try very hard
additional_notes: Literally 'to put it all there'. Common in spoken Italian to say someone gives maximum effort. Often appears in conjugated/clitic forms (e.g., "Ce l'ho messa tutta", "Ce la metterò tutta"). Can be used in various tenses and persons.
target_language_example: Ho deciso di mettercela tutta per superare l'esame.
native_language_example: I decided to do my best to pass the exam.

meaning: to put in a good word for someone; to recommend or speak positively about someone to help them
additional_notes: Used when you ask someone to briefly recommend or praise another person to improve their chances (for a job, favor, etc.). Often preceded by a pronoun/subject: 'Mi puoi metterci una buona parola?' or 'Gli ha messa una buona parola.' The phrase is idiomatic — the literal parts (mettere = put, una buona parola = a good word) do match the figurative meaning.
target_language_example: Puoi metterci una buona parola con il direttore per il mio colloquio?
native_language_example: Can you put in a good word for me with the manager for my interview?

meaning: to put (someone or something) to sleep; to lay down to sleep (literally) — can also mean to euthanize an animal in sensitive contexts
additional_notes: Commonly used for putting a child, baby, or pet to bed (e.g., mettere il bambino a dormire). In informal or euphemistic contexts, especially about animals, it can mean to have them euthanized. Use context to judge meaning. Usually follows pattern: mettere + (object) + a dormire.
target_language_example: Devo mettere a dormire il bambino prima di uscire.
native_language_example: I need to put the baby to sleep before going out.

meaning: to put (someone) to bed; to lay down (a child, patient) to sleep or rest.
additional_notes: Commonly used when talking about putting children or people who need care into bed. Can imply helping someone get ready for sleep (changing clothes, tucking in). With reflexive pronoun 'mettersi a letto' it means 'to go to bed' (oneself).
target_language_example: Devo mettere a letto il bambino entro le otto.
native_language_example: I have to put the child to bed by eight.

meaning: to knock down/knock out; to overwhelm or defeat someone completely
additional_notes: Literal image: 'put (someone) on the mat' (boxing/wrestling). Used both for physical knockout (sports, fights) and figurative defeat (arguments, competition, exhausting someone). Often followed by a direct object (mettere qualcuno al tappeto).
target_language_example: Il pugile avversario lo ha messo al tappeto nel secondo round.
native_language_example: The opposing boxer knocked him out in the second round.

meaning: to test; to put to the test; to try someone or something
additional_notes: Used to indicate checking reliability, skill, courage, or the truth of an idea. Can be used with hypotheses (mettere alla prova un'ipotesi), people (mettere alla prova qualcuno), or one's own abilities (mettere alla prova il proprio coraggio). Often implies a deliberate challenge or experiment.
target_language_example: Voglio mettere alla prova le tue capacità prima di assumerti.
native_language_example: I want to test your skills before hiring you.

meaning: 'to put an end to' or 'to end' (something)
additional_notes: A common phrasal verb used with a direct object: mettere fine a + noun (e.g., mettere fine a una relazione). It can be used for relationships, conflicts, situations, habits, etc. More formal than casual verbs like 'finire' in some contexts. Often followed by 'a' before the thing being ended.
target_language_example: Ha deciso di mettere fine alla relazione.
native_language_example: He decided to put an end to the relationship.

meaning: to put an end to this behavior / to stop this behavior.
additional_notes: A common phrase used to tell someone (or say about someone) that they need to stop a particular behavior. 'Mettere fine a' = 'to bring to an end' and is followed by the thing to end. Polite or neutral; can be used in commands or statements. Conjugate 'mettere' as needed (devo/ devi/ deve/ dobbiamo/ dovete/ devono) and change 'questo/questa' for gender/number if required.
target_language_example: Devi mettere fine a questo comportamento subito.
native_language_example: You must put an end to this behavior immediately.

meaning: to put down; to hang up (the phone); to write down; to dismiss or belittle (context-dependent).
additional_notes: Literal meaning: 'to put/place down.' Common uses: mettere giù il telefono = to hang up the phone; mettere giù qualcosa = to put something down physically; mettere giù per/ mettere giù su carta = to write down (informal). In spoken Italian it can also mean to dismiss, belittle, or speak down to someone (mettere qualcuno giù). Context and reflexive/active construction determine the nuance.
target_language_example: Ho deciso di mettere giù il telefono prima che la conversazione degenerasse.
native_language_example: I decided to hang up the phone before the conversation degenerated.

meaning: to put/place my (singular masculine noun).
additional_notes: Used when asking where to place or put something you own. 'Mio' agrees in gender/number with the noun (mio, mia, miei, mie). Common in questions: 'Dove devo mettere il mio ...?' or with polite forms 'Mi può dire dove mettere il mio ...?'.
target_language_example: Puoi dirmi dove mettere il mio telefono?
native_language_example: Can you tell me where to put my phone?

meaning: to make clear; to clarify or explain something so it's understood
additional_notes: Used when clarifying information, correcting misunderstandings, or making details explicit. Common in both spoken and written Italian. Often followed by a clause or the thing being clarified (e.g., mettere in chiaro i fatti / mettere in chiaro che...).
target_language_example: Voglio mettere in chiaro che non ero presente quel giorno.
native_language_example: I want to make it clear that I wasn't there that day.

meaning: to bring (someone or something) to its knees; to severely weaken or cripple
additional_notes: Used figuratively to describe causing great damage, hardship, or loss of strength/power (e.g., an economy, a company, a person). Can also be literal (to force someone to kneel), but most common use is figurative. Often followed by the thing being affected (mettere [qualcosa/qualcuno] in ginocchio).
target_language_example: La crisi è riuscita a mettere in ginocchio molte piccole imprese.
native_language_example: The crisis managed to bring many small businesses to their knees.

meaning: to start (an engine or a process); to set in motion
additional_notes: Commonly used for starting a vehicle or machine (literally 'to put in motion') and also used figuratively for beginning a process or project (e.g., 'mettere in moto una serie di eventi').
target_language_example: Ho deciso di mettere in moto il progetto questa settimana.
native_language_example: I decided to set the project in motion this week.

meaning: to put together; to assemble; to piece together; also: to organize or form (e.g., a group, a plan, a budget).
additional_notes: A versatile phrasal verb. Literally 'to put together'. Use for assembling physical objects (mettere insieme un mobile), compiling or organizing things (mettere insieme un dossier), or forming/bringing together people/resources (mettere insieme una squadra, mettere insieme i soldi). Context determines nuance: can mean 'to manage to get' in informal contexts (e.g., riuscire a mettere insieme i soldi).
target_language_example: Devo mettere insieme tutti i documenti per la riunione.
native_language_example: I need to put together all the documents for the meeting.

meaning: to get involved with, handle, tamper with, or take control of something (literally 'to put one's hands on').
additional_notes: Used in several senses depending on context: neutral (to handle or take care of something), informal (to meddle or tamper with), or idiomatic (to get one's hands on something = obtain or take control). Often followed by su/nei/in/di + noun (e.g. mettere le mani su qualcosa = get hold of something; non mettere le mani = don't touch). Tone depends on verbs and context.
target_language_example: Non mettere le mani sulla mia scrivania senza chiedere.
native_language_example: Don't put your hands on my desk without asking.

meaning: to lay hands on someone; to physically assault or grab someone
additional_notes: Used to describe physically touching someone in an aggressive or unwanted way (e.g., hitting, grabbing, assault). Often appears in negative contexts: non mettere le mani addosso (don't touch/assault). Not used for neutral, casual touching.
target_language_example: Se torna a minacciarti, non esitare a chiamare la polizia: non puoi permettergli di mettere le mani addosso.
native_language_example: If he threatens you again, don't hesitate to call the police: you can't let him lay hands on you.

meaning: to get involved in, to start fixing or handling something; to edit or tamper with (literally 'to put a hand on').
additional_notes: Common idiom used when someone begins to work on, repair, change, or interfere with something. Context determines tone: neutral when meaning 'start working on' (e.g., mettere mano a un progetto), cautionary when meaning 'tamper with' (e.g., non mettere mano ai documenti). Often followed by a noun introduced by a or su (mettere mano a qualcosa / mettere mano su qualcosa).
target_language_example: Devo mettere mano al vecchio programma per correggere i bug.
native_language_example: I need to get to work on the old program to fix the bugs.

meaning: to set foot (in/on); to go into or visit a place (often with a negative: non mettere piede = never set foot in); can also mean to get involved in something (figurative).
additional_notes: Literally 'to put foot'. Commonly used with a location (mettere piede in/nel/alla) or in negative forms (non mettere mai piede / non mettere piede). Can be used both literally (entering a place) and figuratively (entering a field, getting involved). Conjugates as a verbal phrase (mettere piede, ho messo piede, mettere piede).
target_language_example: Non voglio mettere piede in quel negozio dopo l'incidente.
native_language_example: I don't want to set foot in that shop after the incident.

meaning: to put (something) under; to place beneath; can also mean to subject someone/something to (pressure, control, tests)
additional_notes: Literal meaning is 'to put under' (mettere = to put, sotto = under). Used with a direct object (mettere qualcosa sotto). Can be used literally (mettere sotto il tavolo) or figuratively (mettere sotto pressione = to put under pressure; mettere sotto controllo = to bring under control). Conjugate mettere normally; 'sotto' remains after the verb or sometimes after the object. Word order examples: 'mettere sotto qualcosa' or 'mettere qualcosa sotto'.
target_language_example: Devo mettere sotto il vaso prima che cada.
native_language_example: I need to put the flowerpot under (something) before it falls.

meaning: 'to put on', 'to start/turn on', or 'to set up' depending on context
additional_notes: A versatile phrasal verb. Common uses: mettere su (la radio/playlist) = to play or turn on; mettere su (un'attività/una cena) = to prepare or arrange; mettere su (qualche chilo) = to gain weight. Context determines the nuance.
target_language_example: Posso mettere su la musica mentre cucino?
native_language_example: Can I put on the music while I cook?

meaning: to gain weight (lit. 'to put on weight').
additional_notes: Common informal phrase used to say someone has gained body weight. Often used with subjects (e.g., 'Ho messo su peso' = 'I've put on weight'). Can be used in various tenses: mettere su peso / avere messo su peso / sto mettendo su peso. Similar to ‘ingrassare’ (more neutral).
target_language_example: Ultimamente sto cercando di non mettere su peso dopo le vacanze.
native_language_example: Lately I'm trying not to put on weight after the holidays.

meaning: to put away; to save (money or things).
additional_notes: Common phrasal verb: means physically putting something in its place (put away) or saving money for later. Context determines whether it's about objects or savings. Often used in present forms: metto via, metti via, mette via; past participle: messo via.
target_language_example: Devo mettere via questi libri prima di uscire.
native_language_example: I need to put these books away before going out.

meaning: to get me into (trouble); to cause me problems or trouble.
additional_notes: Literally 'to put me in...' — usually completed with 'guai' (trouble). Contains the object pronoun 'mi' (me) and is commonly used to express fear or accusation that someone's actions will cause trouble, blame, or consequences. Pronouns can be changed (metterti, metterlo, metterla, metterci, etc.). Informal to neutral register depending on context.
target_language_example: Lo sai che potresti davvero mettermi nei guai?
native_language_example: You know you could really get me into trouble?

meaning: to make oneself comfortable; to sit/settle in comfortably.
additional_notes: Used when inviting someone to relax or when describing that you are taking a comfortable position (e.g., sitting down, getting cozy). Often used reflexively with mettersi + adjective (comodo). Can be used literally (sit down and relax) or slightly figuratively (get ready to spend time doing something). Common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Appena arrivato, si è messo comodo sul divano e ha acceso la TV.
native_language_example: As soon as he arrived, he made himself comfortable on the couch and turned on the TV.

meaning: to turn out badly; to get into a bad situation
additional_notes: Informal phrase used to describe a situation that is deteriorating or likely to have negative consequences (e.g., relationships, plans, health, finances). Often used impersonally with 'si' (si mette/si sono messe) or with a person (mi/ti/ci si mette). Common tenses: 'si mette male' (it's getting bad), 'si è messo/a male' (it turned out badly).
target_language_example: Se non paghi le bollette, la situazione si mette male.
native_language_example: If you don't pay the bills, the situation turns bad.

meaning: imperative 'put' (you) + definite article 'the' for plural masculine nouns (e.g. 'put the...').
additional_notes: Metti is the informal imperative (tu) of mettere (to put). 'I' is the plural masculine definite article (the). Together they appear before plural masculine nouns: 'metti i piedi' = 'watch where you put your feet' or literally 'put the feet'. Used for commands or instructions. For polite/formal commands use 'metta' (Lei). Word order: metti + i + noun.
target_language_example: Metti i piatti nella credenza, per favore.
native_language_example: Put the plates in the cupboard, please.

meaning: in the middle of / among (followed by a masculine singular noun)
additional_notes: A colloquial contraction of 'in mezzo al' used before a masculine singular noun (al = a + il). It indicates location 'in the middle of' or 'among' something (e.g., in mezzo al deserto = in the middle of the desert). Can be used literally (physical location) or figuratively. If the noun is feminine, use 'in mezzo alla'. For plural use 'in mezzo ai'/'in mezzo alle'.
target_language_example: L'ho trovato in mezzo al parco.
native_language_example: I found it in the middle of the park.

meaning: in the middle of / among (followed by a plural feminine noun introduced by 'le').
additional_notes: Used to say something is located or happening amid/among other things or people. 'Mezzo' here means 'in the middle' or 'amidst'. It commonly appears as 'in mezzo alle' + plural feminine noun (e.g., foglie, sedie, grida). You can also see 'in mezzo ai' (before plural masculine nouns) or 'in mezzo al' (singular masculine).
target_language_example: La chiave è in mezzo alle piante sul balcone.
native_language_example: The key is among the plants on the balcony.

meaning: in the middle of / in the midst of
additional_notes: Used to indicate being in the center or middle of a place, event, or situation (literal or figurative). Commonly appears in the fixed phrase "nel mezzo di" or "nel mezzo del/ della/ dei"; in casual speech you also hear "nel mezzo del nulla" (in the middle of nowhere) or "nel mezzo del concerto" (in the middle of the concert).
target_language_example: Siamo rimasti bloccati nel mezzo del bosco.
native_language_example: We got stuck in the middle of the woods.

meaning: literally 'middle/means of the' or 'half of the' depending on context; often part of phrases like 'a mezzo della strada' (in the middle of the street) or 'mezzo della popolazione' (half of the population).
additional_notes: mezzo can mean 'middle', 'half', 'means' or 'medium'. When followed by the definite article della (di + la), it links to a feminine singular noun: 'mezzo della casa' (middle of the house) or 'mezzo della popolazione' (half of the population). Context determines whether it means 'middle of' (position) or 'half of' (portion). Use 'del' for masculine nouns (mezzo del), 'dei/degli/delle' for plurals as needed.
target_language_example: La sedia è al mezzo della stanza.
native_language_example: The chair is in the middle of the room.

meaning: 'loves me only' or 'only loves me' (implying for one reason only).
