additional_notes: Used to question or state that someone's love is based solely on a single reason (e.g., appearance, nationality). Often appears in questions: 'Mi ama solo perché...?' = 'Does he/she love me only because...?' Emphasizes exclusivity or doubt about sincerity.
target_language_example: Mi ama solo perché sono diverso?
native_language_example: Does he/she love me only because I'm different?

meaning: 'you love me only' / 'you only love me'
additional_notes: Used to accuse or question someone about the sole reason they love or like the speaker. Often followed by a reason introduced with perché (because...). Voi/tu forms depend on number/formality: 'mi amate' = you (plural) love me; 'mi ami solo' would be singular informal. 'Solo' here means 'only' (not 'just' in the sense of 'a moment ago').
target_language_example: Mi amate solo perché parlo la vostra lingua?
native_language_example: You only love me because I speak your language?

meaning: my name is
additional_notes: Used to say your name when introducing yourself. It comes from the reflexive verb chiamarsi, so it literally works like "I call myself," but in natural English it is usually "my name is." It's normally followed by a name: mi chiamo Luca.
target_language_example: Ciao, mi chiamo Sara.
native_language_example: Hi, my name is Sara.

meaning: 'I bought myself' (past, passato remoto — 'I bought' / 'I purchased' for myself)
additional_notes: Reflexive use of comprare (comprare → comprarsi) meaning to buy something for oneself. 'Mi comprai' is the passato remoto (simple past) first-person singular, used more in written Italian and in some spoken varieties (especially in the north/center/southern storytelling). In everyday spoken Italian many speakers prefer passato prossimo ('mi sono comprato/a'). The gender of the speaker affects agreement in passato prossimo but not in passato remoto here (mi comprai stays the same).
target_language_example: Mi comprai un paio di scarpe nuove per l'estate.
native_language_example: I bought myself a new pair of shoes for the summer.

meaning: ‘(he/she) told me that (he/she) ...’ — introduces reported speech about someone’s state or actions.
additional_notes: Common in reported speech. mi disse = '(someone) told me' (past). che introduces the reported clause. si is a reflexive/third-person pronoun used with verbs like sentirsi, divertirsi, stare (si sentiva = he/she felt). The subject of si is the person being reported (he/she). In English you usually render the sequence as 'told me that he/she ...' Adjust verb tense when translating (imperfetto: si sentiva = was feeling/felt).
target_language_example: Luisa mi disse che si sentiva stanca dopo il viaggio.
native_language_example: Luisa told me that she felt tired after the trip.

meaning: 'never told me' (used to say someone did not tell the speaker something)
additional_notes: Comprised of the indirect object pronoun mi (to me), passato remoto/pretérito-like form disse (he/she told) and mai (never). In everyday spoken Italian, passato prossimo (non mi ha mai detto) or imperfect/past constructions (non mi disse mai) are more common depending on region and formality. Use non before the verb for negation: non mi disse mai = he/she never told me. Can be followed by a clause introduced by che (that) or by a direct object (una parola).
target_language_example: Marco non mi disse mai la verità.
native_language_example: Marco never told me the truth.

meaning: tell me
additional_notes: Literally means "you tell to me." Used with voi (you plural) to ask for information or an opinion: Mi dite... ? = "can you tell me...?" / "tell me..." In statements, it can also mean "you tell me," as in fare come mi dite = "do as you tell me."
target_language_example: Mi dite dove possiamo mangiare bene qui vicino?
native_language_example: Can you tell me where we can eat well nearby?

meaning: it/he/she/they have changed me / it changed for me
additional_notes: Literally 'has changed me' (mi = to/for me; ha cambiato = has changed). Context determines if it means someone/something changed the speaker (e.g., 'He changed me' meaning altered me as a person) or if it means something was exchanged/changed for the speaker (e.g., 'He changed it for me' or 'He replaced it for me'). To be clearer, Italians often add an object or context: 'mi ha cambiato la vita' (changed my life) or 'mi ha cambiato la gomma' (he changed my tire).
target_language_example: Quella esperienza mi ha cambiato la vita.
native_language_example: That experience has changed my life.

meaning: ‘(someone) told me that he/she/they…’ — introduces reported speech with a reflexive or pronominal verb.
additional_notes: Used to report what someone told the speaker. mi ha detto = ‘(he/she) told me’. che introduces the content. si is a reflexive/impersonal pronoun attached to the verb that follows (e.g. si era sbagliata, si sentiva, si stava divertendo). English equivalent often uses 'that' plus a reflexive sense (he/she had mistaken herself / felt better / was enjoying himself/herself). Pay attention to agreement and gender in the following verb's past participle or adjective (e.g. si era sbagliata — feminine).
target_language_example: Marco mi ha detto che si sentiva stanco.
native_language_example: Marco told me that he felt tired.

meaning: ‘(he/she/you formal) ever told me that…’ — used to ask or state whether someone has at any time told you something
additional_notes: Literal parts: mi = to me, ha detto = has said/told, mai = ever/never, che = that. Used in questions (e.g., “Mi ha mai detto che…?”) to ask if someone has ever told you something; can also appear in negative contexts with 'non' (e.g., “Non mi ha mai detto che…”) meaning 'has never told me that…'. The subject is third person singular (lui/lei/Lei). For first/second person subjects, the auxiliary changes (mi hai mai detto che, mi hai mai detto che).
target_language_example: Mi ha mai detto che arriva più tardi?
native_language_example: Has he/she ever told me that he/she is arriving later?

meaning: he/she showed me the (masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: Literal: 'mi' = to me, 'ha mostrato' = has shown / showed (passato prossimo), 'il' = the (masculine singular). Used to say someone showed you a specific masculine thing (album, giardino, telefono). Change 'il' to other articles as needed (la, l', i, gli, le) depending on the noun. Common in spoken and written Italian.
target_language_example: Luca mi ha mostrato il suo libro ieri.
native_language_example: Luca showed me his book yesterday.

meaning: 'has ... me anymore' or 'no longer ... me' (part of a negative perfect construction meaning someone stopped doing something to me).
additional_notes: Usually appears in negative sentences with 'non' before it: 'non mi ha più ...' = 'he/she hasn't ... me anymore' or 'he/she no longer ... me'. Common with verbs like 'rivolgere la parola' (speak), 'dire' (tell), 'lasciare' (let). Literally 'has more to me' but functions idiomatically to express 'anymore' or 'no longer' in the present perfect (passato prossimo).
target_language_example: Da quel giorno non mi ha più chiamato.
native_language_example: Since that day he hasn't called me anymore.

mi ha raccomandato di leggere questi libri

target_language_multi_word_term: mi ha raccomandato di leggere questi libri
meaning: He/she recommended that I read these books.
additional_notes: A complete sentence: 'mi ha raccomandato' = 'he/she recommended to me' (past tense), followed by an infinitive clause 'di leggere questi libri' = 'to read these books'. Common way to report someone’s advice or recommendation. Can be adjusted for person/tense (mi raccomanda di..., mi ha raccomandato di..., mi raccomanderebbe di...).
target_language_example: Il professore mi ha raccomandato di leggere questi libri prima dell'esame.
native_language_example: The professor recommended that I read these books before the exam.

meaning: literally 'it saved my ...' — used to say something/somebody saved me from trouble or helped me out (often followed by a noun).
additional_notes: This phrase is the start of a sentence: 'mi ha salvato la ...' (e.g. 'mi ha salvato la vita' = 'saved my life'). It's common to use with nouns like 'vita' (life), 'giornata' (day), 'serata' (evening), or 'situazione'. The grammatical structure: mi (to me) + ha salvato (has saved) + la + noun. In spoken Italian you may hear shortened or emphatic forms (e.g. 'mi ha salvato, la verità è che...').
target_language_example: Quella telefonata mi ha salvato la giornata.
native_language_example: That phone call saved my day.

meaning: 'they have ever/never (to me)'; used in negative sentences to mean 'they have never (told/done) me'.
additional_notes: This phrase combines the indirect object pronoun mi (to/for me), the auxiliary verb hanno (they have), and the adverb mai (ever/never). In Italian, mai usually means 'ever' in questions and 'never' in negatives when paired with non or another negative word. Most natural use is with non: "Non mi hanno mai..." = "They never... me" (e.g. told me, shown me, made me pay). In affirmative questions it can mean 'have they ever... me?'. Word order can vary, but the typical beginner pattern is 'Non mi hanno mai + past participle'.
target_language_example: Non mi hanno mai detto la verità.
native_language_example: They have never told me the truth.

meaning: they never told me that / they've never told me that
additional_notes: A common phrase used to report that someone has never informed the speaker about something. Structure: mi (to me) + hanno (they have) + mai (ever/never in negative context) + detto (told) + che (that) + [clause]. In English we often say "they never told me that...". Can be used for past states or actions (perfect/imperfect context) depending on the following clause.
target_language_example: Non mi hanno mai detto che parlavi italiano.
native_language_example: They never told me that you spoke Italian.

meaning: I miss you
additional_notes: Common way to say 'I miss you' in Italian. Literally 'you are missing to me' (the person who is missed is the subject in Italian: 'tu mi manchi' = 'you miss me' literally). Used for expressing emotional longing; can be emphatic (Oh, come mi manchi!) or simple (Semplicemente mi manchi).
target_language_example: Mi manchi molto quando non ci sei.
native_language_example: I miss you a lot when you're not here.

meaning: 'he/she/it put (on/onto) me' or 'he/she/it placed me' (past, literary/formal past tense)
additional_notes: Literal meaning is 'put me' or 'placed me.' Common uses: physically placing something on or near the speaker (e.g., 'mi mise un cerotto' = 'he/she put a plaster on me') or placing the speaker in a situation (e.g., 'mi mise in una situazione delicata'). 'Mi mise' is the third-person singular passato remoto of mettere + the indirect object pronoun mi. In spoken contemporary Italian, the passato prossimo ('mi ha messo') is more common; passato remoto appears in written narratives, formal speech, or regional uses.
target_language_example: Mi mise una giacca addosso perché avevo freddo.
native_language_example: He/she put a jacket on me because I was cold.

meaning: he/she/it speaks to me; he/she/it talks to me.
additional_notes: mi = 'to me' (indirect object pronoun). Parla is the third-person singular present of parlare (to speak/talk). Used for someone speaking to the speaker (Tom mi parla = Tom talks to me). Can also be used with non-human subjects (Dio non mi parla = God doesn't speak to me) or to introduce what someone says (Poi mi parla del peccato = Then he talks to me about sin). Context determines whether it's literal (speaks to me) or figurative (addresses me, mentions me).
target_language_example: Luisa mi parla spesso dei suoi viaggi.
native_language_example: Luisa often talks to me about her travels.

meaning: 'I like ... about (someone/something)' — used to specify a particular quality or aspect you like.
additional_notes: This structure is less common and somewhat formal; speakers more often say "mi piace" alone (I like) or use "mi piace di..." to introduce a specific trait (e.g. "Mi piace di lei la gentilezza" = "What I like about her is her kindness"). Often replaced by "quello che mi piace di..." or "mi piace in..." in everyday speech. Follow with a noun phrase indicating the aspect.
target_language_example: Mi piace di lui la pazienza quando parla con i bambini.
native_language_example: What I like about him is his patience when he talks with children.

meaning: I like to play (a sport or game).
additional_notes: Use before the name of a sport or game introduced with the preposition 'a' (e.g., a calcio, a tennis, a carte). 'Mi piace' expresses liking; 'giocare a' means 'to play' (used with many sports/games). For some sports Italian omits 'a' (e.g., giocare a calcio often used, but giocare a pallacanestro or giocare a calcio are common; with instruments or activities different verbs may be used).
target_language_example: Mi piace giocare a basket con gli amici il sabato.
native_language_example: I like to play basketball with friends on Saturdays.

meaning: I like the way (in which)... / I like how...
additional_notes: This phrase begins a comment about how something is done or the manner of something. In Italian you'd normally complete it with a verb or clause: e.g. "mi piace il modo in cui lavori" (I like the way you work) or "mi piace il modo in cui è scritto il libro". You can also use the shorter "mi piace il modo in cui" or simply "mi piace come" for the same idea. "Mi piace il modo in" by itself is incomplete and needs the rest of the clause.
target_language_example: Mi piace il modo in cui spieghi le cose.
native_language_example: I like the way you explain things.

meaning: i like you
additional_notes: Literally, this is more like 'you please me': Italian uses piacere differently from English. With a person, it can mean simple personal liking or romantic/physical attraction, depending on context.
target_language_example: Mi piaci molto, ma sono troppo timido per dirtelo.
native_language_example: I really like you, but I'm too shy to tell you.

meaning: 'are you making fun of me?' / 'are you kidding me?' (literally: 'are you taking me for the ass')
additional_notes: Informal and vulgar. Used when someone thinks another person is mocking, deceiving, or not taking them seriously. Can be a question (surprise/anger) or a statement (I'm being made fun of). Avoid in polite/formal situations.
target_language_example: Ma davvero pensi che non lo sapessi? Mi prendi per il culo?
native_language_example: Do you really think I didn't know? Are you kidding me / Are you making fun of me?

meaning: he/she lent me the ... (past tense).
additional_notes: mi = to me; prestò = third-person singular passato remoto or passato prossimo form of prestare (here: 'lent'); il = definite article 'the' before a masculine singular noun. Commonly used to say someone lent something to you in the past: e.g. 'Mary mi prestò il suo computer' = 'Mary lent me her computer.' In spoken Italian past tense often appears as passato prossimo ('mi ha prestato il...') instead of passato remoto in many regions.
target_language_example: Luca mi prestò il libro quando ero in vacanza.
native_language_example: Luca lent me the book when I was on holiday.

meaning: I think / it seems to me / I guess
additional_notes: Common informal expression used to give an opinion or guess based on impression or likelihood. Often followed by 'che' + clause (Mi sa che...) or by a short answer (Mi sa di no). Equivalent to 'I suppose' or 'it looks like'. Tone ranges from neutral to conversational.
target_language_example: Mi sa che pioverà stasera.
native_language_example: I think it will rain tonight.

meaning: excuse me
additional_notes: Formal/polite form used to get someone's attention, apologize, or ask for forgiveness. Used with strangers, elders, or in polite situations. It literally means 'excuse me' (literally 'excuse me' or 'forgive me') and is the formal version; the informal equivalent is 'scusa' (to one person) or 'scusami'. Can be used before a brief interruption ('Mi scusi un secondo') or to apologize for a nuisance ('Mi scusi per il disturbo').
target_language_example: Mi scusi, può ripetere per favore?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can you repeat that please?

meaning: to me, you are
additional_notes: `mi` means "to me" and `sei` means "you are" or works as the auxiliary "you have." In expressions like `mi sei mancato` and `mi sei piaciuto`, Italian is structured differently from English: `mi sei mancato` means "I missed you," and `non mi sei mai piaciuto` means "I never liked you." The participle changes to match the person spoken to: `mancato/piaciuto` for a man, `mancata/piaciuta` for a woman.
target_language_example: Mi sei mancato durante il viaggio.
native_language_example: I missed you during the trip.

meaning: first-person singular reflexive + present subjunctive of 'essere' or auxiliary in compound subjunctive ("that I have/been"; used in phrases like "that I have" or "that has happened to me").
additional_notes: Appears in subordinate clauses with the subjunctive (e.g. 'che mi sia ...'). 'Mi' is the reflexive or indirect object pronoun meaning 'to me' / 'myself'. 'Sia' is the present subjunctive of 'essere' and is used as an auxiliary in compound subjunctive forms (e.g. 'mi sia successo', 'mi sia sembrato') or in expressions of doubt, emotion, or judgment. Common in phrases: 'che mi sia laureato' (that I graduated), 'cosa mi sia preso' (what has come over me), 'mi sia sbagliato' (I was wrong). Translate according to context: often 'that I have' / 'that I am' / 'that happened to me'.
target_language_example: Non so cosa mi sia successo ieri sera.
native_language_example: I don't know what happened to me last night.

meaning: 'have I ever worried about' (used in questions or rhetorical statements).
additional_notes: This is the first-person singular perfect tense of preoccuparsi (mi sono preoccupato/a) with 'mai' (ever) and the preposition 'per' introducing the object of worry. Use 'mi sono mai preoccupato per...' to ask if you have ever been worried about something (often rhetorical). Adjust gender: 'preoccupato' for masculine speaker, 'preoccupata' for feminine. In spoken Italian 'mai' can also convey 'ever' in negative or surprised questions. For present-tense questions use 'mi sono mai preoccupato/a...?' or for general 'mi preoccupo mai...' (less common).
target_language_example: Mi sono mai preoccupato per le piccole cose? No, penso di no.
native_language_example: Have I ever worried about the small things? No, I don't think so.

meaning: 'finds me' / 'do you find me' (literal) — used to say where someone can find you, to ask whether someone finds you attractive, or to indicate that something (a machine, system, or danger) detects or locates you.
additional_notes: Literally 'mi' (me) + 'trova' (he/she/it finds). Common uses: (1) telling where someone can be reached: 'Mi trova qui' or 'Mi trova al caffè' (you can find me here/at the café); (2) asking about perception or attraction: 'Mi trova attraente?' (Do you find me attractive?); (3) indicating detection by systems or threats: 'Tangerine mi trova' (Tangerine finds/detects me). Context and intonation determine meaning. Not an idiom; grammatical and compositional.
target_language_example: Mi trova qui.
native_language_example: You can find me here.

meaning: he/she/it sees me; (formal) you see me
additional_notes: Present tense of vedere with the indirect object pronoun mi (me). In spoken Italian, context determines the subject: può essere 'lui/lei' (he/she/it sees me) or the formal 'Lei' (do you see me?). Common in questions ('Mi vede?') to check if someone (or a camera) can see you, or in exclamations ('Ma qui non mi vede nessuno!') meaning 'nobody sees me here.'
target_language_example: Scusi, mi vede se accendo la videocamera?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can you see me if I turn on the webcam?

meaning: '(that) something happen to me' / '(that) someone come to me' depending on context; often used in exclamations or commands with subjunctive
additional_notes: Two common uses here: 1) Exclamatory idiom with Che mi venga un colpo! meaning 'May I drop dead!' or more softly 'What a shock!' (literally 'that a blow come to me') — expresses surprise or alarm. 2) Imperative/subjunctive use with verbs of motion + mi venga a + infinitive (e.g. non mi venga a dire / non mi venga a salvare) meaning 'don't you come and tell me' or 'don't come to save me' — used to tell someone not to do/say something. The verb venga is the third-person singular present subjunctive of venire. Tone can be strong; common in spoken Italian.
target_language_example: Non mi venga a dire che non puoi venire al lavoro.
native_language_example: Don't you come and tell me that you can't come to work.

meaning: they want me / they like me / they need me (depending on context)
additional_notes: Literal verb 'volere' (to want) in 3rd-person plural + object pronoun 'mi' (me). Can mean 'they want me' (desire), 'they want me on the team' (to have someone), or in negative contexts 'they don't want me' (they reject me). Tone and meaning depend on context (e.g., professional, social, or emotional). Common in spoken Italian.
target_language_example: Mi vogliono nella loro squadra di calcio.
native_language_example: They want me on their soccer team.

meaning: wanted me to
additional_notes: Commonly used to report someone else's desire about the speaker. 'Mi' is the indirect/object pronoun 'me'; 'voleva' is the imperfect of 'volere' (wanted). In reported speech it often corresponds to English 'he/she wanted me to...' or 'he/she wanted to...me' (e.g. 'mi voleva sposare' = 'he wanted to marry me'). Can imply an ongoing or past desire. Word order in Italian places the pronoun before the verb ('mi voleva'), unlike the English infinitive construction.
target_language_example: Luca mi voleva chiamare ieri ma non ce l'ha fatta.
native_language_example: Luca wanted to call me yesterday but couldn't.

meaning: literally 'to me ever' — used with past participles to mean 'I have never (done/experienced/liked) ...'.
additional_notes: Common in negative sentences: 'Non mi è mai + past participle' = 'I have never ...' or 'It has never happened to me...'. 'Mi' is the indirect object ('to me'), 'è' is the present form of 'essere' used in compound tenses for intransitive verbs or states, and 'mai' means 'ever/never' (with negation). In English learners' terms: treat 'Non mi è mai + past participle' as a fixed pattern meaning 'I have never + past participle' or 'It has never happened to me that...'.
target_language_example: Non mi è mai passato per la testa di trasferirmi all'estero.
native_language_example: It never occurred to me to move abroad.

meaning: my (female) friend has (done something to/for me)
additional_notes: Literal parts: 'mia amica' = my (female) friend; 'mi' = to/for me (indirect object) or me (direct object in some constructions); 'ha' = has (third-person singular of avere). Together they begin a past-tense (passato prossimo) clause: 'mia amica mi ha + past participle' = 'my friend has [verb] me/to me' (e.g. helped me, sent me). Agreement of the past participle depends on the object: with direct-object 'mi' (female speaker) the participle can agree (aiutata vs aiutato) in spoken/written Italian when the object precedes the verb; in many contexts non-agreement (aiutato) is also heard. 'Una mia amica' means 'a friend of mine'.
target_language_example: La mia amica mi ha mandato un messaggio.
native_language_example: My friend sent me a message.

meaning: my authority; my right or power to give orders, make decisions, or be obeyed.
additional_notes: Used to refer to someone's authority or power in a context (e.g., parental, managerial, official). Common in questions like "Stai/State sfidando la mia autorità?" meaning "Are you challenging my authority?" Can be used formally or informally depending on context. "Autorità" is feminine; possessive agrees with the possessor (mia = my).
target_language_example: Non metterti contro la mia autorità.
native_language_example: Don't go against my authority.

meaning: my bicycle / my bike.
additional_notes: Possessive phrase: mia is the feminine singular possessive adjective matching bicicletta (feminine noun). Use mia bicicletta for 'my bike' (when referring to one bike). In spoken Italian you can drop the noun if context is clear: 'È la mia.' Also common in everyday contexts (repair, theft, lending).
target_language_example: Posso prendere la mia bicicletta e venire con voi?
native_language_example: Can I take my bicycle and come with you?

meaning: my beer (literally), used to indicate a beer that belongs to or is for the speaker
additional_notes: Literal possession: 'mia' = my, 'birra' = beer. Used both literally (the beer I bought/ordered) and idiomatically in casual contexts (e.g., 'Tieni la mia birra' can mean 'Hold my beer' as in 'let me do this' or simply 'take my beer'). Adjust formality and verb (tieni/tenga) depending on tu/Lei. Plural/other genders change the possessive (la mia birra, le mie birre).
target_language_example: Qualcuno ha bevuto la mia birra.
native_language_example: Someone drank my beer.

meaning: 'my bottle' (possessive phrase)
additional_notes: Used to indicate ownership of a bottle (of wine, water, etc.). 'Mia' is the feminine singular possessive for 'my' when the noun is singular and either has no article or article is omitted; in full form you can also say 'la mia bottiglia'. Common in everyday speech to ask, claim, or complain about a bottle.
target_language_example: Dove hai messo la mia bottiglia d'acqua?
native_language_example: Where did you put my water bottle?

meaning: 'my shirt' (feminine singular).
additional_notes: Possessive + noun: 'mia' is the feminine singular form of 'my' used with feminine nouns like 'camicia'. In Italian the adjective (possessive) agrees in gender/number with the noun. Use 'il mio' for masculine singular (e.g., il mio libro) and 'le mie'/'i miei' for plural. Commonly used to indicate ownership or to ask/claim an item.
target_language_example: Hai lavato la mia camicia?
native_language_example: Did you wash my shirt?

meaning: my guitar in the...
additional_notes: This phrase combines a possessive (mia chitarra = my guitar) with the preposition 'nel' (in + il). 'Nel' must agree with the following noun (il + noun). In the example sentences it's followed by places like 'suo ufficio' / 'tuo ufficio' / 'vostro ufficio' (his/her/your/their office). You will normally say 'la mia chitarra nel suo ufficio' or place the possessive before the noun: 'la mia chitarra nel suo ufficio' (note: definite article 'la' is commonly used with feminine singular possessives in Italian: 'la mia chitarra').
target_language_example: Ho lasciato la mia chitarra nel mio armadio.
native_language_example: I left my guitar in my closet.

meaning: my (Internet) connection
additional_notes: Used to refer to your internet connection or any network link you personally use. Often appears with 'a Internet' or just 'Internet' (e.g. "la mia connessione Internet"). Common in everyday complaints about speed, stability or outages.
target_language_example: La mia connessione è molto lenta oggi.
native_language_example: My connection is very slow today.

meaning: 'my family is' — a simple subject + verb phrase to describe the state, identity or qualities of one's family.
additional_notes: Use to say where your family is, how they feel, their religion, qualities, or other states. 'Mia famiglia' = 'my family'; 'è' is the third-person singular of 'essere' (to be). For plural ideas you may also hear 'la mia famiglia sono' in casual speech, but standard grammar uses 'è'. Add adjectives (al sicuro, fiera, orgogliosa), nouns (musulmana), locations (qui, a casa) or clauses after 'è'.
target_language_example: Mia famiglia è molto unita e ci vediamo spesso.
native_language_example: My family is very close and we see each other often.

meaning: 'my ... party' (possession + type of celebration).
additional_notes: This is a fragment combining mia (my, feminine singular) + festa (party) + di (of/for). In natural Italian you'd usually complete it with the occasion after di (e.g. mia festa di compleanno = my birthday party) or use mia festa alone. Remember agreement: mia matches the feminine noun festa. If the following word begins with a vowel, pronunciation flows (mia festa d'addio).
target_language_example: Hai visto le foto della mia festa di compleanno?
native_language_example: Have you seen the photos of my birthday party?

meaning: my sentence / my phrase
additional_notes: A simple possessive phrase: mia = my (feminine singular), frase = sentence/phrase. Used to refer to a sentence or phrase that belongs to or was spoken/written by the speaker. Agreement: 'mia' matches the gender/number of the noun (e.g. 'il mio discorso', 'le mie frasi').
target_language_example: Aspetta: la mia frase non è ancora finita.
native_language_example: Wait: my sentence isn't finished yet.

meaning: 'my (female) cat is' — a subject phrase used to describe or give information about one's female cat.
additional_notes: Mia gatta è combines the possessive + noun (mia gatta = my female cat) with the verb essere (è = is). Use it to start a description, state a condition (e.g., in heat = in calore), give a quality (grande, adorabile), or report events (è morta = is dead/has died). If referring to a male cat use 'il mio gatto è'. Agreement: 'mia' is feminine singular to match 'gatta'.
target_language_example: La mia gatta è molto timida con gli estranei.
native_language_example: My cat (female) is very shy with strangers.

meaning: my (female) cat.
additional_notes: Literal possession: 'mia' = my, 'gatta' = female cat. Use 'mio gatto' for a male cat. In Italian, possessive agrees in gender/number with the noun (mia gatta, miei gatti, nostre gatte, etc.). Common in everyday speech to talk about pets.
target_language_example: La mia gatta dorme sul divano tutto il pomeriggio.
native_language_example: My cat (female) sleeps on the sofa all afternoon.

meaning: my camera is
additional_notes: A simple subject + verb phrase: 'mia macchina fotografica' = 'my camera' and 'è' = 'is' (3rd person singular of essere). Use to describe possession and give a quality, state, or identity of the camera (e.g., physical trait, comparison, brand). You can replace 'mia' with other possessive adjectives (tua, sua, nostra, vostra) and change the adjective, noun complement, or noun phrase after 'è'.
target_language_example: La mia macchina fotografica è vecchia ma funziona bene.
native_language_example: My camera is old but works well.

meaning: my apple.
additional_notes: Possessive phrase: mia is the feminine singular form of 'my' (mio) used before feminine singular nouns like mela. Use 'mio'/'mia'/'miei'/'mie' to match gender and number of the noun. Common in simple possession statements and everyday actions (washing, eating).
target_language_example: Hai preso la mia mela senza chiedere.
native_language_example: You took my apple without asking.

meaning: 'my opinion is' — used to state your view or stance on something.
additional_notes: A simple way to introduce how you feel or think about a topic. Followed by adjectives (diversa, contraria, simile, ecc.) or clauses. Can be made formal/informal by changing possessive (mia, nostra) or pronouns (tua, sua, vostra).
target_language_example: La mia opinione è diversa da quella di Marco.
native_language_example: My opinion is different from Marco's.

meaning: my part / on my side (depending on context).
additional_notes: Can mean 'my share' (a portion I should receive) or 'on my side'/'in my favor' when used in expressions like 'dalla mia parte'. Context determines whether it refers to a portion (la mia parte) or support/advantage (essere dalla mia parte).
target_language_example: Se c'è da dividere i soldi, voglio la mia parte.
native_language_example: If there's money to split, I want my share.

meaning: my gun / my pistol
additional_notes: A simple possessive phrase: mia (my, feminine singular) + pistola (feminine noun meaning gun/pistol). Used to indicate ownership or to ask for/offer the speaker's gun. Tone can be neutral, but context (weapons) may be sensitive. For other possessives use mio/tuo/suo depending on gender and number (e.g., il mio coltello, le mie chiavi).
target_language_example: Ridammi la mia pistola, per favore.
native_language_example: Give me back my gun, please.

meaning: my pronunciation
additional_notes: Used to talk about how you pronounce words or sounds. 'Mia' is the possessive for 'my' (feminine to match 'pronuncia'). Common in phrases asking for correction or improvement (e.g., correggi/correggete la mia pronuncia; migliorare la mia pronuncia).
target_language_example: Per favore, ascolta la mia pronuncia e dimmi se è corretta.
native_language_example: Please listen to my pronunciation and tell me if it's correct.

meaning: my little sister (affectionate/diminutive)
additional_notes: Sorellina is the diminutive of sorella, used to mean 'little sister' or to express affection. Mia indicates possession ('my'). Can be used literally (a younger sister) or affectionately about a sister of any age. Tone can be tender, playful, or emphatic depending on context and intonation.
target_language_example: La mia sorellina mi ha aiutato a preparare la torta.
native_language_example: My little sister helped me bake the cake.

meaning: 'my room is' — a simple subject + verb phrase used to describe your room.
additional_notes: Use to give information about the location, size, condition, or qualities of your room. 'Mia stanza' = 'my room'. The verb 'è' is the third-person singular of 'essere' (to be). Word order in Italian is usually 'La mia stanza è ...' (include the article 'la' before 'mia stanza' in full sentences).
target_language_example: La mia stanza è sempre pulita.
native_language_example: My room is always clean.

meaning: my keyboard
additional_notes: Possessive phrase: mia (my, feminine singular) + tastiera (keyboard). Use mia for feminine nouns; for masculine singular use mio. Commonly used for computer or musical keyboards. Can appear in questions or statements about condition, repair, or cleanliness.
target_language_example: La mia tastiera è rotta, puoi aiutarmi?
native_language_example: My keyboard is broken, can you help me?

meaning: my theory
additional_notes: A possessive phrase: 'mia' = my (feminine singular) and 'teoria' = theory. Used to refer to an idea, explanation, or hypothesis that the speaker proposes. In spoken Italian you might also hear 'la mia teoria' with the definite article, but 'mia teoria' can appear without it depending on context (e.g., titles or shortened phrases).
target_language_example: La mia teoria è che arriveranno in ritardo.
native_language_example: My theory is that they will arrive late.

meaning: my university
additional_notes: Possessive phrase: mia (my, feminine singular) + università (university, feminine). Use mia for 'my' because università is feminine. In Italian the possessive often includes the definite article (la mia università) in normal speech, but without the article it's still correct and common in short phrases. Can refer literally to the school someone attends or metaphorically (e.g., "La prigione era la mia università" = prison was my school of life).
target_language_example: La mia università ha molti corsi internazionali.
native_language_example: My university has many international courses.

meaning: my life in (used to specify location, situation or state affecting 'my life')
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom by itself but a fragment: 'mia vita' = 'my life', and 'in' introduces where or in what condition (e.g. 'in prigione', 'in pericolo', 'in questo momento'). Combine with a noun or phrase after 'in' to complete the meaning. Common in everyday speech to talk about location, danger, circumstances, or time.
target_language_example: La mia vita in città è molto più tranquilla.
native_language_example: My life in the city is much calmer.

meaning: not bad; pretty good (mild praise or surprise).
additional_notes: Informal conversational expression used to give a positive, often slightly surprised evaluation. 'Mica' is a negation intensifier here that softens the phrase—literally 'not bad' but often implies 'quite good' or 'not too shabby.' Common after statements or alone as a short reply. Tone and context determine strength (from mild approval to genuine praise).
target_language_example: Questa pizza è mica male.
native_language_example: This pizza is not bad / pretty good.

meaning: 'my resignation' (i.e., the act of resigning from a job/position)
additional_notes: Used to refer to a person's resignation. Dimissioni is plural in Italian (even when referring to a single act of resigning). Often appears with verbs like offrire, chiedere, dare, accettare, entrare in vigore. Use 'le mie dimissioni' (with the definite article) in most contexts.
target_language_example: Ho dato le mie dimissioni ieri.
native_language_example: I gave my resignation yesterday.

meaning: my letters (written letters, notes)
additional_notes: Used to refer to letters (correspondence, written notes) that belong to the speaker. 'Lettere' is feminine plural; 'mie' is the feminine plural possessive. Context can be literal (paper letters) or figurative (letters as messages). Word order is standard: possessive before noun (mie lettere).
target_language_example: Hai visto le mie lettere sul tavolo?
native_language_example: Have you seen my letters on the table?

meaning: my hands are (…)
additional_notes: A simple phrase used to describe the condition or state of the speaker's hands. 'Mie mani' is the feminine plural possessive 'my hands' (more common is 'le mie mani'). In normal Italian you'd usually say 'le mie mani sono…' but in casual speech the article can be dropped after certain verbs or for emphasis. Follow with an adjective or past participle: e.g. fredde (cold), bagnate (wet), legate (tied), morbide (soft), sporche (dirty).
target_language_example: Le mie mani sono fredde perché fa freddo.
native_language_example: My hands are cold because it's cold.

meaning: a vulgar expression meaning 'my ass' / 'yeah right' used to show strong contempt, disbelief, or dismissal
additional_notes: Very rude/informal. Literally 'my testicles' (coglioni = testicles), used sarcastically after a noun to reject or insult what was just said (like 'as if!' or 'my ass!' in English). Common in spoken Italian but avoid in polite company. Tone: contempt, disbelief, or annoyance.
target_language_example: Ispettore dei miei coglioni! Non ha capito nulla.
native_language_example: Inspector, my ass! He understood nothing.

meaning: my companions/peers/classmates/teammates (plural, masculine or mixed).
additional_notes: Used to refer to people who are with you in a group (classmates, teammates, colleagues). 'Miei' is the possessive 'my' for plural masculine nouns; if the group is all female, use 'mie compagne'. Can be followed by a specification like 'di scuola', 'di squadra', or 'di classe'.
target_language_example: I miei compagni di classe sono molto simpatici.
native_language_example: My classmates are very nice.

meaning: toward me / in relation to me (refers to someone's feelings, actions, or attitude directed at the speaker).
additional_notes: Used to talk about how someone feels or behaves toward the speaker. Often appears as part of the fixed prepositional phrase 'nei miei confronti' (nei = in + the, plural). Common with verbs and nouns expressing feelings, judgments, or actions (es. essere critico, avere sentimenti, fare un attacco). Formality: neutral; used in both spoken and written Italian.
target_language_example: Era critico nei miei confronti e non lo capivo.
native_language_example: He was critical toward me and I didn't understand it.

meaning: "my children are" (used to describe the state or qualities of one's children).
additional_notes: A possessive phrase: 'miei figli' = 'my children/sons' and 'sono' is the 3rd-person plural of 'essere' (to be). Use to describe age, feelings, appearance, condition, etc. If speaker is female, 'miei' remains the same. For one child, use 'mio figlio è' (singular).
target_language_example: I miei figli sono stanchi dopo la scuola.
native_language_example: My children are tired after school.

meaning: my situation; my shoes (figurative) — used in 'mettiti nei miei panni' = 'put yourself in my shoes'.
additional_notes: A figurative expression meaning 'my circumstances' or 'my perspective'. Commonly used in the set phrase 'mettiti nei miei panni' (put yourself in my shoes) to ask someone to empathize. Grammar: 'miei' agrees with plural masculine 'panni' (clothes/shoes). You can replace 'miei' with other possessives (es. 'nei tuoi panni').
target_language_example: Mettiti nei miei panni e capirai perché sono preoccupato.
native_language_example: Put yourself in my shoes and you'll understand why I'm worried.

meaning: my feet are (used to describe the state or characteristics of someone's feet)
additional_notes: A subject phrase combining the possessive 'miei' (my) + noun 'piedi' (feet) followed by the verb 'sono' (are). Use it to state physical conditions (caldi, freddi), size (piccoli, grandi) or comparisons (più piccoli dei tuoi). Remember agreement: 'miei' matches the plural masculine noun 'piedi'. For other persons: 'i tuoi piedi sono', 'i suoi piedi sono', etc.
target_language_example: I miei piedi sono stanchi dopo la camminata.
native_language_example: My feet are tired after the walk.

meaning: 'my parents are' (used to say where your parents are or how they are)
additional_notes: I miei literally means 'my ones' and is a colloquial way to refer to your parents (short for i miei genitori). Sono is the 3rd-person plural of essere ('they are'). Use to state location, condition, opinion, or characteristics of your parents. Context determines the translation (e.g. 'I miei sono in città' = 'My parents are in town'; 'I miei sono peggio' = 'My parents are worse').
target_language_example: I miei sono in vacanza questa settimana.
native_language_example: My parents are on vacation this week.

meaning: honey in / honey into (literally 'honey in the...')
additional_notes: Commonly used when saying you put honey into something (e.g., tea, yogurt). 'Nel' is the contraction of 'in' + 'il' (in the + masculine singular noun). Change 'nel' depending on the article (nella, nello, nei, negli, nella, etc.) to match the gender/number and sound of the following noun.
target_language_example: Ho messo del miele nel tè caldo.
native_language_example: I put some honey in the hot tea.

meaning: to improve the (masculine singular) — 'migliorare' = to improve; 'il' = the (masc. sing.).
additional_notes: Used before a masculine singular noun (e.g., il mio inglese, il francese) to say you want to improve that skill or thing. In practice you will usually see other determiners after 'migliorare' (migliorare il mio..., migliorare il tuo...) or no article with general nouns (migliorare l'inglese / migliorare l'italiano). Verb 'migliorare' is regular and commonly followed by direct object (what you improve) or by 'in'/'su' to indicate area (migliorare in matematica).
target_language_example: Voglio migliorare il mio inglese prima del viaggio.
native_language_example: I want to improve my English before the trip.

meaning: better in / the best in (depending on context).
additional_notes: Used to compare quality or ability with respect to a place, field, or context. "Migliore" can be comparative (better) or superlative (the best) when combined with articles: "il migliore in" = the best in. Often followed by a noun or clause introduced by "in" or by a relative clause introduced with "in cui" (e.g., "migliore in cui vivere").
target_language_example: Lei è migliore in matematica che in storia.
native_language_example: She is better in math than in history.

meaning: better/best for; used to say the most suitable way or method to do something.
additional_notes: Commonly follows words like 'il modo', 'il metodo', or 'il sistema' (e.g., 'il modo migliore per...') and is used before an infinitive verb or noun phrase to indicate the best approach or purpose. Can be translated as 'the best way to' or 'better for' depending on context.
target_language_example: Il modo migliore per risparmiare è fare un budget mensile.
native_language_example: The best way to save is to make a monthly budget.

meaning: the best (years/experiences) of my life
additional_notes: Used after a noun (often years, moments, experiences) to say those were the best that the speaker personally had. Literally 'best of my'. Common in phrases like 'gli anni migliori della mia vita' (the best years of my life). Can be used with singular or plural nouns depending on context (e.g. 'la migliore della mia vita' for a singular feminine noun).
target_language_example: Quei mesi sono stati i migliori della mia vita.
native_language_example: Those months were the best of my life.

meaning: threatened to (do something).
additional_notes: Used with a verb in the infinitive to say that someone threatened to perform that action. Common in past tenses (ha minacciato di = he/she threatened to). Can express threats toward others or self (minacciato di uccidersi = threatened to kill himself/herself).
target_language_example: Lui ha minacciato di parlarmi male se non glielo davo.
native_language_example: He threatened to speak badly about me if I didn't give it to him.

meaning: any idea / the slightest idea (usually in negative/questions)
additional_notes: Used with negation or questions to mean 'not even a little idea' or 'do you have even the slightest idea'. Common structure: (non) avere la minima idea di + clause/noun. Emphasizes lack of knowledge or awareness.
target_language_example: Non ho la minima idea di dove sia il treno.
native_language_example: I don't have the slightest idea where the train is.

meaning: minutes per (time period) — used to express a rate (e.g. minutes per day).
additional_notes: Commonly appears in phrases like "minuti al giorno" (minutes per day) to indicate how many minutes something gains/loses or how often something happens. Used with verbs like perdere (to lose time), andare indietro (to run slow), or with expressions of duration (parlare trenta minuti al giorno = speak thirty minutes a day). The preposition following 'al' often specifies the period (giorno, mese, ora).
target_language_example: Il cronometro perde cinque minuti all'ora.
native_language_example: The stopwatch loses five minutes per hour.

meaning: 'minutes to' or 'minutes to (do something)' — indicates how many minutes are needed or available before an action or event.
additional_notes: Commonly used after a number (e.g., 'venti minuti per...') to say how long something takes or how much time someone has. Often followed by an infinitive verb (per lavarmi, per organizzare) or by a purpose. Can mean 'it will take X minutes to...,' 'give me X minutes to...,' or 'you have X minutes to...'.
target_language_example: Dammi cinque minuti per finire e torno.
native_language_example: Give me five minutes to finish and I'll be back.

meaning: a minute earlier / one minute before
additional_notes: Used to indicate that something happened or should happen one minute earlier than a referenced time. Can be used literally (exactly 60 seconds) or more loosely to mean 'just a minute earlier.' Often follows a verb or time expression: e.g., 'È arrivato un minuto prima.'
target_language_example: Sono arrivato un minuto prima dell'appuntamento.
native_language_example: I arrived one minute before the appointment.

meaning: comfortable; at ease (with oneself or in a situation).
additional_notes: Used in the fixed expression 'essere a mio agio' (or 'a tuo/nostro agio') to say you feel comfortable, relaxed, or at ease. Often used with a person, group, situation, or activity. The literal words ('my ease') don't convey full meaning in English, so translate as 'comfortable' or 'at ease.' Negative form 'non sono a mio agio' = 'I don't feel comfortable.'
target_language_example: Mi sento a mio agio con questo gruppo.
native_language_example: I feel comfortable with this group.

meaning: my apartment is
additional_notes: A simple subject + verb phrase used to describe or locate your apartment. 'Mio' is the possessive adjective 'my' (agrees in gender: mio appartamento). The verb 'è' is third-person singular of 'essere' (to be). Common follow-ups are adjectives (e.g., piccolo), location phrases (e.g., qua vicino), or identifiers (e.g., quello in fondo al corridoio).
target_language_example: Il mio appartamento è al secondo piano.
native_language_example: My apartment is on the second floor.

meaning: my bus
additional_notes: Simple possessive phrase: mio (my) + autobus (bus). Use mio before masculine singular nouns. If you want to be more specific with gender/number agreement: il mio autobus (my bus), i miei autobus (my buses). Common in everyday speech to indicate the bus you usually take or the one you're waiting for.
target_language_example: Il mio autobus arriva tra cinque minuti.
native_language_example: My bus arrives in five minutes.

meaning: my ticket
additional_notes: A simple possessive phrase: 'mio' (my) + 'biglietto' (ticket). Used when referring to a ticket for travel, events, entrance, etc. Word order is the same as English (possessive before noun). You may also hear other possessives (tuo, suo, nostro) depending on the owner. Definite article is often omitted in spoken phrases like 'Ho dimenticato il mio biglietto' but can appear ('il mio biglietto').
target_language_example: Hai visto il mio biglietto? Non lo trovo.
native_language_example: Have you seen my ticket? I can't find it.

meaning: 'my dog is' (simple subject + verb: describes your dog's state or qualities).
additional_notes: A basic possessive phrase: mio = my (masculine singular), cane = dog, è = is (third person singular of essere). Use when describing your dog (age, condition, mood, appearance). If the noun were feminine you'd use mia; plural would be i miei cani. Word order is the same as in English: possessive + noun + verb + adjective/complement.
target_language_example: Il mio cane è molto affettuoso.
native_language_example: My dog is very affectionate.

meaning: my boss is
additional_notes: Used to describe a characteristic, opinion, ability, or trait of your boss. 'Capo' means boss/manager; 'mio' is 'my'. Common in everyday speech to give opinions (e.g., strict, curious, deaf) or comments about skills (e.g., language ability). Followed by an adjective, noun phrase, or clause.
target_language_example: Il mio capo è sempre disponibile ad aiutare.
native_language_example: My boss is always willing to help.

meaning: my brain
additional_notes: Possessive phrase: mio (my) + cervello (brain). Used literally (anatomy, medical exams) and figuratively (self-critical or joking comments like "my brain is stupid" or "make my brain disappear" meaning mental tiredness or wanting to stop thinking). In full sentences the adjective or article must agree (e.g., il mio cervello).
target_language_example: Il mio cervello non vuole smettere di pensare.
native_language_example: My brain doesn't want to stop thinking.

meaning: my last name is / my surname is
additional_notes: Used to give your family name. 'Cognome' = surname/last name. 'Mio' is the possessive 'my' (agreeing in gender/number with the noun: mio cognome, mia sorella, i miei amici). The verb 'è' (third-person singular of essere) links the subject (implied 'il mio cognome') to the name. You can also say 'Il mio cognome è...' (with the article) or omit 'Il' in informal introductions.
target_language_example: Il mio cognome è Rossi.
native_language_example: My last name is Rossi.

meaning: my birthday is ...
additional_notes: Used to state when or where your birthday falls. Followed by a time expression (month, day, relative phrase like 'lunedì prossimo'), a location phrase ('vicino a ...'), or other descriptors. In Italian the possessive 'mio' agrees with the noun (compleanno is masculine singular) and the verb 'è' (is) links to the information. To say 'my birthday was ...' use passato (e.g. 'Il mio compleanno è stato ...').
target_language_example: Il mio compleanno è il 12 marzo.
native_language_example: My birthday is March 12th.

meaning: my computer (has) ... (used with reflexive/passive verbs to say something happened to the computer, e.g. 'my computer froze/ broke').
additional_notes: The pattern 'mio computer si è + past participle' uses the reflexive/passive si to describe something that happened to the computer (common verbs: bloccato, piantato, rotto). In English you translate depending on the verb: 'si è bloccato/si è piantato' = 'my computer froze/locked up'; 'si è rotto' = 'my computer broke'. This is an informal, everyday way to report a problem with a device.
target_language_example: Il mio computer si è bloccato durante la presentazione.
native_language_example: My computer froze during the presentation.

meaning: 'my computer is' (simple present with possession).
additional_notes: A short phrase combining the possessive adjective mio (my), the noun computer, and the verb è (is). Used to state the location, condition, or possession of the computer. In everyday speech you might hear the article (il) included: il mio computer è — both are correct; omitting the article is common in quick spoken phrases. For gender/number agreement: mio becomes mia for feminine singular (mia macchina), miei/mie for plural.
target_language_example: Mio computer è spento, devo riaccenderlo.
native_language_example: My computer is off, I need to turn it on again.

meaning: my money.
additional_notes: A simple possessive phrase: 'mio' (my) + 'denaro' (money). Used to indicate ownership of money or to demand/get back money. Can be used in both formal and informal contexts; tone depends on the rest of the sentence. 'Denaro' is interchangeable with 'soldi' (more common in spoken Italian).
target_language_example: Mi restituisci il mio denaro, per favore?
native_language_example: Will you give me back my money, please?

meaning: my wish / my desire
additional_notes: Used to express something someone wants or hopes for. Can refer to a specific wish (e.g., for Christmas) or a general desire (e.g., a career goal). Commonly followed by 'di' + infinitive (Il mio desiderio è di + infinitive) or by a clause introduced with 'che' or an infinitive without 'di' (Il mio desiderio è andare...). Informal use in questions when sharing a personal wish (Ti dico il mio desiderio?).
target_language_example: Il mio desiderio è visitare Roma il prossimo anno.
native_language_example: My wish is to visit Rome next year.

meaning: my dictionary
additional_notes: A possessive phrase: 'mio' (my) + 'dizionario' (dictionary). Used to indicate ownership. Gender/number must agree with the noun (e.g., la mia penna, i miei dizionari). Often used before or after the noun (normally before in Italian).
target_language_example: Hai visto il mio dizionario sulla scrivania?
native_language_example: Have you seen my dictionary on the desk?

meaning: my rifle / my gun (possessive phrase)
additional_notes: A simple possessive phrase: 'mio' = 'my' (masculine singular) and 'fucile' = 'rifle' or 'gun'. Used to indicate ownership or to ask someone to give/take the speaker's firearm. In everyday civilian contexts 'fucile' can also refer to a shotgun ('fucile da caccia') or even a rifle for sport; in informal speech 'pistola' is used for handgun. Adjust verb forms and politeness (Prendi = you singular informal; Prendete = you plural) as in the examples.
target_language_example: Mi restituite il mio fucile, per favore?
native_language_example: Will you give me back my rifle, please?

meaning: my cat is
additional_notes: A simple subject–verb phrase used to describe the speaker's cat. 'Mio gatto' = 'my cat' (masculine); 'è' is the 3rd-person singular of 'essere' (to be). Can be followed by adjectives, states, or past participles (e.g. morto). Word order is normal for Italian: possessive + noun + verb. For a female cat you'd say 'mia gatta è'.
target_language_example: Il mio gatto è molto curioso.
native_language_example: My cat is very curious.

meaning: my hobby is… (used to say what you like to do in your free time).
additional_notes: Common way to introduce a hobby. 'Hobby' is a masculine noun in Italian (il hobby) but often used unchanged. After 'è' you can use an infinitive verb (collezionare, nuotare, suonare) or a noun (la pesca, lo shopping). For variety you can also say 'Il mio passatempo è…' or 'Il mio hobby sono…' if listing multiple hobbies.
target_language_example: Il mio hobby è leggere romanzi gialli.
native_language_example: My hobby is reading mystery novels.

meaning: my English (language ability).
additional_notes: Used to talk about one's own ability in the English language. Common in phrases about skill level (e.g., 'il mio inglese è tremendo' = 'my English is terrible') or the need to practice/improve. 'Mio' agrees with the speaker; you can replace it with other possessives (tuo, suo, nostro).
target_language_example: Devo praticare il mio inglese ogni giorno.
native_language_example: I must practice my English every day.

meaning: my (male) teacher of / my teacher for (a subject).
additional_notes: Used to say which subject your teacher teaches. 'Mio' is the possessive 'my' and agrees in gender/number (mio insegnante = my (male) teacher). To refer to a female teacher use 'la mia insegnante di' or more commonly 'la mia professoressa di'. The subject follows 'di' (e.g. 'di francese'). Common in spoken and written Italian.
target_language_example: Il mio insegnante di matematica è molto bravo.
native_language_example: My math teacher is very good.

meaning: my laptop (my portable computer).
additional_notes: Possessive phrase: 'mio' = my (masculine singular). 'Laptop' is commonly used in Italian as a loanword; can also say 'il mio portatile' or 'il mio computer portatile'. Agreement: use 'mia' if you use a feminine noun (e.g. 'la mia macchina'). Often appears with articles: 'il mio laptop' or without in casual speech.
target_language_example: Dove hai messo il mio laptop?
native_language_example: Where did you put my laptop?

meaning: my job/work is...
additional_notes: Use this phrase to state something about your job or what work you are doing. In Italian, possession uses 'mio' (my) before the noun: 'mio lavoro' = 'my job' or 'my work'. The verb 'è' (is) links to a description, status, or action (e.g. 'Il mio lavoro è molto interessante' = 'My job is very interesting'; 'Il mio lavoro è pulire' = 'My job is to clean'). Often you will hear 'il mio lavoro è...' with the definite article 'il' before 'mio lavoro' as in the examples, but omitting 'il' (just 'mio lavoro è') is also understood in casual speech.
target_language_example: Il mio lavoro è aiutare i clienti ogni giorno.
native_language_example: My job is to help customers every day.

meaning: my best (as in 'do my best')
additional_notes: Commonly appears in the fixed expression 'fare del mio meglio' meaning 'to do my best' or 'I'll do my best'. Used to promise effort but not guarantee success. In Italian you usually say 'farò del mio meglio' (I will do my best) or 'ho fatto del mio meglio' (I did my best).
target_language_example: Farò del mio meglio per finire il progetto entro domani.
native_language_example: I'll do my best to finish the project by tomorrow.

meaning: Not a standard Italian phrase — likely a mistaken or nonstandard combination. If intended, it could be an attempt to say "my best for" or "my best to/for", but native speakers would not use this exact sequence.
additional_notes: This exact phrase is not idiomatic in Italian. Possible intended expressions: "il mio meglio" (my best, e.g. 'ho dato il mio meglio' = I gave my best) or "per il meglio" (toward the best) or "il meglio per [qualcuno]" (the best for [someone]). If you meant to say "my best wishes for..." use "i miei migliori auguri per...". If you meant "I'll do my best for..." say "farò del mio meglio per...".
target_language_example: Farò del mio meglio per aiutarti.
native_language_example: I'll do my best to help you.

meaning: my best friend is ...
additional_notes: Used to state something about your best friend (location, nationality, identity, a joking metaphor, or an attribute). 'Mio' can contract to 'il mio' as in examples; word order is flexible: you can say 'Il mio migliore amico è...' or drop 'il' in casual speech. Be careful: some example sentences include offensive language — avoid using slurs.
target_language_example: Il mio migliore amico è insegnante.
native_language_example: My best friend is a teacher.

meaning: my boyfriend / my romantic partner (male).
additional_notes: Moroso is an informal word used in some regions (especially northern Italy) for 'boyfriend' or 'partner'. It usually refers to a male romantic partner. Tone can be casual; use ragazzo/ragazzo mio or fidanzato for more neutral or formal contexts. "Mio" indicates possession: 'my'.
target_language_example: Mi ha telefonato il mio moroso ieri sera.
native_language_example: My boyfriend called me last night.

meaning: 'my name' + negation (used when saying that your name is not something / not on a list / don't say my name)
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself but a fragment showing 'il mio nome non...' or 'il mio nome non è…' (my name is not…). It appears in contexts: denying your identity (Il mio nome non è Tom), saying your name isn't on a list (il mio nome non era nella lista), or warning someone not to mention you (Se fai il mio nome non ci sono più — 'If you say my name I'm gone/there will be trouble'). Use with verbs like essere (è), essere presente (era nella lista), or fare (fai il mio nome).
target_language_example: Il mio nome non è Marco, è Marco Rossi.
native_language_example: My name is not Marco; it's Marco Rossi.

meaning: 'my name is'.
additional_notes: Used to introduce yourself. More natural in Italian is 'Mi chiamo [Name]' but 'Il mio nome è [Name]' is also correct and slightly more formal or literal. Remember to include the article 'Il' when saying the full phrase: 'Il mio nome è...'.
target_language_example: Il mio nome è Marco.
native_language_example: My name is Marco.

meaning: my parrot
additional_notes: A simple possessive phrase: mio = my (masculine singular), pappagallo = parrot. Use mio with masculine singular nouns; change depending on gender/number (mia, miei, mie). Can be used literally (a pet parrot) or humorously to refer to someone who repeats things.
target_language_example: Il mio pappagallo imita sempre le conversazioni in cucina.
native_language_example: My parrot always imitates the conversations in the kitchen.

meaning: my hobby is / my pastime is
additional_notes: Used to say what someone does for fun. Followed by an infinitive verb (collezionare), a noun (la lettura, la pesca) or a clause (quello di + infinitive). Common in informal and neutral speech. You can also say "il mio hobby è" (loanword) or invert word order: "il mio passatempo preferito è..."
target_language_example: Il mio passatempo è guardare film stranieri.
native_language_example: My hobby is watching foreign films.

meaning: my dream is (to)...
additional_notes: Used to introduce a personal aspiration, wish, or ideal. Often followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., diventare, stare) or a noun phrase. Literal translation is 'my dream is'. Common in both spoken and written Italian.
target_language_example: Il mio sogno è viaggiare per il mondo.
native_language_example: My dream is to travel the world.

meaning: 'my success' — refers to achievements or accomplishments that belong to the speaker.
additional_notes: Composed of the possessive adjective mio (my) + successo (success). Used to talk about personal achievements, reputation, or favorable outcomes. Can appear in different genders/numbers (il mio successo, i miei successi). Common in both spoken and written Italian.
target_language_example: Il mio successo non sarebbe stato possibile senza la tua guida.
native_language_example: My success would not have been possible without your guidance.

meaning: my phone is ... (used to describe the phone's state or qualities).
additional_notes: A simple subject + possessive + verb structure: 'mio telefono' = 'my phone' and 'è' = 'is'. Common completions include adjectives (carino, comodo) or states (morto = dead, meaning out of battery). Native speakers often say 'il mio telefono' with the article ('Il mio telefono è...'), but dropping the article can occur in quick speech or notes. To say 'the battery of my phone is almost dead' use 'La batteria del mio telefono è quasi scarica.'
target_language_example: Il mio telefono è morto, devo trovarlo un caricabatterie.
native_language_example: My phone is dead, I need to find a charger.

meaning: my train.
additional_notes: Used to refer to the specific train the speaker is travelling on or expecting. Common in travel contexts (tickets, schedules, delays). 'Mio' agrees in gender/number with the noun (il mio treno). Can be replaced by other possessives (tuo treno, il suo treno).
target_language_example: Devo correre, il mio treno parte tra cinque minuti.
native_language_example: I have to run, my train leaves in five minutes.

meaning: 'my old' as in 'my (longtime)'.
additional_notes: Used before a noun (often 'amico') to mean a long-standing or former relationship — 'my old friend' = a friend you've known for a long time. Not referring to someone's age; conveys familiarity or affection. Can appear as 'mio vecchio amico' or in address 'mio vecchio' (colloquial).
target_language_example: Ho incontrato il mio vecchio vicino al mercato.
native_language_example: I ran into my old neighbor at the market.

meaning: 'my real' or 'my true' (as in 'my real name' or 'my true self').
additional_notes: Used before a noun to indicate the genuine or actual quality (e.g., mio vero nome = my real name; mio vero io = my true self). Often appears in expressions about identity or authenticity. 'Vero' modifies the noun and agrees in gender/number (es. la mia vera identità).
target_language_example: Il mio vero nome non è famoso.
native_language_example: My real name is not famous.

meaning: mission accomplished; the mission has been completed.
additional_notes: Used to report that a task or mission has been successfully finished. Can be literal (military/official missions) or ironic/colloquial for everyday tasks. Often said as a short statement or exclamation. Tone can be proud, factual, or humorous depending on context.
target_language_example: Ho finito il rapporto: missione compiuta.
native_language_example: I finished the report: mission accomplished.

meaning: "the mission is" (used to introduce what the mission involves or its state)
additional_notes: A common word order in Italian to describe or define a mission: missione + essere. Use it to state the mission's objective, condition, or outcome. Followed by a past participle (e.g., "stata" for passive/result) to say what happened, or by an adjective/phrase to describe the mission's status or task. In English it usually translates as "the mission is" or "your mission is" depending on context (compare "La vostra missione è..." = "Your mission is...").
target_language_example: La missione è recuperare il documento entro stasera.
native_language_example: The mission is to recover the document by tonight.

meaning: an expression, saying, or idiom; a way of saying something.
additional_notes: Used to refer to a phrase or common expression rather than a literal meaning. Often implies figurative or conventional language (an idiom). Can be used to downplay a literal statement by calling it only an expression.
target_language_example: È solo un modo di dire; non intendevo offenderti.
native_language_example: It's just a way of saying it; I didn't mean to offend you.

meaning: way of behaving / way of doing (something)
additional_notes: Used to describe someone's manner, style, or method. Can refer to personal behavior (modo di fare freddo = a cold manner) or to a general approach or technique (modo di fare un film, modo di fare le cose). Often followed by an activity introduced with di + infinitive or a noun.
target_language_example: Mi piace il suo modo di fare: è gentile e calmo.
native_language_example: I like his way of behaving: he's kind and calm.

modo migliore per aiutarci è di contribuire

target_language_multi_word_term: modo migliore per aiutarci è di contribuire
meaning: the best way to help us is to contribute
additional_notes: A full phrase used to request help or contributions. You can change the possessive/pronoun (sua, tua, vostra) to match formality and number. Often followed by where/how to contribute (e.g., 'nella tua lingua madre', 'con una donazione', 'con del tempo'). In everyday speech the 'di' after 'è' is sometimes omitted: 'Il modo migliore per aiutarci è contribuire...'.
target_language_example: Il modo migliore per aiutarci è di contribuire nella tua lingua madre.
native_language_example: The best way to help us is to contribute in your native language.

meaning: the wife and her children
additional_notes: A straightforward phrase used to refer collectively to a man's (or someone's) wife and her children. Gender and possession: "moglie" = wife (singular), "i suoi figli" = her children (could be biological or stepchildren depending on context). Use "i suoi" because "figli" is masculine plural; for daughters only you'd say "le sue figlie."
target_language_example: Ha invitato la moglie e i suoi figli alla cena.
native_language_example: He invited his wife and her children to dinner.

meaning: 'my wife has' (used to say what my wife did).
additional_notes: This is the verb phrase 'moglie mi ha' = 'wife (has) to me/for me has...' In Italian the subject (moglie) + indirect object pronoun (mi = to me) + auxiliary (ha) is common in sentences like 'Mia moglie mi ha chiamato' (My wife called me) or 'Tua moglie mi ha detto...' (Your wife told me...). Depending on context the sentence may continue with a past participle (ha chiamato, ha detto) or other complements. Note: word order can vary (e.g., 'Sua moglie mi ha chiamata' if the speaker is female; agreement of past participle with direct object applies when using avere only in some regional/colloquial cases).
target_language_example: Mia moglie mi ha preparato la cena.
native_language_example: My wife has prepared dinner for me.

meaning: my/your/his/her wife is very ... (used to say someone’s wife has a strong quality or emotion).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom but a common structure: 'Mia/Sua moglie è molto + adjective' = 'My/His/Her wife is very ...'. Replace the possessive (mia, tua, sua, etc.) as needed. 'Molto' intensifies the adjective. Word order: possesive + moglie + è + molto + adjective.
target_language_example: La mia moglie è molto gentile con i bambini.
native_language_example: My wife is very kind with children.

meaning: he/she quit/gave up his/her job (colloquial)
additional_notes: Mollare means to let go or give up; here it's used colloquially about leaving a job. The subject (he/she/they) is implied by context; "mollato il suo impiego" is a past participle phrase meaning someone has quit. More neutral/standard verbs: "ha lasciato il suo impiego", "ha rassegnato le dimissioni".
target_language_example: Dopo mesi di stress, ha mollato il suo impiego senza troppi rimpianti.
native_language_example: After months of stress, he quit his job without much regret.

meaning: quit his/her job; left his/her job.
additional_notes: Informal past-tense phrase using 'mollare' (slang for 'to quit/leave' or 'to let go of'). Used to say someone stopped working at a place. Replace 'suo' with the appropriate possessive (mio/tuo/suo/nostro) and adjust gender/number if needed (e.g., 'ha mollato il suo lavoro' or 'ha mollato il lavoro'). Common in spoken Italian; more formal alternatives: 'ha lasciato il suo lavoro' or 'si è dimesso' (for resigning).
target_language_example: Giulia ha mollato il suo lavoro per viaggiare.
native_language_example: Giulia quit her job to travel.

meaning: very angry (feminine singular).
additional_notes: An adjective phrase: molto = very (adverb) + arrabbiata = angry (feminine singular form of arrabbiato). Use 'molto arrabbiato' for a man or mixed/male subject. Often followed by 'con' to indicate who someone is angry with (e.g., 'arrabbiata con me').
target_language_example: Dopo la riunione era molto arrabbiata con il collega.
native_language_example: After the meeting she was very angry with the colleague.

meaning: a lot (to) / much (to) — indicates there is a large amount left to do, learn, say, give, etc.
additional_notes: Used before an infinitive or a past participle/gerund-like idea to say there's a large quantity or extent of something related to an action or object. Common patterns: "molto da" + infinitive (e.g., "molto da imparare" = a lot to learn) or "molto da" + noun (contextual, e.g., "molto da mangiare" = a lot to eat / a lot of food). Can be used with "ancora" to mean "still a lot to..."
target_language_example: Abbiamo ancora molto da fare.
native_language_example: We still have a lot to do.

meaning: very generous (feminine form)
additional_notes: Used to describe a woman (or feminine noun) who gives freely—of money, time, help, etc. Change ending for gender/number: molto generoso (m. sing.), molto generosi (m. pl.), molto generose (f. pl.). 'Molto' intensifies the adjective 'generosa'.
target_language_example: La professoressa è molto generosa con gli studenti.
native_language_example: The (female) teacher is very generous with the students.

meaning: 'very kind of (someone)' — used to thank or acknowledge someone's kindness or polite action.
additional_notes: Commonly appears as 'molto gentile da parte tua/ sua/ vostra/ loro' to specify who acted kindly. Used to express gratitude or appreciation; equivalent to 'that's very kind of you' in English. Can be followed by a gesture or specific action (e.g. 'molto gentile da parte tua ad aiutarmi').
target_language_example: Molto gentile da parte tua ad avermi aiutato oggi.
native_language_example: Very kind of you to have helped me today.

meaning: very grateful for / very thankful for
additional_notes: Formal/standard phrase used to express strong gratitude. Often used with indirect object pronouns or polite forms: 'Le sono molto grato per…' (I am very grateful to you — formal), 'Ti sono molto grato per…' (informal singular), 'Vi sono molto grato per…' (plural or formal). Can be followed by a noun, clause, or phrase describing what you're grateful for.
target_language_example: Ti sono molto grato per il tuo supporto durante l'esame.
native_language_example: I am very grateful to you for your support during the exam.

meaning: very important for / crucial to
additional_notes: Used to say that something is particularly significant or essential for a person, thing, purpose, or outcome. Followed by a noun, infinitive, or clause introduced by a pronoun (e.g., per me, per il progetto, per ottenere). Common in both spoken and written Italian.
target_language_example: È molto importante per il successo del progetto rispettare le scadenze.
native_language_example: It is very important for the project's success to meet the deadlines.

meaning: very careless / very reckless
additional_notes: Used to describe someone’s behavior or an action that lacks caution or good judgment. Can modify a person (È molto imprudente) or a specific action (È molto imprudente lasciare ...). "Molto" intensifies "imprudente". Common in both spoken and written Italian.
target_language_example: È molto imprudente guidare senza cintura di sicurezza.
native_language_example: It's very careless to drive without a seatbelt.

meaning: much better (by far); significantly better
additional_notes: Combines 'molto' (very/much) + 'migliore' (better). Used to emphasize a large difference in quality or ability between two people or things. Often appears before a comparison introduced by 'di' or 'di quanto'. Word order: 'molto migliore di [persona/cosa]' or 'molto migliore di quanto...'.
target_language_example: Questa macchina è molto migliore della mia.
native_language_example: This car is much better than mine.

meaning: very optimistic
additional_notes: Used to describe a person or attitude that is highly hopeful or positive about outcomes. 'Molto' intensifies the adjective 'ottimista'. Can describe current state (è molto ottimista) or reported speech (ha detto che era molto ottimista).
target_language_example: Lei è molto ottimista riguardo al futuro.
native_language_example: She is very optimistic about the future.

meaning: much older than
additional_notes: Used to compare ages. 'Molto' intensifies 'più vecchio di' (older than). Followed by a noun, pronoun, or phrase indicating the person (di + name/pronoun/possessive). For subject pronouns use stressed forms (di me, di noi). Word order: [Subject] + è + molto più vecchio di + [other person].
target_language_example: Lui è molto più vecchio di me.
native_language_example: He is much older than me.

meaning: very sure/confident about (someone/something).
additional_notes: Used before an object or reflexive pronoun (e.g., 'sé' for oneself) to say someone is very confident or sure. When talking about a person's confidence in themselves, Italian uses 'sicuro/a di sé' (note placement of 'di'). Agreement: 'sicuro' changes for gender (sicura for feminine). Commonly appears with verbs like 'essere' or 'sembrare'.
target_language_example: Lei è molto sicura di sé.
native_language_example: She is very confident in herself.

meaning: 'very lonely' or 'very alone'.
additional_notes: Combines the adverb molto (very) with solo (alone/lonely). Used to express a strong feeling of loneliness or being alone right now or in general. Can describe emotional loneliness (mi sento molto solo) or physical solitude (sono molto solo) depending on context. If referring to location rather than emotion, Italian might prefer "da solo" for 'by oneself' (e.g. "sono molto da solo" is less common than "sono da solo").
target_language_example: In questi giorni mi sento molto solo.
native_language_example: These days I feel very lonely.

meaning: very often (in the context of playing or doing a sport or game).
additional_notes: Commonly used before a sport or game introduced with the preposition 'a' (e.g., 'a tennis', 'a calcio'). 'Molto spesso' means 'very often' and 'a' links to the activity. Word order: 'Gioca molto spesso a tennis?' = 'Does he/she play tennis very often?'. Works with different subjects and verb forms.
target_language_example: Gioco molto spesso a calcio nel weekend.
native_language_example: I play soccer very often on weekends.

meaning: a long time
additional_notes: Used to indicate a long period of time or that something happened long ago. Commonly appears in phrases like 'molto tempo fa' (long ago) or 'per molto tempo' (for a long time). Word order may change: 'molto tempo fa' = 'long ago'; 'per molto tempo' = 'for a long time.'
target_language_example: È passato molto tempo da quando ci siamo visti.
native_language_example: It's been a long time since we saw each other.

meaning: moments in (which/when) — used to introduce times or situations when something happens.
