additional_notes: Usually appears as part of the phrase "momenti in cui" (= "moments when/which") or "momenti in famiglia" (= "family moments"). It introduces specific times or situations (e.g., emotional states, events). Common in both general statements (Ci sono momenti in cui...) and in noun phrases (i momenti in famiglia).
target_language_example: Ci sono momenti in cui bisogna fermarsi e riflettere.
native_language_example: There are moments when you need to stop and reflect.

meaning: the crucial moment; the moment when truth/outcome is revealed
additional_notes: Used to indicate a decisive or critical point when results become clear or the real situation is revealed. Can be used literally (a test revealing truth) or figuratively (a decisive moment in events). Common in formal and informal speech.
target_language_example: Domani sarà il momento della verità per il progetto.
native_language_example: Tomorrow will be the moment of truth for the project.

meaning: the right moment; the appropriate or opportune time
additional_notes: Used to say something happens at an advantageous, timely, or appropriate moment. Can be used literally (timing of events) or figuratively (saying/doing the right thing). Often appears with verbs like arrivare, venire, capitare, essere, agire, dire.
target_language_example: Aspetterò finché non arriverà il momento giusto.
native_language_example: I'll wait until the right moment arrives.

meaning: the world that / the world which (introduces a clause describing 'the world')
additional_notes: A combination of mondo (world) + the relative pronoun che. Used to refer to 'the world' and immediately add information about it with a relative clause. Can introduce a literal world, a social/environmental context, or a situation. Word order: 'il mondo che...' or 'nel mondo che...' depending on preposition.
target_language_example: Il mondo che conosci è cambiato.
native_language_example: The world that you know has changed.

meaning: the world is full of / there are many (people/things) — used to say something is common or abundant.
additional_notes: Literal: 'the world is full of...'. Used to downplay uniqueness or emphasize abundance (e.g., many people, many tragedies). Can introduce a noun phrase (gente, tragedie, femmine). Common in spoken and written Italian.
target_language_example: Il mondo è pieno di opportunità, non aver paura di provarci.
native_language_example: The world is full of opportunities; don't be afraid to try.

meaning: A sequence of the adjective or noun 'moroso' followed by the verb 'è' ('is'). Context determines meaning: 'moroso' can mean 'in arrears/delinquent' (financial) or informal 'boyfriend'. The ordering 'moroso è' typically appears in clauses or as part of larger sentences.
additional_notes: The token 'moroso è' by itself is not a fixed idiom; it's simply 'moroso' + 'è'. To interpret it, check surrounding words: if referring to a person or relationship, 'moroso' = boyfriend (informal). If referring to payments/accounts, 'moroso' = late/in arrears. Word order 'moroso è' may appear in inverted or stylistic constructions (e.g., 'Moroso è chi non paga' — 'Delinquent is he who does not pay'). Watch pronunciation: the vowel e in 'è' is stressed.
target_language_example: Moroso è chi non paga le bollette.
native_language_example: Delinquent is someone who doesn't pay the bills.

meaning: 'dead of' (cause of death) OR idiomatic 'very' when followed by a noun expressing strong feeling/need (feminine).
additional_notes: Two uses: 1) Literal: 'morta di' + illness/condition = 'died of' (e.g., 'morta di cancro'). 2) Idiomatic/exclamatory (colloquial): 'morta di' + hunger/fatigue/fear = 'very' or 'so' (emphasizes extreme state) — note gender agreement (morta = feminine). For masculine subjects use 'morto di'. Context and following word show which meaning is intended.
target_language_example: Maria è morta di freddo quella notte.
native_language_example: Maria died of cold that night.

meaning: 'dead in' or 'found dead in' — indicates someone (female) died or was found dead at/in a place or manner.
additional_notes: Morta is the feminine past participle of 'morire' (to die). 'Morta in' is used before mentioning the place or circumstance (e.g., 'morta in un vicolo', 'morta in pace nel sonno'). If referring to a male, use 'morto in'. To say 'was found dead', Italian often uses 'trovata morta' (feminine) or 'trovato morto' (masculine).
target_language_example: La nonna è morta in casa sua la scorsa notte.
native_language_example: Grandmother died in her home last night.

meaning: dead for (a length of time).
additional_notes: Used to state how long someone or something has been dead. Followed by a time expression (e.g., 'due giorni', 'molto tempo', 'appena due mesi'). Equivalent to English 'dead for X (time)'. In spoken Italian you may also hear 'è morto X fa' in some regions, but 'morto da' + time is common.
target_language_example: Il mio cane è morto da tre anni.
native_language_example: My dog has been dead for three years.

meaning: died of (indicates cause of death)
additional_notes: Used to specify the cause of someone's death. Typically follows a subject with the verb 'essere' (e.g., 'È morto di...') or appears in a descriptive clause. Commonly followed by an illness, accident, or descriptive phrase (e.g., 'tumore', 'infarto', 'una morte triste'). Not used when no cause is given; for general 'to die' use 'morire' or 'è morto' without 'di'. 'Morto' is the past participle/adjective meaning 'dead'; 'di' introduces the cause.
target_language_example: Lui è morto di una morte triste.
native_language_example: He died of a sad death.

meaning: dead for three years / died three years (ago).
additional_notes: Used with a subject and typically the auxiliary essere to indicate someone died three years ago or has been dead for three years. Often appears as part of a phrase like "è morto tre anni fa" (he/she died three years ago) or in other contexts without "fa" when followed by additional temporal phrasing (e.g., "Tom è morto tre anni più tardi"). Verb agreement: past participle "morto" agrees with auxiliary essere (e.g., "Lui è morto").
target_language_example: Lui è morto tre anni.
native_language_example: He died three years ago.

meaning: died of a (followed by a description of the death)
additional_notes: Used to describe someone's death, followed by a noun phrase like 'morte pacifica', 'morte orribile', etc. 'Morì' is the past historic (passato remoto) or literary/simple past of 'morire' (to die). In spoken Italian, passato prossimo ('è morto/è morta') is more common: 'è morto di una morte...' is possible but sounds redundant; more natural is 'morì di...' in written or formal contexts. The construction literally means 'died of a (death)'.
target_language_example: Il vecchio morì di una morte serena.
native_language_example: The old man died a peaceful death.

meaning: to show the
additional_notes: Literal combination of the verb mostrare (to show) + the definite article il (the). Used before a masculine singular noun: mostrare il buon esempio = to show the good example / set a good example. In sentence 3 the phrase appears in a colloquial/vulgar context (mostrare il culo = to show one's butt). Use depends on the noun that follows; the full meaning comes from the whole phrase (mostrare + noun).
target_language_example: Devi mostrare il documento all'ufficiale.
native_language_example: You must show the document to the officer.

meaning: shown the (feminine singular object).
additional_notes: ‘Mostrato’ is the past participle of mostrare (to show). In these examples it appears in compound past tense with a person (mi, gli, le, ci) + avere: [person] + ha/ho/hanno + mostrato + la + [noun]. 'La' is the feminine singular direct object pronoun or article before a feminine noun (e.g., la sua auto, la fotografia). For masculine objects you'd see 'lo' or 'il'.
target_language_example: Mi ha mostrato la foto delle vacanze.
native_language_example: He/she showed me the vacation photo.

meaning: shown a photo of
additional_notes: Used to say someone showed (past tense) a picture of someone or something. 'Mostrato' is past participle of 'mostrare' (to show); in full sentences you normally include a helping verb (e.g., 'ha mostrato', 'mi ha mostrato'). 'Una foto di' = 'a photo of' (possessive can follow: 'di sua madre' = 'of his/her mother').
target_language_example: Ieri mi ha mostrato una foto di suo padre.
native_language_example: Yesterday he showed me a photo of his father.

meaning: 'show the' (formal/imperative or subjunctive/indicative form of mostrare + definite article 'il')
additional_notes: Mostri is either: 1) the formal/informal polite imperative (Lei) of mostrare meaning '(please) show' when addressing someone politely (e.g., "Mi mostri il passaporto, per favore" = 'Please show me the passport'), or 2) the third-person present subjunctive/indicative form 'he/she shows the' depending on context (e.g., "credi che questo specchio mostri il futuro?" = 'do you think this mirror shows the future?'). Always followed by a masculine singular noun introduced by 'il'. Common in polite requests and in subordinate clauses.
target_language_example: Mi mostri il biglietto, per favore.
native_language_example: Please show me the ticket.

meaning: please/show me the (plural feminine) — polite/request form of 'to show' plus the feminine plural direct object article.
additional_notes: From the verb mostrare (to show). 'Mi mostri le ...' is a polite/request structure meaning 'will you show me the ...' or 'show me the ...' (formal or neutral). The article 'le' marks a feminine plural noun (e.g., foto, chiamate, dita, carte). In informal familiar contexts you'd hear 'mi fai vedere le...' or 'fammi vedere le...'. Word order: object follows the verb. Depending on context, tone and verb form (mostri vs mostra) can be formal (subjunctive/polite) or imperative-like.
target_language_example: Mi mostri le chiavi, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you show me the keys, please?

meaning: a motel in the area / nearby motel
additional_notes: Used to ask or refer to motels located in the surrounding area or nearby neighborhood. Common in questions when asking for recommendations or directions. 'Zona' means area/zone; can be formal or informal depending on context. You can replace 'motel' with other accommodation types (hotel, ostello) or change 'nella zona' to 'nelle vicinanze' (nearby).
target_language_example: Sai se c'è un buon motel nella zona?
native_language_example: Do you know if there's a good motel in the area?

meaning: search engine (website or tool that finds information online).
additional_notes: Used for web search services (e.g., Google, Bing). Literally 'engine of search'. Common in tech contexts and everyday speech when referring to searching the internet. Can also refer to internal search tools on a website.
target_language_example: Ho trovato la risposta usando un motore di ricerca.
native_language_example: I found the answer using a search engine.

meaning: I'm dying to / I really want (to do/have something).
additional_notes: An emphatic, colloquial way to say you really want or crave something. Usually followed by 'voglia di' + noun or verb (infinitive). Often used in informal spoken Italian. Literal image: 'I'm dying from (the desire)'.
target_language_example: Muoio dalla voglia di un gelato.
native_language_example: I'm dying to have an ice cream.

meaning: imperative 'move the' (singular, informal/plural depending on context) — command to move something (masculine singular noun follows).
additional_notes: Muovi is the (tu) imperative of muovere (to move). 'Muovi il' is followed by a masculine singular noun (e.g., muovi il tavolo). Used to tell someone directly to move an object. For polite/formal commands use 'muova il' (Lei) or plural 'muovete il' (voi). If telling a group formally, prefer 'muovano il' (Loro, rare).
target_language_example: Muovi il tavolo, per favore.
native_language_example: Move the table, please.

meaning: a wall of (used figuratively to mean a strong, sudden presence of something, often negative)
additional_notes: Literally 'wall of'. Commonly used figuratively in Italian to describe an overwhelming, impenetrable, or abrupt occurrence (e.g., 'muro di silenzio' = a wall of silence, meaning strong or complete silence; 'muro di calore' = wall of heat). Follows with a noun. Tone is neutral; usage is natural in both spoken and written Italian.
target_language_example: Quando ho chiesto spiegazioni, mi ha risposto con un muro di indifferenza.
native_language_example: When I asked for an explanation, they replied with a wall of indifference.

meaning: 'the museum is' (statement about the museum's state or condition).
additional_notes: Use before adjectives or past participles to describe the museum (e.g., aperto/chiuso, grande, moderno). In sentences it's simply the noun 'museo' + third-person singular of essere (è). Common in questions and statements about opening hours or condition: 'Il museo è aperto?' 'Il museo è chiuso oggi.'
target_language_example: Il museo è sempre chiuso il martedì.
native_language_example: The museum is always closed on Tuesdays.

meaning: classical music
additional_notes: Refers to Western art music tradition (e.g., Bach, Mozart, Beethoven) and more generally to orchestral, chamber, choral, or solo repertoire from Baroque, Classical, Romantic and later styles. Used like English: posso ascoltare musica classica / suonare musica classica. 'Musica' is feminine singular; adjectives follow gender/number (musica classica, musiche classiche).
target_language_example: Tom ascolta solamente musica classica.
native_language_example: Tom listens only to classical music.

meaning: a type or style of music for/associated with (something).
additional_notes: Used like 'musica da X' to mean music meant for or characteristic of a place, occasion, or purpose (e.g., musica da discoteca = music for the club; musica da chiesa = church music; musica da funerale = funeral music). Often followed by a noun indicating the setting or function. Not a fixed idiom — it's compositional.
target_language_example: Preferisco ascoltare musica da spiaggia in estate.
native_language_example: I prefer to listen to beach music in summer.

meaning: 'the birth of' or 'the origin/founding of'.
additional_notes: Used to indicate the birth of a person (literal) or the origin/founding/start of something (figurative, e.g., a country, idea, tradition). Followed by a noun or pronoun introduced by di + noun/pronoun (di vostro padre, di questo paese).
target_language_example: La nascita di mia sorella è stata una grande festa per la famiglia.
native_language_example: The birth of my sister was a big celebration for the family.

meaning: hide the
additional_notes: A verb phrase: nascondere = to hide; la is the feminine singular direct object pronoun or article ('the' before a feminine noun). In the examples 'nascondere la' appears before a feminine noun (la rotta) or with a following noun phrase (la realtà) or with a possessive idea ('la loro confusione' = their confusion). Use 'nascondere' with a direct object: nascondere la verità = hide the truth. If the object is not feminine singular, the article/pronoun changes (nascondere il, nascondere lo, nasconderli, nasconderla, etc.).
target_language_example: Hanno provato a nascondere la verità.
native_language_example: They tried to hide the truth.

meaning: 'hidden the' (past participle used with a plural masculine noun) — indicates someone hid something (plural or masculine noun).
additional_notes: Nascosto is the past participle of nascondere (to hide). Here it's used with the definite article i, so it appears before a plural masculine noun (i fiammiferi, i soldi, i contanti). In Italian spoken/written sentences you'd usually see the past participle after an auxiliary (ha/sono) or with a subject: e.g. 'Hai nascosto i fiammiferi?' or 'Ha nascosto i soldi'. The examples show transitive use: someone hides (has hidden) objects. For beginner learners: pay attention to the auxiliary (ha/hanno) and agreement when using past participles with avere (nascosto does not change for gender/number with avere).
target_language_example: Hai nascosto i documenti in un posto sicuro?
native_language_example: Did you hide the documents in a safe place?

meaning: has hidden the / hid the (feminine singular object).
additional_notes: Past participle 'nascosto' (from nascondere) used with a definite article + feminine noun (la ...) to say someone hid something specific: e.g. 'ha nascosto la scatola' = 'he/she hid the box'. Form changes with tense/person (hai nascosto, ha nascosto, avete nascosto). Often appears in questions about location: 'Dove hai nascosto la chiave?'
target_language_example: Hai nascosto la lettera sotto il letto?
native_language_example: Did you hide the letter under the bed?

meaning: past participle + article meaning 'hidden the' (e.g. 'has hidden the...').
additional_notes: This combines the past participle 'nascosto' (hidden) with the feminine singular definite article 'la' that precedes a feminine noun (la moneta, la verità, la chiave, la scatola). In the examples, verbs like 'ha nascosto' (he/she has hidden) or questions use the past participle to refer to something someone hid. For beginners: learn the verb nascondere (to hide) and remember agreement of articles with nouns; the past participle itself does not change for gender when used with avere (ha nascosto).
target_language_example: Marco ha nascosto la lettera sotto il libro.
native_language_example: Marco has hidden the letter under the book.

meaning: 'adhesive tape' or 'tape' (sticky tape used for sealing, wrapping, fixing).
additional_notes: Common, general term for rolls of sticky tape (like Scotch tape, parcel tape). Used in shops, offices, and homes. Can refer to different types (transparent tape, brown packing tape) — specify if needed (e.g., nastro adesivo trasparente, nastro da pacchi).
target_language_example: Hai del nastro adesivo per chiudere la scatola?
native_language_example: Do you have any adhesive tape to close the box?

meaning: born to / born for (used figuratively to express a purpose or destiny).
additional_notes: Combines nata (past participle of nascere, 'to be born') with per ('for/to') to say someone was 'born to' do something or be something. Used figuratively to express natural aptitude, destiny, or purpose (e.g., 'nata per cantare' = 'born to sing'). Remember to match gender/number: nata (feminine singular), nato (masculine), nati/nate (plural). Often followed by an infinitive verb or a noun phrase.
target_language_example: Sono nata per aiutare gli altri.
native_language_example: I was born to help others.

meaning: human nature; the typical qualities, instincts, or behaviors of humans.
additional_notes: Used to talk about what is natural or typical for people (e.g., instincts, desires, tendencies). Can be used in philosophical, literary, or everyday contexts. Often appears with adjectives (fondamentalmente buona — fundamentally good) or verbs (essere, fare a meno).
target_language_example: Secondo me la natura umana cerca sempre la compagnia.
native_language_example: In my opinion human nature always seeks company.

meaning: 'nature is' — used to describe qualities of nature (or someone's nature).
additional_notes: A simple subject + verb phrase: 'natura' (nature) as the subject and 'è' (is) as the verb. Usually followed by an adjective or noun phrase (e.g., 'La natura è bella' = 'Nature is beautiful'). Can also refer to a person's character when modified (e.g., 'la tua buona natura' = 'your good nature').
target_language_example: La natura è piena di colori in autunno.
native_language_example: Nature is full of colors in autumn.

meaning: notice it / realize it (referring back to something already mentioned)
additional_notes: This is part of the pronominal verb accorgersi (to notice/realize). 'Ne' refers to 'of it/about it' or 'about that' (something previously mentioned). In full forms you'd see 'se ne accorge' = 'he/she/it notices it' or 'ti/mi/ci se ne accorge' with other reflexive pronouns. Common in questions and exclamations: 'Non se ne accorge?' = 'Doesn't he/she notice it?'.
target_language_example: Non se ne accorge che il regalo è per lui?
native_language_example: Doesn't he realize that the gift is for him?

meaning: he/she/it will notice it / realize it
additional_notes: Verb accorgersi (to notice/realize) used with the reflexive pronoun 'si' and the particle 'ne' (referring to 'of it' or 'about it'). In the future tense for third person singular: 'si accorgerà' = 'he/she/it will notice'; with 'ne' placed before the verb: 'se ne accorgerà' = 'he/she/it will notice it/about it' or 'someone will notice'. 'Ne' often refers back to something already mentioned (it/the fact/of it). In spoken English this can be translated as 'he'll notice', 'she'll notice', 'they'll notice', or 'someone will notice'.
target_language_example: Non ti preoccupare, prima o poi se ne accorgerà.
native_language_example: Don't worry, sooner or later he/she/they will notice it.

meaning: I left (went away); I walked out.
additional_notes: Informal past tense of andarsene (to leave). Uses clitic pronouns: me (me/myself) + ne (away/from here). Commonly used to say you left a place or left with someone. Equivalent to 'me ne sono andato' in perfect tense. Gender/number can change (me ne andai = I left, passato remoto; me ne sono andato/a = present perfect).
target_language_example: Me ne andai prima che iniziasse la riunione.
native_language_example: I left before the meeting started.

meaning: (that) he/she/it would leave; (that) someone go away (subjunctive, polite or hypothetical)
additional_notes: Combines the reflexive pronoun se (himself/herself), the particle ne (away/from here/about it) and the verb andare in the imperfect subjunctive andalus form andasse. Often appears in clauses after verbs expressing desire, preference, doubt or hypothetical situations (e.g., voleva che..., preferirei che..., e se...). Use to talk about someone leaving or to suggest someone should go. Tone can be polite or indirect. Literal sense: 'would go away.'
target_language_example: Preferirei che se ne andasse prima che arrivi la riunione.
native_language_example: I'd prefer that he/she leave before the meeting starts.

meaning: 'you will leave (from here/of it) / you'll go away' (second person singular, future tense, with particle 'ne' meaning 'from here' or 'of it').
additional_notes: Combines the particle 'ne' (meaning 'of it', 'from there', or indicating movement away) with the future form 'andrai' (you will go). Common in questions and statements about someone leaving. In spoken Italian the full phrase often appears as 'te ne andrai' (with clitic 'te' for emphasis). Can also be used in contexts like 'after X, you will leave' (e.g. 'Finita la scuola, te ne andrai').
target_language_example: Quando avrò finito, te ne andrai senza dire niente?
native_language_example: When I'm finished, will you leave without saying anything?

meaning: 'I would leave (from here / of it) / I'd go away' — first person conditional of 'andarsene' with the particle 'ne' (indicating movement away from a place or situation).
additional_notes: Ne is a particle that often means 'from here/from there' or 'of it/about it' and combines with verbs of movement like 'andarsene' (to go away). 'Me ne andrei' literally = 'I would go away from here/from it' and is used to say you'd leave a place or situation. Commonly appears in conditional or hypothetical sentences (e.g., 'Se fossi in te, me ne andrei' = 'If I were you, I'd leave').
target_language_example: Se la festa non migliora, me ne andrei.
native_language_example: If the party doesn't get better, I'd leave.

meaning: I will leave (from here / of it) — 'me ne andrò' = 'I'll go away' or 'I'll leave (of it/from here)'.
additional_notes: This is the first-person singular future of the pronominal verb 'andarsene' (to go away/leave). 'Ne' is a particle meaning 'of it' or 'from here/about it' and moves before the verb with the pronoun 'me' (me + ne + andrò → me ne andrò). Use to say you'll leave a place or situation. Common in spoken and written Italian.
target_language_example: Se non mi ascoltate, me ne andrò.
native_language_example: If you don't listen to me, I will leave.

meaning: 'he/she/they left without (doing something)'.
additional_notes: This is a past tense construction with the verb andare (to go/leave) plus the pronoun 'ne' and 'senza' (without). 'Se ne andò senza...' means someone left without doing or saying something. 'Ne' here is a particle that often combines with 'andarsene' (to go away). Subject can change (io, tu, lui/lei, loro). You can replace the action after 'senza' with an infinitive (senza salutare), a noun (senza di me), or a clause (senza dire una parola).
target_language_example: Lei se ne andò senza spiegare niente.
native_language_example: She left without explaining anything.

meaning: 'I must (of it/of them)' or 'I have to (of it/of them)'; combines the partitive/pronoun 'ne' with the modal verb 'devo' (must/have to).
additional_notes: ne is a pronoun that replaces quantities or things introduced earlier (meaning 'of it', 'of them', 'some'). When placed before the conjugated verb, it comes before devo: 'ne devo' = 'I must [have/ buy/leave] of it/them' or 'I must have some'. In reflexive constructions with movement verbs, 'me ne devo andare' means 'I have to leave (from here)' — literally 'I must go away from it/from here'. Word order: object pronouns (ne, mi/me) come before devo. In questions the order stays the same: 'Me ne devo andare?' = 'Do I have to leave?'.
target_language_example: Ne devo comprare uno nuovo.
native_language_example: I have to buy a new one (of them).

meaning: what do you think (about it)
additional_notes: Used to ask someone's opinion about something already mentioned or suggested. Often appears in questions like "Cosa ne dici?" (What do you think?) or with suggestions: "Cosa ne dici se..." (How about if...). "Ne" refers back to the topic; you can change word order (e.g. "Tu che cosa ne dici?").
target_language_example: Cosa ne dici se andiamo al cinema stasera?
native_language_example: What do you think if we go to the cinema tonight?

meaning: How about (doing) — used to suggest playing something (e.g., a sport or game).
additional_notes: Common phrase for making a suggestion. Often appears as 'Che ne dici di...' or 'Cosa ne dici di...' followed by an infinitive (here 'giocare'). Can be used for activities beyond games (e.g., 'Che ne dici di uscire?'). Polite and neutral in tone.
target_language_example: Che ne dici di giocare a calcio domani?
native_language_example: How about playing soccer tomorrow?

meaning: How about a / What do you say to a (suggestion for something singular).
additional_notes: Used to make a suggestion or propose doing/trying something. Often appears as 'Che ne dici di una ...?' or 'Cosa ne dici di una ...?'. 'Ne' refers to the idea being proposed; 'una' agrees with a feminine singular noun (use 'un' for masculine). Common in spoken and polite conversation.
target_language_example: Che ne dici di una passeggiata?
native_language_example: How about a walk?

meaning: (in 'Che ne dite...?') 'What do you think about...?' or 'How about...?' (asking for opinions or suggestions)
additional_notes: Usually appears in the fixed question form 'Che ne dite di...?' when offering a suggestion or asking for others' opinions. Can be singular 'Che ne dici...?' (informal you) or plural/formal 'Che ne dite...?' (you plural). 'Ne' refers back to the idea mentioned; literal: 'of it/about it.'
target_language_example: Che ne dite di andare al cinema stasera?
native_language_example: How about going to the cinema tonight? / What do you think about going to the cinema tonight?

meaning: How about (having) a ...? / What do you think about a ...?
additional_notes: Common colloquial phrase used to make a suggestion or offer something to a group. Often appears as 'Che ne dite di...' or 'Cosa ne dite di...' followed by a noun (una birra, una partita, una canzone). 'Ne' refers to the idea/proposal; 'dite' is the 2nd-person plural of 'dire'.
target_language_example: Che ne dite di una passeggiata questo pomeriggio?
native_language_example: How about a walk this afternoon?

meaning: 'ne' refers to something already mentioned; 'fa' = 'does/makes' — together used in phrases like 'what do you do with it/that?', 'uses it', or 'make (of it)'.
additional_notes: The pronoun 'ne' replaces a previously mentioned thing or idea (meaning 'of it', 'about it', 'from it', or 'some of it'). 'Fa' is the third-person singular of 'fare' (to do/make). Depending on context, 'ne fa' can mean: • ask what someone does with something (Che se ne fa di quel casco? = What are they doing with that helmet?/What use is it to them?), • say someone uses something (La vittima ne fa uso? = Does the victim make use of it?), • tell someone to stop caring about something (non se ne fa niente = he/she/they do not care / nothing will come of it), or • form idioms like 'farne una regola' (make it a rule). Pay attention to reflexive/impersonal 'se' that often appears: 'se ne fa' or 'non se ne fa niente'.
target_language_example: Non se ne fa nulla: buttarlo o regalarlo?
native_language_example: They won't do anything with it: throw it away or give it away?

meaning: 'care about' or 'be concerned with' (used in negative/indifferent contexts: 'not care about' or 'who cares about').
additional_notes: Commonly appears in the fixed expression 'se ne frega (di)' or 'te ne frega (di)' to express indifference or lack of concern. Often used colloquially and can be rude when combined with strong language (e.g., 'che cazzo te ne frega'). 'Ne' refers back to the thing being cared about; word order: subject + 'se/te/gliene' + 'frega' + 'di' + object. To say someone cares, use 'gliene frega' or 'si frega' rarely — more natural is 'gli importa' or 'le importa'.
target_language_example: A me non me ne frega di quello che pensano.
native_language_example: I don't care about what they think.

meaning: I don't care / it doesn't matter to me.
additional_notes: Colloquial and often used in negative constructions with a pronoun (non me ne frega niente). Means 'I don't care at all' or 'it doesn't bother me'. Can be directed at others (Non te ne frega niente di...) to say 'you don't care about...'. Tone can be blunt or rude depending on context; common in spoken Italian.
target_language_example: Non me ne frega niente di quello che dicono.
native_language_example: I don't care at all about what they say.

meaning: 'I care about it' / 'it matters to me' (used with numbers/amounts: 'I care one [of them]')
additional_notes: Colloquial expression based on the verb fregare (here impersonal). Commonly appears in phrases like 'non me ne frega un' (I don't care at all) or 'me ne frega uno' (I care one — usually sarcastic). Alone as 'ne frega un' is incomplete; it needs a subject (e.g. 'a me') and often a negation. Used in spoken, informal Italian to indicate how much someone cares (often minimally).
target_language_example: A me non me ne frega un accidente di quella storia.
native_language_example: I don't care one bit about that story.

meaning: I don't care / I couldn't care less (strong, dismissive).
additional_notes: Informal and somewhat rude; expresses strong indifference or defiance. Often used alone (Me ne frego.) or after a statement to dismiss it (Non lo so, e me ne frego!). Literally contains 'ne' (about it/of it) but the whole phrase is idiomatic. Avoid in polite/formal contexts.
target_language_example: Se non ti va di venire, me ne frego e vado lo stesso.
native_language_example: If you don't want to come, I don't care and I'll go anyway.

meaning: 'has/have ever of it/about it' (used to ask or state whether someone has ever done something regarding something previously mentioned).
additional_notes: Ne is a pronoun replacing 'di + thing' or 'of it/them' (about it/them). 'Ha' is the 3rd-person singular of avere; in questions with Lei it can be formal 'you have'. 'Mai' means 'ever' (in negative sentences it becomes 'never' when combined with non). Typical patterns: 'Ne ha mai parlato?' = 'Have you/has he ever talked about it?' In negative: 'Non ne ha mai parlato.' = 'He/you/they have never spoken about it.' Word order: ne comes before the conjugated verb (ha) and mai follows it.
target_language_example: Ne ha mai parlato con il dottore?
native_language_example: Have you ever talked to the doctor about it?

meaning: 'you have the' used in fixed expressions like 'se ne hai il coraggio' = 'if you have the courage'
additional_notes: This structure combines 'ne' (referring back to something like 'courage' or 'right'), 'hai' (you have) and the definite article 'il' before a noun (e.g. 'coraggio', 'diritto'). Common in expressions: 'se ne hai il coraggio' (if you have the courage), 'non ne hai il coraggio' (you don't have the courage), 'non ne hai il diritto' (you don't have the right). 'Ne' points back to the quality/thing; word order is standard: 'se ne hai il + noun'.
target_language_example: Se ne hai il coraggio, dillo a suo padre.
native_language_example: If you have the courage, tell his father.

meaning: 'I have never (of it/them) / I've never' (referring back to something mentioned)
additional_notes: Combines pronoun 'ne' (about it/them/of them/of it), auxiliary 'ho' (I have), and 'mai' (never). Used to say you've never done, seen, tasted, heard of, or doubted something mentioned before. English often omits a direct translation of 'ne' and uses 'of it/them' or nothing: e.g. "I have never tried one" or "I've never heard of it." Word order: 'Non ne ho mai…' or shorter 'Ne ho mai…' in some responses. 'Ne' must refer to a previously mentioned noun or idea.
target_language_example: Non ne ho mai provato uno.
native_language_example: I've never tried one.

meaning: 'I have seen (one/of them/of it)'.
additional_notes: Ne is a pronoun that replaces a quantity or a thing introduced earlier (of it/them/of them/of it). Combined with ho visto (I have seen) it usually means 'I have seen one' or 'I have seen some/of them/its [something]'. The exact translation depends on context: if referring to a singular item, translate as 'I've seen one'; if referring to an unspecified part or reflection (as in example 2), translate as 'I've seen it/of it'.
target_language_example: Ne ho visto tre al mercato la settimana scorsa.
native_language_example: I saw three of them at the market last week.

meaning: 'what do you think about it' (asking someone's opinion).
additional_notes: Often appears in the set phrase che te ne pare? / che ve ne pare? / cosa te ne pare? The pronoun 'ne' refers to 'about it' or 'of it' (something already mentioned). 'Te' (informal you singular) or 've' (informal/plural you) mark the person asked. Use 'che ne pare?' when context makes the referent clear. Formal alternative: 'che cosa ne pensa?'
target_language_example: Che te ne pare del film che abbiamo visto ieri?
native_language_example: What do you think about the movie we watched yesterday?

meaning: 'what do you think about/of (the)...' (asks for someone's opinion about a specific thing)
additional_notes: This is a shortened/informal structure used in questions. Full forms include 'Che ne pensi della ...?' or 'Cosa ne pensi della ...?'. 'Ne' refers back to the topic already mentioned or implied; 'della' = 'of the' (feminine singular) and will change to 'del/degli/dello/delle' depending on the noun's gender/number. Use to ask someone's opinion about a person, thing, idea, or situation.
target_language_example: Che ne pensi della città?
native_language_example: What do you think of the city?

meaning: 'you will regret it' (informal warning/prediction)
additional_notes: From the verb pentirsi (to regret). The pronoun 'ne' refers to the thing or action being regretted (about it/of it). Commonly used to warn someone or predict they'll regret a choice. Often appears with 'te' (te ne pentirai) meaning 'you will regret it'. Tone can be strong depending on context (friendly reassurance or sharp warning).
target_language_example: Se non studi ora, te ne pentirai più tardi.
native_language_example: If you don't study now, you'll regret it later.

meaning: 'I knew about it' (used in negative phrases to mean 'I didn't know about it').
additional_notes: Often appears in negative constructions with 'non' plus 'niente' or 'nulla': 'Non ne sapevo niente/nulla' = 'I didn't know anything about it.' The particle 'ne' refers back to whatever topic or thing was mentioned earlier (about it/of it). In positive sentences 'ne sapevo' can mean 'I knew about it' but is most commonly heard in the negative form in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Non ne sapevo nulla fino a ieri.
native_language_example: I didn't know anything about it until yesterday.

meaning: you have
additional_notes: Used with tu in the passato prossimo of reflexive or pronominal verbs. Here sei is the auxiliary for “you,” and ne is a pronoun that is often part of the verb itself. The exact meaning depends on the past participle that follows: te ne sei andato/a = “you left / went away,” te ne sei accorto/a = “you noticed it / realized it.”
target_language_example: Quando te ne sei accorto?
native_language_example: When did you notice it?

meaning: I left (from there/of it); I went away.
additional_notes: This is the first-person singular feminine past perfect/perfect tense of 'andarsene' (to leave/go away). 'Ne' refers to 'from there' or 'of it' and combines with 'andare' + the reflexive particle 'se' (me ne sono andata). Use 'me ne sono andato' for masculine speakers. Often appears with pronoun 'me' (me ne sono andata) or without subject pronoun (Me ne sono andata.).
target_language_example: Me ne sono andata prima che iniziasse la riunione.
native_language_example: I left before the meeting started.

meaning: they left (of them); they have gone away.
additional_notes: Ne refers back to a group or quantity mentioned earlier (of them / of it). 'Sono andati' is the present perfect (passato prossimo) of 'andare' for a plural, masculine or mixed-gender subject. Use 'ne sono andate' if the group is all feminine. Common in sentences like 'Dei libri? Ne sono andati tre' or 'I ragazzi? Ne sono andati due.'
target_language_example: I ragazzi erano in classe, ma alla fine ne sono andati due.
native_language_example: The boys were in class, but in the end two of them left.

meaning: they all left / everyone has gone away
additional_notes: A full sentence typically uses the clitic se (or se ne) + essere + past participle (se ne sono andati) to mean 'have left' or 'went away'. 'Ne' here emphasizes 'from here/from the place' or is part of the pronominal verb 'andarsene' (to go away). 'Tutti' means 'all/everyone'. Use 'se ne sono andati tutti' for a mixed/generic group (masculine or plural); use 'se ne sono andate tutte' for an all-female group. In spoken Italian the subject is often omitted because it's clear from context.
target_language_example: Se ne sono andati tutti prima della fine della festa.
native_language_example: They all left before the end of the party.

meaning: I completely (forgot about it/them) / I totally (lost track of it/them).
additional_notes: Used with verbs of forgetting or losing track (dimenticare, scordare). 'Me ne sono completamente...' literally: 'I of it am completely...' — 'me' = to/for me, 'ne' refers to 'of it' or 'about it', 'sono' is auxiliary for past tense (passato prossimo). Commonly followed by a past participle (dimenticato/a, scordato/a). Gender and number agreement applies to the participle when appropriate (dimenticato/dimenticata/dimenticati/dimenticate).
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, me ne sono completamente dimenticato.
native_language_example: Sorry, I completely forgot about it.

meaning: 'is leaving' or 'is going away' (right now; progressive)
additional_notes: A present progressive construction meaning someone is in the process of leaving. 'Se ne sta andando' combines the reflexive particle 'se', the pronoun 'ne' (here roughly 'away/from here'), and 'sta andando' (is going). Common in spoken Italian. Can be shortened (e.g. 'se ne va'). Use with a name or subject: 'Tom se ne sta andando' = 'Tom is leaving now.'
target_language_example: Sta piovendo e Tom se ne sta andando via adesso.
native_language_example: It's raining and Tom is leaving away right now.

meaning: was leaving (just then); was in the process of going away
additional_notes: Combines the pronoun 'ne' (meaning 'away from here' / 'of it/them' depending on context) + imperfect progressive 'stava andando' (was going). Used to say someone was in the act of leaving. Common in past narrative: "sono arrivato proprio quando se ne stava andando" = "I arrived just as he/she was leaving." 'Se' is part of the reflexive/pronominal verb 'andarsene' (to go away).
target_language_example: Sono arrivata proprio quando se ne stava andando.
native_language_example: I arrived right when he/she was leaving.

meaning: go away
additional_notes: Usually appears as te ne vai, from the verb andarsene, meaning "to go away" or "to leave." The ne is part of this expression and normally isn’t translated separately in English. It can describe simply leaving, or be used more forcefully as "go away."
target_language_example: Te ne vai già?
native_language_example: Are you leaving already?

meaning: 'it's worth it' (literally: 'it is worth it of it')
additional_notes: This is a shortened, colloquial fragment of the full expression "ne vale la pena" meaning "it's worth it" or "it's worth the trouble/effort." Native speakers often drop "pena" in casual speech or writing when context makes the meaning clear, but the complete phrase is safer for learners. Use with third-person singular verbs (vale) and the particle "ne" which refers back to the thing or action discussed (equivalent to 'of it' / 'about it').
target_language_example: Se hai tempo per visitare il museo, ne vale la — è bellissimo.
native_language_example: If you have time to visit the museum, it's worth it — it's beautiful.

meaning: 'it was worth it' (literally: 'it was worth the pain/effort')
additional_notes: Commonly used as 'ne valeva la pena' to say something was worthwhile despite costs or effort. 'Ne' refers back to the situation or thing previously mentioned. Can appear in statements and questions. Often used in past tense to evaluate an action or choice.
target_language_example: Ho studiato tutta la notte, ma ne valeva la pena.
native_language_example: I studied all night, but it was worth it.

meaning: 'I want (of/from) it' or 'I want (to) of it' — used with the pronoun 'ne' to refer back to something previously mentioned; often means 'I want any/that/of it' or in negative sentences 'I don't want it/any of it'.
additional_notes: Ne is a clitic pronoun that replaces a quantity or a part introduced earlier (di + something) or 'of it/them'. 'Voglio' is the first-person singular of volere (to want). Together 'ne voglio' literally means 'I want some/of it'. In negative sentences 'non ne voglio' = 'I don't want any (of it)'. You can add adverbs: 'non ne voglio più' = 'I don't want it anymore'. Context determines whether 'ne' refers to quantity ('some') or to a thing previously mentioned.
target_language_example: Non ne voglio più; buttiamolo via.
native_language_example: I don't want any more of it; throw it away.

meaning: wanted to leave (from there); wanted to go away
additional_notes: Se ne voleva andare combines: 'volere' (to want) in the imperfect ('voleva'), the verb 'andare' (to go), and the particles 'se' + 'ne' which together indicate leaving from a place or situation ('to go away from it/from there'). Common in reported speech (he/she said they wanted to leave). Use tense as needed (e.g., 'se ne vuole andare' present, 'se ne è voluto andare' past).
target_language_example: Mi ha detto che se ne voleva andare prima della riunione.
native_language_example: He told me he wanted to leave before the meeting.

meaning: he/she left (from there); has gone away
additional_notes: Used with third-person singular (often with a name or pronoun before it). The particle 'ne' emphasizes movement away from a place or situation (roughly 'away from here/there/from it'). Common in conversational Italian. For female subjects use 'se n'è andata' (agreement), and plural 'se ne sono andati/e'.
target_language_example: Dopo la lite, Marco se ne è andato senza guardare indietro.
native_language_example: After the argument, Marco went away without looking back.

meaning: denied (doing something) / denied that one did something.
additional_notes: Used with a verb in the infinitive to report that someone denies having done or knowing something. Common in reported speech: 'Ha negato di + [infinitive]'. English equivalents: 'he/she denied (having) ...' or 'denied that ...'.
target_language_example: Luca ha negato di aver visto il film.
native_language_example: Luca denied having seen the movie.

meaning: lately; in recent times.
additional_notes: Used to talk about events or states that have occurred or changed during a recent period (days, weeks, months). Equivalent to 'recently' or 'lately' in English. Can be placed at the start of a sentence (often followed by a comma) or before the verb.
target_language_example: Negli ultimi tempi ho dormito meno del solito.
native_language_example: Lately I've been sleeping less than usual.

meaning: literally "the shop is" — the construction used to describe or ask about a shop (its location, status, characteristic).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom but the noun negozio (shop/store) followed by the verb è (is). Use to state facts about a shop: its opening hours, location, condition, price, or to ask what kind of shop it is. In questions the word order may change (Che tipo di negozio è quello?).
target_language_example: Il negozio è aperto dalle nove alle diciotto.
native_language_example: The shop is open from nine to six.

meaning: 'in case' / 'if (happens that)' — used to talk about a possible event or as a conditional phrase.
additional_notes: Commonly used to introduce a precaution, hypothetical, or conditional clause. Can be followed by a clause with indicative or subjunctive depending on formality and likelihood (e.g., 'nel caso tu venga...' uses subjunctive). In informal speech it can also stand alone as 'nel caso' meaning 'just in case' or 'by the way / in case you didn't know' depending on context. Often interchangeable with 'in caso (che)'.
target_language_example: Porta un ombrello nel caso piova.
native_language_example: Bring an umbrella in case it rains.

meaning: in the center of (the)...
additional_notes: Used to say something is located in the central area of a place (usually a city or town). 'Nel' = in + il (preposition + definite article). 'Centro' = center. 'Della' = of the (feminine singular). Follow with a feminine noun like città (nel centro della città). Can be used more broadly (nel centro della piazza, nel centro della città).
target_language_example: Il ristorante è nel centro della città.
native_language_example: The restaurant is in the center of the city.

meaning: in the middle of (the) — used for times, especially 'in the middle of the night'.
additional_notes: Literally 'in the heart of the'. Commonly used with time expressions (e.g., 'notte') to mean deep/center of that time period (e.g., late at night). Often conveys suddenness or inconvenience (waking/calling someone). Use with definite article matching the noun (nel cuore della notte, nel cuore del giorno).
target_language_example: Mi hai chiamato nel cuore della notte.
native_language_example: You called me in the middle of the night.

meaning: 'in the meantime' / 'meanwhile'.
additional_notes: Used to indicate something that happens or should happen during the time between two events. Can be placed at the beginning of a sentence (often followed by a comma) or inside a sentence. Neutral register and very common.
target_language_example: Posso cucinare io; nel frattempo puoi apparecchiare la tavola.
native_language_example: I can cook; in the meantime you can set the table.

meaning: 'at the moment when' / 'the moment in which'.
additional_notes: Used to introduce the precise time or instant when something happens. Often followed by 'cui' or 'che' + clause (e.g. 'nel momento in cui...'). Can be used for both literal and figurative moments (first meeting, realization, death, etc.).
target_language_example: Ci ho capito tutto nel momento in cui me l'hai spiegato.
native_language_example: I understood everything at the moment when you explained it to me.

meaning: deeply; in the depths (emotionally or mentally).
additional_notes: Used to describe feelings, thoughts or character that lie deep inside someone (emotionally or mentally). Commonly translated as "deep down" or "deeply" in English. Can modify verbs (mi ha ferito nel profondo = it hurt me deeply) or describe a person's true nature (nel profondo è buono = deep down he is good).
target_language_example: Nel profondo sa che ha fatto la cosa giusta.
native_language_example: Deep down he knows he did the right thing.

meaning: in the photograph / in the photo.
additional_notes: Used to point to or describe something or someone that appears inside a photo. 'Nella' = 'in the' (feminine singular) + 'fotografia' (photo). Common in questions (e.g., asking if you know the person shown) and descriptions (e.g., who is smiling in the photo).
target_language_example: Chi è la donna nella fotografia?
native_language_example: Who is the woman in the photograph?

meaning: intended to mean 'in the apartment/door next to (ours)', but note the phrase contains a spelling mistake.
additional_notes: This entry preserves the user-provided misspelling 'accando'. Correct Italian is 'nella porta accanto alla'. 'Porta' can colloquially refer to an apartment/door number in a building. More natural alternatives: 'nell'appartamento accanto (al/alla nostro/a)', 'accanto a', 'di fianco a', or 'vicino a'. Common verbs: abitare, vivere. If you intend to be grammatically correct, replace 'accando' with 'accanto'.
target_language_example: Lei abita nella porta accando alla nostra.
native_language_example: She lives in the apartment next to ours.

meaning: in the hands of; under the control, care, or influence of someone or something.
additional_notes: Used to say that a person or thing is under someone else's control, protection, responsibility, or influence. Can be literal (physically in someone's hands) or figurative (entrusted to, dependent on, or at the mercy of). Common with people, groups, or abstract forces (e.g., Dio). Often preceded by a pronoun (sono/siamo/sei nelle mani di...).
target_language_example: Non voglio lasciare i bambini nelle mani di estranei.
native_language_example: I don't want to leave the children in the hands of strangers.

meaning: 'nero' = black; 'è' = is. Together they form the predicate 'is black' (verb 'to be' + adjective) used after a noun or pronoun.
additional_notes: Not an idiom — simply the adjective nero (which agrees in gender/number: nero/nera/neri/nere) with the third-person singular of essere (è). In normal declarative word order you usually see '... è nero' (noun + è + nero). The sequence 'nero è' can appear in specific constructions (e.g. contrast, inversion, apposition, or within a larger phrase) or when the clause fragment ends with 'nero è'. Examples may include proper names, emphasis, or part of a longer sentence. 'Il lavoro nero' is a fixed compound meaning 'undeclared/illegal work' and when followed by 'è' yields 'Il lavoro nero è...'.
target_language_example: Il lavoro nero è un problema serio.
native_language_example: Il lavoro nero è un problema serio. (Undeclared work is a serious problem.)

meaning: nobody to (do something) / no one to (help, etc.)
additional_notes: Used before an infinitive introduced by 'ad' (a variant of 'a' used before verbs) to say there is nobody available to perform an action for someone. Common in spoken and written Italian: 'nessuno ad aiutarla' = 'no one to help her.' You can also see 'nessuno a' instead of 'nessuno ad' in many contexts; 'ad' appears before vowels for euphony.
target_language_example: Non ha nessuno ad aiutarla con i bagagli.
native_language_example: She has no one to help her with the luggage.

meaning: nobody was / no one was
additional_notes: Combines 'nessuno' (nobody/no one) with the imperfect tense of 'essere' (era). Used to describe states or abilities in the past (e.g., nobody was able to, nobody was interested, nobody was rich). Often followed by an adjective, past participle, infinitive construction (in grado di + infinitive), or a clause introduced by 'che' or 'a'.
target_language_example: Nessuno era in grado di risolvere il problema.
native_language_example: No one was able to solve the problem.

meaning: nobody was in / no one was (at) home or inside
additional_notes: Common informal phrase used to say that no person was present at a location (often followed by a place: in casa, in ufficio, in stanza). Can be used in past descriptions (imperfetto) to describe a general situation in the past. Context determines the exact English translation: 'in' is short for 'in casa/ufficio' or 'in quella stanza'.
target_language_example: Ieri, quando siamo passati, nessuno era in casa.
native_language_example: Yesterday, when we passed by, nobody was home.

meaning: nobody cares / no one cares
additional_notes: Used to say that something is unimportant to people in general. Often appears as 'a nessuno importa (di) ...' + clause or noun. Can be blunt or rude depending on context; stronger versions add swear words (e.g. 'a nessuno importa un cazzo'). Common in spoken Italian to dismiss concerns or feelings.
target_language_example: A nessuno importa di quello che dici.
native_language_example: Nobody cares about what you say.

meaning: no one (cares/about) what / nobody (knows) what
additional_notes: This sequence combines 'nessuno' (no one) with 'quello che' (what/that which). Used to say that nobody cares about, knows, or was told something. Often appears in clauses with verbs like importare, dire, raccontare, confessare. Word order: 'a nessuno quello che...' or 'a nessuno quello che + verb/phrase'. In spoken Italian you may also hear 'a nessuno quello che' shortened to 'a nessuno quel che'.
target_language_example: Non ho detto a nessuno quello che mi hai raccontato.
native_language_example: I didn't tell anyone what you told me.

meaning: 'no one' (with reflexive/partitive particle 'se ne' indicating leaving, noticing, or taking care of something).
additional_notes: Nessuno means 'no one'. In the example sentences it appears with the clitic particles se/ne (se ne) which together modify verbs like andarsene (to go away), accorgersene (to notice), and occuparsi (to take care of). The full verbal idea is often split: e.g. "nessuno se ne è occupato" = "no one took care of it". Word order: nessuno + se ne + verb (or auxiliary + past participle). Useful with verbs that require the pronominal particles se/ne.
target_language_example: Nessuno se ne è accorto quando è successo.
native_language_example: No one noticed when it happened.

meaning: snow in (a time or season) — used to say when snow occurs or where someone is (on the snow).
additional_notes: Often appears with a month or season after 'in' (e.g., 'in gennaio', 'in inverno') to indicate when snow falls. In sentence 5 it combines with a location-like phrase ('sulla neve in costume da bagno') where 'in' introduces what someone is wearing/doing while on the snow. Common pattern: 'neve in + [time period]'.
target_language_example: In montagna c'è spesso molta neve in inverno.
native_language_example: In the mountains there is often a lot of snow in winter.

meaning: nothing to do with; nothing to see (no relation)
additional_notes: Used to say that two things are unrelated or that something has no connection/relevance to something else. Often appears in negative comparisons like "non ha niente a che vedere con..." (has nothing to do with...). Can be followed by "con" + noun or clause. Informal/neutral register.
target_language_example: La sua opinione non ha niente a che vedere con i fatti.
native_language_example: His opinion has nothing to do with the facts.

meaning: I have nothing to tell you / I have nothing to say to you.
additional_notes: Common phrase used to say you have no information, comment, or response for the other person. Can be neutral (no new info) or slightly dismissive depending on tone and context. Word-for-word: 'nothing to tell you'. Often used with pronoun (ti) — 'dirti' = 'to tell you'.
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, in questo momento non ho niente da dirti.
native_language_example: I'm sorry, at the moment I have nothing to tell you.

meaning: 'nothing at all' or 'absolutely nothing'.
additional_notes: An emphatic repetition used to stress complete absence of something. Common in spoken Italian; can be used alone as a short answer. Tone can be slightly informal or conversational. Equivalent to 'niente' but stronger.
target_language_example: Ho cercato ovunque, ma non ho trovato niente di niente.
native_language_example: I searched everywhere, but I found absolutely nothing.

meaning: 'not bad' / 'pretty good'.
additional_notes: Common informal phrase used to give a modest positive evaluation (of something, someone, an idea, performance). Can be standalone as a short response. Tone ranges from neutral to mildly approving depending on context and intonation.
target_language_example: Hai passato l'esame? — Sì, niente male.
native_language_example: Did you pass the exam? — Yes, not bad.

meaning: we play (we are playing).
additional_notes: First-person plural present tense of the verb giocare (noi = we). Used to say that a group including the speaker plays a sport or game. Often followed by 'a' + the sport (e.g. a calcio, a basket) or by the name of the game. Can indicate a habitual action ('we play every Saturday') or a present/near-future plan ('we are playing this afternoon').
target_language_example: Noi giochiamo a tennis ogni domenica.
native_language_example: We play tennis every Sunday.

meaning: we often play (we often play [a game/sport]).
additional_notes: A present-tense, first-person-plural phrase: noi = we, giochiamo = (we) play, spesso = often. Commonly followed by a game or sport introduced with a/alla/ai (e.g. a carte, a tennis) or no preposition when context is clear. Can be used with insieme/assieme for 'together' (optional).
target_language_example: Noi giochiamo spesso a calcio al parco.
native_language_example: We often play soccer at the park.

meaning: we like (something) — incorrect; standard form is 'ci piace' or 'a noi piace' for emphasis.
additional_notes: Italian uses an indirect-object construction for 'like': literally 'to (us) it pleases.' The correct neutral form is 'ci piace' (we like it). 'A noi piace' adds emphasis ('we, we like'), and 'noi piace' without the preposition 'a' is ungrammatical in standard Italian. Use 'ci piacciono' for plural things (we like them). Example: 'Ci piace il gelato.'
target_language_example: A noi piace il gelato, ma ci piacciono anche i sorbetti.
native_language_example: We like ice cream, but we also like sorbets.

meaning: we (female speakers) ourselves; ourselves (reflexive/emphatic, feminine plural)
additional_notes: Used when the group speaking is all female (or identifying as female). Combines 'noi' (we) with the feminine plural reflexive/emphatic pronoun 'stesse' to emphasize that the action is done by ourselves. For mixed-gender or all-male groups use 'noi stessi'. Common in reflexive verbs (ci prendiamo cura di noi stesse) or for emphasis (lo facemmo noi stesse = we did it ourselves).
target_language_example: Abbiamo riparato la macchina noi stesse.
native_language_example: We repaired the car ourselves.

meaning: 'ourselves' (reflexive/emphatic pronoun for 'we')
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that the action or state involves the speaker and others (we). Functions as a reflexive or emphatic pronoun after verbs or prepositions: e.g. doing something ourselves (noi stessi) or talking to ourselves. In Italian, 'noi' = we; 'stessi' agrees in gender/number (noi stessi for a mixed/male group, noi stesse for an all-female group).
target_language_example: Abbiamo risolto il problema noi stessi.
native_language_example: We solved the problem ourselves.

meaning: we three / the three of us
additional_notes: Used to refer specifically to a group of three people that includes the speaker. Common in spoken Italian. Can be used as subject or object (e.g., 'Siamo noi tre' = 'It's the three of us' or 'parlava di noi tre' = 'he/she was talking about the three of us').
target_language_example: Noi tre andremo al cinema domani.
native_language_example: The three of us will go to the cinema tomorrow.

meaning: 'the name that' or 'name which' — used to introduce or refer to a specific name.
additional_notes: Combines nome (name) + che (that/which). Used to point to or describe a particular name (e.g., the name someone uses, inherits, or that appears somewhere). Common in relative clauses: 'il nome che...' = 'the name that...'. Word order may vary in Italian; context determines whether it refers to a name someone has, uses, or that is written/specified.
target_language_example: Il nome che uso sui social è MarcoRossi.
native_language_example: The name that I use on social media is MarcoRossi.

meaning: common name; a name that many people share (first name or surname).
additional_notes: Used to ask or state whether a given personal name is widespread in a place or among people. 'Nome' = name, 'comune' = common. Can refer to first names or family names depending on context. Example questions often use prepositions: 'nel tuo paese' (in your country), 'dove abiti?' (where you live).
target_language_example: Marco è un nome comune in Italia?
native_language_example: Is Marco a common name in Italy?

meaning: 'the name of this' or 'this one's name'.
additional_notes: A simple possessive phrase made of nome (name) + di (of) + questo (this). Used to ask or give the name of a nearby or just-mentioned thing or person. In natural speech Italians often use 'come si chiama?' for people or 'come si chiama questo?' to ask 'what is this called?'. For objects you can also say 'il nome di questo è...' or more naturally 'questo si chiama...'.
target_language_example: Qual è il nome di questo animale?
native_language_example: What is the name of this animal?

meaning: the name of this game
additional_notes: A simple noun phrase used to ask for or state the title/name of a game. Common in contexts like asking someone what a game is called or pointing out the game's name. Can be used with verbs like "qual è" (What is) or "come si chiama" (what is called).
target_language_example: Qual è il nome di questo gioco?
native_language_example: What is the name of this game?

meaning: a name for the (masculine noun); used when asking or talking about choosing a name for something or someone (masculine).
additional_notes: Commonly appears in questions about deciding a name: 'un nome per il gatto' (a name for the cat) or 'un nome per il bebè' (a name for the baby). The phrase uses the masculine definite article 'il' because the noun that follows is masculine (gatto, bebè). If the noun is feminine, use 'la' (nome per la...). Often shortened in speech to 'un nome per...'.
target_language_example: Hai un nome per il cane?
native_language_example: Do you have a name for the dog?

meaning: will not go / will not work / will not succeed (future tense negative of andare)
additional_notes: Non andrà is the future tense negative of andare (to go). Depending on context, it can mean someone/something 'will not go' (physically), 'will not attend', or metaphorically 'will not work/succeed'. The subject is usually third person (lui/lei/esso) but can refer to things or events. Informal or formal usage depends on context; it's neutral language.
target_language_example: Se non studi, il piano non andrà.
native_language_example: If you don't study, the plan will not work.

meaning: don't give up; to not surrender or quit.
additional_notes: Negative form of the reflexive verb 'arrendersi' (to give up/surrender). Often used as advice, encouragement, or general statement: can appear as an infinitive (non arrendersi), in reported speech (di non arrendersi), or as an imperative (non arrenderti). Common in motivational contexts.
target_language_example: La cosa più importante è non arrendersi anche quando è difficile.
native_language_example: The most important thing is not to give up even when it's difficult.

meaning: doesn't listen (to); is not listening
additional_notes: Negative form of 'ascoltare' used for third person (he/she/it/you formal) or as a general statement. Can mean 'doesn't listen' habitually (e.g. 'non ascolta mai' = never listens) or 'is not listening' in the moment. Often followed by a direct object or preposition 'a' when specifying whom/what is not being listened to (e.g. 'non ascolta sua madre' or 'non ascolta nessuno').
target_language_example: Lui non ascolta quando gli parlo.
native_language_example: He doesn't listen when I talk to him.

meaning: 'not to listen' or 'to ignore (someone or something)'.
additional_notes: Used to tell someone not to pay attention to what another person says or to indicate someone is ignoring advice/words. Can be literal (not hearing) or figurative (ignoring, dismissing). Often followed by a clause (ciò che, quello che) or direct object (quelle stronzate) or reflexive pronoun (non ascoltare i miei consigli).
target_language_example: Non ascoltare chi ti dice di mollare.
native_language_example: Don't listen to anyone who tells you to give up.

meaning: if I didn't have
additional_notes: Usually appears in hypothetical sentences, especially after se: se non avessi... = 'if I/you didn't have...'. Avessi is the imperfect subjunctive of avere, so the subject can be io or tu depending on context.
target_language_example: Se non avessi tempo, te lo direi subito.
native_language_example: If I didn't have time, I would tell you right away.

meaning: you (plural) do not have the (right/permission).
additional_notes: Commonly starts sentences denying someone permission or right. 'Non avete' is the 2nd-person plural of 'avere' (you have not). 'Il' is the masculine singular definite article and usually followed by a noun like 'diritto' (right). In everyday English this translates as 'you don't have the right' or 'you don't have the permission.' Can be adapted to other nouns: e.g. 'Non avete il permesso...' Note: tone can be firm or confrontational depending on context.
target_language_example: Non avete il permesso di entrare qui.
native_language_example: You don't have permission to enter here.

meaning: 'didn't have the' (masculine singular), used to say someone lacked something or a quality/feeling.
additional_notes: Literal negative past form of avere (aveva) + definite article il. Used for physical objects (non aveva il resto — didn't have the change) and abstract nouns/qualities (non aveva il coraggio — didn't have the courage). Context determines translation; often translates as "didn't have" or "didn't possess". For feminine nouns change il to la (non aveva la) and for plurals use i/ le (non aveva i/le).
target_language_example: Non aveva il permesso di entrare.
native_language_example: He didn't have the permission to enter.

meaning: not to drink / don't drink (depending on context).
additional_notes: Used either as an infinitive verb phrase meaning 'to not drink' (e.g., Ho deciso di non bere = I decided not to drink) or as an imperative negative 'don't drink' (e.g., Non bere dalla bottiglia = Don't drink from the bottle). Context and sentence structure determine whether it's a command or a statement about not drinking.
target_language_example: Per favore, non bere alcolici stasera.
native_language_example: Please don't drink alcohol tonight.

meaning: I don't understand
additional_notes: Common first-person present negative of capire (to understand). Used to express lack of comprehension about a situation, statement, or reason. Can be followed by a clause (e.g., "non capisco perché..."), an object, or used alone. The second example includes strong vulgar emphasis ("un cazzo")—avoid in polite contexts.
target_language_example: Non capisco perché è successo questo.
native_language_example: I don't understand why this happened.

meaning: I can't (do it) / I am not able to (do it).
additional_notes: Common colloquial phrase: 'ci' refers to a previously mentioned action or situation (it/there), and 'posso' is the first-person singular of 'potere' (can/to be able to). Often used to refuse or say you can't manage something. Full forms include 'non ci posso andare' (I can't go there) or 'non ci posso riuscire' (I can't manage it). Tone ranges from neutral to apologetic depending on context.
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, non ci posso venire stasera.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can't come there/I'm not able to come tonight.

meaning: you (plural) don't believe
additional_notes: Second-person plural form of 'non credere' (voi). Used to tell or ask a group of people that they do not believe something. Can be a statement ('you don't believe') or, with question intonation and/or a question mark, a question ('don't you believe...?'). In informal regions Italians often use 'voi' or 'voi non...' but spoken forms may vary (e.g., 'non credete?' or 'non credete voi?').
target_language_example: Non credete a tutto quello che leggete online.
native_language_example: You (plural) don't believe everything you read online.

meaning: don't tell her
additional_notes: A negative imperative phrase: non + infinitive (dire) + indirect object pronoun (le = to her). Used to tell someone not to tell or say something to a female person. Can appear with niente/nulla (nothing) or with a direct object implied. Word order: in modern spoken Italian you often hear 'non dirle' or 'di non dirle' after verbs like 'dire di' (e.g. 'mi ha detto di non dirle').
target_language_example: Mi ha chiesto di non dirle la verità.
native_language_example: He asked me not to tell her the truth.

meaning: don't argue / do not discuss (imperative or negative infinitive)
additional_notes: Used to tell someone not to argue with someone or not to discuss a topic. Can be a general instruction (non discutere di X = don't discuss X) or a direct command (Non discutere! / Non discutere con me!). Tone can be neutral or forceful depending on context and punctuation.
target_language_example: Non discutere con me, per favore.
native_language_example: Don't argue with me, please.

meaning: you shouldn't
additional_notes: Negative form of dovreste, from dovere. It is used with voi to give advice, warnings, or mild criticism. In a question, it can mean "shouldn't you...?" to express expectation.
target_language_example: Non dovreste uscire senza cappotto.
native_language_example: You shouldn't go out without a coat.

meaning: 'was not at' or 'wasn't in/at (a place)'.
additional_notes: A negated past-tense phrase using essere (non era = he/she/it was not). Followed by a place or location (a + noun) or by a question tag. Common in spoken and written Italian to say someone wasn't somewhere: e.g. non era a casa, non era a scuola. If referring to 'I' or 'you' change verb: non ero, non eri, etc.
target_language_example: Maria non era a lavoro ieri.
native_language_example: Maria wasn't at work yesterday.

meaning: was not in / was not (able) to (depending on context).
additional_notes: This phrase combines the negation 'non' + past imperfect of 'essere' ('era') + 'in'. Meaning depends on what follows: often part of 'non era in grado di...' (= 'was not able to...') to express inability in the past. It can also appear literally to say someone 'was not in' (in a place) when followed by a location or context.
target_language_example: Non era in grado di finire il lavoro ieri.
native_language_example: He/she was not able to finish the work yesterday.

meaning: we were not (or we weren't).
additional_notes: Negative past-tense form of essere (to be) for 'noi' (we). Used to say something the group did not do or was not. Can be followed by adjectives, nouns, prepositional phrases or subordinate clauses. Pronunciation: non e-RAH-voh-mah.
target_language_example: Non eravamo pronti per la pioggia.
native_language_example: We weren't ready for the rain.

meaning: not be
additional_notes: Literally the negative infinitive of essere. It is often used after another verb, especially modal verbs: potrebbe non essere = 'might not be'. With tu, Italian also uses the infinitive for negative commands: Non essere ridicola! = 'Don't be ridiculous!'
target_language_example: Potrei non essere pronto domani.
native_language_example: I might not be ready tomorrow.

meaning: keeps doing nothing but / does nothing except (keeps on doing something repeatedly).
additional_notes: Used with 'che' + verb (non fa altro che + infinito) to emphasize that someone repeatedly does only that action, often with a negative or critical tone. Can also appear with a clause (non fa altro che + verb phrase) meaning 'only serves to' or 'only does'.
target_language_example: Non fa altro che lamentarsi tutto il giorno.
native_language_example: He does nothing but complain all day.

meaning: not suitable for me / not for me (I don't like it or it doesn't suit me).
additional_notes: Used to say something isn't right for the speaker — can refer to people, places, activities, weather, or situations. Polite and common in everyday speech. Tone can be neutral or gently dismissive depending on context. Literal words mean 'doesn't make for me' but the idiomatic sense is 'it's not my thing' or 'it doesn't suit me.'
target_language_example: Il lavoro è interessante, ma non fa per me.
native_language_example: The job is interesting, but it's not for me.

meaning: you do nothing but / you only (keep) — expresses that someone only does one thing, often with annoyance
additional_notes: Usually followed by 'che' + verb (informal spoken Italian). Used to complain that someone repeatedly does the same action (e.g., only talks, only complains). Tone is often negative/critical. Can be used with other persons by changing the verb (non faccio altro, non fate altro, etc.).
target_language_example: Non fai altro che lamentarti, prova a trovare una soluzione.
native_language_example: You do nothing but complain, try to find a solution.

meaning: to be unable to cope anymore; to no longer be able to go on or manage (physically or emotionally)
additional_notes: Used to express that someone cannot continue a situation, action, or endure something any longer. Common in spoken Italian; often appears with a subject and the clitic 'ce' (e.g., 'Non ce la faccio più'). Can refer to physical exhaustion, emotional overwhelm, or inability to handle responsibilities.
target_language_example: Non farcela più è stato difficile da ammettere, ma alla fine ho chiesto aiuto.
native_language_example: Not being able to cope anymore was hard to admit, but in the end I asked for help.

meaning: to do nothing but / to only do (something); often conveys annoyance or inevitability about an action that is repeated
additional_notes: Used before an infinitive to indicate that someone does nothing but perform that action (e.g., 'non fare che + infinito'). Common in spoken and written Italian. Can suggest irritation or emphasize repetition ('all they do is...').
target_language_example: Non fare che lamentarti non risolverà nulla.
native_language_example: Doing nothing but complaining won't solve anything.

meaning: 'were not' / 'had not been' (subjunctive negative used in hypothetical or past-counterfactual clauses)
additional_notes: Used with the imperfect subjunctive of essere (fosse) to express wishes, hypothetical situations, or counterfactual ideas (e.g., 'as if it were not', 'I wish he had not'). Often appears in phrases like 'come se non fosse...' (as if it had not been) or 'vorrei che non fosse...' (I wish that he/it were not). Context (present vs. past meaning) depends on surrounding verbs.
target_language_example: Vorrei che non fosse successo nulla.
native_language_example: I wish that nothing had happened.

meaning: "if it had not been for" (used to credit someone/something for preventing a negative outcome or enabling a positive one).
additional_notes: Used in conditional sentences (past counterfactual) to say that because of X something happened (or did not happen). Often appears as part of 'Se non fosse stato per...' or shortened to 'Non fosse stato per...' followed by a noun or pronoun. Common in spoken and written Italian to express gratitude, blame, or explanation of past events.
target_language_example: Non fosse stato per il tuo consiglio, avrei preso la decisione sbagliata.
native_language_example: If it hadn't been for your advice, I would have made the wrong decision.

meaning: if it weren't for / were it not for (used to introduce the thing that prevents or makes something possible)
additional_notes: Used in conditional sentences (often with 'se' before it) to say that something/someone is the reason a situation exists or is prevented. Common in spoken and written Italian. Can be followed by a noun or pronoun (e.g., 'il mio mal di testa', 'lui'). When negated like this it expresses a counterfactual: the situation would be different without that cause.
target_language_example: Se non fosse per la pioggia, andremmo al parco.
native_language_example: If it weren't for the rain, we'd go to the park.

meaning: did not [verb] / was not (simple past — passato remoto).
additional_notes: Used to negate verbs in the passato remoto (remote/simple past) tense. Common in written Italian, literature, historical narratives, and formal speech. In spoken everyday Italian, the passato prossimo (non è stato/ non ha ...) is more common. After 'non fu' comes a past-participial or adjective depending on the verb: e.g. 'non fu lei a uccidere' (she did not kill), 'non fu la fine del mondo' (it was not the end of the world).
target_language_example: Non fu una decisione facile.
native_language_example: It was not an easy decision.

meaning: has no right (to do something)
additional_notes: Used to say someone is not entitled or authorized to do something. Often followed by an infinitive with di (di + verb) or by a clause. Can be formal or neutral. You can drop the subject (e.g., "Non ha alcun diritto...") when context makes it clear who you mean.
target_language_example: Non ha alcun diritto di decidere per me.
native_language_example: He/she has no right to decide for me.

meaning: 'doesn't have the' (masculine singular noun follows)
additional_notes: A negated phrase using the verb avere (to have) + definite article il. It means someone/something lacks a specific (masculine singular) thing or quality named after it. The article changes with the gender/number of the noun (non ha la, non hanno i, etc.). Often used for abstract qualities (il coraggio, il diritto) or concrete items (il telefono, il ragazzo).
target_language_example: Marco non ha il tempo per venire.
native_language_example: Marco doesn't have the time to come.

meaning: 'doesn't have time' (he/she/it doesn't have time)
