additional_notes: Used to say someone lacks time or is too busy for something. Commonly followed by 'per' + noun/infinitive (e.g. 'per me', 'per queste cose', 'per leggere') or an infinitive verb. Subject is third person singular (lui/lei/Lei); for other persons use 'non ho tempo', 'non hai tempo', 'non abbiamo tempo', etc.
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, non ha tempo di aiutarti oggi.
native_language_example: Sorry, he/she doesn't have time to help you today.

target_language_multi_word_term: non ho niente a (che fare con ...)
meaning: 'I have nothing to do with ...' / 'I'm not involved with ...'
additional_notes: Used to deny involvement, responsibility, or connection with a person, event, or thing. Often appears as the full phrase non ho niente a che fare con ... or with colloquial contractions (col = con il). Can be used in formal and informal contexts to distance oneself from something.
target_language_example: Non ho niente a che fare con quel problema.
native_language_example: I have nothing to do with that problem.

meaning: 'I don't have any money with me' (I don't currently have cash on me).
additional_notes: Used to say you don't have money on your person right now. Often completed as "non ho soldi con me" or simply "non ho soldi" in informal speech. Common in everyday situations (can't pay, borrow, or buy). Not a fixed idiom beyond literal meaning.
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, non ho soldi con me adesso.
native_language_example: Sorry, I don't have any money with me right now.

meaning: I won't tell it / I will not say it.
additional_notes: Literal: non (not) + lo (it/him) + dirò (I will say). Used to promise confidentiality or to refuse to reveal information. Often followed by a person or group (a nessuno = to anyone). Tone can be reassuring or emphatic depending on context and use of 'mai' (never).
target_language_example: Puoi fidarti: non lo dirò a nessuno.
native_language_example: You can trust me: I won't tell anyone.

meaning: ‘may not be it’ / negative subjunctive: expresses doubt or denial about something (that it is/exists/is so).
additional_notes: Phrase uses the negative particle non + lo (a neutral direct object pronoun referring to a previously mentioned idea/thing) + sia, the present subjunctive of essere. Common in subordinate clauses after verbs of doubt, desire, fear, or expressions like «spero che», «temo che», or in formulas like «penso che non lo sia» (I think it isn't). Depending on context lo can refer to a thing, a situation, or an abstract idea. In casual speech you might also hear «non è» (indicative) instead of the subjunctive.
target_language_example: Penso che non lo sia, quindi non dobbiamo preoccuparci.
native_language_example: I think it isn't, so we don't need to worry.

meaning: I don't know
additional_notes: Very common everyday phrase used to say you don't know something or are unsure. Can be shortened in speech to just "boh" or used with emphasis (e.g., "non lo so davvero" = "I really don't know"). Often followed by a comma and additional comment (e.g., "non lo so, può darsi" = "I don't know, maybe").
target_language_example: Non lo so se verrò alla festa.
native_language_example: I don't know if I'll come to the party.

meaning: 'not far' / 'not far away' (close by, nearby).
additional_notes: Used to indicate that a person or place is relatively close in distance or time. Often followed by 'da' + a place/person (non lontano da...). Can be used alone for emphasis (Non lontano ormai = not far now). Neutral register.
target_language_example: Il ristorante è non lontano da casa mia.
native_language_example: The restaurant is not far from my house.

meaning: 'is not lacking' / 'there is no ...' / 'doesn't miss' (depends on context)
additional_notes: Common negative construction with the verb mancare. Can mean 'there is no (something)' or 'something is not lacking' (e.g. 'qui non manca niente' = 'nothing is missing/you have everything'). It can also be used idiomatically: 'non manca molto' = 'there isn't much left' / 'it won't be long', and with people it can mean 'someone doesn't fail to (do something)' when followed by a verb (non manca mai di + inf.). Context and word order determine the exact English translation.
target_language_example: Qui non manca nulla, puoi stare tranquillo.
native_language_example: Nothing is missing here; you can relax.

meaning: I don't give a damn / I don't care (strong, coarse).
additional_notes: Colloquial and vulgar expression used to show strong indifference. Usually completed with a coarse noun (e.g. 'cazzo') but can be left trailing in speech. Conjugates with the person (here 'me' = 'to me'). Avoid in formal contexts; use 'non mi interessa' or 'non me ne importa' instead.
target_language_example: Non me ne frega un cazzo di quello che dici.
native_language_example: I don't give a damn about what you say.

meaning: I don't expect (that) someone will [do something for] me.
additional_notes: Used to express low or no expectation that someone will help or do something for the speaker. Followed by a verb (e.g. aiuti, dia) describing the action you don't expect. Common in contexts about help, support, or assistance. Literal components: non (not) + mi (to me) + aspetto (I expect) + che mi (that to me) — compositional and can be translated literally.
target_language_example: Non mi aspetto che mi aiuti, ma apprezzo che sia stata onesta.
native_language_example: I don't expect him/her to help me, but I appreciate that they were honest.

meaning: 'don't tell me' or an exclamation meaning 'no way!' / 'you don't say!'
additional_notes: Used literally to ask someone not to tell you something (don't tell me that...). Very commonly used as an interjection to express surprise, disbelief, shock, or strong emotion (similar to English 'You don't say!' or 'Oh, come on!'). Tone and context decide whether it's a request or an exclamation. Can be followed by a clause (Non mi dire che...) or stand alone (Non mi dire!).
target_language_example: Non mi dire che hai già finito il lavoro!
native_language_example: Don't tell me you've already finished the work!

meaning: literally 'it is not to me' — used to say 'I am not allowed' or 'it is not allowed for me' (negation + indirect object), often followed by a past participle or adjective.
additional_notes: Common construction to express prohibition or lack of permission for the speaker: non mi è permesso/consentito + infinitive or past participle. 'Mi' is the indirect object pronoun (to me). You can also use other pronouns (non ti è, non gli è, etc.). In casual speech you may hear 'non posso' (I can't) as an alternative.
target_language_example: Non mi è permesso entrare dopo le 22.
native_language_example: I am not allowed to enter after 10 p.m.

meaning: not dead; undead (literally 'not dead').
additional_notes: Used literally to state someone/something is not dead (e.g., after an injury) or as a noun/adjective meaning 'undead' in supernatural contexts (zombies, vampires). Context and syntax determine whether it's a negation ('non morto' as part of a clause) or a label ('i non morti' = 'the undead'). Pronunciation: non = /non/, morto = /ˈmɔr.to/.
target_language_example: Il soldato è non morto dopo l'attacco? No, è sopravvissuto; non è un non morto.
native_language_example: Is the soldier 'non morto' after the attack? No, he survived; he is not an undead.

meaning: 'I can't take it (any)more' or 'I'm fed up (with it/them)'.
additional_notes: Shortened form of 'non ne posso più' (literally: 'I can't [of it] more'). Used to express strong frustration, exhaustion, or being fed up with a situation or thing. 'Ne' refers back to whatever you're fed up with (work, people, tasks, etc.). Often said alone as an exclamation. Informal but common in spoken Italian.
target_language_example: Non ne posso più di questo rumore!
native_language_example: I'm fed up with this noise!

meaning: 'it's not worth it' (used to say something is not worth the effort, cost, or trouble).
additional_notes: This is a shortened/colloquial phrase often completed as "non ne vale la pena" or "non ne vale la pena farlo". You will frequently hear the full form "non vale la pena" (without "ne") meaning the same. Use to advise against doing something or to dismiss an action as not worthwhile.
target_language_example: Non ne vale la pena spendere così tanto per quella borsa.
native_language_example: It's not worth spending that much on that bag.

meaning: 'don't miss the' or 'don't lose the' (use depends on context)
additional_notes: This is a short phrase combining the negative 'non perdere' with the masculine singular article 'il'. In Italian, 'perdere' can mean 'to miss' (an event, opportunity, transport) or 'to lose' (an object). Which meaning applies depends on the noun that follows: e.g. 'non perdere il treno' = 'don't miss the train'; 'non perdere il documento' = 'don't lose the document'. It's followed by a masculine singular noun. For polite or formal commands you can also use 'non perda il' (lei form) or 'non perdete il' (voi).
target_language_example: Non perdere il treno domani mattina.
native_language_example: Don't miss the train tomorrow morning.

meaning: 'they/do not like me' or 'I am not liked' (literally: 'I do not please')
additional_notes: Used with the indirect object introduced by 'a' to say who doesn't like the speaker: 'non piaccio a [nome/qualcuno]'. It's the first-person singular of piacere (to be pleasing) in the present. English often uses 'like' where Italian uses piacere with reversed subject/object order.
target_language_example: Non piaccio a tutti i miei colleghi.
native_language_example: Not all of my colleagues like me.

meaning: to have no choice but to; to be unable to do anything other than (do something)
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to express lack of alternative or necessity (equivalent to English 'can only' or 'have no choice but to'). Italian often uses forms like 'non poter che + infinitive' or conjugated forms 'non posso che...', 'non potevo che...'. Register: neutral/formal depending on context.
target_language_example: Non potere che chiedere scusa è frustrante quando l'errore non dipende da te.
native_language_example: Having no choice but to apologize is frustrating when the mistake isn't your fault.

meaning: to be fed up; to not be able to stand something anymore (emotionally or physically exhausted/frustrated)
additional_notes: Literal components: 'non' (not) + 'poterne' (to be able of it/about it — 'potere' + clitic 'ne') + 'più' (anymore/any longer). Common construction appears as 'Non ne posso più' or in infinitival form 'non poterne più' when embedded (e.g., 'Ho smesso perché non potevo non poterne più' is awkward; more commonly: 'Non poterne più di...' in reported or infinitive contexts like 'Dire di non poterne più'). Can express physical exhaustion (I'm exhausted) or annoyance/fed up (I've had enough). Register: colloquial to neutral; more common in spoken Italian.
target_language_example: Dopo cinque ore di riunioni, non poterne più era inevitabile.
native_language_example: After five hours of meetings, not being able to take it anymore was inevitable.

meaning: 'doesn't feel' / 'doesn't try' / 'doesn't prove' (depends on context)
additional_notes: This phrase combines the negative particle non + the verb provare. Provare has several meanings: to try (attempt), to feel (an emotion or pain), and to prove (demonstrate). Translate based on context: e.g. 'non prova a chiamare' = 'doesn't try to call', 'non prova dolore' = 'doesn't feel pain', 'non prova nulla' = 'proves nothing' (or 'doesn't prove anything' when used with negation).
target_language_example: Perché non prova a parlare con lei?
native_language_example: Why don't you try talking to her?

meaning: you can't
additional_notes: Second-person plural of riuscire with non. It is usually followed by a + infinitive: non riuscite a vedere, non riuscite a trovare. It often suggests difficulty or failure to do something, rather than lack of permission.
target_language_example: Con questo rumore non riuscite a dormire.
native_language_example: With this noise, you can't sleep.

meaning: Don't run away / don't escape; don't run off.
additional_notes: Imperative negative of scappare (to run away/escape). Used to tell someone not to leave, flee, or run off — can be urgent or emotional. Often appears alone as a command (Non scappare!) or followed by adverbs like via. Tone depends on context and intonation.
target_language_example: Per favore, non scappare, resta con me.
native_language_example: Please, don't run away, stay with me.

meaning: There's no question of it / it's out of the question / we can't talk about it (for now).
additional_notes: Used to refuse or rule out something, or to say a topic/situation is not possible or not being discussed. Tone can range from neutral (temporarily not possible) to emphatic refusal depending on context and intonation. Often followed by intensifiers: "non se ne parla proprio" (absolutely not). Literal parts: "se ne" refer to 'about it' or 'of it'.
target_language_example: Mi chiedi di partire domani? Non se ne parla, ho già impegni.
native_language_example: You're asking me to leave tomorrow? That's out of the question, I already have plans.

meaning: 'you are not mine' / 'you are not my (female) ...' depending on context
additional_notes: Used to tell someone they are not (your) [family member/friend/partner]. Mia agrees in gender with the noun omitted or implied (mia = my (feminine)). In short sentences like the examples, the noun (amica, madre, sorella) is omitted because it's understood. Tone can be strong or defensive; word order is the normal negative form (non + verb).
target_language_example: Non sei mia amica, quindi non puoi decidere per me.
native_language_example: You are not my friend, so you can't decide for me.

meaning: they are not useful / they are not needed
additional_notes: Plural form of 'non servire' used to say that people or things are useless, unnecessary, or not needed in a situation. Subject is plural (they). Can refer to objects (e.g., soldi, minacce) or people (e.g., dottori, attrici). Often followed by 'a' + infinitive or noun phrase (non servono a niente, non servono per questo). Tone can be neutral or dismissive depending on context.
target_language_example: Queste regole non servono più.
native_language_example: These rules are no longer useful.

meaning: 'doesn't complain' (he/she/it doesn't complain).
additional_notes: Present-tense, third-person singular of 'lamentarsi' (to complain) with the negative 'non'. Used to describe someone or something that does not complain. Can refer to people, animals, or situations. In Italian the reflexive pronoun 'si' indicates the subject is he/she/it (lui/lei) when the subject is clear from context or a name is used (e.g., "Tom non si lamenta").
target_language_example: Mio fratello non si lamenta mai del lavoro.
native_language_example: My brother never complains about work.

meaning: you never know; you can't be sure.
additional_notes: Used to express uncertainty or caution about possible outcomes. Often said as a short comment to justify being careful, taking precautions, or keeping options open. Common in spoken Italian; can appear alone as a response.
target_language_example: Porta un ombrello, non si sa mai.
native_language_example: Bring an umbrella, you never know.

meaning: negative subjunctive of 'essere' — 'is not' / 'be not' used after verbs or expressions that trigger the subjunctive (e.g., hope, fear, doubt, unless).
additional_notes: Used when the subordinate clause requires the subjunctive (che + subjunctive) and is negated. Common after verbs like sperare, temere, dubitare, and in conditional phrases introduced by a meno che (unless). Don't translate word-for-word; render naturally in English (e.g., 'I hope it isn't...', 'unless...is not...'). Pronunciation/grammar point: 'non' is the negation and 'sia' is the present subjunctive of 'essere' (io/tu/lui/lei).
target_language_example: Spero che non sia difficile per te.
native_language_example: I hope it isn't difficult for you.

meaning: 'are not' or 'aren't' in subordinate (subjunctive) clauses
additional_notes: Non siano is the negative form of 'siano', the third-person plural present subjunctive of essere (to be). It appears after verbs/expressions that trigger the subjunctive (e.g., sperare che, sembra che, sicuro che?) and is used for doubt, hope, emotion, judgment, or hypothetical situations. In simple statements you would use 'non sono' instead. Example translations depend on context: 'I hope they aren't...', 'It seems that they aren't...', 'Are you sure they aren't...?'.
target_language_example: Spero che non siano troppo stanchi dopo il viaggio.
native_language_example: I hope they aren't too tired after the trip.

meaning: I don't know what / I don't know how to (do something).
additional_notes: Used to express uncertainty about what to do, say, think, or what would have happened. Often followed by an infinitive (fare, dire) or a subordinate clause (succedeva, avrei fatto). In conversational Italian it can be shortened to "non so" plus context. Tone ranges from neutral to worried.
target_language_example: Sono in difficoltà e non so che fare.
native_language_example: I'm in trouble and I don't know what to do.

meaning: you are not
additional_notes: A negated, familiar (tu) form of 'stare'. Used to say someone is not in a certain state (e.g. not well: "non stai bene") or to form questions/commands ("Perché non stai zitto?" = "Why don't you be quiet?/Why won't you be quiet?"). Context determines exact translation: as a question it can mean "aren't you...?/don't you...?/won't you...". Commonly used in spoken Italian. "Non stai con Nadia?" means "You're not going out/living with Nadia?/You're not with Nadia?" depending on context.
target_language_example: Non stai bene: dovresti andare dal medico.
native_language_example: You aren't well: you should go to the doctor.

meaning: 'was not' or 'wasn't' (imperfect of stare in negative)
additional_notes: Common negative form of the imperfect tense of stare. Depending on context it can mean 'was not' (location, condition, or ongoing state) or 'wasn't feeling well'. In some idiomatic uses it appears in expressions like "non stava né in cielo né in terra" (made no sense). In questions it can mean "Wasn't (he/she/it) ...?" (Non stava con te? = Wasn't he/she staying with you?).
target_language_example: Ieri mia zia non stava bene, così è andata dal dottore.
native_language_example: Yesterday my aunt wasn't well, so she went to the doctor.

meaning: 'not everything that' / 'not all that'.
additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause (usually followed by 'che' + clause) meaning that not every item or statement in the following group is true or applies. Common structure: 'Non tutto quello che + [verb/clause] + ...'. Often interchangeable with 'non tutto ciò che' or 'non tutto quello che'.
target_language_example: Non tutto quello che ti dicono è utile.
native_language_example: Not everything that they tell you is useful.

meaning: don't use (do not use).
additional_notes: Imperative or negative infinitive form: 'non' + verb 'usare' (to use). Common when giving instructions or warnings. When addressing people directly, context determines tone (command, advice, request). Object follows the verb (e.g., non usare quella / non usare le braccia).
target_language_example: Non usare il mio telefono senza permesso.
native_language_example: Don't use my phone without permission.

meaning: you don't go
additional_notes: From non + vai, where vai is the tu form of andare. It can describe a habitual action ('you don't go') or a current/planned action ('you're not going'), depending on context. The subject pronoun tu is usually omitted in Italian.
target_language_example: Stasera non vai al ristorante con loro.
native_language_example: You're not going to the restaurant with them tonight.

meaning: not worth the (something) / it doesn't count as the (something)
additional_notes: This is a fragment often followed by a noun (e.g. 'pena', 'spesa', 'pena la pena') or an expression; full phrases include 'non vale la pena' (it's not worth it) and 'non vale la pena di...' or 'non vale la pena fare...' It can also appear in contexts meaning 'doesn't count' (e.g. 'non vale la regola' = the rule doesn't apply). You normally need the rest of the phrase to know the exact meaning.
target_language_example: Non vale la pena continuare se non siamo felici.
native_language_example: It's not worth continuing if we're not happy.

meaning: you will not see
additional_notes: Second-person singular future of 'vedere' with negation. Used to tell someone they will never or will not see something (can be literal or figurative, e.g. 'you will never get/experience that' or 'you won't see it happen'). Tone can be neutral or strong depending on context (e.g. promise, warning, statement of fact).
target_language_example: Non vedrai mai la fine di questo progetto se non aiuti.
native_language_example: You won't ever see the end of this project if you don't help.

meaning: don't sell the (feminine singular noun).
additional_notes: Imperative or negative infinitive construction. 'Non vendere' = don't sell. 'La' is the feminine singular definite article (the) and agrees with a feminine noun like 'auto' or 'automobile'. Used to tell or advise someone not to sell a specific item. For masculine nouns you'd use 'non vendere il' (or 'non vendere lo'/'non vendere l\'').
target_language_example: Non vendere la macchina prima di parlarne con me.
native_language_example: Don't sell the car before talking to me.

meaning: 'is not at' or 'is not in (the)' — negation of 'è al' (he/she/it is at the/to the).
additional_notes: Commonly used to say someone or something is not at a specific place or not available at a location (e.g., non è al lavoro, non è al telefono). 'Al' is the contraction of 'a' + 'il' (to the/at the). The full subject (lui/lei/esso) is often omitted because the verb form 'è' already indicates third person singular.
target_language_example: Marco non è al lavoro oggi.
native_language_example: Marco is not at work today.

meaning: not what (it/he/she) is; 'it's not what...' — used to say something is different from what was expected or described.
additional_notes: Ciò means 'that' or 'what' in a more formal or neutral register. 'Non è ciò che...' is followed by a clause describing the expectation, impression, or promise being denied. Common in sentences like 'Non è ciò che sembra' (It's not what it seems). You can often replace 'ciò' with 'quello' or 'ciò che' with 'quello che' in informal speech.
target_language_example: Questa non è ciò che mi avevi detto.
native_language_example: This is not what you told me.

meaning: 'is not with' or 'not with' (used to say someone/something is not accompanying, supporting, or involved with someone).
additional_notes: Commonly used to indicate lack of accompaniment, support, involvement, or target of an action. Followed by a pronoun, name, or noun (e.g., non è con me / non è con te). Can express 'it's not about' someone in contexts like 'Non è con me che devi scusarti' = 'You don't have to apologize to me.' Tone and meaning depend on context (literal physical presence vs. figurative support/involvement).
target_language_example: Non è con noi che devi parlare, è con lui.
native_language_example: You don't have to talk to us, it's him you should talk to.

meaning: it's not certain / not necessarily so
additional_notes: Used to express doubt or to say that something is not guaranteed or obvious. Often followed by che + clause (Non è detto che...) to introduce an alternative possibility or to soften a claim. Can stand alone as a short reply meaning "that's not certain" or "not necessarily."
target_language_example: Non è detto che riesca a venire domani; ha molto da fare.
native_language_example: It's not certain that he'll be able to come tomorrow; he has a lot to do.

meaning: 'the problem/issue is not the' or more generally 'it is not the (thing)'.
additional_notes: Used to negate that a specific noun (usually introduced right after) is the cause, problem, or defining feature. Often followed by a noun phrase (e.g., 'la caduta', 'la sua lingua materna'). Context determines the exact English rendering: 'it's not the ...', 'the problem isn't ...', or 'it's not that ...'. Pronoun 'la' agrees with a feminine noun or stands in for 'that/it' as a feminine idea.
target_language_example: Il problema non è la mancanza di tempo.
native_language_example: The problem is not the lack of time.

meaning: it's not far (feminine) / it isn't far
additional_notes: Used to say that a place or person (feminine noun implied by agreement) is nearby or not far away. Commonly followed by a location introduced with da (e.g. da qui, da qua, da Parigi). Can be adjusted for gender/number: non è lontano (masculine), non sono lontane/i (plural).
target_language_example: La biblioteca non è lontana da qui.
native_language_example: The library isn't far from here.

meaning: not mine / not my (one). Used to deny possession or that someone/something belongs to the speaker.
additional_notes: Used to deny ownership or a familial/relational bond when referring to a masculine singular noun or person. For a feminine singular use 'non è mia'. For plural: 'non sono miei' (masculine or mixed) / 'non sono mie' (feminine). Word order: 'non' (not) + 'è' (is) + 'mio' (my/mine). Can apply to things (objects) or people (to indicate not one's relative/friend).
target_language_example: Tom non è mio figlio.
native_language_example: Tom is not my son.

meaning: it's not all / that's not all / not everything
additional_notes: Used to say that something is not complete or that there is more to add. Can be used literally (not everything) or as a set phrase meaning "that's not all" when introducing further information. Tone depends on context and intonation; often appears in conversational speech. In questions (e.g. "E non è tutto lo stesso?") it can express surprise or doubt.
target_language_example: Ho finito il primo capitolo, ma non è tutto: devo ancora correggere gli esercizi.
native_language_example: I've finished the first chapter, but that's not all: I still need to correct the exercises.

meaning: grandfather and… (the phrase 'nonno e' is not a standalone fixed expression; it appears as 'nonno e' when listing or connecting 'grandfather' with something/someone else)
additional_notes: This is simply the noun nonno (grandfather) followed by the conjunction e (and). It's used when naming or describing multiple people or items, e.g. 'nonno e nonna' (grandfather and grandmother) or 'nonno e io' (grandfather and I). There are no special idiomatic meanings. Pay attention to word order and articles: 'il nonno e la nonna' or more naturally 'il nonno e la nonna vengono domani.'
target_language_example: Il nonno e la nonna arrivano domani.
native_language_example: Grandfather and grandmother arrive tomorrow.

meaning: despite the (plural masculine noun); 'despite' or 'in spite of' used before a plural masculine noun
additional_notes: Nonostante is a preposition meaning 'despite' or 'in spite of'. When followed by the plural masculine definite article 'i' it introduces a plural noun (e.g., nonostante i problemi = despite the problems). Use nonostante il (singular masculine), la (singular feminine), le (plural feminine) as needed. Can be followed by a noun or a clause (nonostante + noun or nonostante che + verb).
target_language_example: Nonostante i ritardi, siamo arrivati in tempo.
native_language_example: Despite the delays, we arrived on time.

meaning: our (female) teacher.
additional_notes: Nostra = our. Insegnante is 'teacher' and can refer to a woman or man; here the feminine article/agreement (if used) or context indicates a female teacher. You might also hear 'il nostro insegnante' for a male teacher. Agreement: adjectives and possessives agree in gender and number with the noun (nostra insegnante, i nostri insegnanti, le nostre insegnanti).
target_language_example: La nostra insegnante parla molto chiaramente.
native_language_example: Our teacher (female) speaks very clearly.

meaning: our situation; the circumstances we are in.
additional_notes: A simple, neutral phrase used to talk about the condition, status, or circumstances affecting a group that includes the speaker (we/us). Can refer to practical, emotional, financial, or any other kind of situation depending on context. 'Nostra' = our; 'situazione' = situation/condition.
target_language_example: Dobbiamo parlare della nostra situazione prima di decidere.
native_language_example: We need to talk about our situation before deciding.

meaning: our vacation / our holiday.
additional_notes: A possessive phrase: nostra (our, feminine singular) + vacanza (vacation/holiday). Use nostra when the speaker refers to a feminine singular noun they share with others (la vacanza). For other nouns/genders/number change the possessive (il nostro viaggio, le nostre vacanze). Common in everyday speech to talk about upcoming or past trips.
target_language_example: Siamo tutte impazienti per la nostra vacanza.
native_language_example: We're all excited for our vacation.

meaning: our old (feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used before a feminine noun to mean 'our old' (as in former or previously owned/used). 'Nostra' agrees with a feminine singular noun; if noun is masculine use 'nostro' (nostro vecchio). Can indicate age ('old') or previous possession/association ('our former'). Word order is typical: possessive + adjective + noun (e.g., la nostra vecchia casa).
target_language_example: Ho ritrovato la nostra vecchia foto.
native_language_example: I found our old photo.

meaning: our homework / our tasks.
additional_notes: Plural phrase: 'nostri' is the plural possessive for 'we' (our) used before a masculine plural noun; 'compiti' commonly means school homework but can also mean general tasks or chores. Word order: possessive + noun (nostri compiti = our homework).
target_language_example: Abbiamo finito i nostri compiti prima di cena.
native_language_example: We finished our homework before dinner.

meaning: 'our men' — our people/men (often refers to members of a group, team, staff, soldiers, or workers).
additional_notes: Literal plural of 'nostro uomo' (our man). Used to refer to people who belong to or work for 'us' (e.g., team members, employees, soldiers, agents). Context determines whether it means literally men or more generally our people; in military/police contexts it often means personnel. Can sound formal or neutral depending on situation.
target_language_example: I nostri uomini sono già arrivati al posto di comando.
native_language_example: Our men have already arrived at the command post.

meaning: our plane / our flight.
additional_notes: A simple possessive phrase: 'nostro' (our) + 'aereo' (plane). Used to talk about a plane or flight that belongs to or is associated with the speaker and others (e.g., a booked flight). Can appear with articles ('il nostro aereo') as in the examples. Commonly used when discussing departure, arrival, delays, or schedules.
target_language_example: Il nostro aereo atterra alle sette di sera.
native_language_example: Our plane lands at seven in the evening.

meaning: our dog is
additional_notes: A simple subject-verb phrase: 'nostro' = our (masculine singular), 'cane' = dog, 'è' = is. Use to describe states, characteristics, location, or events about a shared/owned dog. Adjust gender/number if needed (nostro/nostra, cane/cani, è/sono).
target_language_example: Il nostro cane è molto affettuoso con i bambini.
native_language_example: Our dog is very affectionate with children.

meaning: a way to say 'ours is' or 'ours/our [thing] is' (emphasizing possession and identity).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something belongs to or characterizes 'us' (our country, our world, our service). Often followed by a noun or adjective phrase (e.g., 'il nostro è il miglior servizio...', 'il nostro è un mondo terribile'). Word order may vary: 'Il nostro è...' = 'Ours is...' or 'Our ... is...'.
target_language_example: Il nostro è un problema da risolvere insieme.
native_language_example: Ours is a problem to solve together.

meaning: 'noticed some' or 'noticed any' (past participle + partitive article)
additional_notes: Combines the past participle 'notato' (noticed) with 'degli' (partitive plural meaning 'some' or used in questions as 'any'). Common in questions asking whether someone has observed some/countable things (e.g. errors). Word order often appears in questions: 'Hai notato degli errori?'
target_language_example: Hai notato degli errori nel documento?
native_language_example: Did you notice any errors in the document?

meaning: news of his/her/its (something); information about someone's (e.g., death).
additional_notes: Used to introduce what the news concerns (often followed by a noun like 'morte', 'assenza', 'guarigione'). 'Sua' agrees with a previously mentioned person or thing (his/her/its). Common in formal or neutral contexts. Word order can vary: 'la notizia della sua morte' or 'si è diffusa la notizia della sua morte.'
target_language_example: Abbiamo ricevuto la notizia della sua guarigione.
native_language_example: We received the news of his/her recovery.

meaning: news or information for (someone).
additional_notes: Used to say you have or are asking for news/information intended for a particular person or group. Often appears with pronouns or names (per me, per te, per voi, per lui/lei). Can be singular (una notizia) or plural (qualche notizia / delle notizie).
target_language_example: Ho una notizia per te.
native_language_example: I have some news for you.

meaning: 'numbers of' or '...numbers' (used with a noun to indicate possession or type, e.g. 'numeri di telefono' = phone numbers).
additional_notes: Commonly appears in the phrase 'numeri di telefono' (phone numbers). 'Numeri di' is followed by a noun that specifies what kind of numbers they are (telefono, cellulare, conto, ecc.). Agreement: the verb and any adjectives agree with 'numeri' (plural). In spoken Italian you may hear simply 'i numeri' when context makes the type clear.
target_language_example: Hai i numeri di emergenza?
native_language_example: Do you have the emergency numbers?

meaning: telephone number; phone number.
additional_notes: Common everyday phrase used to ask for or give someone's phone number. Often shortened in speech to "numero" or "numero di cell(ulare)" when specifying a mobile. Use with verbs like dare (to give), avere (to have), chiedere (to ask), dimenticare (to forget).
target_language_example: Mi puoi dare il tuo numero di telefono?
native_language_example: Can you give me your phone number?

meaning: number one; the best; first (in order or rank).
additional_notes: Used both literally (room number one, first in a list) and figuratively to mean 'the best' or 'top-ranked' (e.g., fan number one, the number-one tennis player). Can be masculine or feminine depending on the person referred to: 'il numero uno' (m.) / 'la numero uno' (f.). Also used alone as an exclamation ('Numero uno!') to praise someone.
target_language_example: Sei il numero uno della squadra.
native_language_example: You are the number one on the team.

meaning: to swim with (someone).
additional_notes: A verb phrase: 'nuotare' (to swim) followed by the preposition 'con' (with) + person(s). Used to say you swim together with others. Commonly appears with articles/pronouns (con le loro amiche, con i miei amici, con voi).
target_language_example: Domani vado a nuotare con Laura e Marco.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I'm going to swim with Laura and Marco.

meaning: to swim with us (invitation or statement that someone joins our group to swim).
additional_notes: Used to invite someone or say that someone will/does/wants to join the speaker and others for swimming. Often follows verbs of asking, wanting, or coming (chiedere, volere, venire). 'Con noi' = 'with us'. Formality: neutral; suitable in casual and polite contexts.
target_language_example: Vuoi venire a nuotare con noi sabato?
native_language_example: Do you want to come swim with us on Saturday?

meaning: to swim in (a body of water).
additional_notes: Used with a preposition + place (mare, piscina, fiume, spiaggia) to say where someone swims. Common construction: 'nuotare in + [noun]' for enclosed or named waters (in piscina, in mare, in fiume). For beaches Italians also say 'a nuotare in spiaggia' or more often 'in spiaggia' to indicate location. Verb is infinitive; conjugate as usual (io nuoto, noi nuotiamo).
target_language_example: Andiamo a nuotare in piscina questo pomeriggio.
native_language_example: Let's go swim in the pool this afternoon.

meaning: to swim in (the).
additional_notes: A verb phrase: nuotare = to swim; nel = in + definite article (in the). Use with specific bodies of water (il fiume, il lago, il mare). Can be combined with different articles: nuotare nel (il), nella (la), nello (lo), nei/nelle (plural). Often used with andare a nuotare (to go swimming) or with a subject who swims regularly.
target_language_example: Andiamo a nuotare nel lago questo pomeriggio.
native_language_example: Let's go swim in the lake this afternoon.

meaning: I swim the river / to swim across the river (literal).
additional_notes: This phrase is a literal combination of the verb 'nuotare' (to swim) and the direct object 'il fiume' (the river). In natural Italian you would normally say 'nuotare nel fiume' (to swim in the river) or 'attraversare il fiume a nuoto' (to cross the river by swimming). 'Nuoto il fiume' by itself sounds unusual or ungrammatical in many contexts; to express present action say 'Nuoto nel fiume' or 'Sto nuotando nel fiume.' If intending to convey 'I swim across the river' more idiomatically use 'Attraverso il fiume a nuoto.'
target_language_example: Durante l'allenamento, dissi al gruppo: «Nuoto il fiume per primo e vi aspetto sulla riva opposta.»
native_language_example: During training, I told the group: "I'll swim the river first and wait for you on the opposite bank."

meaning: a new business, venture, or activity (often a newly started business or project).
additional_notes: Commonly used to refer to starting a new business or undertaking (avviare una nuova attività = to start a new business/project). Can also mean a new activity in a more general sense (e.g., a new task or class activity). Context (business vs. general) is usually clear from surrounding words.
target_language_example: Ha deciso di aprire una nuova attività in centro.
native_language_example: He decided to open a new business in the city centre.

meaning: a new identity (taking on a different name/persona).
additional_notes: Used to say someone adopted or assumed a different identity—could be literal (legal identity change) or for disguise, witness protection, or reinvention. Common verbs: assumere/assunse/ha assunto una nuova identità. Not inherently formal or informal.
target_language_example: Dopo lo scandalo, ha creato una nuova identità e si è trasferito all'estero.
native_language_example: After the scandal, he created a new identity and moved abroad.

meaning: a new technique / a new method
additional_notes: Used to describe a recently learned or tried way of doing something (in art, sports, work, etc.). 'Nuova' = new (feminine) because 'tecnica' is feminine. Can be used in various tenses: Ha provato una nuova tecnica = He/She tried a new technique; Provò una nuova tecnica = He/She tried (past simple).
target_language_example: Abbiamo imparato una nuova tecnica in laboratorio.
native_language_example: We learned a new technique in the lab.

meaning: brand new; completely new.
additional_notes: An idiomatic expression used to describe something very new or unused (objects, clothes, websites, etc.). Equivalent to 'brand-new' or 'mint condition' in English. Common in everyday speech. Literally 'new of (a) tack', but not used literally.
target_language_example: Ho comprato una macchina nuovo di zecca.
native_language_example: I bought a brand-new car.

meaning: a new dictionary
additional_notes: Literal phrase: nuovo = new, dizionario = dictionary. Used to refer to a recently released or newly acquired dictionary (physical or digital). Common verbs with it: procurarsi (to get/obtain), prendere (to take/buy), pubblicare (to publish).
target_language_example: Ho deciso di comprare un nuovo dizionario italiano-inglese.
native_language_example: I decided to buy a new Italian–English dictionary.

meaning: 'new to' or 'new on' — indicates someone is inexperienced with or recently arrived at a place, site, topic, or activity.
additional_notes: Commonly used with a person or thing: 'sono nuovo su [piattaforma]' = I'm new to this platform. Often followed by the name of a site, topic, or activity. Can also appear in constructions like 'qualcosa di nuovo su cui...' (something new to think about / write about).
target_language_example: Sono nuovo su questo forum e sto imparando le regole.
native_language_example: I'm new to this forum and I'm learning the rules.

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase; a sequence of the adjective "nuovo" (new) followed by the feminine demonstrative "quella" (that/that one). In Italian the normal order is "quella nuova" (that new one). As written, "nuovo quella" is ungrammatical in standard Italian and likely a mistaken word order.
additional_notes: Treat as a fragment or error rather than an established expression. Possible intended meanings: "that new (one)" referring to a feminine noun — correct form: "quella nuova"; or simply the words appearing next to each other in speech/writing due to error. Use proper agreement: "nuovo" → "nuova" to match feminine "quella". The phrase can appear in informal contexts as a slip, but it is not idiomatic.
target_language_example: Ho letto "nuovo quella" nella nota e sono rimasto confuso; probabilmente volevano scrivere "quella nuova".
native_language_example: I read "nuovo quella" in the note and was confused; they probably meant to write "quella nuova".

meaning: or I'll call the (police). (used as a threat or warning)
additional_notes: Commonly followed by 'polizia' (the police). It's an informal, direct warning meaning 'do this or I'll call the police' / 'leave or I'll call the police'. Used to force someone to stop a behavior or to leave. Tone is firm/angry; not polite. Structure: 'Vattene, o chiamo la polizia' = 'Go away, or I'll call the police.'
target_language_example: Smettila subito o chiamo la polizia!
native_language_example: Stop that now or I'll call the police!

meaning: 'or like' / 'or as' — used to offer an alternative, to introduce a comparison, or to mean 'someone like' when referring to a person.
additional_notes: Depends on context. 1) As a simple alternative: 'o' = 'or' and 'come' = 'as/like' (e.g., 'o come socio' = 'or as a partner'). 2) In comparisons or examples, 'come' means 'like' (e.g., 'uno come te' = 'someone like you'). 3) Can appear in rhetorical lists: '...o ... o ...' = '...or... or...'. Not idiomatic slang. Word order is flexible depending on the phrase.
target_language_example: Vuoi restare a casa o come me partire per il viaggio?
native_language_example: Do you want to stay home or, like me, leave for the trip?

meaning: 'or against' — used to present an alternative or to indicate opposition/contrast
additional_notes: Commonly appears in lists or contrasts (e.g., "a favore o contro" = "for or against"). Can be used literally (physically against) or figuratively (opinions, positions). When meaning 'versus' in contests, Italian also uses 'contro' alone or 'contro' with team names (e.g., "Juventus contro Milan").
target_language_example: Sei a favore o contro questa proposta?
native_language_example: Are you for or against this proposal?

meaning: or against the
additional_notes: A short sequence of words used when presenting alternatives or oppositions involving a masculine singular noun introduced by the definite article 'il'. Common in phrases like 'squadra A o contro il squadra B' (though grammar usually prefers 'contro' without repeating the article). More naturally, you'd often see 'o contro' (or vs.) or 'o... contro...' in sports or debates: 'A o B, contro C' — be careful: native speakers may omit or reorder articles for fluidity.
target_language_example: La partita è Juve o contro il Milan?
native_language_example: Is the match Juventus or against Milan?

meaning: or some/of the (masculine partitive) — used to offer a choice between items, often with partitive articles.
additional_notes: Combines the conjunction o (or) with the masculine singular partitive article del (di + il). Common in offers/choices: 'del tè o del caffè' = 'some tea or some coffee' / 'tea or coffee'. The partitive can be omitted in English; in Italian it signals an unspecified quantity. Forms change with gender/number: della (fem.), dei (masc. pl.), delle (fem. pl.).
target_language_example: Vuoi del pane o del formaggio?
native_language_example: Do you want some bread or some cheese?

meaning: 'or do you have' — used to offer an alternative question or choice, often introducing the second option in a yes/no question.
additional_notes: Commonly appears in spoken Italian to present two possibilities (A o hai B?). Often follows a positive clause or implied option and introduces a contrasting possibility (usually a problem, fear, need, or alternative). In many cases it functions like English '... or are you...' or '... or do you...' depending on context. Tone can be neutral or challenging depending on intonation; in informal speech contraction and rhythm matter.
target_language_example: Vuoi venire con noi o hai già altri piani?
native_language_example: Do you want to come with us, or do you already have other plans?

meaning: 'or' used before a plural masculine/feminine noun with the definite article 'i' (the).
additional_notes: This is the conjunction 'o' (or) followed by the definite article 'i' (the, plural). In Italian you usually include the article before nouns, so you'll often see 'o i' when offering a choice between two plural nouns. Word order: noun + o + i + noun (or noun + o + noun with articles as needed). Pronunciation: the 'o' is pronounced like the English 'o' in 'or'.
target_language_example: Preferisci il tè o i biscotti?
native_language_example: Do you prefer tea or the cookies?

meaning: or by car / or in the car (used to offer 'by car' as an alternative).
additional_notes: Commonly used after another transport option (a piedi, in autobus, ecc.) to give 'or by car' as the alternative. 'Macchina' = car; 'in macchina' = by car / in the car. Used in questions about means of transport: 'Andiamo a piedi o in macchina?' = 'Shall we go on foot or by car?'.
target_language_example: Preferisci andare in treno o in macchina?
native_language_example: Do you prefer to go by train or by car?

meaning: 'or else' (used to introduce a consequence or threat); can also be literal 'or it/her' in choices depending on context.
additional_notes: Often used colloquially to present two alternatives where the second part is an implied consequence (equivalent to 'or else' in English). Context determines whether 'la' is a pronoun ('it'/'her') or a feminine direct object; with commands it often signals a threat or negative consequence. In choices between actions (question form) it can simply join options: 'Do you eat it here or take it away?'.
target_language_example: Fai attenzione, o la perdi.
native_language_example: Be careful, or else you'll lose it.

meaning: or rather / rather (to correct or refine what was just said).
additional_notes: Used to correct, soften, or refine a previous statement. Often placed at the start of a clause ("O meglio, ...") or between two options to replace the first with a more accurate expression. Common in both spoken and written Italian.
target_language_example: Non è un problema, o meglio, lo risolvo io.
native_language_example: It's not a problem, or rather, I'll solve it myself.

meaning: 'or not' (used after a clause to indicate alternative possibility)
additional_notes: Placed after a verb clause or question word (e.g., se, che) to mean 'or not' / 'whether or not'. Common in both spoken and written Italian. Can appear as part of 'se ... o meno' (whether ... or not) or after verbs like 'ricordi o meno'.
target_language_example: Non so se venire o meno alla festa.
native_language_example: I don't know whether to come to the party or not.

meaning: 'or are you...' — used to offer an alternative or ask which of two possibilities is true (often followed by an adjective or brief clause).
additional_notes: Common in questions to present two alternatives: first option, then 'o sei' + second option. Can be used with verbs, adjectives, or short clauses. In short answers or informal speech you may also hear just 'o sei?' to challenge or ask for clarification. Word-for-word literal translation is 'or are (you)'.
target_language_example: Vuoi uscire o sei troppo stanco?
native_language_example: Do you want to go out or are you too tired?

meaning: or sisters (used after 'fratelli' to mean 'brothers or sisters')
additional_notes: Commonly appears after 'fratelli' to ask about siblings in general. 'Fratelli o sorelle' = 'brothers or sisters' (i.e., siblings). Word order can vary (e.g., 'fratelli o sorelle' or 'sorelle o fratelli') but the phrase is simply the disjunction 'or sisters'. Used in questions about family or shared living arrangements.
target_language_example: Quanti fratelli o sorelle hai?
native_language_example: How many brothers or sisters do you have?

meaning: or wine (used to offer/ask preference between beer and wine).
additional_notes: Used when offering choices or asking preferences. Often follows another option with 'o' (or). In these examples it's paired with 'birra' (beer): 'Birra o vino?' = 'Beer or wine?'. Can be used in informal and formal contexts depending on tone and verb form.
target_language_example: Vuoi acqua o vino?
native_language_example: Do you want water or wine?

meaning: 'the eyes are' — the subject 'occhi' (eyes) plus verb 'sono' (are).
additional_notes: A simple subject + verb phrase used to describe someone's eyes (color, appearance, condition). In Italian, 'occhi' (eyes) is plural, so it takes the plural form of 'essere' → 'sono'. Often followed by an adjective (blu, belli, rossi) or a phrase describing state. Can be part of a full sentence (e.g., 'I suoi occhi sono blu' = 'His/her eyes are blue').
target_language_example: I tuoi occhi sono verdi?
native_language_example: Are your eyes green?

meaning: sunglasses (pair of glasses to protect from sunlight).
additional_notes: Used in plural to refer to a pair of sunglasses. You can say 'un paio di occhiali da sole' (a pair of sunglasses) or 'degli/questi occhiali da sole'. 'Occhiali' is plural; singular 'occhiale' is rare and not used for a pair.
target_language_example: Ho messo gli occhiali da sole prima di uscire.
native_language_example: I put on my sunglasses before going out.

meaning: green eye (literally); can refer to someone with green eyes or, figuratively, to jealousy (less common than 'essere geloso' or 'avere invidia').
additional_notes: Literally means 'green eye'. Used to describe the color of an eye: singular 'l'occhio verde' or plural 'gli occhi verdi'. The figurative use (e.g., 'avere l'occhio verde' to imply jealousy) is uncommon; Italians typically say 'essere geloso' or 'provare invidia'. Agreement and article must match number and gender when used in context.
target_language_example: Ha l'occhio verde che risalta nel viso.
native_language_example: He/She has a green eye that stands out on the face.

meaning: 'to take care of / to be in charge of / to deal with'
additional_notes: Used with a subject (often the reflexive pronoun si) to indicate who handles, looks after, or is responsible for something. Common questions: 'Chi si occupa di...?' (Who takes care of...?), statements: 'Si occupa di [argomento/attività]' (He/She/You formal deals with ...). Can refer to caring for people or animals, managing tasks, or working in a field. Verb base: occuparsi di.
target_language_example: Chi si occupa di Quicky?
native_language_example: Who takes care of Quicky?

meaning: busy (doing something); occupied with an activity.
additional_notes: Used with the feminine form 'occupata' (masculine: 'occupato') plus 'a' and an infinitive or gerund-like action. It describes someone being engaged in or busy with a specific task (e.g., 'occupata a cucire' = busy sewing). Common in everyday speech to explain why someone is unavailable.
target_language_example: Lei è occupata a rispondere alle email.
native_language_example: She is busy answering emails.

meaning: too busy to (do something); occupied/unavailable for
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive or a task implied by context. 'Occupate' is the feminine plural form of 'occupato' — adjust gender/number (occupato, occupata, occupati, occupate) to match the speaker(s). Common structure: [subject] + essere + troppo occupato/a/i/e + per + [infinitive/phrase].
target_language_example: Siamo troppo occupate per aiutarti oggi.
native_language_example: We are too busy to help you today.

meaning: 'busy (doing something)'; used before an infinitive to say someone is occupied with an action.
additional_notes: Combine 'occupato' (busy) with 'a' + infinitive verb to describe what someone is busy doing. Common structure: 'essere occupato a' + verb-infinite. Can describe temporary actions. Agreement: 'occupato' agrees in gender/number if used as adjective (e.g., 'occupata', 'occupati', 'occupate').
target_language_example: Sono occupato a finire il rapporto.
native_language_example: I'm busy finishing the report.

meaning: busy (in/with) — used to say someone is occupied at a particular time or with something
additional_notes: Usually appears as 'occupato in quel momento' (busy at that moment) or 'occupato in [something]' (busy with something). Common in past reports: 'mi ha detto che era occupato in quel momento' = 'he told me he was busy then.' Can be followed by an activity, a location, or a time expression. Formality: neutral.
target_language_example: Mi ha chiamato, ma era occupato in quel momento con lavoro urgente.
native_language_example: He called me, but he was busy at that moment with urgent work.

meaning: 'will take care of' / 'will deal with' (someone or something).
additional_notes: Third-person singular future of 'occuparsi di' (reflexive): 'si occuperà di' means 'he/she/it/you(formal) will take care of' or 'will handle' a person, task, or situation. Commonly followed by a noun or relative clause introduced by 'di' (e.g., 'di tutto', 'di ciò di cui avete bisogno').
target_language_example: Non preoccuparti: Maria si occuperà di tutto domani.
native_language_example: Don't worry: Maria will take care of everything tomorrow.

meaning: you (plural) hate (someone/something) so much / hate so much
additional_notes: Odiare = to hate. 'Odiate' is the second person plural (voi) present subjunctive or imperative form, but in questions like the examples it functions as the present indicative for 'you (plural) hate' in colloquial speech or when addressing a group. 'Così' means 'so' or 'so much' and intensifies the hatred. Common in questions: 'Perché odiate così (tanto) ...?' = 'Why do you all hate ... so much?'. Use with direct objects (people, places, things).
target_language_example: Perché odiate così il nuovo professore?
native_language_example: Why do you (all) hate the new teacher so much?

meaning: 'I hate (someone/something) so much' or 'I hate (him/her/it) so deeply'.
additional_notes: Used to intensify the verb 'odiare' (to hate). 'Odio' is the first-person singular present ('I hate'); 'così' means 'so' or 'so much'. In sentences with an object pronoun, the pronoun can appear before the verb (Lo odio così tanto) or the person's name follows (Odio così tanto Tom). It's strong/emotional language — avoid in polite contexts.
target_language_example: Ti odio così tanto dopo quello che hai fatto.
native_language_example: I hate you so much after what you did.

meaning: I hate everything / I hate all of (someone or something).
additional_notes: Used to express strong dislike of everything about a person or thing. Often followed by 'di' or 'riguardo a' + person/pronoun (e.g., 'di lei', 'di loro') or a noun. 'Odio' is first-person singular of 'odiare' (to hate). This is a strong phrase—use carefully; in softer contexts use 'non mi piace' (I don't like).
target_language_example: Odio tutto di quella situazione.
native_language_example: I hate everything about that situation.

meaning: 'the offer is' — a short phrase used to describe the state or quality of an offer
additional_notes: Commonly appears with adjectives or short phrases to say whether an offer is valid, reasonable, expired, offensive, etc. In Italian word order the noun (offerta) comes before the verb (è). Often used formally in business or everyday contexts when discussing proposals, prices or invitations.
target_language_example: La tua offerta è ancora valida?
native_language_example: Is your offer still valid?

meaning: I offer my (…), e.g. life or death.
additional_notes: A verb phrase using offro (first-person singular of offrire) + la mia (feminine singular possessive). The noun that follows (vita, morte, etc.) is often omitted in speech if clear from context. Literally 'I offer my…'. Common in dramatic or formal contexts.
target_language_example: Ti offro la mia vita per proteggerti.
native_language_example: I offer you my life to protect you.

meaning: offered to (do something).
additional_notes: Past tense (passato remoto) of 'offrirsi di' — 'to offer to do something' (volunteer/help). Commonly used with a verb in infinitive after 'di'. In spoken Italian, passato prossimo ('si è offerto di') is more frequent than passato remoto in many regions.
target_language_example: Si offrì di riparare la porta.
native_language_example: He/she offered to repair the door.

meaning: 'that's enough for today' / 'that's all for today'.
additional_notes: Used to stop an activity, end a session, or tell people to stop doing something for the rest of the day. Often appears as 'per oggi basta' or 'per oggi basta così'. Polite or neutral depending on tone; can be used by a leader (teacher, boss) or informally to friends.
target_language_example: Per oggi basta: riposatevi e ne riparliamo domani.
native_language_example: That's enough for today: rest and we'll talk about it again tomorrow.

meaning: 'every case' or in phrases like 'in ogni caso' = 'in any case' / 'anyway'.
additional_notes: 'ogni caso' by itself literally means 'every case'. More commonly you'll see the fixed phrase 'in ogni caso' used to mean 'in any case', 'anyway', or 'regardless'. Used to introduce a conclusion, to change topic, or to emphasize something despite previous points.
target_language_example: In ogni caso, dobbiamo decidere entro domani.
native_language_example: In any case, we must decide by tomorrow.

meaning: every day
additional_notes: A common time expression used to talk about habits or repeated actions. It can appear at the beginning or end of a sentence.
target_language_example: Studio italiano ogni giorno.
native_language_example: I study Italian every day.

meaning: in any case / anyway
additional_notes: Used to introduce a statement that remains true despite other facts or to change/close a topic. Similar to 'comunque' or 'in ogni caso'. Common in spoken and written Italian. Can appear as part of phrases like 'in ogni modo' (more formal).
target_language_example: Non so se verrà, ma ogni modo andremo al cinema.
native_language_example: I don't know if they'll come, but in any case we'll go to the cinema.

meaning: every (one) of his/her/its; each of his/her/its
additional_notes: Used before a noun or noun phrase to indicate that something applies to every item associated with a third-person singular possessor (sua = his/her/its). The gender of 'sua' matches the noun that follows (e.g., ogni sua mossa, ogni sua parola, ogni sua domanda). Context determines whether 'sua' means his, her, or its.
target_language_example: Controlla ogni sua email prima di rispondere.
native_language_example: Check every one of his/her emails before replying.

meaning: every now and then; occasionally; from time to time.
additional_notes: Used to indicate something that happens irregularly but more than rarely. Common in speech and writing; can appear at beginning or inside a sentence. Synonyms: ogni tanto = di tanto in tanto, ogni tanto e comunque.
target_language_example: Ogni tanto vado al cinema con gli amici.
native_language_example: Every now and then I go to the cinema with friends.

meaning: every three (units of time).
additional_notes: Used before a time unit (giorni, settimane, mesi, anni, ore, minuti) to mean 'every three [units]'. Place 'ogni tre' directly before the plural noun. For other numbers replace 'tre' with the number: e.g. 'ogni due', 'ogni quattro'.
target_language_example: Vado dal dentista ogni tre mesi.
native_language_example: I go to the dentist every three months.

meaning: in addition to; besides
additional_notes: Used to add something to what was just mentioned. Can introduce a person, thing, action or clause. Often followed by a noun, pronoun, infinitive or clause (e.g. 'oltre a me', 'oltre a studiare', 'oltre a quello'). In questions it can mean 'what else' or 'besides that'.
target_language_example: Oltre a studiare, lavoro nel fine settimana.
native_language_example: In addition to studying, I work on weekends.

meaning: an umbrella left at/at school (literally: 'umbrella at school').
additional_notes: Used to say someone left or forgot their umbrella at school. It's a simple location phrase: subject + lasciare/scordare + 'il suo ombrello a scuola'. Can be adapted for other items or places (e.g., 'il mio libro a casa').
target_language_example: Ho dimenticato il mio ombrello a scuola ieri.
native_language_example: I forgot my umbrella at school yesterday.

meaning: an opinion of/about (someone or something).
additional_notes: Used to indicate what someone thinks about a person or thing. Often appears with adjectives (buona opinione di = a good opinion of) or verbs like 'avere' (to have an opinion). Followed by a person, thing, or pronoun (di lui, di te, di me).
target_language_example: Ho una cattiva opinione di quel ristorante.
native_language_example: I have a bad opinion of that restaurant.

meaning: now I am
additional_notes: This is a colloquial informal contraction of 'ora sono' used in speech or casual writing. 'Or' here is a variant of 'ora' (now). It precedes a verb (usually 'sono' = 'I am' or 'we are') to indicate a current state. Often used to give an update or contrast with the past: e.g. 'or sono stanco' = 'now I am tired'.
target_language_example: Or sono molto occupato, non posso venire.
native_language_example: Now I am very busy, I can't come.

meaning: 'now you have' (present tense: 'now you possess/are given/experience something')
additional_notes: Literal combination of ora (now) + hai (you have, second-person singular of avere). Used to say that someone currently has or is experiencing something (possession, attention, time, marks, etc.). Can introduce a consequence or prompt (e.g., 'now that you have...').
target_language_example: Ora hai tutto il necessario per partire.
native_language_example: Now you have everything you need to leave.

meaning: now (you) me / now I (do something to/for) me — 'ora' = now, 'mi' = me (direct or indirect object or reflexive).
additional_notes: Common combination used to place 'mi' (me/myself) after 'ora' to mean 'now [you] me' or 'now I [do something to/for myself]'. Depending on the verb, 'mi' can be indirect object (mi lasci = you leave me), direct object (mi hai visto = you saw me) or reflexive (mi riprendo = I recover). Word order 'ora mi' is natural in spoken and written Italian for emphasis on the time ('now').
target_language_example: Ora mi prendo una pausa.
native_language_example: Now I'm taking a break.

meaning: Now (I'll) ... / now I will ... (spoken; introduces an immediate action toward 'you')
additional_notes: Colloquial spoken Italian. 'Ora' = now; 'te' is the unstressed object pronoun (to you / for you). Often followed by a verb phrase with a clitic (lo/la/ne) attached (e.g. 'te lo spiego', 'te la leggo') or a verb like 'spiego', 'dico', 'porto'. It signals the speaker will do something right away for/ to the listener. Equivalent to English 'I'll (do it) for you now' or 'Now I'll... you'.
target_language_example: Sta arrivando il pacco? No, ora te lo porto io.
native_language_example: Is the package arriving? No, I'll bring it to you now.

meaning: 'now is in' (referring to someone's current location)
additional_notes: Used to say where a person (or sometimes thing) is right now: subject + ora è a + place. Often follows a name or noun: "Maria ora è a Milano." Can also appear in questions with inversion or with "sapere/sa/tu sai" to ask if someone knows that fact. Literal translation is possible.
target_language_example: Marco ora è a Firenze per lavoro.
native_language_example: Marco is now in Florence for work.

meaning: 'it's time that you' / 'now that you' (used to say someone should do something now)
additional_notes: Used to introduce that someone should start or do something now; often followed by a subjunctive verb (faccia, decida, venga). Can express urgency, recommendation, or a change of state. Context determines tone (gentle suggestion vs. firm command).
target_language_example: È ora che tu parli con lui.
native_language_example: It's time that you talk to him.

meaning: 'time to go to' or 'it's time to go to (somewhere/action)'
additional_notes: Common phrase used to say it's time to leave or to start going somewhere or to begin doing something. Usually followed by a place or a verb in the infinitive (e.g., 'ora di andare a scuola' = time to go to school, or 'ora di andare a dormire' = time to go to sleep). Can be used in everyday contexts like leaving the house, ending an activity, or prompting someone.
target_language_example: È ora di andare a scuola, sbrigati!
native_language_example: It's time to go to school, hurry up!

meaning: literally 'now it is the' — not a complete fixed phrase; likely the beginning of a sentence like 'ora è la...' (e.g. 'Ora è la mia occasione' = 'Now it's my chance').
additional_notes: This is not a standalone idiom. 'Ora è la' will normally be followed by a noun or clause to complete the idea (la + feminine noun). 'Ora' = now; 'è' = is; 'la' = the (feminine) or pronoun 'her/it'. Common continuations: 'ora è la mia occasione', 'ora è la verità', 'ora è la tua scelta'. Pay attention to gender: 'la' agrees with a feminine noun. If the following noun is masculine use 'il' or the appropriate form.
target_language_example: Ora è la mia occasione di brillare.
native_language_example: Now it's my chance to shine.

meaning: to order (some) — used before an uncountable or partitive noun (e.g., 'order some pizza').
additional_notes: Ordinare = to order (food, items). 'Della' is the partitive article (di + la) meaning 'some' or 'some of the'. Use 'ordinare della' when talking about ordering an unspecified quantity of a feminine singular noun that normally uses 'la' (e.g., la pizza → della pizza). For other nouns/forms use the matching partitive: del (m. sing), dello (m. sing before s+consonant/z), dei (m. pl), delle (f. pl). Common in spoken Italian when suggesting or describing ordering food.
target_language_example: Stasera possiamo ordinare della pasta e guardare un film.
native_language_example: Tonight we can order some pasta and watch a movie.

meaning: 'ordered the dog' or 'told the dog (to do something)'.
additional_notes: This phrase is the past participle form of 'ordinare' used with a direct object (the dog) plus an infinitive clause implied (e.g. di sedersi = to sit). In English you'd say 'ordered the dog to sit' or 'told the dog to sit.' It appears in compound past tenses (ho/ha/abbiamo ordinato). Use 'ordinare a qualcuno di + infinitive' to mean 'to order/tell someone to (do something)'.
target_language_example: Il proprietario ha ordinato al cane di non abbaiare.
native_language_example: The owner ordered the dog not to bark.

meaning: 'ordered some' (past tense) — used with uncountable or partitive nouns like 'pizza' to mean 'ordered some pizza'.
additional_notes: ordinato is the past participle of ordinare (to order). della is the partitive article (di + la) used to indicate 'some' of a feminine singular noun (e.g., della pizza = some pizza). Together they appear in sentences like 'Ha ordinato della pizza' = 'He/She ordered some pizza.' Subject and tense can change (Ho ordinato della pizza = I ordered some pizza).
target_language_example: Ieri abbiamo ordinato della pizza per cena.
native_language_example: Yesterday we ordered some pizza for dinner.

meaning: ordered a/one (he/she/you formal ordered a ...).
additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of ordinare (to order). 'Ordinato un' is followed by an item (e.g., 'ordinato un bicchiere di birra'). It indicates someone ordered one of something. Subject is usually third person singular (ha ordinato) but form can match other subjects (ho/abbiamo/avete ordinato).
target_language_example: Ieri ha ordinato un panino al prosciutto.
native_language_example: Yesterday he/she ordered a ham sandwich.

meaning: '(the) orders are' — a short phrase used when talking about orders/instructions (often followed by what the orders are or to emphasize that orders must be followed).
additional_notes: Literal combination of ordini (orders/instructions) + sono (are). Common in contexts where someone reports or enforces instructions (e.g. military, boss), or to dismiss objections by saying 'orders are orders.' Can introduce the content of the orders (Gli ordini sono di...) or be used idiomatically to mean 'orders must be followed.'
target_language_example: I medicI hanno deciso: gli ordini sono di aspettare qui.
native_language_example: The doctors decided: the orders are to wait here.

meaning: used to emphasize a duration or to link hours with additional time (e.g. 'hours and hours', 'three and a half hours').
additional_notes: Commonly appears as part of the repeated phrase 'ore e ore' meaning 'hours and hours' to emphasize a long time. Also used in constructions like 'tre ore e mezzo' (three and a half hours) or 'tre ore e sei minuti' (three hours and six minutes) to add minutes/halves. In spoken Italian the 'e' simply means 'and'.
target_language_example: Siamo rimasti lì per ore e ore.
native_language_example: We stayed there for hours and hours.

meaning: hours in/inside (used to say spending time in a place).
additional_notes: Combines ore (hours) + nella (in the + feminine singular: in + la). Used to indicate that someone spent hours inside a specific place (e.g., nella giornata = in the day; nella moschea = in the mosque). Nella contracts in + la. Use delle ore nella / passare/trascorrere ore nella to say 'spend hours in'.
target_language_example: Ho passato molte ore nella biblioteca a studiare.
native_language_example: I spent many hours in the library studying.

meaning: the ears are / my ears are (plural subject + verb 'to be').
additional_notes: A simple subject-verb phrase using 'orecchie' (ears, plural) and the present tense of 'essere' (sono). Use with plural subjects: 'le orecchie sono...' For possession, include possessive adjective before 'orecchie' (e.g., 'le mie orecchie sono...'; 'le sue orecchie sono...'). Common in descriptions or questions about appearance, size, color, pain, etc.
target_language_example: Le mie orecchie sono fredde.
native_language_example: My ears are cold.

meaning: a watch/clock given to (someone); 'an [item] to [person]'.
additional_notes: This phrase shows the noun orologio (watch/clock) followed by the preposition a introducing the indirect object (the person who receives it). In Italian, a marks the recipient: 'dare un orologio a Maria' = 'to give a watch to Maria'. Word order can vary: 'Ho dato a Maria un orologio' is also correct. The examples mix past tenses (demmo, ha dato).
target_language_example: Ho comprato un orologio a Luca per il suo compleanno.
native_language_example: I bought a watch for Luca for his birthday.

meaning: 'the watch/clock is' or 'the clock/watch is' (simple predicative structure).
additional_notes: Combines orologio (watch/clock) with the verb essere (to be) in third person singular. Used to describe location, condition, price, or state of a watch/clock. Replace orologio with mio/tuo/questo/etc. as needed (e.g., il mio orologio è...). Verb agreement stays with orologio (singular).
target_language_example: Il mio orologio è rotto.
native_language_example: My watch is broken.

meaning: psychiatric hospital; mental hospital.
additional_notes: Refers to a medical facility specializing in psychiatric care and treatment for people with severe mental disorders. In modern usage, many speakers prefer ospedale psichiatrico specialistico or centro di salute mentale (mental health center) for less institutional connotations. Can be used formally; may carry heavy or historical connotations depending on context.
target_language_example: Mio zio è stato ricoverato in un ospedale psichiatrico per ricevere cure adeguate.
native_language_example: My uncle was admitted to a psychiatric hospital to receive proper care.

meaning: to observe the (plural, masculine) — 'to watch/observe the...'
additional_notes: Osservare = 'to observe/watch'. 'gli' is the masculine plural definite article used before certain consonant clusters and all vowels for plural masculine nouns (e.g., gli uccelli, gli insetti). Together they begin phrases like 'osservare gli uccelli' (to watch the birds). In spoken Italian you might also see 'guardare gli' (to look at/watch the...).
target_language_example: Mi piace osservare gli uccelli al parco.
native_language_example: I like to watch the birds in the park.

meaning: 'obtained the' or 'got the' (past participle + definite article)
additional_notes: Ottenuto is the past participle of ottenere (to obtain/get). Combined with il it literally means 'obtained the...' and is used before a masculine singular noun (il + noun). It appears in compound tenses (e.g., ho ottenuto = I obtained/got) or as an adjective describing a masculine noun. Equivalent to 'got the' or 'received the' in English depending on context.
target_language_example: Ho ottenuto il permesso ieri.
native_language_example: I got the permission yesterday.

meaning: around eight (o'clock) / at eight (when followed by time of day).
additional_notes: Used to refer to the hour 'eight' with a specification of time of day (mattina, sera, etc.). Common patterns: 'alle otto (di) mattina/sera' = at eight in the morning/evening; 'per le otto' = by eight; 'prima delle otto' = before eight. In everyday speech the phrase often appears as 'alle otto' or 'per le otto' — 'di' links to 'mattina/sera' (e.g. 'otto di mattina' ≈ 'eight in the morning').
target_language_example: Ci vediamo per le otto di sera, va bene?
native_language_example: Let's meet by eight in the evening, OK?

meaning: "eight hours a" (used before a time period like giorno = day) — e.g. "eight hours a day".
additional_notes: This is a fixed-looking chunk combining a number + unit + preposition. It needs a following time period (giorno, settimana, mese) to complete the phrase: otto ore al giorno = eight hours a day; otto ore alla settimana = eight hours a week (note agreement: alla for feminine singular like settimana). Common in expressions about sleep or work.
target_language_example: Dovresti riposare otto ore al giorno.
native_language_example: You should rest eight hours a day.

meaning: 'the father of' (used before a feminine singular noun or phrase).
additional_notes: Literally 'father of the'. Used to indicate possession/relationship (e.g., father of the girl, father of the bride). 'Della' is the contraction of 'di' + 'la' and agrees with a feminine singular noun. For masculine singular use 'padre del' (di + il).
target_language_example: Tom è il padre della sposa.
native_language_example: Tom is the father of the bride.

meaning: father of the family; family man (the head or male parent responsible for a household).
additional_notes: Used literally to refer to a man who is a father and usually the head of a household. Can also be used more broadly to describe a respectable family man or emphasize someone's family responsibilities. Context may make it sound approving, neutral, or slightly critical/surprised (e.g., implying ordinary life vs. other roles).
target_language_example: Marco è un padre di famiglia che lavora tutto il giorno.
native_language_example: Marco is a father of the family who works all day.

meaning: the phrase 'padre e' literally means 'father and' — it is the word 'padre' followed by the conjunction 'e' ('and'); used when listing or linking 'father' with another noun or idea.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom: it's simply the noun padre ('father') plus the conjunction e ('and'). You will see it when someone lists family members (e.g., 'padre e madre'), pairs of roles/relations ('padre e fratello') or when padre is part of a longer list. Watch word order and articles: in Italian articles or prepositions may appear before the nouns (e.g., 'di padre e di madre', 'a tuo padre e tornare').
target_language_example: Mio padre e mia madre vengono domani.
native_language_example: My father and my mother are coming tomorrow.

meaning: my father and my mother; my parents.
additional_notes: Used to refer to both parents together. More natural in Italian is 'mio padre e mia madre' or simply 'i miei genitori'. Word order can vary, but possessive 'mio/mia' normally appears before each noun (mio padre e mia madre) or before the plural (i miei genitori).
target_language_example: Vivo con mio padre e mia madre in campagna.
native_language_example: I live with my father and my mother in the countryside.

meaning: his/her/my/your father was
additional_notes: Combines padre (father) + era (third-person singular imperfect of essere — 'was' / 'used to be'). In context the subject (my/your/his/her) comes from the possessive (mio, tuo, suo) or from context. Use to describe past states, occupations, origins, habits, or ongoing past situations. English translation depends on possession: "mio padre era" = "my father was", "suo padre era" = "his/her father was". 'Era' is imperfect, so it often implies a background action or repeated/continuous state in the past (e.g. "era sempre arrabbiato" = "he was always angry" / "he used to be always angry").
target_language_example: Mio padre era stanco dopo il lavoro.
native_language_example: My father was tired after work.

padre era ancora a casa quando

target_language_multi_word_term: padre era ancora a casa quando
meaning: '(my) father was still at home when...'
additional_notes: This phrase is a clause used to say that someone's father was still at home at the moment another action happened. The examples show different past tenses and gender endings (me ne sono andata/o, partii, sono partito/a) — adjust the past participle/gender to match the speaker. You can replace 'padre' with other subjects (mia madre, lui, etc.).
