target_language_example: Mio padre era ancora a casa quando sono entrata.
native_language_example: My father was still at home when I came in.

meaning: my/your/his/her/our/their father works (or 'father works').
additional_notes: A simple subject + verb phrase meaning 'father works.' In Italian the possessive (mio, tuo, suo, nostro, vostro, loro) usually appears before padre (e.g. mio padre = my father). The verb lavora is the third-person singular of lavorare (to work). Context and the possessive determine whose father is meant. Use different prepositions for workplace: in (in), a/ad (in/at for cities), alla/allo/alla/ai (with articles for specific places like 'alla banca' = at the bank).
target_language_example: Tuo padre lavora in ospedale?
native_language_example: Does your father work in a hospital?

meaning: 'my father has' (used as the beginning of a sentence meaning 'my father has [done/has/had …]').
additional_notes: This is the sequence of words you get when talking about something your father has or has done. In Italian the object or past participle usually follows: e.g. 'Padre mi ha aiutato' = 'My father helped me' or 'Mio padre mi ha dato un libro' = 'My father gave me a book.' Note that Italians more commonly place the possessive before the noun ('mio padre') rather than 'padre mio'.
target_language_example: Mio padre mi ha insegnato a cucinare.
native_language_example: My father has taught me how to cook.

meaning: my/your/the father was not / the father wasn't (present/at home/etc.) — negative past description about 'father'.
additional_notes: This is the phrase 'padre' (father) combined with the past-tense negative 'non era' (was not). The subject (my/your/his) is usually shown by a possessive (mio, tuo, suo) before 'padre', e.g. 'mio padre non era' = 'my father wasn't'. The exact nuance depends on context: it can describe absence (not present, not at home) or a character trait (wasn't scared, wasn't like others). Verb tense is imperfetto (imperfect), used for habitual or background actions in the past.
target_language_example: Mio padre non era spesso a casa quando ero piccolo.
native_language_example: My father wasn't often at home when I was little.

meaning: our Father; the opening words of the Lord's Prayer in Italian (also used to refer to the prayer itself).
additional_notes: Literally 'father our' in Italian word order, but used like English 'Our Father'. Most commonly refers to the Christian Lord's Prayer (Il Padre Nostro). Can also be used when talking about 'our father' in a religious or liturgical context. Capitalization: when referring to the prayer title it's often capitalized (Il Padre Nostro).
target_language_example: Recitiamo il Padre Nostro prima della messa.
native_language_example: Let's recite the Our Father before Mass.

meaning: '(my/your) father is in' — used to say where or in what condition someone's father is.
additional_notes: Combine with a place, condition, or state after 'in'. Subject can change (e.g., 'mio padre', 'tuo padre'). Common constructions: 'è in + luogo' (è in giardino), 'è in + condizione/stato' (è in buona salute, è in pericolo, è in galera), or idiomatic uses like 'è in linea' (he's online/on the phone). The literal translation is 'father is in', but you must supply the rest (place/state).
target_language_example: Mio padre è in ufficio adesso.
native_language_example: My father is in the office right now.

meaning: ‘(your/my/his/etc.) father is a…’ — used to say someone’s father has a certain profession or role.
additional_notes: This phrase combines a possessive + 'padre' (father) with 'è un' (is a + masculine indefinite article). Change the possessive (mio, tuo, suo, nostro, vostro, loro) to match the subject. Use 'è una' if the noun that follows is feminine (e.g. 'è una dottoressa'). In questions comfortingly the structure can stay the same but with rising intonation and a question mark: 'Suo padre è un prete?'.
target_language_example: Il mio padre è un musicista.
native_language_example: My father is a musician.

meaning: 'owner of' / 'master of' / 'in control of'
additional_notes: Used to indicate ownership, control, or authority over someone/something. Can mean literal owner (e.g., of a house or property) or figurative control (e.g., being master of oneself). Gender and number may change the noun (padrone/padrona; padroni). Often followed by the thing or person owned/ruled.
target_language_example: È il padrone di quella barca.
native_language_example: He is the owner of that boat.

meaning: landlord; owner of the house or building where people live.
additional_notes: Used to refer to the person who owns or rents out a house, apartment, or building. Can mean the owner of a private home or the landlord of a rental property. In some contexts (older or rural usage) it can mean 'master of the house' but in modern everyday speech it usually means 'landlord'.
target_language_example: Il nostro padrone di casa ha cambiato il rubinetto ieri.
native_language_example: Our landlord changed the faucet yesterday.

meaning: "the country has" or "each/any country has" (paese = country; ha = has).
additional_notes: A simple subject-verb phrase combining paese (country; can also mean village or hometown) and ha (third-person singular of avere = to have). Used to state that a country possesses or experiences something (e.g., a capital, a tradition, resources). In examples with ogni (every/each) or il nostro (our) the sense changes slightly: ogni paese ha = every/each country has; il nostro paese ha = our country has. Paese can also mean 'town' or 'home town' in informal contexts; adjust translation accordingly.
target_language_example: Il paese ha una torre antica.
native_language_example: The country has an ancient tower.

meaning: the (country) that is the most / the ...-est (superlative for countries)
additional_notes: Used to form superlatives with 'paese' + 'più' + adjective (e.g. 'paese più grande' = 'largest country'). Often followed by a prepositional phrase indicating the scope: 'del mondo', 'della Scandinavia', 'del Sudamerica', etc. Can be used with 'qual è' to ask questions ('qual è il paese più piccolo?').
target_language_example: Qual è il paese più popoloso d'Europa?
native_language_example: Which is the most populous country in Europe?

meaning: pays (us/them) every — used to state a recurring payment frequency.
additional_notes: Used with a subject (e.g., lui, lei, Tom) and an object (often 'ci' = 'us'). 'Ogni' means 'every' and is followed by a time period (mese, settimana) or a weekday (venerdì). Verb tense here is present: 'paga' = he/she/it pays. For other persons: 'paghi' (tu), 'paghiamo' (noi), 'pagate' (voi), 'pagano' (loro).
target_language_example: La società ci paga ogni mese.
native_language_example: The company pays us every month.

meaning: to pay his/her/its (something) — literally 'to pay the his/her'.
additional_notes: Used with a masculine noun that follows (e.g., affitto, conto, prestito). In Italian the possessive (suo) agrees in gender/number with the thing owned, not the owner: pagare il suo affitto (his/her rent). Context determines whether 'suo' means his, her, or its. Common verbs: pagare il suo affitto, pagare il suo conto, pagare il suo prestito.
target_language_example: Domani devo pagare il suo affitto per conto suo.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I have to pay his/her rent for him/her.

meaning: to pay the (feminine singular noun).
additional_notes: Literal phrase combining the verb pagare (to pay) + the feminine definite article la. Used before feminine singular nouns like multa (fine), tassa (tax), bolletta (bill), multa, multa, finestra (window) in contexts meaning 'to pay for the [thing]'. In Italian the article agrees with the noun: use pagare il for masculine nouns. Can be followed by direct object without preposition (pagare la multa) or with di/per to indicate 'pay for' in some contexts.
target_language_example: Devo pagare la bolletta dell'elettricità oggi.
native_language_example: I have to pay the electricity bill today.

meaning: paid the
additional_notes: Combination of the past participle 'pagato' (paid) and the definite article 'il' (the). Appears in sentences like 'Ho pagato il conto' (I paid the bill) or 'Ha pagato il biglietto' (He/She paid the ticket). Use with masculine singular nouns following 'il'. Verb tense and subject must be expressed elsewhere (e.g. with an auxiliary: 'ho pagato il...').
target_language_example: Ho pagato il conto ieri.
native_language_example: I paid the bill yesterday.

meaning: paid a lot / well-paid
additional_notes: Used to say someone receives a high amount of pay. Common with passive constructions (vengo pagato molto = I am paid well) or with a subject (sono pagato molto). Can refer to being paid a large sum or to being well-compensated relative to the job. Word order is typical: verb + pagato + molto, or subject + vengo/sono + pagato + molto.
target_language_example: Lavoro poche ore, ma vengo pagato molto.
native_language_example: I work few hours, but I'm paid a lot.

meaning: the ball to / the ball at (used to indicate who receives or is targeted by the ball).
additional_notes: Used after verbs of throwing/passing (lanciare, passare, ecc.) to show the recipient or target: 'lanciare una palla a qualcuno' = 'to throw/pass a ball to someone'. Word order: verb + 'la palla a' + recipient. The preposition 'a' marks the indirect object (to/at).
target_language_example: Gli ho passato la palla a Marco durante la partita.
native_language_example: I passed the ball to Marco during the game.

meaning: 'ball of' or 'ball/sphere made of'
additional_notes: A compositional phrase used to describe a ball or sphere made of something or belonging to someone (possession: 'la palla di Pedro' = Pedro's ball). Can indicate material ('palla di formaggio' = ball of cheese) or a specific named ball/event (e.g. 'palla di Capodanno' = New Year's ball). Word order: 'palla di + noun' or 'palla di + proper name'.
target_language_example: La palla di stoffa è sul tavolo.
native_language_example: The cloth ball is on the table.

meaning: literally 'ball in' — not a fixed phrase; 'palla' = ball and 'in' = in/inside (preposition).
additional_notes: This is not a set expression. 'Palla' is a noun meaning 'ball' (feminine: la palla). 'In' is the preposition 'in' (meaning 'in', 'inside', or 'into'). In the example sentences the full idea is 'una palla in giardino' = 'a ball in the garden'. Word order is noun + preposition phrase. Use articles (una, la) and agree adjectives with palla (feminine).
target_language_example: Ho trovato una palla in casa.
native_language_example: I found a ball in the house.

meaning: fastball (a fast pitch); literally 'fast ball'.
additional_notes: Commonly used in sports (especially baseball/softball) to describe a fast pitch. Literally compositional: palla = ball, veloce = fast. Can also be used more generally to mean a fast-moving ball in other contexts.
target_language_example: Il lanciatore ha appena tirato una palla veloce.
native_language_example: The pitcher just threw a fastball.

meaning: to play volleyball with (someone).
additional_notes: Combines the sport 'pallavolo' (volleyball) with the preposition 'con' (with) + a person or group. Often used with verbs like giocare/giocava/sta giocando and invitations (Vieni a giocare a pallavolo con noi). Use 'a pallavolo' to indicate the sport and 'con' to name who you're with.
target_language_example: Giochiamo a pallavolo con i nostri colleghi domani?
native_language_example: Shall we play volleyball with our colleagues tomorrow?

meaning: volleyball, used in choices: 'pallavolo o ...' = 'volleyball or ...'.
additional_notes: Used when giving options between sports or activities. In Italian you can say 'giocare a pallavolo' (to play volleyball). When listing alternatives with 'o' (or), the preposition 'a' can be repeated or omitted: 'giocare a pallavolo o a basket' or 'giocare a pallavolo o basket' (both are heard colloquially).
target_language_example: Vuoi giocare a pallavolo o a calcio questo pomeriggio?
native_language_example: Do you want to play volleyball or soccer this afternoon?

meaning: a short list starter meaning 'bread, sausage and...' used when listing food items (often followed by another item).
additional_notes: This phrase is an example of listing items in Italian using commas and 'e' (and) before the final item. In the example sentences the speaker is asking if the listener needs/wants those items (pane, salsiccia e formaggio). You will normally complete the list after 'e' (e.g., 'formaggio'). Use the appropriate verb form for the subject (Avete, Le servono, Ti servono).
target_language_example: Vorresti pane, salsiccia e verdure?
native_language_example: Would you like bread, sausage and vegetables?

meaning: 'the bread is' (simple subject + verb to be)
additional_notes: A very basic structure: pane (bread) + è (3rd person singular of essere = to be). Used to describe the state, quality, or characteristic of bread (e.g., duro, fresco, buono). Replace 'pane' with other nouns to form similar sentences. Common in everyday speech and essential for beginners practicing adjectives and agreement.
target_language_example: Il pane è appena sfornato.
native_language_example: The bread is just out of the oven.

meaning: ‘my dad (to me)’ — the subject 'dad' plus the indirect object pronoun 'mi' meaning 'to me' or 'for me'.
additional_notes: Used to say that your father did something for or to you. 'Papà' is the subject (dad); 'mi' is the unstressed indirect-object pronoun meaning 'to me' or 'for me'. In spoken and written Italian the pronoun can appear before the verb (Mio papà mi ha comprato...) or after in some past-tense constructions (Papà mi comprò...). Common verbs with 'papà mi' include comprare (to buy), dare (to give), raccontare (to tell).
target_language_example: Papà mi ha preparato la colazione stamattina.
native_language_example: My dad made breakfast for me this morning.

meaning: ‘Dad/father’ + ‘you’ (direct or indirect object): 'Dad (will) ... you' or 'Dad ... you'.
additional_notes: Combination of papà (dad) with the clitic pronoun ti (to/you). Used when dad is the subject and 'you' is the object (direct or indirect) of the verb. English equivalents depend on the verb: 'Dad loves you', 'Dad wants you', 'Dad will put you in time-out', etc. Word order in Italian places the pronoun after the noun subject in spoken/neutral sentences (papà ti ...).
target_language_example: Papà ti comprerà un gelato domani.
native_language_example: Dad will buy you an ice cream tomorrow.

meaning: to park the (feminine noun follows — e.g. la macchina, la auto).
additional_notes: Parcheggiare = to park (a vehicle). 'La' is the feminine definite article used when the noun that follows is feminine (la macchina, la automobile, la moto). In spoken Italian 'auto' is often used instead of 'automobile'. Word order: parcheggiare la + [noun]. You can also say 'devo parcheggiare qui' (I must park here) without repeating the noun.
target_language_example: Devo parcheggiare la macchina davanti al negozio.
native_language_example: I need to park the car in front of the shop.

meaning: amusement park; theme park (a place with rides and entertainment)
additional_notes: Used for places with roller coasters, rides, games, attractions and shows. Can be large (theme park) or smaller (local amusement park). 'Divertimenti' comes from 'divertire' (to amuse). Not formal or slang—neutral noun phrase. Use with verbs like 'andare a', 'visitare', or 'essere' (e.g., 'il parco divertimenti è aperto').
target_language_example: Andiamo al parco divertimenti questo weekend.
native_language_example: Let's go to the amusement park this weekend.

meaning: 'at the park yesterday' (parco = park; ieri = yesterday).
additional_notes: This is a short combination of a place (parco) and a time adverb (ieri). In natural Italian you'd normally include a preposition when needed (e.g. 'al parco ieri' = 'to/at the park yesterday'). Sentences in the examples show different subject pronouns and past tenses (sono andato/a, ti ho visto). Remember to match gender in past participles with essere (sono andato/andata) and agreement for direct objects in passato prossimo with avere only in some cases (e.g. 'vi ho viste' if the group is feminine).
target_language_example: Siamo andati al parco ieri per fare un picnic.
native_language_example: We went to the park yesterday to have a picnic.

meaning: park for playing / a park where you play sports or games.
additional_notes: Used to describe a park intended or used for play or sports (e.g., baseball, tennis). Can follow verbs of motion (andare, venire, andare al parco per giocare = go to the park to play). The phrase is compositional and literal: parco = park, per = for/to (purpose), giocare = to play.
target_language_example: Andiamo al parco per giocare a calcio questo pomeriggio.
native_language_example: Let's go to the park to play soccer this afternoon.

meaning: relatives in/at (a place) — used to say you have family who live in a specific city or area.
additional_notes: Common construction: 'ho/abbiamo/avete parenti a [luogo]'. 'Parenti' = relatives. Use 'a' for cities and some towns (a Milano, a Napoli). For countries/regions you may use 'in' (in Italia) or still 'a' for cities. Can be definite with 'dei parenti a' to mean 'some relatives in...'.
target_language_example: Hai parenti a Roma?
native_language_example: Do you have relatives in Rome?

meaning: literally 'speaks like' — used to say someone speaks in the manner/style of someone or something.
additional_notes: Followed by a noun phrase introduced by 'un/una' or by a noun (e.g. una persona, un gruppo, a profession). It describes manner, accent, vocabulary, tone or style of speech. Can be neutral (Parla come un adulto) or pejorative depending on the noun (e.g. parla come un camionista). Be aware: one example contains an offensive racial slur in Italian — avoid using such language; it's included only from the source sentences.
target_language_example: Lei parla come una professore, usa parole eleganti.
native_language_example: She speaks like a teacher; she uses elegant words.

meaning: he/she/you (formal) speaks English (or 'do/does [someone] speak English?' depending on context).
additional_notes: Parla is the third-person singular (and formal 'you' lei) form of parlare. Use parla inglese to say someone speaks English, to ask if someone does (e.g., 'Parla inglese?'), or to state a lack with non (e.g., 'Non parla inglese'). For informal 'you' (tu) say 'parli inglese'.
target_language_example: Parla inglese con un perfetto accento americano.
native_language_example: He/She speaks English with a perfect American accent.

meaning: to speak now / to talk right now (asking or stating about doing it at this moment).
additional_notes: Used to ask or say whether someone can or is speaking at this moment. Often appears in questions (Posso parlare adesso? / Possiamo parlare adesso?) and in negative/ongoing contexts (Non posso parlare adesso). 'Adesso' = now/right now; interchangeable with 'ora' in many contexts.
target_language_example: Non posso parlare adesso, chiamami più tardi.
native_language_example: I can't talk right now, call me later.

meaning: to speak well (a language) — to have good ability or speak correctly/fluently.
additional_notes: Commonly used with a language after it (e.g., parlare bene l'inglese). Can refer to pronunciation, grammar, fluency or general competence. Often appears with verbs like sapere, poter, riuscire, or modal verbs (devi cercare di...). Word order: parlare bene + [language].
target_language_example: So parlare bene l'italiano dopo molti anni di studio.
native_language_example: I can speak Italian well after many years of study.

meaning: to speak with one's mouth (usually followed by 'piena') — i.e. to speak with a full mouth; 'don't talk with your mouth full.'
additional_notes: Frequently used in the fixed phrase parlare con la bocca piena (to speak with your mouth full). Used to give polite table manners advice or commands. Can appear with different subjects and verb forms (Non dovresti..., Non parlare..., Non si deve...).
target_language_example: Per favore, non parlare con la bocca piena durante la cena.
native_language_example: Please don't speak with your mouth full during dinner.

meaning: to speak/talk with my (female family member).
additional_notes: This phrase combines the verb parlare (to speak) + con (with) + mia (my, feminine singular). It must be followed by a feminine family noun (sorella, moglie, figlia) or another feminine noun. For a masculine noun use mio (e.g., parlare con mio padre). Common in requests and statements: Fammi parlare con mia sorella = Let me speak with my sister. Pronunciation and word order are the same as in English: parlare con mia + [feminine noun].
target_language_example: Devo parlare con mia madre subito.
native_language_example: I need to speak with my mother right away.

meaning: to speak/talk with my (followed by a family member).
additional_notes: Used before a family-member noun (mio fratello, mio figlio, mio marito) to say you want to talk with that person. 'Mio' agrees in gender/number with the possessor, not the thing: for feminine singular use 'mia' (mia madre), for plural use 'miei/mie' (i miei genitori, le mie sorelle). In formal situations you might hear 'parlare con mio marito' or the more polite 'parlare con mio marito, per favore'.
target_language_example: Devo parlare con mio padre domani.
native_language_example: I need to talk with my father tomorrow.

meaning: to talk with (a) [female or unspecified singular person]; 'parlare con una persona' = to talk with a person.
additional_notes: Literally 'to speak with a (feminine/indefinite)'. In Italian, 'una' is the indefinite article for feminine singular and often appears before a noun (una persona, una ragazza). In many contexts speakers omit the noun if it's understood (e.g., 'parlare con una' implies 'with a woman/girl' or 'with someone/female'). If you mean any person regardless of gender, use 'una persona' or simply 'qualcuno' (parlare con qualcuno). For a male person say 'parlare con un'.
target_language_example: Devo parlare con una persona domani.
native_language_example: I have to speak with a person tomorrow.

meaning: to talk about what (has) happened / to discuss what is/was the case
additional_notes: Used to introduce a discussion about a specific event or situation. In examples it appears with verbs like "successo" (happened) after it: "parlare di quello che è successo" = "talk about what happened." Can be used in present or past contexts; often followed by time markers (ieri, oggi).
target_language_example: Dobbiamo parlare di quello che è successo ieri.
native_language_example: We need to talk about what happened yesterday.

meaning: to speak badly of someone; to badmouth or talk negatively about someone
additional_notes: Used with di + person (e.g., parlare male di lei = speak badly about her). Common in commands or requests to stop someone from criticizing or insulting another. Can be conjugated normally (parlo male, parlavano male). Neutral register; not slang.
target_language_example: Per favore, non parlare male dei tuoi colleghi.
native_language_example: Please don't speak badly about your colleagues.

meaning: 'to speak now' or 'to talk now' — used to ask or tell someone about speaking at the present moment.
additional_notes: Combines the verb parlare (to speak) with ora (now). Common in questions (Possiamo parlare ora? — Can we talk now?) and requests (Le chiedo di non parlare ora — I ask you not to speak now). Often used to check if it's a good moment to start or continue speaking. Word order can vary (e.g., 'posso parlare ora?').
target_language_example: Scusa, posso parlare ora?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can I speak now?

meaning: to speak more than three (languages).
additional_notes: Used to ask or state whether someone can speak more than three languages. Replace 'tre' with another number to change the quantity (e.g., parlare più di due). Common in questions: Puoi/è in grado di/Sai parlare più di tre lingue? 'Parlare' here refers to language ability.
target_language_example: Sai parlare più di tre lingue?
native_language_example: Can you speak more than three languages?

meaning: to speak only (with someone) / to speak only about (something) — depends on context
additional_notes: Can mean 'to speak only with' someone (followed by 'con [someone]') or 'to speak only about' a subject (followed by 'di [topic]'). In colloquial use it can also complain that someone is the only one talking ('Vuoi parlare solo tu?') or that a person talks exclusively about one thing. Word order and context determine whether 'solo' modifies the person you speak with or the topic/extent of speaking.
target_language_example: Preferisco parlare solo con il direttore.
native_language_example: I prefer to speak only with the manager.

meaning: to talk on/about a platform or topic; often 'talk on' (e.g. on a website or app).
additional_notes: Commonly used with online platforms (e.g. 'parlare su Facebook' = 'to start talking on Facebook'). Can mean 'talk about' when followed by a topic, but in these examples it indicates the place/channel where the conversation happened. Use with preposition 'su' + platform or topic.
target_language_example: Ci siamo messi a parlare su Instagram.
native_language_example: We started talking on Instagram.

meaning: 'to speak to you for' (used to ask for someone's brief attention/time)
additional_notes: Common informal polite request meaning 'Can I speak to you for a moment?' or 'Do you have a minute?'. It combines the verb parlare + indirect object pronoun ti (to you) + a time word like attimo or momento. You will often hear full forms: 'Posso parlarti un attimo?' or 'Vorrei parlarti un momento.'
target_language_example: Posso parlarti un attimo in privato?
native_language_example: Can I speak to you for a moment in private?

meaning: spoken with the (feminine singular noun) / talked to the
additional_notes: This is the past participle 'parlato' (spoken) + 'con' (with) + the definite article 'la' used before a feminine singular noun (e.g., la polizia, la gente, la famiglia, la stampa). Use 'parlato con il' for masculine singular (il), 'parlato con i' for masculine plural, and 'parlato con le' for feminine plural. It can mean 'spoke with' (a conversation) or 'talked to' (addressed someone). Context determines whether the following noun is the person/people or a group/institution.
target_language_example: Ho parlato con la polizia ieri.
native_language_example: I spoke with the police yesterday.

meaning: spoken about his/her/its (something).
additional_notes: Combines the past participle 'parlato' (spoken) with 'della sua' (of/about his/her/its [feminine noun]). Use 'del suo' for masculine nouns; 'dei/degli/delle' for plurals as needed. Refers to someone having talked about something that belongs to or concerns them. Person/gender is determined by context (e.g., 'la sua famiglia' = his/her family).
target_language_example: Ha parlato della sua famiglia ieri.
native_language_example: He/She talked about his/her family yesterday.

meaning: spoken in (a language or medium).
additional_notes: Used after parlare (past participle parlato) with in + language/medium to say which language or channel something was spoken in: e.g. "ha parlato in francese" = "he/she spoke in French". Also used for media ("in TV"). Agreement of subject is with avere (ha/hanno) or essere (if required by context), but the phrase focuses on the language/medium used.
target_language_example: Ieri hanno parlato in italiano durante la riunione.
native_language_example: Yesterday they spoke in Italian during the meeting.

meaning: 'speak to' or 'talk to' (subjunctive or imperative forms: 'you speak to' / 'let [someone] speak to').
additional_notes: Commonly appears in commands or requests with lasci(a)/lasci che (let [someone]) + (mi/ti/ci) parli da sola/da solo meaning 'let her/him speak to him/her alone' or as part of reported speech (e.g. 'Me ne parli da tre giorni' = 'You have been talking to me about it for three days'). 'Parlare a/da' can vary with pronouns: 'parli a lui/lei' (speak to him/her) and 'parli da sola' here means 'on her own' or 'alone' depending on context. In sentences 1–4, the structure is 'Lascia/Lasci che [pronoun] parli da sola' = 'Let her/him talk to him/her alone.' In sentence 5, 'parli da tre giorni' uses 'parlare di/da' to indicate duration: 'has been talking about it for three days.' Check context: 'parlare a' = speak to someone; 'parlare da' can mean 'speak from the position of' or indicate duration when followed by a time expression.
target_language_example: Lascia che gliene parli da sola.
native_language_example: Let her talk to him about it by herself.

meaning: I speak in
additional_notes: Literally "I speak in." It is usually followed by a language or way of speaking, for example parlo in italiano = "I speak in Italian." Parlo is the first-person singular form, so it refers to "I."
target_language_example: Parlo in italiano con i miei amici.
native_language_example: I speak in Italian with my friends.

meaning: 'I'll speak' / 'I'll talk (to them/about it)'.
additional_notes: Used to offer to take responsibility for speaking, intervening, or clearing up a situation. Often said to indicate the speaker will handle the conversation or contact someone to avoid misunderstandings. Can be used alone as an offer ('I'll handle it') or followed by a prepositional phrase (e.g. 'con i residenti', 'ci').
target_language_example: Non preoccuparti: ci parlo io domani con il direttore.
native_language_example: Don't worry: I'll speak to the director about it tomorrow.

meaning: literally 'spoke with the mouth' — most commonly appears in the full phrase 'parlò con la bocca piena' meaning 'spoke with his/her mouth full'. Used to describe someone speaking while eating.
additional_notes: Typically used in past tense forms (e.g., 'parlò' passato remoto or 'ha parlato' passato prossimo). In practice you'll often see the complete phrase 'parlò con la bocca piena' or variations with different subjects/persons: 'Lui parlò con la bocca piena', 'Mary parlò con la bocca piena'. The literal translation corresponds to the idiomatic meaning here.
target_language_example: Lui parlò con la bocca piena a tavola.
native_language_example: He spoke with his mouth full at the table.

meaning: 'word in' — used to say a word is in a certain language or to talk about a word inside something (e.g., a dictionary).
additional_notes: Common pattern: parola + in + language (e.g. parola in inglese, parola in berbero). Can also be used literally to mean 'a word in [something]' (e.g. in a dictionary or sentence). The preposition in indicates language or location. Word order: "parola in [lingua/luogo]". If plural use "parole in".
target_language_example: Conosco una parola in spagnolo.
native_language_example: I know one word in Spanish.

meaning: word for word; literally (exact, literal translation).
additional_notes: Used to describe a literal, exact translation or rendering of text, often implying it may be awkward or incorrect in the target language. Commonly follows verbs like tradurre, rendere, or parlare (e.g., 'tradurre parola per parola').
target_language_example: Ha tradotto il testo parola per parola, ma suona strano in italiano.
native_language_example: He translated the text word for word, but it sounds odd in Italian.

meaning: "words in" — used to indicate the language, location, or context that follows (e.g. words in Arabic, words in this list).
additional_notes: Commonly appears before a language (parole in italiano/inglese/arabo) or before a noun phrase to specify the context or medium where the words appear or are used. Can also be part of idiomatic expressions (e.g. mille parole in certi momenti). The preposition in here is literal (inside/in) or idiomatic depending on context.
target_language_example: So dire poche parole in francese.
native_language_example: I can say a few words in French.

meaning: ‘words’ followed by the indirect object 'mi' (to/for me) — used to say that someone's words affect the speaker (hurt, please, comfort, make me think, etc.).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but a common combination: parole (words) + mi (to me). In English you often translate as 'your words hurt me', 'those words give me comfort', 'these words made me think'. The verb comes after and determines the exact meaning (hanno ferito, rendono felice, danno conforto, hanno fatto pensare). 'Mi' is the first-person indirect object pronoun placed before the verb in compound tenses or before the verb in simple tenses.
target_language_example: Le sue parole mi hanno dato coraggio.
native_language_example: His/her words gave me courage.

meaning: words are / my/your/his/her words are (short clause: 'words are...')
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but simply the noun 'parole' (words) followed by the verb 'sono' (they/you formal are). Used to make statements about words (e.g., 'Le parole sono potenti' = 'Words are powerful'). The subject pronoun (le, le sue, queste, etc.) usually appears before 'parole'. Adjust possessive or demonstrative as needed: 'le parole sono', 'le sue parole sono', 'queste parole sono'.
target_language_example: Le parole sono importanti per comunicare.
native_language_example: Words are important for communicating.

meaning: part of the / some of the (used before a plural noun to indicate a portion of a group)
additional_notes: Often appears in the expression "la maggior parte delle" meaning "the majority of" or "most of". "Parte delle" by itself means "part of" or "some of" and is followed by a plural noun with the definite article (delle = di + le). Use when referring to a portion of a group or quantity.
target_language_example: Parte delle mele sono ancora verdi.
native_language_example: Some of the apples are still green.

meaning: 'the right side' or 'the right place/direction' (physically or metaphorically: the correct side/position or heading the right way).
additional_notes: Used literally to mean the correct side or direction (e.g., standing on the right side, going the right way) and figuratively to mean being on the correct/opportune side (e.g., morally or strategically). Commonly appears in the expression 'dalla parte giusta' (on the right side).
target_language_example: Se vuoi essere sicuro, vai dalla parte giusta dell'edificio.
native_language_example: If you want to be sure, go to the right side of the building.

meaning: 'to take part in' or 'to participate in'.
additional_notes: Used with the preposition 'a' plus an event, activity, meeting, conference, festival, etc. Commonly followed by a noun (partecipare a una festa / a una conferenza) or by a verb in the infinitive introduced by 'a' less often. Use appropriate preposition 'a' even when English uses 'in' or 'to'.
target_language_example: Vorrei partecipare a quel corso di cucina il mese prossimo.
native_language_example: I would like to take part in that cooking course next month.

meaning: a game/match of (a particular sport or game).
additional_notes: Used with a specific game or sport after 'a' (e.g., partita a scacchi, partita a poker, partita a biliardo). Commonly means a single contest, match or round. Can refer to both casual games and organized matches. Often used with verbs like fare, giocare, sfidare, vincere (to play, to challenge, to win).
target_language_example: Vuoi fare una partita a carte stasera?
native_language_example: Do you want to play a card game tonight?

meaning: it all passes / everything will pass (used to say a difficult situation will get better)
additional_notes: Commonly used to reassure someone that a problem, pain, or bad time is temporary. Tone can be comforting or a bit dismissive depending on context. Can be literal (everything goes through) but usually figurative: 'this too shall pass.' Often used alone as a short reassurance: 'Passa tutto.'
target_language_example: Non ti preoccupare per adesso: passa tutto.
native_language_example: Don't worry for now: everything will pass.

meaning: a passage/passage excerpt from (a feminine source); 'passage from the...'
additional_notes: Used to introduce an excerpt taken from a work (book, poem, Bible, article, etc.). 'Dalla' is the contraction of 'da' + 'la' and agrees in gender with the feminine noun that follows or is understood (e.g., 'dalla Bibbia', 'dalla poesia'). If the source is masculine use 'dal' (da + il) or other contractions (dallo, dall', dagli, dalle) as appropriate.
target_language_example: Ha letto un passaggio dalla poesia durante la lezione.
native_language_example: He read a passage from the poem during the lesson.

meaning: I spent a (period of time)... (passato remoto of 'passare')
additional_notes: Used to say you spent a certain amount of time doing something (e.g. passai una settimana = I spent a week). 'Passai' is the first-person singular passato remoto of 'passare' (more common in written/narrative Italian; in spoken Italian speakers often use passato prossimo: 'ho passato una settimana'). Followed by a time period or event (una settimana, una buona estate, ecc.) and often a phrase introducing where or how (a Berlino, vivendo... / abitando...).
target_language_example: Passai una settimana al mare con gli amici.
native_language_example: I spent a week at the seaside with friends.

meaning: A fragment of verb phrase used with a noun to mean 'to spend/pass (some) [time/part] of' or 'to go through/experience (some) [period/part]'; incomplete on its own and requires completion (e.g., 'passare del tempo').
additional_notes: On its own 'passare del' is not a complete expression; it must be followed by a noun or phrase (commonly 'tempo'). Common full phrases: 'passare del tempo', 'passare del tempo con qualcuno', 'passare del tempo a fare qualcosa'. Meaning varies with context because 'passare' has several senses (spend, pass, happen). For learners: memorize common complete forms rather than using 'passare del' by itself.
target_language_example: Vorrei passare del tempo con te questo fine settimana.
native_language_example: I would like to spend some time with you this weekend.

meaning: to drop by to pick up (someone or something); to call by and collect
additional_notes: Commonly used when arranging to pick someone up (e.g., by car) or to collect an item. Often followed by a person or thing: passare a prendere Marco / passare a prendere il pacco. Tense and subject change normally: passo a prendere, passerò a prendere, sono passato a prendere. Can be casual or neutral—used in spoken and written Italian.
target_language_example: Dovrei passare a prendere Marco prima di cena.
native_language_example: I should drop by to pick up Marco before dinner.

meaning: to pass (something) — with the definite article 'gli' before a masculine plural noun (e.g. exams, spaghetti).
additional_notes: passare is a verb meaning 'to pass', 'to hand over', 'to spend (time)', or 'to pass an exam' depending on context. 'Gli' is the masculine plural definite article used before nouns starting with z or s+consonant and some vowels (e.g. gli esami, gli spaghetti). Together 'passare gli ___' requires an object noun after 'gli' (e.g. passare gli esami = to pass the exams; passare gli spaghetti = to pass the spaghetti [hand them over]). Imperative and subjunctive forms in your examples (Assicurati di passare gli esami; Potrebbe passare gli spaghetti?) show different moods: here 'passare' stays infinitive after modal/auxiliary verbs or expressions like 'assicurarsi di' and 'potrebbe'.
target_language_example: Devi studiare molto per passare gli esami.
native_language_example: You must study a lot to pass the exams.

meaning: to stop by/visit briefly at a place (usually a specific location like a shop, office, or room).
additional_notes: Commonly used with places introduced by a noun without an article (in + place) to mean dropping in briefly or going to a particular location. Often implies a short, purposeful visit (e.g., to pick something up, check something, or deliver a message). Can be preceded by verbs like ricordare (remember) or devo (I must).
target_language_example: Devo passare in posta prima di tornare a casa.
native_language_example: I have to stop by the post office before going home.

meaning: to pass more / to spend more time (literal); by itself it's incomplete—usually needs context or an object.
additional_notes: On its own 'passare più' is not a complete phrase in Italian. 'Passare' means 'to pass', 'to go by', or 'to spend (time)'; 'più' means 'more' or 'anymore' depending on placement. You will typically see it in longer expressions like 'passare più tempo' (to spend more time), 'non passa più' (he/she/it doesn't pass anymore), or 'passare più tardi' (to come by later). Pay attention to word order and the verb's meaning in context.
target_language_example: Vorrei passare più tempo con la mia famiglia.
native_language_example: I would like to spend more time with my family.

meaning: 'a pastime is' / 'a hobby is' (used to define or describe a pastime)
additional_notes: Passatempo means 'pastime' or 'hobby'. The phrase 'passatempo è' would begin a sentence that defines or describes what a pastime is (e.g., 'Passatempo è fare una passeggiata' — 'A pastime is taking a walk'). In natural Italian you might more often see just 'È un passatempo...' (It's a pastime...) or 'Un passatempo è...' (A pastime is...).
target_language_example: Un buon passatempo è leggere un libro la sera.
native_language_example: A good pastime is reading a book in the evening.

meaning: to spend (the holidays/vacation).
additional_notes: Commonly used to say where or how someone spent a period of time such as 'le vacanze' (the holidays). Conjugate 'passare' for the subject and include the article + period (e.g. le vacanze, le ferie). Word order: passato le -> passato le vacanze (ho passato le mie vacanze).
target_language_example: Ho passato le vacanze al mare con la famiglia.
native_language_example: I spent the holidays at the seaside with my family.

meaning: spent (all) — used to say you spent all of a period of time doing something or being somewhere.
additional_notes: Usually part of the past tense expression 'ho/ho/abbiamo passato tutta la giornata/la notte/la vita...' followed by an activity or place (a + infinitive or con/in/ a location). 'Passare' here means 'to spend (time)'. Agreement: 'tutta' agrees with a feminine noun (la giornata, la notte, la vita). For masculine periods you'd hear 'tutto' (e.g. 'tutto il giorno').
target_language_example: Ho passato tutta la serata a cucinare per la famiglia.
native_language_example: I spent the whole evening cooking for the family.

meaning: spent a (time period)
additional_notes: This sequence appears as part of verb phrases with passato (past participle of passare) + a + a time or event. Common uses: 'ho passato una settimana' (I spent a week), 'mi è passato una brutta tosse' (I got over a bad cough — note different constructions with essere), or 'è passato l'una' (it's past one o'clock). Meaning depends on verb construction and context: with direct object it often means 'to spend' (time); with intransitive 'passare' + time expression it means 'to pass' (time or a clock hour).
target_language_example: Ho passato una settimana al mare.
native_language_example: I spent a week at the seaside.

meaning: a walk (to/at) — used with a specific place (e.g., al parco = a walk in/at the park).
additional_notes: Passeggiata means 'walk' or 'stroll'. When followed by 'al' (a + il) it links to a masculine singular place: 'passeggiata al parco' = 'a walk in/at the park'; 'passeggiata alla' would be used for feminine places. Commonly used to suggest going for a casual walk or describe having taken one.
target_language_example: Vuoi fare una passeggiata al parco questo pomeriggio?
native_language_example: Do you want to take a walk in the park this afternoon?

meaning: a walk with me / 'take a walk with me' (invitation to walk together).
additional_notes: Used to invite someone (formal or informal depending on verb form) to go for a walk together. Common verbs: fare una passeggiata con me (to take/go for a walk with me) or imperatives: Faccia una passeggiata con me (formal 'please take a walk with me') and Fate una passeggiata con me (plural/informal group). Vorresti/Vorreste fare una passeggiata con me? are polite ways to ask 'Would you like to take a walk with me?'
target_language_example: Vorresti fare una passeggiata con me stasera?
native_language_example: Would you like to go for a walk with me tonight?

meaning: 'Could you pass me that...' (polite request to hand something over)
additional_notes: A common way to ask someone to hand you an object. 'Mi' = to me, 'passi' is the polite (Lei) or informal (tu) imperative/indicative depending on context but here used as a polite request (could you pass), and 'quel' = that (masculine singular). Change 'quel' to 'quella/quello/quell'' to match the gender/number of the noun. You can add 'per favore' to be more polite.
target_language_example: Mi passi quel bicchiere, per favore?
native_language_example: Could you pass me that glass, please?

meaning: I/you/he/she spend(s) a lot (of time) — literally 'I spend a lot'.
additional_notes: Used with 'tempo' (time) to say you spend a lot of time doing something: 'passo molto tempo a + infinitive' or 'passo molto tempo con/in + noun'. Conjugate 'passo' for person (passo, passi, passa, passiamo, passate, passano). 'Molto' modifies 'tempo' (a lot).
target_language_example: Passo molto tempo a imparare l'italiano.
native_language_example: I spend a lot of time learning Italian.

meaning: a step forward; progress or an advance toward a goal.
additional_notes: Used both literally (a physical step forward) and figuratively to mean progress, improvement, or being ahead. Common in contexts about development, solutions, achievements, or being more advanced than someone/something.
target_language_example: È un piccolo passo avanti per il progetto, ma stiamo migliorando.
native_language_example: It's a small step forward for the project, but we're improving.

meaning: spent the
additional_notes: This is a fragment, not a fixed expression. passò is the third-person singular passato remoto of passare. With time words such as il Natale, il tempo, or il resto del viaggio, it usually means 'spent'. With physical objects, it can mean 'passed' or 'handed'. The article changes with the noun: for example, passò la notte. This tense is especially common in written stories and historical narration; in everyday speech, Italians often say ha passato instead.
target_language_example: Passò il pomeriggio a leggere.
native_language_example: He spent the afternoon reading.

meaning: 'the meal is' or 'the meal was' (subject + verb 'essere').
additional_notes: A simple combination of the noun pasto (meal) and the verb è (is) or è stato (was) when used in past. Used to describe the quality or state of a meal: e.g. 'Il pasto è stato ottimo' = 'The meal was excellent.' This phrase is compositional and literal — it's just subject + form of 'essere'.
target_language_example: Il pasto è molto abbondante oggi.
native_language_example: The meal is very abundant today.

meaning: fried potato; typically a single piece of fried potato or, by extension, a French fry/item of deep-fried potato.
additional_notes: Often used in singular to name one fried potato piece or generically in recipes. In spoken Italian, plural 'patatine fritte' is more common when ordering fries. Usage can vary by region and context (slices, wedges, or sticks). Informal contexts may prefer diminutives like 'patatina fritta'.
target_language_example: Ho trovato una patata fritta nel piatto del gatto.
native_language_example: I found a fried potato in the cat's plate.

meaning: fried potatoes; French fries / fries.
additional_notes: Commonly refers to sliced or cut potatoes fried in oil (what English speakers call 'French fries' or simply 'fries'). Can be singular in context as "una porzione di patate fritte". Often served with ketchup, mayonnaise, or other sauces. Plural in Italian and used with verbs for eating/serving (mangia, mangiate, fai/fagli).
target_language_example: Vorrei una porzione di patate fritte, per favore.
native_language_example: I'd like a portion of French fries, please.

meaning: a (single) french fry; a small fried potato slice (singular, often used affectionately).
additional_notes: Literal: 'little fried potato'. Used for one fry or a small portion; can be affectionate or playful (e.g., calling someone 'patatina fritta' like 'sweetie' in very informal contexts). Plural is 'patatine fritte' (french fries). Common in Italy to refer to fries served as a side or snack.
target_language_example: Vorrei una patatina fritta, per favore.
native_language_example: I would like one french fry, please.

meaning: French fries; fried potato chips (hot, thinly cut potatoes).
additional_notes: Commonly used in Italy to mean 'French fries' served hot (often with ketchup or alongside sandwiches/pizza). 'Patatine' alone can mean chips (snack) or fries depending on context; 'patatine fritte' specifies they are fried/hot. Plural only in normal use. Used with articles and partitive (delle, alcune, il) as in the examples.
target_language_example: Vorrei un piatto di patatine fritte, per favore.
native_language_example: I'd like a plate of French fries, please.

meaning: 'afraid of that' or 'fear of that (one)'.
additional_notes: Literal combination of paura (fear) + di (of) + quel (that; masculine singular demonstrative). Used before a masculine noun or implied masculine thing: e.g. paura di quel cane (afraid of that dog) or paura di quel (implying 'that one' when the noun is known). Not a fixed idiom — it's compositional and literal. Make sure the noun that follows is masculine; for feminine use paura di quella.
target_language_example: Ho paura di quel cane quando viene di notte.
native_language_example: I'm afraid of that dog when it comes at night.

meaning: afraid of his/her (own) — used to say someone is afraid of a specific person (his/her).
additional_notes: Paura = 'fear' or 'afraid'. 'Suo' is a possessive meaning 'his' or 'her' (formal/third-person). In these sentences it follows the preposition 'di' to mean 'afraid of his/her [father, husband, etc.]'. Gender/number of the possessed noun (padre, marito, nonno) is shown in the noun; 'suo' agrees with the possessor (third person) and not with the speaker. Context decides whether 'suo' refers to 'his' or 'her'. For clarity, Italian often repeats the person's name or uses context to show whose father/husband is meant.
target_language_example: Luca ha paura di suo fratello.
native_language_example: Luca is afraid of his brother.

meaning: the patient is … (used to describe a patient's condition/state).
additional_notes: Used in medical or reporting contexts to state a patient's condition. 'Paziente' can be masculine (il paziente) or feminine (la paziente). The verb 'è' is the third-person singular of 'essere' (to be). Combine with adjectives or phrases (e.g., 'in condizioni critiche', 'malata', 'morta'). Not an idiom—it's simply a subject + verb construction.
target_language_example: La paziente è stabile dopo l'intervento.
native_language_example: The patient is stable after the surgery.

meaning: to make things worse / to worsen them (the feminine plural object 'le' = 'them').
additional_notes: Pecciorare = to worsen; when combined with the pronoun 'le' it refers to feminine plural things/situations previously mentioned (e.g., 'le cose'). Commonly used in imperatives/advisives: 'Non peggiorare le cose' = 'Don't make things worse.' Verb conjugates normally: peggiorare, peggioro, peggiori, peggiora, peggioriamo, peggiorate, peggiorano. The clitic pronoun can attach before the verb (non le peggiorare — less common) or after in some constructions (peggiorarle in infinitive), but in everyday speech 'peggiorare le cose' or 'peggiorare le' (with context) is understood.
target_language_example: Non peggiorare le cose, cerchiamo di risolvere il problema.
native_language_example: Don't make things worse; let's try to solve the problem.

meaning: ‘the worst is’ or ‘my/ the worst ___ is…’
additional_notes: Used to introduce the worst thing/aspect about someone or something. Often appears as part of phrases like "la cosa peggiore è..." (the worst thing is...) or with a noun (e.g. "il mio vizio peggiore è..."). Common in both neutral and negative statements to emphasize a downside or problem.
target_language_example: La cosa peggiore è che non lo sanno ancora.
native_language_example: The worst thing is that they still don't know.

meaning: 'skin and' — the phrase combines pelle (skin) with e (and), used when listing skin together with another noun (e.g., i capelli = hair).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase; it’s just the noun pelle followed by the conjunction e. In normal Italian you would say pelle e i capelli (skin and hair) when describing both. Watch word order and articles: include articles for the following noun when needed (pelle e i capelli). The example sentence 'Pelle e una manciata di capelli.' is ungrammatical or awkward in Italian — you would say 'Pelle e una manciata di capelli' only in a very stylized/contextual way; more natural is 'La pelle e i capelli' or 'Ha la pelle e pochi capelli.'
target_language_example: Ha la pelle e i capelli chiari.
native_language_example: She has fair skin and hair.

meaning: 'worth' or 'worth the trouble of' when used with verbs/nouns; can indicate pity/compassion in some contexts
additional_notes: Commonly appears in the expression 'valere la pena (di) + infinitive' meaning 'to be worth (doing)'. 'Pena di' after a noun can mean 'sorrow/pity for' (e.g. 'pena di entrambe' = 'pity for both'). Use context to determine whether it expresses 'worth' (positive value) or 'pain/pity'.
target_language_example: Vale la pena di provare questo ristorante.
native_language_example: It's worth trying this restaurant.

meaning: death penalty; capital punishment.
additional_notes: Used to refer to state-imposed execution as a legal punishment. Common in legal, political, and ethical discussions. Can appear in phrases like "abolire la pena di morte" (to abolish the death penalty) or "essere condannato a morte" (to be sentenced to death).
target_language_example: Molti paesi hanno abolito la pena di morte.
native_language_example: Many countries have abolished the death penalty.

meaning: used to describe the type of pen by its tip or function (e.g. penna a sfera = ballpoint pen, penna a inchiostro = ink pen).
additional_notes: This is a connector: penna + a + noun describes what kind of pen (tip, ink, use). Common combos: 'penna a sfera' (ballpoint pen), 'penna a inchiostro' (fountain/ink pen in some contexts), 'penna a gel' (gel pen). Not used alone; you need the following noun (sfera, gel, china, inchiostro, biro, etc.).
target_language_example: Vorrei una penna a sfera, per favore.
native_language_example: I'd like a ballpoint pen, please.

meaning: ballpoint pen
additional_notes: Common everyday term for a pen that writes with a tiny rotating ball (ballpoint). Used for asking, giving, or mentioning this kind of pen. Countable (una penna a sfera, due penne a sfera).
target_language_example: Mi passi una penna a sfera, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you pass me a ballpoint pen, please?

meaning: 'think of' / 'what do you think of (about)' (used to ask someone's opinion about something)
additional_notes: Usually appears in the question form 'Che/Cosa/Lei cosa ne pensa del...' or 'Che ne pensa di...'. The pronoun 'ne' refers back to the thing/topic. 'Del' = di + il (about the). Use with nouns: 'del film', 'del libro'. Formal questions may use 'Lei cosa ne pensa...'.
target_language_example: Che ne pensa del nuovo ristorante in centro?
native_language_example: What do you think of the new restaurant downtown?

meaning: 'think of the new...' (asks someone's opinion about a new person or thing).
additional_notes: This appears as part of the question structure 'Che/Cosa ne pensa della nuova ...?' meaning 'What do you think of the new ...?' 'Ne' refers back to the person/thing being discussed (or to the general topic). Use 'nuova' to agree in gender with the noun that follows (nuovo/nuova). Commonly used in polite/formal questions (pensa = Lei/lei/lui). Informal variants: 'Che ne pensi della nuova ...?' (tu form).
target_language_example: Che ne pensa della nuova collega?
native_language_example: What do you think of the new colleague?

meaning: You take care of it / You handle it (imperative; asking or telling someone to do something).
additional_notes: Informal command phrase formed from 'pensarci' (to think about/take care of it) + 'tu' for emphasis. Used to ask or tell someone to handle a task or problem. Tone depends on context: can be neutral, commanding, or annoyed (e.g., calling someone lazy). Common in spoken Italian.
target_language_example: Alfredo, pensaci tu, per favore: chiama il meccanico.
native_language_example: Alfredo, you take care of it, please: call the mechanic.

meaning: thinking about (someone or something)
additional_notes: Used to say what or whom you have in mind. Often appears in the structure 'non sto pensando ad altro che a ...' (I'm thinking of nothing else but ...). 'Ad' is a variant of 'a' used before vowels or for emphasis; interchangeable with 'a' in many contexts. Can be followed by pronouns (me/te/lei/voi) or nouns.
target_language_example: Sto pensando ad Anna tutto il giorno.
native_language_example: I'm thinking about Anna all day.

meaning: 'think that way' or 'think so'
additional_notes: Used to say that people hold a certain opinion. Often follows a neutral subject (alcune persone, la maggior parte, pochi, ecc.) and refers back to an idea mentioned earlier (la). 'Così' means 'like that' or 'so'.
target_language_example: Molti pensano così, ma non è sempre vero.
native_language_example: Many people think that way, but it's not always true.

meaning: think of
additional_notes: Used with a person, thing, idea, or topic to indicate directing one's thoughts toward it. 'Pensare a' and 'pensare ad' are the same verb phrase; 'ad' is used before words starting with a vowel for euphony (e.g., 'pensare ad altro'). Can be used both transitively (pensare a qualcosa) and reflexively in expressions like 'pensare ad altro' (to think of something else).
target_language_example: Non posso pensare ad altro!
native_language_example: I can't think of anything else!

meaning: to think carefully; to consider something thoroughly before deciding
additional_notes: Used when advising caution or reflection. Often appears with an infinitive (pensare bene prima di fare qualcosa) or with a direct object (pensare bene una decisione). Can imply weighing pros and cons. Neutral register — can be used in both formal and informal contexts.
target_language_example: Devi pensare bene prima di firmare il contratto.
native_language_example: You must think carefully before signing the contract.

meaning: to think in (a particular way or language).
additional_notes: Used to indicate the mode, style, or language of thought. Often followed by a noun or an adverbial phrase (e.g. 'modo creativo' = 'in a creative way', or a language name to mean 'think in [that language]'). Common in contexts about mindset, problem-solving, or bilingual thought.
target_language_example: Prova a pensare in termini di soluzioni, non di problemi.
native_language_example: Try to think in terms of solutions, not problems.

meaning: 'do you (plural) think that (someone) is ...' — used to ask for others' opinion about an ongoing action or situation.
additional_notes: This is the plural, informal/formal 'you' (voi) of pensare + subjunctive 'stia' (from stare) to introduce a clause about what someone is doing or what is happening now. Common in questions: 'Cosa pensate che stia facendo?' = 'What do you think he/she is doing?' The subject of 'stia' can be implicit (he/she/it) or explicit (e.g., 'lei/il ragazzo'). Use when asking a group for their opinion about a current action or situation.
target_language_example: Voi cosa pensate che stia facendo Marco in questo momento?
native_language_example: What do you (all) think Marco is doing right now?

meaning: have you/they ever thought of becoming (to consider becoming).
additional_notes: Commonly used to ask whether someone has ever considered a particular career, role, or life change. Built from the verb pensare (to think) + di + diventare (to become). Use with different subjects and professions: e.g. "Hai mai pensato di diventare medico?" Tense can change (Ha mai pensato = Have you ever thought; Pensavi = Did you ever think).
target_language_example: Hai mai pensato di diventare cuoco?
native_language_example: Have you ever thought of becoming a chef?

meaning: I thought that the
additional_notes: A common way to introduce a past-tense opinion or assumption about a specific noun (il + masculine singular noun). 'Pensavo' is first-person imperfect of pensare (I thought/was thinking). It is followed by 'che' + a clause in the imperfect/subjunctive or past tense depending on meaning (e.g. 'fosse' subjunctive for uncertainty, or 'era' for a factual past). Replace 'il' with the appropriate article (la, i, le) when the noun has different gender/number.
target_language_example: Pensavo che il treno fosse in ritardo.
native_language_example: I thought that the train was delayed.

meaning: 'what do you think about/of' (used to ask someone's opinion about plural or masculine/feminine nouns introduced by 'dei')
additional_notes: Commonly appears as 'cosa ne pensi (di)...' or 'che cosa pensi dei...' The construction asks for an opinion about something (people, things, ideas). 'Dei' is the partitive/article used with plural nouns (e.g., 'dei film', 'dei bambini'). You can also use 'del', 'della', 'dei', 'degli', 'delle' depending on the noun.
target_language_example: Cosa pensi dei miei amici?
native_language_example: What do you think of my friends?

meaning: what do you think of his/her/its...
additional_notes: Used to ask someone's opinion about something that belongs to or is associated with a third person (suo = his/her/its). Often appears with 'che cosa' or 'cosa' and sometimes with the clitic 'ne' (che ne pensi del suo...) which emphasizes 'about that' or refers back to a previously mentioned idea. Choose 'suo' meaning from context (his, her, its, your formal).
target_language_example: Cosa pensi del suo progetto?
native_language_example: What do you think of his/her project?

meaning: 'we'll take care of it' / 'we'll handle it'.
additional_notes: Used to reassure someone that the speaker and their group will deal with something. Often preceded by 'ci' (Ci pensiamo noi) meaning 'we'll think about it / take care of it'. Can be used alone as a short reply. Tone can be comforting or confident; common in spoken Italian.
target_language_example: Non ti preoccupare per la cena: ci pensiamo noi.
native_language_example: Don't worry about dinner: we'll take care of it.

meaning: "I think that mine" (feminine noun)—used when referring to something that belongs to the speaker and is feminine in Italian.
additional_notes: This is a fragment rather than a complete sentence; it combines the verb phrase penso che (I think that) with la mia (the feminine possessive pronoun 'mine' or 'my one'). You would complete it with a verb or clause: e.g. penso che la mia sia migliore (I think mine is better). Use la mia when the thing you mean is singular and grammatically feminine (la casa, la macchina, la penna). For masculine singular use il mio; for plural use i miei / le mie depending on gender and number.
target_language_example: Penso che la mia macchina sia più veloce.
native_language_example: I think that mine (my car) is faster.

meaning: I only think / I'm just thinking
additional_notes: Used to limit or soften what you're saying: either to say you only think something (and nothing more) or to indicate you're just thinking aloud. Often followed by 'che' + clause (I just think that...) or 'a' + person/thing (I only think about...). Context decides whether it's 'only' (solamente) or 'just' (solo/juste).
target_language_example: Penso solo che dovremmo aspettare.
native_language_example: I just think that we should wait.

meaning: to help them (feminine) / in order to help them.
additional_notes: Per + infinitive (per aiutare) expresses purpose: 'in order to help.' The final -le is a direct or indirect object pronoun referring to a group of females or feminine nouns (them/her). In spoken Italian the meaning is usually 'to help them' (female people) or 'to help her/them' depending on context. If referring to mixed or masculine groups, use 'per aiutarli'.
target_language_example: Sono qui per aiutarle se hanno bisogno.
native_language_example: I'm here to help them (female) if they need it.

meaning: for some / for a few (feminine plural).
additional_notes: Used before feminine plural nouns or expressions (e.g., 'ore', 'persone', 'delle cose' where 'alcune' agrees in gender/number). Can mean 'for a few' (time, quantity) or 'for some' (people/opinions). Often followed by a noun or a partitive phrase.
target_language_example: Restiamo per alcune ore.
native_language_example: We'll stay for a few hours.

meaning: moreover; besides; additionally
additional_notes: Used to add another reason or point. Similar to 'inoltre' or 'per di più'. Often appears in formal or neutral contexts: e.g., giving an extra argument, clarification, or exception. Can precede a clause or phrase (Per altro, non abbiamo abbastanza tempo) or be integrated in the sentence (È costoso e, per altro, inutile).
target_language_example: Non posso venire; per altro ho già un impegno.
native_language_example: I can't come; besides, I already have an appointment.

meaning: 'for love' / 'out of love' — because of love or for someone's sake; also an exclamation meaning 'for heaven's sake!'
additional_notes: Usually means doing something because of love or devotion (e.g., risking everything for love). As an interjection (often with 'del cielo' or alone), it expresses exasperation or a plea: 'Per amore del cielo!' = 'For heaven's sake!'. Context determines whether it's literal (motivation) or emphatic (exclamation).
target_language_example: Lui ha lasciato il lavoro per amore.
native_language_example: He quit his job for love.

meaning: for the sake of; out of love for; for (someone/something)
additional_notes: Used to indicate motivation or reason—often emotional—behind an action (e.g., doing something for the sake of a person, an idea, peace, etc.). Common with people (per amore di Maria), principles (per amore della pace), or abstract things. Can be followed by a noun or pronoun; if the noun requires an article, include it (per amore della mamma).
target_language_example: Lui ha cambiato lavoro per amore di sua figlia.
native_language_example: He changed jobs for the sake of his daughter.

meaning: to go to (someone's place) / to go to (a person)
additional_notes: Used to indicate purpose or direction toward a person or their place. Often followed by a person's name, a pronoun (me, lui, lei), or a noun indicating a place. Example: "per andare da Marco" = "to go to Marco's (house)". If you mean going to a location (not a person), Italian more commonly uses "per andare a" + place (e.g., "per andare a Roma").
target_language_example: Devo prendere l'autobus per andare da mia sorella.
native_language_example: I need to take the bus to go to my sister's (place).

meaning: for having written the… (introduces the reason: 'because he/she wrote the...')
additional_notes: This phrase combines 'per' (for) + the perfect infinitive 'aver scritto' (to have written) + the masculine singular article 'il'. It's used to give the reason or cause for something, often followed by a noun (e.g. il libro). In English you can translate it as 'for having written the…' or more naturally 'for writing the…'. The structure is common in formal speech or writing; in everyday speech Italians may also say 'perché ha scritto il' or 'per aver scritto il libro' is fine.
target_language_example: È stato arrestato per aver scritto il giornale.
native_language_example: He was arrested for having written the newspaper.

meaning: respectable, well-behaved; properly, thoroughly (depending on context).
additional_notes: Used either as an adjective phrase meaning 'respectable' or 'decent' (una persona per bene = a respectable person), or adverbially to intensify an action meaning 'properly,' 'thoroughly,' or colloquially 'really' (often in informal/strong contexts). Tone can be neutral or judgmental; in some contexts it contrasts with immoral or rude behavior. Watch for ironic or vulgar contexts (example 4 uses strong language).
target_language_example: Pensavo fosse un ragazzo per bene, invece era scaltro.
native_language_example: I thought he was a decent guy, but he was clever/ruined me.

meaning: for dogs; intended for dogs (e.g., food, treats, products).
additional_notes: Used to label items or describe something designed for dogs. Commonly appears after a noun (cibo per cani = dog food). Not idiomatic — literal and straightforward.
target_language_example: Ho comprato dei giochi per cani al negozio.
native_language_example: I bought some toys for dogs at the store.

meaning: please (used to express strong plea, to beg, or to reject/emphasize 'no, please' or 'for heaven's sake').
additional_notes: Common exclamation. Depending on context it can be: a polite plea ('please, be careful'), a strong refusal or disgust ('no, please!' / 'for heaven's sake!'), or an urgent request. Tone and intonation determine whether it's gentle or emphatic. Not literal religious meaning in everyday use.
target_language_example: Per carità, non fare così!
native_language_example: Please, don't do that!

meaning: by chance
additional_notes: Used to ask politely or express that something happened unintentionally or unexpectedly. In questions it often corresponds to English 'by any chance' (softening the question). In statements it means 'by chance' or 'accidentally'.
target_language_example: Sei per caso passato da casa mia ieri?
native_language_example: Did you happen to stop by my house yesterday?

meaning: 'percent' or 'percent of' (used to express a proportion out of 100).
additional_notes: Used after a number to form percentages (e.g., 'dieci per cento' = 10%). In Italian you can also write the symbol '%' after the number. When followed by a noun, it indicates the proportion of that noun (e.g., 'il novanta per cento delle persone' = 90% of the people).
target_language_example: Il venti per cento degli studenti ha superato l'esame.
native_language_example: Twenty percent of the students passed the exam.

meaning: so to speak; as it were (used to soften or qualify an expression).
additional_notes: Used to indicate that a phrase is figurative, approximate, or not to be taken literally. Often inserted mid-sentence with commas: "..., per così dire, ..." Can stand alone as a brief comment. Common in spoken and written Italian.
target_language_example: Lui è, per così dire, un dizionario ambulante.
native_language_example: He is, so to speak, a walking dictionary.

meaning: to believe; used in phrases meaning 'to have reason to believe' or 'to be willing/able to believe'.
additional_notes: Often appears after expressions indicating reason, ability, or degree (e.g., 'abbiamo motivi per credere', 'sufficientemente ... per credere'). It can mean 'to believe' in a neutral sense or imply being gullible when combined with adjectives like 'sufficientemente stupido' or 'grande'. Context determines whether it's about justified belief ('reason to believe') or the capacity/willingness to believe.
target_language_example: Non ho prove, ma ho motivi per credere che arriverà in tempo.
native_language_example: I don't have proof, but I have reason to believe he will arrive on time.

meaning: 'to cook' or 'for cooking' (indicates purpose or intended use related to cooking).
additional_notes: Can indicate purpose ('for cooking' — e.g., strumenti per cucinare) or intent/role when used with a verb like assumere: 'assumere qualcuno per cucinare' = 'hire someone to cook'. Context shows both meanings: purpose/use and infinitive purpose with verbs. Common in everyday speech; neutral form.
target_language_example: Ho comprato una pentola nuova per cucinare la pasta.
native_language_example: I bought a new pot to cook pasta.

meaning: 'for which', 'because of which', or 'why' (introduces a reason or object related to something mentioned).
additional_notes: Used to introduce the reason, cause, purpose, or the thing/person for which something applies. Can translate as 'for which', 'that/which', 'because of which', or simply 'why' depending on context. Appears in both relative clauses (e.g., 'the reason for which') and in expressions meaning 'so/therefore' in spoken Italian ('per cui' = 'so'). Context determines whether it points to a cause, an object, or functions as a discourse connector.
target_language_example: Questa è la ragione per cui sono rimasto.
native_language_example: This is the reason why I stayed.

meaning: 'for which' / 'because of which' + negation — used to introduce a reason followed by 'not' (why not...)
additional_notes: Used to introduce the reason or cause of something, often followed by a clause with negation (non). Can appear inside questions (Qual è il motivo per cui non...?) or statements (È morto, per cui non lo sono più.). In many contexts it is interchangeable with 'per cui' (for which) combined with 'non' in the following clause. Tone: neutral; common in spoken and written Italian.
target_language_example: Qual è il motivo per cui non vieni alla festa?
native_language_example: What is the reason why you are not coming to the party?

meaning: 'really' or 'for real' (used to emphasize that something is true or genuine)
additional_notes: Used to add emphasis or to ask/confirm sincerity. Can appear in statements or questions. Similar to davvero or sul serio; slightly more emphatic or colloquial than just 'davvero' in some contexts. Works after verbs or phrases (e.g., 'sei per davvero?', 'l'ha visto per davvero').
target_language_example: Sei per davvero convinto di partire domani?
native_language_example: Are you really sure you're leaving tomorrow?

meaning: moreover; furthermore; on top of that; besides
additional_notes: Used to add extra information that reinforces or emphasizes a point, often introducing something surprising, negative, or additional to what was already said. Can appear at the start or middle of a sentence and is fairly neutral (used in both spoken and written Italian).
target_language_example: Non solo ha sbagliato, per di più non si è scusato.
native_language_example: Not only did he make a mistake, and moreover he didn't apologize.

meaning: for ten (used with time, distance, quantity — 'for ten [units]').
additional_notes: Used to indicate a duration, distance, number of people, etc., expressed as 'for ten' + unit (mesi, chilometri, persone, ore). In contexts like 'per dieci persone' it means 'suitable for/for ten people'. Can appear in emphatic counts or approximations (e.g., 'per dieci, venti' = 'for ten, twenty' meaning 'for a short while' or 'for ten or twenty').
target_language_example: Rimango qui per dieci giorni.
native_language_example: I'll stay here for ten days.

meaning: by mistake; accidentally
additional_notes: Used to say that something happened unintentionally. It typically precedes or follows the verb and is interchangeable with 'per sbaglio' in most contexts. Neutral register (not slang).
target_language_example: Ho cancellato il messaggio per errore.
native_language_example: I deleted the message by mistake.

meaning: for example; as an example.
additional_notes: Used to introduce an example or to ask for one. Can appear at the start of a sentence (Per esempio, ...) or after the noun/verb it refers to (Prendi me, per esempio). Common in both spoken and written Italian.
target_language_example: Per esempio, prendimi come esempio.
native_language_example: For example, take me as an example.

meaning: to be in love (used with expressions like 'too... to be in love')
additional_notes: Literally 'to be in love'. Commonly used after adjectives or phrases expressing degree, e.g. 'troppo giovane per essere innamorato' ('too young to be in love'). Uses the infinitive 'essere' + past participle 'innamorato' functioning adjectivally. Gender agreement: innamorato (masculine), innamorata (feminine). Can be modified with adverbs (davvero, veramente).
target_language_example: Lei è troppo giovane per essere innamorato.
native_language_example: She is too young to be in love.

meaning: for doing any (kind of) / to do whatever
additional_notes: This sequence combines per + infinitive (per fare = in order to do) with qualsiasi (meaning 'any' or 'whatever'). It's usually followed by a noun or clause (e.g. qualsiasi cosa, qualsiasi lavoro). On its own 'per fare qualsiasi' is incomplete in Italian — you normally add a noun or 'cosa' (anything) or specify what kind of thing. Use it to express purpose with a sense of 'any' or 'whatever'.
target_language_example: Devo avere gli strumenti per fare qualsiasi lavoro in casa.
native_language_example: I need the tools to do any job in the house.

meaning: please
additional_notes: Used to make a polite request. It can come at the beginning or end of a sentence, and in urgent or emotional situations it can sound like a plea: "please!"
target_language_example: Mi aiuti, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you help me, please?

meaning: 'in order to stop' or 'to stop' (indicating purpose or goal)
additional_notes: Commonly used to express purpose: someone does something per fermare qualcosa (to stop something). Can also appear after verbs like cercare/un modo/fare il possibile: 'per fermare Tom' = 'to stop Tom'. Not idiomatic or slang. Often followed by a noun or infinitive depending on structure (e.g. 'per fermare la macchina' or 'troviamo un modo per fermare Tom').
target_language_example: Ho chiamato la polizia per fermare il problema.
native_language_example: I called the police to stop the problem.

meaning: 'fortunately' / 'luckily'.
additional_notes: Used to express relief or that something turned out well by luck or circumstance. Often placed at the start of a sentence or before the clause it modifies. Tone is neutral and common in spoken and written Italian.
target_language_example: Per fortuna ho trovato le chiavi prima di uscire.
native_language_example: Fortunately I found the keys before leaving.

meaning: 'necessarily' / 'by force' depending on context; often means 'must/necessarily' or 'unavoidably'.
additional_notes: Common idiomatic phrase. Used to express necessity or inevitability (e.g., 'non deve restare per forza' = 'he doesn't have to stay necessarily'). In informal contexts it can also imply compulsion or forcing (literal 'by force') or be used sarcastically ('Gli è piaciuto per forza!' = 'He liked it, as if he had to'). Tone and meaning depend on context.
target_language_example: Non devi venire per forza se sei stanco.
native_language_example: You don't have to come if you're tired.

meaning: 'for fun' / 'as a joke' / 'just playing' (not seriously)
