additional_notes: Used to say an action was done playfully, jokingly, or without serious intent. Can imply harmless fun (e.g., playing a prank) but context may show more serious or upsetting behavior — tone and context determine whether it's lighthearted or inappropriate. Common with verbs of doing, throwing, teasing, pretending.
target_language_example: L'ho detto solo per gioco, non volevo offendere nessuno.
native_language_example: I said it just for fun; I didn't mean to offend anyone.

meaning: 'for hamburgers' (used to indicate purpose or intended use, e.g. buns or steaks meant to make hamburgers)
additional_notes: Commonly used after a noun to show what that item is intended for (e.g. panini per hamburger = buns for hamburgers; bistecche per hamburger = patties for hamburgers). 'Per' here means 'for' (purpose). Word order: noun + per + item.
target_language_example: Ho comprato il pane per hamburger.
native_language_example: I bought the buns for hamburgers.

meaning: for the best; hoping for a good outcome.
additional_notes: Used when expressing hope that things will turn out well or that a situation is favorable. Common in phrases like "sperare per il meglio" (to hope for the best) and "andare per il meglio" (to go well). Not formal or slang—neutral everyday expression.
target_language_example: Speriamo per il meglio domani.
native_language_example: Let's hope for the best tomorrow.

meaning: for the moment; for now; at the moment
additional_notes: Used to indicate a temporary state or decision that may change later. Often appears at the beginning or end of a sentence: 'Per il momento, no.' or 'Non per il momento.' Common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Per il momento sto bene, grazie.
native_language_example: For the moment I'm fine, thanks.

meaning: for the rest / for the remainder (of time or things)
additional_notes: Used to refer to what remains (time, things, circumstances) or to introduce a general comment about other matters. Can mean 'for the rest of your life', 'for the rest (of it)', or 'otherwise/in other respects' depending on context. Often followed by a time expression (della vita, dei tuoi giorni) or used parenthetically ('Per il resto, ...') to mean 'otherwise' or 'apart from that.'
target_language_example: Per il resto, possiamo andare avanti domani.
native_language_example: Otherwise / For the rest, we can continue tomorrow.

meaning: for learning the… (used before a masculine singular noun)
additional_notes: A common phrase fragment meaning 'in order to learn the [something]'. 'Per' = 'for/to (in order to)', 'imparare' = 'to learn', and 'il' is the masculine singular definite article. You'll usually see it followed by a noun (e.g., per imparare il vocabolario, per imparare il pianoforte). It is compositional and literal. If the noun is feminine use 'la' (per imparare la) or if plural use 'i/ le' (per imparare i/le).
target_language_example: Sto studiando tutti i giorni per imparare il vocabolario.
native_language_example: I'm studying every day to learn the vocabulary.

meaning: completely; in full
additional_notes: Used to indicate that something was done or given in its entirety (e.g., read an entire book, pay the full amount). Common in both spoken and formal Italian. Can follow verbs or direct objects: leggere il libro per intero, pagare qualcuno per intero.
target_language_example: Ho mangiato la torta per intero.
native_language_example: I ate the whole cake.

meaning: 'to/for the station' (direction or purpose).
additional_notes: Commonly used to indicate direction (e.g., asking which bus/train goes to the station) or purpose (e.g., something intended for the station). In spoken Italian it often appears when asking for travel directions: 'Come vado per la stazione?' can mean 'How do I get to the station?'. If referring specifically to a railway station, 'la stazione' usually means the train station.
target_language_example: Scusi, come arrivo per la stazione?
native_language_example: Excuse me, how do I get to the station?

meaning: an exclamation meaning 'for heaven's sake' or 'damn it'—expresses annoyance, surprise, or frustration.
additional_notes: Used as an interjection to show irritation, disbelief, or emphasis. Less strong than some swear words; can be used in informal situations but is mild and broadly acceptable. Often appears alone or inserted into a sentence (e.g., "Non è giusto, per la miseria."). Tone depends on intonation and context.
target_language_example: Per la miseria, chiudila un attimo!
native_language_example: For heaven's sake, be quiet for a moment!

meaning: for (the) lessons / for class (attendance).
additional_notes: Used to talk about being late, early, or prepared with respect to scheduled classes or lessons. 'Le lezioni' usually means school or university classes. In English you might say 'for class' or 'to class' depending on context. If speaking about a single lesson, Italians could say 'per la lezione'.
target_language_example: Sono in ritardo per le lezioni stamattina.
native_language_example: I'm late for class this morning.

meaning: for a long time; dragging on (takes too long)
additional_notes: Used to say something lasts a long time or is being prolonged/dragged out. Often appears in expressions like "andrà per le lunghe?" (will it take long?/will it drag on?) or "tirarla per le lunghe" (to prolong something, delay). Can describe events, conversations, or days that are extended beyond expectation.
target_language_example: Non tirare per le lunghe la riunione, abbiamo poco tempo.
native_language_example: Don't drag out the meeting, we have little time.

meaning: by the hand of; by (someone) — used to indicate the author, creator, or person responsible for something
additional_notes: Literally 'by the hand of.' Often used in formal or literary contexts to name the creator or author (e.g., a work, a statement, a gesture) — similar to English 'by the hand of' or 'by.' Can also appear in descriptions like 'firmato per mano di...' (signed by the hand of...). Not very common in everyday spoken Italian; more likely in written, formal, historical, or literary language.
target_language_example: Il dipinto è attribuito per mano di un maestro del Rinascimento.
native_language_example: The painting is attributed to the hand of a Renaissance master.

meaning: for me, the ... (used to give a personal opinion about something specific).
additional_notes: Per me = 'for me' or 'in my opinion'. When followed by 'il' + noun it introduces the speaker's personal stance about that noun (e.g. 'per me il problema', 'per me il rispetto'). Common in spoken and written Italian to emphasize subjectivity. You can replace 'il' with other articles (la, i, le) depending on the noun.
target_language_example: Per me il lavoro deve avere un senso.
native_language_example: For me, work must have meaning.

meaning: by midnight; until midnight (indicating a deadline or time frame)
additional_notes: Used to specify that something should happen no later than midnight or to indicate a time span that reaches midnight. Can be used with verbs (e.g., arrivare, finire, consegnare) or in descriptions of opening hours and deadlines. Context determines whether it means 'by' (deadline) or 'until' (duration).
target_language_example: Devi finire il lavoro per mezzanotte.
native_language_example: You must finish the work by midnight.

meaning: by means of; through; via
additional_notes: Used to indicate the method, instrument, channel, or agent by which something is done. Formal or neutral register; common in written Italian. Can be replaced in many contexts by 'tramite', 'attraverso', or 'via'.
target_language_example: Ho inviato il documento per mezzo di email.
native_language_example: I sent the document by means of email.

meaning: not at all; for nothing; completely (in negative contexts)
additional_notes: Commonly used to emphasize a negative (with non/negation): 'non ... per niente' = 'not at all'. Alone, 'Per niente.' can mean 'Not at all.' or 'No way.' In contexts like 'messo per niente' or 'tornato per niente' it means 'for nothing' / 'to no avail'. Tone can be neutral or emphatic depending on context.
target_language_example: Non mi interessa per niente questo progetto.
native_language_example: I'm not interested in this project at all.

meaning: for now; for the time being
additional_notes: Used to talk about the present situation or temporary state. Often placed at the beginning or within a sentence. Can imply that things may change later.
target_language_example: Per ora, tutto procede bene.
native_language_example: For now, everything is going well.

meaning: for eight (periods of time, e.g. months/years).
additional_notes: Used before a time unit (mesi, anni, settimane, ecc.) to indicate a duration of eight of those units. Common in past or present perfect contexts: 'per otto mesi/anni'. Translate as 'for eight months/years'.
target_language_example: Ha vissuto a Roma per otto anni.
native_language_example: He lived in Rome for eight years.

meaning: 'to think' or 'for thinking' (used to indicate time or purpose for thinking)
additional_notes: Commonly follows expressions of time (e.g., 'ho tempo per pensare' = 'I have time to think') or refers to having time/space to reflect before deciding. It can express purpose ('in order to think') or indicate that available time is used for thinking. Neutral register.
target_language_example: Ho bisogno di un giorno per pensare prima di rispondere.
native_language_example: I need a day to think before answering.

meaning: please
additional_notes: A polite expression used to make a request or appeal, similar to "please" in English. It often comes at the end of a sentence. In everyday Italian, "per favore" is more common.
target_language_example: Chiudi la porta, per piacere.
native_language_example: Close the door, please.

meaning: for a short/small amount (of time or number); 'for a few'.
additional_notes: Used before a plural noun (often time expressions) to say 'for only a few' or 'for a short period'. Can describe days, months, people, items. Tone is neutral and common in speech and writing. Example sentences show time (months/days).
target_language_example: Resterò in città per pochi giorni.
native_language_example: I will stay in the city for a few days.

meaning: for a short time; barely/almost (with verbs like 'mancare')
additional_notes: Common phrase with two related uses: 1) temporal — 'for a short time' or 'only briefly' (e.g. Mi fermo per poco = I'll stop/be here only a little while). 2) margin/degree — 'by a small amount' or 'almost' when used with verbs like 'mancare' (Oggi li abbiamo mancati per poco = We missed them by a small margin / we almost caught them). Context shows which sense applies.
target_language_example: Resto qui per poco, torno subito.
native_language_example: I'll stay here for a short while, I'll be right back.

meaning: to carry / to bring / in order to carry (depends on context)
additional_notes: Per portare is a combination of the preposition 'per' and the infinitive 'portare'. It can express purpose ('in order to carry/bring') or simply be part of constructions needing 'to carry/bring' (e.g., needing help to carry something). Context determines whether it's 'to carry', 'to bring', or 'in order to carry'.
target_language_example: Ho bisogno di qualcuno per portare il tavolo in soggiorno.
native_language_example: I need someone to carry the table into the living room.

meaning: in order to be able to pass / so that (one) can pass
additional_notes: A purpose phrase: combines 'per' (for/in order to) + 'potere' (to be able to) in the infinitive 'poter' + verb 'passare' (to pass). Commonly used to explain why someone studied or worked hard — expresses intention or goal (to succeed in a test/attempt). Can be shortened to 'per passare' in everyday speech, but 'per poter passare' emphasizes ability.
target_language_example: Ho studiato tutta la settimana per poter passare l'esame.
native_language_example: I studied all week in order to be able to pass the exam.

meaning: so that I can / in order for me to (be able to)...
additional_notes: Combines 'per' (for/in order to) + the infinitive with the clitic pronoun 'mi' attached to the infinitive (potere → potermi). Used to express purpose or reason emphasizing the subject 'me' and ability. Equivalent to 'per poter(m) ...' but with the pronoun attached. Common in spoken and written Italian.
target_language_example: Sono rimasta a casa per potermi riposare.
native_language_example: I stayed home so that I could rest.

meaning: first (in order or turn); 'before others' (masculine singular form).
additional_notes: Used to say someone goes or speaks before others, or arrived before others. Matches the gender/number of the noun it refers to (per prima, per primi, per prime). Common in phrases like 'posso andare per primo?' (Can I go first?) or 'sono arrivato per primo' (I arrived first). Often used in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Posso andare per primo?
native_language_example: Can I go first?

meaning: for protecting the (feminine singular noun).
additional_notes: A prepositional phrase used before a feminine singular noun to state purpose — 'to/for protecting the ...'. You will see it in instructions or explanations (e.g. 'per proteggere la pelle' = 'to protect the skin'). Change 'la' to 'il', 'i', or 'le' to match gender/number of the noun: 'per proteggere il', 'per proteggere i', 'per proteggere le'.
target_language_example: Metti la crema per proteggere la pelle dal sole.
native_language_example: Put on the cream to protect the skin from the sun.

meaning: 'for how long' (used to ask or refer to duration)
additional_notes: Commonly appears as 'per quanto tempo' to explicitly ask about duration. 'Per quanto' alone can sometimes introduce a clause (e.g., 'per quanto ne so' = 'as far as I know'), but in these examples it is shortened part of 'per quanto tempo'. Use with present/future/past verbs to ask about ongoing, future, or past durations.
target_language_example: Per quanto tempo resterai in città?
native_language_example: For how long will you stay in the city?

meaning: as far as; with respect to; in my/one's opinion (depends on context).
additional_notes: Used to introduce the speaker's point of view or limit knowledge. Common fixed phrases: "Per quanto mi riguarda" (as far as I'm concerned) and "Per quanto ne so" or "Per quanto a mia conoscenza" (as far as I know). Often followed by a clause or a personal pronoun + riguarda/so/mi riguarda.
target_language_example: Per quanto mi riguarda, andrei subito in vacanza.
native_language_example: As far as I'm concerned, I'd go on holiday right away.

meaning: for almost / for nearly (a duration or extent).
additional_notes: Used before time expressions or quantities to mean 'almost' or 'nearly' (e.g., 'per quasi tre anni' = 'for almost three years'). It can also modify general statements ('succede così per quasi tutti' = 'this happens to almost everyone') and appear with amounts (e.g., 'per quasi niente' = 'for almost nothing'). Used in both spoken and written Italian.
target_language_example: Ha aspettato per quasi un'ora.
native_language_example: He waited for almost an hour.

meaning: for what/for the amount that it/they has/have (lit. 'for what it has') — used to qualify value, usefulness or abilities
additional_notes: This phrase is a clipped or colloquial way to comment on something's worth, qualities, or resources: e.g. 'per quello che ha' often follows a noun to mean 'given what it/they have' or 'for what he/she has'. Context (gender/plural) may require adjusting pronoun: 'per quello che ha' (masculine singular), 'per quello che hanno' (they), or 'per quello che ho' (I). It can be followed by a clause: 'per quello che ha, se la cava' = 'given what he/she has, they manage.'
target_language_example: Per quello che ha, la macchina va ancora bene.
native_language_example: For what it has, the car still runs well. (meaning: given what it has/considering its condition)

meaning: for what you have (done); for what you've done
additional_notes: Used to refer to actions someone has done (often followed by a past participle: "per quello che hai fatto"). Common in phrases expressing respect, forgiveness, gratitude, or reproach. Literally 'for that which you have'. You can shorten to "per quello" in casual speech, but the full form clarifies the subject's action.
target_language_example: Ti sono grato per quello che hai fatto per me.
native_language_example: I'm grateful to you for what you've done for me.

meaning: for what happened / because of what happened (referring to an event)
additional_notes: Used to refer back to a previously mentioned or understood event (what happened). Often followed by a past participle (e.g., successo). Can be shortened to 'per quello che è successo' or simply 'per quello che è' when context makes the event clear.
target_language_example: Per quello che è successo, capisco la sua rabbia.
native_language_example: Because of what happened, I understand their anger.

meaning: for this
additional_notes: Literally means "for this." It can refer back to something already mentioned (for example, a task, object, or situation), and at the start of a sentence it often means "for this reason" or "that's why."
target_language_example: Per questo non voglio aspettare.
native_language_example: That's why I don't want to wait.

meaning: 'to know the' or 'in order to find out the' (feminine singular noun follows)
additional_notes: This is a short phrase combining the preposition 'per' (for / in order to) + the verb 'sapere' (to know) + the feminine singular article 'la'. It's used before a feminine noun to indicate wanting to know or find out something: e.g. 'per sapere la data' (to find out the date). Often appears in questions or clauses expressing purpose ('per sapere') followed by a specific feminine noun or clause. If the thing to know is masculine, you'd use 'per sapere il' (or 'per saperlo' / 'per saperne di più').
target_language_example: Ho chiamato l'ufficio per sapere la data dell'appuntamento.
native_language_example: I called the office to find out the date of the appointment.

meaning: by mistake; accidentally.
additional_notes: Used to say that something happened unintentionally. Common in spoken and written Italian. Can be used with verbs (ho fatto, ha preso, si è chiuso) and with people as subject. Equivalent to 'by accident' or 'by mistake' in English.
target_language_example: Ho cancellato il documento per sbaglio.
native_language_example: I deleted the document by mistake.

meaning: forever
additional_notes: Used to express an indefinite, often permanent duration. Commonly translated as "forever" or "always." In contexts like goodbyes (e.g., "Addio per sempre!") it can mean "for good." Can be used both literally (eternal time) and figuratively (lasting memories, feelings, decisions).
target_language_example: Ti amerò per sempre.
native_language_example: I will love you forever.

meaning: in order to hear / to feel; used to express purpose (to hear/feel) or ability/distance (too far to hear).
additional_notes: Commonly appears with verbs of perception (sentire = to hear/to feel). Context determines whether it means 'in order to hear/feel' (purpose) or indicates inability because of distance/conditions ('too far to hear', 'too drunk to feel'). Often followed by an infinitive or used after expressions of degree (troppo... per sentire).
target_language_example: Sono rimasto vicino alla finestra per sentire la musica.
native_language_example: I stayed near the window to hear the music.

meaning: in order to stop (doing something); to stop (doing something).
additional_notes: Used before an infinitive to express purpose or the action of quitting a habit or activity. Commonly followed by verbs like 'fumare' (to smoke). Often interchangeable with 'per smettere' when context is clear.
target_language_example: Ho bisogno di aiuto per smettere di fumare.
native_language_example: I need help to stop smoking.

meaning: 'to study the' (used before a masculine singular noun)
additional_notes: A combination of the preposition 'per' (for/to) + the verb 'studiare' (to study) + the masculine singular definite article 'il'. It introduces purpose or intention: 'to study the ...' — e.g. 'per studiare il libro' ('to study the book') or 'per studiare il diritto' ('to study law'). In spoken Italian you may also see contractions or different word order depending on context (e.g. 'per studiare l'italiano'). Make sure the noun after 'il' is masculine singular; if the noun starts with a vowel use 'l'' (per studiare l'università is incorrect — you'd say 'per studiare all'università').
target_language_example: Sono venuto in biblioteca per studiare il libro di storia.
native_language_example: I came to the library to study the history book.

meaning: for his/her uncle (works for his/her uncle).
additional_notes: Used to say someone works or does something on behalf of or employed by their uncle. 'Suo' can mean his, her, or your (formal) depending on context—Italian uses possessive adjectives; gender/number of the possessor is inferred from the subject. If you need to specify gender, use 'di lui' (of him) or 'di lei' (of her) after the noun: e.g., 'per lo zio di lei' = 'for her uncle'.
target_language_example: Lavora per suo zio adesso.
native_language_example: He/She is working for his/her uncle right now.

meaning: on time; in time (early enough or at the right time)
additional_notes: Used to indicate doing something with enough time before a deadline or event, or being punctual. Can mean 'in time' (preventing something) or 'on time' (arriving punctually) depending on context. Common in spoken and written Italian.
target_language_example: Sono arrivato per tempo alla riunione.
native_language_example: I arrived on time for the meeting.

meaning: on the ground / on the floor
additional_notes: Used to say that something or someone is located on the ground or floor. Can refer to outdoors (ground/earth) or indoors (floor) depending on context. Common in commands (e.g., 'posa per terra') and descriptions ('steso per terra', 'sputò per terra').
target_language_example: Non lasciare le scarpe per terra.
native_language_example: Don't leave your shoes on the floor.

meaning: for the whole
additional_notes: Usually followed by a feminine singular noun, often with an article, as in per tutta la notte or per tutta la vita. It can refer to an entire period of time or to a whole group. The form changes to match the noun: per tutto il giorno, per tutti gli anni, per tutte le persone.
target_language_example: Ho studiato per tutta la mattina.
native_language_example: I studied all morning.

meaning: for further / for additional (used before nouns like informazioni, dettagli).
additional_notes: Common formal phrase used in written and spoken Italian to introduce extra information or instructions (e.g., 'per ulteriori informazioni' = 'for further information'). Often followed by a plural noun. Can appear in emails, notices, websites, and polite requests. Tone is neutral-to-formal.
target_language_example: Per ulteriori informazioni, scriva alla segreteria.
native_language_example: For further information, write to the office.

meaning: last; in the last position; finally (with order/time).
additional_notes: Used to indicate someone/something that comes last in a sequence (order of people, events, actions). Common in contexts like meetings, races, or when leaving a place. Equivalent to 'last' or 'last of all'. Not the same as 'infine' (which means 'finally' in the sense of 'in conclusion').
target_language_example: Sono entrati tutti, io sono arrivato per ultimo.
native_language_example: Everyone went in; I arrived last.

meaning: for a couple (of); for a pair (of) — used with countable nouns to mean 'for two' or 'for a few'.
additional_notes: Commonly followed by a noun (e.g. 'per un paio di giorni', 'per un paio di scarpe'). Often used to mean 'for a couple of' (a small, approximate number, usually two). Can also imply a short duration when used with time expressions.
target_language_example: Rimango qui per un paio di giorni.
native_language_example: I'll stay here for a couple of days.

meaning: by a hair; barely; narrowly (used to say something almost happened or was missed)
additional_notes: Used to describe a very small margin — success, escape, or failure that happened only just. Common in spoken Italian. Equivalent to English 'by a hair', 'by the skin of one's teeth', or 'just barely'. Can be used alone as an exclamation.
target_language_example: Ho preso il treno per un pelo.
native_language_example: I caught the train by a hair / I just barely caught the train.

meaning: because of; due to; as a result of
additional_notes: Used to give a cause or reason for something. Neutral register and common in spoken and written Italian. It often precedes nouns or noun phrases (e.g., per via di una lunga passeggiata). Can be used with people, events, or circumstances. Synonymous with "a causa di" or "a causa de" (note: correct is "a causa di").
target_language_example: Sono stanco per via di una lunga passeggiata.
native_language_example: I'm tired because of a long walk.

meaning: at a time; each time
additional_notes: Used to indicate how many items or events occur in one instance or repetition. Commonly appears in expressions like "uno per volta" (one at a time) or with numbers: "due per volta" (two at a time). Can refer to frequency (each time) or quantity per instance.
target_language_example: Prendi una palla per volta, per favore.
native_language_example: Take one ball at a time, please.

meaning: 'why do we have' / 'why do we need' (asks for a reason about something we possess or require)
additional_notes: Used to ask why 'we' (noi) have, need, or experience something. Often followed by nouns (es. i compiti), verbs in infinitive with 'bisogno di' (es. bisogno di trovarla), or prepositional phrases (es. paura della morte). Common in questions seeking purpose, necessity, or cause.
target_language_example: Perché abbiamo bisogno di aiuto?
native_language_example: Why do we need help?

meaning: 'why does (he/she/it) do' or 'why do (you/they) do' depending on subject; used to ask the reason for an action (present tense).
additional_notes: Perché = why. Fa is the 3rd-person singular present of fare (to do/make). In questions like these the subject can be he/she/it, or formal you (Lei) is also conjugated fa. Context (tone, previous sentence) tells the exact subject. For other subjects use different conjugations (fai, facciamo, fanno). Common in spoken Italian: Perché fa questo? = Why is he/she/it doing this? or Why do you (formal) do this?
target_language_example: Perché fa sempre così quando arriva tardi?
native_language_example: Why does he/she/it always do that when they arrive late?

meaning: why does he/she/it have
additional_notes: Used to ask why someone has something, needs something, or is in a certain state. Ha is the present tense of avere for he/she/it and also formal you (Lei), and Italian usually leaves the subject pronoun unstated. In English, this often needs do/does: perché ha due automobili? = 'why does he/she have two cars?'
target_language_example: Perché ha tre valigie?
native_language_example: Why does he/she have three suitcases?

meaning: why on earth / why ever (expresses surprise, disbelief, or strong questioning)
additional_notes: Used to emphasize amazement, incredulity, or to challenge a suggestion. Often appears at the start of a question (Perché mai...?) and is stronger than plain perché. Can be translated as 'why on earth', 'why ever', or simply 'why' depending on tone.
target_language_example: Perché mai dovrei aiutarti se non ti interessa?
native_language_example: Why on earth should I help you if you don't care?

meaning: 'why not' or 'of course / sure (why not)'.
additional_notes: Used to agree to a suggestion or to ask rhetorically why something shouldn't be done. Tone can be casual or neutral depending on context. Can function as a short affirmative reply ("Sure, why not?") or as a prompt to consider objections ("Why not?").
target_language_example: Vuoi venire al cinema stasera? — Perché no!
native_language_example: Do you want to come to the cinema tonight? — Why not!

meaning: 'why do you (plural) think' or 'why do you (plural) believe'.
additional_notes: Used to ask a group (voi / voi implied) for their reasons or opinions. Followed by a subordinate clause introduced by che (that) or directly by a verb-subjunctive/indicative depending on nuance. In spoken English you can translate as "why do you think...". Stress that pensate is the 2nd person plural present of pensare (you all think).
target_language_example: Perché pensate che non sia una buona idea?
native_language_example: Why do you (all) think it's not a good idea?

meaning: why (of all people/things) — expresses surprise, frustration, or emphasis about why something affects a particular person, time, or thing.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize disbelief, annoyance, or unfairness. Common in questions like 'Perché proprio io?' ('Why me of all people?') or 'Perché proprio ora?' ('Why now?'). Tone can be emotional (upset, resigned) or exasperated. Followed by a noun, pronoun, or time.
target_language_example: Perché proprio a me deve succedere proprio oggi?
native_language_example: Why does this have to happen to me of all days?

meaning: 'why these' or 'why are these' (used to ask why certain things happen to someone or why these [things]...)
additional_notes: Combine perché (why) + queste (these, feminine plural). Often followed by a noun like 'cose' (things) or 'foto' (photos): 'Perché queste cose...' = 'Why do these things...'. Used to ask why something (plural, feminine) occurs. Word order: perché + queste + noun + verb. If referring to masculine plural use 'questi'.
target_language_example: Perché queste foto sono così importanti per te?
native_language_example: Why are these photos so important to you?

meaning: why (he/she/it) seems; why does (someone/something) appear (in a certain way)
additional_notes: Used to ask for the reason or cause of someone's appearance, mood, or behavior. 'Perché' = why; 'sembra' is the third-person singular of sembrare (to seem/appear). Can refer to people, things, or situations. Common follow-ups are adjectives or clauses (e.g., così arrabbiata, sempre stanco, burbero).
target_language_example: Perché sembra così nervoso oggi?
native_language_example: Why does he seem so nervous today?

meaning: 'because (I) look like' or 'because (I) resemble'
additional_notes: Used to ask or state that someone's reason is appearance-based: 'perché' = 'because/why', 'assomiglio a' = 'I resemble' or 'I look like' someone. Conjugation of 'assomigliare' changes with subject (assomiglio, assomigli, assomiglia, assomigliamo, assomigliate, assomigliano). Common in questions: 'Mi ami solo perché assomiglio a [nome]?' = 'Do you love me only because I look like [name]?'
target_language_example: Mi ami solo perché assomiglio a tua sorella?
native_language_example: Do you love me only because I look like your sister?

meaning: 'why the sky is' (beginning of a question asking for a reason about why the sky has a certain property)
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom but the phrase perché + subject + verb used to ask for a reason. Here 'il cielo è' means 'the sky is' and is commonly followed by an adjective (e.g., blu) or clause. Often appears in questions like 'Sai perché il cielo è blu?' ('Do you know why the sky is blue?'). Use intonation or question words (Sai/Sapete/Tu lo sai...) to form different question styles.
target_language_example: Sai perché il cielo è grigio oggi?
native_language_example: Do you know why the sky is gray today?

meaning: 'because she' or 'because her' (giving a reason related to a female person).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a reason that involves a female third person (lei = she/her). Can appear in clauses explaining motives, causes, or justifications. Word order: perché + subject (lei) + verb for explanations (Perché lei ha studiato...), or perché + object/pronoun when referring to cause with an implied verb (Non vuoi più i soldi perché lei ti ha fatto cambiare idea). Tone is neutral; context determines whether 'lei' is subject or object of the clause.
target_language_example: Non vado alla festa perché lei lavora stasera.
native_language_example: I'm not going to the party because she is working tonight.

meaning: 'why they' or 'why are they' (used to ask about reasons concerning 'them').
additional_notes: Perché + subject pronoun (loro) is used to ask why 'they' do something or feel a certain way. In spoken Italian, subject pronouns are often omitted because the verb form shows the subject; saying "perché loro" adds emphasis or clarification (e.g., distinguishing 'they' from 'we' or 'he/she'). For questions with verb inversion, native speakers may say "Perché hanno litigato?" instead of "Perché loro hanno litigato?", but including "loro" is correct and natural when you want to stress 'them'.
target_language_example: Perché loro non vengono alla festa?
native_language_example: Why aren't they coming to the party?

meaning: why him / why he (used to ask or explain reasons related to a specific male person)
additional_notes: Used to question or explain the reason concerning a particular male person. Depending on word order and punctuation it can be a question (Perché lui non è venuto?) or part of a subordinate clause (Mi chiedo perché lui non è venuto). In speech, subject pronoun lui is often stressed to single out 'him' (as opposed to someone else).
target_language_example: Mi chiedo perché lui abbia detto così.
native_language_example: I wonder why he said that.

meaning: 'because now' — gives a reason tied to the present moment or recent change.
additional_notes: Used to explain why something is true or happening now (often after a change in knowledge, situation, or presence). Can introduce a cause linked to the current moment (e.g., 'because now I know', 'because now I'm here'). Often follows a comma or begins a clause. Not slang.
target_language_example: Non preoccuparti, perché ora ci sono io.
native_language_example: Don't worry, because now I'm here.

meaning: because it was raining
additional_notes: Used to give a reason in the past (imperfect tense pioveva = 'it was raining'). Commonly follows a main clause: subject + restare/rimanere + a casa + perché pioveva. Can be used with different subjects and past forms (sono rimasto/a, rimase, etc.).
target_language_example: Siamo usciti tardi perché pioveva.
native_language_example: We went out late because it was raining.

meaning: loses the
additional_notes: From perdere ('to lose'). Perde is the present tense for 'he/she/it loses' and also formal 'you lose'; il means 'the' before a masculine singular noun. The phrase is fully compositional and is often translated more naturally in English depending on the noun, for example perde il posto = 'loses their job'.
target_language_example: Se continua così, perde il lavoro.
native_language_example: If he keeps going like this, he loses his job.

meaning: 'to lose sight of' or 'to lose track of' (physically or figuratively).
additional_notes: Used both literally (losing visual contact with someone or something) and figuratively (losing contact with someone, forgetting about an issue, or no longer following a situation). Common constructions: perdere di vista + noun (e.g., una persona, un problema). Past participle often used (l'ho perso di vista / l'ho persa di vista).
target_language_example: Ho iniziato a perdere di vista i dettagli della conversazione dopo tanta confusione.
native_language_example: I began to lose track of the details of the conversation after so much confusion.

meaning: to miss the train; to fail to catch the train.
additional_notes: Common literal phrase used both literally (not catching a train) and sometimes figuratively (missing an opportunity). Often appears with verbs like perdere, correre, arrivare in time expressions. Use 'non perdere il treno' to say 'don't miss the train.' Tense of surrounding verbs changes normally (past: ho perso il treno / avevo perso il treno).
target_language_example: Ho corso per non perdere il treno.
native_language_example: I ran so I wouldn't miss the train.

meaning: to lose one's patience; to become annoyed or frustrated
additional_notes: Common idiom used when someone becomes impatient, irritated, or can no longer tolerate a situation. Often used with a person as subject (e.g., "Ho perso la pazienza" = "I lost my patience"). Can appear in various tenses (perdere la pazienza, ho perso la pazienza, perderò la pazienza, potrei perdere la pazienza).
target_language_example: Stavo aspettando da quaranta minuti e alla fine ho iniziato a perdere la pazienza.
native_language_example: I had been waiting for forty minutes and in the end I began to lose my patience.

meaning: to lose one's head; to become very upset, irrational, or out of control (often emotionally).
additional_notes: Idiomatic expression used when someone becomes overly emotional, panicked, or behaves irrationally (e.g., from anger, fear, love). Not literal. Common forms: "perdere la testa" (infinitive), "ha perso la testa" (he/she lost his/her head), "sta perdendo la testa" (is losing his/her head).
target_language_example: Ha perso la testa quando ha visto quelle foto; davvero ha perso la testa.
native_language_example: He lost his head when he saw those photos; he really lost his head.

meaning: 'to lose one's life' — a formal/neutral way to say someone died (often used for accidental or violent deaths).
additional_notes: Commonly used in news reports and formal contexts to report deaths (e.g., accidents, disasters, crimes). It emphasizes the loss of life rather than manner; for a more neutral/less formal verb, use 'morire'. Often appears in past periphrasis: 'ha perso la vita' or 'hanno perso la vita'.
target_language_example: Durante l'incidente, due passeggeri hanno perso la vita.
native_language_example: During the accident, two passengers lost their lives.

meaning: to lose one's temper; to get very angry or lose self-control
additional_notes: Idiomatic expression. Literally 'to lose the stirrups/braces', but it means to become furious or lose composure. Often used with past forms like 'ha perso le staffe' or reflexive-like constructions. Common in both spoken and written Italian.
target_language_example: Non voglio che tu perda le staffe per un malinteso.
native_language_example: I don't want you to lose your temper over a misunderstanding.

meaning: to waste time; to cause someone to lose time.
additional_notes: Commonly used both reflexively (io perdo tempo = I waste time) and transitively (far perdere tempo = to make someone lose time). Can be used reproachfully: 'Stai perdendo tempo' or 'Mi fai perdere tempo!'. Neutral contexts also possible (e.g., avoiding delay: 'non far perdere tempo').
target_language_example: Non voglio perdere tempo, iniziamo subito.
native_language_example: I don't want to waste time, let's start right away.

meaning: dangerous for / harmful to
additional_notes: Used to say that something or someone poses a danger to a person or group. Followed by a noun or pronoun (e.g., per lei, per i bambini, per tutti voi). Common with people, groups, or categories (anziani, malati). Word order: adjective per + object.
target_language_example: È pericoloso per i bambini giocare vicino alla strada.
native_language_example: It's dangerous for children to play near the road.

meaning: 'lost his/her' (past tense of perdere, used with a third-person subject)
additional_notes: Perse is the passato remoto (or passato remoto form) of perdere (to lose). In contemporary spoken Italian the passato prossimo ('ha perso') is far more common; passato remoto appears in written narrative or regional/historical usage. 'Suo' is the possessive adjective meaning 'his/her/your (formal)' and normally accompanies a definite article in many contexts (e.g. 'il suo figlio'), though omission of the article can occur in specific stylistic or dialectal contexts. The sequence 'perse suo' without an article is grammatically possible (especially in literary or newspaper headlines) but may sound stilted or dialectal in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Una donna perse suo figlio.
native_language_example: A woman lost her son.

meaning: lost all the… (he/she/it lost all the [masculine plural noun]).
additional_notes: Uses the passato prossimo/simple past root of perdere (perse = he/she lost or in literary contexts past remote). Typically followed by tutti i + masculine plural noun (e.g., soldi, capelli, libri). For feminine nouns use tutte le; for different subjects use other verb forms (ho perso, abbiamo perso, avete perso, persero). Can combine with possessives (i suoi, i miei) or determiners. Tone: neutral; can appear in both formal and informal contexts depending on vocabulary.
target_language_example: Mary perse tutti i soldi che aveva.
native_language_example: Mary lost all the money she had.

meaning: they lost the (plural) — past tense of perdere (to lose) with a plural definite article.
additional_notes: Persero is the third-person plural passato remoto (simple past) of perdere: 'they lost.' In spoken Italian, passato prossimo (hanno perso) is more common, but passato remoto appears in written or narrative contexts. 'I' is the plural definite article 'the' used before a masculine plural noun (i loro = their). The structure 'persero i + [noun]' means 'they lost the [plural noun].' Replace the noun as needed (autobus, occhiali, soldi, ombrelli).
target_language_example: Persero i documenti importanti durante il viaggio.
native_language_example: They lost the important documents during the trip.

meaning: 'lost their' (something belonging to them).
additional_notes: Used after a subject (often plural) to say they lost something that belongs to them. 'Perso' is the past participle of 'perdere' (to lose); agreement with a plural feminine/masculine subject is shown with the auxiliary (here omitted because sentence uses past participle in compound tense). 'I loro' means 'their' (plural possession). Commonly followed by a noun: perso i loro autobus / passaporti / soldi.
target_language_example: Hanno perso i loro biglietti per il treno.
native_language_example: They lost their train tickets.

meaning: lost his/her/its
additional_notes: Used to say someone has lost something that belongs to a third person or third thing (his/her/its). "Suo" agrees with the owner (third person) and is neutral for gender here; the possessed noun follows (e.g., "il suo libro", "il suo lavoro"). Can refer to physical objects, information (numero, indirizzo), abstract things (appetito, tocco) or events (treno). In English choose his/her/its according to context. Tense: "perso" is past participle used with avere (ha perso, ho perso).
target_language_example: Ho perso il suo biglietto, mi dispiace.
native_language_example: I lost his/her ticket, I'm sorry.

meaning: lost your (something).
additional_notes: Used to ask if someone has lost a specific possession. 'Perso' is the past participle of 'perdere' (to lose); 'il tuo' means 'your' (masculine singular). Match gender/number: 'la tua' (feminine), 'i tuoi' (plural masculine), 'le tue' (plural feminine). Can be used alone in a question when context supplies the noun (e.g., 'Hai perso il tuo?').
target_language_example: Hai perso il tuo zaino ieri?
native_language_example: Did you lose your backpack yesterday?

meaning: lost (literal) / lost one's temper (idiomatic in 'perso le staffe').
additional_notes: Literal: past participle of perdere + feminine plural article 'le' (e.g., perso le matite = lost the pencils). Idiomatic: 'perdere le staffe' means to lose control or lose one's temper. Context determines meaning; look at the noun that follows. Agreement: 'perso' can also appear as 'persa/persi/persone' depending on gender/number, but with object following you often keep 'perso' in spoken Italian.
target_language_example: Quando ha visto il disordine, ha perso le staffe.
native_language_example: When she saw the mess, she lost her temper.

meaning: 'lost a lot' or 'lost much' — used with time, blood, money, etc.
additional_notes: Common past participle construction with perdere (perso) + molto. Can describe losing quantities (time, blood, money, sleep) or missing out. Word order: 'perso molto tempo', 'ho perso molto sangue'. If subject is plural, auxiliary uses abbiamo/sono as required by verb (perdere uses avere: abbiamo perso).
target_language_example: Ho perso molto tempo ieri pomeriggio.
native_language_example: I lost a lot of time yesterday afternoon.

meaning: lost in (somewhere).
additional_notes: Used with a person or animal (si è perso) to say they became lost inside/within a place. Combine with different places (bosco, parco, deserto, museo, centro storico). In Italian the reflexive verb perdersi is common: "si è perso nel..." = "he got lost in...". If the person is female, use "persa nel". Agreement and definite articles follow normal gender/number rules (es. "si sono persi nel bosco").
target_language_example: Il ragazzo si è perso nel bosco.
native_language_example: The boy got lost in the woods.

meaning: lost her/his son in (a specific event).
additional_notes: Used to indicate that someone lost their son as a result of an event (e.g., an accident, war). 'Perso' is the past participle of 'perdere' (to lose). Note: More natural Italian often uses the definite article ('ha perso il figlio') or possessive with article ('ha perso suo figlio' is acceptable but less common). The preposition 'in' introduces the cause or event (e.g., 'in un incidente', 'in guerra'). Ensure agreement/context for gender and formality.
target_language_example: Ha perso suo figlio in un incidente stradale.
native_language_example: She lost her son in a road accident.

meaning: lost all of his/her (something).
additional_notes: Used with a masculine past participle (perso) + quantity (tutti) + possessive (i suoi) to say someone lost all of their (masculine plural) belongings or money. The gender/number of the possessed noun affects the possessive: 'tutti i suoi risparmi' (masculine plural), 'tutte le sue cose' (feminine plural). Context usually implies money or possessions.
target_language_example: Ha perso tutti i suoi documenti durante il viaggio.
native_language_example: He/She lost all of his/her documents during the trip.

meaning: lost everything.
additional_notes: Used to say someone has lost all possessions, money, or hope. 'Perso' is the past participle of perdere (to lose); 'tutto' means everything. Can refer to literal loss (e.g., belongings, money) or more figurative loss (e.g., opportunities, reputation). Commonly appears in sentences like 'Ho perso tutto' (I lost everything) or 'Se perdi, hai perso tutto' (If you lose, you've lost everything).
target_language_example: Dopo l'incendio, abbiamo perso tutto.
native_language_example: After the fire, we lost everything.

meaning: lost a / missed a (masculine singular object).
additional_notes: Perso is the past participle of perdere (to lose, to miss). 'Perso un' appears before a masculine singular noun: e.g. perso un braccio (lost an arm), perso un orecchino (lost an earring), perso un treno (missed a train). Use with feminine nouns: 'persa una' (e.g. 'persa una occasione'). Can mean either physically lost or missed (an opportunity/transport). Context determines whether it's literal (lost something/body part) or figurative (missed a train/opportunity).
target_language_example: Ho perso un portafoglio ieri.
native_language_example: I lost a wallet yesterday.

meaning: 'lost a' (feminine singular object) — indicates someone has lost one of something (a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Perso is the past participle of perdere (to lose). When followed by una it refers to a lost feminine noun (una donna, una gamba, una scarpa, una visita, una ruota). Context determines whether it means 'lost' (misplaced), 'missed' (an event/appointment), or 'lost' in the sense of 'no longer has' (e.g., lost a limb). Agreement: if the lost item is masculine, you'd use perso un. For formal writing you might see perso/a or perso·a depending on style.
target_language_example: Ho perso una cintura ieri, non la trovo.
native_language_example: I lost a belt yesterday; I can't find it.

meaning: the most (person) — used to form superlatives about people (e.g., most important, happiest person).
additional_notes: Combine persona + più + adjective (often with article and noun) to say someone is the 'most' something. Word order: la/persona + più + adjective (or la persona più + adjective + del/dei + noun). You may also see è diventata / divenne (became) with this structure. In English you often translate as 'the most ... person' or simply 'the ...-est person.'
target_language_example: Luca è la persona più generosa che conosca.
native_language_example: Luca is the most generous person I know.

meaning: 'people of' or 'people from' (people belonging to a place, group, or context).
additional_notes: A combination of persone (people) + del (contraction of di + il = of the / from the). Used to link people to a location, group, institution, or category: persone del mio paese (people from my town), persone del nostro ufficio (people in our office), persone del centro anziani (people at the senior center). Replace del with della/dell'/dei/delle as needed for gender/number and vowel/consonant rules (es. persone della città, persone dell'azienda, persone dei vicini).
target_language_example: Le persone del quartiere hanno organizzato una festa.
native_language_example: The people of the neighborhood organized a party.

meaning: 'people in' (used before a masculine singular place or time introduced by 'il' contracted with 'in' → 'nel')
additional_notes: Persone = people. Nel is the contraction of 'in' + 'il' (in the). Use 'persone nel' to say 'people in the' + a masculine singular noun (e.g., nel parco, nel dormitorio, nel nostro ufficio). For feminine nouns you'd say 'persone nella' (in + la) or with plural articles ('nelle', 'nei') as appropriate. Commonly used to describe people located within or associated with a place, region, or group.
target_language_example: Ho incontrato molte persone nel quartiere ieri.
native_language_example: I met many people in the neighborhood yesterday.

meaning: people in/inside (followed by a feminine singular noun: e.g. nella città = in the city)
additional_notes: A combination of 'persone' (people) + the contraction 'nella' (in + la). Used to say how many people are in or live in a place. 'Nella' agrees with a feminine singular noun that follows (nella città, nella nostra famiglia, nella cucina). If the noun is masculine use 'nel' (nel mio paese) or other contractions (nello, nell', nei, nelle) as needed.
target_language_example: Ci sono quattro persone nella cucina adesso.
native_language_example: There are four people in the kitchen right now.

meaning: weighs a / it weighs a (used to state the weight of something).
additional_notes: Common construction with verbs of weight: 'pesa' (he/she/it weighs) + 'una' (a) + noun indicating unit (e.g. 'tonnellata' = ton). Used both in literal measurements and hyperbolically (e.g. 'pesa una tonnellata' = 'it's extremely heavy'). To ask weight, use 'Quanto pesa ...?' (How much does ... weigh?).
target_language_example: Questa valigia pesa una decina di chili.
native_language_example: This suitcase weighs about ten kilos.

meaning: to end up with the last one; to draw or get the last (item/choice), often with an undesirable result
additional_notes: Informal expression. 'Pescare' here means 'to draw' (as in drawing lots or cards); 'lo scorso' refers to 'the last one'. Can be literal (drawing the final card/ticket) or figurative (being left with the last/least desirable option). Less common than variants like 'pescare l'ultimo' or 'essere l'ultimo'.
target_language_example: Alla fine del gioco ho pescato lo scorso e sono rimasto senza mosse.
native_language_example: At the end of the game I drew the last one and had no moves left.

meaning: fish for (used to indicate fish as the choice or purpose, e.g. 'fish for dinner').
additional_notes: Often appears as 'pesce per [pasto]' to say which meal will include fish (e.g. 'pesce per cena' = 'fish for dinner'). Can also be literal when followed by a destination or purpose (e.g. 'pesce per il mercato' = 'fish for the market' / 'fish to take to market'). Word order is flexible: you may see 'pesce per cena' or a full sentence like 'Abbiamo pesce per cena'.
target_language_example: Stasera abbiamo pesce per cena.
native_language_example: Tonight we have fish for dinner.

meaning: goldfish; literally 'red fish'.
additional_notes: Commonly used to refer to the small pet fish (goldfish). Can also be used humorously to describe someone with a very short memory (e.g. 'ha la memoria di un pesce rosso' = 'has the memory of a goldfish'). Gender: il pesce rosso (singular). Plural: i pesci rossi.
target_language_example: Ho comprato un pesce rosso per la bambina.
native_language_example: I bought a goldfish for the girl.

meaning: insult meaning 'piece of shit' — a strong, vulgar way to call someone scum/jerk.
additional_notes: Very vulgar and offensive. Used to insult someone directly (often angrily). Equivalent in tone to English 'piece of shit' or 'you shitty bastard'. Avoid in polite/company contexts. Can be used alone or after a name/pronoun; common in heated arguments, films, or informal speech. Not appropriate for learners to use except when explaining or recognizing the insult.
target_language_example: Non guardarmi, pezzo di merda!
native_language_example: Don't look at me, you piece of shit!

meaning: an important/big shot; someone with power, influence, or high rank.
additional_notes: Used informally to refer to a powerful or important person (boss, official, big executive, crime boss, etc.). Can be neutral or slightly dismissive depending on tone. Often translated as "big shot," "bigwig," or "heavy."
target_language_example: Voglio parlare col pezzo grosso.
native_language_example: I want to speak with the big shot.

meaning: '(they) also like' or '...also please (someone)'; used with plural subjects/things to say someone likes them too.'
additional_notes: Piacciono is the third-person plural form of piacere (to be pleasing). In Italian structure, the person who likes something is expressed with an indirect object pronoun or prepositional phrase (mi, ti, gli, le, ci, vi, a + name). 'Anche' means 'also/too' and is placed near piacere or the thing liked. For singular things use 'mi piace anche'. Word order examples: 'A Maria piacciono anche le banane' or 'Le piacciono anche i libri.'
target_language_example: A Marco piacciono anche i film italiani.
native_language_example: Marco also likes Italian films.

meaning: 'I/they really like the...' or '...really like the...' (expressing strong liking for plural nouns).
additional_notes: Combines the verb piacere in plural form (piacciono) + adverb davvero (really) + definite article i (the, for masculine plural). In Italian the person who likes is indicated with an indirect object (mi, ti, a lui/lei, etc.): e.g. Mi piacciono davvero i tuoi dipinti = I really like your paintings. Use this structure for plural things; for singular use 'piace davvero il/la/lo' or 'mi piace davvero'.
target_language_example: A lei piacciono davvero i film italiani.
native_language_example: She really likes Italian films.

meaning: '(they) like seafood' (literal fragment: 'like the fruits of') — used to say someone likes seafood (frutti di mare).
additional_notes: This phrase is a fragment combining the verb piacere (piacciono: plural) + 'i frutti di …' (literally 'the fruits of ...'). In the example sentences it is completed as 'i frutti di mare' = 'seafood' (literally 'fruits of the sea'). Piacere works differently than English 'to like': the grammatical subject is the thing liked (i frutti di mare) and the person who likes it is an indirect object introduced by 'a' or expressed with a pronoun (mi, ti, gli, le, ci, vi, loro). Use 'piacciono' when the thing liked is plural (i frutti), 'piace' when singular. Common pattern: 'A [person] piace/piacciono [thing].' Contractions: 'A noi ci piacciono i frutti di mare' can be shortened to 'Ci piacciono i frutti di mare.'
target_language_example: A Marco e Lucia piacciono i frutti di mare.
native_language_example: Marco and Lucia like seafood.

meaning: they/you (formal) like his/her/your (plural).
additional_notes: This is the verb piacere + possessive phrase. In Italian, piacere works like 'to be pleasing to' so the thing liked is the subject (piacciono = plural things) and the person who likes is indicated by an indirect object (a lei, mi, ti, gli, le, etc.). 'i suoi' means 'his', 'her', or formal 'your' (plural nouns). Context or a pronoun before the verb clarifies whose things are liked and who likes them: e.g. 'A lei piacciono i suoi insegnanti.' = 'She likes her teachers.' 'Mi piacciono i suoi cani.' = 'I like his/her/your dogs.'
target_language_example: A Marco piacciono i suoi amici.
native_language_example: Marco likes his friends.

meaning: they/you (formal/plural) like the... (used with plural feminine noun); literally 'are pleasing to (someone) the...'.
additional_notes: Piacciono is the third-person plural form of piacere, used when the thing liked is plural. Structure in Italian places the thing liked as the subject and the person who likes it as an indirect object (mi, ti, gli, le, ci, vi). 'Le' after 'piacciono' here is the definite article for a plural feminine noun (e.g., 'le nere' = 'the black ones' or 'black (plural feminine) items'). Translate into English as 'I/you/he/she/we/they like the.../like them' depending on the indirect object pronoun used.
target_language_example: Mi piacciono le scarpe rosse.
native_language_example: I like the red shoes.

meaning: they/all of them please (he/she/you like all of them).
additional_notes: Form of piacere + tutti/tutte. 'Piacciono' is the third-person plural of piacere (to be liked), so it's used when the subject is plural (e.g., 'le insegnanti', 'le gonne', 'le verdure'). 'Tutte' means 'all' (feminine plural); use 'tutti' for masculine plural. Word order: indirect object (mi/ti/gli/le) + piacciono + tutte + noun (optional).
target_language_example: A Maria piacciono tutte le canzoni di quell'album.
native_language_example: Maria likes all the songs from that album.

meaning: they/all of them are liked (he/she/they/you like them) — 'everyone/all of them please' in sense of liking every item.
additional_notes: From the verb piacere (to be pleasing). Italian uses an indirect object to indicate who likes something: 'mi/piace/piacciono' with the thing as subject. 'Piacciono tutti' means 'all of them are liked' or 'likes all kinds'. The full sentence often includes the person: 'A lui/le/lei/mi piacciono tutti i tipi di ...' or subject like 'tutti i cani'. Use plural 'piacciono' with plural things. For English, reverse the order: 'Mi piacciono i cani' = 'I like dogs.'
target_language_example: A noi piacciono tutti i tipi di musica.
native_language_example: We like all kinds of music.

meaning: do(s/he/you) really like the mushroom soup (literal fragment).
additional_notes: This is a fragment used in questions to ask if someone truly likes a specific soup (here 'zuppa ai funghi' = mushroom soup). 'Piace' is the verb piacere ('to please' → 'to like' in English) and agreement in Italian uses indirect object pronouns or 'a + name/pronoun' to indicate who likes something (e.g., 'A te piace...?', 'Ti piace...?'). 'Davvero' = 'really'. The phrase as given is not a complete independent expression but appears at the start of a question: 'A lei piace davvero la zuppa ai funghi?' or more naturally 'Le piace davvero la zuppa ai funghi?'.
target_language_example: Le piace davvero la zuppa ai funghi?
native_language_example: Does she really like the mushroom soup?

meaning: I like the ... more / I prefer the ... (subject: io/mi/a me).
additional_notes: Used to compare preferences. Common patterns: 'A me piace di più il/la [X] (del/de la/che) [Y]' or shorter 'Mi piace di più [X]'. 'Piace di più' means 'like more' or 'prefer'. Use definite article with nouns (il/la/lo/ i/le) and compare with 'del' (di + il), 'della', or 'che' before the second item. 'A me' or 'mi' indicate 'to me'.
target_language_example: A me piace di più il gelato della torta.
native_language_example: I prefer ice cream to cake.

meaning: likes to be with (someone) / enjoys being with (people)
additional_notes: This is a combination of piacere (to like) used impersonally and essere con (to be with). In natural speech you'd usually see it as "(A lui/lei/mi/ci) piace essere con..." or more commonly as "gli/le/mi piace stare con..." Piacere agrees with the thing/person liked (e.g. "Mi piace essere con te" = I like being with you). Use pronouns or names to show who likes it: "A Marco piace essere con gli amici."
target_language_example: Mi piace essere con i miei amici il sabato sera.
native_language_example: I like being with my friends on Saturday night.

meaning: likes to do (some)... — expresses that someone enjoys doing a plural/activity (followed by a plural noun).
additional_notes: Common structure: (A lui/lei/Gli/Le) + piace + fare + delle + [plural noun]. 'Piace' agrees with the activity (singular infinitive phrase). 'Fare delle' introduces a nonspecific plural amount ('some' or 'a few') of activities: fare delle passeggiate = to take some walks / go for walks. Use 'fare del'/'della'/'dei' depending on the noun; 'delle' is used before feminine plural nouns.
target_language_example: A noi piace fare delle gite il weekend.
native_language_example: We like to go on outings on the weekend.

meaning: 'to like doing (the...)' — used with plural nouns (e.g. i compiti = the homework/assignments).
additional_notes: This is the structure piacere + verb infinitive + plural definite article + noun. Piace agrees with the activity (singular or plural). With plural nouns use 'piace fare i ...' (e.g. 'Vi piace fare i compiti?'). For polite/formal singular 'Le piace...?', for informal singular 'Ti piace...?'. When the thing liked is plural, Italian still often uses 'piace' (not 'piacciono') if followed by an infinitive construction (piace fare i compiti).
target_language_example: Ci piace fare i giochi da tavolo il sabato.
native_language_example: We like playing board games on Saturdays.

meaning: 'like to watch old (ones)' — used to say someone likes watching old films (or other old things).
additional_notes: This is a fragment built from the verb piacere + infinitive (guardare) + adjective (vecchi). In full sentences you'd usually add the noun (e.g. film): 'Ti piace guardare i vecchi film?' = 'Do you like watching old films?'. Remember Italian uses indirect-object pronouns with piacere: 'mi/ti/gli/le/ci/vi/agli' or the stressed form 'a me/a te/a lui...' before piacere. The verb stays singular when referring to an activity (guardare) or a singular thing: 'Mi piace guardare i vecchi film.'
target_language_example: A me piace guardare i vecchi film durante il weekend.
native_language_example: I like to watch old films during the weekend.

meaning: '(someone) likes butter' — literal phrasing used to ask or state that butter is liked.
additional_notes: Piace is the third-person singular form of piacere (to be pleasing). In Italian you say 'A [person] piace il burro?' or 'Ti/Vi piace il burro?' to ask if someone likes butter. The subject of piace is the thing liked (il burro) and the indirect object indicates who likes it (a lei, a te, a voi, ti, vi). For other persons use piacciono with plural things (e.g. 'Ti piacciono i burrotti?').
target_language_example: A Marco piace il burro sul pane caldo.
native_language_example: Marco likes butter on warm bread.

meaning: likes the way (in which)... / I/you/he/she like(s) the way in which...
additional_notes: This is not a fixed set phrase but looks like part of a sentence: 'piace il modo in cui...' or 'mi/ti/gli piace il modo in cui...' meaning someone likes the manner or way something is done. Commonly used with a pronoun (mi/ti/gli/le/ci/vi/gli) and often followed by 'in cui' or 'in cui + verb' (e.g. 'mi piace il modo in cui parla'). If standalone 'piace il modo in' is incomplete; use the full connector 'in cui' or 'in cui + verb'.
target_language_example: Mi piace il modo in cui cucini le lasagne.
native_language_example: I like the way you cook lasagna.

meaning: to enjoy learning / (it) pleases (me/him/etc.) to learn
additional_notes: Combines the verb piacere (to like/please) with the infinitive imparare (to learn). Piacere is used with an indirect object: A Tom piace imparare = Tom likes to learn (literally: learning pleases Tom). For English speakers, translate as 'to like/enjoy doing (something)'. Conjugate piacere for the person who experiences the liking (Mi piace imparare = I like to learn).
target_language_example: A Maria piace imparare nuove parole ogni giorno.
native_language_example: Maria likes to learn new words every day.

meaning: you/he/she/they like meat (literally: 'meat is pleasing')
additional_notes: Piace is the third-person singular form of piacere, which works differently than English 'to like'. The structure is often: (indirect object pronoun) + piace/piacciono + subject. For example, 'Mi piace la carne' = 'I like meat.' In the given phrase 'piace la carne' the full sentence needs an indirect object (mi, ti, gli, le, ci, vi, loro) to show who likes the meat. Use 'piacciono' when the thing liked is plural (e.g., 'mi piacciono le carni' or more commonly specific plural foods).
target_language_example: Ti piace la carne alla griglia?
native_language_example: Do you like grilled meat?

meaning: like the soup / (someone) likes soup.
additional_notes: This phrase uses the verb piacere ('to like') which is structured differently than English: the thing liked (la zuppa) is the subject, and the person who likes it is an indirect object (mi, ti, gli/le, ci, vi, loro). Example sentences show common varieties: 'Mi piace la zuppa' = I like soup; 'Ti piace la zuppa?' = Do you like soup? Use the appropriate indirect-object pronoun (mi, ti, gli/le, ci, vi, loro) to match the person who likes it. For plural things, use 'piacciono' (e.g. 'Mi piacciono le zuppe').
target_language_example: A Marco piace la zuppa di pollo.
native_language_example: Marco likes chicken soup.

meaning: likes the
additional_notes: Used with the verb piacere. Literally, piace means "is pleasing," so a lui piace lo sport means "sport is pleasing to him" = "he likes sport." Lo is the masculine singular definite article used before nouns like sport, studente, zaino, etc.
target_language_example: A mia sorella piace lo yoga.
native_language_example: My sister likes yoga.

meaning: likes to speak (in) — used to say someone enjoys speaking in a particular language or context.
additional_notes: Common construction with the indirect object pronoun or prepositional phrase: 'A [name/pronoun] gli/le piace parlare in [lingua/luogo]'. 'Piace' agrees with the activity (parlare). Often shortened: 'Gli piace parlare in inglese.' Can refer to language ('in inglese') or place/context ('in pubblico').
target_language_example: A Maria piace parlare in italiano con gli amici.
native_language_example: Maria likes to speak in Italian with her friends.

meaning: I really like reading (something).
additional_notes: Common phrase to express strong liking for reading a specific thing (e.g., a blog, a book). 'Mi piace' or 'A me piace' mean 'I like'; 'veramente' (= really) adds emphasis. Followed by a direct object introduced by the verb 'leggere' (to read). Use 'il tuo/vostro blog', 'i tuoi/vostri articoli', etc., to specify what you like. 'A me' is optional and used for emphasis or contrast.
target_language_example: Mi piace veramente leggere il tuo blog ogni mattina.
native_language_example: I really like reading your blog every morning.

meaning: A form of the verb piacere used in progressive or impersonal constructions where the thing that pleases is the grammatical subject and the person who experiences the liking is expressed as an indirect object. It conveys meanings like “is/was enjoying” or “is/was pleasing (to someone).”
additional_notes: Piacere normally behaves as “to be pleasing to” rather than a direct transitive “to like.” Progressive uses combine stare + piacendo (e.g., gli sta piacendo la festa = the party is pleasing to him / he is enjoying the party). Word order often places the thing that pleases (the subject) after the verb; the experiencer is marked by a prepositional phrase (a + name) or an indirect-object pronoun (mi, ti, gli, le, ci, vi, loro). The exact multi-word sequence “piacendo la” can appear when piacendo is followed directly by a feminine singular noun (la + noun) that functions as the subject: e.g., “le stava piacendo la festa.”
target_language_example: Disse che le stava piacendo la festa.
native_language_example: She said she was enjoying the party.

meaning: Please listen (plural or formal).
additional_notes: Per piacere is a polite way to say “please.” Ascoltate is the second-person plural imperative of ascoltare (to listen), so it addresses more than one person or a single person formally in some regions. Used to politely ask a group to pay attention; word order can vary ("Ascoltate, per piacere"). For a singular informal request use "per favore, ascolta" or "ascolta, per favore."
target_language_example: Per piacere, ascoltate questo messaggio importante.
native_language_example: Please listen to this important message.

meaning: 'please, call me' (a polite request asking someone to call you)
additional_notes: Combines 'per piacere' (please) with an imperative/infinitive request. 'Chiamatemi' is the polite or plural imperative form meaning 'call me' (from 'chiamare' + 'mi'). Commonly followed by a time expression (e.g. domani, stasera, più tardi). Use 'chiamami' for informal singular (one person, familiar).
target_language_example: Per piacere, chiamatemi domani mattina.
native_language_example: Please, call me tomorrow morning.

meaning: 'please, give me' (polite request: ask someone to hand or give something)
additional_notes: Combines 'per piacere' (please) and 'datemi' (give me — imperative plural of dare). Use when politely asking a group or a person you address formally in plural 'voi' situations (also common with staff in shops/restaurants). For singular polite formal (Lei) use 'mi dia' instead. Can be used with objects: 'datemi il menù', 'datemi due hot dog'.
target_language_example: Per piacere, datemi un bicchiere d'acqua.
native_language_example: Please, give me a glass of water.

meaning: Please bring me / Please bring us (formal or plural 'me' depends on context).
additional_notes: A polite request formula. 'Per piacere' = 'please'. 'Portatemi' is the imperative of 'portare' + clitic 'mi' (to me) in the voi form (you plural) or polite plural; in many regions it's also used to address a single person politely. If you want to address one person informally, use 'portami'. To ask for something for someone else, replace the clitic: 'portaci' (bring us), 'portale' (bring them/her) etc.
target_language_example: Per piacere, portatemi un bicchiere d'acqua.
native_language_example: Please bring me a glass of water.

meaning: to take pleasure in / to enjoy (doing something)
additional_notes: Used to say someone enjoys or takes pleasure in an activity. Followed by an infinitive verb (nel + [verb] is a contraction of in + il, often before a noun or verbal phrase: 'piacere nel parlare' = 'to enjoy speaking'). Common in formal or literary contexts; in everyday speech Italians may also say 'mi piace' + infinitive or noun (e.g. 'mi piace parlare').
target_language_example: Trovo piacere nel leggere prima di dormire.
native_language_example: I find pleasure in reading before sleeping.

meaning: to be glad/pleased that; it pleases (me/you/etc.) that
additional_notes: Common impersonal construction with 'fare' (mi/ti/gli/le/ci/vi/gli fa piacere) + che + subjunctive or indicative. Used to express pleasure or satisfaction about a fact or action. After 'mi/ti/gli fa piacere' the verb following 'che' often appears in the subjunctive (especially for personal reactions) but indicative can occur depending on certainty.
target_language_example: Mi fa piacere che tu sia qui oggi.
native_language_example: I'm glad that you're here today.

meaning: Nice to meet you (formal).
additional_notes: Polite, formal phrase used when meeting someone for the first time. 'Conoscerla' uses the formal 3rd-person singular pronoun (Lei). For informal situations with peers or friends, use 'piacere di conoscerti'. Often said after introductions: 'Piacere di conoscerla, signora Rossi.'
target_language_example: Piacere di conoscerla, sono Marco Bianchi.
native_language_example: Nice to meet you, I'm Marco Bianchi.

meaning: was liked by
additional_notes: Imperfect tense of piacere + indirect object introduced by 'a'. Used to say someone/something was liked by someone in the past (ongoing or repeated state). Structure: [Subject = thing or person who is liked] + piace/piaceva + a + [person who likes]. English uses subject and 'by' or 'was liked by' (e.g. "He was liked by everyone"). With people it's common to use forms like "a + me/te/lui/lei/noi/voi/loro" or names/pronouns: "piaceva a tutti", "piaceva a lei". For present tense use 'piace a'.
target_language_example: Lui piaceva a tutti al liceo.
native_language_example: He was liked by everyone in high school.

meaning: he/she/they liked his/her/their
additional_notes: This phrase combines the imperfect form of piacere (piaceva) with a possessive phrase (il suo). In Italian piacere is used differently than English: the item liked is the grammatical subject and the person who likes it is the indirect object introduced by a/mi/ti/gli/le/ci/vi/loro. In the examples the full structure is 'A [name] piaceva il suo [noun]' meaning '[Name] liked his/her [noun]'. The gender/number of 'suo' agrees with the possessed noun (il suo lavoro, la sua casa, i suoi amici). 'Piaceva' (imperfect) indicates a past habitual or ongoing liking; in simple past use 'è/piaciuto/a' (gli è piaciuto il suo lavoro).
target_language_example: A Lucia piaceva il suo insegnante.
native_language_example: Lucia liked her teacher.

meaning: 'he/she/they/you liked that' or 'liked what/that (was happening)'.
additional_notes: Combination of the verb piacere (imperfect tense 'piaceva' = 'was pleasing' / 'liked') with 'quello' ('that' / 'what' in these contexts). Used to say someone liked something that was happening or something previously mentioned. Subject is expressed with an indirect object (A Maria, a loro, gli, ti) and the thing liked is 'quello'. Common in past descriptions (imperfect) to report feelings or preferences.
target_language_example: A noi piaceva quello che facevamo al mare.
native_language_example: We liked what we used to do at the beach.

meaning: liked the wine (past tense: it pleased someone)
additional_notes: Piaciuto is the past participle of piacere, used with an indirect object to say someone liked something. Italian uses piacere differently than English: the thing liked is the subject (here 'il vino') and the person who likes it is an indirect object (mi, ti, gli/le, ci, vi, etc.). Example forms: 'Mi è piaciuto il vino' = 'I liked the wine.' For plural things use 'sono piaciuti' (e.g., 'Mi sono piaciuti i vini').
target_language_example: A lei è piaciuto il vino della Toscana.
native_language_example: She liked the wine from Tuscany.

meaning: I enjoyed working with (someone).
additional_notes: Combines the past participle piaciuto (from piacere = to please/like) with lavorare con (to work with). Used to say you liked working with a particular person or group. Subject is the speaker (mi / a me), structure: (A me) mi è/piaciuto lavorare con + object (lui, te, voi, Tom). For plural speakers or plural liked thing use sono piaciuti, but for 'working with X' the impersonal 'mi è piaciuto' is common. You can change person: "Ti è piaciuto lavorare con..." (Did you enjoy...), "Ci è piaciuto lavorare con..." (We enjoyed...).
target_language_example: Mi è piaciuto lavorare con il team internazionale.
native_language_example: I enjoyed working with the international team.

meaning: 'liked reading this' (refers to enjoying reading something).
additional_notes: A phrase built from the past participle of piacere + infinitive leggere + demonstrative questo. Commonly used with indirect object pronouns (mi, ti, gli/le, ci, vi) or dative nouns: Mi è piaciuto leggere questo = I liked reading this. Piacere uses a reverse construction: the thing is the grammatical subject and the person pleased is expressed by a pronoun or indirect object. Agreement: when the thing is plural, use piaciuti (e.g. Ci sono piaciuti leggere questi racconti → more commonly Ci è piaciuto leggere questi racconti is avoided; instead say Ci sono piaciuti questi racconti or Ci è piaciuto leggere questi racconti with singular neutral). For beginners, stick to: Mi è piaciuto leggere questo (I liked reading this) and Ti è piaciuto leggere questo? (Did you like reading this?).
target_language_example: Mi è piaciuto leggere questo romanzo la scorsa estate.
native_language_example: I liked reading this novel last summer.

meaning: liked this
additional_notes: Commonly appears with a pronoun + è/mi/ti/ci/vi to express who liked something (e.g. "Mi è piaciuto questo" = "I liked this"). The past participle "piaciuto" agrees in gender/number with the subject when using the auxiliary "essere" in some constructions (but in common spoken Italian you normally say "Mi è piaciuto" for "I liked this" regardless of the object's gender). "Questo" means "this" and refers to the item liked (book, game, video...).
target_language_example: Mi è piaciuto questo film.
native_language_example: I liked this movie.

meaning: 'the planet is' — subject 'pianeta' + verb 'è' (is).
additional_notes: This is simply the noun 'pianeta' (planet) followed by the third-person singular of 'essere' (to be). Use it to describe the state, location, or characteristics of a planet. Word order in Italian is flexible, but 'pianeta è' is used when the speaker has just mentioned or focused on 'pianeta'. For questions about which planet (e.g., 'Quale pianeta è...') use the same structure.
target_language_example: Il pianeta è ricoperto di foreste.
native_language_example: The planet is covered in forests.

meaning: to cry about / to cry for (someone or something)
additional_notes: Used to indicate crying because of a person, event, or reason. Common with direct objects (piangere per lei, per la perdita, per la notizia). Can be both literal (shedding tears) and emotional (grieving, feeling sad). Often appears with verbs like riuscire a (non riesco a piangere per...), continuare a, or expressions like non poter fare a meno di.
target_language_example: Non voglio piangere per quel ricordo.
native_language_example: I don't want to cry about that memory.

meaning: I cry every ... (beginning of a sentence indicating a repeated event)
additional_notes: This is the first part of a verb phrase: 'piango' = 'I cry' (present tense, io piango).
