Often used in negative constructions: 'Non farmi prendere in giro' (Don't make fun of me / Don't take me for a fool). Can also imply deception (to trick) depending on context and intonation.
target_language_example: Non mi prendere in giro: lo so già.
native_language_example: Don't make fun of me: I already know.

meaning: to take note; to write down or make a note of something
additional_notes: Used to record information (mentally or in writing) for future reference. Common in both formal and informal contexts. Can be followed by di/about or directly by an object: prendere nota di un appuntamento / prendere nota della tua osservazione. Also used figuratively: 'Prenderò nota' = 'I'll keep that in mind.'
target_language_example: Puoi ripetere l'indirizzo? Devo prendere nota.
native_language_example: Can you repeat the address? I need to take note.

meaning: to take part / to participate (in something).
additional_notes: Commonly used with a preposition: prendere parte a qualcosa (to take part in something). Formal or neutral register. Can refer to joining an event, discussion, competition, etc. Often appears as prendere parte a + noun.
target_language_example: Molti studenti hanno deciso di prendere parte al progetto.
native_language_example: Many students decided to take part in the project.

meaning: to make fun of someone; to tease, mock, or deceive someone in a rude/vulgar way
additional_notes: Informal and vulgar expression. Used when someone is joking at another's expense, lying to them, or intentionally deceiving them in a mocking way. Comparable to 'to pull someone's leg' (milder) or 'to take the piss out of' (closer in tone). Avoid in formal contexts.
target_language_example: Stai solo cercando di prendere per il culo Marco, non prendere sul serio quello che dice.
native_language_example: You're just trying to make fun of Marco; don't take what he says seriously.

meaning: 'to take a position' or 'to take a stand' (express an opinion or adopt a stance on an issue).
additional_notes: Used when someone expresses their opinion, chooses a side in a debate, or publicly states how they feel about a topic. Can be used in both literal sense (physically take a position/place) and, more commonly, figurative (political, moral, professional stance). Often followed by su (prendere posizione su qualcosa) or nei confronti di (prendere posizione nei confronti di qualcuno).
target_language_example: Il sindaco ha deciso di prendere posizione sulla questione ambientale.
native_language_example: The mayor decided to take a stand on the environmental issue.

meaning: to take a seat / to sit down; also to take someone's place or to occupy a position
additional_notes: Commonly used when asking or describing someone sitting down (e.g., in a room, at a table, on public transport). Can also mean to occupy a spot or role (e.g., 'ha preso il suo posto' — he/she took his/her place). Use pronominal/finite forms with subject: 'prende posto', 'ha preso posto', 'prenderà posto'. Can be used formally or neutrally; in very informal speech people may say 'sedersi' instead.
target_language_example: Per favore, prendi posto: la riunione sta per cominciare.
native_language_example: Please take a seat: the meeting is about to start.

meaning: to take/get something from (somewhere or someone)
additional_notes: Common phrasal structure: prendere qualcosa da + source (e.g., una persona, un luogo, un negozio). Can mean physically taking (pick up) or obtaining (buy, borrow). Context determines nuance: prendere qualcosa da mangiare (get something to eat), prendere qualcosa da qualcuno (take/borrow something from someone). If used with a verb or adjective after 'da', it can introduce purpose or reason (less common).
target_language_example: Posso prendere qualcosa da bere dal frigorifero?
native_language_example: Can I get something to drink from the fridge?

meaning: to take this medicine without (a prescription).
additional_notes: Common phrase seen on over-the-counter drug labels or when asking if a medicine requires a prescription. The phrase often appears as "prendere questa medicina senza ricetta" or shortened to "senza ricetta". Conjugate prendere to match the subject (posso prendere, puoi prendere, può prendere, possiamo prendere, potete prendere, possono prendere).
target_language_example: Posso prendere questa medicina senza ricetta?
native_language_example: Can I take this medicine without a prescription?

meaning: take this
additional_notes: A polite request asking someone to take or pick up a specific (feminine) item: la/questa (this) refers to a feminine noun previously indicated (e.g., una borsa, una scatola). The verb form may change (prendi/prendete) depending on formality/number; examples use conditional/polite forms (potresti/potreste/potete). Often followed by 'per favore' or 'per piacere'.
target_language_example: Potresti prendere questa, per favore?
native_language_example: Could you take this, please?

meaning: Ask someone politely to take or pick up this (object) — equivalent to 'could you take this, please?'.
additional_notes: Used to make a polite request for someone to take or pick up an item. You will see variations in the subject/formality: 'Potrei/ Potresti/ Potrebbe/ Potreste' depending on who you ask (I/we/you formal/you plural). 'Per favore' and 'per piacere' are interchangeable polite endings. The comma in the input separates the object and the polite particle but in normal speech you would say 'Prendere questo, per favore?' or more naturally 'Puoi prendere questo, per favore?'.
target_language_example: Potresti prendere questo, per favore?
native_language_example: Could you take this, please?

meaning: to buy time; to delay making a decision or giving an answer
additional_notes: Used when someone intentionally delays, hesitates, or asks for more time before responding or acting. Common in conversations, negotiations, or when avoiding a direct answer. Can be literal (to take extra time) but usually figurative.
target_language_example: Posso prendere tempo prima di rispondere?
native_language_example: Can I buy some time before answering?

meaning: to take/get a cup (of something).
additional_notes: Commonly used when referring to grabbing a cup (e.g., of coffee, tea). Can mean picking up an empty cup or getting a cup filled. Informal, everyday phrase; context (coffee, tea) clarifies whether you mean prepare/get a drink or literally take a cup.
target_language_example: Vado in cucina a prendere una tazza di caffè.
native_language_example: I'm going to the kitchen to get a cup of coffee.

meaning: to come to life; to begin to exist or develop; to become lively or animated.
additional_notes: Used both literally (something becomes alive) and figuratively (a project, idea, or event starts to take shape or gain energy). Common in contexts like stories, plans, projects, or atmospheres. Often conjugated with avere in compound tenses for transitive senses (ha preso vita) and with essere rarely when referring to intransitive change; passive or reflexive forms may appear. Register: neutral.
target_language_example: Dopo mesi di lavoro, il progetto ha cominciato a prendere vita.
native_language_example: After months of work, the project began to come to life.

meaning: to take care (of)
additional_notes: Reflexive verb phrase used when someone cares for or looks after a person, animal, or themselves. Often appears as prendersi cura di + object (e.g., prendersi cura di noi) or prendersi cura di sé (to take care of oneself). Conjugate the reflexive pronoun to match the subject (si prende cura, mi prendo cura, etc.).
target_language_example: Deve prendersi cura di noi domani.
native_language_example: He/She must take care of us tomorrow.

meaning: 'to make fun of' or 'to mock' (someone)
additional_notes: Reflexive construction (prendersi + gioco). Often used with di + qualcuno to indicate the target (prendersi gioco di qualcuno). Conjugate prendersi like a reflexive verb (si prende, mi prendo, ecc.). Expresses annoyance or disapproval when someone is mocked. Can be used in various moods and tenses (Cercano di prendersi gioco di me!, La smetta di prendersi gioco di me!).
target_language_example: Cercano di prendersi gioco di me!
native_language_example: They're trying to make fun of me!

meaning: to take one's time; to give oneself enough time
additional_notes: Reflexive construction (prendersi) with a possessive phrase (il suo) referring to the person's own time. Often appears in full as 'prendersi il suo tempo' but can be used with context-implied 'tempo'. Used to tell or describe someone not to hurry. Can be conjugated and combined with pronouns/names (e.g., 'Mary si prende il suo').
target_language_example: Dissi a Mary di prendersi il suo tempo.
native_language_example: I told Mary to take her time.

meaning: will take care (of).
additional_notes: Future tense of prendersi cura di (to take care of). Used with a subject who will look after someone or something. Often appears with a reflexive pronoun (si prenderà cura di ...) and followed by 'di' + person/thing. Polite and neutral; can refer to practical care, responsibility, or emotional support.
target_language_example: Lui si prenderà cura del gatto mentre siamo in vacanza.
native_language_example: He will take care of the cat while we're on vacation.

meaning: worries about
additional_notes: A form of preoccuparsi (to worry). In sentences like those given, the subject (e.g., Tom, Mary) is the person who worries and the object introduced by 'per' is the cause/person/thing of concern. In Italian you often see the reflexive form 'si preoccupa per...' (he/she worries about...). Can be used with people, things, or abstract ideas (e.g., la salute, il peso, tutto).
target_language_example: Marco si preoccupa per il suo esame.
native_language_example: Marco worries about his exam.

meaning: worries too much / is too worried
additional_notes: Used to describe someone who is excessively worried about something or someone. Often appears with a subject pronoun (si, lei, lui, Tom) and optionally followed by a preposition phrase (di, per) indicating what or whom they worry about. Can be used as a short comment: "Si preoccupa troppo."
target_language_example: Marco si preoccupa troppo per l'esame.
native_language_example: Marco worries too much about the exam.

meaning: worried about (plural masculine noun).
additional_notes: Feminine singular adjective 'preoccupata' = 'worried' (for a female speaker/subject). 'per' means 'about' or 'for'. 'i' is the masculine plural definite article 'the' and precedes a masculine plural noun (e.g., 'i suoi voti' = 'his/her/their grades'). Use 'preoccupato per i' for a male subject. For plural subjects use 'preoccupate' (feminine) or 'preoccupati' (masculine/mixed).
target_language_example: Anna è preoccupata per i compiti dei bambini.
native_language_example: Anna is worried about the children's homework.

meaning: 'was worried about' (past tense, third person singular of preoccuparsi + preposition per).
additional_notes: Preoccuparsi di/ per means 'to worry about'. In these examples the verb is in passato imperfetto (si preoccupava) describing an ongoing or repeated past worry. Use si preoccupa (present) to say 'he/she worries'. Common prepositions: per (about/for) or di (about); both are often interchangeable depending on context. The reflexive pronoun (si/mi/ti/ci/vi) agrees with the subject: mi preoccupo, ti preoccupi, si preoccupa, ci preoccupiamo, ecc.
target_language_example: Anna si preoccupava per i risultati dell'esame.
native_language_example: Anna was worried about the exam results.

meaning: (you) worry about; used to indicate that someone (second person singular) is worried about a person or thing.
additional_notes: This is the verb preoccupare in the 2nd person singular form (ti preoccupi) followed by the preposition 'per' to mark the object of worry. Common in everyday speech and in questions or reassurances. The reflexive form preoccuparsi can take 'per' or 'di' (preoccuparsi di is slightly more common), but 'preoccupi per' is natural when addressing someone directly (e.g., 'Ti preoccupi per...').
target_language_example: Perché ti preoccupi per Cahit?
native_language_example: Why are you worried about Cahit?

meaning: to worry about (someone or something).
additional_notes: Used with reflexive verb form (preoccuparsi): mi preoccupo per + person/thing. Commonly followed by a person (per te, per voi, per Tom) or situation. Tone can be serious or caring; not informal slang. English equivalents: 'I'm worried about...' or 'I worry about...'.
target_language_example: Mi preoccupo per la salute di Marco.
native_language_example: I'm worried about Marco's health.

meaning: preparing dinner / making dinner (right now).
additional_notes: Present continuous form (stare + gerund) used to say someone is in the process of making the evening meal. Can be used with a subject (Lei, Tom) and optionally with details like location (in cucina) or recipient (per me). Common in everyday conversation.
target_language_example: Sto preparando la cena adesso.
native_language_example: I'm preparing dinner right now.

meaning: making/preparing breakfast.
additional_notes: Present progressive form (stare + gerund) used to describe someone currently preparing breakfast. 'La colazione' = breakfast. Can be used with different subjects (Mamma, Tom, names). Common in everyday conversation to say someone is in the process of making the morning meal.
target_language_example: Sto preparando la colazione per tutti.
native_language_example: I am preparing breakfast for everyone.

preparare il nostro matrimonio e la nostra

target_language_multi_word_term: preparare il nostro matrimonio e la nostra
meaning: to prepare our wedding and our (…); starts the phrase 'prepare our wedding and our honeymoon'.
additional_notes: This is a fragment used when talking about planning both a wedding and something belonging to the couple (most commonly 'luna di miele' = honeymoon). The examples show gender/number agreement in the preceding adjective: 'impegnati/occupati' (masculine or mixed group) vs 'impegnate/occupate' (feminine group). Complete the phrase with the noun (e.g. 'luna di miele'). Common verbs: preparare (to prepare/plan), siamo impegnati/occupati a + infinitive.
target_language_example: Noi siamo impegnati a preparare il nostro matrimonio e la nostra luna di miele.
native_language_example: We are busy preparing our wedding and our honeymoon.

meaning: prepared some / made some (of something).
additional_notes: Used to say someone prepared or made an unspecified amount of a food or drink. Italian often uses partitive 'del' (di + il) before a noun to mean 'some' or 'some of the'. 'Preparato del' appears when the past participle 'preparato' (prepared/made) is followed by the partitive + noun: e.g. 'ha preparato del tè' = 'he/she prepared some tea.'
target_language_example: Ho preparato del pane per la cena.
native_language_example: I prepared some bread for dinner.

meaning: prepared for; got ready for (someone/something).
additional_notes: Used to say that a person or group made preparations or got ready in advance for an event, situation, person, or outcome. Can be followed by a noun (il festival, la chiesa) or an infinitive/idea (morire, il peggio). In reflexive forms (si è preparato) it means 'he/she prepared himself/herself.' When used with a person as indirect object (preparare qualcosa per qualcuno) it means 'to prepare something for someone.'
target_language_example: Mi sono preparato per l'esame tutta la settimana.
native_language_example: I prepared for the exam all week.

meaning: he/she prepared the (feminine singular noun) — past simple (passato remoto) of 'preparare' with the feminine direct object article 'la'.
additional_notes: Used to say someone prepared something feminine (e.g., la colazione, la cena). In modern spoken Italian, passato prossimo (ha preparato la) is more common than passato remoto (preparò la) except in some regions or narratives. Can appear with indirect objects: 'preparò la colazione a Mary' or 'per Mary'. With reflexive 'si preparò la colazione' it means 'he/she made breakfast for himself/herself.'
target_language_example: Maria preparò la cena prima di uscire.
native_language_example: Maria prepared the dinner before going out.

meaning: prepared for (past tense, he/she/it).
additional_notes: Preparò is the passato remoto or passato prossimo form of preparare depending on context (here presented as 'he/she prepared'). 'Preparò per' + noun or phrase means to get ready/prepare oneself or something for a specific event or purpose. More commonly in spoken Italian you'd hear 'si è preparato per' (passato prossimo) or 'si preparava per' (imperfetto). When reflexive (si preparò per) it means someone prepared themselves; without 'si' it can mean someone prepared something for someone/something.
target_language_example: Si preparò per l'esame tutta la notte.
native_language_example: He prepared for the exam all night.

meaning: presented a / filed a (something) — past participle + indefinite article
additional_notes: Composed of the past participle 'presentato' (from presentare: to present, to submit, to file) and the article 'un' (a). Used before a masculine singular noun: e.g. presentato un reclamo (filed a complaint), presentato un rapporto (submitted a report). The exact nuance depends on context: can mean 'submitted', 'filed', 'introduced' or 'presented'.
target_language_example: Hai presentato un reclamo ieri?
native_language_example: Did you file a complaint yesterday?

meaning: introduced (someone) to (someone).
additional_notes: Past-tense of presentare: 'presentò a' means 'he/she introduced (someone) to someone else' or 'introduced himself/herself to' when reflexive (si presentò a). Use with indirect object (a + person). Common with mi/ti/ci etc. Example sentences show both transitive (Mary mi presentò a sua sorella = Mary introduced me to her sister) and reflexive use (si presentò a Tom = she introduced herself to Tom).
target_language_example: Luca mi presentò a sua madre ieri.
native_language_example: Luca introduced me to his mother yesterday.

meaning: 'took two' or 'I/you/they took two' (past tense of prendere + numeral)
additional_notes: Presi is the passato remoto or colloquially the passato prossimo first-person past of prendere (in spoken Italian 'ho preso' is more common for passato prossimo). Here 'presi due' means '(I) took/bought two' or '(I) got two' (objects). Often used with 'ne' to mean 'of them' (e.g. 'Ne presi due' = 'I took two of them'). It can appear with expressions like 'al prezzo di uno' (for the price of one).
target_language_example: Ne presi due al mercato.
native_language_example: I took/bought two of them at the market.

meaning: 'borrowed (taken in)'; indicates that someone took something temporarily, typically from a person or institution, with the implication it will be returned.
additional_notes: Usually appears as part of the phrase 'presi in prestito' (borrowed). 'Presi' is the past tense (first or third person singular in passato remoto or past participle form in some constructions); context determines exact tense/person. Commonly followed by the source introduced with 'da' (from) or by the noun of the item borrowed. Use for temporary borrowing of objects, money, books, etc.
target_language_example: Presi in prestito questo libro dalla biblioteca.
native_language_example: I borrowed this book from the library.

meaning: I made/took (the) ... (simple past of prendere + definite article).
additional_notes: ‘Presi’ is the passato remoto (simple past) of prendere for io (I) and is used to describe a completed action in the past; in spoken Italian and many regions, passato prossimo (ho preso) is more common. 'La' is the feminine singular definite article 'the' and refers to a feminine noun (e.g., decisione). Together 'presi la decisione' = 'I made/took the decision.'
target_language_example: Io presi la decisione giusta prima di partire.
native_language_example: I made/took the right decision before leaving.

meaning: 'taken care (of)' — part of the past participle form of prendersi cura di (to take care of).
additional_notes: Appears as part of the reflexive verb prendersi cura di. Commonly used in perfect tenses (mi sono preso cura, si è presa cura) to say someone cared for or looked after someone/something. Agreement in gender/number can occur with past participle when used with reflexive pronouns (e.g., «si è presa cura» for feminine). Often followed by di + person/thing.
target_language_example: Mi sono preso cura del gatto mentre eri via.
native_language_example: I took care of the cat while you were away.

meaning: took/got some (of) — used to say someone took or obtained an unspecified amount of something (often food/drink).
additional_notes: Preso is past participle of prendere (to take/get). 'Del' = di + il, a partitive article meaning 'some' or 'any' before a masculine singular noun. Use with uncountable or mass nouns (ketchup, latte, miele, tè). In questions it asks whether someone got/served/ate some of that item. For feminine nouns use 'della' and before vowels 'dell\''; plural 'dei/degli/delle'.
target_language_example: Hai preso del pane per la cena?
native_language_example: Did you get some bread for dinner?

meaning: taken the
additional_notes: A fragment built from preso (past participle of prendere, 'to take/get') + i ('the' for masculine plural nouns). It usually appears with a form of avere, for example hai preso i...? = 'did you take/get the...?'
target_language_example: Ho preso i biglietti per il concerto.
native_language_example: I got the tickets for the concert.

meaning: 'taken in' / part of several verbs meaning 'to take in', 'to take into consideration', 'to borrow', 'to take into custody' depending on context.
additional_notes: Preso in is the past participle (preso) plus the preposition in and appears in many compound verbs: prendere in considerazione (to consider), prendere in prestito (to borrow), prendere in custodia (to take into custody), prendere in giro (to tease). You must look at the verb phrase that follows to know the meaning. Commonly used in formal and informal contexts.
target_language_example: Ho preso in considerazione la tua proposta.
native_language_example: I took your proposal into consideration.

meaning: rented a (masculine/singular) — 'have/has/had rented a ...'.
additional_notes: From the verb phrase prendere in affitto (to rent). 'Preso' is the past participle used with avere (ho, hai, ha, abbiamo, hanno). The phrase is followed by a masculine singular noun (e.g. appartamento). Use prendere in affitto when you mean renting from someone (tenant perspective).
target_language_example: Abbiamo preso in affitto un monolocale per l'estate.
native_language_example: We rented a studio for the summer.

meaning: borrowed a (masculine singular) — 'took (something) on loan'.
additional_notes: Used to say someone borrowed one masculine singular item (e.g., un libro, un dizionario). The full verb phrase is 'prendere in prestito' (to borrow). Conjugate 'prendere' for tense/person (qui 'ha preso' = he/she borrowed). For feminine or plural items change the article: 'presa in prestito una', 'presi in prestito dei/alcuni', etc. Often followed by 'da' or 'dalla/dal' to indicate whom or where it was borrowed from.
target_language_example: Lei ha preso in prestito un romanzo dalla biblioteca.
native_language_example: She borrowed a novel from the library.

meaning: borrowed a (feminine singular noun)
additional_notes: This is a fragment combining the past participle preso (taken) with the expression in prestito (on loan / borrowed) and the feminine indefinite article una. It would typically appear before a feminine noun (e.g., 'preso in prestito una macchina', though macchina is feminine? 'auto' is feminine). More naturally you'd say 'ho preso in prestito una [cosa]' (I borrowed a ...). Use with appropriate auxiliary and noun: 'Ho preso in prestito una bicicletta.'
target_language_example: Ho preso in prestito una bicicletta dal mio vicino.
native_language_example: I borrowed a bicycle from my neighbor.

meaning: took mine / took my (feminine noun).
additional_notes: Composed of the past participle 'preso' (taken) and the possessive phrase 'la mia' (my/mine for a feminine singular noun). Used after a subject (Chi ha preso la mia? — Who took my...) or with reflexive/pronominal forms (Si è preso la mia vita — He/She took my life). The exact English translation depends on the noun being referred to (biro, automobile, mano, borsa, decisione, medicina, vita).
target_language_example: Hai preso la mia chiave?
native_language_example: Did you take my key?

meaning: literally 'took the' or 'caught the' — past participle (masculine) of prendere + feminine singular article; used before a feminine noun to say you took/caught/received something
additional_notes: Used with a feminine noun that follows (e.g., presa la medicina, preso la medicina). In spoken Italian, the past participle can agree in gender when using avere in some colloquial or regional varieties (e.g., "io ho preso la donna" meaning "I took the woman"). Standard Italian normally uses "ho preso" without changing to "presa" for feminine objects, so "preso la" is simply the sequence of verb + article; be careful with word order: more common is "ho preso la medicina" or "ho preso la donna."
target_language_example: Ho preso la medicina prima di dormire.
native_language_example: I took the medicine before sleeping.

meaning: taken nothing / didn't take anything
additional_notes: A negative short phrase used after avere (past participle preso) to say someone took nothing. Common in spoken Italian: 'non ha preso nulla' = 'he/she didn't take anything'. Can be used with different subjects (ho/ha/hai/abbiamo). Word order: negation 'non' comes before the verb. 'Nulla' is equivalent to 'niente' (both mean 'nothing').
target_language_example: Io non ho preso nulla stamattina.
native_language_example: I didn't take anything this morning.

meaning: 'taken/got those' (past participle + demonstrative; used to ask where someone got or took those [things])
additional_notes: Combines the past participle 'preso' (from prendere = to take/get) with the demonstrative 'quelle' (those, feminine plural). Common in questions asking where someone obtained or took particular items: 'Dove ha preso quelle...?' (Where did he/she take/get those...?) or 'Dove hai preso quelle...?' (Where did you get those...?). The gender and number of 'quelle' must match the noun it refers to (quelle = feminine plural). For masculine plural use 'quei/quegli' depending on context.
target_language_example: Dove hai preso quelle scarpe?
native_language_example: Where did you get those shoes?

meaning: blood pressure
additional_notes: Refers to the force of blood against the walls of the arteries. Often used with adjectives like alta (high) or bassa (low) and verbs like controllare, misurare, avere. Common in medical contexts and everyday health conversations.
target_language_example: Devo misurare la pressione sanguigna ogni mattina.
native_language_example: I need to measure my blood pressure every morning.

meaning: to pay attention; to pay close attention to something or someone.
additional_notes: Commonly used with a person or thing introduced by a preposition (a/di/alle etc.). Often appears as 'prestare attenzione a' + noun/pronoun. Can be used in imperative and past forms (e.g., 'presta attenzione', 'ha prestato attenzione').
target_language_example: Devi prestare attenzione alla lezione.
native_language_example: You must pay attention to the lesson.

meaning: borrowing jewelry (a loan of jewelry).
additional_notes: Literally 'loan of the jewels.' Used to describe the act of borrowing jewelry from someone (friends, acquaintances). In Italian sentences the verb phrase is usually 'prendere in prestito dei gioielli' or 'prendere in prestito i gioielli di...'. Can refer to temporary use (e.g., for an event).
target_language_example: Lei prende in prestito dei gioielli dalle sue amiche per la festa.
native_language_example: She borrows jewelry from her friends for the party.

meaning: borrowing books (the act or a loan of books).
additional_notes: Used to talk about borrowing books (typically from a library or a person). Commonly appears with verbs like prendere in prestito / prendere (in) prestito dei libri. 'Prestito' here is a noun meaning 'loan' or 'borrowing'.
target_language_example: Posso fare il prestito dei libri oggi alla biblioteca?
native_language_example: Can I borrow the books today at the library?

meaning: 'a loan of money' or 'borrowing money'.
additional_notes: Used to refer to money that is lent or borrowed. More commonly in Italian you'd say prendere in prestito dei soldi (to borrow money) or prestito (loan) when referring to the concept. 'Prestito dei soldi' is literal and understandable but not the most natural fixed phrase; context often uses 'un prestito' (a loan) or the verb phrase 'prendere in prestito (dei) soldi'.
target_language_example: Ho dovuto chiedere un prestito dei soldi per riparare la macchina.
native_language_example: I had to ask for a loan of money to fix the car.

meaning: quickly/early to (followed by a noun or infinitive context) — 'presto' = early/soon/quickly; 'al' = to the/at the (a + il).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but the sequence of the adverb 'presto' and the preposition contraction 'al' (a + il). In many examples 'presto' means 'early' (alzarsi presto al mattino = get up early in the morning) or 'soon/quickly' (abituerai presto al cibo = you'll get used to the food soon). 'Al' introduces the noun that follows (al mattino = in the morning; al lavoro = to work). Word order can vary: 'presto al mattino' or 'presto al lavoro'.
target_language_example: Arriveremo presto al cinema.
native_language_example: We'll arrive at the cinema early.

presto e bene non vanno insieme

target_language_multi_word_term: presto e bene non vanno insieme
meaning: You can't do something quickly and well at the same time; haste and quality don't mix.
additional_notes: A proverb used to warn that rushing (presto) usually reduces quality (bene). Used to advise taking time to do a job properly. Equivalent to English sayings like "haste makes waste" or "you can't have it fast and good." Common in spoken and written Italian.
target_language_example: Non fare il lavoro di fretta: presto e bene non vanno insieme.
native_language_example: Don't do the work in a hurry: haste and quality don't go together.

meaning: 'too early to' / 'early for' (used to say that the time is too soon or appropriate for something)
additional_notes: Used before an infinitive or a noun to comment on timing. With 'troppo' it means 'too early to' (neglecting readiness); without 'troppo' it can mean simply 'early for' (e.g., arriving early for an event). Common structure: 'troppo presto per + [infinitive or noun]' or 'presto per + [noun]'.
target_language_example: È troppo presto per partire, aspettiamo un'altra ora.
native_language_example: It's too early to leave; let's wait another hour.

meaning: to foresee/predict the (something); literally 'to foresee the'.
additional_notes: Prevedere means 'to foresee' or 'to predict'. When followed by the definite article (il, la, i, le) it indicates predicting a specific noun (e.g., il futuro = the future). In sentences like the examples, 'prevedere il futuro' = 'to predict the future'. Commonly used with verbs like riuscire/riuscire a (to be able to) or dire di (to claim to).
target_language_example: Credo di poter prevedere il risultato dell'esame.
native_language_example: I think I can predict the result of the exam.

meaning: forecasts of / predictions for (often followed by a noun like 'tempo' = weather).
additional_notes: Commonly used in the fixed phrase 'previsioni del tempo' (weather forecast). 'Previsioni' is plural; 'del' is the contraction of 'di' + 'il' and links to the noun that follows (e.g. 'previsioni del tempo' = 'forecasts of the weather'). You will often hear it in news and everyday conversation about weather, planning, and expectations.
target_language_example: Ho ascoltato le previsioni del tempo prima di uscire.
native_language_example: I listened to the weather forecast before going out.

meaning: prices on / prices for (something listed on a platform or document)
additional_notes: Used to indicate the prices shown on a list, website, menu, or for specific items/services. Often followed by the platform or document (e.g., 'prezzi su Amazon') or by a noun introduced by 'di'/'per'. Context determines exact translation: it can mean 'prices on' (a website) or 'prices for' (an item).
target_language_example: I prezzi su quel sito sono più bassi.
native_language_example: The prices on that site are lower.

meaning: the price of (the).
additional_notes: A common combination: prezzo (price) + del (contraction of di + il = of the). Use before masculine singular nouns: prezzo del caffè, prezzo del pane. For feminine nouns use 'prezzo della' (e.g. prezzo della benzina). Can refer to literal prices or be used figuratively (e.g. 'il prezzo del successo' = the cost/price of success).
target_language_example: Il prezzo del pane è aumentato.
native_language_example: The price of bread has increased.

meaning: 'the price of' (feminine singular noun follows).
additional_notes: Used to talk about the cost or value of something. 'Prezzo' is masculine, but the phrase 'prezzo della' combines prezzo + definite article + feminine noun (della = di + la). For masculine nouns use 'prezzo del' (di + il). For plural: 'prezzo dei' (dei = di + i) or 'prezzo delle' (di + le) for plural feminine. Common collocations: 'prezzo della benzina' (price of petrol), 'prezzo della macchina' (price of the car).
target_language_example: Qual è il prezzo della casa?
native_language_example: What is the price of the house?

meaning: 'the price is' (used to state or describe the price or cost of something)
additional_notes: Common phrase used to give information about cost or to comment on whether a price is fair/acceptable. Often followed by an adjective (buono, ragionevole) or a number (trecento). In dialogue it can be used to insist on a set price (Il mio prezzo è quello = That's my price). Word order: in Italian the verb 'è' (is) follows the noun 'prezzo'.
target_language_example: Il prezzo è cinquanta euro.
native_language_example: The price is fifty euros.

meaning: 'first of all' or 'first and foremost'.
additional_notes: Used to introduce the first point, priority, or most important consideration. Common in spoken and written Italian to start explanations, lists, or arguments. Can be followed by a clause or used alone at the start of a sentence.
target_language_example: Prima di tutto, grazie per essere venuto.
native_language_example: First of all, thank you for coming.

meaning: before taking a (feminine) — used to introduce an action that happens prior to taking something (often a decision, object, or opportunity).
additional_notes: This phrase combines 'prima di' (before) with the verb 'prendere' (to take) and the feminine indefinite article 'una'. It usually precedes a noun or verb phrase (e.g., 'prima di prendere una decisione', 'prima di prendere una medicina'). Use 'un' for masculine nouns: 'prima di prendere un...'. If followed by a verb, use the infinitive: 'prima di prendere una decisione' or 'prima di prendere una decisione importante'.
target_language_example: Prima di prendere una decisione, parlane con la famiglia.
native_language_example: Before making a decision, talk about it with your family.

meaning: 'sooner or' used in the fixed expression 'prima o dopo' meaning 'sooner or later' or in comparisons like 'prima o seconda' = 'first or second'.
additional_notes: In practice 'prima o' appears in two common short patterns: 'prima o dopo' (sooner or later / before or after) and 'prima o seconda' (first or second). Alone 'prima o' is incomplete; it needs 'dopo' or another alternative to complete the phrase. Used in both literal time-sense (before/after) and idiomatic sense (eventually/sooner or later).
target_language_example: Prima o dopo dovremo parlarne.
native_language_example: Sooner or later we'll have to talk about it.

meaning: 'sooner or later' / 'eventually'.
additional_notes: Used to say that something will happen at some unspecified time in the future; can express inevitability or expectation. Common in spoken and written Italian. Interchangeable with 'ad un certo punto' in some contexts but more idiomatic for inevitability.
target_language_example: Prima o poi dovrai affrontare la verità.
native_language_example: Sooner or later you will have to face the truth.

meaning: before it's too (late/soon); used to warn to do something in time (usually 'before it's too late').
additional_notes: Often completed by 'tardi' in full phrase 'prima che sia troppo tardi' meaning 'before it's too late'. Commonly used to urge action or warn that delay may cause negative consequences. Follows subjunctive (sia) because it expresses a condition or fear about the future. Can be used alone as a short warning: 'Prima che sia troppo.'
target_language_example: Parla con lui adesso prima che sia troppo tardi.
native_language_example: Talk to him now before it's too late.

meaning: 'first person' (the first individual; also 'I' / grammatical first person in other contexts)
additional_notes: Used to indicate the first/primary person in a sequence or as the first to do/experience something (e.g., the first person police would look for; the first person who believed me). In grammar, it can mean the first person (io). Context determines if it refers to position ('the first person') or the grammatical person. Common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Sei stata la prima persona a cui ho telefonato.
native_language_example: You were the first person I called.

meaning: 'first girlfriend' (the first romantic female partner someone has had)
additional_notes: Used to refer to the first girl someone dated or had a romantic relationship with. Can be used with past tense (è stata la mia prima ragazza) or in questions (la tua prima ragazza?). Gender of speaker affects agreement (prima ragazza for a female partner; if referring to a first male partner you'd say primo ragazzo). Not idiomatic or slang — literal meaning.
target_language_example: Lei è stata la mia prima ragazza.
native_language_example: She was my first girlfriend.

meaning: for the first time (in/of) — used to say something happens for the first time in someone's life or experience
additional_notes: Usually appears in the full phrase 'per la prima volta nella mia/tuo/sua vita' (for the first time in my/your/his/her life) or 'per la prima volta nella nostra/vostra vita'. Often preceded by 'per' as 'per la prima volta' and followed by a noun like 'vita' (life) or a period/context. Use to emphasize that an action or event is happening for the very first time in that person's life or experience.
target_language_example: Per la prima volta nella mia vita ho parlato in pubblico.
native_language_example: For the first time in my life I spoke in public.

meaning: prime minister; head of government.
additional_notes: Used to refer to the head of government in parliamentary systems. Can be used with an article (il primo ministro) or with a name (il primo ministro Conte). In informal speech you might hear abbreviations like 'Premier' (also used in Italian).
target_language_example: Il primo ministro ha tenuto una conferenza stampa.
native_language_example: The prime minister held a press conference.

meaning: the first step is...
additional_notes: Used to introduce a statement about the initial action or stage of a process. Often followed by an adjective, clause or description (e.g. important, difficult, fun). Common in both literal and figurative contexts (starting a task or beginning a change). Word order: Il primo passo è + [complement].
target_language_example: Il primo passo è chiedere aiuto.
native_language_example: The first step is to ask for help.

meaning: 1) 'first floor' (above ground level in many European buildings); 2) 'foreground' or 'front/priority' (figurative: something prominent).
additional_notes: Has two main uses: literal (a level of a building: il primo piano = the floor above the ground floor in Italy) and figurative (metaphorical emphasis: mettere qualcosa in primo piano = to put something in the foreground or make it a priority). Context tells which meaning is intended.
target_language_example: Hanno affittato la camera al primo piano.
native_language_example: They rented the room on the first floor.

meaning: the crown princes/princesses of (literally: 'hereditary princes of')
additional_notes: Used to refer to heirs to a throne (male or female). 'Principi ereditari' is plural; follow with the country using 'di' + country (e.g. 'di Svezia'). Can be used with past tenses as in the examples: 'hanno incontrato i principi ereditari di...'.
target_language_example: I turisti hanno fotografato i principi ereditari di Norvegia.
native_language_example: The tourists photographed the crown princes/princesses of Norway.

meaning: 'for or against' (asking whether someone supports or opposes something).
additional_notes: Used in questions like "sei pro o contro...?" to ask if someone is in favor (pro) or against (contro) a proposal, idea, plan, etc. 'Pro' is borrowed from Latin/English and means 'in favor of'; 'contro' means 'against'. Common in spoken and written Italian.
target_language_example: Sei pro o contro la nuova regola?
native_language_example: Are you for or against the new rule?

meaning: probably has / has probably (done something).
additional_notes: probabilmente = 'probably' (adverb). When followed by the auxiliary verb 'ha' (3rd person singular of avere), it forms a phrase used to express that someone likely did something (present perfect: has + past participle). Word order can vary: adverb before or after the subject (e.g., 'Mary probabilmente ha perso...' or 'Probabilmente ha perso.').
target_language_example: Luca probabilmente ha dimenticato le chiavi.
native_language_example: Luca has probably forgotten the keys.

meaning: 'probably is' (used before a present continuous verb: likely doing something right now)
additional_notes: Combines the adverb probabilmente (probably) with the present progressive auxiliary sta (he/she/it is / you formal are). Use before a gerund (verb‑ing) to say someone is likely doing something now. Can be placed before a subject for emphasis (e.g., Tom probabilmente sta dormendo). Formality: neutral; common in spoken and written Italian.
target_language_example: Probabilmente sta aspettando alla fermata.
native_language_example: He/She is probably waiting at the stop.

meaning: a problem that someone tried to solve but without success; indicates the attempt to address the problem was unsuccessful — 'in vain' or 'unsuccessfully'.
additional_notes: This is a noun ('problema') followed by the adverb 'invano' (in vain). 'Invano' modifies the preceding clause to show the effort was useless. In Italian it commonly follows the verb phrase or clause describing the attempt: e.g. "Ha cercato di risolvere il problema, invano." The comma before 'invano' is optional but often used for emphasis. Can be used with various tenses and subjects.
target_language_example: Dick cercò di risolvere il problema, invano.
native_language_example: Dick tried to solve the problem, in vain.

meaning: 'bigger/more serious problems' (used to compare problems; literally 'problems more')
additional_notes: Commonly appears as 'problemi più + adjective' or 'problemi più + verb phrase' to compare severity or size (e.g. 'problemi più grandi', 'problemi più gravi', 'problemi più importanti'). Often followed by 'di' or 'da' + infinitive/verb to indicate what to worry about or face (e.g. 'di cui preoccuparsi', 'da affrontare'). Word order in Italian places 'più' after the noun when used this way.
target_language_example: Abbiamo problemi più urgenti da risolvere.
native_language_example: We have more urgent problems to solve.

meaning: female teacher/professor of (a subject).
additional_notes: Used to say a female teacher's subject: professoressa (female) + di + subject. Common for school teachers and university professors. Use 'professore di' for a male. To indicate possession use 'la mia professoressa di...' (my teacher of...).
target_language_example: La professoressa di storia ha spiegato bene la lezione.
native_language_example: The history teacher explained the lesson well.

meaning: a plan/project of (used to specify what the project is about)
additional_notes: Commonly followed by a noun (e.g., costruzione, legge, [person's name]) to indicate the subject or type of the project: progetto di costruzione, progetto di legge, progetto di Abby. Use with preposition 'di' to link the project to its content or owner.
target_language_example: Stiamo lavorando al progetto di ristrutturazione della cucina.
native_language_example: We are working on the kitchen renovation project.

meaning: 'progress in' or 'advances in' (making improvements or developments within a field or activity).
additional_notes: Used to talk about improvements, developments or advances in a particular area (e.g., progresso in medicina → progressi in medicina). Typically followed by a noun indicating the field or activity. Common in formal and neutral contexts.
target_language_example: Negli ultimi anni abbiamo visto molti progressi in tecnologia.
native_language_example: In recent years we have seen a lot of progress in technology.

meaning: promised to leave me (alone).
additional_notes: Promesso is the past participle used with avere to form 'have promised'. 'Lasciarmi' = lasciare + mi (to leave me). Often used with 'da sola/da solo' (alone). Depending on subject, agreement of 'solo/sola' matches the speaker's gender. Common in sentences where someone pledges to stop bothering or to let the speaker be.
target_language_example: Mi hai promesso di lasciarmi da sola.
native_language_example: You promised to leave me alone.

meaning: ready to do anything (for someone or to achieve something).
additional_notes: Often completed with 'cosa' or another noun/verb phrase (e.g. 'pronta a fare qualunque cosa'). Expresses willingness to take any action, sometimes extreme or sacrificial. Agreement in gender/number: 'pronta' (feminine singular) / 'pronto' (masculine). Commonly followed by 'per' + person/purpose or 'pur di' + infinitive to indicate motive.
target_language_example: Sono pronta a fare qualunque cosa per aiutarti.
native_language_example: I am ready to do anything to help you.

meaning: ready to speak / willing to speak (feminine singular).
additional_notes: Literal: 'ready to speak'. 'Pronta' is feminine singular; masculine would be 'pronto a parlare' and plural 'pronti/pronte a parlare'. Used to say someone is prepared or willing to talk, give a statement, or answer questions. Common in contexts like interviews, confessions, or when asking if someone is willing to discuss something.
target_language_example: Sono pronta a parlare se vuoi ascoltare.
native_language_example: I'm ready to speak if you want to listen.

meaning: ready for (something) — 'prepared for' or 'ready to face' (followed by a masculine singular noun through the contraction al = a + il).
additional_notes: Used before a masculine singular noun (al = a + il). Adjust for gender/number: 'pronta alla' (feminine + singular), 'pronti ai' (masculine plural), 'pronte alle' (feminine plural). Common in expressions like 'pronto al peggio' (ready for the worst) or 'pronto al lancio' (ready for launch). Can describe people, objects, or systems. Tone is neutral; register varies with context.
target_language_example: Dovrebbe essere pronto al peggio.
native_language_example: He/It should be ready for the worst.

meaning: owner of; someone who owns something.
additional_notes: Used to indicate ownership. Followed by the thing owned (often introduced by 'di' + noun or name). Can refer to people or businesses (e.g., 'proprietario di un negozio'). Formal/neutral register.
target_language_example: Il signore è il proprietario di quella casa.
native_language_example: The man is the owner of that house.

meaning: a strong/real need for something (really need)
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that someone truly needs something in the moment. Common with verbs or nouns: 'ho proprio bisogno di...' (I really need to...). 'Proprio' strengthens the noun 'bisogno'. Can express physical needs (shower, rest), emotional wants (vacation), or urgent practical needs (a job).
target_language_example: Ho proprio bisogno di un caffè stamattina.
native_language_example: I really need a coffee this morning.

meaning: exactly her / it is her (indeed her).
additional_notes: Used to identify or emphasize a specific female person (lei). 'Proprio' adds confirmation, emphasis, or surprise: 'exactly/precisely/indeed her.' Can express recognition ('That's her!'), insistence, or contrast ('of all people, her'). Tone depends on context—can be neutral, admiring, disbelieving, or dismissive.
target_language_example: Quando ho visto la foto ho capito: è proprio lei.
native_language_example: When I saw the photo I knew: it's exactly her.

meaning: You're absolutely right / you are completely correct.
additional_notes: Used to strongly agree with someone. 'Proprio' here intensifies 'ragione' (reason/right). Common in spoken Italian: 'Hai proprio ragione.' = 'You are really right.' Can be directed (hai) or impersonal (ha).
target_language_example: Hai proprio ragione: dobbiamo partire ora.
native_language_example: You're absolutely right: we must leave now.

meaning: 'really a' / 'truly a' — adds emphasis before a noun phrase.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize the quality, identity or intensity of the noun that follows. Common in spoken Italian. Can be positive, neutral or insulting depending on context and tone (e.g., 'proprio una signora' = 'really a lady'; 'proprio una merda' = 'truly a piece of shit'). When placed before adjectives + noun it stresses surprise or admiration ('proprio una splendida idea').
target_language_example: Con quel comportamento sei proprio una persona coraggiosa.
native_language_example: With that behaviour you are really a brave person.

meaning: the next time that / the next time when
additional_notes: Used to refer to a future occasion when something will happen. Often followed by a verb in the indicative or subjunctive depending on certainty or context (e.g., 'prossima volta che vieni' = next time you come). Can be shortened in speech to 'la prossima volta che' or simply 'la prossima volta'.
target_language_example: La prossima volta che vieni, portami quel libro.
native_language_example: The next time you come, bring me that book.

meaning: next time I (will) ... (followed by an action directed at 'you').
additional_notes: A phrase used to introduce what the speaker will do the next time something happens. 'Prossima volta' = 'next time'; 'ti' = direct object 'you' (informal singular). Often followed by a verb in present or future (faccio, farò, porterò, sparo) describing an action toward the listener. Can be threatening or neutral depending on context. Use 'la prossima volta' in full for natural speech.
target_language_example: La prossima volta ti aiuterò con i compiti.
native_language_example: Next time I'll help you with the homework.

meaning: to protect (the) — feminine plural direct object (e.g., 'protect the women/girls').
additional_notes: Proteggere = to protect. The article 'le' is the feminine plural definite article or a clitic direct object pronoun for feminine plural (them, feminine). In examples here 'le' refers to 'le tue donne', 'le sue figlie', 'le ragazze' (the women/girls). Use 'proteggere i' for masculine plural (e.g., i ragazzi) and 'proteggere la' for singular feminine.
target_language_example: Dobbiamo proteggere le bambine del quartiere.
native_language_example: We must protect the neighborhood girls.

meaning: to protect their (plural possessive).
additional_notes: Proteggere = to protect. Le loro is the feminine plural possessive 'their' used before a feminine plural noun (e.g., famiglie). Use 'i loro' before masculine plural nouns (e.g., amici). The phrase is often followed by the thing/people being protected: proteggere le loro famiglie / proteggere le loro case. Verb can appear in different tenses (cercarono di proteggere le loro = they tried to protect their...).
target_language_example: Hanno fatto di tutto per proteggere le loro famiglie.
native_language_example: They did everything to protect their families.

meaning: proof/evidence of (something); test of/of the
additional_notes: A short phrase made of the noun prova (proof, test, trial) followed by the preposition del (di + il = of the). It is used before a noun to indicate evidence, a demonstration, or a trial related to that noun: e.g. 'prova del crimine' (proof of the crime) or 'prova del funzionamento' (test of the functioning). Choose the correct article after di (del, della, dei, degli, delle) depending on the noun that follows.
target_language_example: Questa è la prova del furto.
native_language_example: This is the proof of the theft.

meaning: trying to lose (something) or trying to be defeated / trying to miss (an opportunity) — literal: 'trying to lose'.
additional_notes: This is the gerund phrase of provare a + infinitive perdere. Context determines what is being lost: perdere can mean 'to lose' (an object), 'to miss' (a bus/opportunity), or 'to be defeated' (a game). 'Provando a perdere' describes an ongoing attempt to cause or experience loss/defeat. It's neutral/informal depending on context; not an idiom.
target_language_example: Sta provando a perdere la partita per vedere se l'arbitro reagisce.
native_language_example: He is trying to lose the match to see if the referee reacts.

meaning: to try something / to try something out.
additional_notes: Common phrase used to say you want to attempt, test, or experience an item, activity, or idea. 'Provare' can mean 'to try' (attempt) or 'to taste/try on' depending on context. 'Qualcosa' = 'something'. Use with infinitives or adjectives: 'provare qualcosa di nuovo/differente' = try something new/different.
target_language_example: Voglio provare qualcosa di tipico della cucina locale.
native_language_example: I want to try something typical of the local cuisine.

meaning: tried to hide the (feminine noun).
additional_notes: A common verb phrase: provare a + infinitive = 'to try to'. 'Nascondere la' means 'to hide the' followed by a feminine noun (e.g., ansia, confusione, paura, scocciatura). Use with appropriate possessive or article (la loro, la sua, la mia). If the noun is masculine, use 'nascondere il' or 'nascondere i'.
target_language_example: Hanno provato a nascondere la vergogna.
native_language_example: They tried to hide the embarrassment.

meaning: tried to hide his/her/their (something).
additional_notes: Very common phrase structure: provare a + infinitive (attempt to do something) + nascondere la sua + noun (emotion, reaction, object). 'Sua' agrees with possessor (his/her) but does not change for gender of the noun; context or name (e.g., Mary/Tom) clarifies gender. Use 'provato a nascondere il/la loro' for 'their' or change 'sua' to 'mia/tua/nostra/vostra' for other possessors.
target_language_example: Luca ha provato a nascondere la sua delusione, ma si vedeva sul viso.
native_language_example: Luca tried to hide his disappointment, but it showed on his face.

meaning: tried not to / attempted not to
additional_notes: Used with a verb infinitive to say someone attempted to avoid doing or feeling something. Common structure: [ha/ho/han provato] + a + non + [infinitive]. Equivalent to English 'tried not to...'. Tense and subject change (ho provato, ha provato, abbiamo provato).
target_language_example: Ho provato a non ridere durante la riunione.
native_language_example: I tried not to laugh during the meeting.

meaning: have tried the / tried the (past participle + definite article) — used when asking if someone has tried a specific thing (food, activity, etc.).
additional_notes: Combines the past participle 'provato' (tried) with the definite article 'il' (the). Common in questions: 'Hai provato il...?' or 'Hai mai provato il...?' ('Have you ever tried the...?'). Use 'hai' for tu/you singular; for other nouns change the article (la, i, le) or the form (hai provato la pasta; avete provato i dolci). 'Provato' agrees only when used as an adjective with essere, but in these expressions it stays unchanged after avere.
target_language_example: Hai mai provato il gelato artigianale?
native_language_example: Have you ever tried artisanal ice cream?

meaning: to clean their (plural belongings, e.g. rooms)
additional_notes: Pulire = to clean. Le loro is the feminine plural possessive meaning “their” (agrees with a feminine plural noun like stanze). In Italian the possessive normally agrees with the thing owned, not the owners. Commonly appears before a noun (pulire le loro stanze). If context already makes ownership clear you might also hear pulirle / pulirli in spoken Italian when attaching a clitic, but standard form is pulire le loro + noun.
target_language_example: Dobbiamo pulire le loro auto prima di partire.
native_language_example: We need to clean their cars before leaving.

meaning: keep ... clean
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself but an example of the adjective pulita (clean) used with the definite article la after an imperative or modal verb. In the example sentences the structure is [imperative/modal verb] + tenere/tieni + pulita + la + [noun implied or stated], meaning 'keep the (room/desk/etc.) clean' or 'keep your ... clean.' The adjective agrees in gender (pulita = feminine singular) with the noun (la camera, la stanza, la aula, la postazione).
target_language_example: Tieni pulita la cucina, per favore.
native_language_example: Keep the kitchen clean, please.

meaning: ‘cleaned my’ (past participle + feminine singular possession).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but a sequence: pulito (past participle of pulire = 'to clean'), la (feminine singular definite article), mia (my; feminine). Used when saying you cleaned a feminine noun you possess (e.g., stanza, camera). Word order in Italian places the past participle before the object: Ho pulito la mia stanza = I cleaned my room. For masculine nouns you'd say 'pulito il mio'.
target_language_example: Ho appena pulito la mia cucina.
native_language_example: I just cleaned my kitchen.

meaning: tip/point of (something); used to indicate the very end or extremity of an object or a small amount/trace of something
additional_notes: Literally 'tip of'. Followed by a noun: punta di spillo (needle's tip), punta di vento (gust of wind) or figuratively punta di speranza (a small trace of hope). Also used in expressions like 'alla punta di' (at the tip of). Not a fixed idiom by itself — meaning depends on the noun that follows.
target_language_example: Ho trovato una punta di sale sul tavolo.
native_language_example: I found a grain (tiny bit) of salt on the table.

meaning: weak point; vulnerability; weakness.
additional_notes: Used to refer to someone's or something's weakness — a personal vulnerability, a flaw, or an area where one is not strong. Can be literal (physical weak spot) or figurative (emotional, skill-related). Common in phrases like "trovare il punto debole" (to find someone's weak spot).
target_language_example: Il suo punto debole è che non sa dire di no.
native_language_example: His weak point is that he can't say no.

meaning: strength, strong point; someone's or something's best quality or skill.
additional_notes: Used to ask or say what someone or something is particularly good at. Common in job interviews or casual questions about abilities. Plural: punti di forza. Can refer to skills, talents, or advantages (personal or of an object/idea).
target_language_example: La comunicazione è il mio punto di forza.
native_language_example: Communication is my strength.

meaning: point of view; perspective; standpoint
additional_notes: Used to express someone's perspective, opinion, or a particular vantage (practical, professional, legal, etc.). Commonly introduced with prepositions: 'da un punto di vista' (from a point of view), 'dal punto di vista' (from the ... standpoint). Can refer to opinion (il mio punto di vista) or to a specific perspective (punto di vista legale).
target_language_example: Dal punto di vista pratico, dobbiamo risparmiare tempo.
native_language_example: From a practical point of view, we must save time.

meaning: 'you can count on' / 'you can rely on'.
additional_notes: Used to assure someone that a person or group will provide help, support, or reliability. Usually followed by a pronoun or noun introduced with 'di' (e.g. 'su di me', 'su di lei', 'su di noi') or sometimes without the 'di' in casual speech ('puoi contare su me' is less common). Common in both everyday and semi-formal contexts.
target_language_example: Puoi contare su di me se hai bisogno di aiuto.
native_language_example: You can count on me if you need help.

meaning: you can do that / you can do it
additional_notes: A casual way to tell someone they are allowed or able to do something. Often used in spoken Italian; context determines whether it's permission ('you may do that') or ability ('you are able to do that'). You can replace 'quello' with a specific action or object (e.g. 'puoi fare quello oggi' = 'you can do that today').
target_language_example: Se non hai tempo, puoi fare quello domani.
native_language_example: If you don't have time, you can do that tomorrow.

meaning: snowman (a figure made of snow, usually with coal/buttons for eyes, carrot nose, etc.)
additional_notes: A compound noun: pupazzo (doll/figure) + di neve (of snow). Used to refer to the typical winter figure built outdoors. Can be singular or plural (pupazzi di neve).
target_language_example: I bambini hanno fatto un pupazzo di neve nel giardino.
native_language_example: The children made a snowman in the garden.

meaning: mashed potatoes
additional_notes: A common side dish made from boiled potatoes mashed with butter, milk (or cream), salt and sometimes pepper or nutmeg. Used like any noun for food: un purè di patate (rare), il purè di patate, del purè di patate. Pronunciation: [puˈrɛ di paˈtaːte].
target_language_example: Per cena preparo purè di patate e pollo arrosto.
native_language_example: For dinner I'm making mashed potatoes and roast chicken.

meaning: can trust (someone)
additional_notes: Commonly appears as si può fidare di + person (or pronoun) to mean 'one/you can trust someone' or 'you can trust someone' in polite/general statements. Often used with reflexive 'si' (impersonal or polite you). With names/pronouns: 'di Tom', 'di lei', 'di me'. Alternative word order: 'ci si può fidare di...' or more naturally 'ci si può fidare' (without repeating 'di') or simply 'puoi fidarti di...' for informal direct address.
target_language_example: Ci si può fidare di Tom.
native_language_example: You can trust Tom.

meaning: Can I/We know what...? / May I ask what...?
additional_notes: Polite or neutral formula used to ask someone to explain what they are doing, feeling, or what happened. Often appears as 'Si può sapere...' (impersonal/passive) meaning 'Can one know...?' In informal/emphatic contexts it can be stronger (e.g., with expletives) and sound confrontational. Commonly followed by a verb in the present or past (che stai facendo? / che ti è successo?).
target_language_example: Si può sapere che cosa stai facendo qui?
native_language_example: Can I know what you are doing here?

meaning: can sit / may sit (polite, formal impersonal or passive construction).
additional_notes: Used to offer permission or ask politely if someone may sit (often directed at a stranger or in formal contexts). The construction 'si può sedere' is impersonal/formal — literally 'one can sit' or 'you may sit' — and is common in polite requests or offers. For more casual speech you might hear 'puoi sederti' (informal singular) or 'potete sedervi' (informal plural).
target_language_example: Si può sedere qui, signore?
native_language_example: May you sit here, sir? / Could you sit here, sir?

meaning: can play the (something) — used to ask or state whether someone is able to play a musical instrument.
additional_notes: Common structure: [Name/Pronoun] può suonare il + [instrument]. 'Può' is the third-person singular of potere (can/may). Use 'suonare' for playing instruments. For instruments beginning with a vowel or feminine forms, the article changes (e.g. 'suonare il violino', 'suonare la chitarra', 'suonare l'organo'). In questions, intonation or question mark is used: 'Può suonare il pianoforte?'
target_language_example: Lucia può suonare il violino.
native_language_example: Lucia can play the violin.

meaning: right here/now; come here now (context-dependent).
additional_notes: Qua means 'here' (near the speaker). Ora means 'now'. Together they emphasize immediacy and proximity: 'here now' or used as an imperative 'come here now'. Common in spoken Italian; placement can vary (e.g., 'vieni qua ora' or 'qua ora vieni').
target_language_example: Vieni qua ora, per favore.
native_language_example: Come here now, please.

meaning: here to play (something).
additional_notes: Used to say that someone is at a place for the purpose of playing a sport or a game. 'Qua' = here (colloquial), 'per' = for/to (purpose), 'giocare' = to play. Followed by the sport with 'a' (e.g., 'giocare a tennis'). Common in spoken Italian.
target_language_example: Siamo qua per giocare a calcio.
native_language_example: We're here to play soccer.

meaning: here/around for the whole (period); throughout (a time span) in this place
additional_notes: Used to say someone or something stayed 'here' (qua) for the entire duration of a specified time (per tutta la settimana, per tutta la vita, per tutta la notte). 'Qua' emphasizes 'here/around' (near the speaker). You can replace 'qua' with 'qui' in many contexts; both mean 'here' but 'qua' is more colloquial/spoken. Commonly followed by a time expression introduced by 'per tutta' + feminine noun (la settimana, la vita, la notte).
target_language_example: Sono qua per tutta la giornata.
native_language_example: I'm here for the whole day.

meaning: here for a (short time) / come here for a (moment/object).
additional_notes: Used to tell someone to come here briefly or to say someone is here in order to get or use something (e.g., 'qua per un minuto' = 'here for a minute'). Common in spoken Italian; context (time vs. purpose) clarifies meaning: 'qua per un minuto' = here for a minute (duration), 'qua per un computer' = here to get/use a computer (purpose). Often followed by a noun or time expression.
target_language_example: Vieni qua per un momento, devo chiederti qualcosa.
native_language_example: Come here for a moment, I need to ask you something.

meaning: "the painting is" or "a/that painting is" (simple present of essere with quadro)
additional_notes: This is just the noun quadro (painting, picture, frame) followed by the verb è (is). Use depends on context: un quadro = a painting; quel quadro = that painting; il quadro = the painting. È is the 3rd-person singular of essere (to be). Common in simple descriptions or location statements (e.g., "Il quadro è appeso...").
target_language_example: Quel quadro è molto famoso in questa città.
native_language_example: That painting is very famous in this city.

meaning: some good (a few good — used before a singular noun to mean 'some' or 'a few' good ...)
additional_notes: Qualche means 'some' or 'a few' and is always followed by a singular noun; buon is the short form of 'buono' used before nouns (buon ristorante). Together they indicate an unspecified small number of good things (restaurants, books, advice). Word order: 'qualche buon + [singular noun]'.
target_language_example: Conosci qualche buon film da guardare questo weekend?
native_language_example: Do you know any good movie to watch this weekend?

meaning: a few days later / a few days afterwards
additional_notes: Used to indicate that something happened a few days after a previously mentioned event. Commonly appears as "qualche giorno più tardi" or in spoken/written Italian you may also see "qualche giorno dopo". Can be used with past tenses (passato prossimo, passato remoto) or simple past narration.
target_language_example: È morto qualche giorno più tardi.
native_language_example: He died a few days later.

meaning: for some reason; for whatever reason
additional_notes: Used to introduce an unexplained or unknown cause for something. Often appears as 'per qualche motivo' (literally 'for some reason') and is followed by a clause describing the unexpected event or feeling. Neutral register and common in spoken and written Italian.
target_language_example: Per qualche motivo, ho dimenticato le chiavi a casa.
native_language_example: For some reason, I forgot my keys at home.

meaning: for some reason; for some unspecified reason
additional_notes: Used to indicate that the speaker doesn't know or doesn't state the exact reason. Often appears as 'per qualche ragione' or 'per una qualche ragione'. Natural alternatives: 'per qualche motivo' (more common) or 'per qualche motivo/strano motivo'. Slightly formal/neutral; not slang.
target_language_example: Per qualche ragione non ha risposto al messaggio.
native_language_example: For some reason he didn't reply to the message.

meaning: sometimes; every so often.
additional_notes: Used to indicate that something happens on occasion but not regularly. Interchangeable with 'a volte' in many contexts. Placed before or after the verb/clause: 'qualche volta vado' or 'vado qualche volta'.
target_language_example: Qualche volta vado al cinema da solo.
native_language_example: Sometimes I go to the cinema alone.

meaning: 'something too' or 'something as well' — used to include someone or something in addition to others.
additional_notes: Combines qualcosa (something) with anche (also/too). Common in offers, requests, or suggestions to include an extra person or item. Word order can vary: anche può precede o seguire qualcosa (e.g. 'anche qualcosa' less common). Often used in imperatives or questions: 'Portami qualcosa anche' / 'Porti qualcosa anche a me?'.
target_language_example: Portami qualcosa anche, per favore.
native_language_example: Bring me something too, please.

meaning: 'something I must/need to (do/say)'.
additional_notes: Used to introduce an action or statement the speaker has an obligation, need, or intention to perform. Followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., dire, fare) or by a clause with a pronoun/object. Can be formal or informal depending on context; pronoun after verb changes the listener (dirle = to her, dirvi = to you plural).
target_language_example: Ho qualcosa che devo dirti.
native_language_example: I have something I need to tell you.

meaning: 'something with' / 'something (to do) with'
additional_notes: Used to talk about 'something' together with someone or something, or to mean 'something' in a general sense when paired with 'con' to indicate accompaniment or instrument. Common in informal spoken Italian: e.g. 'bere qualcosa con (qualcuno)' = 'have a drink with (someone)'. Can also appear in questions about earning/making something 'qualcosa con' (e.g. 'guadagni qualcosa con i tuoi disegni?' = 'do you make any money from your drawings?').
target_language_example: Vuoi prendere qualcosa con me stasera?
native_language_example: Do you want to get something (to eat/drink) with me tonight?

meaning: something cold to (do/use) — used before a verb like 'bere' (to drink) or implicit action
additional_notes: This phrase is incomplete on its own; it expects an infinitive verb after 'da' (e.g., 'da bere' = 'to drink') or context that makes the action clear. It's a common way to ask for or offer 'something cold to drink/put on/etc.' in everyday Italian. Word-for-word: 'something of cold to...'.
target_language_example: Vorrei qualcosa di freddo da mangiare.
native_language_example: I'd like something cold to eat.

meaning: something there / something over there (referring to a thing in a nearby place).
additional_notes: Combines 'qualcosa' (something) with 'lì' (there). Used to ask or point out the presence of an unspecified object in or at a nearby location. Tone is neutral; context and intonation can indicate more precise distance (lì = relatively close) or attention to a specific spot.
target_language_example: C'è qualcosa lì sotto il tavolo?
native_language_example: Is there something under the table there?

meaning: 'something today' — used to ask or say whether something happened or was done today.
additional_notes: Qualcosa = 'something' (indefinite pronoun). Oggi = 'today'. Combined, it's used in questions and statements about events, actions, or experiences that occurred (or not) today. Typical word order: verb + qualcosa oggi (e.g., Hai fatto qualcosa oggi?). In casual speech you might also hear 'qualcosa di interessante oggi?' or the words separated by tense/negation (e.g., Non ho fatto niente oggi = I didn't do anything today).
target_language_example: Hai visto qualcosa oggi?
native_language_example: Did you see anything today?

meaning: someone else; somebody else.
additional_notes: Used to refer to another person (not the one mentioned or present). Common in questions, requests, and statements (e.g., asking if another person can do something, or saying something was done by someone else). Often appears as 'qualcun altro?' in short spoken exchanges. Written form: 'qualcun' + 'altro' (no apostrophe).
target_language_example: Può rispondere qualcun altro?
native_language_example: Can someone else answer?

meaning: 'someone who can' (someone able to ...)
additional_notes: Used to refer to a person who has the ability, possibility or permission to do something. Often followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., aiutarti, aiutarci, aiutarla). Can appear in conditional or indicative sentences (e.g., Potrei conoscere qualcuno che può...).
target_language_example: Conosco qualcuno che può riparare la macchina.
native_language_example: I know someone who can fix the car.

meaning: someone with (someone who has/with whom)
additional_notes: Used to talk about an unspecified person combined with either possession (someone with + object) or a relationship/connection + cui (with whom). When followed by a noun (e.g. "un coltello"), it means "someone with [something]". When followed by "cui" or "con cui" or another clause, it expresses "someone to/with whom" (someone to do something with). For beginner learners: remember to add "con cui" or restructure the sentence when you need "with whom" before a verb (e.g. "qualcuno con cui parlare").
target_language_example: Cerco qualcuno con cui andare al cinema.
native_language_example: I'm looking for someone to go to the cinema with.

meaning: 'does anyone care' / 'someone cares' (literal: 'to someone it matters')
additional_notes: Used to ask whether anyone cares about something (often rhetorical) or to say that something matters to somebody. In questions it's commonly phrased 'A qualcuno importa?' or 'A qualcuno importa davvero?/veramente?' In statements it appears as 'a qualcuno importa' following verbs like 'so' or 'sento' (e.g. 'Ho bisogno di sapere che a qualcuno importa' = 'I need to know that someone cares'). Tone can be neutral or emotional depending on context. Literal translation is 'to someone it matters.'
target_language_example: Dopo tutto quello che è successo, a qualcuno importa?
native_language_example: After everything that happened, does anyone care?

meaning: someone to/for (used to say you hire, pay, or get someone to do something).
additional_notes: Used with verbs like assumere (to hire) or pagare (to pay) + an infinitive to indicate hiring or paying a person to perform an action (e.g., "assumere qualcuno per + [infinitive]"). Common structure: [verb] qualcuno per [infinitive]. Not a fixed idiom — compositional and literal: "qualcuno" = someone, "per" = to/for. Can be used for neutral tasks (train a dog) or criminal acts (hire someone to kill), so context matters.
target_language_example: Ho assunto qualcuno per ristrutturare la cucina.
native_language_example: I hired someone to renovate the kitchen.

meaning: 'someone' (somebody) + reflexive/pronoun 'si' used with verbs to mean 'someone will/has to/... (do something to themselves or generally)'.
additional_notes: Qualcuno means 'someone' or 'somebody'. When followed by the clitic si (reflexive/impersonal pronoun) it appears before a verb to form phrases like 'someone must/ will/ could ...' where the action is reflexive or generic. English often uses 'someone' + auxiliary + verb (e.g. 'Someone has to take care of...'; 'Someone will get hurt'). Word order in Italian is: Qualcuno si + verb (si precedes the verb). Not all verbs with si are truly reflexive here; si can also make a general/impersonal sense.
target_language_example: Qualcuno si occuperà dei bambini domani.
native_language_example: Someone will take care of the children tomorrow.

meaning: which bottle of (used to ask which specific bottle of something, usually wine or other drink)
additional_notes: Common in questions when choosing among several bottles. Followed by the item (e.g., vino, acqua, champagne). Can be used with formal (lei) or informal/plural (voi/voi, voi/consigliate) verb forms. Word order: 'Quale bottiglia di + [noun] + [verb]'.
target_language_example: Quale bottiglia di vino preferisci per la cena?
native_language_example: Which bottle of wine do you prefer for dinner?

meaning: 'what reason' or 'which reason' (used to ask or refer to the reason for something).
additional_notes: Often appears in questions or phrases asking why something happened. Can be followed by verbs or clauses (e.g., 'Quale motivo hai?' or more commonly 'Quale motivo hai di...'). In everyday spoken Italian, people more often say 'perché' for 'why' or 'che motivo'/'che ragione' for 'what reason'. 'Quale motivo' is slightly more formal/neutral.
target_language_example: Quale motivo ti ha fatto cambiare idea?
native_language_example: What reason made you change your mind?

meaning: which reason; what reason (for)...
additional_notes: Used to ask or refer to the cause or motive for something. Often appears in questions or relative clauses: e.g. "Per quale ragione..." (For what reason...). On its own "quale ragione" is slightly formal; in spoken Italian you may hear "perché" more often. Followed by verbs or clauses that explain the reason.
target_language_example: Per quale ragione non sei venuto alla festa?
native_language_example: For what reason didn't you come to the party?

meaning: 'for what reason is' / 'why is' (formal)
additional_notes: Used to ask why someone or something is in a certain state or place. More natural alternatives: "Per quale ragione..." + verb, or simply "Perché...". "Per quale ragione è qui stamattina?" = "Why is he/she here this morning?" Slightly more formal or emphatic than just "Perché è...?"
target_language_example: Per quale ragione è qui oggi?
native_language_example: For what reason is he/she here today? / Why is he/she here today?
