additional_notes: Used to refer to what remains of a group, quantity, or situation. Can be followed by a noun, pronoun, or clause. In informal speech it may appear in various constructions (e.g., 'il resto di voi' = 'the rest of you', 'il resto di questa storia' = 'the rest of this story'). Also appears as a fixed phrase in expressions like 'resto di guardia' (the remaining time on guard / I'm still on guard) depending on context.
target_language_example: Il resto di pizza lo porto a casa.
native_language_example: I'll take the rest of the pizza home.

meaning: the rest (of it) — used with a pronoun/verb to mean 'the rest (of that) you/they know/do/etc.'
additional_notes: Resto means 'the rest' or 'what remains'. When followed by a clitic pronoun (here 'lo') it refers back to something already mentioned. Common in spoken Italian: e.g. 'Il resto lo sapete' = 'You know the rest.' Word order can vary ("il resto lo sapete", "il resto lo buttate?"). Use to avoid repeating details.
target_language_example: Ho spiegato la prima parte, il resto lo sapete già.
native_language_example: I explained the first part; you already know the rest.

meaning: to get something back (the) — 'riavere' = to get back; 'il' is the masculine singular definite article placed before a noun.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom but a combination of the verb riavere (to regain, receive back) followed by the definite article il before a masculine singular noun. Use riavere + il + noun to say you got that masculine singular thing back: riavere il libro = to get the book back. Conjugate riavere according to tense and subject (io riavrò, tu hai riavuto, noi riavremo, etc.).
target_language_example: Spero di riavere il libro che ho prestato.
native_language_example: I hope to get back the book I lent.

meaning: Can I get my ... back? / to get my ... back
additional_notes: Used to ask (or talk about) getting back a possession that belonged to the speaker. Followed by the noun for the item (il mio + noun). Common in requests or questions. The verb riavere = ri- (again) + avere (to have) and implies recovering possession. You can also use 'riavere indietro' for emphasis ('get back').
target_language_example: Posso riavere il mio portafoglio?
native_language_example: Can I get my wallet back?

meaning: rich in; full of; having a lot of (something).
additional_notes: Used to describe something or someone that contains or possesses an abundance of a quality, resource, or substance (e.g., ricco di risorse, ricco di calcio, ricco di esperienza). Can be used with people, places, foods, abstract qualities. For comparing wealth, use constructions like 'più ricco di' = 'richer than.'
target_language_example: Il latte è anche ricco di calcio.
native_language_example: The milk is also rich in calcium.

meaning: 'received the' (past participle + definite article) — indicates that someone has received specific items.
additional_notes: Ricevuto is the past participle of ricevere (to receive). In Italian, past participles combine with auxiliary verbs (avere/essere) to form perfect tenses: (hai/ha/abbiamo) ricevuto. In the examples, ricevuto i = 'received the' followed by a plural masculine noun (i + noun). For questions use the auxiliary (Hai ricevuto i fiori?) and in hopes/wishes use the present perfect in the subjunctive (Spero che tu/lei abbia ricevuto...).
target_language_example: Hai ricevuto i documenti che ti ho mandato?
native_language_example: Did you receive the documents I sent you?

meaning: received the (masculine singular noun or date) — often used in formal/administrative contexts to say 'received the [document/date]'.
additional_notes: Combines the past participle ricevuto (received) with the article il. Common in written notes, emails, or forms to acknowledge receipt of something: e.g. «ricevuto il documento», «ricevuto il 10/03/2026». Agreement: if the noun is feminine use ricevuta la. Can appear without an explicit noun when the context provides it (e.g. on a stamped document).
target_language_example: Ricevuto il pacco, grazie.
native_language_example: Received the package, thank you.

meaning: received his/her/your (formal) — 'ricevuto' is the past participle of 'ricevere'; 'il suo' agrees as a neutral possessive meaning 'his', 'her', or formal 'your' (Lei).
additional_notes: Commonly appears in perfect tense constructions with 'avere' (e.g., 'Ha ricevuto il suo...') to say someone received something. 'Il suo' can mean 'his', 'her' or formal 'your' (Lei) depending on context; gender/number of the possessed noun may change the article and possessive (e.g., 'la sua lettera', 'i suoi messaggi'). Word order: past participle before the possession is normal in Italian ('ho ricevuto il suo messaggio').
target_language_example: Hai ricevuto il suo messaggio?
native_language_example: Did you receive his/her/their message?

meaning: received a (masculine singular noun); past participle + indefinite article used to say you got something
additional_notes: Ricevuto is the past participle of ricevere (to receive). In these examples it appears with the indefinite article un before a masculine singular noun (un avvertimento, un bonus, un telescopio, un sacco). Use ho/abbiamo/ha + ricevuto + un ... to say 'I/we/they received a ...'. For feminine nouns you'd say ricevuta una. Can also be used with expressions (e.g. ricevuto molti messaggi).
target_language_example: Ho ricevuto un regalo ieri.
native_language_example: I received a gift yesterday.

meaning: received a
additional_notes: Passive/perfect participle construction: ricevuto is the past participle of ricevere (to receive). 'ricevuto una' commonly appears in sentences meaning 'I/you/he/etc. received a ...' followed by a feminine singular noun (una lettera, una chiamata, una notizia). In full sentences the auxiliary (avere/essere) or subject may appear before (e.g. Ho ricevuto una...).
target_language_example: Ieri ho ricevuto una email importante.
native_language_example: Yesterday I received an important email.

meaning: 'received an answer' or 'got a reply'.
additional_notes: Past participle phrase used to ask or state whether someone has gotten a reply from someone else. Common in questions (Hai ricevuto una risposta?) and negative statements with avere + mai (Non ho mai ricevuto una risposta). You can change the subject/person by conjugating avere (ho, hai, ha, abbiamo, avete, hanno) and keep 'ricevuto una risposta' after it.
target_language_example: Hai ricevuto una risposta dalla scuola?
native_language_example: Did you receive an answer from the school?

meaning: call me back later / call me again later
additional_notes: Used when asking someone to call you back at a later time. 'Richiamarmi' = 'call me back' (richiamare = to call back). 'Più' here is a shortened form of 'più tardi' (later) and often follows the verb. Formality varies with the verb: 'Potrebbe' (formal), 'Potresti' (informal), 'Potreste' (plural/formal). In spoken language 'più' alone is common, but 'più tardi' is clearer in writing.
target_language_example: Potrebbe richiamarmi più tardi?
native_language_example: Could you call me back later?

meaning: grateful/thankful for
additional_notes: Used to express gratitude toward a thing, person, or situation. Often follows the verb essere (sono riconoscente per) or is used with indirect-object pronouns (Le sono riconoscente per = I am grateful to you for). Formal but common in both spoken and written Italian. Can be followed by a noun, clause, or infinitive (e.g., riconoscente per il tuo aiuto; riconoscente per avermi aiutato).
target_language_example: Sono riconoscente per il tuo sostegno in questo periodo.
native_language_example: I am grateful for your support during this time.

meaning: to recognize the / to acknowledge the
additional_notes: Riconoscere is a verb meaning 'to recognize' (a person, object) or 'to acknowledge/admit' (a fact, debt, right). 'Il' is the masculine singular definite article 'the'. Together 'riconoscere il ...' begins a phrase like 'recognize the ...' or 'acknowledge the ...' and must be followed by a masculine singular noun (e.g., 'riconoscere il problema'). Use appropriate subject and tense: 'io riconosco il', 'lui ha riconosciuto il', etc.
target_language_example: Dobbiamo riconoscere il problema prima di risolverlo.
native_language_example: We must acknowledge the problem before solving it.

meaning: 'do you/it remember the' or 'it reminds (one) of the' depending on context.
additional_notes: Depending on sentence structure, ricorda il can be either: (1) third-person singular 'ricorda' meaning 'it reminds (one) of' (e.g., 'Il colore ... ricorda il tramonto' = 'The color ... reminds one of the sunset'), or (2) second-person imperative/question/statement with a subject omitted (tu/Lei) 'ricorda il ...?' meaning 'do you remember the ...?' In spoken Italian the subject (tu/Lei) is often dropped. If addressing someone formally, use 'ricorda' (Lei) or 'si ricorda' for politeness. For 'remember' in general conversation you may also hear 'ti ricordi' (informal) or 'si ricorda' (formal).
target_language_example: Ti ricorda il concerto dello scorso anno?
native_language_example: Does it remind you of last year's concert? / Do you remember last year's concert?

target_language_multi_word_term: ricorda il suo / si ricorda il suo
meaning: Do you remember his/her/your (formal) ...? / Remember his/her/your ...?
additional_notes: Used to ask if someone remembers a piece of personal information (name, number, surname, etc.). 'Ricorda il suo...' is the informal second-person form (tu): 'Ricorda il suo numero?' would be used in casual speech. 'Si ricorda il suo...' is the formal or polite form (Lei) used when addressing someone respectfully. The possessive 'suo' agrees with the person being referred to (his/her/your formal). Context determines whether 'suo' refers to 'his', 'her', or the formal 'your'.
target_language_example: Si ricorda il suo indirizzo e-mail?
native_language_example: Do you remember his/her email address?

meaning: reminds (you/her) of / do you remember the... (polite or informal forms).
additional_notes: From the verb ricordare. Depending on context and pronouns, 'ricorda la' can mean 'it reminds (someone) of...' (e.g., 'La fotografia mi ricorda la mia famiglia' = 'The photo reminds me of my family') or be an imperative/question addressing someone about remembering a feminine noun (la domanda = the question). In questions and polite forms you'll often see reflexive 'si ricorda' (formal 'do you remember?') or 'ti ricordi' (informal). Word order and pronouns change the meaning: 'ricorda la mia faccia!' (remember my face! — imperative), 'Lei ricorda la domanda?' (formal 'Do you remember the question?').
target_language_example: Ti ricorda la canzone di quando eravamo bambini?
native_language_example: Does it remind you of the song from when we were kids?

meaning: to remember the (masculine) / to recall the
additional_notes: ricordare = 'to remember' or 'to remind'. When followed by 'il' it indicates remembering a specific masculine noun (e.g., il passato, il nome, il numero). In Italian the article agrees with the noun: you would say ricordare la, ricordare i, ricordare le accordingly. Can be transitive (ricordare qualcosa) or pronominal (ricordarsene).
target_language_example: Devo ricordare il suo compleanno.
native_language_example: I must remember his/her birthday.

meaning: Do you remember what (I) told you / what happened to you?
additional_notes: Common spoken phrase used to ask if someone remembers something that was said to them or done to them. Often appears as 'Ricordi cosa ti ho detto?' or with subject pronoun 'Ti ricordi cosa ti ho detto?'. 'Ricordi' is the second-person singular present of 'ricordare' (informal 'you remember'); 'ti' is the indirect object 'to you' or reflexive 'yourself'. Use with past actions or earlier statements.
target_language_example: Ti ricordi cosa ti ho detto ieri al bar?
native_language_example: Do you remember what I told you yesterday at the bar?

meaning: filled the (masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: A past participle phrase: riempito (filled) + il (the). Used before a masculine singular noun: e.g. "ha riempito il bicchiere" = "he/she filled the glass." Depending on context, it can be part of passato prossimo (e.g. "ho riempito il...") or a passive-like construction. Conjugation of the auxiliary verb (avere) is required to form full sentences.
target_language_example: Ho riempito il bicchiere d'acqua.
native_language_example: I filled the glass with water.

meaning: is able to understand the (masculine singular).
additional_notes: Riesce a capire = 'can / is able to understand'. Followed by a noun with definite article (il) = 'the' (masculine singular), e.g. il francese = French (language). Common in questions (formal or neutral). Use 'riesci a capire' for tu, 'riuscite a capire' for voi, 'riusciamo a capire' for noi. You can omit 'il' with names of languages in some contexts (e.g. 'capisce il francese' vs 'capisce francese'); both are used, but with 'il' is more explicit.
target_language_example: Riesce a capire il medico quando parla?
native_language_example: Can (he/she) understand the doctor when he speaks?

meaning: is able to play (an instrument) / manages to play
additional_notes: Riesce a + infinitive expresses ability or successful effort (he/she/it/you formal manages to...). Here used with musical instruments: 'suonare' = to play (an instrument). 'Riesce' is 3rd-person singular of 'riuscire'. For other subjects use: riesco a suonare, riesci a suonare, riusciamo a suonare, riuscite a suonare, riescono a suonare.
target_language_example: Lei riesce a suonare il violino molto bene.
native_language_example: She is able to play the violin very well.

meaning: I'm unable to stop (doing something) / I can't stop (doing something).
additional_notes: Common construction with the verb riuscire (riesco = I manage) + a + infinitive smettere di + infinitive. In these examples the speaker says they can't stop doing an action or thinking about something (emotional or repetitive actions). To change person, conjugate riuscire (e.g., non riesci a smettere di, non riusciamo a smettere di). Often appears with gerund-like meaning but followed by the infinitive verb (smettere di + verb).
target_language_example: Non riesco a smettere di guardare il telefono.
native_language_example: I can't stop looking at my phone.

meaning: 'I can no longer (do something)' or 'I'm no longer able to...'
additional_notes: Used with a verb in the infinitive to say you have lost the ability, capacity, or willingness to do something now (often because of a change or problem). Commonly appears as 'non riesco più a...' (I can no longer...).
target_language_example: Non riesco più a dormire quando sento quel rumore.
native_language_example: I can no longer sleep when I hear that noise.

meaning: made (or did) the same (thing), e.g. repeated the same mistake.
additional_notes: Commonly used after a past participle (rifatto = re-done) plus 'lo stesso' to say someone did the same thing again or repeated the same error. Often refers to mistakes or actions already mentioned. You can change the subject and auxiliary (ho/ha/abbiamo/avete/anno) to match tense and person.
target_language_example: Hai rifatto lo stesso errore di prima.
native_language_example: You made the same mistake as before.

meaning: to refuse his/her/its (something).
additional_notes: Rifiutare = to refuse/decline. "La sua" is a feminine singular possessive (her, his, its, your formal) that agrees with the noun that follows (which is omitted here). Together "rifiutare la sua" would appear before a feminine noun or imply one already mentioned (e.g., "rifiutare la sua offerta" = refuse his/her offer). The gender and number of the possessive must match the noun: for a masculine singular noun use "il suo"; for plural, "i suoi" or "le sue". The subject (who refuses) is usually explicit or clear from context.
target_language_example: Ho deciso di rifiutare la sua offerta.
native_language_example: I decided to refuse his/her offer.

meaning: refused to accept
additional_notes: Passive/participial form used with a feminine subject (rifiutata). Often appears with si è rifiutata di + infinitive to say 'she refused to...'. Change gender/number: rifiutato (m sg), rifiutati (m pl), rifiutate (f pl). Common with objects like soldi, denaro, regali, offerte.
target_language_example: Si è rifiutata di accettare il regalo.
native_language_example: She refused to accept the gift.

meaning: refused the (masculine singular noun) — 'rifiutare' in past participle + definite article 'il'.
additional_notes: Used to report that someone declined or turned down something (an offer, invitation, item). The phrase combines the past participle 'rifiutato' (has refused/ refused) with the masculine singular article 'il' before a masculine noun (e.g., 'il cibo', 'il mio invito'). For feminine nouns you would see 'rifiutata la' (or other gender/number forms). Context determines whether it's present perfect ('ha rifiutato il...': has refused) or simple past in English.
target_language_example: Lei ha rifiutato il mio invito alla festa.
native_language_example: She refused my invitation to the party.

meaning: refused (something feminine singular) / rejected her/it
additional_notes: Past participle 'rifiutato' (refused/rejected) followed by the feminine singular article 'la' typically introduces the object being refused (la proposta, la chiamata, la offerta) or can mean 'rejected her' when referring to a person. You will more often see the full noun after 'la' (e.g. 'rifiutato la proposta') or a pronoun (e.g. 'l'ha rifiutata'). Word order and clitic pronouns change in compound tenses: 'l'ho rifiutata' = I refused/rejected her/it.
target_language_example: Ho rifiutato la proposta perché le condizioni non erano buone.
native_language_example: I refused the proposal because the terms weren't good.

meaning: refused to
additional_notes: Past tense (passato remoto or simple past) of 'rifiutarsi di' meaning 'to refuse to (do something)'. Commonly used with a verb after 'di' (e.g. rifiutò di pagare = refused to pay). Can also appear as 'si rifiutò di' (he/she refused to) when reflexive. In everyday speech you will more often hear passato prossimo (si è rifiutato di / ha rifiutato di).
target_language_example: Si rifiutò di rispondere alle domande.
native_language_example: He refused to answer the questions.

meaning: refused to accept
additional_notes: Past tense (passato remoto) of 'rifiutarsi di accettare' — used to say someone refused something. In spoken Italian, passato prossimo (si è rifiutato/a di accettare) is more common for recent events; context shows refusing money, defeat, gifts, etc. The reflexive form 'si rifiutò di...' is typical.
target_language_example: Luigi si rifiutò di accettare l'aiuto degli altri.
native_language_example: Luigi refused to accept help from others.

meaning: "reflection in the" (used to say someone or something seen reflected in a surface, e.g. a mirror).
additional_notes: riflesso = reflection; nello = in + il (in the). Used before a masculine singular noun starting with a consonant (e.g. nello specchio = in the mirror). Commonly appears with verbs like guardare, vedere, notare. Literal translation corresponds to English word order: "reflection in the..."
target_language_example: Vedo il mio riflesso nello specchio ogni mattina.
native_language_example: I see my reflection in the mirror every morning.

meaning: 'remains in' / 'stays in' (literally) or 'keeps/maintains (something) in' depending on context.
additional_notes: Used with different nouns to mean either 'stay/continue to be inside or at' (e.g., rimane in un motel = stays in a motel) or 'remain/keep in contact' when followed by a noun phrase like 'contatto'. Can also appear with time expressions (il tempo che ti rimane = the time you have left). Verb form is rimanere (to remain/stay) + preposition in. Choose meaning from context.
target_language_example: Lei rimane in città per un'altra settimana.
native_language_example: She stays in town for another week.

meaning: to feel hurt, upset, or disappointed (about something someone said or did).
additional_notes: Commonly used to describe an emotional reaction when someone's words or actions offend, upset, or let you down. Often used in the past: 'sono rimasto/a male' = 'I felt bad/upset'. Gender agreement matters in the past participle when using essere (rimasto/rimasta). Can be followed by 'per' + reason (e.g. 'rimanere male per quello che ha detto').
target_language_example: Sono rimasta male quando sono venuta a sapere che non mi avevano invitata; sono rimasta male sul serio.
native_language_example: I felt really hurt when I found out they hadn't invited me to the party; I was genuinely upset.

meaning: stayed at
additional_notes: Feminine past participle form (rimasta) of rimanere + preposition a. Used with a location (e.g., casa) to mean 'stayed at' or 'remained at'. For a male speaker you'd say 'rimasto a'. Often appears with essere in passato prossimo (sono rimasta a...).
target_language_example: Sono rimasta a casa tutto il giorno.
native_language_example: I stayed at home all day.

meaning: stayed with / remained with (feminine singular past participle + preposition 'with').
additional_notes: Rimasta is the past participle of 'rimanere' agreeing with a feminine singular subject. 'Con' means 'with'. Used to say someone stayed with or remained alongside someone else (e.g., stayed at someone's place or stayed to look after them). For other subjects/forms use: sono rimasto/a, siamo rimasti/e, è rimasto/a, sono rimasti/e. Common in contexts of staying for company or care (e.g., 'grazie per essere rimasta con lui' = 'thanks for staying with him').
target_language_example: Sono rimasta con mia sorella tutta la notte.
native_language_example: I stayed with my sister all night.

meaning: stayed with (someone).
additional_notes: Past participle 'rimasto' (from rimanere) + preposition 'con' means to have stayed or remained with a person. Common in thank-you phrases: 'Grazie per essere rimasto con [nome]' = 'Thanks for staying with [name]'. Use 'rimasta' for feminine speaker or to agree with subject if needed (e.g., 'è rimasta con lei'). The infinitive form in these examples is 'essere rimasto/a'.
target_language_example: Sono rimasto con mia sorella tutta la notte.
native_language_example: I stayed with my sister all night.

meaning: was injured in a (…)
additional_notes: Passive/experience construction using the past participle 'rimasto' + adjective 'ferito' means 'was injured' or 'got injured'. Followed by 'in un' + noun to indicate the event/place (e.g. 'incidente', 'incidente stradale'). Common in spoken and written Italian to describe someone who suffered an injury. You can replace 'un' with other articles or determiners: 'in un incidente', 'in un incidente stradale', 'in un'esplosione', or use prepositions like 'in' or 'in seguito a'. Verbs often used with this phrase: essere rimasto ferito, è rimasto ferito, sono rimasti feriti.
target_language_example: È rimasto ferito in un incidente stradale la scorsa notte.
native_language_example: He was injured in a road accident last night.

meaning: 'stayed/left in' or part of the passive/perfect expression meaning 'remained in (a state or place)'
additional_notes: Combines the past participle 'rimasto' (remained/stayed) with a following preposition 'in'. Often used with a noun or phrase after 'in' (e.g. 'in silenzio' = 'in silence') to indicate someone remained in that state. In sentence 3 the structure is different ('Se è rimasto in vita qualcuno' uses 'rimasto in vita' = 'remained alive'); note that 'rimasto' can appear with different prepositions (in, con, a) depending on the phrase. Common in spoken and written Italian.
target_language_example: Sono rimasto in silenzio per tutta la riunione.
native_language_example: I stayed silent for the whole meeting.

meaning: thanked (someone) for
additional_notes: Past participle 'ringraziato' (from ringraziare) used with a person as subject and 'per' to introduce the reason (often followed by an infinitive clause: 'per aver...'). Commonly appears as 'mi ha ringraziato per...' = 'he/she thanked me for...'.
target_language_example: Mi ha ringraziato per avermi aiutato.
native_language_example: He/She thanked me for helping him/her.

meaning: he/she thanked (me) for having (her) — expresses thanks for a past action involving a female person.
additional_notes: Ringraziò is the passato remoto (simple past) of ringraziare (to thank). 'Per averla' = 'for having (her)' + past participle that follows (e.g., assunta, avvertita, salvata). The object 'la' refers to a feminine singular person or thing. In spoken Italian, passato prossimo (mi ha ringraziato) is more common than passato remoto in many regions.
target_language_example: Mi ringraziò per averla aiutata quando era in difficoltà.
native_language_example: She thanked me for having helped her when she was in trouble.

meaning: 'to repair the' (plural masculine noun).
additional_notes: Riparare = to repair/fix. The phrase riparare i is used before a plural masculine noun (e.g., i computer = the computers). In the examples the object is implied as 'computer'. Conjugate riparare to match the subject (io riparo, tu ripari, lui/lei ripara, noi ripariamo, voi riparate, loro riparano).
target_language_example: Io so riparare i telefoni.
native_language_example: I know how to repair the phones.

meaning: 'may he/she rest in peace' (a polite formula said about someone who has died).
additional_notes: Used to express a wish that a deceased person find peace. It's the formal/subjunctive form (lei/egli) of 'riposare' used as a set phrase. Can be said alone ('Riposi in pace.') or inserted after mentioning the deceased. Tone can be respectful, but in some contexts it may sound ironic if said about someone disliked.
target_language_example: Mio nonno, riposi in pace, era molto generoso.
native_language_example: My grandfather, may he rest in peace, was very kind.

meaning: global warming; the long-term rise in Earth's average temperature.
additional_notes: Used to talk about climate change and environmental issues. Can refer to the phenomenon itself or to debates/policies related to it (e.g., cause, effects, prevention). Formal and widely used in media, science, and everyday conversation.
target_language_example: Il riscaldamento globale sta causando lo scioglimento dei ghiacciai.
native_language_example: Global warming is causing glaciers to melt.

meaning: 'risk of' or 'chance of' (something happening).
additional_notes: Used to express the possibility or danger that an event will occur. Commonly followed by an infinitive verb (rischio di + fare) or a noun (rischio di + incendi). Can be used with verbs like correre (correre il rischio di = to run the risk of).
target_language_example: Corri il rischio di perdere i soldi se investi troppo.
native_language_example: You run the risk of losing the money if you invest too much.

meaning: brown rice (whole-grain rice)
additional_notes: Refers to rice that still has the bran and germ (not polished), often considered healthier than white rice. Used like a food item: il riso integrale, del riso integrale. Can be contrasted with "riso bianco" (white rice).
target_language_example: Preferisco il riso integrale con le verdure.
native_language_example: I prefer brown rice with vegetables.

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase; literal reading: 'rice every' or 'laughter every' depending on context.
additional_notes: This exact two-word sequence 'riso ogni' is not a common Italian phrase on its own. 'Riso' can mean 'rice' (food) or 'laughter' (noun). 'Ogni' means 'every' or 'each' and must be followed by a singular noun (e.g., 'ogni giorno' = every day, 'ogni persona' = every person). If you see 'riso ogni' it is likely a fragment or a word order mistake. Correct phrases would be 'ogni riso' (every rice / every laugh — rare) or more naturally 'riso ogni giorno' (rice every day) should be 'riso ogni giorno' is understandable but better as 'riso tutti i giorni' or 'mangio riso ogni giorno' (I eat rice every day). For 'laughter every ...' you would say 'risate ogni ...' (plural) or 'una risata ogni ...'.
target_language_example: Mangio riso ogni giorno.
native_language_example: I eat rice every day.

meaning: 'the rice is...'.
additional_notes: A simple subject-verb phrase: riso (rice) + è (is). Used to describe the state or quality of rice (temperature, condition, composition, etc.). Replace the adjective or phrase after 'è' to change the meaning (e.g., caldo, bruciato, pieno di...). Useful for making basic descriptive sentences.
target_language_example: Il riso è troppo salato.
native_language_example: The rice is too salty.

meaning: natural resource (materials or features from nature used by people)
additional_notes: Refers to elements like water, forests, minerals, soil, and fossil fuels. Used in environmental, economic, and policy contexts. Plural is risorse naturali. Can be preceded by adjectives (e.g., scarse, rinnovabili).
target_language_example: L'acqua è una risorsa naturale preziosa.
native_language_example: Water is a precious natural resource.

meaning: respect my (something) — used before a feminine noun like 'privacy'.
additional_notes: Commonly followed by a feminine noun (e.g., privacy, decisione? though 'decisione' is incorrect; use 'decisione' is 'decisone'—stick to privacy). Use with different subjects and verbs (devi, deve, dovete) to tell someone to respect your rights, privacy, space, etc. 'La mia' agrees in gender with a feminine noun; for masculine nouns you'd say 'il mio'.
target_language_example: Per favore, rispettare la mia privacy.
native_language_example: Please respect my privacy.

meaning: compared to; in relation to
additional_notes: Used to compare two things, times, people, quantities, or situations. Often followed by a noun, pronoun, place, or time (e.g., ieri, me, Hong Kong). Can express similarity, difference, or change (e.g., 'più... rispetto a', 'meno... rispetto a').
target_language_example: Lei è più tranquilla rispetto a prima.
native_language_example: She is calmer compared to before.

meaning: to answer/respond to this (feminine singular noun or idea)
additional_notes: A short phrase combining the verb rispondere (to answer) with the preposition a (to) and the demonstrative questa (this, feminine). Use when referring to replying to a specific feminine noun already mentioned (e.g., questa domanda, questa email, questa richiesta) or to 'this' idea/situation. For a masculine noun you'd say rispondere a questo; for plural, rispondere a queste/questi. Common in spoken and written Italian.
target_language_example: Devo rispondere a questa email entro stasera.
native_language_example: I have to respond to this email by tonight.

meaning: to answer/respond to my (feminine plural noun that follows, e.g. 'domande' — questions).
additional_notes: This is the verb 'rispondere' (to respond) followed by the prepositional phrase 'alle mie' (a + le + mie), used when the thing being responded to is feminine plural. It must be followed by a feminine plural noun (e.g. domande, email, richieste). Example uses often include 'domande' (questions). Note the construction can appear in different tenses and with negation or auxiliary verbs (e.g. 'ha evitato di rispondere alle mie domande').
target_language_example: Evitò di rispondere alle mie domande.
native_language_example: He avoided answering my questions.

meaning: a (any) reply/answer from (someone).
additional_notes: Used to indicate who provides (or fails to provide) an answer. Often appears with negation (nessuna/mai/non) to say someone did not get a reply from a person or group. The preposition da = 'from' here; the noun risposta may be modified (nessuna risposta = no reply).
target_language_example: Non ho ricevuto nessuna risposta da Marco.
native_language_example: I didn't receive any reply from Marco.

meaning: answered all (feminine plural or implied 'questions')
additional_notes: Literally 'answered to all'. Commonly follows the indirect object (e.g., 'le domande' implied). 'Tutte' agrees with a feminine plural noun like 'domande' (questions). Use 'risposto a tutti' for masculine or mixed plural. Can appear in questions and negatives with auxiliary 'ha/ha' (present perfect) or 'hai' (you).
target_language_example: Hai risposto a tutte le email?
native_language_example: Did you answer all the emails?

meaning: answered/responded to (masculine/neutral subject) + definite article + noun; past participle with 'a' contracted with 'il/lo/la' as 'al'.
additional_notes: From the verb rispondere (to answer/respond). 'Risposto' is the past participle used in compound tenses (with avere) or as an adjective. 'Al' is the contraction of 'a + il' meaning 'to the' or 'to the (phone)'. Commonly used with objects like 'telefono', 'messaggio', 'telegramma' or people (e.g. 'ha risposto al ragazzo'). In English you can often translate as 'answered the phone' or 'responded to the telegram'.
target_language_example: Non ha risposto al messaggio di ieri.
native_language_example: He/She didn't reply to yesterday's message.

meaning: 'responded to' or 'replied to' (feminine/masculine singular agreement depends on subject)
additional_notes: Past participle of rispondere (risposto) + preposition a. Used to say someone replied/answered to something (una email, una chiamata, una domanda). The subject determines auxiliary in compound tenses (ha risposto). 'Alla' = a + la (to the). Can appear with other articles: 'al', 'alle', 'ai'.
target_language_example: Ho finalmente risposto alla sua email questa mattina.
native_language_example: I finally replied to his/her email this morning.

meaning: 'answered that' or 'replied that' (introduces reported speech).
additional_notes: Used to report what someone said. Typically follows a subject (Ha risposto che...) and is followed by a clause with the reported content. In English you'd use 'answered/replied that' or more naturally 'said that'. Past participle 'risposto' comes from the verb rispondere. Common in both spoken and written Italian.
target_language_example: Gli ho risposto che sarei arrivata tardi.
native_language_example: I answered him that I would arrive late.

meaning: that new restaurant
additional_notes: Used to talk about a recently opened or newly discovered restaurant. 'Quel' (that) commonly appears before it in examples (quel ristorante nuovo). Can be used in questions, suggestions, or statements about trying or giving opinions. Word order 'ristorante nuovo' (noun + adjective) is standard in Italian.
target_language_example: Vorrei provare quel ristorante nuovo stasera.
native_language_example: I'd like to try that new restaurant tonight.

meaning: delay because of / late due to
additional_notes: Used to say something or someone is late or delayed because of a reason. Usually followed by di/ della/ del + noun (ritardo a causa della neve, ritardo a causa del traffico). Formal-neutral; interchangeable with "in ritardo a causa di" or more simply "a causa di" + noun.
target_language_example: Il volo è in ritardo a causa del vento forte.
native_language_example: The flight is delayed because of the strong wind.

meaning: 'delay due to' or 'delay because of'.
additional_notes: Used to explain the cause of a delay. Common in announcements (trains, flights, meetings) or in everyday speech to give a reason: ritardo per traffico (delay due to traffic). Often followed by a noun or verb in the gerund (e.g., ritardo per un guasto / ritardo per il maltempo).
target_language_example: Siamo in ritardo per traffico.
native_language_example: We are delayed because of traffic.

meaning: 'returned to' (feminine singular) + preposition 'to/at'.
additional_notes: Ritornata is the past participle of 'ritornare' used with 'essere' for feminine singular subjects (io/lei). Use 'ritornato' for masculine singular, 'ritornati'/'ritornate' for plurals. Followed by 'a' to indicate the place someone returned to (e.g., 'a casa', 'a Boston'). In spoken Italian you may also hear 'sono tornata a' (tornare = to return/come back) which is more common in some regions.
target_language_example: Sono ritornata a casa tardi ieri sera.
native_language_example: I returned home late last night.

meaning: return to (a place) / comeback into
additional_notes: Used when talking about returning to a location, situation, or state introduced by a following noun or place name: 'ritorno in Italia' = 'I return to Italy.' In Italian you often see 'ritorno a' or just 'ritorno' depending on the verb/phrase; use 'in' when the destination takes the preposition 'in' (countries/regions/rooms: in Italia, in ufficio, in montagna). Verb forms usually accompany it (torno/tornerò/ho fatto ritorno).
target_language_example: Farò il mio ritorno in Italia il mese prossimo.
native_language_example: I will make my return to Italy next month.

meaning: the meeting was (something).
additional_notes: This phrase combines 'riunione' (meeting) with the passive past construction 'è stata' (feminine singular of 'essere' + past participle). Use it to say what happened to a meeting: e.g. was canceled, postponed, closed. Change the participle to match the action (annullata, rimandata, chiusa, convocata).
target_language_example: La riunione è stata confermata per domani alle 10.
native_language_example: The meeting was confirmed for tomorrow at 10.

meaning: could no longer (do something); was no longer able to
additional_notes: Used to say someone lost the ability or strength to continue an action or feeling. Often followed by an infinitive verb (e.g. reggere, sopportare, contenere, controllarsi). Nuance: expresses a progressive inability—"no longer" rather than a one-time failure.
target_language_example: Non riusciva più a sopportare la situazione e se ne andò.
native_language_example: He could no longer bear the situation and left.

meaning: French magazines (literally: magazines that are French).
additional_notes: Plural phrase: 'riviste' = magazines (feminine plural). 'francesi' is the adjective 'French' agreeing in number and gender. Used to refer to magazines from France or in French. Often appears after verbs like 'avere' (to have) and with partitive 'delle' (some) or as a direct noun phrase.
target_language_example: Hai delle riviste francesi da prestarmi?
native_language_example: Do you have any French magazines I can borrow?

meaning: a colloquial sequence meaning 'stuff and...' used to link taking/bringing 'stuff' with then doing something (e.g. 'take your stuff and...').
additional_notes: roba = 'things, stuff' (very common, informal). When followed by a verb introduced with e (and) the phrase links the action involving 'stuff' with a subsequent action: 'take your stuff and leave', 'grab the stuff and let's go'. The examples show several clitics combined with verbs (vattene, ce ne andiamo, me ne andai) — pay attention to placement of pronouns. Common in spoken Italian.
target_language_example: Prendi la tua roba e vattene subito.
native_language_example: Take your stuff and leave right away.

meaning: to annoy/bug someone a lot; to be a pain in the ass
additional_notes: Very informal and vulgar. Used to tell someone to stop bothering, annoying, or making things difficult. Can be directed at someone (imperative) or used generally. Avoid in formal situations; use milder alternatives like "dar fastidio" or "dare noia".
target_language_example: Per favore, smettila di rompere i coglioni con quella questione.
native_language_example: Please stop annoying me about that issue.

meaning: to annoy, bother, or piss someone off (very vulgar).
additional_notes: Strong vulgar expression. Literally 'to break the dick', used to say someone is being extremely annoying or a nuisance. Common in spoken Italian among friends or in angry contexts; avoid in formal situations. Can be directed at a person (Mi stai rompendo il cazzo — You're pissing me off) or used generally (Questo mi rompe il cazzo — This pisses me off).
target_language_example: Mi stai rompendo il cazzo, smettila.
native_language_example: You're pissing me off, stop it.

meaning: to annoy, to bother, to be a pain (colloquial/strong)
additional_notes: Very informal and somewhat vulgar — literally 'to break the balls'. Used to say someone or something is annoying, pestering, or making life difficult. Often used in the present tense (mi rompe le palle = it annoys me) or as an imperative (smettila di rompermi le palle). Avoid in formal situations.
target_language_example: Il tuo vicino non fa altro che rompere le palle con la musica alta.
native_language_example: Your neighbor does nothing but annoy everyone with loud music.

meaning: is broken
additional_notes: This phrase is the past participle 'rotta' (feminine singular) plus the definite article 'la'. It appears in impersonal or reflexive constructions with 'si' (si è rotta la ...), meaning 'the ... got broken' or 'she/it broke' when referring to a feminine noun (la macchina, la gamba, la teiera, la videocamera). Use rotta (fem.) for feminine singular nouns; for masculine singular you'd see rotto il (e.g. si è rotto il vetro). Context determines whether it refers to an object or a body part (e.g. 'si è rotta la gamba' = 'she broke her leg' or 'her leg got broken').
target_language_example: Si è rotta la finestra ieri durante il temporale.
native_language_example: The window broke yesterday during the storm.

meaning: spilled his/her/its (something); knocked over his/her/its
additional_notes: Rovesciare means to overturn or spill. "Rovesciato il suo" is the past participle phrase used in reported statements or questions to say someone spilled their (masculine) thing: e.g. "Ha rovesciato il suo caffè" = "He/She spilled his/her coffee." The possessive (suo) agrees with the owner, not the object; use "la sua" for feminine nouns (la sua tazza) and "il suo" for masculine nouns (il suo caffè). In spoken Italian the subject pronoun is often omitted: context (or a preceding name) tells you who "ha" refers to.
target_language_example: Marco ha rovesciato il suo bicchiere sul tavolo.
native_language_example: Marco spilled his glass on the table.

meaning: ruined (something/someone) — past participle + direct object article (feminine).
additional_notes: Rovinato is the past participle of rovinare (to ruin). In examples it’s used with a feminine singular noun introduced by la (e.g., la vita, la carriera, la festa). In English you would usually say “ruined my life,” “ruined her career,” etc. Word order: subject + ha/hanno/ho + rovinato + la + noun. Can refer to damaging reputation, plans, events, life, career, etc.
target_language_example: Quel errore mi ha rovinato la giornata.
native_language_example: That mistake ruined my day.

meaning: to steal my
additional_notes: Literal meaning is 'to steal my...'. In spoken Italian this phrase is used figuratively about people (e.g. 'rubarmi il fidanzato/il ragazzo/il moroso') meaning 'to steal my boyfriend' — i.e. to try to take someone who is in a relationship with the speaker. The structure is verb + clitic object ('rubare' + 'mi' → 'rubarmi') followed by the definite article and noun. Context determines whether it's literal theft or emotional/relational 'stealing'.
target_language_example: Ha cercato di rubarmi il fidanzato al bar.
native_language_example: She tried to steal my boyfriend at the bar.

meaning: 'stolen the' (past participle + definite article) — indicates that someone stole some specific plural noun (e.g., 'rubato i soldi' = 'stolen the money').
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but a combination of the past participle 'rubato' (from rubare = to steal) followed by the definite article 'i' (the, plural masculine). It's used in perfect or past constructions (often with avere: 'ha rubato i...') to say someone stole something specific. Context determines the following noun (e.g., documenti, soldi). In English you usually translate as 'stole my...' or 'stole the...'.
target_language_example: Ha rubato i documenti importanti.
native_language_example: He stole the important documents.

meaning: 'stolen my' (past participle + definite article + possessive — used to say someone stole something of mine)
additional_notes: Combines the past participle rubato (stolen) with the article il and the possessive mio. Used after a subject: e.g. "Ha rubato il mio telefono" = "He/She has stolen my phone." Can be adjusted for gender/number: rubato il mio (masc. sing.), rubata la mia (fem. sing.), rubati i miei (masc. pl.), rubate le mie (fem. pl.).
target_language_example: Qualcuno ha rubato il mio portafoglio.
native_language_example: Someone has stolen my wallet.

meaning: stolen the / (someone) stole the
additional_notes: Combines the past participle 'rubato' (stolen) with the feminine definite article 'la' before a feminine noun (e.g., 'la borsetta') or with a noun phrase; used in statements about something being stolen. In examples with a person as subject, you may see 'mi hanno rubato la...' (they stole my...) or 'gli hai rubato la...' (you stole his/her...). Word order and agreement follow the noun that comes after 'la'.
target_language_example: Mi hanno rubato la giacca ieri.
native_language_example: They stole my jacket yesterday.

meaning: stolen (feminine plural direct object) — 'has/have stolen the...'.
additional_notes: Rubato is the past participle of rubare (to steal). In Italian compound past with avere uses the past participle that agrees in gender/number with a preceding direct object pronoun, but not with a following noun; here 'le' is the feminine plural direct object pronoun/article matching a feminine plural noun (e.g., le uova, le scarpe, le idee). Typical translations: 'stole the...' or 'has/have stolen my/your/...'.
target_language_example: Mi ha rubato le chiavi della macchina.
native_language_example: He/she has stolen my car keys.

meaning: stolen a (something).
additional_notes: Past participle of rubare (to steal) used with a feminine singular noun introduced by 'una'. Indicates that someone stole one item (feminine noun). In sentences the subject can be explicit (Fadil ha rubato una macchina) or implied (Ha rubato una macchina fotografica). Use 'rubato un' before masculine nouns (e.g., 'rubato un libro').
target_language_example: Lui ha rubato una borsa ieri.
native_language_example: He stole a bag yesterday.

meaning: broke both (the...)
additional_notes: Past simple (passato remoto) of rompersi used with a body part: 'si ruppe entrambe le braccia' = 'he/she broke both arms'. 'Entrambe le' means 'both (the...)' and agrees with a plural feminine noun (le + plural noun). Common in narratives; in spoken Italian, passato prossimo ('si è rotto/rota/rotti/rote') is more frequent.
target_language_example: Maria si ruppe entrambe le gambe in montagna.
native_language_example: Maria broke both legs in the mountains.

meaning: 'knows how to play' (used with sports/games).
additional_notes: Formed from the verb sapere (to know) + giocare (to play). Use sa (he/she/you formal) or so/ sai/ sappiamo/ sapete/ sanno for different subjects. Usually followed by a sport or game introduced by a (e.g., a tennis, a baseball) or by a direct object (giocare bene). Common structure: [Subject] + sa + giocare + (a + sport).
target_language_example: Maria sa giocare a pallavolo molto bene.
native_language_example: Maria knows how to play volleyball very well.

meaning: Not a standard or grammatical Italian multi-word expression; likely a mistaken, misheard, or incomplete phrase. Could result from a typo or from combining parts of correct phrases such as "sa che" (he/she knows that) or "sa a chi" (he/she knows whom/to whom).
additional_notes:
As written, "sa a che" does not occur in standard Italian. If encountered in text or speech, check for errors or missing words. Possible intended alternatives:
- "sa che" (compositional) — "he/she knows that" or polite/formal "you know that".
- "sa a chi" — "he/she knows whom/to whom".
- "sa a che punto" — a grammatical phrase meaning "knows at what point" (note the addition of "punto").
If the context shows an extra word after "che" (e.g., "sa a che ora"), the phrase becomes grammatical ("knows at what time").
target_language_example: Non so cosa intendeva quando ha scritto "sa a che"; sembra un errore.
native_language_example: I don't know what he/she meant when they wrote "sa a che"; it looks like a mistake.

meaning: he/she knows that I (something) — 'sa' = knows; 'che' = that; 'mi' = me/to me (often introduces a verb phrase like 'mi piace').
additional_notes: This is a common structure where 'sa' (3rd person singular of sapere) + 'che' introduces a clause about the speaker. 'Mi' is an indirect object pronoun meaning 'to me' or 'me' and usually connects to a verb (e.g., 'mi piace' = 'I like' / 'it pleases me'). Depending on context, 'mi sa che...' is an idiomatic expression meaning 'I think/it seems to me that...'. Word order can vary: 'Lo sa che mi piace' (he knows it that I like) or simply 'Sa che mi piace'.
target_language_example: Sa che mi piacciono i film di fantascienza.
native_language_example: He/She knows that I like science-fiction movies.

meaning: doesn't know anything / knows nothing
additional_notes: Formed with the verb sapere (sa = he/she/you formal knows) + nulla (nothing). Common negated pattern in Italian is non + verb + nulla (or non + verb + niente). In spoken Italian you may also hear "non sa niente". Context decides subject (he/she/you formal/it/they with plural verb).
target_language_example: Lui non sa nulla della festa.
native_language_example: He knows nothing about the party.

meaning: knows this / knows that (referring to a fact or piece of information)
additional_notes: Combination of the verb sapere (sa = he/she/you formal knows) + questo (this/that when pointing to a specific fact). Used to say someone knows a particular thing. Word order can vary: 'Lo sa questo' adds the pronoun lo (it/that) to refer to the specific fact; 'Sa questo' is a shorter version. Context determines whether sa = he/she knows or (formal) you know.
target_language_example: Lui sa questo dettaglio importante.
native_language_example: He knows this important detail.

meaning: knows everything
additional_notes: A phrase using the verb sapere (to know) in the 3rd person singular + tutto (everything). Used to say someone knows everything or knows a lot about a topic. Context can mean literal omniscience (joking) or simply that the person is well informed about a subject (e.g., "sa tutto sui gatti" = knows everything about cats). Replace subject and topic as needed.
target_language_example: Marta sa tutto sui film italiani.
native_language_example: Marta knows everything about Italian films.

meaning: 'Saturday is' (used to state something about Saturday).
additional_notes: sabato means 'Saturday'. When followed by the verb è (is), it introduces a description, characteristic, or fact about Saturday (e.g. 'Saturday is the day when...' or 'Saturday is sacred'). Italians also sometimes drop the article and say simply 'Sabato è...' to mean 'Saturday is...'. If you want to say 'on Saturday' use 'di sabato' or 'il sabato' depending on context.
target_language_example: Il sabato è il giorno in cui mi rilasso.
native_language_example: Saturday is the day when I relax.

meaning: sleeping bag.
additional_notes: A common camping item. Used to refer to an individual sleeping bag (masculine noun: il sacco a pelo). Can be used in questions (Di chi è questo sacco a pelo?) and statements about bringing or preparing one.
target_language_example: Porto il mio sacco a pelo per il campeggio.
native_language_example: I'll bring my sleeping bag for the camping trip.

meaning: ‘sacrificed his/her/its (… )’ — indicates someone gave up something belonging to them (often 'life' or a game piece).
additional_notes: Usually follows a subject and precedes the thing sacrificed (la sua + noun). Commonly used with 'vita' (la sua vita = his/her life). Can also be used in other contexts (e.g., chess: 'ha sacrificato la sua torre' = he sacrificed his rook). Gender and number of the possessed noun are shown by the article and adjective (la sua = his/her (feminine) or your formal). Context or preceding subject clarifies whether 'sua' refers to he/she/you/it.
target_language_example: Ha sacrificato la sua carriera per la famiglia.
native_language_example: He/she sacrificed his/her career for the family.

meaning: 'do you know what (someone) was ...' — a spoken lead-in used to introduce something someone was doing or feeling (often followed by a gerund or clause).
additional_notes: This is an informal conversational phrase: 'sai' = 'you know' (from sapere), 'cosa' = 'what', 'stava' = imperfect of 'stare' ('was' + gerund). It typically precedes a gerund (stava + -ando/-endo) or a clause that explains what someone was doing or what was happening. Example continuation: 'sai cosa stava facendo?' (do you know what he/she was doing?). Can be used to get someone's attention before telling a story or describing a past scene.
target_language_example: Sai cosa stava facendo ieri sera?
native_language_example: Do you know what he/she was doing last night?

meaning: 'do you know which' (informal second-person singular)
additional_notes: Used to ask someone if they know which specific things/items/answers are being referred to. 'Sai' is the informal 'you know' (tu form of sapere). 'Quali' is the plural form of 'which/what (ones)'. Often followed by 'sono' or a noun/phrase: 'Sai quali sono...?' = 'Do you know which ones they are?'. For formal situations use 'sa quali' (lei form).
target_language_example: Sai quali sono le ore del concerto?
native_language_example: Do you know which hours the concert is at?

meaning: engine room; machinery room (on a ship, train, or building).
additional_notes: Refers to the room where engines, motors, boilers, or other mechanical systems are housed. Common in maritime and railway contexts (e.g., ship's engine room). Can be used with determiners or as a label (Sala macchine principale).
target_language_example: Torniamo alla sala macchine per controllare la caldaia.
native_language_example: Let's go back to the engine room to check the boiler.

meaning: operating room; surgical theater (where surgeries take place).
additional_notes: Used for the room in a hospital where operations are performed. Often preceded by articles or phrases indicating presence (in sala operatoria = in the operating room) or purpose (per la sala operatoria = for the operating room). Formal medical term; not slang.
target_language_example: Il medico entra in sala operatoria alle otto.
native_language_example: The doctor enters the operating room at eight.

meaning: smoked salmon.
additional_notes: A food term: 'salmone' = salmon, 'affumicato' = smoked. Used to refer to smoked salmon in general (with partitive 'del') or a specific portion (with definite article 'il'). Common on menus and in sandwiches, salads, antipasti. Pronunciation: sal-MO-ne af-fu-mi-CA-to.
target_language_example: Ho comprato del salmone affumicato per l'antipasto.
native_language_example: I bought some smoked salmon for the starter.

meaning: literally 'sausage and' — used when listing items (e.g., salsiccia e funghi = sausage and mushrooms).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself but the start of a compound food name or a list (salsiccia e patate, salsiccia e peperoni). You'll usually see it in menus or when naming combinations. Pronunciation: /salˈsi(t)ːtʃa e/. Followed by another noun.
target_language_example: Pizza con salsiccia e funghi.
native_language_example: Pizza with sausage and mushrooms.

meaning: (he/she/it) jumps into; (you) jump into — literal or figurative 'jump in' (salta is imperative or present of saltare + preposition in).
additional_notes: Commonly appears as part of phrases like 'salta in auto' (jump into the car) or 'salta in mezzo' (jump in the middle). 'Salta' is the third-person singular present (or the tu/imperative form) of the verb 'saltare' (to jump). With 'in' it can be literal (physically entering) or figurative (join, interrupt, get involved): e.g. 'Salta in macchina!' (Get in the car / Jump in the car) or 'Salta in conversazione' (jump into the conversation). Conjugation and subject depend on context.
target_language_example: Salta in macchina, partiamo!
native_language_example: Jump in the car, let's go!

meaning: 'to pop up', 'to appear suddenly', or 'to come out (unexpectedly)'.
additional_notes: Informal phrasal expression. Used when something or someone appears abruptly or unexpectedly (an idea, a problem, a person, a detail). Often used in spoken Italian and can refer to things that emerge during discussion or investigation. Can be conjugated (e.g., è saltato fuori, saltò fuori, saltano fuori).
target_language_example: Durante la riunione è saltare fuori un problema con il budget.
native_language_example: During the meeting a problem with the budget popped up.

meaning: to blow up; to cause to explode (literal) — also used figuratively for 'ruin' or 'destroy'.
additional_notes: Commonly used to describe making something explode (bombs, bridges, ships). Can be used figuratively to mean 'spoil/destroy something' (e.g., 'you messed everything up'). Subject often is someone who triggers the explosion: fare saltare in aria qualcosa = to blow something up. Colloquial but neutral in register when describing violent actions.
target_language_example: Hanno fatto saltare in aria il magazzino durante la guerra.
native_language_example: They blew up the warehouse during the war.

meaning: 'skip' or 'miss' (a feminine noun) — to not attend or to jump over something.
additional_notes: Used with a feminine singular noun (la + noun). Common meanings: skip (e.g., a stop, a class) or make something 'jump'/'explode' in slang/violent contexts. Context determines whether it's neutral (saltare la fermata = miss/skip the stop; saltare la scuola = skip school) or violent (far saltare la testa = blow someone's head off). Be careful: can be used literally (make something jump) or idiomatically (skip).
target_language_example: Dovremo saltare la nostra prossima fermata.
native_language_example: We'll have to miss/skip our next stop.

meaning: mental health
additional_notes: Refers to emotional, psychological, and social well‑being. Used in medical, everyday and public-health contexts. Can appear with articles (la salute mentale) or as a general concept (per la salute mentale).
target_language_example: Dormire a sufficienza aiuta la salute mentale.
native_language_example: Getting enough sleep helps mental health.

meaning: 'health is' — used to state something about health (often followed by an adjective or clause).
additional_notes: A phrase combining salute (health) and the verb è (is). Commonly used to make general statements about health (e.g., its importance, condition). In Italian word order, è follows salute here; you will often see full sentences like "La salute è importante."
target_language_example: La salute è fondamentale per vivere bene.
native_language_example: Health is essential for living well.

meaning: health is more (important) — used to say health is more important than something else.
additional_notes: Often appears in comparisons: 'La salute è più importante di...' or with possessive: 'La tua salute è più importante.' The word 'più' means 'more' or 'most' depending on context; in these examples it implies 'more important.' You can complete the phrase with 'di' or 'del/della' + noun (di + il = del, di + la = della).
target_language_example: La salute è più importante della carriera.
native_language_example: Health is more important than a career.

meaning: to save the (masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: Combines the verb salvare (to save) with the definite article il (the) before a masculine singular noun (e.g., il pianeta). Commonly used in sentences like 'salvare il pianeta' — 'to save the planet'. Conjugate salvare according to subject (io salvo, tu salvi, lui/lei salva, noi salviamo, voi salvate, loro salvano). If the noun begins with a vowel, use 'l'' (salvare l'...); for feminine nouns use 'la' or 'l''; for plural use 'i' or 'le'.
target_language_example: Dobbiamo salvare il mare prima che sia troppo tardi.
native_language_example: We must save the sea before it's too late.

meaning: calmness under pressure; cool-headedness (literally "cold blood").
additional_notes: Used to describe someone who stays calm, composed, and unflustered in stressful, dangerous, or tense situations. Can refer to deliberate, unemotional behavior (e.g., taking decisive action) or simply remaining calm. Commonly used in expressions like "avere sangue freddo" (to have/keep a cool head).
target_language_example: Ha avuto sangue freddo e ha chiamato subito i soccorsi.
native_language_example: He kept his cool and called for help right away.

meaning: “blood on” — used to say there is blood on something (literal).
additional_notes: This is not an idiom: sangue = blood, sul = su + il (on the). Use with a noun: sangue sul pavimento (blood on the floor), sangue sul labbro (blood on the lip). In sentence 1 the phrase is figurative/colloquial meaning to put a lot of effort or intensity on stage ('leave a lot of blood on the stage'), but usually the expression is literal. Choose the article (sul/sulla/sui/sulle) to agree with the following noun.
target_language_example: C'è ancora sangue sul vetro.
native_language_example: There is still blood on the glass.

meaning: safe and sound; unharmed.
additional_notes: Used to say someone (or something) has returned or arrived without injury or harm. Commonly follows verbs like arrivare, tornare, ritornare. Formality: neutral — suitable in spoken and written Italian.
target_language_example: È tornato a casa sano e salvo.
native_language_example: He returned home safe and sound.

meaning: an exclamation like 'oh my goodness' or 'good heavens' used to express surprise, shock, or annoyance.
additional_notes: Used as an interjection. Can be mild or emphatic depending on context and intonation. Common in spoken Italian and interchangeable with expressions like 'oddio', 'per l'amor del cielo', or 'cielo santo'. Not formal; polite enough for most situations but not used in very formal writing.
target_language_example: Santo cielo, hai dimenticato le chiavi di nuovo!
native_language_example: Good heavens, you forgot your keys again!

meaning: not knowing what to do
additional_notes: A short subordinate phrase used to explain why someone did something. It literally means "knowing what to do" but with 'non' before it (often in full sentence as "Non sapendo cosa fare") it expresses lack of knowledge about what to do. Common with a main clause showing the resulting action (e.g., se ne andò, chiese aiuto). Use appropriate subject/person and tense in the main clause; the gerund phrase itself is invariant.
target_language_example: Non sapendo cosa fare, Marta chiamò un amico.
native_language_example: Not knowing what to do, Marta called a friend.

meaning: do you know about
additional_notes: Form of sapere (voi) + preposition di. Used to ask if someone knows information about a person, thing, or topic. In questions it often appears as 'sapete di + [noun]' (do you know about X), 'sapete di chi...' (do you know whose...), or 'sapete di cosa...' (do you know what/what it's about). Informal/formal register depends on context; 'sapete' addresses multiple people (you plural).
target_language_example: Sapete di quel ristorante nuovo in centro?
native_language_example: Do you know about that new restaurant downtown?

meaning: knows the
additional_notes: This is the verb sapere (subjunctive form 'sappia') followed by the definite article 'il'. Seen in sentences like 'Penso che Tom sappia il francese' = 'I think that Tom knows French.' In English you usually say 'know French' without 'the', but Italian uses 'il' with some languages and abstract nouns. 'Sappia' here is present subjunctive used after verbs expressing opinion (penso che). When addressing different subjects the verb changes (sappia = lui/lei/Lei or io in subjunctive).
target_language_example: Penso che Maria sappia il motivo.
native_language_example: I think that Maria knows the reason.

meaning: we know about / we know that (followed by information or topic)
additional_notes: Commonly used with a person, thing, or fact after 'di' (e.g. 'di lei', 'di Tom', 'di chi'). Can mean 'we know about' (knowledge concerning someone/something) or introduce what is known (often followed by a clause or noun). In spoken Italian 'sappiamo' = 'noi sappiamo' (we know).
target_language_example: Sappiamo di quel progetto da tempo.
native_language_example: We have known about that project for a long time.

meaning: we know nothing / we don't know anything
additional_notes: A negative statement using the verb sapere (to know). In spoken Italian, the particle 'niente' (nothing) often follows the verb: 'non sappiamo niente' or informally 'sappiamo niente?' in questions/expressions of ignorance. Can be used alone as a short reply: 'Non sappiamo niente.'
target_language_example: Dopo l'incidente, sappiamo niente sui testimoni?
native_language_example: After the accident, do we know anything about the witnesses?

meaning: 'you will be the' (future tense + definite article)
additional_notes: Combines the 2nd-person singular future form of essere (sarai = 'you will be') with the masculine singular definite article il. Used before a noun to say someone will become or will be a specific person/thing in the future: e.g. 'sarai il prossimo' = 'you will be the next one'. Change the article for gender/number (sarai la, sarete i, ecc.).
target_language_example: Sarai il capitano della squadra l'anno prossimo.
native_language_example: You will be the team captain next year.

meaning: 'they will be the' (future tense + definite article for a masculine plural noun)
additional_notes: Combines the future tense of essere (saranno = 'they will be') with the masculine plural definite article gli. Used before masculine plural nouns that require gli (e.g. attori, esami). Common in statements and questions about who or what will be something. Word order can vary (e.g. 'Chi saranno gli attori?' or 'Saranno gli attori?').
target_language_example: Saranno gli studenti a vincere la competizione?
native_language_example: Will they be the students to win the competition?

meaning: they will be the / there will be (with feminine plural noun).
additional_notes: A combination of the future tense verb 'saranno' (they will be) plus the feminine plural definite article 'le'. Used either to say 'they will be [something]' when referring to a feminine plural subject, or in impersonal/existential expressions with 'ci saranno le' meaning 'there will be the [events/people]' (feminine plural). English translation depends on context: 'they will be the...', 'there will be the...'.
target_language_example: Domani ci saranno le riunioni importanti.
native_language_example: Tomorrow there will be the important meetings.

meaning: would go to
additional_notes: Conditional past of andare. It is often used in reported speech after a past verb: ha detto che sarebbe andato a Venezia = 'he said he would go to Venice.' Before an infinitive, it can mean 'would go and do something': sarebbe andato a pescare = 'would go fishing.' With negation, it can mean 'wouldn't go.' The participle changes to match the subject: andata, andati, andate.
target_language_example: Mi aveva promesso che sarebbe andato a trovarla.
native_language_example: He had promised me that he would go visit her.

meaning: would be the / would be (emphatic), used to form conditional statements.
additional_notes: Combines the conditional form of 'essere' (sarebbe = 'would be') with the definite article 'la'. Appears in phrases like 'sarebbe la fine' (would be the end) or in emphatic questions ('Questa sarebbe la tua saggezza?'). Often used in hypothetical or conditional sentences. Word order and exact meaning depend on the words that follow 'la'.
target_language_example: Questa sarebbe la soluzione migliore?
native_language_example: Would this be the best solution?

sarebbe un buon nome per un

target_language_multi_word_term: sarebbe un buon nome per un
meaning: would be a good name for a (would make a good name for a ...)
additional_notes: Used to ask or say that a suggested word would be a suitable name for something (often a pet). It follows the suggested name: e.g. "Cookie sarebbe un buon nome per un cane?" Polite/neutral; can be used with different nouns (cane, gatto, bambino, personaggio). Verb mood: conditional ('sarebbe' = would be).
target_language_example: Pensi che Luna sarebbe un buon nome per un gatto?
native_language_example: Do you think Luna would be a good name for a cat?

meaning: will be at
additional_notes: Future form of essere + al (= a + il). It is used to say that someone or something will be at a place, event, or position. Before vowels, Italian uses all' instead of al.
target_language_example: Marco sarà al ristorante alle otto.
native_language_example: Marco will be at the restaurant at eight.

meaning: will really be
additional_notes: A combination of sarà ("will be") and davvero ("really"). It is used to emphasize that something will truly be a certain way. In questions, it can also express surprise or doubt, like "could it really be...?"
target_language_example: Sarà davvero difficile.
native_language_example: It will be really difficult.

meaning: 'what will become of us' / 'what will happen to us'.
additional_notes: Used in questions expressing worry or uncertainty about the future of the speaker and others. Often appears with 'che' or 'cosa' and the clitic 'ne' (che ne sarà di noi?), where 'ne' refers to the situation/thing previously mentioned. Formal and informal contexts; common in everyday speech and literature.
target_language_example: Che ne sarà di noi quando partirete?
native_language_example: What will become of us when you leave?

meaning: will be my
additional_notes: Uses the future tense of essere (sarà = "will be") with il mio ("my" / "mine"). It is used to say that something will belong to you or will be your event, role, gift, friend, etc. il mio is the masculine singular form; with other nouns the form changes, for example la mia, i miei, le mie.
target_language_example: Domani sarà il mio turno.
native_language_example: Tomorrow it will be my turn.

meaning: to be wrong to (do something); 'you/ I made a mistake by ...'.
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive after 'a' to say someone made a mistake in doing (or not doing) something. Common pattern: 'Hai sbagliato a + infinitive' = 'You were wrong to.../You shouldn't have...'. Can be used in past or present contexts about specific actions.
target_language_example: Hai sbagliato a non fidarti di lui.
native_language_example: You were wrong not to trust him.

meaning: 'have been wrong' or 'was wrong' + and (connects to next clause).
additional_notes: This is the past participle sbagliato (from sbagliare = to be wrong/make a mistake) used with a helping verb (e.g., mi sono sbagliato / ho sbagliato) followed by e meaning 'and'. Common in sentences admitting a mistake and then adding a consequence, apology, explanation, or intention to fix it. Agreement in gender/number: mi sono sbagliato (masculine speaker) / mi sono sbagliata (feminine).
target_language_example: Mi sono sbagliato e adesso voglio rimediare.
native_language_example: I was wrong, and now I want to make amends.

meaning: I was making so many mistakes / I was so wrong (in the past).
additional_notes: Past imperfect (sbagliavo) + intensity (così tanto). Used to describe a repeated or ongoing past state of being wrong or making many mistakes. Tone depends on context: can be literal (making many errors) or figurative (being very mistaken). Often follows a clause explaining what was wrong.
target_language_example: All'inizio sbagliavo così tanto che ci voleva più tempo per correggere gli errori che per scrivere il testo.
native_language_example: At first I was making so many mistakes that it took longer to correct them than to write the text.

meaning: 'chess with' (used to say you played chess with someone)
additional_notes: scacchi = chess. The preposition con means 'with' and is used to indicate the person you played chess with. Commonly appears after verbs like giocare a (giocare a scacchi = to play chess). Word order: giocare a scacchi con + [person].
target_language_example: Ho giocato a scacchi con Marta ieri sera.
native_language_example: I played chess with Marta last night.

meaning: 'climbed the' (past participle form used with avere: 'have you climbed the...')
additional_notes: Scalato is the past participle of scalare (to climb). In questions like the examples, it appears with the auxiliary avere to form the present perfect (Hai mai scalato il Monte Everest? = Have you ever climbed Mount Everest?). The article (il) must match the noun that follows (il Monte, la montagna, etc.).
target_language_example: Hai mai scalato il Colle vicino al paese?
native_language_example: Have you ever climbed the hill near the village?

meaning: This scandal will probably ruin the (something) — used to say a scandal is likely to damage someone's chances or prospects.
additional_notes: Commonly followed by 'sue/sue/nostre/vostre possibilità' (his/her/your/our chances) or other plural nouns. 'Probabilmente' = probably. 'Rovinerà' = will ruin (future of rovinare). 'Le' is the feminine plural definite article matching a plural noun like 'possibilità'. For masculine plural nouns you'd see 'i' (e.g. 'rovinerà i suoi piani').
target_language_example: Questo scandalo probabilmente rovinerà le nostre possibilità di vincere.
native_language_example: This scandal will probably ruin our chances of winning.

meaning: 'shoes for' (used to specify the purpose or activity the shoes are for)
additional_notes: Used before a noun that names the activity or purpose (passeggio, ballo, tennis, ginnastica). Literally 'shoes for ...'. Common in everyday speech to specify types of shoes (scarpe da ginnastica = sneakers/trainers, scarpe da ballo = dance shoes). Follow with the activity/noun; if the noun is an activity, often use the noun for that activity (es. tennis, ballo).
target_language_example: Ho comprato delle scarpe da corsa nuove.
native_language_example: I bought new running shoes.

meaning: literally 'shoes before (doing something)'; used in phrases telling someone to take off or clean their shoes before an action.
additional_notes: Not a fixed idiom by itself — it's the noun 'scarpe' (shoes) followed by a time/ordering phrase 'prima di' (before). Common verbs that pair with it: togliersi (to take off), lucidare/lucidarsi (to polish), indossare (to put on). Use appropriate reflexive form and imperatives when giving instructions (e.g., 'Togliti le scarpe prima di entrare' = 'Take off your shoes before entering').
target_language_example: Togliti le scarpe prima di sederti sul divano.
native_language_example: Take off your shoes before sitting on the sofa.

meaning: a box for (something) — used with a noun to indicate the box's intended contents or use (e.g. "scatola da scarpe" = "shoe box").
additional_notes: This phrase is compositional: scatola = box, da = for/of (indicating purpose or association). It's followed by the noun that specifies what the box is for (often a compound like "scatola da scarpe", "scatola da gioielli"). In these example sentences it appears in the fixed phrase "scatola da scarpe" meaning a shoebox used to store money. Use gender and number agreement for adjectives elsewhere as needed (scatola is feminine: la scatola).
target_language_example: Ho trovato una vecchia scatola da libri in soffitta.
native_language_example: I found an old box for books in the attic.

meaning: empty box
additional_notes: Literal phrase: 'scatola' = box, 'vuota' = empty (feminine). Used to describe a container that contains nothing. Can refer to a physical empty box or be used metaphorically in context (e.g., something that looks like it should contain value but doesn't). Agreement: if plural, use 'scatole vuote'.
target_language_example: Ho trovato una scatola vuota sotto il tavolo.
native_language_example: I found an empty box under the table.

meaning: this box is / the box is
additional_notes: A simple subject + verb phrase: scatola (box) + è (is). Used to describe the state or material of a box. In natural Italian you'd usually include the definite or demonstrative article ('la scatola è' or 'questa scatola è'). Here 'scatola è' shows how to combine a noun with the verb 'essere' (to be). Use adjectives or prepositional phrases after 'è' (fatta di…, piena di…, vuota).
target_language_example: Questa scatola è pesante.
native_language_example: This box is heavy.

meaning: taken in a (place) — used to say a photo was taken in a specific location (masculine/feminine form agrees with 'foto/fotografia').
additional_notes: Scattata is the past participle of scattare (to take a photo). 'In uno' means 'in a' before a masculine noun starting with certain consonant clusters (e.g., uno zoo). Use scattato if the subject is masculine (e.g., 'il film fu scattato' — though 'scattare' for photos uses feminine when referring to 'la foto/la fotografia'). Common full phrase: 'Quella foto è stata scattata in uno zoo' = 'That photo was taken in a zoo.'
target_language_example: La foto è stata scattata in uno zoo lo scorso weekend.
native_language_example: The photo was taken in a zoo last weekend.

meaning: 'the ... scene' (used to specify a scene in a film/play by naming the location or setting).
additional_notes: Common in filmmaking, theatre, or describing sequences: 'scena' = scene; 'della' = 'of the' (feminine singular). Combine with a place or setting (piscina, piazza, cucina) to say 'the ... scene' (e.g. 'la scena della cucina' = the kitchen scene). Used when referring to shooting, editing, or talking about parts of a performance.
target_language_example: Domani registriamo la scena della spiaggia.
native_language_example: Tomorrow we'll film the beach scene.

meaning: 'never jokes' or 'is never joking' (about something).
additional_notes: Literal components: scherzare = to joke, mai = never. Used to say someone does not joke (often about a specific topic). In positive sentences the negative is usually placed before the verb (Non scherza mai = He/She never jokes). Can be followed by su/ riguardo a + topic (e.g., sul suo lavoro).
target_language_example: Lui non scherza mai sul denaro.
native_language_example: He never jokes about money.

scivolare su una buccia di banana

target_language_multi_word_term: scivolare su una buccia di banana
meaning: to slip on a banana peel; figuratively, to make an embarrassing mistake or blunder
additional_notes: Literal image of slipping on a banana peel is used in Italian like in English to describe a physical slip or, more commonly, an embarrassing social or professional error. Can be used humorously. Context will tell whether it's literal or figurative.
target_language_example: Durante la riunione ho scivolare su una buccia di banana e tutti hanno riso; volevo dire qualcosa di importante e ho fatto una figura imbarazzante.
native_language_example: During the meeting I slipped on a banana peel and everyone laughed; I wanted to say something important and I made an embarrassing mistake.
