Can be followed by 'per' + infinitive or 'a' + verb to express purpose (e.g., 'si sono girati per guardare' / 'si sono girati a guardare'). Agreement: if subject is feminine/ singular/plural, past participle may agree (e.g., 'si sono girate' for a group of women).
target_language_example: Si sono girati per vedere cosa succedeva.
native_language_example: They turned (around) to see what was happening.

meaning: 'they met' (referring to a past event; reflexive/reciprocal: met each other).
additional_notes: Used with plural subjects (they). The verb is incontrarsi (to meet each other); in passato prossimo it uses essere + past participle (si sono incontrati). Indicates two or more people met one another or met up. Word order often: [Names] si sono incontrati + (a/in/alla) + place / (per la prima volta). If subject is mixed-gender or all-male, incontrati is masculine plural; for all-female use incontrate.
target_language_example: Marco e Giulia si sono incontrati al parco ieri pomeriggio.
native_language_example: Marco and Giulia met at the park yesterday afternoon.

meaning: 'I fell in love with' (female speaker).
additional_notes: This is the past perfect construction (mi sono innamorata di) used by a woman to say she fell in love with someone. Use 'innamorato' (male) or 'innamorati/innamorate' as needed for gender/number. Commonly followed by a person: 'di lui/di lei/di [name]'.
target_language_example: Mi sono innamorata di Marco l'estate scorsa.
native_language_example: I fell in love with Marco last summer.

meaning: 'I am in love with' (male speaker).
additional_notes: Used to say you are in love with someone. The form 'sono innamorato di' is for a male speaker in the singular; a female speaker would say 'sono innamorata di'. Often followed by the person or pronoun (e.g., 'di te' = 'with you'). 'Innamorato' is an adjective formed from the past participle of 'innamorare'.
target_language_example: Sono innamorato di lei, ma ho paura di dirglielo.
native_language_example: I am in love with her, but I'm afraid to tell her.

meaning: 'they broke up' (referring to a couple who have ended their relationship)
additional_notes: Literal verb: lasciare (to leave/end a relationship). 'Si sono lasciati' is the passato prossimo (present perfect) of the pronominal verb 'lasciarsi' used for couples: 'si' shows the reciprocal action (they left each other / broke up). Use with plural subject (they). To ask 'Why did they break up?' you say 'Perché si sono lasciati?'. In informal speech you may also hear 'si sono lasciati da poco' (they broke up recently) or 'si sono lasciati anni fa' (they broke up years ago).
target_language_example: Anna e Marco si sono lasciati il mese scorso.
native_language_example: Anna and Marco broke up last month.

meaning: 'I washed myself' (feminine speaker) — reflexive past tense (passato prossimo).
additional_notes: Used with the reflexive verb lavarsi in passato prossimo (mi sono lavata = I washed/washed up). Form agrees in gender and number with the subject: sono lavata (feminine singular), sono lavato (masculine singular), ci siamo lavati/e (we), etc. Often followed by an object (e.g., i capelli, le mani) or used alone to mean 'I washed up.'
target_language_example: Mi sono lavata i capelli prima di uscire.
native_language_example: I washed my hair before going out.

meaning: 'I have never been to' (said by a female speaker).
additional_notes: Very common way to say you have never visited a place. 'Sono stata' is the passato prossimo of 'essere' used with verbs of movement; 'mai' = never. Because the past participle 'stata' agrees in gender/number with the subject, a male speaker would say 'sono mai stato a'. For places use 'a' (to/in) before city names. To make it negative in full: 'Io non sono mai stata a...'.
target_language_example: Io non sono mai stata a Roma.
native_language_example: I have never been to Rome.

meaning: I have never been to
additional_notes: First-person singular, feminine form of the present perfect (passato prossimo) with essere + past participle (stata). Used to say you (female speaker) have never visited a place. For a male speaker use "sono mai stato in". You can drop the subject "io" (both forms in examples). If speaking about plural or other persons, conjugate the verb (e.g. "non siamo mai stati in...").
target_language_example: Non sono mai stata in Giappone.
native_language_example: I have never been to Japan.

meaning: 'I have never been to' (said by a male speaker).
additional_notes: Literal structure: sono (I am) + mai (never) + stato (been, past participle of essere) + a (to). Used to say you have never been to a place or attended an event. If a female speaker, use 'sono mai stata a'. In informal speech the subject 'io' is often omitted ('Non sono mai stato a...'). For plural/singular persons change verb: 'non siamo mai stati a' (we have never been to).
target_language_example: Non sono mai stato a Roma, ma vorrei andarci.
native_language_example: I have never been to Rome, but I'd like to go.

meaning: 'I am hidden' or 'I hid myself' (female speaker).
additional_notes: Reflexive past form: 'sono nascosta' uses the verb nascondersi (to hide oneself) in the passato prossimo with auxiliary essere. It can describe a current state ('I am hidden') or a completed action ('I hid myself') depending on context. The form shown is feminine singular; a male speaker would say 'sono nascosto'. Common with location phrases (in soffitta, sotto il letto, etc.).
target_language_example: Mi sono nascosta dietro la porta quando è arrivato.
native_language_example: I hid myself behind the door when he arrived.

meaning: 'I am hidden' or 'I hid myself' (first person, passive/state or reflexive perfect).
additional_notes: Literally from 'essere nascosto' or reflexive 'nascondersi'. In present tense 'sono nascosto' describes being hidden (state). In past/perfect, speakers usually say 'mi sono nascosto' (I hid myself / I have hidden myself) — note the reflexive pronoun 'mi'. Context shows locations (under table/bed, behind a tree). Use 'mi sono nascosto' to say you hid; use 'sono nascosto' to say you are (currently) hidden.
target_language_example: Mi sono nascosto dietro la porta e nessuno mi ha visto.
native_language_example: I hid behind the door and no one saw me.

meaning: 'I'm lost' (literally 'I am lost'); can be used literally (lost physically) or figuratively (confused, missed something).
additional_notes: Often used with the reflexive pronoun mi (mi sono perso) for first person. Can mean: 1) physically lost (e.g. wandered off), 2) confused or not following (e.g. in a conversation), or 3) 'What did I miss?' when used in questions (Che/Cosa mi sono perso?). Tone can be neutral; adding strong language (e.g. 'cazzo') makes it informal/colloquial. For feminine speaker: mi sono persa.
target_language_example: Mi sono perso durante la gita e ho perso il gruppo.
native_language_example: I got lost during the trip and lost the group.

meaning: they have taken / they took (used in reflexive or passive-like expressions: 'they made fun of', 'they took credit', 'they took care').
additional_notes: Sono presi is the passé composé (loro si sono presi) of prendersi. Prendersi is reflexive and changes meaning with different objects: prendersi gioco di = to make fun of; prendersi il merito = to take credit for; prendersi cura di = to take care of. English translations depend on the object following prendersi. In spoken Italian the subject pronoun (loro) is often dropped: Si sono presi ...
target_language_example: Si sono presi cura del cane mentre ero via.
native_language_example: They took care of the dog while I was away.

meaning: 'they refused to' (past tense).
additional_notes: Plural third-person past of the reflexive verb rifiutarsi di — used to say that people declined or refused to do something. Italian uses the reflexive pronoun (si) plus essere in passato prossimo: si sono rifiutati di + infinitive. For feminine plural use si sono rifiutate di. Can refer to individuals or groups.
target_language_example: Si sono rifiutati di pagare il conto.
native_language_example: They refused to pay the bill.

meaning: I'm broken / I broke (a body part) — feminine speaker (used with body parts: 'mi sono rotta il braccio' = I broke my arm).
additional_notes: Literally 'I am broken', but in these sentences it's the reflexive past (passato prossimo) used to say you broke a body part: mi sono rotta + definite article + body part. The form 'rotta' is feminine singular — a woman or girl says this. A male speaker would say 'sono rotto' and the verb agrees with the subject. For injured body parts you can also use 'mi sono rotto il/lo/la...' or say 'mi sono rotto/a un/una...' depending on whether you use the definite or indefinite article.
target_language_example: Mi sono rotta la mano giocando a pallone.
native_language_example: I broke my hand playing soccer.

meaning: I'm broken
additional_notes: Used to say you have broken something, usually a bone or tooth. Commonly appears with a reflexive verb (mi sono rotto/a) to mean 'I broke (my...)'. Change gender (rotto → rotta) to match the speaker. Followed by the body part: mi sono rotto il braccio = I broke my arm. Not used to mean 'I'm tired' or 'I have no money' (do not confuse with informal 'essere al verde' etc.).
target_language_example: Mi sono rotto la gamba giocando a calcio.
native_language_example: I broke my leg playing soccer.

meaning: I forgot to / I forgot (about) — feminine speaker (past tense).
additional_notes: Literal verb: scordare = to forget. 'Mi sono scordata di...' is a reflexive past (passato prossimo) used by a female speaker to say she forgot to do something or forgot someone/ something. For a male speaker say 'mi sono scordato di'. Common synonyms: 'ho dimenticato di...'. Use 'di' before an infinitive or before a noun/pronoun (e.g. di chiamare, di loro).
target_language_example: Mi sono scordata di chiudere la porta.
native_language_example: I forgot to close the door.

meaning: I forgot to / I have forgotten to (expressing that the speaker forgot something).
additional_notes: Common conversational way to say 'to forget' in Italian using 'scordarsi' (often reflexive). Typically used with a reflexive pronoun (mi/ti/si/ci/vi) + essere as auxiliary in compound tenses: mi sono scordato di + infinitive or di + noun. More neutral alternative: 'ho dimenticato di'.
target_language_example: Mi sono scordato di chiudere la porta.
native_language_example: I forgot to close the door.

meaning: 'I apologized' (said by a female speaker).
additional_notes: This is the first-person singular perfect (passato prossimo) of scusarsi (to apologize), used with the reflexive pronoun mi: mi sono scusata. It indicates a completed action in the past. If a male speaker, use mi sono scusato. Common variants: "Io mi sono scusata" (with subject pronoun for emphasis) or shortened "Mi sono scusata".
target_language_example: Mi sono scusata con il professore per il ritardo.
native_language_example: I apologized to the teacher for being late.

meaning: 'I have always wondered' (literally: 'I have always asked myself').
additional_notes: This is the passato prossimo reflexive construction of chiedersi (mi sono chiesto/a) used to say you have long wondered about something. With 'mi' or 'io mi' it refers to 'I'; gender agreement matters in past participle when subject is feminine (mi sono chiesta). Often followed by a subordinate clause introduced by cosa, a che ora, perché, etc. Common in spoken and written Italian.
target_language_example: Mi sono sempre chiesto cosa succedeva in quella casa.
native_language_example: I have always wondered what was happening in that house.

target_language_multi_word_term: mi sono sentito / mi sono sentita
meaning: I felt (emotion or state); I felt/considered myself (followed by adjective).
additional_notes: Reflexive passato prossimo of sentirsi (to feel). Use mi sono sentito (masculine speaker) or mi sono sentita (feminine). Describes an emotional or physical feeling in the recent past and is often followed by an adjective or past participle (e.g. 'stupido', 'solo', 'male'). Note that the auxiliary is essere, so the past participle agrees in gender and number with the subject.
target_language_example: Ero confuso e mi sono sentito stupido.
native_language_example: I was confused and I felt stupid.

meaning: 'I am married' (said by a woman) or 'I got married' depending on context.
additional_notes: Literally 'I am married' (sono = I am, sposata = married, feminine). Often used both to state current marital status ('I am married') and in perfect tense with 'mi sono sposata' to mean 'I got married' (past action). If speaker is male, masculine form is 'sono sposato'.
target_language_example: Mi sono sposata lo scorso sabato a Roma.
native_language_example: I got married last Saturday in Rome.

meaning: 'I am married' (said by a man) or literally 'I got married' depending on context.
additional_notes: Form of essere + sposato. As an adjective, 'sono sposato' = 'I am married' (state). In past-event contexts (with 'mi sono sposato' or time expressions) it uses the reflexive passato prossimo 'mi sono sposato' = 'I got married' (I married). The masculine form is 'sposato'; a woman would say 'sono sposata'. Can be used with a time phrase: 'Mi sono sposato ieri' = 'I got married yesterday.'
target_language_example: Mi sono sposato l'anno scorso.
native_language_example: I got married last year.

meaning: 'I'm tired of' / 'I've had enough of' (expressing annoyance, fatigue, or fed-up feeling with someone or something).
additional_notes: Commonly used with a noun, phrase introduced by di, or a verb in the infinitive. Often appears in the reflexive perfect form (mi sono stancato/a) to indicate personal experience; match gender (stancato for masculine, stancata for feminine). Can be informal or neutral depending on context. Frequently used to express both physical tiredness and emotional/mental exasperation.
target_language_example: Mi sono stancato di aspettare Tom, così sono andato a casa.
native_language_example: I'm tired of waiting for Tom, so I went home.

meaning: "I was bitten" (male speaker) or more generally "I have been bitten."
additional_notes: Passive past tense: sono (I am) + stato (been) + morso (bitten). Use to say you were bitten by someone/something. Change gender to morsa (sono stata morsa) for a female speaker? Note: past participle must agree in gender/number when using essere; masculine singular is morso, feminine singular mor sa -> "morsa". To specify the agent, add "da + [animal/person]" (e.g. da un cane).
target_language_example: Sono stato morso da un cane mentre correvo nel parco.
native_language_example: I was bitten by a dog while I was running in the park.

meaning: 'I was at home.' (first person singular, past)
additional_notes: Perfect tense (passato prossimo) of 'stare' or 'essere' + past participle 'stato'. Used to say you spent time at home or returned home. Can also imply a completed action (e.g., 'I was at home [and not elsewhere]'). For a female speaker use 'sono stata a casa'. In informal speech speakers may shorten to 'stato a casa' in context, but full form is standard.
target_language_example: Ieri sono stato a casa tutto il giorno.
native_language_example: Yesterday I was at home all day.

sono stato a casa tutto il

target_language_multi_word_term: sono stato a casa tutto il
meaning: 'I was at home all the...' (start of a sentence meaning you stayed home the whole [time period], e.g. day)
additional_notes: This is the beginning of a common sentence pattern: sono stato a casa tutto il + [periodo] (giorno, pomeriggio, weekend, tempo). Sono stato = 'I was' (masculine speaker or neutral in writing); feminine speakers say sono stata. Often completed as 'tutto il giorno' = 'all day'. It's past tense (passato prossimo) describing a completed action/state.
target_language_example: Sono stato a casa tutto il giorno ieri.
native_language_example: I was at home all day yesterday.

meaning: 'they took off' or 'they removed (for themselves)'.
additional_notes: Reflexive past (passato prossimo) of togliersi (to take off/remove from oneself). Used when subjects remove clothing or accessories themselves. Structure: subject + si sono tolti + noun. For mixed-gender or feminine groups the past participle agrees (si sono tolti / si sono tolte).
target_language_example: Si sono tolti gli zaini prima di entrare.
native_language_example: They took off their backpacks before going in.

meaning: ‘they have moved’ (to a new home or location).
additional_notes: Passive/reflective with si (si sono trasferiti) or with subject + sono trasferiti: refers to people relocating (moving house or moving to a different city/country). Use past participle trasferiti (masc. pl.); agree with subject (trasferita/o/i/e). Commonly appears with in/ a + place (si sono trasferiti a Roma / in Russia).
target_language_example: Si sono trasferiti in un'altra città l'anno scorso.
native_language_example: They moved to another city last year.

meaning: I moved / I have moved (residence or workplace).
additional_notes: First-person singular passato prossimo of trasferirsi (reflexive). Used to say you changed home, city, country, or workplace. Often appears with prepositions: a (to a city), in (into a country/region), da (from). For feminine speaker use sono trasferita. Can refer to recent or past moves depending on context.
target_language_example: Mi sono trasferito a Roma l'anno scorso.
native_language_example: I moved to Rome last year.

meaning: 'they are killed' (passive) or 'they killed themselves' (reflexive past) depending on context; in your examples it means 'they killed themselves' (they committed suicide).
additional_notes: Structure depends on presence of 'si'. With 'si sono uccisi' it's the passato prossimo of the reflexive verb 'uccidersi' = 'to kill oneself' → 'they killed themselves'. Without reflexive 'si' but with 'sono uccisi' it can be a passive form meaning 'they are killed' (or 'they were killed' in past contexts). Word order and pronouns matter in Italian; here 'si' makes it reflexive/reciprocal (they killed each other or themselves).
target_language_example: Dopo la tragedia, si sono uccisi senza lasciare spiegazioni.
native_language_example: After the tragedy, they killed themselves without leaving an explanation.

meaning: 'I joined the' (part of the compound reflexive perfect construction 'mi sono unito/a alla' meaning 'I joined the [feminine noun]')
additional_notes: This appears as part of the reflexive passato prossimo 'mi sono unito/a alla' from the verb 'unirsi a' (to join). Gender agreement: 'unito' for masculine speaker, 'unita' for feminine speaker. The form 'sono unito alla' without the reflexive pronoun 'mi' is unusual in isolation; typically you say 'mi sono unito/a alla [squadra/partito/gruppo]'. The following article contracts as usual (al = a + il, alla = a + la, all' before vowels, ai/agli for plurals). Informal alternatives: 'mi sono aggregato/a', 'mi sono iscritto/a' (depending on context).
target_language_example: E non mi sono unito alla PDZ per fare il poliziotto.
native_language_example: And I didn't join the PDZ to become a policeman.

meaning: 'were needed' / 'it took (time)'.
additional_notes: Used with indirect-object pronouns (mi, ti, le, ci, etc.) and a time expression to say how long something took or how much was needed. Literal structure: 'a me ci sono voluti tre giorni' = 'for me, there were needed three days' → 'it took me three days'. Use plural/masculine agreement (voluti/volute/voluto) to match the implied noun (giorni, minuti, anni). Often appears as 'ci sono voluti X' or with a person emphasized ('a me/mi ci sono voluti...').
target_language_example: Mi ci sono voluti tre mesi per imparare le basi.
native_language_example: It took me three months to learn the basics.

meaning: I am in favor (of) / I support (something).
additional_notes: Used to state support or approval for a proposal, idea, or person. Conjugate 'essere' for different subjects (sono a favore, sei a favore, è a favore, siamo a favore, siete a favore, sono a favore). Often followed by 'di' or 'della' + noun or 'della tua/vostra proposta'.
target_language_example: Sono a favore del nuovo orario di lavoro.
native_language_example: I am in favor of the new work schedule.

meaning: there are some / they are some
additional_notes: A short phrase combining the verb 'sono' (they are / there are) with 'alcuni' (some, a few). It can mean 'there are some' when referring to the existence of plural items (impersonal 'ci sono' is more common for 'there are'), or 'they are some' when describing a group ('sono alcuni miei amici' = 'they are some of my friends' but more natural: 'alcuni di loro sono miei amici'). Alone, 'sono alcuni' is uncommon; you usually need more context (e.g. nouns or clauses after 'alcuni').
target_language_example: Sono alcuni problemi che dobbiamo risolvere.
native_language_example: There are some problems that we need to solve.

meaning: 'there are other' (used with a plural noun)
additional_notes: This is the plural form of 'c'è un/una' (there is) — 'ci sono' means 'there are'. When followed by 'altre' (feminine plural) it agrees with a feminine plural noun (altre cose, altre persone, altre donne). Use 'altri' for masculine or mixed-gender plural (es. ci sono altri libri). Common in questions and statements to ask if additional items/people/options exist.
target_language_example: Ci sono altre informazioni che dovrei conoscere?
native_language_example: Are there any other pieces of information I should know?

meaning: there are other (there aren't other... when used with 'non').
additional_notes: Used with 'ci sono' (there are) to say that additional people, options, choices, solutions, etc. exist. In negative sentences ('Non ci sono altre...') it means 'there are no other...'. 'Altre' agrees in gender/number with the noun it modifies: altre (f. pl.), altri (m. pl.), altra (f. sing.), altro (m. sing.).
target_language_example: Non ci sono altre informazioni disponibili.
native_language_example: There is no other information available.

target_language_multi_word_term: sono altri / ci sono altri / ce ne sono altri
meaning: there are others / there are more
additional_notes: Used to say that additional people or things exist. Common patterns: "ci sono altri" (there are others), "ce ne sono altri" (there are others of them / more of them — includes pronoun 'ne' referring back to something mentioned), and "sono altri" can appear within sentences as part of these expressions. Use to indicate more people/items in a place or more people like someone. "Ci sono altri che..." introduces other people who do something.
target_language_example: Ci sono altri che vogliono partecipare.
native_language_example: There are others who want to participate.

meaning: I am handsome
additional_notes: Used by a male speaker to describe his appearance. In questions like "Sono bello?" it often means "Do I look good?" For a female speaker, use "sono bella."
target_language_example: Con questa giacca nuova, sono bello?
native_language_example: Do I look good in this new jacket?

meaning: 'they are flowers' or 'these are flowers' (a statement identifying something as flowers).
additional_notes: Sono is the 3rd-person plural of essere (to be). Use 'sono fiori' to identify or confirm that multiple items (or people metaphorically) are flowers. Context determines translation: can mean 'they are flowers', 'these are flowers', or emphatically 'they are flowers!' If referring to people metaphorically (e.g. 'Le donne sono fiori') it's a poetic or figurative expression. To ask 'Are these real flowers?' you would say 'Questi sono fiori veri?'.
target_language_example: Guarda: sono fiori nel vaso sul tavolo.
native_language_example: Look: they are flowers in the vase on the table.

meaning: 'what are his/her/their plans' (literally: 'are his/her/their plans')
additional_notes: Used to ask about someone's plans or intentions. The possessive 'suoi' agrees with the person being asked about and can mean his, her, or their depending on context. Formal (Chieda) and informal (Chiedi) imperatives appear in the examples; the question form often starts with 'Quali sono i suoi piani?'
target_language_example: Se non può venire, quali sono i suoi piani per domani?
native_language_example: If she can't come, what are her plans for tomorrow?

meaning: 'what are his/her/their plans for...' or 'what are your (formal) plans for...'
additional_notes: Used to ask about someone's plans for a specific time or event. 'Suoi' is formal (third person or polite 'you'); context determines whether it refers to 'his', 'her', 'their', or polite 'your'. You can replace 'suoi' with 'tuoi' for informal you (Quali sono i tuoi piani per...? ). Common time words: oggi (today), stasera (tonight), questo fine settimana/questo weekend (this weekend), Natale (Christmas).
target_language_example: Quali sono i suoi piani per domani?
native_language_example: What are his/her/your (formal) plans for tomorrow?

meaning: what are your plans / what do you plan (to do)
additional_notes: Used to ask about someone's intentions or arrangements for a specific time (this weekend, Christmas, long term). Often appears in questions with 'Quali' (Which/What) as in 'Quali sono i tuoi piani?' Can be formal or informal depending on context; common in everyday conversation.
target_language_example: Quali sono i tuoi piani per il prossimo mese?
native_language_example: What are your plans for next month?

meaning: 'what are your plans' (literally: 'are your plans')
additional_notes: Used to ask about someone's plans or intentions. 'Vostri' is the plural/formal 'your' (informal singular = 'tuoi'). Commonly appears in questions like 'Quali sono i vostri piani?' You can change the time phrase: 'per Natale', 'per lunedì', 'per questo fine settimana', etc.
target_language_example: Quali sono i vostri piani per il weekend?
native_language_example: What are your plans for the weekend?

meaning: A sequence combining the verb 'sono' (I am / they are) and the prepositional phrase 'in questo' (in this). It can appear in contexts describing someone's state or location relative to 'this' (this moment, this place, this situation). By itself the sequence is uncommon; it usually forms part of a larger sentence (e.g., 'sono in questo momento' = 'I am at this moment').
additional_notes: 'Sono' is first-person singular present of 'essere' (I am) or third-person plural (they are) depending on context. 'In questo' must be followed by a noun or noun phrase (in questo momento, in questo ospedale, in questo caso). The exact string 'sono in questo' is grammatically correct only when what follows contextualizes 'questo' or when embedded in a clause. For existential 'there are' constructions Italian uses 'ci sono' (e.g., 'ci sono in questo ospedale' / more naturally 'quante persone ci sono in questo ospedale?').
target_language_example: Mi domando chi sono in questo gruppo.
native_language_example: I wonder who I am in this group.

meaning: I'm in love with you (said by a female speaker).
additional_notes: Used to confess romantic love. 'Innamorata' is the feminine form; a male speaker would say 'sono innamorato di te'. Can be used in serious or tender contexts. Literal translation: 'I am in love of you.'
target_language_example: Devo dirtelo: sono innamorata di te.
native_language_example: I have to tell you: I'm in love with you.

meaning: 'I am' + linking 'and' (used to contrast or list people/things: 'I am... and...')
additional_notes: A combination of the verb sono (I am) + pronoun io (I) followed by e (and). Used to assert identity or introduce/contrast oneself before adding another clause or item. Often appears in simple sentences like 'Io sono io e tu sei tu' (I am me and you are you) or when pointing out oneself and another person/thing ('Questa sono io e questa è la mia gatta'). Word order can vary (Sono io e... / Io sono io e...) depending on emphasis.
target_language_example: Io sono io e questo è il mio amico.
native_language_example: I am me and this is my friend.

meaning: they/you/he/she/ I am there (depends on subject); 'are/is/am there' — indicates someone or something is located there.
additional_notes: Sono is the present tense of essere (to be). Combined with lì/ là it means 'is/are/am there' depending on the subject: io sono là (I am there), tu sei là (you are there), lui/lei è là (he/she is there), noi siamo là (we are there), voi siete là (you all are there), loro sono là (they are there). In casual speech Italians often use lì or là interchangeably; là can imply a more distant place. The phrase may appear in questions (Sono là?) or statements (Le mie radici sono là).
target_language_example: Io non ci vivo più, ma alcune foto sono là.
native_language_example: I don't live there anymore, but some photos are there.

meaning: I'm not (at all) / I certainly am not — used to deny or reject something emphatically.
additional_notes: Sono + mica is an emphatic negative: mica adds force, meaning 'not at all' or 'definitely not.' It appears after non (the negative) and before the predicate: Non sono mica... Common in spoken Italian to reject an accusation, obligation, or description. Tone can be defensive or dismissive. Mica itself cannot be used alone to negate; it strengthens a negation that includes non.
target_language_example: Non sono mica il tuo dipendente, quindi non posso farlo gratis.
native_language_example: I'm not your employee, so I can't do it for free.

meaning: there are many (feminine plural) / there are a lot
additional_notes: Literal translation: 'are many.' Used with feminine plural nouns (e.g., molte parole). Often appears with 'ci sono' or 'ce ne sono' to say 'there are' or 'there are many of them.' Change to 'sono molti' for masculine plural. Common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Nella biblioteca ci sono molte riviste interessanti.
native_language_example: There are many interesting magazines in the library.

meaning: 'there are many things that' (used to introduce a list or describe many aspects/situations)
additional_notes: Common phrase to start a sentence when you want to say many different things or reasons follow. Often followed by a subordinate clause introduced by che + verb (e.g., che non capisco, che bisogna fare). Can be used in spoken and written Italian. Word order can vary (e.g., 'ci sono molte cose che...').
target_language_example: Sono molte cose che dobbiamo ancora decidere.
native_language_example: There are many things that we still need to decide.

meaning: are many
additional_notes: Often appears in the pattern ci sono molti + plural noun to mean "there are many ..." as in Ci sono molti libri. By itself, sono molti can also mean "they are many" or "there are many," depending on context. With feminine plural nouns, molti becomes molte.
target_language_example: Ci sono molti studenti oggi.
native_language_example: There are many students today.

meaning: 'there are many buildings' (statement about quantity/place).
additional_notes: A simple descriptive phrase using the verb essere (sono) + quantity (molti) + noun (edifici). Commonly used to describe a place or skyline. If referring to a specific location, you might add a prepositional phrase: 'Sono molti edifici qui' (There are many buildings here) or use 'ci sono molti edifici' which is more natural for 'there are many buildings'. 'Molti' agrees in number with a plural noun (edifici).
target_language_example: Ci sono molti edifici nel centro della città.
native_language_example: There are many buildings in the city center.

meaning: they are in
additional_notes: A form of the verb essere (sono = they are / I am) followed by the preposition nella (in + la = in the). Use 'sono nella' when referring to plural subjects or third-person plural being located inside or part of something feminine singular (e.g. nella classe, nella città, nella famiglia). Context determines if 'sono' means 'they are' or (less commonly) the polite/formal 'you are' isn't used here — for first person singular 'I am' you would use 'sono nella' as well (sono = I am), so check subject from context. For other genders/articles adjust: 'sono nel' (in + il), 'sono nello', 'sono nelle' (in + le), 'sono nei' (in + i).
target_language_example: Tom e Mary sono nella stessa classe.
native_language_example: Tom and Mary are in the same class.

meaning: there are in your... (used to ask how many of something exist in someone's...)
additional_notes: This phrase is part of questions asking how many of something exist in someone's place/group (e.g., class, family, city). Often appears with a specific noun after 'tua' (tua classe, tua famiglia). In spoken Italian you may also hear 'ci sono nella tua...' or 'quante ne sono nella tua...'; word order can vary: 'Quante ce ne sono nella tua classe?' and 'Quante persone ci sono nella tua famiglia?' mean the same basic idea. Adjust gender/number: 'tuo'/'tua'/'tuoi'/'tue' depending on the noun.
target_language_example: Quanti libri ci sono nella tua stanza?
native_language_example: How many books are in your room?

meaning: 'they are ours' or 'they are our (plural noun)'.
additional_notes: Used after a plural subject to say that those people/animals/things belong to or are related to us (e.g., our friends, our cousins). In English you often translate it as 'they are our...' or 'they are ours' depending on context. Adjust the noun (nostri/nostre) to match gender of the plural noun (nostri for masculine or mixed, nostre for feminine).
target_language_example: Quei vicini sono nostri amici.
native_language_example: Those neighbors are our friends.

meaning: 'are there any news' or 'is there any news' / 'there are news' (used to ask or say if there are updates)
additional_notes: Usually appears with the impersonal expression 'Ci sono novità' to ask if there are updates or to report that there are updates about a situation. Can be used as a question (Ci sono novità?) or in statements (Ci sono novità sul caso...). In English speakers often say 'any news?' or 'any updates?'.
target_language_example: Ci sono novità sul volo? — No, ancora nulla.
native_language_example: Any updates on the flight? — No, nothing yet.

meaning: used to say 'I am neither... nor...' (negating two or more things).
additional_notes: Combines the verb sono (I am) with né... né... to join two negative alternatives: 'Non sono né A né B' = 'I am neither A nor B.' The first 'non' negates the verb; each 'né' links the items. You can replace sono with other verbs/pronouns (e.g. 'non siamo né... né...').
target_language_example: Non sono né timido né pigro.
native_language_example: I am neither shy nor lazy.

meaning: it's been ten (years/months/etc.).
additional_notes: Used to say that ten units of time have passed. Often followed by the time unit (anni, mesi, giorni) or understood from context. Common structure: 'Sono passati + [number] + [time unit] (da/che...)' or simply 'Sono passati dieci.' Emphasizes the elapsed time since an event.
target_language_example: Sono passati dieci anni da quando ci siamo visti l'ultima volta.
native_language_example: It's been ten years since we last saw each other.

meaning: i am the one
additional_notes: "quella" is the feminine singular form of "quello" and means "the one" or "that one." After "sono," it is used by or about a female speaker/person. It often appears with more words after it, such as "sono quella giusta" (I'm the right one) or "sono quella che..." (I'm the one who... / I am who...).
target_language_example: Sono quella con il cappotto rosso.
native_language_example: I'm the one with the red coat.

meaning: I'm here with (someone/something).
additional_notes: A simple phrase used to say you are physically present together with someone or accompanied by someone (e.g., family, a friend). 'Sono qui' = 'I am here'; 'con' = 'with'. Often followed by a pronoun or noun (te, la mia famiglia). Can express support ('I'm here for you') when said to someone directly.
target_language_example: Sono qui con te; non ti preoccupare.
native_language_example: I'm here with you; don't worry.

meaning: 'they/you (formal)/I am on' — the verb essere (to be) + preposition sulla (su + la = on the).
additional_notes: Sono is the 1st person singular (I am) or 3rd person plural (they are) of essere; context determines meaning. 'Sulla' is the contraction of su + la (on the, feminine singular). Together they appear in sentences like "I numeri sono sulla vetrata" (the numbers are on the window) where sono = they are, or "Sono sulla strada" (I am on the road) where sono = I am. Pay attention to gender/number: su + il = sul, su + lo = sullo, su + la = sulla, su + i = sui, su + gli = sugli, su + le = sulle.
target_language_example: I piatti sono sulla mensola.
native_language_example: The plates are on the shelf.

meaning: 'I am so/very' or in some contexts 'they/objects are so/very' (literal: 'are so').
additional_notes: Sono = 'I am' (or 'they/you are' depending on subject) + tanto = 'so'/'very'/'so much'. Used to intensify an adjective or past participle (e.g. sono tanto felice = I'm so happy). In sentence 1 it appears in a negative construction with 'ne ... sicuro' meaning 'I'm not so sure'. Context determines subject and negation; English translations often use 'so/very' or 'so much'.
target_language_example: Sono tanto felice di vederti.
native_language_example: I'm so happy to see you.

meaning: are too many
additional_notes: Usually said about masculine plural countable things or people. It often appears in the fuller pattern "ci sono troppi ..." = "there are too many ...". With feminine plural nouns, use "sono troppe" instead.
target_language_example: Per questa stanza sono troppi tavoli.
native_language_example: There are too many tables for this room.

meaning: they are all
additional_notes: Not an idiom. Sono is from essere ('to be'), and tutti means 'all'. Before a plural noun, it often means 'all the' or 'all those' (for example, tutti quei lividi = 'all those bruises'). Used on its own, tutti can mean 'everyone' or 'all of them'. Tutti is masculine plural; the feminine plural form is tutte.
target_language_example: Sono tutti pronti per partire.
native_language_example: They are all ready to leave.

meaning: 'I am a lot' / 'I am very' (colloquial) — used to emphasize a quality or feeling, often meaning 'I'm really' or 'I have a lot [of something]'.
additional_notes: This is informal and incomplete on its own: 'un sacco' literally means 'a sack' but idiomatically means 'a lot' or 'very'. In Italian you often see phrases like 'sono un sacco stanco' (I'm really tired) or 'ne ho un sacco' (I have a lot of them). When used with 'sono' it emphasizes the speaker's state or amount. More natural variants: 'sono stanco un sacco' is less common — typical order is 'sono un sacco [adj]'.
target_language_example: Sono un sacco felice per te.
native_language_example: I'm really happy for you.

meaning: I'm one of (the group); I belong to (them/us).
additional_notes: Used to say you are part of a group. Followed by a plural noun or pronoun (e.g. 'voi', 'loro', 'noi') or a noun phrase (e.g. 'quegli uomini'). Often used for emphasis or reassurance: 'Sono uno di voi' = 'I'm one of you.' Negation works the same: 'Non sono uno di loro' = 'I'm not one of them.'
target_language_example: Sono uno di quelli che aiutano sempre.
native_language_example: I'm one of those who always help.

meaning: 'it took' (a certain amount of time).
additional_notes: Used with time expressions to say how long something required. Often appears as "ci sono voluti" (literally "there were needed") followed by a duration and optionally an infinitive or clause. Agreement: the past participle "voluto" agrees in number/gender with the implied subject when used with essere (e.g., "sono voluti" for plural durations). Common structure: "Ci sono voluti [durata] (per/da) ..."
target_language_example: Ci sono voluti due mesi per ristrutturare la casa.
native_language_example: It took two months to renovate the house.

meaning: sister now / (your) sister right now (used to ask what someone's sister is doing at this moment).
additional_notes: This phrase combines 'sorella' (sister) with 'adesso' (now). It's used in questions about the present: e.g. 'Che cosa fa sua sorella adesso?' = 'What is his/her/your (formal) sister doing now?' Note pronouns and possessive adjectives (sua, vostra) change the subject (his/her/your plural). Word order is flexible: 'Cosa sta facendo vostra sorella adesso?' uses the present progressive.
target_language_example: Tua sorella adesso dove è?
native_language_example: Where is your sister right now?

meaning: 'it surprises (me) that' / 'I'm surprised that'.
additional_notes: Used to express surprise about someone or something; typically appears with the subjunctive verb form after 'che' (e.g., 'che tu non abbia...'). The subject (mi, ti, etc.) can change who is surprised: 'mi sorprende' = it surprises me / I'm surprised. Common in spoken and written Italian.
target_language_example: Mi sorprende che non sia venuto alla festa.
native_language_example: I'm surprised that he didn't come to the party.

meaning: sipped his/its (something) — past tense of 'sorseggiare' + article + possessive
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom but a short sequence: 'sorseggiato' is the past participle of 'sorseggiare' (to sip). 'Il suo' is a masculine singular possessive (his / its / yours formal). Together they typically appear before a noun or can stand with the noun understood from context (e.g. 'sorseggiato il suo caffè' = 'sipped his coffee'). You will see other forms depending on gender/number (la sua, i suoi, le sue) and verb tense/person (sorso, sorseggiai, sorseggiava, ha sorseggiato, etc.).
target_language_example: Ha sorseggiato il suo caffè prima di uscire.
native_language_example: He/She sipped his coffee before leaving.

meaning: a sip of; a small drink of (something).
additional_notes: Used to indicate taking or offering a small amount of a drink. Common with beverages (vino, vodka, brandy, acqua). Often used with verbs like bere, offrire, prendere; literal and compositional (sorso = sip, di = of).
target_language_example: Posso avere un sorso di acqua, per favore?
native_language_example: Can I have a sip of water, please?

meaning: under (one's) arm; tucked under the arm or carried under the arm.
additional_notes: Used to describe holding or carrying something pressed against the side of the chest under the arm (e.g., a book, package, umbrella). Can also be used for placing something under the armpit (e.g., a thermometer). Common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Ho messo la giacca sotto il braccio e sono uscito.
native_language_example: I put the jacket under my arm and went out.

meaning: under the
additional_notes: A simple preposition + definite article combination used to indicate physical position beneath a feminine singular noun (la ...). Choose 'sotto il' if the noun is masculine singular. Common in everyday descriptions of location.
target_language_example: La borsa è sotto la sedia.
native_language_example: The bag is under the chair.

meaning: 'underground' or 'below ground' (can mean physically underground or dead/buried).
additional_notes: Used literally for being beneath the surface (in a basement, tunnel, or buried). Also used idiomatically to mean 'dead' or 'buried' (e.g., threats like "ti troverò anche se sei sotto terra"). Common in everyday speech; neutral register.
target_language_example: Dopo la tempesta, molte radici sono sotto terra.
native_language_example: After the storm, many roots are underground.

meaning: 'I'll smash/beat (you) up' — a violent threat (literally 'I break/ smash the ...').
additional_notes: Colloquial and very aggressive. 'Spacco' is first-person singular of 'spaccare' (to break/smash). Often followed by a body part (faccia, testa) or object; here used as a direct threat meaning 'I'll smash your face/head' / 'I'll beat you up'. Do NOT use in polite conversation. Equivalent English tone: 'I'll smash your face in' or 'I'll beat you up.'
target_language_example: Se continui così ti spacco la faccia, smettila subito.
native_language_example: If you keep going I'll smash your face in, stop right now.

meaning: 'the sword is' — a simple subject + verb phrase (spada = sword; è = is).
additional_notes: This is not an idiom but the combination of the noun 'spada' (sword) and the verb 'è' (third-person singular of 'essere' = to be). You'll see it in sentences that describe ownership, condition, location, or qualities of a sword. Replace 'spada' with other nouns to form similar sentences (e.g. 'la porta è', 'il libro è'). In Italian the definite article (la/il) often appears before the noun: 'la spada è tua' = 'the sword is yours'.
target_language_example: La spada è antica ma ben conservata.
native_language_example: The sword is old but well preserved.

meaning: shot at / shot (the) + (masculine singular) (i.e. 'shot the...')
additional_notes: Past participle 'sparato' (from sparare = to shoot) combined with the preposition 'a' + definite article (al = a + il) marks the direct object introduced like 'shot the [masculine noun]'. Used to say someone shot something/someone. Change 'al' when the noun requires a different article (alla, allo, ai, agli, all').
target_language_example: Ieri ho sparato al bersaglio.
native_language_example: Yesterday I shot at the target.

meaning: he/she/it sent a (simple past — passato remoto) — 'spedire' = to send
additional_notes: Spedì is the third-person singular (also used for first person in some contexts?) of the passato remoto of 'spedire' (to send). It expresses a completed action in the past (often used in written/narrative Italian). 'Una' is the feminine indefinite article (a). Together 'spedì una' introduces a feminine singular object (e.g., 'una lettera', 'una cartolina'). In spoken Italian, the passato prossimo ('ha spedito') is more common for past events; passato remoto appears frequently in stories, historical accounts, or some regional uses.
target_language_example: Ieri lui spedì una cartolina dalla Sicilia.
native_language_example: Yesterday he sent a postcard from Sicily.

meaning: turn off the (plural)
additional_notes: Imperative form of spegnere (to turn off) + definite article le (feminine plural). Used to command or ask someone to turn off multiple feminine-plural items (most commonly le luci — the lights, or le candele — the candles). Can be polite with per favore / per piacere. Context determines tone (command, request, or question).
target_language_example: Spegni le luci quando esci dalla stanza.
native_language_example: Turn off the lights when you leave the room.

meaning: spends a lot (of money).
additional_notes: Commonly used with an object introduced by 'in' or a gerund to say what someone spends a lot on (e.g. 'spende molto in scarpe', 'spende molto viaggiando'). Can be used with subject pronouns or names. Literal components: 'spende' = spends, 'molto' = a lot/very much.
target_language_example: Marco spende molto per i libri.
native_language_example: Marco spends a lot on books.

meaning: I hope (that) you... / I hope you... (followed by a verb about the listener).
additional_notes: Common way to express a wish or hope directed at the listener. 'Spero' = 'I hope'; 'ti' = informal singular 'you' (object form). Usually followed by a verb in the subjunctive (e.g. 'piaccia', 'sia divertito') or indicative (especially in spoken/written informal contexts: 'piacerà'). Use 'vi' for plural 'you'.
target_language_example: Spero ti sia piaciuto il film.
native_language_example: I hope you liked the movie.

meaning: 'spent at' or 'spent on (a place/event)'.
additional_notes: Formed from the past participle 'speso' (from 'spendere' = to spend) plus the contracted preposition 'allo' (a + lo). Used to ask or state how much money was spent at a specific place or event: e.g. 'Quanto hai speso allo zoo?' = 'How much did you spend at the zoo?'. The exact form will change with subject and tense (ho speso, hai speso, ha speso, abbiamo speso, avete speso).
target_language_example: Quanti soldi hai speso allo zoo?
native_language_example: How much money did you spend at the zoo?

meaning: spent a lot (of)
additional_notes: Literal phrase combining the past participle 'speso' (from 'spendere' = to spend) with 'molti' (many/a lot). It appears before a noun (e.g., 'speso molti soldi' = 'spent a lot of money') or alone with the object understood (e.g., 'Ho speso molti' — less common; usually include the noun). Use with appropriate auxiliary verb (avere) in the passato prossimo: 'ho speso', 'ha speso', 'hanno speso'.
target_language_example: Ho speso molti soldi per il viaggio.
native_language_example: I spent a lot of money on the trip.

meaning: 'often at' or 'often to the' (used before a masculine singular place introduced by 'a').
additional_notes: spesso = 'often'. al = a + il, meaning 'to the' or 'at the' for masculine singular nouns (e.g. al supermercato, al cinema, al ristorante). Used to say you frequently go to or meet someone at a place, or to think often about something (in which case 'al' can mean 'about the' when followed by a noun like futuro or posto). Word order: adverb 'spesso' usually comes before the prepositional phrase 'al ...'.
target_language_example: Vado spesso al parco il sabato.
native_language_example: I often go to the park on Saturdays.

meaning: often about his/her (own) ...
additional_notes: Used to say someone frequently talks or complains about their own (masculine or neutral) thing (e.g., lavoro, impiego). 'Suo' agrees with the thing owned, not the speaker; context determines gender/number (suo/sua/suoi/sue). Commonly appears as 'parla spesso del suo lavoro' (he/she often talks about his/her job) or 'si lamenta spesso del suo impiego' (he/she often complains about his/her employment).
target_language_example: Luca parla spesso del suo progetto.
native_language_example: Luca often talks about his project.

meaning: often borrowed (on loan); frequently lent out or temporarily given to others
additional_notes: A phrase combining 'spesso' (often) and 'in prestito' (on loan/borrowed). Used to describe objects, books, equipment, or people (e.g., players loaned between teams) that are frequently lent or borrowed. Can refer to something that is commonly borrowed by different people or repeatedly loaned out by the owner.
target_language_example: Questa bicicletta è spesso in prestito ai miei amici.
native_language_example: This bicycle is often on loan to my friends.

meaning: often late to (a place or event).
additional_notes: Used to describe someone frequently arriving late to a specific location or appointment. 'Spesso' = often, 'in ritardo' = late, 'a' introduces the place (e.g. a scuola, al lavoro). Verb must agree in person/tense (arriva, arrivava).
target_language_example: Marco arriva spesso in ritardo al lavoro.
native_language_example: Marco is often late to work.

meaning: often the (feminine singular); 'spesso' = often, followed by the feminine definite article 'la'.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but the adverb 'spesso' (often) followed by the feminine singular article 'la' before a feminine noun (e.g., la madre, la scuola, la TV, la CNN, la granola). Common word order: adverb + article + noun. Use 'spesso il' for masculine nouns and 'spesso i/le' for plurals.
target_language_example: Spesso la studentessa arriva in ritardo.
native_language_example: The female student often arrives late.

meaning: "lo spettacolo è" = "the show is" (used to describe the state or quality of a show/world of entertainment).
additional_notes: This is the phrase 'lo spettacolo è' (or simply 'lo spettacolo' / 'lo spettacolo è...') used to introduce a comment about a performance, the entertainment industry, or an event. It can describe the show itself (e.g. good, ruined, over) or be used more broadly in expressions like "il mondo dello spettacolo è..." meaning "the show business world is...". Use with adjectives (rovinato, finito, vivace) or nouns (un fiasco).
target_language_example: Lo spettacolo è stato molto divertente ieri sera.
native_language_example: The show was very entertaining last night.

meaning: to break someone's heart; to cause deep emotional pain or sadness
additional_notes: Used when something causes strong emotional distress, disappointment, or grief. Often used in contexts of love, loss, betrayal, or sad news. Can be used literally in poetic contexts but is usually figurative. Conjugate the verb (e.g., mi ha spezzato il cuore = it broke my heart).
target_language_example: Mi ha spezzato il cuore sentirlo dire quelle parole; davvero ha saputo spezzare il cuore a tutti noi.
native_language_example: Hearing him say those words broke my heart; he truly managed to break all of our hearts.

meaning: 'I'm sorry, but...'/expressing regret before refusing or correcting someone
additional_notes: A common short phrase using mi spiace (I'm sorry). It softens a refusal, correction, or negative statement that follows (introduced by non). Often used before saying you can't do something, don't know someone/something, or that something isn't true. You can drop "mi" in informal speech ("spiace" alone is less common); standard full form is "Mi spiace, non..."
target_language_example: Mi spiace, non posso venire stasera.
native_language_example: I'm sorry, but I can't come tonight.

meaning: to (go) to the beach with (someone).
additional_notes: Spiaggia = beach. 'In spiaggia con [persona]' is used to say you went/are going/want to go to the beach with someone. In full sentences you'll usually use a verb like andare (andare in spiaggia con...), essere (sono in spiaggia con...) or other tenses. Con is the preposition 'with' and combines with object pronouns or names (con lui, con lei, con Tom).
target_language_example: Domani vado in spiaggia con Giulia.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I'm going to the beach with Giulia.

meaning: 'to explain the' (used before a masculine noun or set phrase like "perché" or other masculine nouns)
additional_notes: spiegare = to explain. il is the masculine singular definite article 'the'. Common collocations: spiegare il perché (to explain the reason), spiegare il piano (to explain the plan), spiegare il taxi (colloquial: explain about the taxi). Use spiegare + a + person when indicating who you explain something to (e.g., spiegare il piano a Fábio). Word order: you can say 'spiegare il perché' or 'spiegare il piano'.
target_language_example: Devo spiegare il problema al professore.
native_language_example: I need to explain the problem to the teacher.

meaning: explained the (feminine noun) — past participle with the definite article 'la'.
additional_notes: This is not a single fixed phrase but the combination of the past participle 'spiegato' (explained) and the feminine definite article 'la' before a feminine noun (e.g., la parola, la lezione, la questione). It appears in sentences with various subjects (ha/ho/mi ha) and means someone explained something (the feminine object). In Italian word order the object often follows the verb: "ha spiegato la lezione" = "he/she explained the lesson."
target_language_example: Il professore ha spiegato la grammatica ieri.
native_language_example: The teacher explained the grammar yesterday.

meaning: 1) spine, backbone (anatomical). 2) figuratively: backbone, courage, moral strength.
additional_notes: Literally refers to the physical spine. Commonly used both in medical contexts (trauma, injury) and figuratively to describe someone's courage or resolve (e.g., 'non avere spina dorsale' = 'to have no backbone' = to be spineless). Context tells which meaning is intended.
target_language_example: Non ha la spina dorsale per dire la verità.
native_language_example: He doesn't have the backbone to tell the truth.

meaning: married and (followed by another fact)
additional_notes: Used by a woman to say she is married (sposata) and then add more information (e = 'and'). Commonly followed by family details (e.g. ho due bambini). For a man use sposato e. Contraction/word order: 'Sono sposata e...' or 'Io sono sposata e...'.
target_language_example: Sono sposata e lavoro part-time.
native_language_example: I'm married and I work part-time.

meaning: married to a (female).
additional_notes: Used to say a man is married to a woman. The phrase agrees in gender/number with the subject and the spouse: 'sposato con una' (male married to a female), 'sposata con un' (female married to a male), 'sposati con' (they are married to…). You can add a noun after 'una' to specify who (e.g. 'una dentista', 'una collega', 'una straniera').
target_language_example: Luca è sposato con una collega dell'ufficio.
native_language_example: Luca is married to a colleague from the office.

meaning: 'married a' (masculine singular) — past participle form used with a masculine singular person
additional_notes: Sposato is the past participle of sposare (to marry). In Italian, married + a man is expressed as "sposato un [uomo/impiegato/canadese]" when describing someone who married a man. The full phrase usually appears in perfect tenses (e.g., "ha sposato un..." = "(she) married a...") or in conditional perfect (e.g., "avessi sposato un..." = "if I had married a..."). Change article/gender for other subjects: "sposata una" for feminine, and verb agreement may appear when using essere (e.g., "è sposato").
target_language_example: Ha sposato un collega lo scorso anno.
native_language_example: She married a colleague last year.

meaning: married a woman.
additional_notes: Literal past-participle structure: 'ha sposato una donna' = 'he/she married a woman' (someone married a woman). Commonly used to say whom someone married (followed by nationality, religion, adjective, or relative clause). In Italian the subject (he/she) can be omitted if clear from context. To specify who did the marrying, use the appropriate form of 'sposare' (e.g., 'ho sposato', 'hai sposato', 'ha sposato').
target_language_example: Lui ha sposato una donna spagnola l'anno scorso.
native_language_example: He married a Spanish woman last year.

meaning: married a (young) woman / got married to a girl/woman.
additional_notes: This is a past-participial phrase built from the verb sposare (to marry). In full correct Italian you would normally use the passato prossimo with an auxiliary (e.g., "Ho sposato una ragazza" = I married a girl/woman). Without the auxiliary it can appear in headlines, notes, or as a fragment. 'Ragazza' usually means 'girl' or 'young woman' (teen to young adult). Use 'donna' for an adult woman. If the subject is female, use the reflexive or passive form ("Mi sono sposata" or "Si è sposata").
target_language_example: L'anno scorso ho sposato una ragazza del mio paese.
native_language_example: Last year I married a girl from my town.

meaning: wasting his/her/one's (time or something belonging to someone).
additional_notes: Literally 'wasting the his/her'. Commonly used with 'tempo' (time): 'sprecare il suo tempo' = 'to waste one's time'. The possessive (suo) agrees with the person whose time/item is being wasted, not necessarily the subject of the sentence; context determines whether 'suo' means his, her, or your (formal). In spoken Italian, object can be omitted: 'sta sprecando il suo' or more often 'sta sprecando il suo tempo' or simply 'sta sprecando tempo'.
target_language_example: Stai sprecando il suo tempo parlando di questo.
native_language_example: You are wasting his time talking about this.

meaning: to waste (the) — used before a plural masculine noun like 'soldi' (to waste money).
additional_notes: Literal verb 'sprecare' = 'to waste'. In examples it's followed by the definite article 'i' (plural masculine) as in 'i soldi' (the money). Use with objects or resources (tempo, soldi, risorse). Common constructions: 'smettila di sprecare i...' (stop wasting the...), imperatives and past tenses shown in examples.
target_language_example: Non sprecare i tuoi soldi per cose inutili.
native_language_example: Don't waste your money on useless things.

meaning: to waste (something) — e.g. to waste the/your/my + noun.
additional_notes: Sprecare means 'to waste'. In examples 'il' is the masculine singular definite article used before a masculine noun (il denaro, il tempo). Replace 'il' with the appropriate article/pronoun for other nouns (sprecarlo = to waste it). Common collocations: sprecare il tempo, sprecare il denaro, sprecare il talento.
target_language_example: Non voglio sprecare il mio tempo.
native_language_example: I don't want to waste my time.

meaning: a waste of (used before a noun, e.g. 'a waste of time').
additional_notes: Used with a noun to say something is wasted (tempo, soldi, energie, ecc.). Common construction: 'uno spreco di [noun]'. Can express regret or criticism. 'Spreco' is masculine; use 'uno spreco di' for singular nouns and adjust article if needed (e.g. 'uno spreco di soldi' or 'una perdita' for feminine synonyms).
target_language_example: È stato uno spreco di soldi.
native_language_example: It was a waste of money.

meaning: literally 'team has'; used when saying something the team possesses, experiences, or has done (subject = la squadra).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but a combination of the noun squadra (team) and the verb avere (to have) in the third-person singular: la squadra ha. It appears in sentences like 'La squadra ha vinto' (The team has won) or 'La squadra ha bisogno di allenamento' (The team needs training). Remember that Italian often omits the subject pronoun, so 'ha vinto' can imply 'the team has won' if context is clear. Adjust the past participle or object after ha depending on tense and meaning.
target_language_example: La squadra ha vinto la partita ieri.
native_language_example: The team won the match yesterday.

meaning: literally 'is going the...' — part of the question 'How is the ... going?' used to ask how an event, situation, or activity is progressing.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed standalone phrase; it's the verb phrase 'sta andando' (is going) followed by a feminine noun with the article 'la' (the). Commonly used in questions: 'Come sta andando la [festa/guerra/ricerca]?' = 'How is the [party/war/job search] going?' Tone is neutral; can be used with formal 'sta' (Lei/eg. 'Come sta andando la sua...') or informal 'sta' for third person. In sentence 6 the same structure appears in a more vulgar/emphatic question ('Dove cazzo sta andando la sua mano?') — note the strong language 'cazzo' (vulgar).
target_language_example: Come sta andando la lezione di italiano?
native_language_example: How is the Italian class going?

meaning: is getting closer / is approaching
additional_notes: Present progressive form of avvicinarsi (si sta avvicinando) used to say something (time, event, person, weather) is drawing near. Common with time expressions (Il suo tempo), events (Natale), or physical things (un temporale). Often appears as 'si sta avvicinando' or invariable 'sta avvicinando' in spoken language when subject is implied.
target_language_example: La scadenza si sta avvicinando, dobbiamo finire il progetto.
native_language_example: The deadline is getting closer; we need to finish the project.

meaning: is behaving / is acting (right now).
additional_notes: Present continuous form of 'comportarsi' (to behave). Used to describe someone's current behaviour; often appears with a reflexive pronoun (si, mi, ti) and adverbs like così, in modo, in maniera. Useful for asking or commenting about how someone is acting.
target_language_example: Perché Marco si sta comportando così con te?
native_language_example: Why is Marco behaving like that with you?

meaning: 'is having fun' / 'is enjoying himself' (progressive present)
additional_notes: This is the present progressive (stare + gerund) of divertirsi (to have fun/to enjoy oneself). It describes someone currently enjoying themselves. With a reflexive pronoun (si) it means 'he/she/they is/are enjoying themselves' or 'you (formal) are enjoying yourself' depending on context. Commonly appears as "si sta divertendo" (is having fun). Use with adverbs like ora/ora stesso/adesso to emphasize the present moment.
target_language_example: Tom si sta divertendo adesso.
native_language_example: Tom is having fun right now.

meaning: 'is doing her/their best' or 'is doing his/her best.'
additional_notes: Used to say someone is trying as hard as they can. The gender/number is determined by context: 'suo' here is neutral in set phrase but agrees with possessor (his/her/their) in meaning; Italian often uses this impersonal construction regardless of explicit possessive. Common in present continuous (sta facendo del suo meglio = is doing his/her best).
target_language_example: Lui sta facendo del suo per risolvere il problema.
native_language_example: He is doing his best to solve the problem.

meaning: is doing the / is doing the (masculine noun) — present continuous 'is doing' + definite article 'il'.
additional_notes: This phrase combines the present continuous verb form (stare + gerund: sta facendo = 'is doing') with the masculine singular definite article 'il' before a noun (e.g., il dottore, il serpente, il bucato is actually 'il bucato' though more commonly 'fare il bucato' = 'do the laundry'). Used to describe what someone or something is doing right now. In many cases the article is required in Italian where English would omit it (e.g., 'sta facendo il bucato' = 'she is doing the laundry').
target_language_example: Che cosa sta facendo il gatto sul tavolo?
native_language_example: What is the cat doing on the table?

meaning: is moving / is starting to move (present continuous of muovere).
additional_notes: Used with a subject (often preceded by a reflexive 'si' for intransitive movement) to describe something or someone in the process of moving. In Italian progressive construction, 'stare' + gerund (sta muovendo) emphasizes an ongoing action. With 'si sta muovendo' it can mean 'it/they are moving' (e.g., traffic, a picture) or 'he/she is moving' depending on context.
target_language_example: La macchina si sta muovendo lentamente.
native_language_example: The car is moving slowly.

meaning: 'is hiding from' (present continuous: someone is currently hiding from someone/something)
additional_notes: Uses the verb nascondere (to hide) in progressive form (stare + gerund). Followed by da to indicate the agent or thing being hidden from (e.g. una persona, la polizia, la pioggia). Can be used for literal hiding and figurative (avoiding). Conjugate stare as needed: sto nascondendo da, stai nascondendo da, sta nascondendo da, etc.
target_language_example: Marco sta nascondendo da sua sorella il regalo.
native_language_example: Marco is hiding the gift from his sister.

meaning: is swimming in the (masculine singular) — present continuous with location
additional_notes: Combines the present progressive (stare + gerund: sta nuotando = 'is swimming') with the preposition + article 'nel' (in + il) used before a masculine singular noun like 'fiume' (river). Use 'nella' for feminine nouns (nella piscina), 'nello' before s+consonant/z/ps/gn (nello stagno), 'nell\'' before vowel (nell'acqua). Replace 'sta' with other forms of 'stare' for different subjects (sto, stai, stiamo, state, stanno).
target_language_example: La bambina sta nuotando nel lago.
native_language_example: The girl is swimming in the lake.

meaning: is getting ready/preparing for (something).
additional_notes: Present continuous form of preparare: 'si sta preparando per' means someone (si) is currently preparing themselves for an event or action. Commonly followed by an infinitive (per + verb) or a noun (per + il/la + noun). Equivalent to 'is getting ready to' or 'is preparing for' in English.
target_language_example: Maria si sta preparando per partire domani mattina.
native_language_example: Maria is getting ready to leave tomorrow morning.

meaning: is cooling; is getting cold.
additional_notes: Present continuous (stare + gerund) meaning something is in the process of becoming cooler. Often used with food or drinks (il cibo, il tè, il caffè). You can change the subject (sto, stai, sta, stiamo, state, stanno) to match who/what is cooling. Alternatively use 'si sta raffreddando' or simply 'si raffredda' for passive/impersonal forms.
target_language_example: Il tè si sta raffreddando, bevilo ora.
native_language_example: The tea is cooling, drink it now.

meaning: it's just / he's just / she is only (doing something)
additional_notes: Combination of the verb stare (sta = he/she/it is or you formal are) + solamente (only, just). Used to downplay or limit an action/state: e.g. 'sta solamente riposando' = 'he's just resting'. Can refer to people or things depending on context. Word order can vary: 'sta solamente' is common before a gerund or adjective; 'è solamente' is also possible with essere.
target_language_example: Non ti preoccupare, sta solamente riposando.
native_language_example: Don't worry, he's just resting.

meaning: is just
additional_notes: Used to downplay or minimize the action that follows (similar to English "is just" or "is only"). Appears before a verb (present continuous) to indicate that someone is merely doing something, often to reassure or explain. Tone can be neutral or defensive depending on context.
target_language_example: Sta solo guardando il telefono.
native_language_example: He's just looking at his phone.

meaning: 'season of' (used to introduce a specific season or period, e.g. 'stagione delle piogge' = 'rainy season').
additional_notes: This is a phrase used before a noun to name a particular season or recurring period. Common collocations: 'stagione delle piogge' (rainy season), 'stagione delle vacanze' (holiday season), 'stagione delle foglie' (autumn foliage season). Use 'la stagione delle ...' for 'the ... season'. Verb forms: 'inizia/è iniziata' or 'comincia/è cominciata' to talk about the season starting.
target_language_example: La stagione delle vacanze inizia a dicembre.
native_language_example: The holiday season starts in December.

meaning: 'you stay at' / 'you are at' (informal, second person singular)
additional_notes: Combination of the verb stare (stai = you stay/are) + the preposition al (a + il = at/to the). Used informally to indicate someone's location, position, or to tell someone to stay in their place/role. Context changes meaning: location (stai al quinto piano = you're on the fifth floor), request/order (stai al tuo posto = stay in your place), or habitual presence (stai al fast food = you're at/working at the fast food place).
target_language_example: Perché stai al tavolo invece di venire con noi?
native_language_example: Why are you staying at the table instead of coming with us?

meaning: 'tired to (do something)'.
additional_notes: Used with an adjective (stanca = tired, feminine) + 'per' + an infinitive to say someone is too tired to do a specific action. Change gender/number as needed (stanco per, stanchi per, stanche per). Common structure: [subject] + essere (conjugated) + troppo/abbastanza + stanco/a/i/e + per + [infinitive].
target_language_example: Sono troppo stanca per uscire stasera.
native_language_example: I'm too tired to go out tonight.

meaning: tired of; fed up with
additional_notes: Used to say you're tired, bored, or fed up with something. 'Stanco' agrees in gender/number with the speaker (use 'stanca' for a female speaker). 'Dei' is the contraction of 'di' + 'i' and introduces a plural masculine noun. For actions, use 'stanco di' + infinitive (e.g., 'Sono stanco di aspettare'). Context and register: neutral to informal.
target_language_example: Sono stanco dei compiti.
native_language_example: I'm tired of the homework.

meaning: 'tired and' — used to link 'tired' with another adjective, noun or verb phrase to indicate two simultaneous states or actions.
additional_notes: Stanco means 'tired'. When followed by e ('and') it connects stanco to another descriptor (e.g., stanco e affamato = tired and hungry; stanco e avevo freddo = tired and I was cold). Common in both spoken and written Italian. Word order is typically 'stanco e + adjective/phrase'. Remember agreement: stanco becomes stanchi/stanca/stanche to match subject gender/number (e.g., sono stanca e felice).
target_language_example: Io ero stanco e avevo freddo.
native_language_example: I was tired and cold.

meaning: 'how are' (for plural subjects) — used to ask or say how people/animals/things are or how something fits/looks (with clothing/body parts).
additional_notes: Stanno is the 3rd-person plural present of stare. Used with plural nouns (i miei ragazzi, i cani, i nostri vecchi). In questions like "Come mi stanno i capelli?" it asks how something looks/fits on the speaker (literally: How do my hair/clothes look on me?). With people/animals it means 'How are they?'. The article (i) shows the noun is plural. For singular use 'sta il/la'.
target_language_example: Stanno i bambini bene dopo la gita?
native_language_example: Are the children okay after the trip?

meaning: 'they are in' or 'they stay in' (third-person plural of stare + preposition in).
additional_notes: Stanno is the third-person plural present of stare (to be/stay). Combined with the preposition in it indicates location or state (e.g., 'stanno in prigione' = 'they are in prison', 'stanno in silenzio' = 'they remain silent'). Use with a place, condition, or phrase introduced by in. For other persons/forms use sto, stai, sta, stiamo, state, stanno accordingly.
target_language_example: Stanno in giardino a parlare.
native_language_example: They are in the garden talking.

meaning: a (bed)room with his/her (someone's) — used to say someone shares a room with another person.
additional_notes: This phrase combines stanza (room) + con (with) + sua (his/her; feminine possessor). In context, 'sua sorella' means 'his sister' or 'her sister' depending on the subject. Italian uses possessive adjectives that agree in gender/number with the possessed noun (la sua stanza) and not always with the possessor. For beginners: focus on 'condividere una stanza con [persona]' = 'to share a room with [person]'.
target_language_example: Marco condivide la stanza con sua sorella.
native_language_example: Marco shares the room with his sister.

meaning: the room of the (plural masculine) — part of the phrase 'stanza degli ospiti' meaning 'guest room'.
additional_notes: Stanza = room. 'degli' is the contraction of 'di' + 'gli', used before masculine plural nouns beginning with a vowel or certain consonant clusters (e.g., 'ospiti'). Alone 'stanza degli' is incomplete — it needs the following noun (e.g., 'ospiti'). Common full phrase: 'stanza degli ospiti' = guest room. Use 'della' for feminine singular, 'dei' for masculine plural before consonants, and 'del' for masculine singular.
target_language_example: Dormiamo nella stanza degli ospiti durante il viaggio.
native_language_example: We sleep in the guest room during the trip.

meaning: a room intended or used for (something/someone) — 'room for' or 'room to'.
additional_notes: Used to indicate the purpose of a room or who it is for. Followed by a noun (person, activity, or thing) introduced directly or with an article: 'stanza per il visitatore' (room for the visitor), 'stanza per studiare' (room to study). Not an idiom; literal and compositional.
target_language_example: Abbiamo una stanza per gli ospiti al piano di sopra.
native_language_example: We have a room for guests upstairs.

meaning: 'the room is' or 'a room is' (literal combination of noun + verb 'essere')
additional_notes: This is simply the noun 'stanza' (room) followed by the verb 'è' (is). Usage depends on the article: 'la stanza è...' = 'the room is...', 'una stanza è...' = 'a room is...'. Common in statements about location (In quale stanza è entrato Tom? = In which room did Tom enter?) or about use/condition (Questa stanza è usata come cucina = This room is used as a kitchen). The verb 'è' can be replaced by passive constructions (è stata preparata) for 'has been'/'was'.
target_language_example: La stanza è pronta per gli ospiti.
native_language_example: The room is ready for the guests.

meaning: to stay in
additional_notes: Used to indicate staying or remaining at a place (city, building, etc.). Often followed by a location (stare a Boston) or by an infinitive/gerund in idiomatic expressions (stare a + verb) to mean 'be doing' or 'be in the habit of' in some contexts. In negative imperative (non stare a + infinitive) it can mean 'don't bother (doing something)' or 'don't go on (doing)'. Common in spoken Italian.
target_language_example: Voglio stare a Roma per una settimana.
native_language_example: I want to stay in Rome for a week.

meaning: to wait and see; to watch what happens (before deciding).
additional_notes: Used to express a wait-and-see attitude — not taking action immediately and observing how a situation develops. Often followed by a clause introduced by "che" or used alone: "stare a vedere cosa succede" or "staremo a vedere" (we'll see). Common in spoken and written Italian.
target_language_example: Dobbiamo solo stare a vedere cosa succede dopo la riunione.
native_language_example: We just have to wait and see what happens after the meeting.

meaning: to keep up with, to follow closely, to stay on top of (someone/something).
additional_notes: Commonly used both literally (to follow or stay behind someone) and figuratively (to keep track of tasks, work, or developments). Often appears with a direct object introduced by a noun or pronoun: stare dietro a qualcosa/qualcuno. Example senses: "Non riesco a stare dietro al lavoro" = I can't keep up with the work; "Stai dietro a lui" = stay behind/follow him. If used with a person it can mean to watch or look after them.
target_language_example: Non riesco a stare dietro a tutte le email.
native_language_example: I can't keep up with all the emails.

meaning: to stand; to be standing
additional_notes: Used for the physical posture 'to stand' (opposite of sitting or lying). Also used figuratively for 'to keep something standing/upright' or 'to make (something) stand' (e.g., far standing a tower). Common in everyday speech: stare in piedi in autobus, non riesce a stare in piedi (can't stand up).
target_language_example: Non posso stare in piedi a lungo.
native_language_example: I can't stand for long.

meaning: to be together; to spend time together (often used for couples or friends).
additional_notes: Commonly used for people being together physically or in a relationship. Can mean 'to be a couple' (we are/should be together) or simply 'to spend time together' for friends or family. Conjugate 'stare' normally (e.g., 'stiamo insieme', 'stava insieme').
target_language_example: Ci piace stare insieme il sabato pomeriggio.
native_language_example: We like to be together on Saturday afternoons.

meaning: to be about to
additional_notes: Usually used as stare per + infinitive to express that something is going to happen very soon. In normal sentences, stare is typically conjugated (for example: sto per uscire = I'm about to go out), but the dictionary form is stare per.
target_language_example: L'espressione stare per + infinito si usa per parlare di un'azione imminente.
native_language_example: The expression stare per + infinitive is used to talk about an imminent action.

meaning: be quiet
