additional_notes: Used to describe or judge someone's behavior. 'Suo' agrees with the possessor (his/her/its) and is formal/neutral; context tells gender. Commonly followed by adjectives (contrario, intollerabile) or clauses. Can be used in written and spoken Italian.
target_language_example: Il suo comportamento è inaccettabile in questo contesto.
native_language_example: His/her behavior is unacceptable in this context.

meaning: his/her/its concert; that concert of his/hers/its.
additional_notes: Suo is a possessive adjective (his/her/its/your formal/their) that agrees in gender and number with the thing possessed. Concerto means 'concert' (a musical performance). In Italian the possessive is usually used with the definite article (e.g., il suo concerto), but in some fixed phrases or titles the article may be omitted. Context determines whether 'suo' refers to he, she, you (formal) or they.
target_language_example: Il suo concerto è stato un grande successo.
native_language_example: His/her concert was a great success.

meaning: his/her/its yard; his/her/its courtyard.
additional_notes: suo is a possessive adjective meaning 'his', 'her', or 'its' (context decides the gender of the owner). cortile means 'yard' or 'courtyard' (outdoor area adjacent to a house). In Italian, suo agrees in gender/number with the owner, not with the noun; cortile is masculine singular so 'suo cortile' is used regardless of the owner's gender. To clarify whose yard in speech or writing, you can add a name or use 'di lui'/'di lei' for emphasis (e.g., il cortile di Tom / il suo cortile).
target_language_example: Maria ha portato i bambini a giocare nel suo cortile.
native_language_example: Maria took the children to play in her yard.

meaning: his/her/their doctor (formal/polite reference).
additional_notes: Suo is the formal or polite third-person possessive (also used in written/literary contexts); the gender/number of the possessed noun determines agreement (il suo dottore — masculine singular). In spoken Italian, context or verb forms usually show whether 'suo' means 'his', 'her', or 'your (formal)'. Use 'il suo dottore' for 'his/her/your (formal) doctor'.
target_language_example: Devo parlare con il suo dottore domani.
native_language_example: I need to speak with his/her/your (formal) doctor tomorrow.

meaning: 'in his/her favor' or 'to his/her advantage'
additional_notes: Used to say that something benefits someone or counts as an advantage for them. 'Suo' agrees with the person (his/her/its). Common in expressions like 'avere un punto a suo favore' (to have a point in one's favor) or 'le probabilità sono a suo favore' (the odds are in his/her favor). Formal/neutral tone.
target_language_example: Le decisioni recenti sono a suo favore.
native_language_example: The recent decisions are in his/her favor.

meaning: his/her engagement (to be married).
additional_notes: Refers to the state of being engaged or to the event/announcement of an engagement. 'Suo' agrees with the person possessing the engagement (his/her/your formal) and can refer to either gender depending on context. Commonly used with verbs like 'annunciare' (to announce) or expressions like 'fare/i congratulare con' (to congratulate).
target_language_example: Hanno festeggiato il suo fidanzamento con una piccola cena.
native_language_example: They celebrated his/her engagement with a small dinner.

meaning: 'his/her son was a ...' (start of a sentence describing someone's son)
additional_notes: This is a fragment: suo = his/her (formal or neutral possessive), figlio = son, era = was (imperfect of essere), un = a/an (masculine). Use to introduce a description, profession, age (with number), or characteristic of someone's son. Adjust suo to agree with context (sua figlia for daughter). If you want "their son" in modern Italian, use il loro figlio. For age, Italian normally uses avere (aveva) not essere: e.g. "suo figlio aveva dieci anni."
target_language_example: Suo figlio era un bravo studente.
native_language_example: His/Her son was a good student.

meaning: literally 'to his/her son a...'; part of a sentence pattern used to say someone gave/told/built something to his/her son (indirect object + direct object).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase—it's the sequence of words that appears when you have an indirect object ('a suo figlio' = to his/her son) followed by a feminine singular direct object introduced by 'una' (a/one). In natural English you'd reorder: 'He told his son a story' / 'He built his son a new house' (more commonly 'He built a new house for his son'). The possessive 'suo' agrees with the owner (his/her) and refers back to the subject of the sentence. 'Una' marks a feminine singular noun (una storia, una casa, una macchina, una fortuna).
target_language_example: Ha dato a suo figlio una bicicletta per il compleanno.
native_language_example: He gave his son a bicycle for his birthday.

meaning: his/her/their textbook
additional_notes: Suo agrees with the owner (his/her/its/their) and libro di testo means 'textbook' (book used for study). In Italian, possessive adjectives (mio, tuo, suo, nostro, vostro, loro) must match the possessor; when referring to a single item like libro di testo, no definite article is required after the possessive in colloquial speech (Mi ha prestato il suo libro di testo). Context determines whether suo means 'his', 'her' or 'their'.
target_language_example: L'insegnante ha chiesto a Marco di portare il suo libro di testo domani.
native_language_example: The teacher asked Marco to bring his textbook tomorrow.

meaning: in its/his/her own way; in a particular manner
additional_notes: Used to say that someone or something does something in a characteristic or individual way. Agrees with the possessor (suo can mean his, her, its, or your formal) and modo is singular masculine. Common in expressions like "a modo suo" (in its/his/her own way).
target_language_example: Lui si esprime a suo modo, ma è interessante ascoltarlo.
native_language_example: He expresses himself in his own way, but he's interesting to listen to.

meaning: 'his/her/its name was' (simple statement of someone's name)
additional_notes: Used to state a person's (or animal/thing's) name in the past or when introducing someone in a narrative. 'Suo' agrees with the possessor (his/her/its) and can be ambiguous without context; gender/number of the named person is not marked here. In spoken/written Italian, you might also hear 'si chiamava' (he/she was called) as a natural alternative.
target_language_example: Il suo nome era Marco, ma tutti lo chiamavano Marc.
native_language_example: His name was Marco, but everyone called him Marc.

meaning: his/her/its new (m.), used before a masculine singular noun to say someone’s new [thing].
additional_notes: Suo is the formal or third-person possessive (his/her/its/your formal). 'Nuovo' agrees in gender and number with the noun it modifies (here masculine singular). In spoken Italian, meaning (his vs. her vs. your formal) is clear from context. For a feminine noun use 'sua nuova' (e.g., la sua nuova casa).
target_language_example: Che ne pensi del suo nuovo lavoro?
native_language_example: What do you think of his/her new job?

meaning: his/her first kiss
additional_notes: Literally 'his/her first kiss'. The possessive 'suo' agrees with the possessor (third person) and not the object; context determines whether it refers to 'his' or 'her'. Commonly used to talk about someone's first romantic kiss or to ask if they remember it.
target_language_example: Ricorda il suo primo bacio?
native_language_example: Do you remember his/her first kiss?

meaning: 'at your service' or 'in his/her/its service' (depends on context).
additional_notes: Common polite formula: "Al suo servizio" = "At your service" (used to offer help or show readiness to serve). Can also mean "at someone's service" in a literal or figurative sense (e.g. an enemy has spies 'at its service' = working for it). Possessive agrees by context: suo can refer to 'your' (formal), 'his', 'her', or 'its' depending on speaker and situation.
target_language_example: Al suo servizio, signore — come posso aiutarla?
native_language_example: At your service, sir — how can I help you?

meaning: his/her/your (formal)/its student — possessive + noun (singular masculine).
additional_notes: Suo is the formal/third-person singular possessive adjective meaning 'his', 'her', 'its', or 'your' (formal). It agrees in gender and number with the noun it modifies. 'Studente' is masculine singular; if referring to a female student use 'sua studentessa'. Context determines whether 'suo' means 'his', 'her', 'its' or the formal 'your' (Lei). To specify gender of the owner, Italian often repeats a subject (e.g., 'la sua professoressa' vs 'la sua madre') or relies on context.
target_language_example: La professoressa ha parlato del suo studente brillante.
native_language_example: The teacher talked about her/his/your (formal) brilliant student.

meaning: his/her/one's time spent studying; (to) spend one's time studying.
additional_notes: This phrase combines "suo tempo" (his/her/one's time) with the verb phrase "a studiare" (to study). It's used to say someone spends or wastes their time studying. In sentences you will often see verbs like "passare" or "trascorrere" (to spend) or "sprecare" (to waste) before it. Gender/number of "suo" agrees with the possessor (suo = his/her/its).
target_language_example: Luca passa tutto il suo tempo a studiare per gli esami.
native_language_example: Luca spends all his time studying for the exams.

meaning: his/her uncle at (the)... — literally 'his/her uncle at'.
additional_notes: This is a short sequence combining a possessive noun (suo zio = his/her uncle) plus the preposition 'al' (a + il) meaning 'at the' or 'to the'. Use 'suo' to mean 'his', 'her', or formal 'your' (Lei) depending on context; gender/number of the possessor can be clarified by context or by using 'di lui/di lei' for clarity. 'Al' contracts 'a' + 'il' and must agree with the definite article (e.g., 'alla' for feminine: 'sua zia alla').
target_language_example: Lei ha incontrato suo zio al mercato.
native_language_example: She met her uncle at the market.

meaning: his/her/their classmates/teammates/companions (used before a noun like 'classe' or 'squadra').
additional_notes: Literally 'his/her/their companions of'. 'Suoi' agrees in gender/number with the possessed plural noun (i suoi, le sue, etc.). Commonly followed by a group noun: 'compagni di classe' (classmates), 'compagni di squadra' (teammates). Context determines the English possessive (his/her/their).
target_language_example: Ha parlato con i suoi compagni di classe dopo la lezione.
native_language_example: He/She talked with his/her classmates after class.

meaning: 'his/her French homework' or 'their French homework' (depending on context).
additional_notes: Literal phrase: suoi = his/her/their (possessive plural agreement with compiti), compiti = homework/assignments, di francese = of French (subject/lesson). Use 'suoi' to match the person being talked about (third person). In English you would usually specify gender/number as 'his' or 'her' or 'their' depending on who 'suo' refers to from context.
target_language_example: Marco ha finito i suoi compiti di francese prima di cena.
native_language_example: Marco finished his French homework before dinner.

meaning: 'his/her/their children' + preposition 'to/at/in' (depends on context).
additional_notes: This phrase combines the possessive 'suoi figli' (his/her/their children) with a following preposition 'a'. The preposition 'a' can mean different things depending on the verb: 'a' + place = 'in/at' (e.g., a Boston, a casa), 'a' + motion = 'to' (e.g., a scuola), and 'a' + infinitive = marks what someone is taught or encouraged to do (e.g., insegnare a giocare). Adjust the English preposition or construction to match the verb.
target_language_example: Ho portato i suoi figli a casa dopo la festa.
native_language_example: I took his/her children home after the party.

meaning: his/her parents were
additional_notes: A phrase using the possessive 'suoi' (his/her — agrees with the possessed plural noun) + 'genitori' (parents) + the imperfect past tense 'erano' (they were). Common for describing states, characteristics, locations, or feelings in the past. Context decides whether 'suoi' refers to 'his' or 'her'.
target_language_example: I suoi genitori erano molto orgogliosi di lui.
native_language_example: His/her parents were very proud of him.

meaning: his/her parents are
additional_notes: Used to talk about someone else's parents (third person). 'Suoi' agrees with the noun 'genitori' (plural) and means 'his' or 'her' depending on context. Word order: subject (i suoi genitori) + verb (sono). Commonly followed by adjectives (divorziati, orgogliosi), states (vivi), origin (della Spagna), or questions.
target_language_example: I suoi genitori sono molto gentili.
native_language_example: His/Her parents are very kind.

meaning: 'his/her/their eyes were' — describes the state or appearance of someone's eyes.
additional_notes: Used to describe how someone's eyes looked or what they expressed (color, emotion, condition). 'Suo/i' agrees in gender/number with the possessor: 'i suoi occhi' = 'his/her/their eyes' (plural). Verb 'erano' is the imperfect of 'essere' (to be) and describes past states or ongoing conditions. For a single eye use 'il suo occhio era'.
target_language_example: I suoi occhi erano pieni di sorpresa.
native_language_example: His/her eyes were full of surprise.

meaning: his/her money; his/her own money (depending on subject).
additional_notes: Literally 'his/her money'. 'Suoi' agrees with the possessor (third-person singular) and the gender/number of the thing possessed: here 'soldi' is plural masculine so 'suoi'. Context determines whether it refers to 'his' or 'her' (eg. 'Egli', 'Lui' → his; 'Mary' → her). Commonly used to talk about how someone handles or spends their own money.
target_language_example: Lei è avara con i suoi soldi.
native_language_example: She is stingy with her money.

meaning: to play (a musical instrument) well
additional_notes: Used with instruments (suonare il pianoforte, la chitarra, il violino, la batteria, ecc.). Suonare means 'to play' (an instrument); bene = 'well'. Commonly appears with verbs like sapere (to know how) or dire (to say).
target_language_example: Sai suonare bene la chitarra?
native_language_example: Can you play the guitar well?

meaning: rang the
additional_notes: Literal past participle phrase: suonato is the past participle of suonare (to ring, to play, to sound). With avere (ho suonato) it forms the passato prossimo: "I rang/played". The direct object follows (il + noun). Use "rang the" for bell/campanello and "played the" for musical instruments (il flauto).
target_language_example: Ho suonato il tamburo ieri sera.
native_language_example: I played the drum last night.

meaning: to (attend) high school in/at; literally 'high school at'.
additional_notes: Used after verbs like andare/essere to say where someone attended high school. 'Le superiori' = secondary school / high school. The preposition 'a' introduces the place (city, school). Can also be used with age: 'lasciare le superiori a diciassette anni' = 'leave high school at seventeen'.
target_language_example: Sono andato alle superiori a Milano.
native_language_example: I went to high school in Milan.

meaning: 'sushi and' (used to join 'sushi' with another item, e.g. a drink)
additional_notes: This is simply the noun sushi followed by the conjunction e (and). In the example sentences it's used with a past tense verb: 'mangiato sushi e bevuto birra' = 'ate sushi and drank beer.' Note that word order and verb forms follow Italian (two past participles after avere: abbiamo mangiato ... bevuto ...). Useful for listing foods or items.
target_language_example: Ieri ho comprato sushi e bevuto del té freddo.
native_language_example: Yesterday I bought sushi and drank iced tea.

meaning: 'to wake the child' (cause the child to stop sleeping).
additional_notes: Used when warning or advising someone not to make noise or do something that will wake a sleeping child. Commonly appears with negative constructions (non svegliare il bambino) and with different polite forms (State attenti/State attente, Stia attento/attenta).
target_language_example: Per favore, non correre nel corridoio: potresti svegliare il bambino.
native_language_example: Please don't run in the hallway: you might wake the child.

meaning: intended to convey 'fully awake' or 'awake the whole (time/night)' (as written, nonstandard form)
additional_notes: Nonstandard or ungrammatical as written. Standard Italian would be 'sveglia tutta' (rare) or more commonly 'svegliata tutta la notte' / 'sveglia tutta la notte' to mean a (female) person was awake all night, or 'completamente sveglia' for 'fully awake'. 'Sveglio'/'sveglia' means 'awake' and must agree in gender with the person; 'tutta' means 'all'/'whole' and must agree with the noun it modifies. Context required — likely an attempt to say a (female) subject was awake the whole time or completely awake.
target_language_example: Sono rimasta sveglio tutta la notte e adesso sono esausta.
native_language_example: I stayed awake all night and now I'm exhausted.

meaning: used to emphasize or strengthen a statement (roughly 'now that's' / 'that really is').
additional_notes: Placed before a clause to highlight or praise something just mentioned. Often translated as 'now that's...', 'that really is...', or 'that's what I call...'. It adds strong affirmation or approval and is not the same as 'sì, che' (yes, that).
target_language_example: Con quella giacca sì che stai elegante!
native_language_example: With that jacket now that's elegant!

meaning: used in the expression 'un giorno sì e un giorno no' meaning 'every other day' or 'one day yes, one day no'.
additional_notes: You won't usually use 'sì e' alone — it's part of the fixed pattern 'un giorno sì e un giorno no' (or 'un giorno sì e uno no') to say something happens every other day. Literal meaning is 'a day yes and a day no'. Commonly used with time words (giorno, settimana, volta).
target_language_example: Vado in palestra un giorno sì e un giorno no.
native_language_example: I go to the gym every other day.

meaning: cut (oneself) with (a knife or sharp object).
additional_notes: Used with a reflexive subject (si/mi/ti) to say someone cut themselves. Followed by 'con' + instrument (un coltello, la lama, ecc.). Tense in examples is passato prossimo (si è tagliato). For gender/number agreement: past participle may agree when used without reflexive or with direct object — with reflexive 'si è tagliato' is standard for masculine singular; a woman would say 'si è tagliata'.
target_language_example: Mi sono tagliato con il coltello mentre preparavo la cena.
native_language_example: I cut myself with the knife while preparing dinner.

meaning: cut the
additional_notes: Past participle construction of tagliare (to cut). 'Tagliato il' appears in perfect or compound contexts: e.g. questions (Avete tagliato il pane? — Have you cut the bread?), statements about having cut something (Ho tagliato il filo — I cut the wire), or in passive/agentive descriptions (Mi ha tagliato il collo — he/she cut my neck). The object follows the phrase (il + noun). Depending on context, it can describe a harmless action (cutting food) or a violent act. Use appropriate past tense (ho/avete/mi ha etc.) before tagliato.
target_language_example: Ho tagliato il prosciutto per il pranzo.
native_language_example: I cut the ham for lunch.

meaning: haircut
additional_notes: Common phrase to talk about someone's hairstyle or haircut. Literally 'cut of hairs'. Used for asking opinions, describing a new style, or asking which style someone prefers.
target_language_example: Mi piace il tuo nuovo taglio di capelli.
native_language_example: I like your new haircut.

meaning: cut (it/her/him) with his/her (own) ... — past tense (he/she/it) + 'with his/her ...'.
additional_notes: This is the passato remoto (simple past) third-person singular of 'tagliare' (to cut) followed by 'con il suo' (with his/her/its). In context the direct object pronoun (lo, la) appears before the verb (e.g. 'lo tagliò' = 'he/she cut it/him'). 'Suo' agrees with the possessor, not the object: 'il suo coltello' = his/her knife. Use passato prossimo (ha tagliato) more often in spoken Italian; passato remoto is common in written/narrative contexts.
target_language_example: Maria lo tagliò con il suo coltello.
native_language_example: Maria cut it with her knife.

meaning: so much (in) cooking / so much fun cooking
additional_notes: Used after verbs like divertirsi to say you had a lot of fun doing the activity 'cucinare' (to cook). Literally 'so much at cooking' but in English you'd say 'had so much fun cooking' or 'enjoyed cooking so much'. Commonly appears as 'così tanto a cucinare' or 'tanto a cucinare' depending on sentence; 'ci siamo divertiti così tanto a cucinare' = 'we had so much fun cooking'.
target_language_example: Ci siamo divertiti tanto a cucinare ieri sera.
native_language_example: We had so much fun cooking last night.

meaning: so much that I / so ... that it causes me to ...
additional_notes: Used to link an action or degree (tanto / così tanto) with a resulting effect on the speaker (mi + verb). Common patterns: 'così tanto che mi...' or 'tanto che mi...' followed by reflexive or impersonal verbs (dimentico, scordo, sento, fa). Literal sense: 'so much that (it) makes me...'.
target_language_example: Ho parlato così tanto che mi è venuta la voce roca.
native_language_example: I talked so much that my voice became hoarse.

meaning: 'so much' (used before a plural noun with the definite article 'i')
additional_notes: Combine tanto (so much/so many) with the definite article i when referring to plural masculine nouns (e.g. i genitori, i cani). Often appears as "così tanto i" or simply "tanto i". Context determines if it expresses strong feeling (Mi mancano così tanto i miei genitori = I miss my parents so much) or a dismissive comment (Tanto i morti non parlano = After all, the dead don't speak). Note: Italian normally places tanto before the noun phrase (tanto i cani). In some spoken/colloquial uses you may see "di tanto in tanto" meaning "from time to time" (different expression).
target_language_example: Odio tanto i ragni.
native_language_example: I hate spiders so much.

target_language_multi_word_term: tanto in / di tanto in tanto
meaning: 'from time to time' / 'now and then'; and "tanto in" alone can appear in expressions like "tanto in collera" meaning "so/very" (context-dependent).
additional_notes: Most example sentences use the fixed expression "di tanto in tanto" meaning "from time to time" or "every so often". Use it to say something happens occasionally: "di tanto in tanto" = "occasionally". Separately, "tanto in" can appear in other combinations (e.g. "tanto in collera") where "tanto" means "so/very" and is not part of the idiom. Pay attention to spacing: the idiom requires the preposition "di" before it: "di tanto in tanto."
target_language_example: Vado al cinema di tanto in tanto.
native_language_example: I go to the cinema from time to time.

meaning: even better / all the better; good news or approval — 'so much the better'.
additional_notes: Used to express that a situation is preferable or that a proposed outcome is welcome. Can be used alone as an exclamation (Beh, tanto meglio!) or as part of a sentence (se... tanto meglio). Tone can be neutral or positive/approving. Often translates as 'so much the better' or 'even better'.
target_language_example: Se trovi un posto vicino, tanto meglio.
native_language_example: If you find a spot nearby, all the better.

meaning: even less / much less / let alone
additional_notes: Used to downplay or exclude something, similar to English 'let alone' or 'much less'. Often follows a negative idea (explicit or implied). Can appear on its own as a short interjection (e.g., 'Tanto meno tu!' = 'Even less you!').
target_language_example: Non ho tempo per uscire, tanto meno per andare al cinema.
native_language_example: I don't have time to go out, much less to go to the cinema.

meaning: as much/as ... as; indicates equality or comparison (quantity, degree, or intensity).
additional_notes: Used after an adjective or verb phrase to compare two subjects or objects (X è/tanto quanto Y = X is as ... as Y). Can follow nouns or pronouns (e.g. tanto quanto noi). Equivalent to English 'as much as' or 'as ... as.' In spoken Italian you may also hear 'quanto' alone in some contexts, but 'tanto quanto' is common for emphasizing equality.
target_language_example: Sono felice tanto quanto te.
native_language_example: I'm as happy as you are.

meaning: literally 'rug/carpet for' — used to say a carpet intended for a specific room or purpose; can also appear in idiomatic expressions (see notes).
additional_notes: Most often used to indicate which room or purpose the carpet is for (e.g., 'tappeto per la stanza' = 'rug for the room'). 'Tappeto' can also appear in idioms: 'mettere al tappeto' (to knock someone out / put someone down) or 'essere al tappeto' (to be floored/knocked out). In everyday speech you will typically see 'un tappeto per [stanza/ingresso/soggiorno]'.
target_language_example: Dobbiamo comprare un tappeto per il soggiorno.
native_language_example: We need to buy a rug for the living room.

meaning: late for (a place or event).
additional_notes: Used to say someone will be or is often late to a specific location; 'al' is the contraction of 'a + il' and agrees with masculine singular nouns (e.g., lavoro, circolo). For feminine nouns use 'tardi alla' (e.g., tardi alla riunione) and for plural use 'tardi ai/alle'. Common in spoken Italian: 'fare tardi' = to be late.
target_language_example: Scusa, torno subito: non voglio fare tardi al treno.
native_language_example: Sorry, I'll be right back: I don't want to be late for the train.

meaning: 'it's late' / 'it's getting late' followed by a consequence or comment (literally: 'late and')
additional_notes: Used to state that it is late (time of day) and then add a result, concern or observation. Common in spoken and written Italian: 'Si sta facendo tardi e...' or 'È già tardi e...' The construction links the time comment to what follows (e.g., worry, need to leave, a missed opportunity).
target_language_example: Si sta facendo tardi e dovremmo andare a casa.
native_language_example: It's getting late and we should go home.

meaning: 'the table is' — a subject (tavolo) + the verb 'essere' (to be) in the present tense.
additional_notes: Used to describe the table's characteristics or state (size, cleanliness, location of something on it, readiness, etc.). 'Tavolo' is masculine singular; 'è' is the 3rd person singular of 'essere'. In sentences you can replace 'tavolo' with other nouns and keep 'è' to say 'is'.
target_language_example: Il tavolo è vicino alla finestra.
native_language_example: The table is near the window.

meaning: 'a taxi for' or 'taxi to/for (someone)'
additional_notes: Used to say someone calls/orders a taxi on behalf of someone else or to indicate the taxi is meant for a particular person. Common structure: chiamare/telefonare un taxi per + pronoun/noun (e.g., per me, per lei, per Marco). Can also mean 'a taxi to' when followed by a destination (less common than 'per' + person).
target_language_example: Puoi chiamare un taxi per mio padre?
native_language_example: Can you call a taxi for my father?

meaning: cup of
additional_notes: Used to talk about a cup containing something (drink or quantity). Follows by a noun: tazza di caffè (cup of coffee), tazza di tè (cup of tea). In Italian 'tazza' is singular; for plural use 'tazze di' (cups of). Often used for both countable servings and approximate quantities (una tazza di farina = one cup of flour).
target_language_example: Vorrei una tazza di caffè, per favore.
native_language_example: I'd like a cup of coffee, please.

meaning: cups of (used to measure quantity of a drink or liquid).
additional_notes: Combine the plural noun tazze (cups) with di + noun to indicate how many cups of something (e.g., tazze di caffè). Use di before a noun without an article. If specifying a definite/specific item, you may need delle/degli or other partitive/definite forms (e.g., due tazze del caffè). Common in everyday speech for ordering or describing consumption.
target_language_example: Vorrei tre tazze di tè, per favore.
native_language_example: I would like three cups of tea, please.

meaning: 'you now' / 'you at the moment' (used to refer to the person addressed in the present time)
additional_notes: Combines the object pronoun 'te' (you, object form) with the adverb 'adesso' (now). Common in spoken Italian to emphasize the current state or situation regarding the person addressed. Word order 'te adesso' is informal and often appears in contexts like 'I have you now', 'I don't trust you now', or when asking if something is clear to the person now. In more formal or standard word order you might see 'adesso te (lo) dico' or 'adesso ti (lo) dico'—note that 'ti' is the clitic subject/object used before verbs (e.g., 'ti vedo'), whereas 'te' is used for emphasis or after prepositions.
target_language_example: È chiaro per te adesso?
native_language_example: Is it clear to you now?

meaning: 'How are you doing?' / 'How's it going for you?'.
additional_notes: Informal Italian phrase used to ask about someone's general well-being or how they are getting by. Often appears in greetings: 'Come te la passi?' = 'How are you doing?'. Literal components: 'te' (to you), 'la' (it), 'passi' (you pass/get along) — somewhat compositional but idiomatic in use. Use with friends, acquaintances or informally; not for very formal situations.
target_language_example: Ciao Marco — come te la passi ultimamente?
native_language_example: Hi Marco — how have you been lately?

meaning: 'do you want to leave/go away (from here)?' (informal you form)
additional_notes: Combines the clitic pronouns 'te' (you, tonic) and 'ne' (away/from here/of it) with the verb 'vuoi' (you want). Commonly used in spoken Italian to ask if someone wants to go or leave a place. Tone is informal; the full sentence often omits rest of phrase (e.g., 'andare' or 'andare via'). Word order often appears as 'Te ne vuoi (andare)?' or with subject 'Tu te ne vuoi...?'
target_language_example: Te ne vuoi andare adesso?
native_language_example: Do you want to leave now?

meaning: 'because of you' or 'why (do you/does...)' depending on word order—two common uses:
additional_notes: When te perché appears as in examples 1–2 (te perché + clause), it means 'because of you' or 'I ... because you ...' and explains a reason related to 'you' (object pronoun te). When seen in questions like 'Secondo te perché...?' it is split: 'Secondo te' = 'in your opinion' and 'perché' = 'why'. In that case it asks 'why, do you think...?' Word order matters: 'te perché' together usually signals 'because of you'; 'Secondo te perché' is a set phrase meaning 'do you think why' / 'why do you think...'.
target_language_example: Mi hai aiutato molto, te perché ti fidi di me.
native_language_example: You helped me a lot, because of you you trust me.

meaning: you like (them)
additional_notes: Second-person singular informal indirect-object + verb piacere in present plural form. Literally 'to you are pleasing' — used to say that something pleases you. Often followed by the thing liked (gli addii, i tortellini, le mele). For singular things use 'ti piace'. In questions the phrase is preceded by 'a' for emphasis: 'A te piacciono...?'
target_language_example: A te piacciono i gelati alla fragola?
native_language_example: Do you like strawberry ice creams?

meaning: 'do you (informal/emphatic) like to play' — used to ask someone whether they enjoy playing a specific game or sport (often appears as 'A te piace giocare a ...?' for emphasis).
additional_notes: This phrase is a variation of 'Ti piace giocare a ...?' where 'A te' provides emphasis or contrast (e.g., 'A te piace...' = 'You, do you like...'). The preposition 'a' is required before the name of many games/sports (giocare a calcio, giocare a carte). Use 'te' instead of 'ti' only in structures with 'a' for emphasis ('A te...') or after pause; 'te piace' alone is nonstandard without 'a'.
target_language_example: A te piace giocare a calcio?
native_language_example: Do you like to play soccer?

meaning: 'do you like the' (informal emphasis on 'you') — used to ask if someone likes a specific thing (masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: A te piace... adds emphasis to 'you' (A te) — similar to 'ti piace...' but more emphatic or contrastive. Use 'ti piace il' before masculine singular nouns (il + noun). For feminine use 'la' (A te piace la...), plural use 'i'/'le' (A te piacciono i/le...). Common in spoken Italian.
target_language_example: A te piace il gelato al cioccolato?
native_language_example: Do you like chocolate ice cream?

meaning: you like the (informal; emphatic form: 'do you like the...?' or 'you like the...').
additional_notes: This is the informal/emphatic way to ask or state that 'you' (tu) like a specific feminine noun (la + noun). 'A te' adds emphasis or contrasts (like 'you, you like...'). For masculine singular nouns use 'ti piace il/lo' or 'ti piace l'' before a vowel; for plural use 'ti piacciono'. 'Ti piace' is the usual unstressed form; 'a te piace' stresses the person.
target_language_example: A te piace la musica italiana?
native_language_example: Do you like Italian music?

meaning: 'you liked' (singular, familiar; imperfect tense — used to talk about a past, ongoing or repeated liking)
additional_notes: Used with the informal singular pronoun 'te' (short for 'a te') to emphasize or clarify who likes something. 'Piaceva' is the imperfect of 'piacere' and describes past states/habits or background information (e.g., 'You used to like...', 'You liked [in general]', or 'You were liking...' depending on context). In questions or tags it can appear with question particles (e.g., 'vero?', 'eh?'). Common structure: 'A te piaceva + [infinitive or noun]'.
target_language_example: A te piaceva leggere quando eri giovane?
native_language_example: Did you used to like reading when you were young?

meaning: yourself (feminine singular).
additional_notes: Reflexive pronoun used when speaking to or about a female person. Used after prepositions or as the object of a verb (e.g., 'con te stessa', 'parlare di te stessa'). For addressing a male, use 'te stesso'. Informal/formal level depends on context; 'te' is the familiar (tu) form.
target_language_example: Prenditi cura di te stessa ogni giorno.
native_language_example: Take care of yourself every day.

meaning: yourself (emphatic reflexive pronoun).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize the reflexive action or state about the same person (you). Common after verbs and prepositions. In Italian, 'te' is the stressed form of the second-person singular object pronoun and 'stesso' adds emphasis meaning 'the same' → 'yourself'. Often appears in expressions like 'aiuta te stesso' (help yourself) or 'non sei più te stesso' (you are not yourself anymore).
target_language_example: Devi prenderti cura di te stesso.
native_language_example: You must take care of yourself.

meaning: 'German (language) is...' — used to make statements about the German language.
additional_notes: Tedesco means 'German' (the language). The phrase 'tedesco è' appears when describing or evaluating the language (e.g., difficulty, quality, ability). In sentences it's usually followed by an adjective, clause, or complement (e.g., 'terribile', 'così difficile da imparare', 'la lingua migliore del mondo'). Use when talking about the language in general. Word order in Italian places the subject (il tedesco) before the verb (è).
target_language_example: Il tedesco è interessante da studiare.
native_language_example: German is interesting to study.

meaning: called (on the phone) to; telephoned someone (to).
additional_notes: Past participle telefonato + preposition a is used to say who was called. Often appears with subject pronouns and auxiliary avere (ho, hai, ha, etc.): Ho telefonato a Maria = I called Maria. Can also be used in questions and with indirect object pronouns (Mi ha telefonato = He/she called me).
target_language_example: Ho telefonato a Luca ieri sera, ma non ha risposto.
native_language_example: I called Luca last night, but he didn't answer.

meaning: called (on the phone) to/onto (a feminine singular noun or organization).
additional_notes: Past participle 'telefonato' + preposition 'a' + definite article 'la' (contracted as 'alla') indicates someone phoned a specific person or organization referred to by a feminine singular noun (e.g., la polizia, la signorina). Use 'telefonato al' for masculine singular (a + il) and 'telefonato ai/alle' for plurals.
target_language_example: Ho telefonato alla reception per chiedere informazioni.
native_language_example: I called the reception to ask for information.

meaning: mobile phone; cell phone.
additional_notes: Common everyday term for a mobile phone. Can be shortened to 'cellulare' in Italian — both are widely used. Used for asking ownership, wanting one, or referring to someone's first phone. Neutral register.
target_language_example: Ho dimenticato il mio telefono cellulare a casa.
native_language_example: I forgot my cell phone at home.

meaning: 'phone' followed by 'da' as part of constructions meaning 'from/at/since/from someone' depending on context; not a fixed phrase on its own.
additional_notes: This is not a single fixed expression. "Telefono" = phone. The preposition "da" can combine with "telefono" in different ways: 1) "il telefono da qualcuno" / "da lui" = taken from or belonging to someone (He took the phone from him). 2) "telefono da qualche parte" appears in informal spoken questions meaning "my phone somewhere?" but more correct is "il mio telefono da qualche parte?" 3) with a time expression, "da" means "since" (È strano che non stia rispondendo al telefono da stamattina = it's strange he hasn't been answering the phone since this morning). 4) with a duration, "da" can mean "for/for the last" (Stai guardando il telefono da un'ora = you've been looking at the phone for an hour). Pay attention to word order and pronouns: "telefono da lui" = phone from him; "il mio telefono" = my phone.
target_language_example: Ha preso il telefono da Marco senza chiedere.
native_language_example: He took the phone from Marco without asking.

meaning: 'phone in' or 'phone inside (a feminine singular place)'.
additional_notes: Composed of telefono (phone) + nella (in the + feminine singular: in + la). Used to say where a phone is located (e.g. 'telefono nella moschea' = 'phone in the mosque'). Change 'nella' according to the gender/number of the noun that follows (nel, nello, nelle, etc.).
target_language_example: Ho lasciato il telefono nella borsa.
native_language_example: I left the phone in the bag.

meaning: phone (is) — fragment often from a sentence like 'il telefono sta...' meaning 'the phone is...'
additional_notes: This is not a standalone fixed phrase; it looks like the subject 'telefono' + the verb 'sta' (third-person singular of stare). You'll commonly see it as part of sentences describing the phone's state or location, e.g. 'Il telefono sta squillando' (The phone is ringing) or 'Il telefono sta nella borsa' (The phone is in the bag). For beginners: use 'il telefono è' (the phone is) for simple descriptions with adjectives or locations, and 'il telefono sta' when followed by a gerund to describe an ongoing action (sta + gerund = 'is ...-ing').
target_language_example: Il telefono sta squillando, rispondi!
native_language_example: The phone is ringing, answer it!

meaning: time at home; time spent at home (e.g., rest, recovery, or remote work)
additional_notes: Commonly used to talk about being at home for a period — e.g., taking time off to stay home, recovering at home, or working from home. Context determines nuance: 'tempo a casa' can mean 'time to spend at home' or refer to a period when one remains at home rather than going out.
target_language_example: Dopo l'operazione ho bisogno di un po' di tempo a casa per riposare.
native_language_example: After the operation I need some time at home to rest.

meaning: time spent playing (doing play or sports).
additional_notes: Used to talk about how much time someone spends playing games or sports. Often appears with verbs like passare, trascorrere, stare + tutto il tempo + a + infinitive (e.g., giocare). Can be followed by a sport introduced with a (giocare a calcio, giocare a golf).
target_language_example: Passiamo molto tempo a giocare a carte il sabato.
native_language_example: We spend a lot of time playing cards on Saturdays.

meaning: literally 'time that'; used to refer to a period or the time when something happens (often 'the time that' or 'the time when').
additional_notes: Combines tempo (time) with the relative pronoun che. Commonly used to introduce a clause about a period or moment: e.g. 'il tempo che ci viene concesso' = 'the time that is given to us'. Not to be confused with weather-related tempo (il tempo) + che as a complement; context shows whether it means 'time that/when' or 'what the weather will be' (see example 2, where tempo refers to weather and che introduces a subordinate clause).
target_language_example: Non sprechiamo il tempo che abbiamo oggi.
native_language_example: Let's not waste the time that we have today.

meaning: 'how long (it) takes' or 'how much time (is) needed' (with 'ci' as an impersonal/neutral particle referring to the action or situation).
additional_notes: In these examples 'tempo' (time) combines with the particle 'ci' to ask or state how much time is required. 'Ci' is an impersonal/clitic particle that often appears with verbs about time and motion (e.g., volere, passare, mettere, vorrà). Common question forms: "Quanto tempo ci vuole?" (How long does it take?), "Quanto tempo ci vorrà?" (How long will it take?), "Quanto tempo ci hai passato sopra?" (How much time did you spend on it?). Use 'ci' even when the exact subject is general or unstated.
target_language_example: Quanto tempo ci vuole per finire questo lavoro?
native_language_example: How long does it take to finish this job?

meaning: 'it takes time' / 'time is needed'
additional_notes: Used to say that something requires time or patience. Often appears in sentences like "Per imparare ci vuole tempo" (To learn, it takes time). Can be used impersonally with 'ci vuole' (singular) for one thing, or 'ci vogliono' (plural) for multiple things. Tone is neutral and common in spoken and written Italian.
target_language_example: Per cucinare questo piatto tempo ci vuole, non è veloce.
native_language_example: It takes time to cook this dish; it's not quick.

meaning: time with him (spending time together).
additional_notes: Used to talk about spending time together with a male person. Common verbs: passare (passare del tempo con...), trascorrere (trascorrere del tempo con...). Can refer to short or long periods depending on context.
target_language_example: Mi piace passare tempo con lui il sabato.
native_language_example: I like spending time with him on Saturdays.

meaning: free time; leisure time.
additional_notes: Used to talk about the time when you're not working or occupied with duties. Commonly appears with verbs like avere (to have), passare (to spend), dedicare (to devote), and activities (fare sport, suonare la chitarra, navigare su Internet). Can be singular only (no plural form).
target_language_example: Nel mio tempo libero leggo e faccio passeggiate.
native_language_example: In my free time I read and go for walks.

meaning: time passes / time goes by
additional_notes: Used to say that time moves on or that it seems to go quickly (often with 'veloce' or 'in fretta'). Common in reflections about change, aging, or when time seems to fly in enjoyable situations. In questions (e.g. 'Quanto tempo passa?') it can ask how much time is spent on something.
target_language_example: Il tempo passa in fretta quando sei felice.
native_language_example: Time passes quickly when you're happy.

meaning: in time for / time to (make it for) — used to say you arrive or are available in time for something or have time for something.
additional_notes: Commonly used with events or deadlines (e.g., il treno, un evento). Can mean both 'in time for' (arriving before something starts) and 'have time for' (having enough time to do something), depending on context. Followed by a noun introduced by the definite article (il, la, etc.).
target_language_example: Siamo arrivati in tempo per il concerto.
native_language_example: We arrived in time for the concert.

meaning: humid/wet weather (damp, muggy conditions).
additional_notes: Used to complain about weather that is damp, muggy or has high humidity. Common in everyday speech when describing uncomfortable, sticky conditions. Can refer to overall weather or a specific period (oggi c'è tempo umido).
target_language_example: Sono stufo di questo tempo umido; rende tutto appiccicoso.
native_language_example: I'm tired of this humid weather; it makes everything sticky.

meaning: 'time flies' — used to say time passes very quickly.
additional_notes: Common idiom used to comment that time seems to pass fast, especially when you're busy or having fun. Can be used alone ('Il tempo vola') or in sentences (e.g. 'Il tempo vola quando...'). Informal/neutral phrase suitable in spoken and written Italian.
target_language_example: È già passato un anno? Tempo vola!
native_language_example: Has a year already passed? Time flies!

meaning: 'to keep under control' or 'to restrain'
additional_notes: Used when talking about controlling emotions, impulses, behavior, or physical forces. Often followed by a noun (e.g., tenere a freno la rabbia) or reflexive ideas (tenersi a freno). It implies deliberate effort to limit or restrain something.
target_language_example: Devo tenere a freno la rabbia prima di parlare.
native_language_example: I have to keep my anger under control before I speak.

meaning: 'to hold one's tongue' — to restrain oneself from speaking or from saying something inappropriate
additional_notes: Idiomatic expression used when someone should avoid commenting, complaining, or revealing something. Often used with reflexive or impersonal constructions: 'Devi tenere a freno la lingua' (You must hold your tongue). Can imply self-control or politeness. Not literal (you're not physically restraining the tongue).
target_language_example: Quando i clienti si lamentavano, ho dovuto tenere a freno la lingua per non rispondere male.
native_language_example: When the customers complained, I had to hold my tongue so I wouldn't answer rudely.

meaning: to take into account; to consider
additional_notes: Used with di/che or a direct object to mean 'to bear in mind' or 'to factor in' when making a decision or judgment. Common in advice or instructions. Conjugate 'tenere' normally (e.g., 'devi tenere conto', 'dovremmo tenere conto').
target_language_example: Dovresti tenere conto del suo lavoro quando prendi la decisione.
native_language_example: You should take his work into account when you make the decision.

meaning: to hold on; to hang in there; to persevere
additional_notes: Used to encourage someone to keep going through a difficult situation. Often used as an infinitive idea (dobbiamo tenere duro) or referenced in the imperative (Tieni duro!). The infinitive form tenere duro is common when describing the need to persevere (e.g., bisogna tenere duro). Common in spoken and written Italian.
target_language_example: Dobbiamo tenere duro fino alla fine.
native_language_example: We must hang in there until the end.

meaning: to hold the
additional_notes: This is the verb tenere ('to hold/keep') followed by the definite article il ('the'). It isn't a fixed phrase by itself — meaning depends on the noun that follows (e.g. tenere il bambino = to hold the baby; tenere il libro = to keep the book). Common uses: physical holding, keeping/retaining something, or maintaining a state (tenere il passo = to keep up the pace). Remember that the article changes with the noun (la, i, gli, le) so you'll often see forms like tenere la, tenere i, etc.
target_language_example: Puoi tenere il mio ombrello per favore?
native_language_example: Can you hold my umbrella please?

meaning: to take into account; to keep (something) in a certain state (context-dependent).
additional_notes: Commonly appears in fixed phrases: 'tenere in considerazione/tenere in conto' = 'to take into consideration/into account'. With 'vita' it becomes 'tenere in vita' = 'to keep alive'. With 'ordine' in sentence 4 the meaning is 'to keep (something) in order/maintained'. The verb needs an object and often a noun that completes the phrase (considerazione, conto, vita, ordine).
target_language_example: Dobbiamo tenere in considerazione le opinioni di tutti.
native_language_example: We must take everyone's opinions into consideration.

meaning: to keep one's mouth shut; to stay silent or not speak.
additional_notes: Commonly used in informal contexts to tell someone to be quiet or to describe keeping a secret. Often appears in commands or advice (e.g., 'Tieni la bocca chiusa') or in reflexive/idiomatic forms. Literal words mean 'to keep the mouth', which makes the phrase fairly compositional.
target_language_example: Meglio tenere la bocca chiusa se non sei sicuro.
native_language_example: It's better to keep your mouth shut if you're not sure.

meaning: to keep/hold (something) — with a feminine plural direct object (le = them).
additional_notes: Tenere is a verb meaning 'to hold/keep'. When followed by the article/pronoun le, it refers to keeping or holding feminine plural things (e.g., le mani, le spalle, le cose). In many contexts le + noun is simply 'the' (le mani = the hands) so 'tenere le mani a posto' = 'keep your hands in place/keep your hands to yourself'. Can be literal (hold the chopsticks) or figurative (keep things as they were). Remember Italian verbs require correct agreement with articles/pronouns.
target_language_example: Tenere le mani a posto è importante durante la lezione.
native_language_example: Keeping your hands to yourself is important during the lesson.

meaning: to hold tight / to hold firmly
additional_notes: Used when someone grips something (or someone) firmly to prevent it from moving or falling, or as an expression of emotional closeness (e.g., holding someone close). Common with objects (tenere stretto il volante) and people (tenere stretto un bambino). Can be used literally and figuratively.
target_language_example: Devi tenere stretto il bambino quando attraversi la strada.
native_language_example: You must hold the child tightly when you cross the street.

meaning: to hold something/someone tightly; to keep close (physically or figuratively)
additional_notes: Commonly used both literally (holding an object or person close) and figuratively (to cherish, to keep something safe or keep a relationship). Reflexive verb construction: tenersi + stretto (or altra parola) with a direct object: tenersi stretto qualcosa/qualcuno. Often followed by a noun or pronoun: tenersi stretto il bambino / tenersi stretto quel ricordo. Can appear in different persons (mi tengo stretto, ti tieni stretto, si tengono stretti).
target_language_example: Mi tengo stretto questo libro quando viaggio.
native_language_example: I hold this book tightly when I travel.

meaning: 'keep' or 'hold' (formal/imperative polite form) + definite article 'the'.
additional_notes: Tenga is the formal (Lei) imperative of tenere (to hold/keep). Used to give polite commands or suggestions: e.g. telling someone to keep the change (Tenga il resto) or to hold/keep something (Tenga il telefono acceso; Tenga il vaso con entrambe le mani). 'Il' is the masculine singular definite article and will change according to the noun (la, lo, i, gli, le) to match gender and number. Common in polite interactions, customer service, instructions, and formal contexts.
target_language_example: Tenga il resto, per favore.
native_language_example: Keep the change, please.

meaning: play tennis with (someone).
additional_notes: Used to say you will or want to play tennis together with a person or group. In Italian the full construction is usually 'giocare a tennis con [nome/pronome]'. 'Con' means 'with' and is compositional and literal here.
target_language_example: Vuoi giocare a tennis con me questo weekend?
native_language_example: Do you want to play tennis with me this weekend?

meaning: to play tennis with her.
additional_notes: A simple phrase combining the activity (giocare a tennis) with 'con lei' ('with her'). Used to say someone plays or should play tennis with a female person (lei = she/her, formal or informal depending on context). Pronoun 'lei' can also be formal 'you' in polite speech, but in these examples it refers to 'her'. Verb forms change with subject (Andate, Giocavo, Voglio, Vada).
target_language_example: Stasera voglio giocare a tennis con lei.
native_language_example: Tonight I want to play tennis with her.

meaning: to play tennis with him
additional_notes: Combines the sport 'tennis' with the prepositional phrase 'con lui' (with him). Used to say someone plays (or wants to play/used to play) tennis together with a male person. Verbs before it change for tense/person (gioca, giocava, vuole giocare, voleva). You can replace 'lui' with other pronouns/names (con me, con lei, con Marco). In Italian you say 'giocare a tennis' (use 'a' before the sport).
target_language_example: Domani voglio giocare a tennis con lui al club.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I want to play tennis with him at the club.

meaning: table tennis (ping-pong).
additional_notes: Refers to the sport played on a table with paddles and a lightweight ball. 'Ping-pong' is a common synonym. Used the same way as 'table tennis' in English.
target_language_example: Gioco a tennis da tavolo ogni sabato al circolo sportivo.
native_language_example: I play table tennis every Saturday at the sports club.

meaning: the sport tennis + the time expression 'yesterday' — used to indicate that someone played tennis the day before (e.g. 'played tennis yesterday').
additional_notes: This is the noun 'tennis' combined with the adverb of time 'ieri' (yesterday). In natural Italian you'd normally include a verb (e.g. giocare) and the preposition 'a' before the sport: "ho giocato a tennis ieri." Word order often places time expressions after the verb or at the end. Formality depends on context; the phrase itself is neutral.
target_language_example: Io ho giocato a tennis ieri.
native_language_example: I played tennis yesterday.

meaning: playing tennis every / tennis every (as part of a time expression).
additional_notes: This combination appears when saying you play tennis on a regular schedule. In Italian the verb and the sport come first (gioco a tennis), then 'ogni' + time period (ogni lunedì, ogni pomeriggio). Use 'ogni' to mean 'every' (each) with days, parts of the day, or other repeated intervals.
target_language_example: Gioco a tennis ogni sabato mattina.
native_language_example: I play tennis every Saturday morning.

meaning: play tennis every Sunday / tennis every Sunday
additional_notes: A simple phrase stating that someone plays or does tennis on Sundays (every Sunday). Can be used as part of a sentence: e.g. "Faccio tennis ogni domenica" (I play tennis every Sunday) or "Gioca a tennis ogni domenica" (He/She plays tennis every Sunday). 'Tennis' in Italian is invariant; use 'a tennis' or the verb 'fare/giocare' to form a full sentence. 'Ogni' means 'every' and is followed by a singular time word like 'domenica' (Sunday).
target_language_example: Faccio tennis ogni domenica con gli amici.
native_language_example: I play tennis every Sunday with friends.

meaning: held the (feminine) — past participle 'tenuto' + direct object article 'la' (e.g. 'held the door').
additional_notes: Common in sentences where someone held something open or kept it closed. 'Tenuto' is the past participle of 'tenere' (to hold/keep). The article 'la' marks a feminine singular noun (e.g. la porta, la bocca). English often uses 'held' or 'kept' + adjective ('open', 'closed') or preposition 'for' to indicate purpose/beneficiary: Ha tenuto la porta aperta per lei = He/she held the door open for her. Word order can vary: 'tenuto la porta' or 'tenuto la bocca'.
target_language_example: Marco ha tenuto la porta aperta per noi.
native_language_example: Marco held the door open for us.

meaning: 'theory is' — the noun 'teoria' (theory) followed by the verb 'è' (is).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but simply the noun 'teoria' plus the third-person singular of 'essere' (to be). You'll see it in sentences like 'teoria è...' meaning 'the theory is...' or in expressions like 'in teoria è...' meaning 'in theory it is...'. Pay attention to context: 'in teoria' (an adverbial phrase) is common and means 'in theory' / 'theoretically'.
target_language_example: In teoria è una buona idea, ma dobbiamo provarla.
native_language_example: In theory it is a good idea, but we need to test it.

meaning: 'the land/ground is' — a short phrase used to describe qualities or possession of a piece of land
additional_notes: Terreno = land, soil, plot; è = is (3rd person singular of essere). Used to say something about the land (quality, ownership, value). In natural speech you would more often see 'il terreno è', 'questo terreno è', or 'quel terreno è' with an article or demonstrative before 'terreno'.
target_language_example: Il terreno è molto fertile.
native_language_example: The land is very fertile.

meaning: 'test of' or 'test for' (used before a noun to indicate what is being tested).
additional_notes: Common in phrases like "test del DNA" (DNA test) or "test del nuovo motore" (test of the new engine). 'Test' is a masculine invariant noun in Italian; use 'del' = di + il before a masculine singular noun. The structure is compositional (literally 'test of the ...'). In many contexts English would flip the order to say '... test' (e.g. 'DNA test' rather than 'test of the DNA').
target_language_example: Hanno fatto il test del sangue ieri.
native_language_example: They did the blood test yesterday.

meaning: ‘test in’ = 'a test/exam in (a subject or language)'; here 'in' marks the subject or medium (e.g. in giapponese = in Japanese).
additional_notes: Commonly used with verbs like passare/passar (to take/pass) or fare (to do). 'Test' is a loanword from English and is masculine (un test). 'In' followed by a language, field, or location indicates the medium/subject (in italiano, in matematica, in laboratorio). Not idiomatic — it's a straightforward combination: test + preposition in + noun.
target_language_example: Ho fatto un test in inglese ieri.
native_language_example: I took/did a test in English yesterday.

meaning: literally 'head with' — used to describe covering, filling, or striking someone's head with something.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom on its own; it appears as part of verbs like coprire la testa con (to cover one's head with), riempire la testa con (to fill someone's head with [ideas/noise]), scuotere la testa con (rare—to shake one's head with), or spaccare la testa con (to smash someone's head with). Context and the verb determine the exact meaning. Use when describing what is on, in, or done to someone's head. Word order: the object (testa) is usually part of the verb phrase (e.g., coprire la testa con + object).
target_language_example: Si è coperto la testa con un cappello per proteggersi dal sole.
native_language_example: He covered his head with a hat to protect himself from the sun.

meaning: insult: 'asshole' / 'dickhead' (very rude)
additional_notes: Strong vulgar insult used to call someone stupid, annoying, or contemptible. Literally 'head of dick' — extremely offensive; avoid in polite company. Common in heated speech, commands, or to express anger. Tone and context determine intensity (direct insult vs. exclamation).
target_language_example: Lasciami in pace, testa di cazzo!
native_language_example: Leave me alone, you dickhead!

meaning: "testa e" is not a fixed phrase on its own; it's the word "testa" (head) followed by the conjunction "e" (and).
additional_notes: You will rarely see "testa e" as an isolated fixed expression. In the example sentences it appears as part of larger instructions or constructions: "la testa e bocca" (the head and mouth), "la testa e le buone maniere" (the head and good manners) and "la testa e vi toccate la fronte" (lower your head and touch your forehead). Learn "testa" (head) and remember "e" means "and" — they combine compositionally.
target_language_example: Abbassa la testa e guarda in basso.
native_language_example: Lower your head and look down.

meaning: eyewitness — a person who personally saw an event happen.
additional_notes: Used to describe someone who directly observed an incident (crime, accident, event). Often used in legal or news contexts. Can be shortened to just 'testimone' if context makes it clear. Not informal.
target_language_example: La polizia ha parlato con il testimone oculare della rapina.
native_language_example: The police spoke with the eyewitness of the robbery.

meaning: I love you
additional_notes: Direct, strong declaration of romantic love (first-person singular + object pronoun). Used for partners, close loved ones; not typically used for casual affection (use ti voglio bene for friends/family). Can appear in emphatic forms (e.g., ti amo immensamente, ti amo con tutto il mio cuore).
target_language_example: Ti amo con tutto il mio cuore.
native_language_example: I love you with all my heart.

meaning: 'is/are enough for you' or 'do you have enough' (asks if something suffices for the person addressed).
additional_notes: A common informal phrase using the verb bastare (to be enough) with the indirect object pronoun ti (to you). Used to ask whether something suffices, is sufficient, or satisfies someone's need/desire. Word order can change (e.g., 'Questo ti basta?' or 'Ti basta questo?'). Can express surprise or mild reproach depending on tone and context.
target_language_example: Ti basta un caffè per ripartire?
native_language_example: Is one coffee enough for you to get going?

meaning: do you think (that) you ...? / you think you ...
additional_notes: Used to question or challenge someone's belief about themselves or their actions. Often appears in structures like "Ti credi di poterlo fare?" (Do you think you can do it?) or "Ti credi migliore di me?" (Do you think you're better than me?). Can be direct/challenging or neutral depending on tone. Followed by an infinitive, an adjective, a clause introduced by "che" or a noun phrase.
target_language_example: Ti credi di poter guidare questa macchina?
native_language_example: Do you think you can drive this car?

meaning: 'let me give you a' / 'may I give you a' (used to offer or propose giving someone something, help, or an action)
additional_notes: ti = 'to you' (indirect object). dia is the present subjunctive of dare ('to give'), often used after verbs like 'vuoi che' or 'lascia che' to make offers, suggestions, or hypothetical/polite actions. Followed by a noun (un passaggio, un abbraccio, un consiglio) or a phrase describing the action. Common in offers: 'Vuoi che ti dia...' or 'Lascia che ti dia...'.
target_language_example: Vuoi che ti dia un consiglio prima di partire?
native_language_example: Do you want me to give you a piece of advice before leaving?

meaning: tell you
additional_notes: Second-person singular indirect object (ti) + subjunctive/infinitive form (dica) of dire; commonly appears after verbs/phrases like bisogna che, lascia che, cosa vuoi che to express 'that I tell you' or 'let me tell you'. Used when the speaker is about to give information, an opinion, or emphasise something. In English translations the subject ('I') is often added even though it's not explicit in the phrase.
target_language_example: Lascia che ti dica la verità.
native_language_example: Let me tell you the truth.

meaning: 'what makes you think that...' / 'why do you think that...'
additional_notes: Used to ask someone for the reason or evidence behind a belief or assumption. Common in conversational Italian. Followed by a clause (subordinate) introduced by che and then a statement or opinion. Can be formalized as "Cosa ti fa pensare che..." or shortened colloquially to "Perché pensi che...?"
target_language_example: Cosa ti fa pensare che non verrà?
native_language_example: What makes you think he won't come?

meaning: I'll blow your (something) up / I'll make (part of you) explode — a violent threat meaning 'I'll kill/injure you' (usually completed with a body part like 'testa').
additional_notes: This is an informal, aggressive threat. In examples it's completed as 'ti faccio saltare la testa' ('I'll blow your head off'). Used to intimidate; extremely rude and violent — avoid using. Structure: 'ti faccio saltare' (I make you blow up/make explode) + definite article + noun (body part).
target_language_example: Non dire altro o ti faccio saltare la testa!
native_language_example: Don't say another word or I'll blow your head off!

meaning: you hurt yourself
additional_notes: Literal components: ti (to yourself) + fai (you do/make). Used in different contexts: 1) warning about self-injury: "ti fai male" = "you'll hurt yourself" or "you hurt yourself"; 2) reflexive/semi-reflexive actions: e.g. "ti fai le seghe" (vulgar) = "you masturbate" (you do it to yourself) or "ti fai un favore" = "you do yourself a favor"; 3) slang for using drugs: "ti fai di coca" = "you do coke / you take cocaine." Tone ranges from neutral to informal/vulgar; often used in spoken Italian. The exact meaning depends on the object or context that follows.
target_language_example: Occhio, così ti fai male!
native_language_example: Careful, you'll hurt yourself like that!

meaning: I saved your life (literally: 'I have saved it for you' — used to mean 'I saved you').
additional_notes: Common informal phrase used to tell someone you rescued or helped them in a serious way. Often said emphatically (Ti ho salvato la vita!) and can be used literally (physical rescue) or hyperbolically (helped someone out of big trouble). The full neutral form is "ti ho salvato la vita"; the provided fragment "ti ho salvato la" is colloquial/incomplete on its own but clearly understood in context. Pronunciation stress typically falls on salvato and vita.
target_language_example: Non dire grazie? Ti ho salvato la vita ieri!
native_language_example: You won't say thank you? I saved your life yesterday!

meaning: How dare you (do/say ...).
additional_notes: Used to express strong surprise or indignation at someone's words or actions. Often appears in the phrase "Come ti permetti... ?" followed by an infinitive (di + verb) or alone as a sharp rebuke. Tone is confrontational; avoid using it in polite contexts.
target_language_example: Come ti permetti di parlarmi così!
native_language_example: How dare you talk to me like that!

meaning: 'do you like to play' (asking if someone enjoys playing a game/sport)
additional_notes: Uses the verb piacere + infinitive; 'ti' = to you. Commonly followed by 'a' + the game/sport (e.g. a calcio, a carte). Use subject implied (you) — Italian treats the thing enjoyed as the subject: literal structure is 'to you is pleasing to play'. For other persons change the pronoun: 'mi piace giocare' (I like to play), 'gli piace giocare' (he likes to play).
target_language_example: Ti piace giocare a tennis?
native_language_example: Do you like to play tennis?

meaning: don't worry about (someone/something).
additional_notes: A casual way to tell someone not to worry. Commonly used with pronouns or nouns after 'per' (per me, per noi, per la situazione). In full imperative form it's usually 'Non ti preoccupare per...' or plural/formal 'Non vi preoccupate per...' or polite 'Non si preoccupi per...'.
target_language_example: Non ti preoccupare per me, vado d'accordo con tutti.
native_language_example: Don't worry about me, I get along with everyone.

meaning: 'I promise you' (I give you my word).
additional_notes: Used to reassure someone or make a commitment. Common in spoken Italian; often followed by a clause starting with 'che' (that) describing what is promised. Tone can be sincere, casual, or emphatic depending on context and intonation.
target_language_example: Ti prometto che verrò alla tua festa.
native_language_example: I promise you that I'll come to your party.

meaning: 'remind you (of)' or 'does it remind you (of)'.
additional_notes: Used to ask if something (a person, object, name, event, etc.) brings to mind or triggers a memory of someone/something. 'Ti' is the informal second-person singular object pronoun (you). With different pronouns it becomes: 'mi ricorda' (reminds me), 'gli/le ricorda' (reminds him/her). Common in questions: 'Ti ricorda qualcosa?' = 'Does it remind you of anything?'.
target_language_example: Questo odore ti ricorda la casa di tua nonna?
native_language_example: Does this smell remind you of your grandmother's house?

meaning: You've lost your mind / You're crazy (lit. 'you drank your...').
additional_notes: Colloquial and idiomatic. Often completed with 'cervello' (brain): 'ti sei bevuto il cervello' meaning 'have you lost your mind?' or 'you're out of your mind'. Used to criticize someone's foolish behavior or choices. Tone can be rude or playful depending on context and intonation.
target_language_example: Ma che fai? Ti sei bevuto il cervello?
native_language_example: What are you doing? Have you lost your mind?

meaning: suits you very well / looks very good on you
additional_notes: Used with clothing or appearance: the verb stare + pronoun 'ti' indicates how something (e.g., a dress) looks on the person. Often followed by 'bene' (well). Word order can vary (e.g., 'ti sta molto bene', 'ti sta molto bene addosso/indosso'). Common in compliments.
target_language_example: Quel colore ti sta molto bene.
native_language_example: That color suits you very well.

meaning: you're behaving/acting in (a certain way).
additional_notes: Used to ask or comment about someone's behavior. Usually followed by manner expressions like 'maniera/ modo + adjective' (e.g., 'in maniera così strana'). Informal to neutral register. Common in questions: 'Perché ti stai comportando in modo/maniera...?'
target_language_example: Perché ti stai comportando in modo così serio?
native_language_example: Why are you behaving so seriously?

meaning: we were (doing something) to/for you — 'we were' + verb in progressive/past continuous with 'ti' (you).
additional_notes: Ti is the direct object 'you' (informal). Stavamo is the first-person plural imperfect of stare used to form the past progressive (we were ...). It's normally followed by a gerund (e.g., aspettando = waiting, cercando = looking for). Common in sentences like 'Ti stavamo aspettando' = 'We were waiting for you.' Context can be neutral, friendly, or confrontational depending on tone and following words (e.g., 'maiale' = insult).
target_language_example: Ti stavamo aspettando alla fermata dell'autobus.
native_language_example: We were waiting for you at the bus stop.

meaning: to you is (doing)
additional_notes: Combines the object pronoun ti (to/for you) + stia (subjunctive of stare) and is used in subordinate clauses to indicate an ongoing action affecting 'you' with a sense of doubt, possibility or emotion (common after verbs like pensare, credere, dire, sospettare). Often followed by a gerund: ti stia dicendo = (that) is telling you. Translate naturally as 'is ... to you' or simply 'is ...ing you' (e.g. 'is telling you', 'is hiding from you').
target_language_example: Pensi che ti stia mentendo?
native_language_example: Do you think he is lying to you?

meaning: I care about you / I love you (affectionate, non-romantic or gentle romantic).
additional_notes: Common affectionate phrase used with family, close friends, or a partner in a gentle way. Less intense than "ti amo" (which is used for romantic love). Can express strong friendship, familial love, or tender romantic feeling depending on context and relationship.
target_language_example: Volevo solo dirti che ti voglio bene e che mi manchi tanto.
native_language_example: I just wanted to tell you that I care about you and that I miss you a lot.

meaning: I love you very much / I care for you deeply (affectionate, often non-romantic).
additional_notes: A warm, affectionate phrase used to express deep care or love. Commonly said to family members, close friends, or children; can be romantic but often implies deep, tender affection rather than passionate love. Literal components: 'ti' (to you), 'voglio' (I want), 'tanto bene' (so much good/well) — together idiomatically 'I love you a lot.' Tone is gentle and sincere.
target_language_example: Ti voglio tanto bene, papà, grazie per tutto.
native_language_example: I love you very much, Dad, thank you for everything.

meaning: I wanted you
additional_notes: Literal meaning is 'I wanted you' (ti = you, volevo = I wanted/used to want). Used both for wanting a person (affection: "ti volevo bene" = I cared for you) and for wanting someone to do/be somewhere ("ti volevo su quella sedia" = I wanted you on that chair). Context and tone change the nuance (desire, intention, past feelings). In spoken Italian, it can also imply a past continuous or a completed desire depending on context. Not reflexive.
target_language_example: Ti volevo vicino quando avevo paura.
native_language_example: I wanted you close when I was scared.

meaning: to you is/has
additional_notes: A common Italian pattern where ti means "to you" and è is either "is" or the auxiliary "has" with verbs that use essere. English often does not translate it literally: ti è successo = "it happened to you," ti è piaciuto = "you liked it," ti è venuto in mente = "it occurred to you."
target_language_example: Ti è arrivato il mio messaggio?
native_language_example: Did you get my message?

meaning: 'holds/keeps the' or 'is holding the' (third-person singular present of tenere + definite article)
additional_notes: Combines the verb tenere (to hold, keep, maintain, take care of) in third-person singular (tiene) with the masculine singular definite article il. Used to say someone is holding or keeping something, or figuratively to mean maintaining (e.g., a position, a grudge, responsibility). Context determines exact translation (physical holding, caring for, keeping a facial expression, or maintaining control). Word order can change in questions or with pronouns (e.g., 'Lo tiene' = 'He/She holds it').
target_language_example: Lui tiene il libro mentre io prendo appunti.
native_language_example: He is holding the book while I take notes.

meaning: keeps the ... always clean / she keeps the ... always clean.
additional_notes: A phrase used to say someone regularly maintains something (usually a room) in a clean state. 'Tiene' is the third-person singular of 'tenere' (to keep), 'sempre' means 'always', 'pulita' agrees in gender with a feminine singular noun (e.g., 'camera' or 'stanza'), and 'la' is the definite article referring to that noun. In English you typically insert the noun after 'keeps': 'keeps the room always clean' → 'keeps the room always clean' (more natural: 'always keeps the room clean').
target_language_example: Lei tiene sempre pulita la sua stanza.
native_language_example: She always keeps her room clean.

meaning: keep the (followed by a plural masculine noun); literally 'keep the...'.
additional_notes: Imperative form of tenere (tieni) + the plural masculine definite article gli. Often used with body parts (e.g., occhi = eyes) or other plural masculine nouns. In English the article is usually omitted: 'keep your eyes open' vs. Italian 'tieni gli occhi aperti'. Use with informal singular you (tu).
target_language_example: Tieni gli occhi aperti quando attraversi la strada.
native_language_example: Keep your eyes open when you cross the street.

meaning: you (informal singular) hold/keep the (plural) — imperative or present tense form with a definite plural object.
additional_notes: From the verb tenere (to hold, keep). 'Tieni' can be either the present indicative 'you hold/keep' (tu tieni) or the imperative 'hold/keep!' (tieni!). 'I' is the plural definite article 'the' (before a masculine plural noun). Used with plural nouns: capelli, libri, soldi, preziosi dubbi. Context and intonation determine whether it's a statement (Do you hold/keep...?) or an instruction (Hold the... / Keep the...).
target_language_example: Tieni i bagagli per un secondo, per favore.
native_language_example: Hold the luggage for a second, please.

meaning: 'keep your mouth (shut)'; telling someone to be quiet or not speak.
additional_notes: Imperative or instructive phrase (second person singular: tu). Often completed as 'tieni la bocca chiusa' for 'keep your mouth shut'. Can be rude or strong depending on tone and context; used to order silence or to tell someone not to reveal information.
target_language_example: Tieni la bocca chiusa se non vuoi creare problemi.
native_language_example: Keep your mouth shut if you don't want to cause trouble.

meaning: 'hold/keep the' (informal imperative, singular you) or 'keep' (with plural feminine noun).
additional_notes: Tieni is the imperative (or present indicative) of tenere for tu (you). With 'le' it precedes a feminine plural noun: e.g. tieni le mani (hold the hands/keep your hands), tieni le chiavi (hold the keys). Common in commands or requests: 'Tieni le dita incrociate' = 'keep your fingers crossed'. Can also mean 'keep something for later' (tieni le noci di cocco per dopo). Tone can be neutral to forceful depending on context; often used in spoken/colloquial commands.
target_language_example: Tieni le chiavi fino a che non torno.
native_language_example: Hold the keys until I come back.

meaning: imperative 'keep' or 'hold' + indefinite article (you keep/hold a ... / you keep ...)
additional_notes: Tieni is the 2nd person singular imperative (or present indicative) of tenere (to hold/keep). 'Tieni un' appears before a noun: it can mean 'hold a ...', 'keep a ...', 'keep (a) ...', or in some idiomatic uses 'keep a low profile' or 'keep an eye'. Depending on context it can be literal (hold an object) or figurative (keep a diary, keep an eye, keep a low profile). For commands, it's direct address: 'Tieni un cetriolo' = 'Hold a cucumber.' For questions it can be used like 'Do you keep a ...?' (Tieni un diario?).
target_language_example: Tieni un occhio aperto quando attraversi la strada.
native_language_example: Keep an eye open when you cross the street.

meaning: too shy to (do something).
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to say someone was or is 'too shy to' do something. Agreement: timida (feminine) / timido (masculine). Often appears as 'troppo timida per...' ('too shy to...'). Can be used in past or present contexts: 'era troppo timida per...' = 'she was too shy to...'.
target_language_example: Ero troppo timida per parlare con lui.
native_language_example: I was too shy to talk to him.
