meaning: to dye (one's) — used with hair (e.g., 'tinta i capelli' = 'dye one's hair')
additional_notes: This is part of the reflexive verb 'tingersi' in past participle form 'tinta' (feminine) used with reflexive pronouns (mi/ti/si) and the body part 'i capelli'. In the examples speakers ask or state that someone (usually female) dyed her hair. For other genders/forms you might see 'tinto i capelli' (masculine/mixed) or 'tinta le capelli' is incorrect — keep 'i capelli'. Use appropriate reflexive pronoun: mi sono tinta(i), ti sei tinta(i), si è tinta/o, ci siamo tinti/e. Common pattern: 'ti sei mai tinta i capelli?' = 'have you ever dyed your hair?'
target_language_example: Mi sono tinta i capelli di biondo l'estate scorsa.
native_language_example: I dyed my hair blonde last summer.

meaning: have dyed (one's) — used with capelli (hair); 'tinto i capelli' = '(someone) dyed their hair'.
additional_notes: The verb here is tingersi / tingere (past participle tinto) used reflexively: 'si è tinto i capelli' = 'he/she dyed his/her hair'. In Italian you often say 'tingersi i capelli' (to dye one's hair). Followed by a color introduced with 'di' (e.g. 'di blu', 'di nero') or by 'del suo stesso colore' (the same color). Agreement: tinto is a participle used adjectivally; the structure is reflexive so the auxiliary is essere (si è tinto).
target_language_example: Mi sono tinto i capelli di rosso la settimana scorsa.
native_language_example: I dyed my hair red last week.

meaning: 'guy who' / 'person who' or 'a kind/type that' depending on context.
additional_notes: Used informally to refer to a person (tipo = guy/person) followed by a relative clause introduced by che: e.g. "un tipo che vive..." = "a guy who lives...". It can also mean 'a kind/type that' when describing objects or abstract things (di un tipo che... = of a kind that...). Tone is casual; choose more specific words (uomo, persona, genere, tipo di) for formal contexts.
target_language_example: Conosco un tipo che parla cinque lingue.
native_language_example: I know a guy who speaks five languages.

meaning: someone who is the kind of person to (do/like) — used to describe a characteristic tendency or preference
additional_notes: Follows a noun or verb phrase: 'tipo da + [noun]' or 'tipo da + [verb/infinitive]' to say someone is the sort of person who would do or be into that thing. Often informal. Tone can be neutral, playful, or slightly judgmental depending on context.
target_language_example: È un tipo da viaggiare all'ultimo momento.
native_language_example: He's the kind of person to travel at the last minute.

meaning: 'type/kind of food'.
additional_notes: Used to ask or talk about what kind of food someone likes, wants, or what a particular food is (e.g., cuisine, category, or specific style). Common in questions: Che tipo di cibo ti/le piace? or Che tipo di cibo è questo? Can refer to general categories (Italian, Chinese, vegetarian, spicy, etc.).
target_language_example: Che tipo di cibo preferisci quando vai al ristorante?
native_language_example: What type of food do you prefer when you go to the restaurant?

meaning: 'the kind/type of person who' — used to describe someone's character or typical behavior
additional_notes: Followed by a verb clause describing what that kind of person does or doesn't do. Common in comparisons or to emphasize contrast (e.g., 'Non sono il tipo di persona che...'). Can be used positively or negatively. Word-for-word compositional and literal in English.
target_language_example: Non sono il tipo di persona che parla alle spalle degli altri.
native_language_example: I'm not the kind of person who talks behind other people's backs.

meaning: 'to get by' or 'to make do / carry on (financially or emotionally)'
additional_notes: Used informally to talk about surviving, managing, or continuing with limited resources or despite difficulties. Can refer to money (getting by financially) or to life/situations (carrying on). Often followed by time expressions or resources.
target_language_example: Con quel salario piccolo, riesco solo a tirare avanti fino alla fine del mese.
native_language_example: With that small salary, I can only get by until the end of the month.

meaning: to take out / pull out; also figuratively 'bring out' (a trait, idea, or object).
additional_notes: Common separable phrasal verb. Can be literal (pull something out: tirare fuori il coltello, il tappo, i giocattoli) or figurative (bring out a personality, an idea, courage). In imperative or with pronouns the particle 'fuori' stays after the verb or pronoun: tiralo fuori, tirare fuori la lingua. Often used with direct objects.
target_language_example: Vidi Tom tirare fuori un coltello.
native_language_example: I saw Tom take out a knife.

meaning: to lift up; to raise; to pull up; also: to bring up (a child) or to cheer someone up depending on context.
additional_notes: A multi-purpose phrasal verb. Literally means 'to pull up' or 'to lift.' Common uses: physical lifting (tirare su la valigia), raising something (tirare su le tapparelle), raising/bringing up a child (tirare su i bambini), or comforting/cheering someone (tirare su di morale). The meaning depends on the object and context. Conjugate with avere (ho tirato su) when transitive.
target_language_example: Dovresti tirare su la finestra, fa freddo.
native_language_example: You should pull up the window, it's cold.

meaning: to pull back; to back out; to withdraw from doing something
additional_notes: Used when someone decides not to take part in an action, plan, or agreement they were expected to join. Can be literal (physically stepping back) but is most often figurative (refusing or backing out). Common with reflexive pronouns: mi tiro indietro, si è tirato indietro.
target_language_example: Alla fine si è tirato indietro; avrebbe dovuto firmare, ma ha deciso di tirarsi indietro.
native_language_example: In the end he backed out; he was supposed to sign, but he decided to pull back.

meaning: pulled the (feminine noun).
additional_notes: Past participle of tirare (to pull) used with a feminine singular noun: 'tirato la [noun]'. Common in everyday contexts (e.g., pulled a strap, rope, key out of a pocket). In sentence 1 'tirare la cinghia' is an idiom meaning 'to tighten one's belt' (to make sacrifices/ live frugally). Make sure the noun after 'la' is feminine singular.
target_language_example: Ha tirato la porta per chiuderla.
native_language_example: He/She pulled the door to close it.

meaning: the title of the (masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used before a masculine singular noun to indicate possession or association (e.g., titolo del libro = the title of the book). 'Del' is the contraction of 'di' + 'il'. For feminine nouns you'd use 'titolo della'. For plural masculine use 'titolo dei'.
target_language_example: Qual è il titolo del libro?
native_language_example: What is the title of the book?

meaning: to hit rock bottom; to reach the lowest point (emotionally, financially, etc.).
additional_notes: Used figuratively to say someone or something has reached a very bad or lowest point. Can describe emotions, situations, finances, relationships, or a group's performance. Often used with past or present perfect (ha toccato il fondo, sta toccando il fondo) or in infinitive constructions (sembra aver toccato il fondo).
target_language_example: Dopo la perdita del lavoro ha toccare il fondo? No — in realtà ha toccato il fondo e ora sta cercando di risalire.
native_language_example: After losing his job did he hit rock bottom? No — actually he hit rock bottom and now he's trying to recover.

meaning: 'to touch (the)'.
additional_notes: Toccare = to touch; 'la' is the feminine singular definite article (the). Together they mean 'to touch the...' followed by a feminine noun (la parete, la sedia, la pietra, la pancia). Use 'toccare' for physical contact. For masculine nouns use 'toccare il/lo/l'' (e.g. toccare il tavolo). Imperative negative (don't touch) is 'Non toccare...'.
target_language_example: Non toccare la porta con le mani sporche.
native_language_example: Don't touch the door with dirty hands.

meaning: touched a / have you ever touched a (masculine singular noun)
additional_notes: Combination of the past participle 'toccato' (from 'toccare' = to touch) with the indefinite article 'un'. Often appears in questions with 'hai/avete/ha mai' = 'have you ever'. Use 'una' for feminine nouns (e.g. 'hai mai toccato una pietra?'). The phrase agrees with the gender of the noun only in the article, not in 'toccato' (which stays the same).
target_language_example: Hai mai toccato un riccio?
native_language_example: Have you ever touched a hedgehog?

meaning: to get out of the way; to remove oneself or someone/something from a situation (literal or figurative).
additional_notes: Used literally (physically moving out of a path) and figuratively (stepping aside, leaving a responsibility, or removing an obstacle). In informal contexts it can imply getting rid of someone. Built from togliersi (reflexive of togliere) + di mezzo. Common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Devi toglierti di mezzo per far passare il carrello.
native_language_example: You need to get out of the way to let the cart pass.

meaning: 'get out of the way' / 'move aside' (informal, often rude).
additional_notes: Imperative phrase using 'togliersi dai piedi' literally 'remove yourself from the feet' — used to tell someone to move away or stop blocking. Common in spoken Italian; can be neutral ('move aside') or aggressive/rude depending on tone and added words (e.g., with insults). Usually addressed to one person (togliti).
target_language_example: Togliti dai piedi, sto cercando di passare.
native_language_example: Get out of the way, I'm trying to pass.

meaning: took off (his/her) glasses.
additional_notes: Past simple (passato remoto) form of 'togliersi gli occhiali' meaning to remove one's glasses. Often used reflexively (si tolse gli occhiali) to indicate the subject removed their own glasses. In spoken Italian, the passato prossimo ('si è tolto gli occhiali' or better 'si è tolto gli occhiali' / 'si è tolti le lenti' depending on gender/number) is more common for recent actions. Adjust gender/number agreement when using passato prossimo (si è tolto, si è tolta, si sono tolti/e).
target_language_example: Si tolse gli occhiali e guardò il documento.
native_language_example: He/She took off his/her glasses and looked at the document.

meaning: took off (his/her) wedding ring / removed the ring
additional_notes: Past tense (passato remoto) of 'togliere' used reflexively with 'si' + 'la fede' = 'si tolse la fede' meaning 'he/she took off the ring' (often a wedding ring). Commonly used to describe removing a ring physically; context may imply end of a relationship. For present tense use 'si toglie la fede' or 'si è tolto/la fede' for passato prossimo.
target_language_example: Lei si tolse la fede e la mise nel cassetto.
native_language_example: She took off her wedding ring and put it in the drawer.

meaning: removed the
additional_notes: Combination of the past participle tolta (feminine singular of tolto, from togliere) plus the definite article la. Used with reflexive si è tolta (she/one removed/took off) or in a phrase like 'tolta la ...' meaning 'apart from' / 'except for' or 'once you remove'. Agreement: tolta matches a feminine singular direct object (la + feminine noun). For masculine objects you'd see tolto il / tolti i / tolte le. In spoken sentences with a person subject, use si è tolta la + clothing/jewelry. 'Tolta la buona condotta' can mean 'aside from good behavior' or 'if you remove good conduct' depending on context.
target_language_example: Si è tolta la giacca prima di entrare in casa.
native_language_example: She took off her jacket before entering the house.

meaning: '(a) mouse of / (a) mouse named' or part of a phrase referring to a mouse (often used in 'topo di peluche' = stuffed mouse); can also appear in insults like 'topo di fogna' = 'sewer rat' (insult).
additional_notes: Literal meaning: 'mouse of' or 'mouse from'. In practice 'topo di' normally appears before a noun to describe a type of mouse (e.g. 'topo di peluche' = stuffed mouse) or in fixed expressions/insults ('topo di fogna' = sewer rat). It is not a standalone phrase; translate according to the noun that follows. Tone can be affectionate (a toy mouse) or offensive (an insult).
target_language_example: Mi ha comprato un topo di peluche con il mio nome.
native_language_example: He bought me a stuffed mouse with my name on it.

meaning: someone who loves reading/studies a lot; a bookworm.
additional_notes: Used to describe a person who spends much time reading, studying, or in libraries. Often neutral or affectionate, sometimes gently teasing. Literal image: 'library mouse'. Can refer to students or anyone very bookish.
target_language_example: Mia sorella è un vero topo di biblioteca: passa ore in biblioteca ogni giorno.
native_language_example: My sister is a real bookworm: she spends hours in the library every day.

meaning: come back/return to (a feminine singular place) — used as an imperative.
additional_notes: This is the imperative form of 'tornare' (to return) + the preposition 'in' + the feminine singular definite article 'la' contracted as 'nella'. It tells someone to go back to a specific place (e.g., la foresta, la camera, la stanza). Use 'torna nel' for masculine singular (nel = in + il), 'torna nello' before masculine s+consonant or z, 'torna nei' for plural, etc. The subject is usually 'tu' (you, singular informal).
target_language_example: Torna nella tua stanza e riposa.
native_language_example: Go back to your room and rest.

meaning: returning to
additional_notes: Gerund form of tornare. With a place, it means returning/going back there: tornando a casa = returning home, often more naturally 'on the way home'. With an infinitive, it can mean coming back to do something: tornando a prenderci = coming back to get us.
target_language_example: Ho ascoltato la radio tornando a casa.
native_language_example: I listened to the radio on the way home.

meaning: to return with (someone or something); to come back accompanied by or carrying something/someone.
additional_notes: Used when saying you will go back somewhere accompanied by a person or bringing something (e.g., money, family, darkness). Context determines whether 'con' refers to a person, object, or abstract (e.g., 'il buio'). 'Tornare' is conjugated as usual and 'con' links the companion/thing. Can be used in questions inviting someone to return together (Vuoi tornare con me?).
target_language_example: Vuoi tornare con me?
native_language_example: Do you want to return with me?

meaning: to go back (in) to — often used with 'tempo' to mean 'to go back in time'.
additional_notes: A common phrase meaning to return to an earlier point. Usually followed by a noun introduced by 'nel' (e.g., 'nel tempo' = 'in time'). Can be used literally (go back physically) or figuratively (go back in time, undo a decision). Conjugate 'tornare' to match the subject (tornare indietro nel tempo, sono tornato indietro nel passato, voglio tornare indietro nel tempo).
target_language_example: Se potessi tornare indietro nel tempo, cambierei alcune scelte.
native_language_example: If I could go back in time, I would change some choices.

meaning: (you plural) return/go back to (the) — used to tell a group to go back to specific places (e.g. seats, tables, studios).
additional_notes: Imperative plural of 'tornare' + preposition 'a' + definite article 'i' (contracted to 'ai'). Used when addressing more than one person (voi). Common in classroom/restaurant/studio contexts: 'tornate ai vostri posti' = 'go back to your seats'. Can be softened with 'per favore'.
target_language_example: Ragazzi, tornate ai vostri banchi subito.
native_language_example: Kids, go back to your desks immediately.

meaning: 'returned to' (masculine singular subject) + definite article + place/person.
additional_notes: Past participle 'tornato' (from tornare) agrees in gender and number with the subject (tornata, tornati, tornate). 'Al' is the contraction of 'a' + 'il' and introduces the destination or place returned to (e.g., al mio posto = to my seat). If the noun requires a different article contraction use 'allo', 'alla', 'all\'', etc. Use 'tornato al' when the subject is masculine singular and the following article is 'il'.
target_language_example: Sono tornato al mio posto.
native_language_example: I returned to my seat.

meaning: "returned here" — past participle (masculine singular shown) + adverb indicating the current location; used to say someone came back to this place.
additional_notes: ‘Tornato’ agrees in gender/number with the subject (tornata, tornati, tornate). Often used with the auxiliary verb essere (e.g., sono tornato qui). Common in statements and questions (Sei tornato qui?). Can be combined with time expressions (ieri, un anno fa, il giorno successivo).
target_language_example: Io sono tornato qui per prendere lo zaino.
native_language_example: I returned here to get my backpack.

meaning: used to describe a cake 'with' a specific flavor or ingredient (e.g. torta al cioccolato = chocolate cake).
additional_notes: This is not a standalone phrase but the beginning of a cake/flan name: torta + al/alla/ai + ingredient. Use al before masculine singular nouns (cioccolato, limone), alla before feminine singular (fragola → torta alla fragola), and ai/alle for plurals. It literally means 'cake of/with'.
target_language_example: Vorrei una torta al cioccolato, per favore.
native_language_example: I'd like a chocolate cake, please.

meaning: chocolate cake.
additional_notes: A common food phrase: torta = cake, al cioccolato = (made) with chocolate. Used to talk about liking, ordering, or describing cakes. Gender is feminine (la torta). You can change cioccolato to other flavors: torta alla frutta, torta alla vaniglia.
target_language_example: Vorrei una fetta di torta al cioccolato, per favore.
native_language_example: I'd like a slice of chocolate cake, please.

meaning: apple pie (apple tart)
additional_notes: Common dessert phrase. Used to refer to a whole apple pie or a slice depending on context. 'Torta' can mean cake or pie; 'torta di mele' is the typical way to say apple pie in Italian. Use with articles (la torta di mele, una torta di mele) and verbs like fare (to make), avere (to have), piacere (to like).
target_language_example: Hai una fetta di torta di mele?
native_language_example: Do you have a slice of apple pie?

meaning: 'the cake is' (subject + verb — used to describe or ask about a cake)
additional_notes: This is simply the noun 'torta' (cake) followed by the verb 'è' (is). Used to describe a cake's qualities (e.g., taste, type) or to ask what kind of cake it is. Word order can change (e.g., 'La torta è saporita' = 'The cake is tasty'; 'Che tipo di torta è?' = 'What kind of cake is it?'). Not an idiom — compositional and literal.
target_language_example: La torta è al cioccolato.
native_language_example: The cake is chocolate.

meaning: underfoot; in the way; bothering or obstructing someone.
additional_notes: Used figuratively to say a person or thing is annoying, intrusive, or blocking you (literally 'between the feet'). Common in everyday speech. Can be used neutrally (someone physically in the way) or more negatively (someone who annoys you).
target_language_example: Non restare sempre tra i piedi quando lavoro.
native_language_example: Don't stay underfoot all the time when I'm working.

meaning: literally 'between/in the (female) his/her' — used to mean 'in his/her arms' (i.e., being held by someone).
additional_notes: Commonly appears before a body part (e.g., 'tra le sue braccia' = 'in his/her arms'). 'Sue' agrees with a feminine plural noun (braccia). The exact possessor (his/her) is determined by context. Used to describe being physically held or cradled; often found in past tenses describing sleeping, dying, comfort, etc.
target_language_example: Si addormentò tra le sue braccia.
native_language_example: She fell asleep in his/her arms.

meaning: between me / among myself (used to indicate something said or done privately, or a choice between options where speaker is involved)
additional_notes: Literally 'between me'. Often used in informal speech to express a personal opinion or a private matter (similar to 'between you and me' or 'for me'). Context determines exact sense: can mean 'between myself and others' (e.g., 'tra me e te' = 'between you and me') or simply 'for me' when contrasting options ('tra me e lui scelgo...' = 'between me and him I choose...').
target_language_example: Tra me e te, preferisco restare a casa stasera.
native_language_example: Between you and me, I'd rather stay home tonight.

meaning: in parentheses; by the way (used to add a side remark)
additional_notes: Literally 'between parentheses' (i.e. inside parentheses). Used both literally (to place text inside parentheses) and idiomatically to introduce a parenthetical remark or aside, similar to 'by the way' or 'incidentally' in English. Often set off by commas: 'tra parentesi, ...'.
target_language_example: Tra parentesi, ieri ho visto quel film di cui parlavi.
native_language_example: By the way, I saw that movie you were talking about yesterday.

meaning: soon; in a little while.
additional_notes: Used to say something will happen shortly. Can refer to minutes or a short, vague future time. Common in everyday speech for departures, arrivals, actions (e.g., 'Ci vediamo tra poco' = 'See you soon').
target_language_example: Ritorno tra poco, aspetta qui.
native_language_example: I'll be back soon, wait here.

meaning: 'in a' (used to say when something will happen, followed by a time period like 'settimana' = week).
additional_notes: Commonly used in spoken and written Italian to indicate a future time measured from now: 'tra una settimana' = 'in a week' (i.e., one week from now). It precedes a singular time unit (una settimana, un'ora). Can be interchangeable with 'fra una' — both are correct. Not used alone; needs the time unit after it.
target_language_example: Ci vediamo tra una settimana.
native_language_example: We'll see each other in a week.

meaning: 'betrayed the' (used before a feminine noun like "fiducia")
additional_notes: Tradito is the past participle of tradire (to betray). When followed by the feminine definite article la, it introduces a feminine noun (e.g., la fiducia = trust). Common in phrases like "tradito la fiducia" (betrayed the trust). The subject who did the betraying is usually expressed earlier (e.g., Ho tradito la fiducia = I betrayed the trust).
target_language_example: Ho tradito la sua fiducia e me ne pento.
native_language_example: I betrayed his/her trust and I regret it.

meaning: translated the (masculine singular direct object).
additional_notes: This is the past participle 'tradotto' (translated) followed by the definite article 'il'. It appears in examples of the passato prossimo or in compound structures: e.g. 'Ha tradotto il romanzo' = 'He/She has translated the novel'. 'Tradotto' agrees only when used with auxiliary 'essere' in some verbs, but with 'tradurre' the auxiliary is 'avere', so no agreement. Common in sentences describing that someone translated a specific masculine noun (il libro, il testo).
target_language_example: Ha tradotto il capitolo ieri sera.
native_language_example: He/She translated the chapter last night.

meaning: to spend more (time).
additional_notes: Used with time expressions (e.g., tempo) to say you want to spend more time doing something or with someone. Typically appears as 'trascorrere più tempo (con...)' or 'trascorrere più (ore/giorni)'. 'Trascorrere' is a regular verb meaning 'to pass/spend (time)'.
target_language_example: Vorrei trascorrere più tempo con i miei amici.
native_language_example: I would like to spend more time with my friends.

meaning: (she/he) spent the whole (time period) — used to say someone spent all of a period (life, day, etc.) doing or being somewhere/something.
additional_notes: 'Trascorse' is the passato remoto (third person singular) of 'trascorrere' (to spend, to pass [time]). In spoken Italian, passato prossimo ('ha trascorso tutta') is more common in many regions; passato remoto is used in narrative or literary contexts. 'Tutta' agrees with a feminine noun (tutta la vita, tutta la giornata). If the noun is masculine use 'tutto' (e.g., 'trascorse tutto il giorno' — literary). The structure: [Name] trascorse tutta + [periodo] + (a/in/da ...).
target_language_example: Luca trascorse tutta la sera al telefono.
native_language_example: Luca spent the whole evening on the phone.

meaning: spent a lot (of time); elapsed a great deal
additional_notes: From the verb trascorrere (to spend time; to pass/ elapse) + molto (a lot). Used to say that a long time has passed or someone spent a lot of time doing something. Usually appears in contexts like "è trascorso molto tempo" (a lot of time has passed) or with a subject who 'trascorre molto tempo' doing an activity. Formality: neutral.
target_language_example: È trascorso molto tempo dall'ultima volta che ci siamo visti.
native_language_example: A lot of time has passed since the last time we saw each other.

meaning: spent three (units of time); used to say you spent three days/weeks/months/years somewhere or doing something.
additional_notes: Used with a time period (giorni, settimane, mesi, anni). Typically appears as 'trascorrere + [time period]' to indicate duration spent in a place or situation. In sentences the auxiliary 'avere' is often used (ho trascorso, abbiamo trascorso). 'Trascorso tre' itself is followed by the unit: e.g. 'trascorso tre giorni'.
target_language_example: Ho trascorso tre settimane al mare.
native_language_example: I spent three weeks at the seaside.

meaning: after/once an entire (period) has passed; literally 'having spent the whole the...'
additional_notes: Usually part of a larger phrase like "trascorso tutta la notte" (after the whole night passed) or "trascorso tutta la settimana". It combines the past participle "trascorso" (spent/passed) with a feminine singular noun phrase introduced by "tutta la". Use with time expressions; the noun must follow (e.g., notte, giornata, settimana).
target_language_example: Trascorso tutta la notte, finalmente è tornata la luce.
native_language_example: After the whole night had passed, the power finally came back.

meaning: spent the entire morning
additional_notes: Used with past participle 'trascorso' (from 'trascorrere') to say someone spent the whole morning doing something or with someone. Can be used with different subjects (io, tu, lui/lei, noi, voi, loro) by changing the auxiliary verb (avere). Typical structure: [subject] + avere (conjugated) + trascorso tutta la mattinata (+ con + person/activity).
target_language_example: Ho trascorso tutta la mattinata con Anna al mercato.
native_language_example: I spent the entire morning with Anna at the market.

meaning: it's/about a (something); introduces what something is (e.g. it's a misunderstanding / it's about a phenomenon).
additional_notes: Common fixed phrase: 'si tratta di un/una...' is used to identify or describe the nature of something (often translated as 'it's a' or 'this is a'). Can introduce a fact, explanation, or classification. Followed by a noun phrase. Neutral register and very common.
target_language_example: Si tratta di un problema semplice da risolvere.
native_language_example: It's a simple problem to solve.

meaning: it's about a / it's a matter of a (used to introduce what something concerns)
additional_notes: Commonly used to introduce the topic or nature of something: tratta di + article + noun or tratta di + infinitive/phrase. Similar to 'si tratta di' (it concerns/is about). Often appears as 'si tratta di una...' when explaining or clarifying what something is.
target_language_example: Si tratta di una vecchia tradizione del paese.
native_language_example: It's about an old tradition of the town.

meaning: deals only with / treats only / concerns only
additional_notes: A short phrase made of the verb trattare (to deal with / to treat / to discuss) + solo (only). Use to say something addresses or concerns only one topic, person, or aspect. Conjugation of trattare changes with subject (es. tratta solo, trattiamo solo, trattano solo). Context determines whether it's about treating medically, handling a topic, or negotiating/doing business.
target_language_example: Questo capitolo tratta solo l'introduzione.
native_language_example: This chapter deals only with the introduction.

meaning: 'it's just/about' or 'it's only a matter of'.
additional_notes: Used impersonally with 'si tratta' to introduce what something consists of or to downplay its importance. Followed by a noun, infinitive, or clause. English equivalents: "it's just about...", "it's only a matter of...", "it's not only about..." when negated (non si tratta solo di...).
target_language_example: Non preoccuparti: si tratta solo di finire il compito.
native_language_example: Don't worry: it's just a matter of finishing the homework.

meaning: held (one's) breath
additional_notes: Used to describe someone briefly stopping or holding their breath, often from surprise, fear, anticipation, or to stay quiet. Commonly appears with past participle (ha trattenuto il fiato) or reflexive forms (si è trattenuto/si è trattenuta il fiato). Context determines gender/subject.
target_language_example: Quando ha visto il regalo, ha trattenuto il fiato.
native_language_example: When she saw the gift, she held her breath.

meaning: three questions for (someone)
additional_notes: A simple phrase used to say you have three questions directed at a person or group. Replace the pronoun after 'per' to indicate the addressee (per me, per te, per lei, per voi, etc.). Common in both formal and informal contexts; tone depends on the pronoun (e.g., 'lei' can be formal). Word order: 'Ho tre domande per + pronoun/name.'
target_language_example: Ho tre domande per te sulla lezione.
native_language_example: I have three questions for you about the lesson.

meaning: 'for three days that' — used to say something has been happening (or not happening) for three days (equivalent to 'it's been three days that' / 'I've/We've/He/She has been ... for three days').
additional_notes: Common spoken way to express duration in Italian: subject + 'sono tre giorni che' + verb (often with present tense to indicate ongoing action/state). Can appear as 'sono tre giorni che non...' to mean 'haven't ... for three days.' English more naturally uses 'it's been three days' or 'I've been ... for three days.'
target_language_example: Sono tre giorni che piove ininterrottamente.
native_language_example: It's been raining for three days straight.

meaning: three or (short for 'tre ore' = three hours) or used in informal speech to mean 'around three' (time).
additional_notes: 'Tre o' by itself is incomplete in standard Italian. It most often appears as a shortened colloquial form of 'tre ore' (three hours) when the final vowel is dropped in casual speech/writing, or as part of a time expression like 'alle tre e...' (at three and...) where 'tre o' could be a misheard/typo. For beginners: say 'tre ore' for 'three hours' and 'alle tre' for 'at three o'clock.'
target_language_example: Ho lavorato per tre ore.
native_language_example: I worked for three hours.

meaning: shivering/ trembling from (because of) — used to say someone is shaking due to something (often cold).
additional_notes: Commonly used with sensations or causes (e.g., dal freddo = from the cold, dal dolore = from pain). 'Dal' is a contraction of 'da' + 'il' (from the). The verb form can change (sto tremando, stava tremando). Typical structure: [subject] + stare + gerund (tremando) + dal + [cause].
target_language_example: Sto tremando dal freddo, metti la giacca.
native_language_example: I'm shivering from the cold, put on a jacket.

meaning: used to ask or say whether someone travels by train or by another means (e.g., car, plane, bus).
additional_notes: A common question pattern: 'Vai in treno o in macchina?' = 'Are you going by train or by car?'. The structure is 'in + mode of transport' for many vehicles (in treno, in macchina, in aereo, in autobus). Often followed by another transport word; the examples show the choice between train and another option.
target_language_example: Andiamo in treno o in macchina domani?
native_language_example: Are we going by train or by car tomorrow?

meaning: about thirty (of); roughly thirty
additional_notes: Used to indicate an approximate quantity of around thirty items/units/people. Can be used with countable nouns and pronouns (quelli/quelle). More generally, -ina suffix makes a rounded estimate (ventina ≈ ~20, trentina ≈ ~30). Common in spoken Italian for 'around' + number.
target_language_example: Ho una trentina di libri nella soffitta.
native_language_example: I have about thirty books in the attic.

meaning: too thin; not thick/strong enough (to do something).
additional_notes: Used to say something lacks sufficient thickness, strength or sturdiness for a purpose (e.g., ice, material, bamboo). Often followed by a verb phrase with 'per' + infinitive (e.g., 'troppo sottile per reggere/sopportare...'). Can describe physical objects; not typically figurative.
target_language_example: Il ponte è troppo sottile per sopportare il carico.
native_language_example: The bridge is too thin to bear the load.

meaning: too shy; overly shy.
additional_notes: An adjective phrase used to describe someone who is excessively timid or reluctant to act or speak. Often followed by 'per' + infinitive to explain what the person is too shy to do (e.g., 'troppo timido per dire...'). Can describe current state or past (era/era troppo timido).
target_language_example: Sono troppo timido per parlare con lei.
native_language_example: I'm too shy to talk to her.

meaning: imperative or present tense of 'trovare' + definite article 'il' — 'find the' (he/she/it finds the; or (you) find the as a command).
additional_notes: Trova is either the third-person singular present tense (he/she/it finds) or the informal imperative (you find!). Combined with 'il' it means 'find the ...' or 'finds the ...' depending on context. Use 'trova il' before a masculine singular noun (il cane, il passaporto, il ristorante, il ragno). For polite/formal commands use 'trovi il' (Lei) or 'trova' with 'non' for negative informal commands: 'Non trovare...' is more usual for the negative imperative; examples show both statements and commands.
target_language_example: Trova il mio libro sul tavolo.
native_language_example: Find my book on the table.

meaning: is found in / is located in (third-person singular present: 'he/she/it is found in' or 'is located in').
additional_notes: Formed from the verb trovare (si trova = 'is found' / 'is located') + nella (in + la = 'in the'). Used to say where someone or something is located or whether something exists within a given domain (literal place or abstract context). Appears in questions and statements. Change the article after 'in' to agree with the noun (p. es. 'si trova nel', 'si trova nello', 'si trova nell\'', 'si trova nelle', etc.).
target_language_example: Il museo si trova nella piazza principale.
native_language_example: The museum is located in the main square.

meaning: finds/find a (feminine singular object) — literal imperative or present tense + indefinite article.
additional_notes: Trova is either the 3rd person singular present of trovare (he/she/it finds) or the informal (tu) imperative form (find!). 'Una' is the feminine singular indefinite article (a/an). Together they appear when the object is feminine: e.g. trova una scuola (there is/find a school), trova una scusa (find a excuse). Context determines whether it's a statement ('he/she/it finds a...') or a command ('(you) find a...'). Use 'trova un' before masculine nouns starting with a consonant, and 'trova uno' before masculine nouns starting with s+consonant or z.
target_language_example: Trova una soluzione e fammi sapere.
native_language_example: Find a solution and let me know.

meaning: to find some / to find (a bit of) — used when referring to an unspecified quantity of something
additional_notes: Del is the contraction of di + il and here means 'some' (partitive). 'Trovare del' is followed by a masculine singular noun (del burro, del latte, del cibo) and expresses finding an unspecified amount. Can also be used figuratively (trovare del tempo = to find some time). For feminine nouns use 'della' (trovare della farina) and for plural 'dei/degli' (trovare dei libri / degli amici).
target_language_example: Posso trovare del pane al negozio vicino?
native_language_example: Can I find some bread at the nearby shop?

meaning: find the
additional_notes: Used for finding a specific masculine singular thing or person: trovare + il + noun. Il means 'the' before many masculine singular nouns. In 'andare a trovare', though, trovare is part of the expression 'to go visit', not just 'find'.
target_language_example: Non riesco a trovare il supermercato.
native_language_example: I can't find the supermarket.

meaning: 'to find the' (feminine plural direct object)
additional_notes: trovare = to find. When followed by a feminine plural noun or pronoun, Italian uses 'le' as the direct object pronoun/article: e.g. trovare le chiavi (to find the keys) or trovarle (to find them). In speech you may see 'trovare le' as part of a longer phrase; if 'le' is a pronoun it is often attached to the infinitive (trovarle).
target_language_example: Devo trovare le chiavi del garage.
native_language_example: I need to find the garage keys.

meaning: literally 'found a' — used to say 'a ... has been found' or 'a ... was found'.
additional_notes: This is the feminine past participle 'trovata' + the indefinite article 'una'. It agrees in gender with a feminine noun that follows (e.g., 'soluzione', 'corrispondenza'). Common in passive or impersonal constructions: 'Deve essere trovata una soluzione' = 'A solution must be found.' Word order often places the noun after these words (trovata una + noun).
target_language_example: È stata trovata una soluzione al problema.
native_language_example: A solution to the problem has been found.

meaning: 'found some' (past participle + partitive article) — indicates finding an unspecified number/amount of something.
additional_notes: Combines the past participle 'trovato' (found) with the partitive 'dei' (some, plural). Use 'dei' before plural masculine nouns to mean 'some' or 'a few'. For feminine plural use 'delle' and for singular partitives use 'del/ della/ dello/ dell'' depending on gender and sound. Common in spoken and written Italian to report discovering objects, signs, money, people, animals, etc.
target_language_example: Ho trovato dei libri interessanti in soffitta.
native_language_example: I found some interesting books in the attic.

meaning: found the (masculine singular object).
additional_notes: Combination of the past participle 'trovato' (found) and the definite article 'il' (the). Used when saying someone has found a specific masculine singular thing (e.g., il libro, il cane, il teatro). Word order in Italian often places the participle after an auxiliary verb (ha trovato = has found) or with a past perfect construction (ho trovato). Change the article for feminine (la) or plural (i, le) nouns: 'trovata la', 'trovati i', 'trovate le'.
target_language_example: Ho trovato il mio portafoglio ieri.
native_language_example: I found my wallet yesterday.

meaning: literally 'found his/its/their' — part of a phrase meaning 'found his/its/their [something]'.
additional_notes: This is not a standalone fixed phrase; it's the past participle 'trovato' ('found') followed by the possessive 'il suo' ('his/its/your formal/their', depending on context). Together they introduce a direct object: e.g. 'ha trovato il suo portafoglio' = 'he/she found his/your/their wallet'. Agreement and gender may change (e.g. 'trovata la sua' for a feminine noun). The exact meaning of 'suo' depends on the subject and context.
target_language_example: Ha trovato il suo passaporto prima del viaggio.
native_language_example: He/she found his/her passport before the trip.

meaning: "found your" (past participle + definite article + possessive) — used to say someone found something that belongs to 'you'.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom but a short phrase built from the past participle 'trovato' (found) + 'il' (the) + 'tuo' (your). It commonly appears in sentences like 'Ho trovato il tuo libro' (I found your book) or questions like 'Chi ha trovato il tuo cane?' (Who found your dog?). Word order may change (e.g. 'Ho trovato il tuo cappello'). Use the appropriate article and possessive form for gender/number: il tuo (m. sing.), la tua (f. sing.), i tuoi (m. plural), le tue (f. plural).
target_language_example: Hai trovato il tuo portafoglio?
native_language_example: Did you find your wallet?

meaning: found my (feminine noun).
additional_notes: This is the past participle construction using 'trovare' (to find) plus the feminine possessive 'la mia' meaning 'my (something feminine)'. It appears in sentences like 'Chi ha trovato la mia borsa?' ('Who found my bag?'). For masculine nouns you would say 'trovato il mio' (or colloquially 'trovato il mio/il mio...'); with plural nouns use 'trovato i miei' (masc.) or 'trovato le mie' (fem.). Remember agreement of articles/possessives: la mia (singular feminine), il mio (singular masculine), le mie (plural feminine), i miei (plural masculine).
target_language_example: Hai trovato la mia giacca?
native_language_example: Did you find my jacket?

meaning: found his/her/its (something) — 'trovato' = found; 'la sua' = his/her/its (feminine noun)
additional_notes: Used after a verb (past participle) plus a possessive phrase referring to a feminine noun (la sua foto, la sua chiave, la sua destinazione). Agreement: 'la sua' matches a feminine singular thing belonging to 'him' or 'her' (context decides gender of owner). For masculine nouns you'd see 'il suo'. Common in questions (Dove avete trovato la sua foto?) and statements (Ha trovato la sua chiave).
target_language_example: Ho finalmente trovato la sua borsa.
native_language_example: I finally found her bag.

meaning: found that / thought that (depending on context); literally 'found that'.
additional_notes: This is the past participle 'trovato' (found) followed by the demonstrative adjective 'quel' (that). In questions like 'Come ha trovato quel film?' it means 'How did you find that film?' (i.e. what did you think of it). In sentences like 'Dove hai trovato quel vestito?' it asks where someone physically found/bought the item. Word order and context determine whether it refers to an opinion (find = think) or a physical act of finding. 'Quel' agrees in gender/number (quel, quella, quei, quelle) with the noun it modifies; here examples use masculine singular "quel + noun."
target_language_example: Hai trovato quel libro interessante?
native_language_example: Did you find that book interesting?

meaning: literally 'found this' — used when referring to something you (or someone) found.
additional_notes: Usually appears in questions or statements about where or how an item or piece of information was discovered. Verb form 'trovato' is the past participle of 'trovare' and agrees with the auxiliary (avere). Word order in Italian often places the demonstrative ('questa') after the participle when pointing to a specific feminine singular noun (questa + noun). In spoken Italian you may also hear 'l'ho trovato/a' (I found it) or full questions like 'Dove hai trovato questa [chiave/lista]?'
target_language_example: Dove hai trovato questa foto?
native_language_example: Where did you find this photo?

meaning: found this / found it (this).
additional_notes: A combination of the past participle 'trovato' (found) and the demonstrative 'questo' (this). Commonly appears in questions with 'come hai/ha trovato questo...?' meaning 'how did you find this...?' (i.e. what did you think of it / how did you discover it?). Also used in statements 'Ho trovato questo...' meaning 'I found this...' (physically discovered or judged/experienced something). Verb form changes with subject (e.g. 'ho trovato', 'hai trovato', 'ha trovato').
target_language_example: Come hai trovato questo film?
native_language_example: How did you find this movie?

meaning: found this / found it
additional_notes: Literal combination of the past participle 'trovato' (found) and the demonstrative 'questo' (this). Used to say you or someone else discovered or located something (often an item, a link, or a piece of information). In questions it can mean 'Did you find this on...?' and in statements 'I found this (for someone).' Context determines whether 'questo' refers to a physical object or something like a web link or article.
target_language_example: L'ho trovato questo articolo interessante.
native_language_example: I found this article interesting.

meaning: found a
additional_notes: Not a fixed expression. trovato is the past participle of trovare ("to find"), and una means "a" before a feminine singular noun. You often see it with forms of avere, especially ho trovato una... = "I found a..." / "I've found a...". Before a vowel, una usually becomes un'.
target_language_example: Ieri ho trovato una chiave per strada.
native_language_example: Yesterday I found a key in the street.

meaning: 'find me/ find (someone) a' or 'find a' (imperative or subjunctive/conditional contexts); used to ask someone to obtain or look for something or someone
additional_notes: Commonly used with verbs like 'trovare' in requests or suggestions: can be a polite imperative (Lei) or present subjunctive/imperative familiar form depending on context. In everyday speech it often means 'get me' or 'find (for me)'. Word order 'mi trovi una ...' adds an indirect object 'mi' (find me a ...). Without 'mi' it can be an exhortation or suggestion to the listener: 'trovi una soluzione' = 'you should find a solution' / 'try to find a solution'. Tone and context determine whether it's a request, suggestion or criticism.
target_language_example: Mi trovi una stanza per favore?
native_language_example: Can you find me a room, please?

meaning: I find (someone/something) in (a certain state) / I am (in a certain situation) — used with 'trovo' (from trovare) + 'in' + noun or adjective phrase.
additional_notes: Common uses: 'ti trovo in gran forma' = 'I find you in great shape' (commenting on someone's condition); 'mi trovo in una situazione...' = 'I find myself in a situation...' (expressing one's circumstances). The subject can be first person ('mi trovo') or another person ('ti trovo', 'la trovo'). After 'in' expect a noun phrase or adjective phrase describing condition or situation. Literal meaning: 'I find (someone) in (state)'.
target_language_example: Mi trovo in difficoltà con questo progetto.
native_language_example: I find myself in difficulty with this project.

meaning: I find the (feminine plural) — 'trovo' = I find, 'le' = the (feminine plural).
additional_notes: Used when the speaker says they find something (opinion or ability to locate) referring to feminine plural nouns. 'Trovo' can mean 'I find' as in opinion (I think) or 'I can't find' in negative sentences (I can't locate). Word order: verb + definite article + noun (e.g., trovo le lingue). Replace 'le' with 'i' for masculine plural nouns (trovo i libri).
target_language_example: Trovo le tue idee molto utili.
native_language_example: I find your ideas very useful.

meaning: he/she/it found the (plural/feminine) or he/she/it found + feminine plural object (past simple).
additional_notes: Trovò is the passato remoto (simple past) of trovare (to find) for third person singular — commonly used in written Italian and in some spoken varieties to tell past events. 'Le' is the feminine plural definite article ('the') or a feminine plural direct object pronoun. In examples, it introduces feminine plural nouns (le chiavi, le scarpe, le tazze). In everyday spoken Italian many speakers use passato prossimo (ha trovato) instead of trovò.
target_language_example: Maria trovò le chiavi nel cassetto.
native_language_example: Maria found the keys in the drawer.

meaning: 'you have a' (used after verbs that trigger the subjunctive)
additional_notes: This phrase combines the subject pronoun tu + the present subjunctive of avere (abbia) + the indefinite article un. It's found in subordinate clauses after verbs/expressions of doubt, hope, supposition, opinion, or emotion (e.g., spero che, sembra che, suppongo che). Use for 'you have a/an' when the speaker expresses uncertainty, desire, or speculation about the person having something.
target_language_example: Spero che tu abbia un buon giorno.
native_language_example: I hope that you have a good day.

meaning: you and (the)... — used to address someone and include a plural noun that follows (e.g. 'you and your friends').
additional_notes: Common structure: 'Tu e i + [noun/possessive + noun]' (informal singular 'tu' + plural group). Often used to point out someone and their group or possessions. Word order is 'tu e i...' (not 'tu e voi'). Use 'tu' for one person; use 'voi' when addressing a group directly. In pronunciation the article 'i' links to the following noun (i tuoi, i miei, i cani).
target_language_example: Tu e i tuoi fratelli siete invitati alla festa.
native_language_example: You and your brothers are invited to the party.

meaning: you (singular, informal) + to him/them (indirect object pronoun).
additional_notes: Tu is the informal singular 'you'. Gli is the indirect object pronoun used for 'to him' and often also for 'to them' (masculine or mixed gender) in colloquial Italian. In standard written Italian, 'gli' primarily means 'to him'; for 'to them' some speakers use 'loro' or 'agli' in more formal contexts, but 'gli' is very common in everyday speech for both. Position: the pronoun follows the subject (tu) and precedes the verb (tu gli dici). In compound tenses and with auxiliaries or infinitives, gli stays before the main verb or attached to an infinitive per normal clitic rules (e.g., voglio che tu gli dica / puoi dirglielo).
target_language_example: Tu gli hai detto la verità?
native_language_example: Did you tell him/them the truth?

meaning: 'you' (subject) + 'them' (direct object).
additional_notes: Tu = informal singular 'you'. Li = masculine plural direct object pronoun 'them' (can refer to people or masculine/neutral objects). In spoken/written Italian the subject pronoun tu is optional (verb endings usually show the subject), but it's used here for emphasis or clarity. Word order is subject (tu) + object pronoun (li) before the verb (e.g., tu li vedi? = Do you see them?). In compound tenses the object pronoun precedes the auxiliary: tu li hai già incontrati? Note agreement of past participle when the direct object pronoun precedes the auxiliary (in passato prossimo the participle agrees in gender/number with the preceding direct object).
target_language_example: Tu li chiami stasera?
native_language_example: Are you going to call them tonight?

meaning: a request or command: 'that you tell me' / 'you tell me' (subjunctive or reported clause)
additional_notes: Used in subordinate clauses after verbs like voglio, chiedo, etc. The form dica is subjunctive (from dire) used for wishes, requests, or indirect commands: voglio che tu mi dica = I want you to tell me. It literally means 'that you tell me' and introduces what the speaker wants to be told. Can appear with different subjects and objects (e.g., come ci sei arrivato/a, la causa, di Tom).
target_language_example: Per favore, voglio che tu mi dica la verità.
native_language_example: Please, I want you to tell me the truth.

meaning: you (subject) + 'ne' (pronoun meaning 'of it/them', 'about it/them', 'from it/of them' or partitive); together often means 'you (of it/them)' or 'you (can/do) ... of it/them'.
additional_notes: Tu = informal singular 'you'. Ne is a clitic pronoun with several uses: replaces phrases introduced by 'di' (of it/them), indicates partitive ('some'), or refers back to something already mentioned ('about it/about them'). Position: ne normally comes before the conjugated verb (tu ne puoi), before a compound auxiliary (tu ne sei), or attached to an imperative (mandane). In English it often translates as 'of it', 'of them', 'about it', 'about them', or is untranslated when meaning 'some'. Context determines the exact translation.
target_language_example: Tu ne sai più di me.
native_language_example: You know more about it than I do.

meaning: do you really think / do you truly think
additional_notes: Used to question or express surprise/doubt about someone's belief or opinion. 'Tu' is the informal singular 'you' (can be omitted in spoken Italian). 'Pensi' is the present of 'pensare'. Often followed by 'che' + a clause. Tone can be skeptical or emphatic depending on intonation.
target_language_example: Tu pensi veramente che lui tornerà?
native_language_example: Do you really think he'll come back?

meaning: you (are) the one (who)... — used to identify or point to a specific person (female) as the one doing or being something.
additional_notes: Combines the subject pronoun tu (you) with quella (that one / the one, feminine). Used in sentences like 'Sei tu quella...' or 'Eri tu quella...' to ask or state whether the addressee is the particular person who did something or has a certain characteristic. Quella agrees in gender (feminine) and can be replaced by quello (masculine) for men. The verb (sei, eri, dovresti essere, etc.) normally appears before questa phrase.
target_language_example: Sei tu quella che ha chiamato ieri?
native_language_example: Are you the one who called yesterday?

meaning: ‘that you know’ used in subordinate clauses to introduce something the speaker wants the listener to be aware of.
additional_notes: This phrase appears in constructions with verbs like volere, avere bisogno, or dire (e.g., "Voglio che tu sappia che..."). It uses the subjunctive form "sappia" (from sapere) because these verbs express desire, necessity, or emotion about the listener's knowledge. In English it's usually translated as "I want/need you to know that..." or "I want you to be aware that...".
target_language_example: Voglio che tu sappia che sarò sempre al tuo fianco.
native_language_example: I want you to know that I will always be by your side.

meaning: the present-subjunctive form of 'stare' for 'you' (singular): 'that you be/stay/feel'.
additional_notes: Used after verbs or expressions that require the subjunctive (e.g., sperare, volere, dubitare). English translations vary by context: 'that you are/are feeling/you stay/you remain'. Common in set phrases like 'Spero che tu stia bene' ('I hope that you are well'). Pronounced with emphasis on the subjunctive mood; not used in simple statements (use 'stai' for indicative).
target_language_example: È importante che tu stia calmo durante l'esame.
native_language_example: It's important that you stay calm during the exam.

meaning: your friendship
additional_notes: Used to refer to the friendship someone has with the speaker. Tone depends on context: can be sincere/affectionate (e.g., "La tua amicizia è molto preziosa") or dismissive/angry when combined with an insult (e.g., "Fottiti tu e la tua amicizia!"). "Tua" is the informal singular 'your'; use "la vostra amicizia" for plural 'your' (formal/plural).
target_language_example: Apprezzo davvero la tua amicizia.
native_language_example: I really appreciate your friendship.

meaning: your attention
additional_notes: Used to ask or thank someone for paying attention (listening or looking). Common in formal and polite contexts (e.g., presentations, announcements) but also in everyday requests. Often appears with verbs like dare/avere (dare la tua attenzione / avere la tua attenzione) or in the phrase "grazie per la tua attenzione."
target_language_example: Per favore, posso avere la tua attenzione per un minuto?
native_language_example: Please, can I have your attention for a minute?

meaning: your photo / a photo of you.
additional_notes: Common, informal way to refer to a picture of the person you're speaking to. 'Tua' is the familiar singular possessive (tu). Use 'la tua foto' for a specific photo (e.g., profile picture). In more formal contexts or to address multiple people, use 'sua foto' (formal) or 'vostra foto' (plural).
target_language_example: Mi puoi mandare una tua foto per la tessera?
native_language_example: Can you send me a photo of yourself for the ID?

meaning: your car is
additional_notes: A simple subject–possessive + noun + verb phrase used to describe or ask about the state, location, or qualities of someone’s car. 'Tua' is the informal singular 'your'. Can be used in statements or questions; word order may change in questions (e.g. 'La tua macchina è nuova?').
target_language_example: La tua macchina è parcheggiata davanti alla porta.
native_language_example: Your car is parked in front of the door.

meaning: your best (feminine form) — used before a feminine noun to indicate the best of something belonging to 'you'.
additional_notes: ‘Tua’ = your (singular informal). ‘Migliore’ = better/best. Because Italian adjectives agree in gender and number with the noun they modify, 'tua migliore' appears before a feminine singular noun (e.g., partita, amica, caratteristica, idea). For masculine nouns you'd see 'tuo migliore' or more commonly 'il tuo migliore...' but often speakers use 'migliore' without the article: 'la tua migliore amica' or simply 'la tua amica migliore'. In everyday speech English speakers often translate as 'your best...' or 'your best friend/idea/feature'.
target_language_example: Sei la tua migliore sostenitrice; credi in te stessa.
native_language_example: You are your own best supporter; believe in yourself.

meaning: your request; your application
additional_notes: Used to refer to something someone has asked for, requested, or applied for. Common in formal and informal contexts (e.g., requests, applications, permissions). 'Tua' is the familiar singular 'your' (use 'la tua richiesta' with article in many contexts). If speaking formally to one person, use 'la Sua richiesta' (capitalized) or 'la vostra richiesta' for plural.
target_language_example: Ho letto la tua richiesta e ti risponderò domani.
native_language_example: I read your request and I will reply tomorrow.

meaning: your theory / your idea (about something)
additional_notes: Literal: 'tua' = your, 'teoria' = theory. Commonly used to refer to someone's explanation, opinion, or hypothesis about a topic. Can be used in informal and formal contexts depending on tone; often appears in phrases expressing disagreement (e.g., 'la tua teoria non è corretta').
target_language_example: La tua teoria non convince tutti.
native_language_example: Your theory doesn't convince everyone.

meaning: 'your stories' — literal; often used to mean 'your tales' or colloquially 'your excuses/long-winded stories'.
additional_notes: Literally 'your stories' (tue = your, storie = stories). Can be neutral (referring to tales, accounts, anecdotes) or negative/colloquial to dismiss someone's long, boring, or dubious explanations (e.g., 'save me your stories' = 'I don't want to hear your excuses'). Tone depends on context and intonation.
target_language_example: Non voglio sentire le tue storie: dimmi la verità.
native_language_example: I don't want to hear your stories: tell me the truth.

meaning: your comfort; feeling at ease (literally 'your ease').
additional_notes: Often used in the fixed expression 'essere a tuo agio' or 'sentirsi a proprio agio' to say someone feels comfortable or relaxed in a situation. Common in questions and invitations (e.g., 'Sei a tuo agio?' = 'Are you comfortable?'). Can refer to physical comfort or emotional/social ease. Use 'a proprio agio' for a more neutral/general form.
target_language_example: Se non sei a tuo agio, dimmelo e cambiamo posto.
native_language_example: If you're not comfortable, tell me and we'll change places.

meaning: a slightly ironic or emphatic way to say 'your' + noun (literally 'your beautiful'), often used sarcastically or to emphasize the noun.
additional_notes: Combines the possessive tuo (your) with the adjective bel (short form of bello before a consonant). Frequently used colloquially to emphasize, mock, threaten, or draw attention to the person or object named; tone and context determine whether it's flattering, sarcastic, insulting, or dramatic. Bel is used instead of bello before masculine singular nouns starting with most consonants (e.g., bel vestito, bel ragazzo, bel muso).
target_language_example: Se continui così, porto via il tuo bel vestito.
native_language_example: If you keep going like that, I'll take your nice dress away.

meaning: for your own good; for your benefit
additional_notes: Used to say that an action or remark is intended to help or protect the person addressed, even if it may be unpleasant or not understood now. Common in sentences like 'lo faccio per il tuo bene' (I do it for your own good). Can sound paternalistic depending on tone. Often appears with 'per' as in 'per il tuo bene.'
target_language_example: Te lo dico per il tuo bene.
native_language_example: I'm telling you this for your own good.

meaning: your horse
additional_notes: A simple possessive phrase: tuo = your (singular, informal), cavallo = horse. Use tuo before a masculine singular noun. For formal or plural 'your' in Italian: 'Suo' (formal singular) or 'vostro' (your, plural). Context can be literal (an actual horse) or exclamatory ('Il tuo cavallo!' as a short remark).
target_language_example: Il tuo cavallo sembra curioso.
native_language_example: Your horse looks curious.

meaning: a rude/emphatic way to say 'your' or 'your damn' (insulting emphasis).
additional_notes: Very vulgar. Literally 'your dick of', but used as an intensifier or to show contempt about something belonging to someone (e.g. your job, your friend, your dog). Use only in very informal, angry contexts; avoid in polite speech. Often placed before a noun to express annoyance, disrespect, or strong emotion.
target_language_example: Non voglio il tuo cazzo di aiuto, vattene.
native_language_example: I don't want your damn help, go away.

meaning: your knife.
additional_notes: A simple possessive phrase: 'tuo' is the informal singular 'your' (addressing one person you know well), and 'coltello' means 'knife'. Use 'tuo' for informal singular, 'suo' for formal or third-person possessive (his/her/your formal), 'vostro' for plural 'your'. Agreement: 'tuo' agrees in gender/number with the noun (tuo coltello — masculine singular).
target_language_example: Posso usare il tuo coltello per tagliare il pane?
native_language_example: Can I use your knife to cut the bread?

meaning: your computer is
additional_notes: A simple subject + verb phrase: tuo = your (informal singular), computer = computer, è = is (3rd person singular of essere). Used to describe the state, characteristics, or actions of someone's computer. In formal situations or when speaking to more than one person, use vostro computer (your, plural/formal) or il suo computer (his/her/your formal). Word order can change (È il tuo computer) but meaning stays the same.
target_language_example: Il tuo computer è spento? Accendilo, per favore.
native_language_example: Is your computer off? Turn it on, please.

meaning: your money (informal, singular 'you').
additional_notes: Combines the possessive adjective 'tuo' (your, singular informal) with 'denaro' (money). Used to indicate money that belongs to the person you're addressing. If speaking formally or to more than one person, use 'il vostro denaro' (formal/plural) or 'il Suo denaro' (formal singular). In Italian possessive adjectives usually include the definite article (e.g., 'il tuo denaro'), which is normal here.
target_language_example: Controlla il tuo denaro prima di uscire.
native_language_example: Check your money before you go out.

meaning: your film / your movie (the movie that belongs to or is preferred by you)
additional_notes: A simple possessive phrase: tuo = your (informal singular), film = film/movie. Used to indicate ownership, preference, or association. Context determines whether it means "your movie" (one you own or made) or "your favorite movie" when combined with words like "preferito." Note: use "tuo" for informal singular 'you'; for polite or plural use "suo" (formal) or "vostro" (plural).
target_language_example: Questo è il tuo film o lo guardiamo insieme?
native_language_example: Is this your movie or shall we watch it together?

meaning: your cat (singular, informal 'you').
additional_notes: 'tuo' is the possessive adjective used with the informal singular 'tu'. Use 'suo' for formal 'you' (Lei) or 'vostro' for plural 'you'. The noun 'gatto' is masculine singular; if referring to a female cat, you can still say 'il tuo gatto' or specify 'la tua gatta'. Include the definite article when needed: 'il tuo gatto' = 'your cat'.
target_language_example: Il tuo gatto è molto carino.
native_language_example: Your cat is very cute.

meaning: 'your cat is' (describing a quality or state of someone's cat).
additional_notes: Used to describe appearance, behavior, or condition of another person's cat. 'Tuo' = your (informal singular). 'Gatto' = cat. 'È' is the third-person singular of 'essere' (to be). You can replace adjectives after 'è' (e.g., carino = cute, grasso = fat, adorabile = adorable). For formal or plural 'your', use 'il Suo gatto è' (formal) or 'il vostro gatto è' (plural).
target_language_example: Il tuo gatto è molto timido.
native_language_example: Your cat is very shy.

meaning: your job / your employment
additional_notes: Used to ask or talk about someone's job or type of employment. Impiego is a slightly more formal word than lavoro and refers to a position or employment. Tuo is the informal singular 'your'.
target_language_example: Il tuo impiego è lontano da casa?
native_language_example: Is your job far from home?

meaning: "your job is" / "your work is" (followed by what the person's job or role consists of, or a comment about their work)
additional_notes: Used to describe someone's job, role, or responsibility (tuo lavoro è + [infinitive] to say someone's job is to do something, or + adjective/noun to describe the work). Informal/formal level neutral — 'tuo' is the familiar 'your' (use 'il suo' for formal). Common in statements and questions.
target_language_example: Il tuo lavoro è aiutare i clienti ogni giorno.
native_language_example: Your job is to help customers every day.

meaning: your moment; the time when something important happens for you (e.g., success, happiness).
additional_notes: Used to refer to a personal moment/opportunity, often for success, recognition, or a significant life event. Common in phrases like "è arrivato il tuo momento" (your time has come) or "il tuo momento di gloria" (your moment of glory). Addressing someone directly (tuo = your).
target_language_example: Preparati: presto arriverà il tuo momento.
native_language_example: Get ready: your moment will arrive soon.

meaning: your name is
additional_notes: Used to state or ask someone's name. 'tuo' = your (informal singular). Often preceded by the subject pronoun 'il/tu/il tuo' as in the examples: 'Il tuo nome è...' is the common full phrase. To ask someone's name more politely or formally, use 'il suo nome è' (his/her or your formal) or ask 'Come ti chiami?' (How do you call yourself?/What's your name?).
target_language_example: Il tuo nome è Marco, vero?
native_language_example: Your name is Marco, right?

meaning: your new (masculine or neutral — modifying a masculine singular noun)
additional_notes: Combines the possessive adjective tuo (your) with the adjective nuovo (new). It agrees in gender and number with the noun it modifies: tuo nuovo (masculine singular), tua nuova (feminine singular), tuoi nuovi (masculine plural), tue nuove (feminine plural). Used to talk about something recently acquired, started, or changed that belongs to the person you're addressing (informal tu).
target_language_example: Hai visto il tuo nuovo telefono?
native_language_example: Have you seen your new phone?

meaning: your watch / your clock.
additional_notes: A simple possessive phrase: 'tuo' (your, singular informal) + 'orologio' (watch/clock). Used to refer to someone's personal wristwatch or a clock. If speaking formally or to multiple people, use 'suo' (formal) or 'vostro' (plural). Word order is the same as in English: possessive + noun.
target_language_example: Mi dai il tuo orologio, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you give me your watch, please?

meaning: your bread (literally) — 'the bread that belongs to you'.
additional_notes: A simple possessive phrase: tuo = your (singular, informal), pane = bread. Use tuo before a masculine singular noun. For polite/formal 'your' use il suo. Can refer literally to bread or be used figuratively in context.
target_language_example: Posso assaggiare il tuo pane?
native_language_example: Can I taste your bread?

meaning: 'your wine' (possessive: the wine that belongs to or is associated with you)
additional_notes: Tuo is the informal singular possessive adjective for 'your' (used with tu). It agrees in gender and number with the noun it modifies: tuo vino = your (male/singular) wine. For formal or plural 'your' use suo (Lei), vostro (voi) or loro as appropriate. Common in everyday speech to indicate preference or ownership.
target_language_example: Hai assaggiato il tuo vino di ieri?
native_language_example: Did you taste your wine from yesterday?

meaning: your hair is / your hair are (description of someone else's hair).
additional_notes: A common phrase to describe another person's hair. 'Tuoi' = 'your' (informal singular tu), 'capelli' = 'hair' (plural in Italian), and 'sono' = 'are' (third-person plural of essere). In English we often say 'your hair is' (singular), but in Italian hair is grammatically plural so you use 'sono'. Use with adjectives: belli (beautiful), brutti (ugly), lunghi (long), corti (short), colorati (colored), ecc.
target_language_example: I tuoi capelli sono molto lucidi oggi.
native_language_example: Your hair is very shiny today.

meaning: your eyes are (…)
additional_notes: A simple subject–predicate phrase used to describe someone's eyes. 'I tuoi occhi' = 'your eyes' (informal/plural agreement with 'tu'). Followed by an adjective or clause: e.g. 'bagnati' (wet), 'belli' (beautiful), 'come...' (like...). Use 'i tuoi occhi sono' to make observations or ask about appearance/condition. For formal or polite 'your' (singular) you'd use 'i suoi occhi sono'.
target_language_example: I tuoi occhi sono così luminosi stasera.
native_language_example: Your eyes are so bright tonight.

meaning: 'shift of' or 'turn to' (indicates someone's shift, turn, or duty for a particular activity).
additional_notes: Used to talk about work shifts (e.g., 'turno di notte' = night shift) or whose turn it is to do something (e.g., 'il mio turno di ascoltare' = my turn to listen). Usually followed by a noun (attività, tipo di turno) or an infinitive/gerund phrase describing the action or duty.
target_language_example: Questa settimana ho il turno di mattina all'ufficio postale.
native_language_example: This week I have the morning shift at the post office.

meaning: the whole morning / all morning
additional_notes: Used to say that an action or state lasted for the entire morning period (from early morning until around midday). Commonly followed by verbs like passare (to spend) or stare (to be). 'Tutta' agrees in gender/number with the noun: mattinata is feminine singular. Equivalent expressions: 'per tutta la mattinata' or simply 'tutta la giornata' for the whole day.
target_language_example: Ho passato tutta la mattinata a leggere libri.
native_language_example: I spent the whole morning reading books.

meaning: all the letters (letters as written messages)
additional_notes: Used to mean 'every letter' (physical written letters, emails less likely unless context). Commonly appears with past-tense verbs (ho bruciato/strappato/buttato via) to say you destroyed or disposed of all the letters someone wrote you. 'Tutte' agrees in gender/number with 'le lettere'.
target_language_example: Ho conservato tutte le lettere che mi avete scritto.
native_language_example: I kept all the letters you wrote me.

meaning: 'both' or 'all (of them)', used with a numeral (e.g. due, tre) to mean 'all of the two/three/etc.'
additional_notes: Combine with a number and a noun or pronoun: 'tutte e due' = both (feminine/plural), 'tutti e due' = both (masculine or mixed). Can be followed by a noun or stand alone as a pronoun. Use 'tutte e tre' = all three, etc. Agreement (tutte/tutti) matches the gender and number of the items.
target_language_example: Ho invitato le sorelle: sono venute tutte e due.
native_language_example: I invited the sisters: both of them came.

meaning: 'all the saints' (literal) — used idiomatically to mean 'all the time' or to intensify exclamations (like 'for heaven's sake').
additional_notes: Literally means 'all the saints'. In everyday Italian it appears in religious contexts (referring to all saints) and in idiomatic/exclamatory phrases to add emphasis or frustration, e.g. 'Per tutti i Santi!' similar to 'for heaven's sake!' or 'good grief!'. It can also appear in place names or holidays (Tutti i Santi = All Saints' Day). Tone depends on context: neutral in calendar/religious use; emphatic or colloquial when used as an exclamation.
target_language_example: Per tutti i Santi, chiudi la porta!
native_language_example: For heaven's sake, close the door!

meaning: every day
additional_notes: A frequency expression used to say something happens each day. Literally it means "all the days." Compare it with "tutto il giorno," which means "all day."
target_language_example: Prendo il caffè tutti i giorni.
native_language_example: I have coffee every day.

meaning: a colloquial way to say 'everyone knows that...' or 'it's obvious to everyone that...'.
additional_notes: Used to introduce a statement presented as common knowledge or an obvious fact. In standard Italian you'd more often see 'tutti sanno che' or 'è chiaro a tutti che'. 'tutti che non' appears in informal speech as a contraction of that idea; avoid in formal writing. The negation 'non' applies to the clause that follows (e.g. 'non esiste...').
target_language_example: Tutti che non vogliono venire, allora rimaniamo noi.
native_language_example: Everyone knows they don't want to come, so we'll stay.

meaning: 'all' with a connector used to add a number or emphasize inclusiveness (e.g. 'tutti e tre' = 'all three')
additional_notes: Used to mean 'everyone' or 'all' and often followed by a number or pronoun with 'e' to link items (e.g. 'tutti e due', 'tutti e tre'). Also appears alone as 'tutti' (everyone); 'tutti e' emphasizes inclusion or adds a specific count. Common in spoken and written Italian.
target_language_example: Siamo andati al cinema tutti e quattro insieme.
native_language_example: We went to the cinema all four of us together.

meaning: all of them; every one of those people
additional_notes: Used to refer to a specific group of people previously mentioned or understood from context. Can be used with verbs in plural (sono, parlano, erano). Informal level: neutral, common in spoken and written Italian.
target_language_example: Ho invitato molti colleghi e tutti loro hanno accettato.
native_language_example: I invited many colleagues and all of them accepted.

meaning: everyone watching / all (of them) are watching
additional_notes: This phrase shows 'tutti' (everyone/all) with the gerund 'osservando' (watching). In natural Italian you'd more commonly say 'tutti stanno osservando' or 'ci stanno tutti osservando' (they're all watching us). Word order can change: 'stanno tutti osservando Tom' = 'they are all watching Tom.' Pronouns can appear before the verb (Mi/Le/Li/ci stanno tutti osservando) meaning 'everyone is watching me/her/them/us.'
target_language_example: Ci stanno tutti osservando mentre parliamo.
native_language_example: Everyone is watching us while we talk.

meaning: everyone; all of you; all of them (informal/emphatic).
additional_notes: Used to address or refer to a whole group in a friendly or emphatic way. Common in spoken Italian. Can be directed at people present (all of you) or used more generally (everyone). Often appears with commands or greetings: 'Andiamo, tutti quanti!' / 'È stato un piacere conoscervi, tutti quanti.'
target_language_example: Grazie a tutti quanti per essere venuti.
native_language_example: Thank you everyone for coming.

meaning: all ears; fully listening and paying attention
additional_notes: Used to say you are ready to listen carefully to what someone is about to say. Equivalent to English 'I'm all ears.' Informal but common in everyday speech. Often used alone as a response.
target_language_example: Dimmi, sono tutto orecchie.
native_language_example: Tell me, I'm all ears.

meaning: 'all the respect' — used to acknowledge or emphasize respect for someone or something (often ironical or formulaic).
additional_notes: Can be used sincerely to express full respect (e.g., praising someone's choice) or ironically/sarcastically to signal polite disagreement. Often appears in phrases like "tutto il rispetto per..." followed by a person or opinion. Common in spoken and written Italian. Followed by "per" + noun/pronoun/phrase.
target_language_example: Tutto il rispetto per lei, ma non sono d'accordo con quella decisione.
native_language_example: All due respect to her, but I don't agree with that decision.

meaning: everything now; all (of it) right now
additional_notes: Used to say that everything (or everything relevant) is happening or should happen immediately. Can express someone 'knowing everything now' (Conosce tutto adesso) or an instruction to explain everything now (Spiegami tutto adesso). Word order is flexible (e.g. 'adesso tutto' is possible but less common).
target_language_example: Spiegami tutto adesso, per favore.
native_language_example: Explain everything to me now, please.

meaning: all good
additional_notes: Common informal greeting or check-in. Can be used as a question (Tutto bene?) to ask someone if they're okay or if everything is fine, or as a response meaning 'all good'. Tone and context determine if it's a question or statement. Suitable in casual and polite contexts (with titles like signorina, signore) — not overly formal.
target_language_example: Tutto bene, come è andata la riunione?
native_language_example: All good — how did the meeting go?

meaning: Is everything okay with / Did everything go well with (someone or something).
additional_notes: Used to ask if things are fine or went well regarding a person or situation. Often appears in the question form 'Va tutto bene con ...?' to check status or well-being. In past tense ('È andato tutto bene con ...') it means 'did everything go well with ...'.
target_language_example: Va tutto bene con il nuovo lavoro?
native_language_example: Is everything okay with the new job?

meaning: all you have to (do) / everything you need to (do).
