target_language_example: Questa vittoria per la squadra è molto importante.
native_language_example: This victory for the team is very important.

meaning: 'no longer lives' or 'lives longer' depending on context (most commonly 'no longer lives').
additional_notes: This phrase combines the verb vivere (to live) with più. In negative sentences (with nessuno, non, etc.) 'vive più' means 'no longer lives' or 'doesn't live here anymore'. In questions about duration (e.g. 'vive più a lungo?') it means 'lives longer' (comparative). Pay attention to surrounding words to choose the correct translation.
target_language_example: Il mio amico non vive più qui.
native_language_example: My friend doesn't live here anymore.

meaning: to make a living as; to live/work as (in a certain role/profession).
additional_notes: Often used with 'si guadagna da vivere come' or 'guadagnarsi da vivere come' to say someone earns their living in a given job. Can also mean 'to live like' in some contexts (e.g., 'vivere come voi' = 'to live as/like you'), so context determines whether it refers to profession (make a living) or manner/condition (live like). When talking about jobs, it's common to use 'guadagnarsi da vivere come' or 'si guadagna da vivere come'.
target_language_example: Luca si guadagna da vivere come falegname.
native_language_example: Luca makes a living as a carpenter.

meaning: 'alive and' (used to connect 'alive' with another idea or emphasize being alive)
additional_notes: Often appears in expressions that emphasize being alive (physically or metaphorically) and is followed by another adjective, verb, or noun. Can be literal (physically alive) or figurative (full of life, active, present). Word order: 'sono vivo e...' = 'I am alive and...'. Not a fixed idiom on its own; meaning comes from the words.
target_language_example: Sono vivo e voglio far sentire la mia voce.
native_language_example: I'm alive and I want to make my voice heard.

meaning: they live (followed by a plural noun/article).
additional_notes: Present tense of 'vivere' for 'loro' (they) followed by the definite article 'i' + plural noun (e.g., 'i tuoi genitori' = your parents). Used to ask or say where or how long plural subjects live. In questions about lifespan, 'Quanto (tempo) vivono i ...?' = 'How long do ... live?'.
target_language_example: Vivono i miei cugini in città.
native_language_example: My cousins live in the city.

meaning: 'the voice (that) ... me' — short for a clause where 'voce' is the subject and 'mi' is an indirect or reflexive object (literally: 'voice to me' or 'voice me').
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom but a common word order in Italian where voce (voice) is the subject and mi (to me / me) marks the person affected. Depending on the verb that follows, mi can be an indirect object (mi ricordò = it reminded me), a reflexive/dative clitic (mi si è bloccata = got stuck in my throat), or a direct/indirect object in perception verbs (sentendo la sua voce mi girai = hearing her voice I turned). Word order can vary: you may also see 'mi ricordò la voce' but placing 'voce' first emphasizes the source (the voice).
target_language_example: La voce mi raccontò una storia.
native_language_example: The voice told me a story.

meaning: very (used to modify voce = voice); 'a very ... voice' or 'speaks very ...' depending on context.
additional_notes: Voce = voice; molto is an adverb/adjective meaning 'very' or 'much'. With a noun (una voce molto bella) it intensifies an adjective describing the voice. With verbs of speaking (parla a voce molto alta) molto modifies the adjective/phrase about volume. Position can change slightly: molto + adjective (molto bella), or molto + adverb/adjective after a preposition (a voce molto alta).
target_language_example: Ha una voce molto profonda.
native_language_example: He/She has a very deep voice.

meaning: the (someone's) voice is / that voice is (followed by an adjective or description).
additional_notes: Voce = 'voice'. 'È' is the third-person singular of 'essere' (to be). Together they form a common way to describe a voice's quality (e.g., profonda, imperiale) or to point out that a voice is real/true. Use with adjectives or clauses: 'La sua voce è profonda' = 'His/her voice is deep.'
target_language_example: La sua voce è dolce e rassicurante.
native_language_example: His/her voice is sweet and reassuring.

meaning: 'want or' used in the expression 'che lo si voglia o no' meaning 'whether one wants it or not' / 'like it or not'.
additional_notes: Usually appears in the fixed expression 'che lo si voglia o no' or 'che tu/voi/lo voglia o no' to say that something will happen regardless of someone’s wishes. Also used in direct questions like 'Mi chiedo se Tom lo voglia o no' = 'I wonder whether Tom wants it or not.' The part 'voglia o' on its own is not commonly used; it's the whole phrase ('...voglia o no') that matters.
target_language_example: Che lo si voglia o no, dobbiamo decidere oggi.
native_language_example: Whether we like it or not, we must decide today.

meaning: how much time it takes to go from (one place) to (another).
additional_notes: This phrase appears inside the question structure Quanto tempo (pensa/pen­sate/pen­si) che ci voglia per andare da X a Y? Literally: “How much time do you think (that) it takes us to go from X to Y?” In spoken Italian you often hear ci voglia (subjunctive) after verbs of thinking. You can replace 'da' with 'da qui/da qua' (from here) or a specific place name. Common with travel verbs and time expressions.
target_language_example: Quanto tempo pensi che ci voglia per andare da Roma a Firenze?
native_language_example: How long do you think it takes to go from Rome to Florence?

meaning: we want a / we want one (feminine singular object)
additional_notes: Vogliamo is the first-person plural of volere (to want). Una is the feminine singular indefinite article, so use 'vogliamo una' before a feminine noun (una decisione, una soluzione, una macchina, una spiegazione). For masculine nouns use 'vogliamo un' or 'vogliamo uno' as appropriate. In spoken Italian the subject pronoun 'noi' is often dropped because the verb form already indicates 'we'.
target_language_example: Vogliamo una pausa adesso.
native_language_example: We want a break now.

meaning: 'I want to live' (expresses desire to live/reside somewhere).
additional_notes: Combines the verb volere (voglio = I want) + abitare (to live/live in). Use with a place introduced by a preposition: a/Città or in/Paese, region, or 'in campagna' (in the countryside). Can be followed by a noun or clause. For polite requests, use vorrei abitare (I would like to live).
target_language_example: Voglio abitare vicino al mare.
native_language_example: I want to live near the sea.

meaning: 'I still want' or 'I want (something) again' depending on context.
additional_notes: Combines the verb voglio (I want) with ancora. Usually means 'I still want' (continuing desire) when used with an infinitive (e.g. Voglio ancora andare = I still want to go). In some contexts it can mean 'I want again' (to do something another time), but for beginners treat it as 'I still want'. Word order: ancora normally follows voglio. Common with verbs in the infinitive.
target_language_example: Voglio ancora parlare con te domani.
native_language_example: I still want to talk with you tomorrow.

voglio avere niente a che fare con

target_language_multi_word_term: voglio avere niente a che fare con
meaning: I want to have nothing to do with (someone/something).
additional_notes: This phrase is an ungrammatical/colloquial negative construction in Italian because it lacks the negation particle "non" before the verb; the standard forms are "non voglio avere niente a che fare con..." or "non voglio avere nulla a che fare con...". Native speakers will understand it, but it sounds nonstandard or emphatic. Use to express a strong desire to avoid involvement or association.
target_language_example: Non voglio avere niente a che fare con quella situazione, ma lui continua a coinvolgermi.
native_language_example: I don't want to have anything to do with that situation, but he keeps involving me.

meaning: I really want (to)
additional_notes: Used to add emphasis to the verb that follows; expresses a strong desire. 'Voglio' = 'I want'; 'davvero' = 'really/truly'. Commonly followed by an infinitive (e.g., 'aiutare', 'vedere', 'impressionare') or a pronoun+infinitive. Formality: neutral.
target_language_example: Voglio davvero parlare con te stasera.
native_language_example: I really want to talk with you tonight.

meaning: 'I want to learn the' (used before a language name with the definite article)
additional_notes: Common phrase to express desire to learn a language. In Italian, names of languages often take the definite article (il, lo, l', la) depending on gender and starting letter: il francese, il tedesco, il berbero; l'inglese, lo spagnolo, la lingua (if generic). You can also say Voglio imparare + (language) without the article in casual speech, e.g. Voglio imparare italiano.
target_language_example: Voglio imparare il giapponese quest'anno.
native_language_example: I want to learn Japanese this year.

meaning: 'I want to return' or 'I want to go back'.
additional_notes: Combines the verb volere (voglio = I want) with ritornare (to return/go back). Use before a place or to a previous state. Can be followed by prepositions: 'a' (to), 'in'/'nel'/'nella' (in/to the), or by clauses (e.g., 'al modo in cui era'). Common in everyday speech; tone is neutral.
target_language_example: Voglio ritornare in Italia questo agosto.
native_language_example: I want to return to Italy this August.

meaning: I just want / I simply want
additional_notes: Used to soften or clarify a desire, emphasizing that the speaker's wish is simple or limited. Follows the verb 'volere' (voglio = I want) and is typically followed by an infinitive verb or a direct object. 'Semplicemente' = 'simply/just.' Tone neutral; can be used in everyday and formal contexts.
target_language_example: Voglio semplicemente parlarti per un minuto.
native_language_example: I just want to talk to you for a minute.

meaning: I only want / I just want
additional_notes: "Voglio" = I want (io form). "Soltanto" = only/just; it emphasizes limitation or simplicity of the desire. Common in spoken and written Italian. Word order can vary: "voglio solo" is also used (both mean the same). Formality: neutral.
target_language_example: Voglio soltanto un po' di tempo per pensarci.
native_language_example: I just want a little time to think about it.

meaning: I want to study / I want to learn (something).
additional_notes: Combines the verb volere (to want) with studiare (to study). Used to express desire to study a subject, a language, a place (study in a country), or to learn a profession. Can be followed by a direct object (il cinese, storia) or 'in' + place (in Australia). For a softer or more polite request, Italians often use 'vorrei studiare' (I would like to study).
target_language_example: Voglio studiare medicina all'università.
native_language_example: I want to study medicine at university.

meaning: 'I want that the...' (used to introduce a clause with plural masculine/feminine-noun subjects after 'voglio che')
additional_notes: This is the verb 'voglio' (I want) + the conjunction 'che' (that) followed by a definite plural article 'i' (the). It introduces a subordinate clause expressing a desire, command, or wish about what someone (plural) should do or be. The verb after 'che' uses the subjunctive mood when expressing desire or opinion (e.g., 'siano', 'vengano'), though in casual speech the indicative sometimes appears. Replace 'i' with other articles/pronouns as needed (e.g., 'voglio che tu...', 'voglio che gli amici...').
target_language_example: Voglio che i bambini finiscano i compiti prima di uscire.
native_language_example: I want the children to finish their homework before going out.

meaning: 'I want that the...' (used to introduce a clause expressing a desire about something/someone).
additional_notes: Voglio che + subjunctive introduces a wish or desire about an action or state. 'Il' is the masculine singular definite article ('the') and will agree with the noun that follows (il mio pensiero, il medico). The verb in the subordinate clause normally appears in the congiuntivo (subjunctive) after 'voglio che' when expressing desire, e.g. 'voglio che il mio nome venga ricordato.' In spoken Italian, the present indicative sometimes replaces the subjunctive, but learners should aim to use the subjunctive.
target_language_example: Voglio che il gatto stia dentro casa stasera.
native_language_example: I want the cat to stay inside tonight.

meaning: 'I want (that) the (feminine plural)...' — introduces a clause expressing desire about feminine plural people or things.
additional_notes: A combination of the main verb voglio (I want) + che (that) followed by a verb phrase referring to a feminine plural subject indicated by le (e.g., le tue amiche = your (female) friends). After 'che' the subordinate clause uses the subjunctive (vengano in the examples) for desires, requests, or doubts. In English you usually translate the structure as 'I want (that) ...' or more naturally 'I want your friends to...'.
target_language_example: Voglio che le mie colleghe partecipino alla riunione.
native_language_example: I want my (female) colleagues to attend the meeting.

meaning: I want (someone/something) out (of here/there/my life).
additional_notes: Common spoken phrase using 'voglio' (I want) + 'fuori' (out). Usually followed by a place (da qui, da qua, dalla mia vita) or implicit context. Agreement with object pronouns: 'lo/la/li/le/vi' indicate whom you want out. Tone is often strong/insistent — can sound angry or commanding. Not a polite request; it's more like an order or demand.
target_language_example: Li voglio fuori da casa mia.
native_language_example: I want them out of my house.

meaning: 'I want to play' (followed by the game or sport).
additional_notes: Used to express desire to play a specific game or sport. In Italian the preposition 'a' is required before the name of many games/sports (giocare a calcio, giocare a carte). For sports like tennis or basketball, Italians often still use 'giocare a' (giocare a tennis). When specifying a person to play with, add 'con' + name/pronoun (con Judy, con lei).
target_language_example: Voglio giocare a basket con Marco questo pomeriggio.
native_language_example: I want to play basketball with Marco this afternoon.

meaning: I want to take / I want to get / I want to borrow
additional_notes: Combines voglio (I want) + prendere (to take/get/borrow). Prendere is versatile: prendere qualcosa (take/get something) or prendere in prestito (to borrow). Context decides translation (e.g., "prendere delle sigarette" = buy/get cigarettes; "prendere in prestito la macchina" = borrow the car). Use voglio prendere to express a desire to do the action now or in the near future; it's informal but common in speech.
target_language_example: Voglio prendere in prestito la tua macchina domani.
native_language_example: I want to borrow your car tomorrow.

meaning: 'I want something' or 'I would like something'.
additional_notes: Used to express a desire for an unspecified thing. Often followed by a specification (da bere, da mangiare, di caldo, di dolce, etc.). Can be polite or direct; for more politeness use Vorrei qualcosa. 'Qualcosa' = 'something'.
target_language_example: Voglio qualcosa di caldo da bere, per favore.
native_language_example: I want something warm to drink, please.

meaning: I want someone / I want somebody (to do or be something).
additional_notes: Used to express desire for a person (someone) to fulfill a role or have a quality. Followed by a relative clause introduced by che, a verb infinitive introduced by a preposition (e.g., con cui, a cui) or by da + infinitive ('da amare'). In casual speech, 'voglio qualcuno' can be followed directly by a verb clause: e.g., 'Voglio qualcuno che mi aiuti.'
target_language_example: Voglio qualcuno che capisca i miei hobby.
native_language_example: I want someone who understands my hobbies.

meaning: 'I want (it) so much' or 'I really want (to).'
additional_notes: Voglio = 'I want' (io voglio). Tanto here intensifies the desire: 'very much' or 'so much'. Can be followed by a noun (voglio tanto quel libro), an infinitive verb (voglio tanto vedere quel film) or stand alone with context (Voglio tanto!). Common in spoken and written Italian.
target_language_example: Voglio tanto visitare Roma quest'estate.
native_language_example: I really want to visit Rome this summer.

meaning: the (subjunctive) form meaning 'that you (plural) go' — used after verbs expressing desire, permission, doubt, etc.
additional_notes: Voi is the plural 'you' (you all). Andiate is the present subjunctive of andare. This phrase appears in subordinate clauses introduced by verbs like volere, poter (negated), desiderare, etc.: e.g. 'I want you (pl.) to go' or 'I can't allow you (pl.) to go'. In everyday spoken Italian, voi is often replaced by voi/voi forms are less common in some regions (use voi or voi/voi?), and the subjunctive is required after the trigger verbs shown in the examples.
target_language_example: Ti chiedo che voi andiate domani mattina.
native_language_example: I'm asking that you (all) go tomorrow morning.

meaning: 'that you (plural) go to...'; present subjunctive used after verbs expressing desire/wish that others go to a place.
additional_notes: Voi andiate is the second-person plural present subjunctive of andare (voi andiate). It's used in subordinate clauses after verbs like volere (to want), desiderare, chiedere, etc., to express wishes, requests, or commands about other people's actions. The preposition a introduces the destination (a Boston, a casa). In everyday spoken Italian, voi is less common in many regions (si usa 'voi' or more often 'voi' replaced by 'voi' forms or 'loro' historically), but the structure remains standard. Use with verbs in the main clause: (Subject) + vuole/voliamo/non voglio + che + voi andiate a + place.
target_language_example: Speriamo che voi andiate a Roma questo inverno.
native_language_example: We hope that you (all) go to Rome this winter.

meaning: you (plural) to/for him or them (indirect object).
additional_notes: Voi = plural 'you'. Gli is an indirect object pronoun meaning 'to him', 'to it' (masculine) or 'to them' in informal spoken Italian; context decides whether it refers to 'him' or 'them'. In standard written Italian, 'gli' for 'to them' is less common (instead 'loro' can appear after a verb), but in speech 'gli' often covers both. The structure 'voi gli + [verb]...' means 'you (plural) [verb] to him/them'. Word order: subject (voi) + indirect object pronoun (gli) + verb.
target_language_example: Voi gli avete detto la verità?
native_language_example: Did you (plural) tell him/them the truth?

meaning: 'you (plural) them' — subject pronoun + direct object pronoun (you all them).
additional_notes: Voi = you (plural). Li is the masculine plural direct object pronoun meaning 'them' (used for groups of males or mixed gender, or when referring to masculine plural nouns). The pronoun order in Italian places the subject (voi) and the object (li) separately; in spoken/written Italian you may also see li directly after a verb (e.g., 'li conoscete?'). In formal sentences with a conjugated verb, the object pronoun usually comes before the verb when combined with auxiliary verbs (e.g., 'voi li avete visti' can become 'li avete visti?').
target_language_example: Voi li avete trovati?
native_language_example: Did you (all) find them?

meaning: 'either you (plural) or...'; used to present an alternative involving 'voi' (you plural).
additional_notes: Usually appears in the structure 'o voi o ...' (either you or ...). It offers a choice/alternative between 'voi' and another person/group. 'Voi' is the plural 'you' (informal or plural formal in Italy). Can be used in commands, questions, or hypothetical statements.
target_language_example: O voi o io dovete decidere subito.
native_language_example: Either you (plural) or I must decide right away.

meaning: 'do you (plural) like' (used to ask if something pleases you all).
additional_notes: Voi is the plural 'you' (used in Italy less often in spoken language; tu/voi distinction is formal/plural). Piacciono is the third-person plural form of piacere, which literally means 'to be pleasing to'. The structure is different from English: the thing liked is the subject and voi is the indirect object (often introduced by 'a'). Questions often include 'A voi' or 'Vi' (e.g. 'Vi piacciono?'). Use 'piace' for singular things and 'piacciono' for plural things.
target_language_example: A voi piacciono i gatti?
native_language_example: Do you (all) like cats?

meaning: you (plural) like
additional_notes: This is actually incorrect in standard Italian. The correct form is 'vi piace' or 'a voi piace' to mean 'you (plural) like'. Italian uses an indirect-object clitic (vi) with piacere: 'Vi piace il gelato?' or the full form 'A voi piace il gelato?'. 'Voi' is the subject pronoun 'you (plural)' and should not replace the clitic 'vi' in this construction. Use 'vi piace' for spoken/written Italian, or 'a voi piace' for emphasis.
target_language_example: A voi piace questo film?
native_language_example: Do you (plural) like this movie?

meaning: you are
additional_notes: present subjunctive of essere with voi (“you” plural). It is used in clauses after che, especially after verbs of wanting, hoping, doubt, or emotion: voglio che voi siate felici = “I want you to be happy.” It can also appear in expressions like ovunque voi siate = “wherever you are.”
target_language_example: Spero che voi siate pronti.
native_language_example: I hope you are ready.

meaning: Are you (plural) in favor of or against...?
additional_notes: A way to ask a group (voi = you plural) whether they support or oppose something. Often completed with 'contrari' (masc. plural) or 'contrarie' (fem. plural) and followed by the thing in question introduced by a preposition (a/al/alla). Common in meetings, discussions, or surveys. You can shorten it in speech to 'Siete favorevoli o contrari a...?' when addressing a group informally.
target_language_example: Voi siete favorevoli o contrari alla nuova regola?
native_language_example: Are you (all) in favor of or against the new rule?

meaning: 'are you in favor' (lit. 'you are pro')
additional_notes: Used to ask a group (voi = you plural) whether they support or are in favor of something. 'Pro' is an Italian loanword from Latin/English meaning 'for' or 'in favor of' and is commonly paired with 'contro' (against). Often used in spoken and informal contexts but also common in neutral speech.
target_language_example: Voi siete pro a favore del nuovo orario di lavoro?
native_language_example: Are you in favor of the new work schedule?

meaning: you (plural, feminine) yourselves / yourselves (reflexive emphasis for a group of women)
additional_notes: Reflexive/emphatic phrase used when addressing a group of females (or a mixed group using feminine form) in the second person plural. Common in imperatives and reflexive constructions: e.g. 'Fatelo voi stesse' = 'Do it yourselves.' Use 'voi stessi' for a group of males or mixed gender if masculine form is intended. In many contexts English simply uses 'yourselves' or 'you' + 'yourself' depending on emphasis.
target_language_example: Raccontateci di voi stesse senza paura.
native_language_example: Tell us about yourselves without fear.

meaning: 'yourselves' (plural reflexive/emphatic form addressing multiple people).
additional_notes: Used when speaking to more than one person. Can be reflexive (acting on yourselves) or emphatic (be yourselves). Formality: 'voi' is the familiar plural 'you' used in Italy; in very formal contexts you might hear 'loro' or 'sé stessi' but 'voi stessi' is common for groups. Pairing: 'voi' + 'stessi' matches gender/mixed group (stessi), for feminine plural use 'voi stesse'.
target_language_example: Siate voi stessi in ogni situazione.
native_language_example: Be yourselves in every situation.

meaning: the present-subjunctive form of 'stare' for 'voi' — 'that you (plural) are' (used in wishes, hopes, requests).
additional_notes: Used with verbs like sperare, volere, desiderare to express wishes, hopes, requests, or hypothetical situations about a group (you plural). Appears only in subordinate clauses after expressions like 'spero che', 'voglio che'. Pronunciation: voi stiate [voɪ ˈstjaːte].
target_language_example: Spero che voi stiate bene durante il viaggio.
native_language_example: I hope that you (all) are well during the trip.

meaning: 'to fly away' or more generally 'to go away quickly/leave'.
additional_notes: Literally means 'to fly away' (volare = to fly, via = away). Used both for literal flying (birds, planes) and figuratively to mean leaving, escaping quickly, or getting rid of someone/something. Can be neutral or informal; can also appear in aggressive/threatening contexts (e.g., 'Ti faccio volare via' as a threat).
target_language_example: Perché non provi a volare via e vedere cosa succede?
native_language_example: Why don't you try to fly away and see what happens?

meaning: "to care for" or "to love (affectionately)" (expresses affectionate, non-romantic love/care).
additional_notes: Used to express affection or care without the romantic intensity of amare. Commonly used for family, friends, pets, or someone you care about. Often followed by an indirect object pronoun (e.g., "Ti voglio bene") or a person introduced with a preposition (less common). Neutral register — everyday language. Conjugation is based on volere (e.g., voglio, volevo, ho voluto).
target_language_example: Ti voglio bene, mamma — ma ti ho sempre voluto bene anche quando litigavamo.
native_language_example: I love you / I care about you, Mom — and I've always cared about you even when we argued.

meaning: to mean
additional_notes: Usually seen in conjugated forms like vuol dire or vuole dire. It is used to explain the meaning of a word, phrase, action, or situation. Literally it is 'to want to say,' but in normal use it often means 'to mean.'
target_language_example: Non capisco che cosa possa volere dire questa frase.
native_language_example: I don't understand what this sentence could mean.

meaning: to want to know about it/them; to care/about something (want to find out)
additional_notes: Idiomatic construction from volere + ne + sapere. The clitic ne refers back to something already mentioned (about it/them). Often appears as saperne or volerne sapere in various tenses (es. Voglio saperne di più, Non ne voglio più sapere). Can express desire for information (Voglio volerne sapere di più) or indifference/refusal (Non ne voglio sapere). Word order and pronoun placement change with tense and mood.
target_language_example: Voglio volerne sapere di più.
native_language_example: I want to know more about it.

meaning: wanted to do it (by) herself / wanted to do it alone
additional_notes: This phrase is part of a larger clause like "voleva farlo da sola" (she wanted to do it alone/by herself). "Voleva" is the imperfect of "volere" (wanted). "Far lo" = "to do it" and "da sola" means "alone/by herself" (feminine singular). Replace "da solo" for a male subject, or omit "da" and say "voleva farlo sola" is not standard—use "da sola". Used to report a past desire or intention.
target_language_example: Ha detto che voleva farlo da sola.
native_language_example: She said she wanted to do it by herself.

meaning: he/she/it wanted to work (or you formal/they in context); imperfect tense indicating a past desire to work.
additional_notes: Voleva lavorare is the third-person singular (lui/lei) form of volere + infinitive in the imperfect (voleva) + lavorare. It expresses an ongoing or repeated past desire or intention to work, or a polite/backstory statement (e.g., 'he wanted to work' / 'she was trying to work'). Depending on context, subject can be implied and may also mean 'you (formal) wanted to work.' Common in storytelling and explanations about past situations.
target_language_example: Quando era giovane, voleva lavorare all'estero.
native_language_example: When she was young, she wanted to work abroad.

meaning: 'wanted to work for' (someone or some organization).
additional_notes: Past imperfect of volere + infinitive lavorare + preposition per. Used to report a past desire or intention to be employed by or work on behalf of a person, company, or group. The indirect object (te, lei, voi, etc.) follows per: e.g. 'lavorare per te' = 'work for you'.
target_language_example: Lei voleva lavorare per quell'azienda, ma ha scelto un'altra offerta.
native_language_example: She wanted to work for that company, but she chose a different offer.

meaning: wanted to die (expresses past desire to die)
additional_notes: Voleva morire is the imperfect of volere + infinitive morire. It reports a past desire or wish (often used to report someone's feelings or statements). In English it usually translates as "wanted to die." Context can indicate literal suicidal desire or be hyperbolic ("I wanted to die" meaning extreme embarrassment). Tense: imperfect (voleva) is used for ongoing, repeated, or reported past states. You can change the subject (volevo morire = I wanted to die; volevamo morire = we wanted to die).
target_language_example: Quando vide il risultato, disse che voleva morire.
native_language_example: When she saw the result, she said she wanted to die.

meaning: wanted to cry / felt like crying.
additional_notes: Past-tense (imperfetto) of volere + infinitive piangere. Used to report someone's desire or emotional state in the past (He/She wanted to cry). Common in reported speech: "Ha detto che voleva piangere" = "He/She said that (they) wanted to cry."
target_language_example: Quando ascoltò la notizia, mi disse che voleva piangere.
native_language_example: When he heard the news, he told me he wanted to cry.

meaning: 'he/she/it wanted to study the' (imperfect tense + infinitive phrase with definite article)
additional_notes: This is a fragment: voleva = 3rd person singular imperfect of volere (to want). Studiare il = to study the (masculine singular noun follows). Commonly used to describe a past desire or intention that may or may not have been fulfilled: e.g. "Voleva studiare il pianoforte" (He/she wanted to study the piano). The pronoun/subject is often clear from context. You will usually see a noun after il.
target_language_example: Quando era giovane, voleva studiare il pianoforte.
native_language_example: When she was young, she wanted to study the piano.

meaning: 'wanted some' (him/her/you/it wanted some) — polite/neutral way to say someone wanted some of something (usually food/drink).
additional_notes: Voleva is the imperfect of volere (to want) and here is used to describe a past desire or to soften a request. Del = di + il (some/of the) used before masculine singular nouns; combine to mean “some” (e.g., del caffè = some coffee). In questions or reported speech it can mean 'would like some' (polite). You can change tense/person: vuole del (wants/sometimes used as 'would you like some?'), vorrebbe del (conditional/polite 'would like some').
target_language_example: Lei voleva del tè dopo cena.
native_language_example: She wanted some tea after dinner.

meaning: he/she/you (formal) wanted some / wanted some of (feminine or plural noun).
additional_notes: Voleva is the imperfect of volere (to want). 'Delle' is the partitive article used before plural nouns (or feminine plural) and often translates as 'some' or 'any' in English. Together they indicate someone wanted some quantity or unspecified items (e.g. 'voleva delle risposte' = 'she/he wanted some answers'). Context tells the subject (e.g. 'Lui voleva...' or 'Mary disse che voleva...').
target_language_example: Lei voleva delle informazioni prima di partire.
native_language_example: She wanted some information before leaving.

meaning: 'wanted the' (third-person singular, imperfect tense)
additional_notes: Voleva is the imperfect of volere (to want). 'Voleva la' is used to describe what someone (he/she/it) wanted in the past or to express a past desire/intent. The noun or phrase following 'la' provides the object (feminine singular) — e.g. la custodia, la polizia. For masculine or plural objects the article changes (il, lo, i, le).
target_language_example: Lei voleva la custodia dei bambini.
native_language_example: She wanted the custody of the children.

meaning: wanted a
additional_notes: Not a fixed expression: voleva is the imperfect of volere ("to want"), so it often means "wanted" or "used to want," depending on context. Una is the feminine singular form of "a/an," so this phrase is used before a feminine singular noun: voleva una casa = "wanted a house."
target_language_example: Da piccola, voleva una chitarra.
native_language_example: When she was little, she wanted a guitar.

meaning: once a week; one time per week.
additional_notes: Used to indicate frequency (how often) something happens. Can appear before or after the verb or at the start of a sentence (e.g., "Una volta a settimana, ..."). Common alternatives: "una volta alla settimana" (same meaning).
target_language_example: Vado al mercato una volta a settimana.
native_language_example: I go to the market once a week.

meaning: '(the) time that/we ...' — used to refer to a particular occasion when something happened (with 'ci' = us/there/each other depending on verb).
additional_notes: Commonly appears in phrases like 'la prima volta che ci siamo.../incontriamo' to talk about a specific occurrence. 'Volta' = 'time' (occasion). 'Che' introduces the clause. 'Ci' can be a reflexive/object pronoun meaning 'each other' or 'us' (ci siamo visti = we saw each other), or an adverbial 'there' in other contexts. Use past tense for completed past events (ci siamo incontrati), present for habitual (ci incontriamo).
target_language_example: La volta che ci siamo incontrati era al concerto.
native_language_example: The time we met was at the concert.

meaning: each time (that) her/it; whenever I/you/we ... her/it
additional_notes: Commonly appears as part of expressions like "ogni volta che..." (every time that...) or "la prima volta che..." (the first time that...). "La" is a direct object pronoun (her/it) referring to a feminine noun previously mentioned. Word order can vary: you may see "ogni volta che la vedo" or "questa è la prima volta che la assaggia" (though standard spelling uses "assaggia" for 'he/she tastes'). Use to introduce repeated reactions or occurrences.
target_language_example: Ogni volta che la vedo, mi viene da sorridere.
native_language_example: Every time I see her, I feel like smiling.

meaning: literally 'time that it/him' — used in phrases like 'every/first time that (you) him/it...' to refer to occasions when something happens involving 'lo' (him/it).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed standalone phrase but a combination: 'volta' (time/occasion) + a clause introduced by 'che' (that) and the object pronoun 'lo' (him/it). Common patterns: 'ogni volta che lo...' (every time that him/it...), 'la prima volta che lo...' (the first time that him/it...). The meaning depends on context and what 'lo' refers to (a person or an object). Word order: 'ogni/questa/la prima volta che lo + verb'.
target_language_example: Ogni volta che lo vedo, gli porto un caffè.
native_language_example: Every time that I see him, I bring him a coffee.

meaning: 'time (that) I' or 'time (that) me' — used to refer to occasions when something happens to or involves the speaker.
additional_notes: This phrase appears in expressions like "la prima volta che mi..." (the first time that I...) or "ogni volta che mi..." (every time that I...). It introduces a clause describing an event affecting the speaker (mi = to me / me). Can be followed by verbs that take an indirect object (capitare, succedere) or reflexive/pronominal verbs (faccio, lavo, bacio with mi/mi).
target_language_example: Ogni volta che mi scrivi, mi illumino.
native_language_example: Every time you write to me, I light up.

meaning: '(the) time that/when you...' — used to refer to an occasion or moment involving 'you'.
additional_notes: Combines 'volta' (time/occasion) with a relative clause introduced by 'che' and the indirect object pronoun 'ti' (to you) or part of the verb phrase addressing 'you'. Common in phrases like 'la prima volta che ti ho visto' (the first time I saw you) or 'ogni volta che ti ...' (every time you ...). Word order can vary (e.g., 'la volta che ti ho visto', 'ogni volta che ti invitiamo').
target_language_example: La prima volta che ti ho parlato eri molto timido.
native_language_example: The first time I spoke to you you were very shy.

meaning: to turn one's back (on someone); to ignore, abandon, or refuse to help someone
additional_notes: Used both literally (physically turning one's back) and figuratively (expressing abandonment, indifference, or betrayal). Often followed by a prepositional phrase indicating whom or what you're turning away from (e.g., 'a qualcuno', 'al passato'). Common in news, literature, and everyday speech describing broken relationships or social rejection.
target_language_example: Dopo il litigio, Marco ha deciso di voltare le spalle a Giulia.
native_language_example: After the argument, Marco decided to turn his back on Giulia.

meaning: 'turned (one's) back (on someone/something)' — i.e., to abandon, ignore, or refuse help.
additional_notes: This is a past participle construction of voltare le spalle (lit. 'to turn the shoulders'). Used to say someone turned their back on someone/something emotionally or physically (abandoned, ignored, refused support). Commonly appears with a person or thing as direct object (e.g., le spalle) and often with a preposition a/di before the person: 'voltare le spalle a qualcuno'.
target_language_example: Non mi aspettavo che mi avresti voltato le spalle.
native_language_example: I didn't expect you to turn your back on me.

meaning: times that
additional_notes: Used to count occurrences or to say how often something happens. Often appears in expressions like "tutte le volte che" (every time that) or with a number + "volte" to mean "(number) times" (e.g. "tre volte che" = "three times that" / "I've called three times"). In English, it's usually translated as "times that/when" or simply "times" depending on context.
target_language_example: Tutte le volte che piove, porto l'ombrello.
native_language_example: Every time it rains, I bring an umbrella.

meaning: sometimes it goes / sometimes it works (depending on context)
additional_notes: A short, informal phrase. 'Volte' = 'sometimes' (plural of 'volta' used adverbially). 'Va' = 'it goes' or 'it works' (3rd person singular of 'andare'). Together, 'volte va' is used in conversational Italian to mean 'sometimes it works/turns out that way' or 'sometimes it's okay' — often part of a larger sentence (e.g. 'A volte va bene' = 'Sometimes it's fine'). Alone it sounds colloquial and may omit words that are understood from context.
target_language_example: Non sempre è perfetto, ma a volte va.
native_language_example: It's not always perfect, but sometimes it works.

meaning: 'how many times (to) you' — used to ask or complain about the number of times something has happened to/for you (plural or polite).
additional_notes: Volte = 'times' (occurrences). Vi is the indirect/direct object pronoun for 'you' (plural or polite). In these examples it's used in questions like 'Quante volte vi devo/chiedo...?' or 'Quante volte vi ho detto...?' to express frustration or to ask how often something happens. Word order: Quante volte + vi + verb. Can be translated as 'How many times do I have to ask you...?' or 'How many times have I told you...?'
target_language_example: Quante volte vi devo ricordare di chiudere la porta?
native_language_example: How many times do I have to remind you to close the door?

meaning: the volume of (the) — referring to sound level of something (e.g., radio, TV).
additional_notes: Used to talk about the loudness of a specific device or source. 'Volume' is masculine in Italian (il volume), so 'del' + noun becomes 'del' or 'della' depending on the following noun's gender: 'il volume della radio' (the volume of the radio). Common verbs with this phrase: abbassare (turn down), alzare (turn up), controllare (check).
target_language_example: Puoi alzare il volume della musica, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you turn up the volume of the music, please?

meaning: wanted to be a (male role/profession) — past participle construction expressing a long-standing desire
additional_notes: Used with ho/ha (or other forms of avere) + voluto + essere + un/una + noun to say someone 'always wanted to be' something. The gender/article (un/una) and the noun change with the role; for female roles use 'una' (e.g., voluto essere una dottoressa). Often preceded by time expressions like 'sempre' (always) or 'da che mi ricordo'.
target_language_example: Da bambino ho sempre voluto essere un pilota.
native_language_example: As a child I always wanted to be a pilot.

meaning: Would you like a (feminine singular noun)? — polite offer or question.
additional_notes: Vorresti is the conditional form of 'volere' (to want) used to make polite offers or requests. 'Una' is the indefinite article for feminine singular nouns (e.g., una banana, una birra, una camera). Change the article to 'un' for masculine nouns (vorresti un caffè?). Common in everyday conversation for offers and suggestions.
target_language_example: Vorresti una mela prima di partire?
native_language_example: Would you like an apple before leaving?

meaning: your house is / is your house (polite/plural 'your').
additional_notes: Vostra is the feminine singular possessive for 'you' (plural or formal) used with casa. È is the third-person singular of 'essere' (to be). Use 'la vostra casa' to say 'your house' when speaking to more than one person or formally; 'la tua casa' for one person familiar. Word order can be the same as English: 'La vostra casa è ...' (Your house is ...), and you can form questions by intonation or adding a question mark.
target_language_example: La vostra casa è vicino al parco?
native_language_example: Is your house near the park?

meaning: your breakfast (plural or formal 'your')
additional_notes: Vostra is the possessive adjective for 'your' when addressing multiple people (voi) or more formal/archaic singular uses; colazione = breakfast. Commonly used when referring to someone's meal in the morning. Use la tua colazione for one person (informal).
target_language_example: La vostra colazione è pronta: venite a tavola.
native_language_example: Your breakfast is ready: come to the table.

meaning: your ideas (plural, polite/formal or plural 'you')
additional_notes: Vostre is the feminine/plural possessive pronoun for 'voi' (you plural). Use 'vostre idee' when speaking to multiple people or formally addressing someone in some regions; 'idee' is feminine plural, so 'vostre' agrees. For one person informal use 'le tue idee'.
target_language_example: Apprezzo molto le vostre idee sul progetto.
native_language_example: I really appreciate your ideas about the project.

meaning: 'your hands are' (plural, polite/informal depending on context) - describing the condition or quality of someone's hands.
additional_notes: Le vostre = your (plural or formal in some regions); mani = hands; sono = are. Use when addressing more than one person or when using the plural polite form. For singular informal 'your' use le tue mani sono; for singular formal use le Sue mani sono (capital S) in very formal writing. Commonly followed by adjectives or descriptions (es. fredde, sporche, morbide).
target_language_example: Le vostre mani sono molto calde oggi.
native_language_example: Your hands are very warm today.

meaning: your money (plural/formal or addressing multiple people).
additional_notes: Vostri is the plural (or formal) second-person possessive adjective meaning 'your' when talking to more than one person or politely to one person in some contexts. Soldi means 'money' (plural). Use il vostro denaro / i vostri soldi; both are common. Word order: possessive before noun. For talking to one person informally use i tuoi soldi.
target_language_example: Posso prendere i vostri soldi per il biglietto?
native_language_example: Can I take your money for the ticket?

meaning: your help for / your help to (do something).
additional_notes: Used to request or mention assistance from a group of people (vostro = your, plural polite/informal). Commonly followed by an infinitive or a noun phrase describing the task or purpose: e.g. "per aiutarla" (to help her) or "per il mio lavoro" (for my work). Equivalent to "il vostro aiuto per" or "ho bisogno del vostro aiuto per..."
target_language_example: Ho bisogno del vostro aiuto per finire questo progetto.
native_language_example: I need your help to finish this project.

meaning: your horse (plural or formal 'your' addressing multiple people or formal singular).
additional_notes: Vostro = possessive adjective meaning 'your' when speaking to more than one person (or in formal contexts in some regions). Cavallo = horse. Use 'vostro cavallo' to say 'your horse' (masculine singular noun). Agreement: for feminine/plural nouns change cavallo -> vostra/vostre/ i vostri as needed.
target_language_example: Il vostro cavallo è molto gentile con i bambini.
native_language_example: Your horse is very gentle with the children.

meaning: your food (plural or formal 'you').
additional_notes: Vostro is the possessive adjective for 'your' when addressing more than one person (voi) or in formal plural contexts; it agrees in number with the possessor, not the thing (cibo stays singular). Use 'il vostro cibo' for masculine singular nouns like 'cibo'. For informal singular 'your' (tu) use 'il tuo cibo'.
target_language_example: Avete mangiato il vostro cibo?
native_language_example: Have you (all) eaten your food?

meaning: your French (language) — polite/plural form
additional_notes: Vostro is the polite or plural possessive 'your' (used for voi or formal you). 'Francese' here means the French language or ability in French. Use to talk about someone's skill in French. For informal singular you (tu), you'd say 'il tuo francese' or simply 'il tuo francese sta migliorando?'.
target_language_example: Il vostro francese è davvero migliorato dall'anno scorso.
native_language_example: Your French has really improved since last year.

meaning: your cat (plural or formal 'your').
additional_notes: Vostro is the possessive adjective meaning 'your' when addressing more than one person (plural) or sometimes used formally. It agrees in gender/number with the noun: vostro gatto = your (male) cat; la vostra casa = your house. In everyday spoken Italian, voi/il vostro is used for plural 'you' in Italy; in many regions or contexts people use 'tu/il tuo' for informal singular and 'voi/il vostro' for plural. Use 'il vostro gatto?' to ask 'Is that your cat?'.
target_language_example: Il vostro gatto è sul divano.
native_language_example: Your cat is on the sofa.

meaning: your game (plural or formal 'your') — can mean a literal game, deck/hand in card games, or figuratively 'your move' or 'your performance'.
additional_notes: Vostro is the plural or formal possessive 'your' (used for voi). Gioco primarily means 'game' (sport, board game, video game), but in card contexts can mean 'hand' or 'play'. In expressions like "Fate il vostro gioco" it can mean "make your move" or "do what you normally do". Register is neutral; use 'tuo gioco' for singular informal you.
target_language_example: Portate il vostro gioco migliore per la serata.
native_language_example: Bring your best game for the evening.

meaning: your English (plural or formal 'your' addressing more than one person or polite singular).
additional_notes: Composed of the possessive adjective 'vostro' (your) + noun 'inglese' (English language). Use 'vostro' when speaking to multiple people or formally to one person in some contexts. For informal singular 'your' use 'tuo' (tuo inglese). 'Inglese' can mean the English language or an English person depending on context, but here it refers to the language.
target_language_example: Il vostro inglese è migliorato molto quest'anno.
native_language_example: Your English has improved a lot this year.

meaning: your [number of] — used to ask for a specific identifying number (account, room, plate, etc.).
additional_notes: Combine 'vostro' (your, plural/formal) + 'numero di' + noun (e.g., conto, stanza, targa). Common when requesting an identifying number. Use 'il vostro numero' before the noun or 'il numero della vostra ...' as alternatives. If speaking to one person informally, use 'tuo numero di'.
target_language_example: Mi puoi dare il vostro numero di telefono?
native_language_example: Can you give me your phone number?

meaning: your bread (plural or formal 'your').
additional_notes: Vostro is the possessive adjective meaning 'your' when addressing more than one person or using a formal plural in Italian; pane means 'bread'. Agreement: 'vostro' matches the possessor (plural/formal), not the noun's gender/number; for a singular/plural distinction the noun changes (il vostro pane = your bread; i vostri pani is uncommon — usually pane is uncountable). Common in contexts like bakeries, meals, or offering food.
target_language_example: Posso assaggiare il vostro pane, per favore?
native_language_example: Can I taste your bread, please?

meaning: your secret (plural or formal 'your').
additional_notes: Vostro is the possessive adjective for 'you' (plural) or polite/formal singular in some contexts; segreto means 'secret'. Use to talk about a secret belonging to the person or group you're addressing. In everyday Italian, for informal singular 'your' you'd use 'tuo segreto'.
target_language_example: Il vostro segreto è al sicuro con noi.
native_language_example: Your secret is safe with us.

meaning: literally 'grades are' or 'votes are' — the start of a sentence stating what the grades/votes are
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself but two separate words: 'voti' (plural of voto) can mean 'grades' (school marks) or 'votes' (in an election). 'Sono' is the third-person plural of 'essere' (to be). You'll see 'i voti sono...' followed by a description or a number (e.g. 'i voti sono alti', 'i voti sono trenta'). In speech the article is often included ('i voti sono').
target_language_example: I voti sono buoni quest'anno.
native_language_example: The grades are good this year.

voti sono stati ben al di sotto

target_language_multi_word_term: voti sono stati ben al di sotto
meaning: grades were well below (something), e.g. the average
additional_notes: Used to say that someone's grades were significantly lower than a reference point (la media = the average). 'Ben al di sotto' intensifies 'al di sotto' (below). Structure: subject + 'voti sono stati ben al di sotto (della media)'. Replace 'voti' with a different noun as needed (e.g. 'i risultati sono stati ben al di sotto').
target_language_example: I miei voti sono stati ben al di sotto della media quest'anno.
native_language_example: My grades were well below the average this year.

meaning: street vendor
additional_notes: Informal and slang expression used in Italy (derived from Southern Italian dialect imitation of 'vuoi comprare?' = 'do you want to buy?'). Refers to non-Italian itinerant sellers who hawk goods in public places (beaches, streets). Can be derogatory or stereotypical; avoid using it in polite/formal contexts. Plural often used as vu cumprà or vu cumpra'.
target_language_example: Sulla spiaggia ci sono sempre i vu' cumprà che vendono coperte e occhiali da sole.
native_language_example: On the beach there are always street vendors selling blankets and sunglasses.

meaning: you want to be
additional_notes: Second-person singular form, used when speaking to one person informally (tu). It combines vuoi (“want”) with essere (“to be”) and is often followed by an adjective or noun: vuoi essere libero, vuoi essere mio amico. In Italian, the same word order can be used for both statements and questions; punctuation and intonation show which one it is.
target_language_example: Vuoi essere felice?
native_language_example: Do you want to be happy?

meaning: 'do you want to return' (or 'you want to return' depending on context).
additional_notes: Vuoi = second-person singular of volere (to want). Tornare = to return/come back. Together usually appears in questions or conditional clauses: 'Se vuoi tornare...' = 'If you want to return/come back...'. In direct questions word order can be 'Vuoi tornare a casa?' (Do you want to go back home?). Use different prepositions after 'tornare' for places: 'tornare a casa', 'tornare in Australia', 'tornare al tuo paese'.
target_language_example: Vuoi tornare in Italia quest'estate?
native_language_example: Do you want to return to Italy this summer?

meaning: you want me to... (start of a subordinate clause asking someone if they want the speaker to do something / go away)
additional_notes: This is the beginning of a common Italian construction: 'Vuoi che...' + subjunctive verb, where 'me' (often followed by pronouns like 'ne' or verbs like 'vada') refers to 'me' (the speaker). In examples it appears as 'vuoi che me ne vada' (do you want me to go away?) or 'vuoi che me ne sbarazzi' (do you want me to get rid of it for you?). The full meaning depends on the rest of the clause. Use subjunctive after 'vuoi che' (e.g. 'vada', 'sbarazzi').
target_language_example: Vuoi che me ne vada adesso?
native_language_example: Do you want me to leave now?

meaning: Do you want some/of the (used before an uncountable noun or a part of something).
additional_notes: Vuoi is the 2nd-person singular informal form of 'volere' (to want). Della is the partitive article (di + la) used to mean 'some' or 'any' before feminine singular nouns that are uncountable or when offering a portion. In questions it’s common in offers (Vuoi della pasta? — Would you like some pasta?). For masculine nouns use 'del' (di + il), for plural use 'dei/degli/delle' as appropriate. You can omit 'della' and use just 'vuoi' + noun if context allows, but the partitive signals an indefinite amount.
target_language_example: Vuoi della cioccolata dopo cena?
native_language_example: Do you want some chocolate after dinner?

meaning: does this mean / does this (feminine) mean?
additional_notes: Informal spoken contraction of 'vuole dire questa' or more commonly part of the question 'Che vuol dire questa?' meaning 'What does this mean?' When addressing a feminine noun (questa) or pointing to something close. Often used in questions to ask for the meaning or explanation of something. More standard: 'Che cosa vuol dire questa?' or 'Cosa vuol dire questa?'.
target_language_example: Che vuol dire questa parola?
native_language_example: What does this word mean?

meaning: wants still / still wants (to)
additional_notes: A common combination of the verb 'volere' (to want) in the third person singular ('vuole') plus the adverb 'ancora' (still/again). Used to say someone continues to want something or to do something. Word order can vary (e.g., 'ancora vuole' is possible but less common). Context determines whether 'ancora' means 'still' (continuation) or 'again'; with actions it usually means 'still'.
target_language_example: Lui vuole ancora parlare con te stasera.
native_language_example: He still wants to talk to you tonight.

meaning: wants me to (leave/ go away/from here).
additional_notes: This is part of the full phrase "(lui/lei) vuole che me ne vada" meaning "(he/she) wants me to leave." "Vuole che" introduces a subordinate clause with the subjunctive (vada). "Me ne" combines the object pronoun "me" (me) and "ne" (away/from here/about it) — together meaning "me away/from here." Common in questions: "Vuole che me ne vada?" = "Does he/she want me to go?"
target_language_example: Maria vuole che me ne vada subito.
native_language_example: Maria wants me to leave right away.

meaning: he/she/you (formal) wants to play
additional_notes: Present-tense, third-person singular of volere + infinitive giocare. Can mean 'he wants to play', 'she wants to play', or polite 'you want to play' (Lei vuole giocare). Followed by 'a' + sport when specifying a game: vuole giocare a tennis/pallavolo. To ask someone directly informally use 'vuoi giocare'.
target_language_example: Vuole giocare a calcio con noi?
native_language_example: Does he/she/you (formal) want to play soccer with us?

meaning: would like a cup (of ...); do you/he/she want(s) a cup
additional_notes: Commonly used to offer or ask if someone wants a cup of a drink (caffè, tè, latte). Vuole is the formal/third-person singular of volere (lei/lui/Lei). In informal plural or singular among friends you might hear 'vuoi una tazza' (tu) or 'volete una tazza' (voi). The phrase is followed by 'di' + the drink: 'una tazza di caffè', etc.
target_language_example: Vuole una tazza di tè?
native_language_example: Would you like a cup of tea?

meaning: to spend the weekend with (someone).
additional_notes: Common way to say you spent or spent time over the weekend with a person or group. Often appears with passato/trascorso (ho passato/ho trascorso) and a pronoun or noun (con lui, con lei, con loro, con mia nonna). 'Weekend' is an English loanword widely used in Italian. Use 'con' + person or pronoun.
target_language_example: Questo weekend passo il weekend con i miei genitori.
native_language_example: This weekend I'm spending the weekend with my parents.

meaning: my aunt (with indirect object pronoun 'mi' = to/for me or 'me' as receiver).
additional_notes: This phrase combines 'zia' (aunt) with the clitic pronoun 'mi' (to me / for me / me). In the examples it appears in two roles: as the subject ('Mia zia mi ha dato...' — 'My aunt gave me...') or before a verb as 'Zia mi insegna...' ('Aunt teaches me...'). Remember Italian often places the pronoun before the verb (mi ha dato, mi insegna) and uses 'mia zia' or just 'zia' depending on context.
target_language_example: Mia zia mi ha comprato un regalo.
native_language_example: My aunt bought me a present.

meaning: my/your/the uncle lives (or 'an uncle lives' depending on possessor).
additional_notes: Combines 'zio' (uncle) with the verb 'abitare' (to live). In the examples 'Mio zio abita…' means 'My uncle lives…'. You can change the possessor (mio, tuo, suo, etc.) or the subject (Il mio zio abita) and adjust the location with 'a' for cities/countries (a Madrid, a New York), 'in' for larger countries/regions (in Australia, in Germania), 'in' for buildings/places (in un appartamento), and 'vicino a' or 'vicino alla' for 'near'.
target_language_example: Tuo zio abita vicino al parco.
native_language_example: Your uncle lives near the park.

meaning: '(my/your/his/her) uncle lives' — a simple noun + verb phrase used to state where an uncle lives. The possessor (mio, tuo, suo, etc.) is often added before 'zio' to show whose uncle.
additional_notes: Not an idiom; compositional phrase: zio (uncle) + vive (he/she/it lives). In Italian the subject pronoun is usually omitted because the verb form indicates person (vive = he/she/it). To specify location use prepositions: 'a' for cities and some islands (a New York, a Tashkent), 'in' for many countries/regions (in Germania, in Svizzera) and for enclosed places (in una villa). Agreement: if you mean 'my uncle lives' say 'Mio zio vive'.
target_language_example: Mio zio vive a New York City.
native_language_example: My uncle lives in New York City.

meaning: ‘sugar, please’ — a polite way to ask for sugar or to request that sugar be added.
additional_notes: Used when asking someone to pass sugar at the table, to request sugar for a drink, or to order a coffee with sugar. Common in spoken and polite contexts. You can change the verb or pronoun (e.g., "Mi passi lo zucchero, per favore?", "Passa lo zucchero, per favore") to match formality and number. "Per favore" softens the request; other options: "per cortesia" (more formal) or just "grazie" after receiving it.
target_language_example: Mi passi lo zucchero, per favore?
native_language_example: Could you pass me the sugar, please?

meaning: sugar in/for (used before a noun with an article, e.g. 'zucchero al tè' = sugar in the tea)
additional_notes: This is a combination of 'zucchero' (sugar) + the preposition 'a' + definite article (il/lo/la → al/allo/alla). 'Zucchero al' appears when saying you add sugar to or put sugar in something (e.g., 'zucchero al tè', 'zucchero al caffè'). In many examples you will see 'dello zucchero' (some sugar) or 'lo zucchero' (the sugar) before 'al'. Literal translation into English is possible but word order differs: English says 'sugar in the tea' or 'sugar to the tea' — more naturally 'sugar in/for the tea' or simply 'add sugar to the tea.'
target_language_example: Metti dello zucchero al caffè, per favore.
native_language_example: Put some sugar in the coffee, please.

meaning: brown sugar; unrefined cane sugar
additional_notes: Refers to sugar made from sugar cane, typically brown and less refined than white sugar. Commonly used in cooking, baking, and to sweeten drinks. In everyday speech it can be shortened to just "zucchero" if context is clear, but "zucchero di canna" specifies the type.
target_language_example: Metti due cucchiaini di zucchero di canna nel caffè.
native_language_example: Put two teaspoons of brown sugar in the coffee.

meaning: sugar in my (…); used to say you add sugar to something you drink (tea, coffee, etc.).
additional_notes: This phrase is followed by the noun for the drink (e.g., tè, caffè). In Italian you can also say "zucchero nel mio caffè/tè" or simply "nel mio" when the drink is clear from context. To state quantity, add a number + measure (due cucchiaini di zucchero). To express frequency, use adverbs like "mai" (never), "raramente" (rarely), "sempre" (always).
target_language_example: Metto un cucchiaino di zucchero nel mio caffè.
native_language_example: I put one teaspoon of sugar in my coffee.

meaning: sugar in his/her/your (formal) — used to say someone puts sugar into their drink (e.g., coffee).
additional_notes: Combines zucchero (sugar) with nel suo (in his/her/your [formal] + masculine singular noun). The possessive suo agrees with the thing possessed (here caffè). In everyday speech Italians often omit the article: "zucchero nel suo caffè" or say "zucchero nel suo" when context (the drink) is clear. To say "in my/your/his/her/our/their" change the possessive (mio, tuo, suo, nostro, vostro, loro) and the article if needed (nel = in + il).
target_language_example: Ha messo dello zucchero nel suo caffè.
native_language_example: He/she put some sugar in his/her coffee.

meaning: is/has become used to; is accustomed to
additional_notes: Literally from abituarsi (to get used to). Used to say someone is accustomed to a situation, place, person, or habit. Commonly appears in passato prossimo (si è abituato) to mean 'has gotten used to'; can take a preposition a (a vivere, a me) or al/alla (al lavoro, al nuovo ambiente). Agreement in gender/number changes (è abituata, sono abituati).
target_language_example: Tom si è abituato alla vita in città.
native_language_example: Tom has gotten used to life in the city.

meaning: 'noticed that' or 'realized that'.
additional_notes: From the verb accorgersi (si è accorto = he/she noticed). Used to say someone became aware of something. Commonly followed by che + clause. Can be reflexive: "si è accorto" (he/she noticed). In questions or negatives the auxiliary changes: "non si è accorto" = didn't notice.
target_language_example: Si è accorto che la porta era aperta.
native_language_example: He noticed that the door was open.

meaning: has noticed / became aware of
additional_notes: Typically appears as part of the reflexive construction "si è accorto di" (past) or "si accorge di" (present) to indicate that someone noticed or became aware of someone/something. The verb agrees with the subject (e.g., "si è accorto" vs "si è accorta"). Often followed by "di" + noun/pronoun. Common in everyday speech; neutral register.
target_language_example: Nessuno si è accorto di lui.
native_language_example: No one noticed him.

meaning: is asleep / has fallen asleep.
additional_notes: Third-person singular of 'essere addormentato' or used in combination with the reflexive 'addormentarsi' (si è addormentato) to indicate someone fell asleep. With a named male subject you often see 'Tom si è addormentato'; for a female use 'si è addormentata'. Context determines whether it reads as a past action ('has fallen asleep') or a present state ('is asleep').
target_language_example: Dopo la lunga passeggiata, Tom è addormentato sul divano.
native_language_example: After the long walk, Tom fell asleep on the sofa.

meaning: 'has gotten up' / 'is up' (refers to someone having risen from bed)
additional_notes: This is the passato prossimo form of alzarsi used with the reflexive pronoun (si è alzato / si è alzata). Used to ask or say that someone got up (from bed) at a particular time or whether they are already up. Agreement changes with gender/number: è alzato (he), è alzata (she), sono alzati (they masc/mixed), sono alzate (they fem). Often appears with time expressions (stamattina, presto, tardi) and in questions: A che ora si è alzato?
target_language_example: A che ora si è alzato stamattina?
native_language_example: What time did he get up this morning?

meaning: she is angry
additional_notes: Refers to a female subject (arrabbiata = feminine). In examples the phrase often uses the passato prossimo (si è arrabbiata) meaning 'she got angry' or 'she became angry'. For a male subject use 'è arrabbiato' / 'si è arrabbiato'. Can be used with 'perché' to ask why someone became angry.
target_language_example: Giulia si è arrabbiata perché ha perso il treno.
native_language_example: Giulia got angry because she missed the train.

meaning: has come true; (something) came true or was fulfilled.
additional_notes: Used to say that a wish, dream, prediction, or expectation has been realized. Often appears as 'si è avverato' (reflexive) with the thing that happened as subject: 'Il mio sogno si è avverato' = 'My dream came true.' Can be used in past tense (si è avverato) or in other tenses (si avvererà = will come true). Formal/neutral register.
target_language_example: Dopo anni di lavoro, il suo sogno si è avverato.
native_language_example: After years of work, his dream came true.

meaning: is closed
additional_notes: Literally 'is closed.' Can describe a place or thing that is closed (the shop è chiuso = the shop is closed) or a person who has shut themself away (si è chiuso in camera = he shut himself in the room). With 'fuori' (si è chiuso fuori) it means 'locked himself out.' With 'a chiave' it emphasizes being locked with a key. Context and reflexive 'si' change the sense.
target_language_example: Si è chiuso in bagno e non apre la porta.
native_language_example: He shut himself in the bathroom and won't open the door.

meaning: 'she bought herself' (reflexive past: she purchased for herself)
additional_notes: Comprata is the past participle of comprare (to buy). With the reflexive pronoun si (si è comprata), it means 'she bought herself' or 'she got herself' — i.e., she purchased something for her own use. Agreement: the past participle agrees in gender and number with the direct object when the direct object precedes the verb or when using a reflexive pronoun acting as a direct object (here, si refers to a female subject, so comprata). Common in spoken and written Italian to indicate buying something for oneself.
target_language_example: Si è comprata una giacca nuova.
native_language_example: She bought herself a new jacket.

meaning: 'is covered' or 'covered himself/oneself' (depending on context).
additional_notes: Often used with reflexive forms (si è coperto) to mean someone covered part of their body (ears, eyes, mouth, head) — e.g. with hands, a pillow, or clothing. Can be used transitively (qualcosa è coperto — something is covered) or reflexively to indicate the subject covered themselves. Context tells whether it's passive ('is covered') or reflexive ('covered himself').
target_language_example: Si è coperto il volto con le mani.
native_language_example: He covered his face with his hands.

meaning: 'has decided' (she/it has made up her mind)
additional_notes: Form of the reflexive verb 'decidersi' (past tense, third person singular). Used to say someone made a decision or finally decided to do something. Often appears as 'si è deciso/a' or 'si è decisa a + infinitive' when followed by an action (e.g., si è decisa a venire). Gender agrees with the subject (deciso for masculine, decisa for feminine). Can be used alone to mean 'she's decided' or 'she made up her mind (some time ago)'.
target_language_example: Dopo tante esitazioni, si è decisa a partire domani.
native_language_example: After much hesitation, she has decided to leave tomorrow.

meaning: is determined/has decided to (do something).
additional_notes: Used with a reflexive verb structure (decidersi) + 'ad' + infinitive to express that someone has resolved or made up their mind to do something. Often appears as 'si è deciso ad...' (he/she has decided to...). Can be formal or neutral. English equivalents: 'he's decided to...', 'he's determined to...'.
target_language_example: Si è deciso ad accettare il lavoro.
native_language_example: He has decided to accept the job.

meaning: 'has forgotten to' (he/she/it has forgotten to ...).
additional_notes: Passive/impersonal-looking construction using the past participle dimenticato with essere + di + infinitive. It describes that someone (often specified earlier) forgot to do something. More common alternatives: "ha dimenticato di" (active: he/she has forgotten to) or "si è dimenticato di" (reflexive: he/she forgot to). Use with an infinitive verb after "di".
target_language_example: È dimenticato di chiudere la finestra.
native_language_example: He/She has forgotten to close the window.

meaning: 'he/she/it/they went toward' or 'headed (to)'.
additional_notes: From the verb dirigersi (to head/steer oneself). Used to say someone moved or went in a particular direction or toward a place. Subject can be la persona/egli/lei/si (reflexive). Common constructions: 'si è diretto a/verso [luogo]'. Use 'a' for a specific destination and 'verso' to indicate direction/toward.
target_language_example: Si è diretto verso la stazione per prendere il treno.
native_language_example: He headed toward the station to catch the train.

meaning: 'had fun' / 'enjoyed (herself)'.
additional_notes: Third-person singular feminine of the reflexive verb divertirsi in the passato prossimo (si è divertita). Used to ask or state that a female person enjoyed herself. For males use 'si è divertito'. With names/pronouns: 'Lei/lei/Mary si è divertita'.
target_language_example: Giulia si è divertita al concerto ieri sera.
native_language_example: Giulia had fun at the concert last night.

meaning: had fun
additional_notes: Reflexive past form of divertirsi (si è divertito) used to say someone enjoyed an activity or had a good time. Commonly followed by a preposition or phrase indicating how or where (a + infinitive, con, al, leggendo, sul serio). Use è divertita for a female subject; plural si sono divertiti/si sono divertite for they.
target_language_example: Dopo la festa, Marco si è divertito molto con gli amici.
native_language_example: After the party, Marco had a lot of fun with his friends.

meaning: it's done
additional_notes: This is the feminine singular form. With di + a material, it means 'is made of' (for example, La borsa è fatta di pelle). On its own, especially in speech, è fatta! means something is completed, settled, or successful: 'it's done' / 'we did it'. For masculine singular nouns, use è fatto.
target_language_example: Abbiamo prenotato i biglietti: è fatta!
native_language_example: We've booked the tickets: it's done!

meaning: was hurt (on the) / got injured (in) — used to say someone injured a specific body part
additional_notes: This is the passive/reflexive perfect form of farsi male: 'si è fatto male alla [parte del corpo]' means 'he/she hurt his/her [body part]'. Use the definite article with body parts (alla = a + la). For other persons change si/è: 'mi sono fatto/a male', 'ti sei fatto/a male', 'ci siamo fatti/e male'. Gender affects past participle agreement when using essere (mi sono fatto — male if male speaker; mi sono fatta if female).
target_language_example: Si è fatto male alla mano mentre cadeva.
native_language_example: He hurt his hand while falling.

meaning: is injured
additional_notes: Third-person singular present of 'essere' + past participle 'ferita' (feminine). Used to say someone (she/it) is injured or hurt. In Italian reflexive construction 'si è ferita' means 'she injured herself' or 'she got hurt' when subject is feminine; context determines whether passive ('is injured') or reflexive ('hurt herself'). For other genders/forms you will see 'è ferito' (masculine) or plural 'sono feriti/ferite'.
target_language_example: Maria si è ferita mentre cadeva.
native_language_example: Maria hurt herself while falling.

meaning: is injured / got injured
additional_notes: Used to say someone is hurt. Often appears with a reflexive/passive construction (si è ferito) meaning 'he/she hurt himself/herself' or with a person's name (Max si è ferito) meaning 'Max injured himself.' Can refer to past action (present perfect) or state depending on context. Commonly followed by body part introduced by 'a' or direct object (e.g. 'alle mani', 'la gamba').
target_language_example: Marco si è ferito al braccio mentre giocava.
native_language_example: Marco injured his arm while playing.

meaning: (she/it) has stopped; came to a stop (third-person singular, feminine)
additional_notes: Form of the verb 'fermarsi' (to stop) in passato prossimo with third-person singular feminine subject: 'è' (auxiliary essere) + past participle 'fermata'. Used for feminine subjects (person, vehicle treated as feminine, or feminine noun) or in constructions like 'mi si è fermata la macchina'. For masculine subjects use 'è fermato'. Reflexive form often appears as 'si è fermata/o'. Can describe stopping movement or a machine stopping. Context determines whether translation is literal or idiomatic.
target_language_example: Un'auto blu si è fermata davanti al portone del palazzo stamattina.
native_language_example: A blue car stopped in front of the building's gate this morning.

meaning: has stopped / stopped (it/he/she is stopped).
additional_notes: From the verb fermarsi (to stop). In the examples the structure si è fermato is the passato prossimo (present perfect) of the pronominal verb fermarsi: 'si è fermato' = 'he/it has stopped' or 'it stopped'. Agreement can change with gender/number (si è fermata, si sono fermati). Use è fermato for third-person singular masculine; context decides whether it refers to a person or thing (e.g. Il motore si è fermato = the engine stopped).
target_language_example: L'autobus si è fermato davanti alla scuola.
native_language_example: The bus stopped in front of the school.

meaning: 'she is hanged' / 'she hanged herself' (female subject)
additional_notes: Used to describe that a female person has been hanged (killed by hanging) or has committed suicide by hanging. Context determines whether it's passive ('was hanged' — e.g., executed) or reflexive ('si è impiccata' — she hanged herself, suicide). The form changes with gender/number (impiccato for male singular, impiccati/impiccate for plural). This is a sensitive, potentially distressing phrase; use with care.
target_language_example: La donna è impiccata nella soffitta; sembra un suicidio.
native_language_example: The woman is hanged in the attic; it looks like a suicide.

meaning: 'she is in love with' or 'she fell in love with'.
additional_notes: A feminine, singular form of the verb phrase innamorarsi + preposition di. Use è innamorata di for 'she is in love with' (present/result state) or si è innamorata di for 'she fell in love with' (past). Change gender/number/pronoun as needed: sono innamorata (I, f.), è innamorato (he is / male), ci siamo innamorati (we fell in love), etc.
target_language_example: Si è innamorata di un cantante famoso.
native_language_example: She fell in love with a famous singer.

meaning: is in love
additional_notes: Used to say someone is in love (with someone or something). Often appears with 'di' to indicate the object of affection (e.g. 'si è innamorato di ...'). Here 'è innamorato' is the present perfect/compound sense 'has become/fallen in love', but in English both 'is in love' and 'has fallen in love' are natural translations depending on context.
target_language_example: Tom si è innamorato di Venezia.
native_language_example: Tom has fallen in love with Venice.

meaning: 'she has washed' or 'she washed' (reflexive, feminine singular, passato prossimo).
additional_notes: Part of the reflexive verb lavarsi (to wash oneself). È lavata is the feminine singular third-person form in the passato prossimo (si è lavata = she washed herself). Often followed by the body part with a definite article (si è lavata le mani = she washed her hands). If subject is masculine use è lavato; plural feminine: sono lavate; plural masculine/mixed: sono lavati.
target_language_example: Si è lavata le mani prima di mangiare.
native_language_example: She washed her hands before eating.

meaning: has washed (himself) / is washed (used with reflexive 'si è lavato' = he washed himself).
additional_notes: This is the past participle form of lavare used with the auxiliary essere in the passato prossimo for reflexive verbs (si è lavato = he washed himself). With plural subjects the past participle agrees in gender/number (si sono lavati / si è lavata). Often used with body parts: si è lavato le mani = he washed his hands. Can also be non‑reflexive with avere (ha lavato = he washed something).
target_language_example: Dopo il gioco, Marco si è lavato le mani.
native_language_example: After playing, Marco washed his hands.

meaning: is/has put on; (she) got/has become (in certain expressions).
additional_notes: Part of the reflexive verb mettersi (to put on, to start, to get into contact, to become). 'Si è messa' = 'she put on' (clothing) or 'she got/has started' (e.g., si è messa a parlare) or 'she got in touch' in fixed phrases like 'si è messa in contatto con...'. In questions like 'Che si è messa?' it can mean 'What did she put on?' Context determines the English translation. The subject is third person singular feminine (lei).
target_language_example: Si è messa la giacca prima di uscire.
native_language_example: She put on her jacket before going out.

meaning: put on (oneself)
additional_notes: Used with a reflexive pronoun (si/mi/ti/ci) to say someone put clothing or an item on themselves (e.g., si è messo la giacca = he put on his jacket). Literally "is put" but functions as the past tense (passato prossimo) of mettersi (to put on). Commonly appears as "si è messo" for he/she/they (formal) or "mi sono messo" for I.
